en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Anudīpanīpāṭha 1.
An Exposition on the Compendium of Consciousness (Cittasaṅgaha).
Having paid homage to the Jina, the possessor of infinite knowledge who brings light to the world,
I shall provide an elucidation for the *Paramatthadīpanī*.
(In this context, "the one who brings light to the world" refers to the one who creates the light of the teaching on the Dhamma of the Four Truths throughout the ten-thousandfold world system.)

Regarding the term *Paramatthadīpanī*: here, "meaning" (*attha*) is twofold—namely, the primary meaning (*padhānattha*) and the figurative meaning (*pariyāyattha*). Among these, the primary meaning is called the ultimate meaning (*paramattha*);
the primary meaning is the principal sense of words and sentences, as well as their direct sense.

Furthermore, some figurative meaning that is logically consistent is also indeed the ultimate meaning. It is called *Paramatthadīpanī* because it illuminates—that is, makes manifest—the ultimate meaning.
Next, providing illumination for the head, the teacher first pays homage to the Blessed Buddha with the words beginning “Udayā yassā.
Therein, “Udayā” means from arising or from rising. “Yassā” means of that Great Hero, the Omniscient Buddha. “Ekassā” means...
"Of the peerless one, there is no rival in splendor. Regarding the phrase "possessing a web of rays of the True Dhamma" (*saddhammaraṃsijālino*):

here, "True Dhamma" (*saddhamma*) refers to the Dhamma of the Teacher’s dispensation. And therein, what is intended is the "True Dhamma of the teaching," comprising the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dhamma.

One who possesses a web of rays consisting of that which is called the True Dhamma is "one possessing a web of rays of the True Dhamma. Of such a one, [it is said]: "They awoke" (*pabujjhiṃsu*), meaning they blossomed.
They reached the full blossoming of the knowledge of the four truths, which expands through the knowledge of the ultimate reality (*tathatā*).

"The lotuses of people" (*janambuja*) means the lotuses that are the people. Here, "people" refers to those beings capable of being awakened in this world, who, having heard the instruction of the Omniscient One, will awaken to the Dhamma of the Four Truths.
"Lotus" (*ambuja*) is a synonym for the *paduma* flower. "In the great lake of the field of birth" (*jātikkhettemahāsare*) refers to what is called the field of birth...
In the great lake of the lotus of humanity, there is what is called the "field of birth," consisting of ten thousand world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*), which is termed a single "Buddha-field.

It is in this field that, for the sake of the Great Beings (*mahābodhisattva*) attaining Buddhahood, events such as the simultaneous trembling of the earth occur at the time of their first great resolve (*pathamamahābhinīhāra*) and so forth;
and it is here that the gods and Brahmās dwelling therein constitute the assembly of the Buddha.

When that one great sun, who possesses a web of rays of the True Dhamma, rises in the great lake of the field of birth, the lotuses of beings awaken in that great lake of the field of birth—this is the first yojana.
"That great sun" refers to the solar orb of the omniscient Buddha, the Great Sun. The "lotuses of beings" refers to the great [awakening] proceeding within the lineages of beings.
It dispels—that is, removes—the darkness of delusion (*moha-tamas*), and by emitting the web of rays of the True Dharma (*saddhamma-raṃsi-jāla*), it causes that [darkness] to vanish;
thus, he is the "Dispeller of the Great Darkness of Delusion" (*mahāmohatamonuda*).
Having thus paid homage to the Buddha, he spoke the words beginning with "Has arisen" (*sañjātam*) while dedicating the purpose of the homage as he himself desired.
The construction is: “May the Soma-hāsa-sūrya dispel that mass of darkness born within my heart. In this context, “born” (*sañjāta*) means well-born;
the meaning is that it has arisen firmly throughout the beginningless cycle of existence (*anamatagga-saṃsāra*).

“Mass of darkness” (*tamokhandha*) refers to the mass of darkness of great delusion (*mahāmoha*), or else to the mass of darkness of all defilements (*kilesa*). Obstructive karmas—those that are oppressive and destructive—are also included within the mass of darkness.
They are indeed included. Likewise, obstructive factors such as diseases are of the nature of darkness in such passages as "darkness whose further end is darkness.
Regarding the word "panūdataṃ," it means: may he remove, may he lead away, may he cause to disappear.

Having thus performed a salutation that possesses a specific purpose, he now states the words beginning with "by the ancients" in order to acknowledge the composition of this work along with its source.
In this context, "nidāna" (the introduction) refers to the proximate cause for the undertaking of the treatise.
It consists of the request made by those who take pride in the essential meaning and the vastness of the compendium.
Therein, with two verses he shows the request together with its reason; again, with two verses he shows the vastness of the meaning through a simile.
With the words beginning “Therefore,” he shows that his claim to authorship of the work is consistent with the nature and qualities of the composition.
Regarding this, the construction of the first verse is as follows: “In this world, many commentaries on the *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha* composed by ancient wise men will be seen.
By “commentaries” (*vaṇṇanā*), the ancient sub-commentaries (*ṭīkā*) are meant. This being so, one might ask: why does he request a new commentary?
The construction is as follows: “Those who pride themselves on [finding] the essential meaning do not find satisfaction in those many ancient commentaries; therefore, we entreat you.
By this, it is also indicated that those ancient commentaries possess little essential meaning. In this context, “satisfaction” (*tuṭṭhi*) means contentment.
“Do not find” (*na vindanti*) means they do not obtain it. “Those who” (*ye*) refers to the people.
They hold fast to the essential meaning (*sāra*) and especially delight in that nature; thus they are called "those who hold fast to the essential meaning" (*sāratthābhimānino*).
This connects with the previous phrase, "by means of that they find. Again, "they" (*te*) refers to those people who do not find satisfaction through those [other things].

"Me" (*maṃ*) is a designation for himself. "Having come together" (*saṅgammā*) means having assembled. Because they request the illumination of the ultimate truth (*paramattha*), this commentary is therefore called the *Paramatthadīpanī*.
Even the name itself is established as accomplished. “In the great ocean” means in the great sea. “Jewels” means jewels such as gold, silver, and so forth.
“Having drawn up” means having brought up from below. “According to their desire” means whatever they wish for; the intended meaning is “as much as they desire.
“They might give” means they should give. The sense is: “let them give as they please. This refers to the optative verbal endings (*eyya*-class).

Because it functions for the sake of consent (*anumati*). Regarding the phrase "the deficiency is not to be stated": the deficiency or loss of the great jewels and treasures is indeed not to be stated.
Why? Because the great ocean has immeasurable jewels as its defining characteristic; hence it is called the "Sāgara" (Ocean).
For its meaning is "Sāgara" because it is like a house or a chamber for those riches and treasures.
“*Tathevetthā*” means in this *Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha*, it is exactly so. “*Vipulatthā*” means vast meanings. “*Ratanūpamā*” means like jewels in the great ocean.
“*Satakkhattumpī*” means even hundreds of times, that is, many hundreds of times. “*Vaṇṇeyyun*” means they might indeed describe them.
“*Pariyādinnā*” means taken completely and without remainder; it is said to mean exhausted.
“*Nahessare*”: they will not exist; they will cease to be. “*Tasmā*”: because they entreat [for it], and because they will cease to exist once [the work] is completed;
therefore. “*Tāsu vaṇṇanāsū*”: in those ancient commentaries (*porāṇa-ṭīkā*). “*Vaṇṇanaṃ*”: a new commentary (*abhinava-vaṇṇana*), meaning they will compose a new commentary (*abhinava-ṭīkā*);
this is the connection. To the question, “What kind of commentary will he compose? he says: “*Nānāsārattha*... [etc.]

"Complete," and so forth. In that context, "with clear words and phrases" means both the words are clear and the sentences are clear. "Neither too concise nor too prolix" means neither too brief nor too extensive.
"Those of dull intellect" refers to those whose understanding is dull. "Dull" means soft or weak. "Intellect" means knowledge.
It awakens—that is, it causes to blossom—the minds of the listeners who possess dull intellect; it brings about the expansion of their knowledge.
“Awakening those of dull intellect. “I shall compose” means I will compose. “That” refers to this commentary. The construction is: “Let those who desire proficiency in the ultimate meanings listen.
Proficiency (*pāṭava*) is the state of being proficient (*paṭu*). “Proficient” means one who is skilled or wise.

Those for whom the purpose is proficiency are “those who desire proficiency” (*pāṭavatthina*). The word “iti” indicates the conclusion. For it marks the conclusion here of the undertaking of the composition of the book.

It is employed at the conclusion of the introductory statement of the work in order to make known its completion; it is likewise employed for the individual sentences of the text. This same method applies everywhere.
The commentary on the introductory verses of the work is finished. 1.
Having thus established the commencement of the work, he now states the words beginning with "Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha" in order to show the connection with the opening verse.

“Connection” (*sambandha*) means the conjunction of cause and fruit. In this context, the delivery of the verses is called the “cause,” while the demonstration of the meaning of the five summaries (*pañcapiṇḍattha*) is called the “fruit.
The conjunction of cause and fruit is what is meant by “connection. “With purpose” (*sappayojane*) means accompanied by the purpose of the fruit.
“To be expressed by the text” (*ganthābhidheyyo*) means that which is to be stated or explained by the treatise. “The action of bowing” (*nipaccaṃ*) refers to the act of prostrating; having bowed...
The compound is: *kiriyā* (action), *nipaccākāra* (service), and *nipaccakārassa karaṇaṃ* (the performance of service). "She" (*sā*) refers to the salutation to the Triple Gem;

the connection has been shown. "Expressed" (*abhihitā*) means spoken; that is to say, it has been made manifest. "Being the primary meaning" (*padhānatthabhūtā*) intends the sense of what is intended (*adhippetatthabhūtā*).
For meaning is twofold: the meaning of the word (*vacanattha*) and the denoted meaning (*abhidhānattha*). In this context, "gone" (*gato*) is that which goes.
Regarding the term "purisa" (person): when it is said that "a person goes," whatever is going is what is meant by the word's referent (*vacanāttha*).

That which is shown by the word "purisa"—namely, the primary meaning (*padhānattha*), the intended meaning (*adhippetattha*), and the denoted meaning (*abhidheyyattha*)—is what is meant here. "Abhidhammattha" (the topics of Abhidhamma):
therein, the topics of Abhidhamma are stated to be fourfold according to the ultimate sense (*paramatthato*).
"Mind, mental factors, matter, and Nibbāna—thus in every way.

Such are the categories of Abhidhamma as they have been stated. And because they have been stated thus, it is understood that these four categories of Abhidhamma alone constitute the primary subject matter here, and that it is precisely these primary subjects that are intended by the title of this treatise. This is the underlying intention.
Some might object: "If those Abhidhamma topics were included within the *Saṅgaha-pakaraṇa*, they would no longer exist as a separate category called 'Abhidhamma topics' (*abhidhammattha*).
To this it is said: "In this context, only those things that serve as a compendium (*saṅgaha*) are intended by way of being the subject matter (*abhidheyya*);
thus it is stated: 'The subject matter is the *Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha*. It is replied: Those Abhidhamma topics [are indeed contained] within the *Saṅgaha-pakaraṇa*.
Even though the categories of the Abhidhamma (abhidhammattha) are thus named, they do not have the name "Saṅgaha" as their individual designation.
For it is said there [in the *Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha*] that they are "the categories of the Abhidhamma stated therein," but it is not said that they are "the categories of the Saṅgaha stated therein.

This being the case, the mere state of being included (saṅgahitabhāva) becomes the distinguishing feature. Therefore, that very state is what constitutes the subject matter (abhidheyya) here; hence it is said: "The state of being included is indeed the subject matter," and so forth.
In this context, "the state of being included" refers to the act of including, such as "inclusion of consciousness" (*cittasaṅgaha*) and "inclusion of mental factors" (*cetasikasaṅgaha*).

That [act] is not something other than the phenomena that are included; rather, it is said that "the state of being included is also indeed denotable" because it is itself included within those very phenomena.
Even if it were not something other than them, it is nonetheless included within them. Furthermore, that is the primary meaning of the treatise.
"It does not exist. And here, since only the purpose of striving (*padhāna*) is intended, it is said, "That is not beautiful.
To the question "Why is it not beautiful?", he says "For it is not... and so forth. Here, the word *hi* (for) indicates that this sentence functions as a statement of reason (*hetuvākya*).

This same method applies elsewhere as well. "From this point onwards," and so forth, is for the purpose of avoiding the heavy burden of the text. In that context, "of this compendium" refers to this *Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha*.

“*Dutiyā*” means the second commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*). “*Dvepi*” means both commentaries. “*Visuddhimaggemahāṭīkā*” refers to the commentary named *Paramatthamañjūsā*, composed by the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla.
It is known as the “Great Commentary” (*Mahāṭīkā*) because it was based upon the “Short Commentary” (*Cūḷaṭīkā*) composed by the Elder residing at Tiriyapabbata in the Brahmaraṭṭha country.
It is with reference to that [Great Commentary] that this was said.
The manner of the book (*ganthappakāra*) is established only together with the phenomena that possess such a manner, and it is not established without them;
this is the intended meaning behind the statement, "It is [designated] by the term *abhidhammatthapada*.

Granted, it is indeed established together with them and not without them; however, the term *abhidhammatthapada* does not express the manner of the act of compilation, and thus it was said, "That is not good."

Name is twofold: a name according to its meaning (*anvatthanāma*) and a conventional name (*ruḷhināma*). Therein, a name that conforms to the actual state of things is a name according to its meaning, such as the name "happy" for a person who is happy.
A name that is devoid of such a meaning and is merely imputed is a conventional name, such as the name "happy" for a person who is suffering.
Here, however, the phrase beginning with "conforming to the meaning" (*atthānugatā*) is stated in order to demonstrate names according to their meaning.
It has been stated. Therein, "conforming to its meaning" means conforming to its own meaning;

what is meant is that it conforms to the cause for the occurrence of the word. "The designation of the compendium" means the conventional designation of the compendium; what is meant is the name of the compendium.

What is called the *Saṅgaha-gantha* (Compendium Text) is a compendium that functions by collecting, in one place and as a homogeneous group, those teachings scattered here and there throughout the Pāḷi.
One who masters that [text] comes to know many teachings with ease through a small amount of wording. Regarding the phrase “by means of its mastery, inquiry, and so forth”:
“its mastery” (*uggaha*) and “inquiry” (*paripucchā*) form a *dvanda* compound. By the word “and so forth” (*ādi*), it includes retention (*dhāraṇā*) and other such qualities.

Among these, “mastery” (*uggaha*) refers to making the recitation committed to memory by voice. “Inquiry” (*paripucchā*) refers to grasping the meaning of that mastered recitation. “Without effort” (*anāyāsato*) means without suffering.
The connection is: “the fruit and its subsequent fruit are to be obtained. *Sarūpāvabodho* means understanding according to the specific form [of the teaching].

By the word “etcetera,” it includes the understanding of characteristics (*lakkhaṇāvabodho*), the understanding of flavors (*rasāvabodho*), and so forth. *Anupādāparinibbānantaṃ* means that which has non-clinging final nibbāna as its end or conclusion.
In this context, “non-clinging final nibbāna” refers to [the cessation] regarding the aggregates through craving and views...
“Parinibbāna without clinging” means parinibbāna without residue (anupādisesa). “Fruit and subsequent fruit” means both the fruit and the subsequent fruit.
Therein, “fruit” refers to the primary fruit; “subsequent fruit” refers to the successive fruit.
“It employs” means it motivates. What does it motivate? It motivates the person seeking the fruit. Where?
He enjoins [the mind] to the action that produces the fruit. For what purpose does he enjoin it? He says: for the sake of performing that action.
They also say that "purpose" (payojana) means that which is employed in the various functions of experiencing the fruit; thus it is for the sake of experiencing the fruit.
"By the force of the statement" (sāmatthiyato) means by the force of the words. What is the force of the words? It is the statement of the cause (kāraṇavacana).
The fruit also illuminates [the cause]. The statement of the fruit also illuminates the cause.
Just as when it is said, "In such-and-such a country there has been good rain," it is understood that "that country has abundant food";

and when it is said, "Such-and-such a country has abundant food," it is understood that "there has been good rain in that country. However, the purpose [of this treatise] is indicated by the term *abhidhammattha*.
There is nothing further to be shown; it is established by the very power of the inclusive term (*saṅgaha*).
With this intention, he said, "by the word *saṅgaha*. However, when demonstrating such power, a perfectly complete expression must be desired.
Otherwise, there might be the risk of an unintended meaning (*aniṭṭhattha*) arising. To show this point, he said, "That is not good," and then [proceeded] with "No," and so forth.
He establishes that meaning by means of a logical statement.
2. Regarding the phrase "Thus, with its purpose, in the fivefold summary-meaning":

having shown the fivefold summary-meaning here, he now states "In that regard," etc., in order to show the five specific purposes for each of those five summary-meanings. "In that regard" refers to among those five.
Regarding the meanings of the terms *piṇḍa* and *attha*: "Incalculable" (*asaṅkhyeyya*) means that which cannot be numbered;

the sense is that it is impossible to count. "Immeasurable" (*appameyya*) means that which cannot be measured; the sense is that it is impossible to measure. Thus, there is an illustration of the meaning of the word *sakka* (possible) in certain conditions of function.
To establish his own statement by means of the canonical text (*pāḷi*), he asks, "As it has been said," and [cites] the canonical verse:
"Āhari. In this context, "yathāha" means "how he said. The meaning should be understood accordingly as follows:
"How did he say it in the Pāḷi? How did he say it in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā)? How did he say it in the Sub-commentary (Ṭīkā)? The construction is:
"Of one who worships those [Buddhas] and others who have attained Nibbāna, which is free from fear. In that phrase, "te" refers to the Buddhas.

“Buddha-sāvake”: those who are like him (*tādise*), endowed with qualities such as the aggregates of virtue (*lakkhandhādi-guṇa-sampanne*). “Nibbute”: extinguished by the extinction of defilements (*kilesa-nibbānena nibbute*).
“Akutobhayā”: those for whom there is no fear from any cause whatsoever; they are non-returners (*anāgāmi*) whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*).
“Bhayaṃ”: the fear of mental terror. “Pūjayato”: of one who worships. “Taṃ payojanaṃ”: that purpose, namely, the Three Jewels (*tiratana-ttaya*).
The purpose of the salutation [is stated]. The term “compilers” (*saṅgahakārā*) refers to the later authors of the commentaries, such as the Venerable Buddhaghosa and others.

Having collected those points from the ancient commentaries that were scattered here and there and connected with various miscellaneous determinations (*vinicchaya*), they composed new commentaries. Therefore, all the new commentaries are called “compilations” (*saṅgaha*).
They are called *ācariyas* (teachers), and they are specifically known as *saṅgahakāras* (compilers). Therefore it was said: "The *saṅgahakāras* are [called] Buddhaghosa... so it is said.
If it is asked, "How is it known that they desire only the removal of obstacles?"—it is shown that this is known from their own words;
thus he cites the verse of the *saṅgahakāra*: "For this single act of homage toward the Three Jewels..."
The construction is: "having completely dried up obstacles by means of his majesty. The word "hi" indicates a reason that makes something known.
"It is said" (vuttam) means it is stated in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*.
3. "And how does it come to be?"—this is the connection; this is the question. "It is said" (vuccate)—the answer is being told.
“*Hī*” indicates the detailed explanation. The connection is: “The stream of merit (*puññappavāha*) is that which brings about the performance of homage.

In the phrase “*aneka...vāre*,” the accusative case is used in the sense of absolute conjunction (*accantasamyoga*). “*Puññābhisando*” means a flood of merit (*puññābhisota*), and “stream of merit” (*puññappavāha*) is a synonym for that very thing.
The connection is: “And that is called ‘meritorious’ (*puññātissaya*). Why is it called “meritorious”?

"It comes about. To show that it comes about through the perfection of the field (*khetta-sampatti*) and the perfection of the underlying intention (*ajjhāsaya-sampatti*), he said "in the unsurpassed," and so forth.
"He was nurtured" (*saṃvaḍḍhittha*) means he was nurtured (*saṃvaḍḍhita*). It is an outflow of merit (*puññābhisanda*).
The state of being nurtured is "nurturedness" (*saṃvaḍḍhitatta*). It was permeated (*paribhāvita*)—like a perfectly pure cloth with fragrances—meaning it was infused by the outflow of merit itself.
The state of being cultivated is *paribhāvitattaṃ*. In both instances, the ablative case (*nissakkavacana*) is used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*).

"Greatly radiant" means possessing great splendor (*mahātejo*). "Of great fruit" means of great fruit by way of its root-fruit (*mūlapphalena*). "Of great benefit" means of great benefit by way of its beneficial fruit (*ānisaṃsapphalena*).
And the "beneficial fruit" is said to be the successive fruit (*paramparāphala*). Surpassing other merit...
It flows and proceeds, thus it is *atisayo*. It is both merit (*puñña*) and an excellence (*atisaya*), thus it is *puññātissayo*.
"Excellence-merit" (*atissayapuñña*) means superlative merit. The connection is: "He gives support and provides an opportunity.
To the questions "How does he give support? And how does he provide an opportunity? he says: "Having himself stood in the state of perfection through application," and so forth.
In this context, "perfection of means" (*payogasampatti*) refers to a supporting kamma that is more powerful than past meritorious deeds.
"Externally" (*bahiddhā*) means from outside one's own continuum (*santāna*). The phrase "conditions for misfortune" and "conditions for prosperity" should be construed together.

Among these, "conditions for misfortune" refers to the conditions for the arising of suffering as they appear in such passages as "from a king," "from thieves," and so forth. "Conditions for prosperity" refers to...
These are the conditions conducive to body and mind. Furthermore, the four requisites, the families of supporters, protective deities, and so forth, are conditions for the arising of happiness.

Through these conditions, because joy abounds in the mental continuum of the Elder, internal temperature, consciousness, and nutriment become exceedingly refined due to the day-and-night occurrence of rapture, tranquility, bliss, and concentration.
Arising from those [nutriments], the bodily constituent elements (*sarīraṭṭhakadhātu*) also become exceedingly refined and nourish [the body].

In this context, the "bodily constituent elements" refer to the earth element and so forth, as well as wind, bile, phlegm, and so on. "He bestows additional strength" means he brings about fresh vigor and power.
"Of the merit-store" refers to the manifold meritorious kamma that produces the result of continued existence (*pavattivipāka*). "Then" means at that time.
“Time” is the meaning. “Having become strong and weak” means having become exceedingly powerful by way of their natural strength.
“In that elder’s continuum” is the connection. “Filled with a density of desirable fruits” means filled with a density of material continua (rūpa-santati) consisting of desirable fruits.
“There is no space” means there is no place for them to be established. “Thus” means therefore.
The connection is: “They are indeed removed from afar.
Those actions which obstruct and ward off the continuity of desirable results are called *upapīḷaka* (afflicting) and *upaghātaka* (injuring) kamma.
Those which produce a continuity of undesirable results, namely unwholesome-producing kamma or demeritorious (*apuñña*) kamma—these three kinds of unwholesome kamma are indeed removed from afar.
The intention is that [the merit] exists by way of not providing an opportunity for the ripening of those [demeritorious deeds]. Therefore, he said "No," and so forth.
"From that" means because demeritorious actions have been removed from afar.

The habit of saluting—consisting in showing respect through the act of salutation toward those who are worthy of salutation, such as mother, father, ascetics, brahmins, and so on—is called "the habit of saluting. One who possesses this is "one whose habit is to salute" (*abhivādanasīlī*).
One who honors those superior in virtue and superior in age by honoring oneself through the practice of humble conduct is called "one who honors the elders" (*vuddhāpacāyī*).
In both instances, the dative case is used. The words "evam" and so forth express the act of going; "nigama" means reaching a conclusion.
The phrase beginning with "tasmā" expresses the qualities that have been attained. "Laddhaguṇo" refers to the complete purification of each respective context.
The meaning obtained by way of derivation is called "purified" (*visuddho*). Likewise, another meaning obtained through the power of the word's inherent capacity (*sāmatthiya*) is also intended here.
The construction is: "And it is not only for the sake of the Elder’s own completion [of the work] without obstacles. The connection is:
"For the sake of the listeners' successful accomplishment of the task of grasping [the teaching]. Those who hear are the "listeners" (*sotāro*); [the word refers to] them.
"Of those who take up" means of those who learn. "For the accomplishment of veneration" means because of the accomplishment of merit through that very threefold veneration.
In the *Javanavinicchaya*, it is stated that the removal of obstacles is indeed the fruit desired in the present life (*diṭṭhadhamma*).

And the present life is the field for the result of the first impulsion (*javana*). Therefore, even after having reached the function of support (*upatthambhana-kicca*), [the veneration fulfills its purpose].

It is stated that "it is experienced in the present life" (diṭṭhadhammavedanīya) with the intention that, in this context, only the first impulsion volition (pathama-javana-cetanā) is the subject under discussion.
However, even when it performs the function of support (upatthambhana-kicca), that first impulsion volition must be considered the weakest of all. Why?
Because it has not received repetition (asevana). The remaining volitions would be stronger. Why? Because they have received repetition (asevana).
"It should be seen. The connection is: "Because it is intended in the context of the seven impulsive moments (javana), and because it is something to be acquired, that is not good.
"Thus" marks the completion of the sentence. "Just as it is trifling, even so it is trifling"—this is how it should be construed.
"For thus" means "for that very reason. Also in the *Paṭṭhāna*: "Edible food is for this body..."

“Conditioned by nutriment” is analyzed as follows: otherwise, it would have been analyzed as “edible food is a condition for matter produced by nutriment, by way of the condition of nutriment. The phrase “in this very life” means in this present existence (*bhava*).
Having thus illustrated the purpose of the salutation, [the author] now states the purpose of the remaining summary points, beginning with “But because... (*yasmā panā*).
It has been said. In that regard, regarding the phrase "When it is known from the beginning," etc.:
upon hearing the words "I shall speak the *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha*," once they have been understood, "exertion arises. [One thinks:

"Having mastered this, we shall come to know the very difficult Abhidhamma meanings without effort, and we shall become partakers of the goal rooted therein, which is final Nibbāna through non-clinging."
The intention is: "because it arises from the arising of consciousness.
The elucidation of the summary meaning is finished.
4. Regarding the meaning of the words: “Bujjhī” means he understood. “Etthā” means in this word. The word “ca” indicates the commencement of the sentence.
"Vākyārambho" means the commencement of the subsequent statement (*anuvākya*) for the purpose of stating whatever remains to be said that was not stated in the root statement (*mūlavākya*).

"Awakening activity" refers to knowledge (*ñāṇa*). Regarding the question, "How does the word *sammā*, occurring in the sense of non-perversion, indicate 'pervading without remainder'?", [the answer is given] through both the method of exclusion (*vyatireka*) and the method of agreement (*anvaya*) with respect to the preceding meaning.
Furthermore, in expanding upon this, he says, "For it is thus," and so forth. Therein, "For it is thus" (*tathāhi*) indicates that this is the expansion of that statement.
"Unmistaken" (*aviparīta*) is an adverbial term qualifying the action. "Only within its own domain" (*attano visaye eva*); the connection is:
"only within the domain of their own knowledge is that [the] domain. Because even a single phenomenon, through distinctions such as time, place, and mental continuum...
There are infinite divisions. Therefore, those who possess only partial knowledge, such as the Paccekabuddhas and others, are not able to know even a single phenomenon in all its aspects.

Thus he said, "By them," and so forth. In that context, "in all aspects" means by way of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), cause (*hetu*), condition (*paccaya*), fruit (*phala*), outflow (*nissanda*), time (*kāla*), place (*desa*), and so on. "Where" means in which [phenomenon].

“Regarding phenomena that are not within one’s domain (*avisaya-dhamme*): ‘They might understand them erroneously; there is no phenomenon whatsoever that is not within one’s domain’—this is the construction. Explaining this in detail, he says “by them,” and so forth.
Therein, “gone through the three times” (*tiyaddhagate*) means occurring throughout the three periods of time. “Released from the three times” (*addhāmuttake*) means liberated from the three times.
“Like gems placed in the palm of the hand” (*hatthamaṇike viya*) means like precious gems set upon the surface of the palm. “All... [The text continues:]... all.
The passage beginning with “dhammā” is the supporting canonical text. Therein, “āpātam” means falling directly toward [the object].
“Ābādham” is also a reading, meaning appearing by way of covering.

“Sabbaññumahābhavaṅgam” refers to the first of the eight great resultant consciousnesses (mahāvipāka) that proceeds from the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) throughout the final existence of all omniscient Buddhas.
The life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*). “Therein” means in that great life-continuum.
“Manifesting at all times” means they remain having attained the mode of manifestation at every moment. Why? Because there is an absence of any obstruction for anyone.
This too is indeed one kind of manifestation. “By adverting” means by the mind-door adverting consciousness. The mental objects (*dhammā*) are great.

The life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is limited. Therefore, the opponent’s intention is that the limited life-continuum cannot, in a single moment, be capable of great phenomena. “This is not to be objected to”:
this point is not to be challenged. Regarding the phrase “of those who have reached the highest excellence,” here “excellence” (ukkaṃsa) means a supreme height or unsurpassed state.
The compound *paramukkaṃsa* is analyzed as “the highest (parama) excellence (ukkaṃsa).”
Having thus analyzed the meaning of the word *sam-*, he now analyzes the meaning of the word *saṃ* by saying, "The prefix *saṃ*," and so forth.

In that context, "prefix" (*upasaggo*) is the term for a prefix. "Regarding the penetrative states" (*paṭivedhadhammesu*) refers to the knowledges that penetrate dependent origination and other such truths.
"One who has no teacher" (*anācariyo*) means one for whom there is no teacher; with the letter *k* added at the end of the compound, it becomes *anācariyako*. Of this *anācariyako*...

The state of being without a teacher is *anācariyakatā*. That is the state of being without a teacher. The third formless attainment (*arūpasamāpatti*) is the jhāna of the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*);
the Blessed One learned that in the presence of Āḷāra. The fourth formless attainment is the jhāna of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*);

he learned that in the presence of Udaka. Thus it is said, "rooted in Āḷāra and Udaka. "Without adorning" refers to [the process] by way of adverting (*āvajjana*), entering (*samāpajjana*), and so forth.
“Without having adorned. This means “without having cultivated. Regarding the phrase “because they have been discarded”:

having seen the disadvantage that these attainments are not sufficient for enlightenment, but rather lead only to the acquisition of the third and fourth formless realms (ārūpyabhava), they are discarded.
“For the act of awakening” refers to the knowledge of penetration (paṭivedha-ñāṇa). “From where [could there be] states of penetration? [This asks: from what source?

From what, then, do these qualities of penetration (*paṭivedha-dhamma*) arise? The intention is that these very qualities of penetration serve as the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for the state of Buddhahood.
In the Pāḷi: “Regarding the Dhammas unheard of before,” this refers to the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths which had not been heard from anyone prior to this existence.
In the phrase “he fully awakened” (*abhisambujjhi*), there is the knowledge of the path to Arahatship known as full awakening (*abhisambodhi*).
It has been said: that very knowledge is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
It is stated, "And therein he attains omniscience," because by means of that [knowledge], immediately thereafter (*tadanantarā*), omniscient knowledge manifests.
The phrase "immediately thereafter" means at the time following both the path-moment of Arahatship and the four moments of reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇa*).
“In the sense of a cause” (*nimittatthe*) means in the sense of a cause (*hetvatthe*).
“Locative” (*bhummam*) is the name for the seventh case-ending as it appears in the *Aṭṭhakathās*.

For in those [works], the names of the seven case-endings have been given in successive order as follows: the nominative, the accusative, the instrumental, the dative, the ablative, the genitive, and the locative.
“In the ten powers of knowledge” means in the ten powers of knowledge beginning with the power of knowing what is possible and impossible (*ṭhānāṭhāna-kosalla-ñāṇa*).
“Mastery” (*vasibhāva*): here, the specific excellence of capability consisting in the ability to bring [the qualities] under one’s own control is called “mastery” (*vāsa*).

[The term *vasī* is used] as in such expressions as “one who possesses mastery” (*vasī*) or “by those possessing mastery” (*vasigaṇehi*). The state of being one who possesses mastery is “mastery” (*vasibhāva*). The meaning is: that mastery. Therefore he said:
“Mastery” (*vasibhāva*) means the state of being a lord (*issarabhāva*). However, in some places the feminine noun “mastery” (*vasī*) is also seen—as in such passages as “these five masteries:
mastery over adverting, mastery over attainment,” and so forth. [This concludes] the section on the term *sammāsambuddha*.
5. *Atulapade*. Veneration performed by means of many words of praise is called "having many words of praise as its object.
"What is the use of the second [word]?"—the meaning is: what purpose is there for the second word, namely *atulapadena* (incomparable word)?
"Not capable"—the construction is: it does not become "not capable"; the intended sense is that it is indeed capable. "Acting with moderation" means acting within measure. "The Elder..."
"And among them, one [did not] make a measure"; therefore, he brought forward the second incomparable word—this is the intended meaning.
"Moreover" (*apica*) means that there is something further to be said. The construction is: "It is not only the prevention of obstacles to veneration that is to be desired.
"Of veneration" (*vandanāya*) means for the sake of veneration. That too refers to such things as proficiency in wisdom.
“*For the purity of the text*”: there are indeed textual faults, such as faults of words, faults of sentences, and faults of meaning.
It is for the sake of the complete purification of this text from those faults. But how can the purpose of proficiency in wisdom and so forth arise from an act of homage?
To answer this, it is said: “*In the bases of recollection,*” and so on. The bases of recollection (*anussatiṭṭhāna*) are the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, virtue (*sīla*), and so forth.
It brings about the concentration of the mind; thus, it is "that which brings about mental concentration" (*cittasamādhānāvaho*).

Regarding the phrase "it flows having become sharp and keen": it flows in a manner that is not dull but is clearly articulated with respect to the meanings and phrasing of profound matters. Regarding the phrase "also for the sake of that": it is also for the sake of such things as proficiency in wisdom.

The meaning of the qualities is evident in sentences where the names of the qualities are analyzed according to their meaning and grammatical form, but it is not evident in established conventional terms.

Therefore, it is said: "For those who do not understand the meaning of the compounds, these [terms] become mere sounds," because they occur even when the meanings of the words as previously stated are applied...
"Those who know the natural language" means those who know the Māgadhī tongue.
The root language, the noble language, the Māgadhī tongue, and the Pāli tongue are all one and the same.

And it is called both "the designation of phenomena" (*dhammanirutti*) and "the designation of intrinsic nature" (*sabhāvanirutti*). Regarding the phrase "empty of the meaning of being" (*bhāvatthasuñña*):

here, the "meaning of being" (*bhāvattha*) refers to the referent of a quality-name (*guṇanāma*), namely the quality itself. That very thing is also called the "proper sense" (*sakattha*), the "lexical meaning" (*vacanattha*), and the "analytical meaning" (*viggahattha*).

This same method applies to action-names (*kiriyanāma*) and so forth as well. "Of the Teacher" (*satthu*) means "of the Teacher" (*satthuno*). "A mere conventional designation" (*samaññāmatta*) means a mere name-concept (*nāmasaññāmatta*).

It is not possible [to be so]. For instance, when the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika arrived at Rājagaha and heard that "a Buddha has appeared in the world," he uttered this inspired utterance: "Even the mere sound of 'Buddha' is rare in this world.
Therefore, even the name "Buddha" is a great and very rare title of excellence in the world. It cannot be said that there is no one who should be called "Sammāsambuddha."

“But for those who do not know the conventional terminology (*sabhāvanirutti*), even if a thousand words are spoken”—let alone a single incomparable word, even a thousand words being spoken result in nothing more than a mere conventional designation by the Teacher.
Such people do not even recognize this as a great term of excellence in the world;
how then could they understand its true meaning?
“*Atula*” means either that he has no equal (*asadiso*) by another, or that there is no other who is his equal; thus the meaning is obtained in two ways.
In the supporting verse, “*paṭipuggalo*” refers to a person who holds a dyad (*yugaggāhī*).
Although Makkhali, Pūraṇa, and others each individually claimed, “I am omniscient and all-seeing,” and “I am the Perfectly Enlightened One,” they were holders of such dyads.
Having offered [the oblation], they wander about. However, according to the nature of things (*dhammata*), near Sineru, the king of mountains, even pebbles and gravel become like jewels.
“Not wonderful” (*anacchariya*) means that it is not something to be marveled at. “Of one who has become a Buddha” (*buddhabhūtassa*) means of one who has attained the state of Buddhahood.
The construction is: “That which is the incomparability of one who has become a Buddha—that is not wonderful. If...
This is not surprising; but what, then, is truly marvelous? To this he said, "Of him who was just born," and so forth.
Therein, "of him who was just born" means even of this Blessed One on the very day of his birth. How is his incomparability made known? To this he said, "For then," and so forth.
"Level ground" (*ekaṅgaṇāni*) means having a single surface. For then, by the power of the Bodhisatta’s merit...
An exceedingly great radiance appears. It is said: "A sublime radiance appeared, surpassing even the divine power of the gods.
All the earth, mountains, and so forth, pervaded by that radiance, become perfectly clear like a mass of pure crystal.
The ten thousand world-systems appear as a single level plane. Therefore it is said: "Many thousands of world-systems..."
"They became one level. "With supreme worship" means with the worship of words of praise and auspiciousness. "Of the world" means from the entire world of sentient beings.
The intention is that he thus uttered fearless speech, being impelled by the natural law (*dhammatā*).
In this context, "fearless speech" means confident speech. There is also a reading, "āsabhiṃ vācaṃ," which means "supreme speech."

“Nicchāresī” means he uttered. This too is not wonderful; rather, it was begun with the words “yadāpana” and so forth to show that there is something even more wonderful than this, namely, his father.
The intention is that, apart from him, there is no one whatsoever equal to him in the qualities of the perfections (pāramitā), nor indeed any other Great Being (mahābodhisatta).
“Assā” means of one who is similar to him. “Natthibhāvo dīpetabbo” means the state of non-existence [of such a being] is to be illustrated.
The connection: “It should be illustrated” means it should be illustrated by bringing [the evidence] from the *Buddhavaṃsa-pāḷi*.

The construction is: “From where will he be able to provide a hundred thousand disciples and bodhisattvas? That which investigates the perfections (*pāramīs*) in their various modes is the investigation of the perfections (*pāramipavicaya*);
it is knowledge (*ñāṇa*). Furthermore, that knowledge arises only in great bodhisattvas; it does not arise in pacceka-bodhisattvas or disciple-bodhisattvas (*sāvaka-bodhisattas*).

It is precisely that which has arisen. And in order to show that this very [arising] is the primary cause for all Bodhisattvas to obtain the prediction of their certainty (*niyatavyākaraṇa*), it was said: “Even those who are Bodhisattvas for the enlightenment of disciples,” and so forth.
In this context, “enlightenment” (*bodhi*) refers to the knowledge of liberation; this is a name for the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*).
They are called “Bodhisattvas” because they go toward (*sajanti*) or cling to (*lagganti*) enlightenment. “They cling” means they are fixed (*niyata*) for the sake of its attainment.

The meaning is that they possess the mind [of enlightenment]. It is also appropriate to call them "bodhisattvas" because beings who have set out for the sake of enlightenment (bodhi) are so designated.

It is said that even in a world empty of a [permanent] Buddha, these beings—standing in the knowledge that one is the owner of their own karma—are seekers of the Dhamma of liberation from the suffering of the round of existence (vaṭṭa).
"In the qualities of the requisites" refers to the tenfold perfections (pāramī-dhamma). They follow and pursue the round of existence; thus they are called "those who follow the round."
"Followers of the round" (*vaṭṭānusārino*). "Worldlings" (*puthujjana*) are so called because they are by nature scattered like dust and powder upon the earth (*pathavī*).
"Great worldlings" (*mahāputhujjana*) means great worldlings. The compound is "those who are followers of the round and are great worldlings.

The analysis of the phrase is "the state (*bhāvo*) of those [worldlings]. This very state is also called their "ground" (*bhūmi*). In terms of meaning, however, it is the lack of regard for the Dhamma of liberation.

Thus it is called "freedom from desire. "Entered" means having entered. There are three kinds of certainty: the certainty of a Bodhisatta, the certainty of a lesser stream-enterer (*cūḷasotāpanna*), and the certainty of a noble stream-enterer (*ariyasotāpanna*).

Among these, the certainty of a Bodhisatta is established by the power of the requisites for enlightenment. The certainty of a lesser stream-enterer is established by the power of the knowledge that awakens to the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*). The certainty of a noble stream-enterer...

[This occurs] by the power of the knowledge of the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga-ñāṇa*). Among those [three types], it is the Bodhisatta who is destined [to enlightenment] that is intended here; thus it is said, "by one method," and so forth.

The intention is that there is no possibility whatsoever of two Bodhisattas—those not yet established [in the certainty of destiny]—receiving the prediction of destiny (*niyata-byākaraṇa*) without the attainment of the knowledge that investigates the perfections (*pāramī-pavicaya-ñāṇa*).

This was stated in the *Vibhāvanī* during the investigation of the derivation of the word *padasiddhi*: "Equal" (*tulya*) means "balanced by a scale" (*tulāya samita*). It is precisely "equal" (*tulya*) through the elision of the letter *y*.

With reference to that, it is said: "by way of the elision of the letter *ya*. Furthermore, it was stated in that very same work: "Alternatively, in the sense of proximity (*samīpa*), [it is] 'equal' (*tulya*) by way of the suffix *aka*.
Thus, 'near a scale' (*tulāya samīta*) [becomes] *tulo*. With reference to that, it is said: "by way of the elision of the letter *a*."

In this context, “tulāya” means by means of wisdom (paññā) which is like a balance-scale used for weighing in the world. “Samīto” means made equal. For it is not appropriate that the word *tula* [itself] be [the agent];
rather, it is appropriate [as an instrument], such is the intention. How is this known? He says: “tulayituṃ,” etc.

Therein, by the expression “incapable of being weighed (*tulayituṃ asakkuṇeyyo*),” he demonstrates that it has the sense of an object (*kamma-sādhana*). “By means of the object-formation alone (*kammasādhaneneva*)” [he says].
“*Tula*” means that which should be weighed (*tulayitabbo*) or measured in comparison with another; thus, it is by this very etymological derivation as an instrument noun (*kamma-sādhana*) used here.
“*Tadatthasiddhito*” means because of the establishment of that twofold meaning stated in its commentary (*vibhāvani*). “*Tato*” means from the word *tula*. What purpose is there for reflection?
There is none at all—this is the intended meaning. “One who speaks by nature” (*vadati sīlena*).
*Vattā*: one who speaks; a person who argues. *Vatticchā*: the desire to speak; they say it means "the desire to speak. *Sammuti*: following after the desire to speak;
a compound meaning established through convention, linguistic usage, and common agreement. "This" (*etaṃ*) refers to this twofold statement of what is established.
"If" (*ce*) is used as a particle of concession. "Not" (*na*) is not appropriate. "As heard" (*yathāsutaṃ*): that which has been heard is weighed (*tula*). "Appropriate" (*yuttaṃ*): as it was heard.

Having excluded [the word] *yutta* by means of the rule of necessity (*niyāmena*). Regarding the term *assutassa*: this refers to the feminine gender marker *-tā* (in *tulā*) and the word *tulya*, both of which are joined with the suffix *-ya*.

Precisely for that reason, in the case of the word *tulya* joined with the suffix *-ya*, and also in the case of the feminine gender, since there is one more *-a* than that, the second secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix *-a* in the sense of proximity is likewise called "unheard" (*assuta*). Regarding the phrase "by way of supposition" (*parikappanāya*): having made a supposition.
For the purpose of explaining. Because there is no purpose [in it], the connection is not logical. The term *atulapada*. 6.
Having thus provided a commentary on the meaning of the two words, he now states "But by these... and so forth, while providing a commentary that extracts their specific meanings.
In that context, "attainments" (*sampadā*) means successes. "The accumulation of the requisites for enlightenment" (*bodhisambhārasambharaṇam*).

The name [of this knowledge] refers to the fulfillment of the thirty perfections (*pāramī*). "Great Vajira-knowledge" is also called the Blessed One’s knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya-ñāṇa*).

Prior to that, for the sake of attaining Buddhahood, there is also the prior-stage insight-knowledge consisting of the daily practice of three million six hundred thousand fruit-attainments (*phala-samāpatti*) by way of the successive-dharma insight (*anupada-dhamma-vipassanā*).
It is called "great diamond-like knowledge" (*mahāvajiraññāṇa*). All of this has been stated in the *Mahāṭīkā*.
"Of the Great Enlightenment" (*mahābodhiyā*) refers to the knowledge of the supreme path, which is designated as the full awakening (*abhisambodhi*) of the omniscient Buddhas.

It is "abandonment" (*pahāna*) because defilements to be abandoned are cast off by it; or, taking it as "abandonment" because they abandon the defilements to be abandoned by means of it—that [knowledge] is also this supreme path-knowledge.
With the intention that "insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) is also called abandoning," it was said: "Or, it is included within the perfection of abandoning.

Regarding the five precepts: among such terms as "the morality of abandoning killing," "the morality of abstention (veramaṇi)," "mental morality," "restraint (saṃvara)," and "non-transgression," here "morality of abandoning" is indeed the morality of abstention in the sense already explained.

It is logical. However, if the intention is that there is no such thing as a dhamma called "abandonment," then those two types of knowledge which accomplish abandonment under the heading of "mindfulness" must be understood metaphorically as abandonment.
Otherwise, it would follow that the perfection of abandonment is without essence and without fruit.
Even when Paccekabuddhas and Buddhas' disciples abandon the defilements, they do so together with the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Because the latent tendency of delusion (*mohavāsanā*) still exists within the continuum of their minds due to its not having been abandoned, they do not attain omniscience.
Therefore, the perfection of abandonment as it pertains to them does not exist in the same way as it does for the omniscient Buddhas;
thus he said, "together with the latent tendencies," and so forth. In the *Vibhāvanī*, the perfection of knowledge is stated first, followed by the perfection of abandonment.

In the *Ṭīkā*, however, the perfection of abandonment (*pahāna-sampadā*) is stated first. Following that, the perfection of attainment (*adhigama-sampadā*) is stated, and then the perfection of knowledge (*ñāṇa-sampadā*).

Within the perfection of abandonment, the knowledge of the supreme path (*aggamagga-ñāṇa*) is shown. The "perfection of attainment" refers to the acquisition of the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*).
Furthermore, within the perfection of knowledge, all the remaining ten powers of knowledge (*dasabala-ñāṇa*) and so forth are shown by means of those two aforementioned knowledges.
Here too, considering the method of the *ṭīkā*, he says: "The 'perfection of abandonment' is itself the removal," and so forth.

"'Having omniscient knowledge as its proximate cause' (*sabbaññutaññāṇappadaṭṭhāna*) means that it has omniscient knowledge as its proximate cause, that is, its immediate condition. For there is no such thing as the 'perfection of abandonment' other than the knowledge of the Path.
The intended meaning is that [such a thing] does not exist in the ultimate sense (*paramatthato*). And this [statement], "There is no dhamma called 'abandonment,'" is found in the *Visuddhimagga*.
This was stated because it is taught that there is nothing other than the mere non-arising of the aforementioned types of killing and so forth.
However, through the undertaking of the states that abandon, the non-arising of the states to be abandoned is indeed a single noble state;
it is a single state of peace. For thus it is said in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*: "Arising is fear; non-arising..."
"Safety" (*khema*) is knowledge regarding the state of peace (*santipada*). "Occurrence" (*pavatti*) is fear; "non-occurrence" (*appavatti*) is safety—this is knowledge regarding the state of peace.

Furthermore, abandonment by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgappahāna*) should be called the non-arising of that very factor; abandonment by suppression (*vikkhambhanappahāna*) is the non-arising through suppression;

and abandonment by eradication (*samucchedappahāna*) is the non-arising through eradication. In this context, however, it is the knowledge of insight (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) that brings about this non-arising.
And it is intended that the knowledge of the path (*maggaññāṇa*) constitutes abandonment by means of access concentration (*upacāra*).

Why? Because it should be understood as being the condition for the perfection of higher knowledges (*upariñāṇa*) and so forth. "Confusion of perfection" (*sampadāsaṅkara*) means the mixing of perfections or the blending of perfections. "Arrived at through the proper method" (*ñāyāgata*) means arrived by way of logical reasoning (*yutti*).

"By means of the qualities of virtue and so forth" (*sīlādiguṇehi*) means by means of the qualities of virtue (*sīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*paññā*), liberation (*vimutti*), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuttiñāṇadassana*). "By means of the phenomena of supernormal power" (*iddhidhammehi*).
“By means of the qualities of psychic power,” such as the supernormal powers of the various kinds of *iddhi*.
“Adorned with the primary and secondary marks” means adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpurisa*) and the eighty minor marks.
“Inclination” (*āsaya*) refers to a particular desire residing within the continuum of the mind. “Of the disposition” (*ajjhāsayassa*) refers to dispositions such as that of non-greed (*alobha*).
“Excellence” (*uḷāratā*) means refinement. “The disposition toward welfare” (*hitajjhāsayatā*) means the desire for the welfare [of others].

Here, it should also be stated that [the Buddha] arrives at the time when the faculties of beings whose faculties have not yet matured reach maturity. “Of those well-known” (*abhiññātānaṃ*) means of those who are very famous.

“The perfection of the two abandonments” (*dvepahānasampadā*) refers to the perfection of the two abandonments and the perfection of knowledge. Regarding the term “Perfectly Enlightened One” (*sammāsambuddha*): “He fully awakened to the truths by himself” (*sāmaṃ saccāni abhisambujjhi*).
Here, the knowledge of the supreme path known as full enlightenment (abhisambodhi) is intended; and that has the function of abandoning as its primary characteristic.

In the phrase "and there he attained omniscience," it is the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa) that is meant. In the phrase "and mastery over the powers," the ten powers of knowledge (dasabalaññāṇa) are intended.
Therefore it was said: "The two... [are] manifested by the title of Perfectly Enlightened One (sammāsambuddha)."
The section on *sampadāna* (the dative case) is concluded. 7. Regarding the phrase *sasaddhammaguṇuttama*:

in the expression *yathā sasaṅghaṃ lokanāyakaṃ namassissaṃ* ("just as I shall pay homage to the Leader of the World together with the Saṅgha"), because the word *saha* has the sense of "conjunction" (*samavāya*), it is understood that the sense of conjunction is intended here, such that one pays homage to both the Leader of the World and the Saṅgha.

Likewise, here too, in order to show that the meaning of "conjunction" (*samavāya*) is indicated by the word *saha* (together) in the phrase "I pay homage to the Perfectly Enlightened One, the True Dhamma, and the Supreme Assembly," it is said:
"From afar... [etc. ...this is how it should be understood. Here, "this" refers to the words "the Perfectly Enlightened One together with the True Dhamma and the Supreme Assembly.
And in this context, "conjunction" refers to two, three, or many meanings [coming together].
*Samavāya* is the coming together, the proceeding, or the conjunction, based on a single substance, quality, or non-action.
Regarding instances such as regret (*paccānutāpa*) or rejoicing (*paccānumodanā*), it is said: "I did not give gifts in the past;

I did not guard my virtue"—thus, even concerning the past, a future verbal form is employed, as in the passage beginning, "I shall wander through the saṃsāra of many births. Therefore, he says: "He shall revere."
They shall pay homage. Regarding the phrase “guṇībhūtānaṃ,” this means those that have become subordinate within a compound word (*samāsapada*), that is, those that have become non-primary.
This suffix *ī* is used here in the sense of becoming something that was not previously so (the formation of an abstract state).

For example: “The crow becomes white” (*setībhavati*) and “the crane becomes black” (*kaṇhībhavati*). In these cases, “becomes white” means it becomes white having not been white before; “becomes black” means it becomes black having not been black before.

This is the meaning. Likewise here as well. In expressions such as "having paid homage to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha," although the Dhamma and the Saṅgha are subordinate (aguṇabhūta) because they are each individually primary [in their own context], they become subordinate to the external referent (aññapadattha) within this compound word.

This is what is called the sense of "the becoming of what was not previously so" (abbhūtatadbhāva). When it is said "the state of having been saluted" (abhivāditabhāva), since the suffix *ta* generally has the past tense as its domain, at the time of commencing the earlier text—

The accomplishment of paying homage to the Dhamma and the Saṅgha is thus demonstrated for the Elder. Furthermore, when it is said, "the state of being worthy of salutation" (*abhivādetabbabhāva*), because the suffix *-tabba* has as its scope the generality of time, it is shown accordingly that the Dhamma and the Saṅgha are to be saluted at all times.
This is just as in such cases as "giving is to be given" (*dānaṃ dātabbaṃ*) or "virtue is to be guarded" (*sīlaṃ rakkhitabbaṃ*);
likewise, the Dhamma and the Saṅgha are to be saluted at all times. Thus, [the Dhamma and the Saṅgha] at all times...
In order to show this meaning—that only the quality of being worthy of salutation has been demonstrated—the passage beginning with “therein” (tatthā) was stated.
Therein, the term “salutation” (abhivādana) is stated by way of showing the occurrence of the action; however, it does not indicate a specific time.
“By way of his own example” means that he came together with his children and wife, having brought them out and shown them by means of his own application. For he...
"Application is the very act of inherence. [Regarding the phrase] "of the inherence of qualities":
here, in the Elder’s statement of homage, it is understood that the Elder pays homage to the Triple Gem through these very words as the doors;

thus, they derive the meaning "having paid homage" (*abhivādiya*) as "having caused [the Triple Gem] to be paid homage to" (*abhivādiya-ādhi*). However, when the verb is subordinate, such a derivation of meaning is not applied.

Not considering it sufficient, he says "Furthermore" (*apica*) and so forth. Therein, the phrase "Furthermore" (*apica*) is a collection of particles used to indicate that there is something further to be said.

"By way of the designation 'book'" (*ganthappaṭiññāya*) means by the expression "designation as a book. "Having joined together" (*sahaghaṭetvā*) means having connected them into one. Regarding the meaning of words:
compounds and derivative words such as *sadhano puriso* (a man with wealth) and *dhanavā puriso* (a man possessing wealth) are for the most part [formed in this manner].
These [terms] indicate the sense of excellence (*atisaya*). For people do not speak in such a manner regarding a small amount of wealth;
therefore, here too, in order to show such an excellent meaning, it is said: "by that which was created by himself... [and so on]... which has become a refuge.
Therein, "by that which was created by himself" means produced by himself. With the words beginning with "For not," he explains that very same meaning through the method of contrast (*vyatireka*).
In this context, “by one created by another” (paranimmitena) means “created by the Buddha”; this is the intended meaning.

“Such praise” (tathā thomanan) refers to the praise: “the supreme assembly together with the True Dhamma. “This too” (idampi): here, the particle *api* is used in the sense of including a second item;
it is not only the first two phrases that constitute qualities unique to the Teacher, but this phrase as well is a quality of the Teacher not shared with Pacceka Buddhas and others.
The construction is: "It is indeed a footprint.
In the sense of expressing a phenomenon (*dhamma*): "It bears" means it carries. In the verse, "it protects" means it protects from the suffering of the states of woe and so forth.

"Of those" refers to the defilements (*kilesa*). "In this sense" refers to the sense of bearing, which is defined as the complete cutting off of the defilements. And "nibbāna" is [to be understood] in its non-figurative sense.

Why was it said, “It is called Dhamma”? Anticipating the objection that the function of Nibbāna is indeed the abandoning by way of escape (*nissaraṇappahāna*), whereas this [Dhamma] is the abandoning by way of eradication (*samucchedappahāna*), he says: “By means of the Noble Path,” and so forth. “Having come into being together with Nibbāna”:
Nibbāna, which has become the object-predominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*) and the object-support (*upanissaya*), is its own foundation.
This is the intended meaning. Furthermore, "complete eradication" (*samuccheda*) and "escape" (*nissaraṇa*) are identical in their essential import.
Therefore, escape should be understood as the primary retention itself. Or rather, it is even more appropriate to say that escape alone is the principal retention.
[The text says: "It is indeed the means for retention; it is not the primary retention. Why? Because it lacks the function of complete eradication.
“These five are indeed states belonging to the method (pariyāya-dhammā). Why? Because they are not assistants to Nibbāna in its function of total eradication.

And here, regarding the term “fruits of recluseship” (sāmaññaphalāni): the state of a recluse (samaṇa) is *sāmañña*; this is a name for the Noble Path. The fruit of *sāmañña* is the fruit of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*).
In the second interpretation, although certain conditions are non-functional (akicca), they are understood in the sense of the object (kamma) because they serve as conditions for what is to be done.
It also elucidates the meaning of the conditions for the tasks (*kicca-paccaya*). As it was stated, "seen, heard, sensed, and cognized," [the phrase] "worthy of being retained" is used.
"Only those phenomena as they have been stated" refers to the five primary phenomena, that is, the five modes of expression regarding phenomena.
"Some" refers to the four paths. Again, "some" refers to Nibbāna alone. Here, the plural number is employed because it falls under the category of a collective term (*sotapatita*).
The plural form is used in a conventional sense (*rūḷha*). Again, “some” refers to the four fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*);

“some” refers to the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti*). Here too, the plural form is included within the scope of the term. In the phrase “bearing one who bears,” it refers to the person who bears [the Dhamma].
In the third alternative, “carrying one who does not fall,” they carry him by making him one who does not fall. In the fourth alternative, “here.”

"In this Dhamma": those for whom the Dhamma is their island are "Dhamma-islanders" (*dhammadīpā*). Those for whom the Dhamma is their refuge are "Dhamma-refuges" (*dhammappaṭisaraṇā*). It is said: "Bhikkhus, be Dhamma-islanders, be Dhamma-refuges, with no other refuge.
Those who have obtained a footing are "those who have obtained a footing" (*laddhappatiṭṭhā*). This is indeed appropriate, because it conforms to the reading "Dhamma-island" (*dhammadīpa*).

This is the intended meaning. In this investigation of the Dhamma, the accuser, perceiving the practice of the Dhamma as something other than the tenfold Dhamma itself, challenges it with the words "Why...
and so forth. However, that practice of the Dhamma is not different from it; rather, he says "And that...
and so on, demonstrating that it is included within that very [Dhamma]. The phrase "it is the preliminary path of the Way" is like the mango tree.
The mango flower is the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the mango fruit by way of being its prior state (*pubbabhāga*).

Why? Because it is from this very [flower] that the fruit is born, and it is in this very [flower] that it grows. Likewise, the practice of the Dharma is the preliminary decisive support (*pubbabhāgūpanissaya*) for the fruit of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*) by way of being its foundation. Why? Because it is from this very [practice] that the fruit is born, and it is in this very [practice] that it grows.

And this has been said in the Mahāvagga Saṃyutta: "Just as, monks, whatever kinds of crops or vegetation reach growth, increase, and abundance, all do so depending on the earth and established upon the earth;
even so, monks, it is by depending on the virtue of a monk and being established in virtue that one develops the Noble Eightfold Path."
"It attains growth, increase, and abundance in wholesome qualities. Regarding the phrase "the prior volition in giving," just as merit is said to be threefold—
merit consisting in giving, merit consisting in virtue, and merit consisting in meditation—
all prior volitions occurring in relation to the act of giving, starting from the search for the object of the gift, are included within the term "giving."

Generosity alone is included within that number. Thus, it is meant to say that this practice-dhamma is included in the expression "the Noble Path," and it has attained the designation of the "Noble Path" itself.
While speaking further that ought to be said regarding this convergence of dhammas, he said, beginning with "Moreover... (*apicā*). Therein, "by which point" (*yadaggena*)...
The meaning of "by way of the causal factor" (*kāraṇakoṭṭhāsena*) and so forth is: by means of the portion consisting of the cause, such as the method for maintaining [the training].

"Worthy of being venerated" (*vandaneyyo*) means one who deserves veneration; [the phrase] "in that one worthy of veneration" refers to this. Regarding the term "a virtuous worldling" (*puthujjanakalyāṇaka*), there are three kinds of virtuous ones:
the virtuous one in the Vinaya, the virtuous one in the Suttanta, and the virtuous one in the Abhidhamma. Among these, it is by virtue of the excellent practice prescribed in the Vinaya...
A bhikkhu who possesses [these qualities] is called "one who is beautiful in the Vinaya.

Here, this bhikkhu should be understood as one who dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, perfect in conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and training himself by undertaking the rules of training.
In that regard, there are two kinds of unwholesome practice prescribed in the Vinaya: first, the beginning...
The virtue of the basic course of the holy life (*brahmacariyakasīla*) is the virtue of the practice of the higher training (*abhisamacārikasīla*).

In this context, the virtue included in the *Ubhatovibhaṅga* is called "the basic course of the holy life" (*ādibrahmacariyaka*), while the virtue included in the *Khandhaka* is called "the practice of the higher training" (*abhisamacārika*).
Whether a householder or one who has gone forth, one who is endowed with the noble practice as described in the *Suttantas* is a *suttantika*.
He is named Kalyāṇaka. Monks, an noble disciple endowed with four qualities has completely transcended all fear of miserable destinies.
With which four? Here, monks, an noble disciple is endowed with verified confidence in the Buddha, thinking:
"Indeed, this Blessed One is... [as before] ...the Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. In the Dhamma...
He is endowed with unwavering confidence (aveccappasāda) in the Dhamma thus: "The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One... to be personally realized by the wise.
He is endowed with unwavering confidence in the Sangha thus: "The Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way...
the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. Here it should be understood that he is endowed with the virtues dear to the noble ones (ariyakanta-sīla).

In this context, "unshakable confidence in the Buddha" refers to the clarity of faith associated with the knowledge that understands the meaning of such quality-terms as "He is an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One," and so forth.
They are called "dear to the Noble Ones" (*ariyakanta*) because they are desired or sought after by the Noble Ones.
This is the name for the perfectly pure virtue consisting of the eight factors of right livelihood. "Monks, there are these four factors of stream-entry. Which four?"
Many discourses should be cited here, such as those beginning with: "Association with superior persons, hearing the true Dhamma, wise attention, and practice in accordance with the Dhamma.
Whether a householder or one gone forth, one who is endowed with this noble practice—whether taught in the Abhidhamma or in the Suttantas—...

Or it is called the "Excellence of the Abhidhamma. Here, the learned noble disciple—one who has seen the noble ones, is skilled in the noble Dhamma, and is disciplined in the noble Dhammas—is to be understood in this context as one who does not regard form as self.
In that regard, "learned" (*sutavā*) refers to one who has mastered the study of the aggregates, bases, elements, dependent origination, and the foundations of mindfulness.

"One who possesses the knowledge of discernment through thorough inquiry—whether a householder or one gone forth, whether a listener or not—is what is described in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) as such.
He alone is called a 'virtuous worldling' (*puthujjana-kalyāṇaka*).
Two types of worldlings were spoken of by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun:"
And it is said: "The worldling alone is blind; the worldling alone is noble.
Furthermore, in the Catukka-nipāta of the Aṅguttara Nikāya, it is asked: "Which person is one who has heard little but is perfected by what he has heard?
Here, someone hears the Dhamma and, having understood the meaning of even a single four-line verse, [realizes] the Dhamma..."
Thinking "Are these phenomena one who has entered into the practice of the Dhamma?"—this is what is meant by "one who has heard little, yet is established through what he has heard.

Furthermore, "one who has heard" (*sutavā*) and "established through what he has heard" (*sutena upapanno*) are identical in meaning. The virtuous worldling (*puthujjana-kalyāṇaka*) is included among the trainees (*sekkha*) within the Saṅgha.
For this is stated in the *Parivāra*: "Who are those training? [The answer is: "The seven noble persons together with the virtuous worldling."
They train. An Arahant whose taints are destroyed is one who has completed the training.

However, in the commentary to the *Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅgasutta*, it is stated that even a lay follower (*upāsaka*) who has gone for refuge to the Triple Gem is included among those practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*).
In this context, "one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry" refers to a noble person (*ariya-puggala*) standing upon the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*).

“Not included” (*asaṅgahito*) is the connection [with the preceding]. “At this point it is rejected” (*ettāvatā paṭikkhittaṃ hoti*) is the connection. “Not included in the Saṅgha” (*saṅghe asaṅgahito*):

when such statements regarding the Saṅgha occur—such as “I go for refuge to the Saṅgha” and “The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way”—one is not included in those words concerning the Saṅgha. For one who goes for refuge, there is no going for refuge that is not beneficial.
The phrase "it is accomplished" is stated here in order to establish that the word "Saṅgha" does not include that particular individual when one says, "I go for refuge to the Saṅgha.

Therefore he said: "That is rejected. However, if one were to go for refuge to the Saṅgha without mentioning the entire Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples, but only to that specific individual—such as saying, "I go for refuge to the Venerable One"—[that would be invalid].

"I am going"—even then, the going for refuge does not yet come to pass. Then, if one were to go for refuge in the presence of the entire Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples, saying, "I go for refuge to the Saṅgha," it indeed comes to pass.
And this is said with reference to the very first going for refuge during one's childhood. For this going for refuge—
Once one has taken the name, for one who does not abandon faith in the Triple Gem, it does not break even throughout their entire life.
There is no need to take it again and again. Even if one takes it repeatedly, there is no fault; rather, merit increases more and more.
Furthermore, at the very first moment of taking it, because it was given by another, it is not something "obtained" [by oneself]; it is obtained through the verbal expression of oneself.
Therefore, for a householder who takes the vocal expression himself without receiving it from another, the going for refuge is indeed accomplished.
The same applies to all the precepts of a householder. However, the going for refuge of a novice monk (sāmaṇera) is obtained only when conferred by a bhikkhu;
moreover, that occurs only when both have attained the status of being a foundation [for the lineage].
It should be understood. “*Vo*” means “of you. “The Dhamma that has been taught and the Vinaya that has been laid down”—“after my passing away” means beyond me;
it is said, “when I have attained final Nibbāna. There is an ellipsis for the words “will be the Teacher.
“*Saṃvaṇṇito*” means well-praised or extolled. “Even while established in the practice of excellence” refers to the three types of excellent practice.
Even one who stands in some form of practice—by the phrase "even though not standing," the intention is that one who is outside of all forms of practice, being immoral and of evil nature—is meant.
Specifically, however, it should be understood that here the "practice" refers specifically to the practice of the Vinaya.
"He"—that is, the immoral person of evil nature—"is not even a refuge for himself. The intention is that he will inevitably go to the states of misery (apāya).
The construction is: “From where will there be refuge? Regarding the phrase “in many thousands of suttas,” numerous passages of reproach are found not only in the Vinaya but also in the Suttanta;
specifically, however, in such discourses as the *Aggikkhandhopama-sutta*.

With respect to the etymological meaning of the term *saddhamma*—namely, that it “calms” (*sameti*) or “pacifies” (*vūpasameti*) the defilements—the phrase “of those whose defilements have been calmed” (*samitakilesānaṃ*) is used, referring to this etymological sense of “peaceful” (*santa*).
It has been said. However, the word *santa* is seen to mean "praised," "honored," "a true person" (*sappurisa*), and "wise.
With reference to this range of meanings, it was stated: "of those who are praised," and so forth. The construction is: "The Dhamma that is real (*sacca*) is the True Dhamma (*saddhamma*).
By this, he shows that it is "real" (*santa*) because it exists and is found by way of its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). "That" refers to the Dhamma of other sectarians.
“Of one who maintains it”: of one who maintains it by way of hearing, grasping, memorizing, practicing, and so forth. “It results only in harm”:
the intention is that for the most part it has a result in the miserable realms (duggati). “But this,” namely, the Teacher’s true Dhamma: “of one who maintains it thus”:
of one who maintains it thinking, “This is for my benefit”; it results only in benefit, because it leads to the happy realms and Nibbāna—this is the intention.
“Of those with identical view and virtue” means those who possess identical views and identical virtues.
