By this, it is shown that a *gaṇa* (group) is so called because people with identical view and virtue are counted together therein; and a *saṅgha* (community) is so called because they are bound together and made into a unity therein.
They practice the Dhamma together as one, thus they are *sahadhammika* (fellow-practitioners). [This refers to] within the Dhamma and Vinaya of a single Teacher.
Those who have gone forth. Of those who share the same Dhamma. The Blessed One’s Saṅgha of disciples is called the "supreme group.
For it has been said: "Whatever groups or assemblies there may be in the world, the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata’s disciples is declared to be the foremost among them.
This very [Saṅgha] is here called the "supreme group" by way of an adjective following a noun; this is the intended meaning. Regarding the word *uttama*:
Because it refers to the qualities themselves, it is said: "It occurs only with respect to the qualities. By the word "tena" (thereby), [it refers to] the word *uttama* (supreme).

"A *gaṇa* is said to be the *saṅgha* itself," because the word *saṅgha* is conventionally established in the sense of a collection; "it is well-known in the disciplinary acts (*vinayakamma*)"—namely, the fivefold *saṅgha*:
the four-membered *saṅgha*, the five-membered *saṅgha*, the ten-membered *saṅgha*, the twenty-membered *saṅgha*, and the *saṅgha* consisting of more than twenty members.
It is well-known and evident as "an act to be performed by a group of four" (*catuvaggakaraṇīyaṃ kammaṃ*), "an act to be performed by a group of five" (*pañcavaggakaraṇīyaṃ kammaṃ*), and so forth.
"Sacrifice" (*dakkhiṇā*) refers to the act of giving—both the ritual act and its fruit—which is offered with faith for the sake of obtaining the result of maturation in the future;
it is called *dakkhiṇā* because beings "prosper" (*dakkhanti*) or "increase" (*vaḍḍhanti*) by means of it. One who is worthy to receive that sacrifice is [an *arahant*].

"An object worthy of offerings" (*dakkhiṇeyya*). He "deserves" it because, by being a distinguished field of merit unsurpassed, he perfectly brings about for the donor the future fruit desired and prayed for;

and because, by not disappointing the donor, he brings about an increase that is incalculable and immeasurable. Indeed, such a gift as this is called a sublime gift. Yet, it is given even to those who are immoral.
Because their field is corrupted, it does not produce the fruit desired and prayed for by the donor;
or it becomes fruitless, or yields only meager fruit. This being so, they are said to "disappoint" the donor and are said to "destroy" the fruits of merit.
Furthermore, by receiving that gift or by consuming it, they cause the offering given in faith to go to waste.
Or they are destined for an unhappy rebirth. Therefore, they are not worthy to receive such a gift.

As for the statement, "The act of full ordination (*upasampadā-kamma*) is called a formal authorization (*sammuti*)," it is called a formal authorization in one sense; for it is certainly included among the formal acts of authorization.
However, because it is accomplished through the authorization of the Saṅgha, which consists of the motion (*ñatti*) and the third proclamation (*kammavācā*), it is [also] a formal act.

"In that sense, it is called a formal act of convention (*sammuti-kamma*). Regarding the phrase "having reached the stage of full ordination" (*upasampannabhūmiṃ patvā*), this means having reached the subsequent higher stage known as the stage of full ordination.
For it is so stated in the *Vinaya*, in the *Bhikkhu-vibhaṅga*:

"By a formal act consisting of a motion and a third proclamation (*ñatti-catuttha-kamma*), which is irreversible and fit for the occasion. In that context, "fit for the occasion" (*ṭhānāraheṇa*) refers to what is reckoned as the stage of full ordination.
The meaning is: "to cause one to reach a higher status. Furthermore, "the stage of full ordination" (*upasampannabhūmi*) refers to the virtue of one who is fully ordained.
"Established in the legal acts of the Vinaya" means well-known in such contexts as "Let the Saṅgha listen, venerable sirs," and so forth.

Moreover, in expressions such as "the Saṅgha by convention" or "the assembly of the gods has gathered," the term *saṅgha* is established through worldly convention in the sense of being a collection of many individuals.
It is also appropriate to say that the Saṅgha is conventional (*sammuti*).

A "collection of noble persons" (*ariyapuggalasamūho*) includes a bhikkhu who is a virtuous worldling (*puthujjanakalyāṇaka*) when he has reached the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*) according to the method previously stated; thus, together with him, there is an eightfold collection of noble persons.

By the statement, “He is indeed included within the conventional Saṅgha,” it is shown that what is called the "Saṅgha worthy of offerings" (*dakkhiṇeyyasaṅgho*) need not be mentioned separately. And in that [conventional Saṅgha]...
If it were not to be stated [as "the Saṅgha"], there would be no need to state that it is "the conventional Saṅgha" (*sammuti-saṅgha*);
rather, it is shown that one must simply say, "the Blessed One’s Saṅgha of disciples" (*bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho*). This is true.

However, here, because the instances where the word "Saṅgha" occurs are of two kinds, the twofold nature of the Saṅgha is mentioned. Among these, the instance where the conventional Saṅgha occurs is in the formal acts of the Vinaya (*vinayakamma*).
This has already been stated. Now, in order to show the place where the Noble Saṅgha is found, he says, "Even so," and so forth.

In that context, within the sections on going for refuge... up to the bases of recollection (anussatiṭṭhāna), only the Bhikkhu Saṅgha who has received full ordination (upasampadā) should be understood.

However, in the section on the purification of offerings (dakkhiṇāvisuddhi), in regard to gifts given to individuals, even a lay follower (upāsaka) or a novice (sāmaṇera) endowed with the four factors of stream-entry (sotāpattiyaṅga) is appropriate.
But regarding gifts for the Saṅgha, it is the community of monks themselves. “Having praised them in such and such a way” means having extolled them well with such phrases as:
“They are worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
That is the Saṅgha worthy of offerings. As for the phrase “the Saṅgha of worldlings,” this refers exclusively to the Saṅgha of worldlings, apart from the noble Saṅgha.
This was said with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*). And here, by the word "Saṅgha," even a single monk included within the Saṅgha is to be understood.
If he is an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), he is not an unsurpassed field of merit; if he is a noble person (*ariya-puggala*), he is an unsurpassed field of merit.

In the *Dakkhiṇavibhaṅgasutta*, regarding gifts dedicated to the Saṅgha, it is said: "But there will come to be, Ānanda, those of the lineage (gotrabhū) with saffron robes around their necks who are immoral and of evil character; yet people will still give gifts dedicated to the Saṅgha for their sake.

At that time, Ānanda, I declare that a gift directed toward the Saṅgha is incalculable and immeasurable. Because of this statement, when [a gift] reaches the status of being dedicated to the Saṅgha, no one...
It should be understood that there is no monk who is not included within the Saṅgha worthy of offerings.
"Corrupting the field" refers to those things which corrupt the field, namely weeds. The weeds are the defilements. For it is said in the Dhammapada:
"Fields have weeds as their blemish; this generation has lust and hatred as its blemish."
Therefore, what is given to those free from passion yields great fruit.
Fields have weeds as their blemish; this generation has hatred as its blemish.
Therefore, what is given to those free from hatred yields great fruit.
"Fields have weeds as their blemish; this generation has delusion as its blemish.
Therefore, what is given to those free from delusion becomes of great fruit.
Here, however, in order to show the defilements that corrupt the field by way of their specific characteristics, [the text says]: "of personality-belief, doubt, and underlying-tendencies."

It has been said: “*Sabbhāvā*”: the analysis is that *sabbhāva* is the state (*bhāva*) of being present (*santa*) or existing (*vijjamāna*). “*Assa*”: of the Saṅgha of ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*).
“*By the method stated in the *Saddhammapada*”* means by the method stated beginning with the words “*Apica yadagge*.
The exposition of the meaning of the supreme term for the assembly possessing the True Dhamma is completed.

8. “Having saluted” (*abhivādiya*) means having caused [them] to say, “May you be well, O noble one. And since salutation (*abhivādana*) is indeed veneration (*vandana*), it is said, “having paid homage” (*vanditvā*).
For one who pays homage causes those worthy of veneration—the elders—to speak in that manner.

Speaking in such a way is the proper conduct (*vatta*) toward those elders worthy of veneration. “Having attended upon” (*paccupaṭṭhāpetvā*) means having attended upon them face-to-face. “Threefold” (*tividhā*)...
It is threefold according to the distinction of doors. “Of those worthy of veneration” refers to the Buddhas and so forth. “Lying down” means prostrating.

“Among those not to be venerated” refers to those such as very junior novices who are not to be venerated by monks. “Phrases of quality” are words that illuminate qualities, such as “Arahant, Perfectly Enlightened One,” and so forth.
In this context, expressions such as “he venerates with the body” are figurative (upacāra) statements, just as one says, “he sees form with the eye. For it is thus:

It is stated in the commentaries: "Having seen a visible form with the eye" means having seen a visible form by means of the visual consciousness (*cakkhu-viññāṇa*), which is conventionally designated as "the eye" in the sense of being the instrument and is capable of seeing forms.
However, the Ancients have said: "The eye does not see the form, because it is devoid of consciousness;
the consciousness does not see, because it is devoid of the eye. But when there is a conjunction of the door, the object, and the [mental] assembly, the basis of the sensitive eye..."
One sees by means of something. However, this kind of expression—such as "one pierces with a bow"—is what is called a "figurative expression" (*sasambhāra-kathā*).
Therefore, in the phrase "having seen a form with the eye," the meaning is precisely that one sees the form by means of visual consciousness.
For in this context, in the case of "with the body," the instrument is the door-form known as bodily intimation (*kāya-viññatti*). Thus, [it is said] "by means of the eye."
When there is figurative speech (*upacāra-vacana*), it is understood that even the expression "by means of the body" is figurative speech.
Likewise, when the word "by the eye" has the meaning "by means of eye-consciousness," it is understood that the word "by the body" also has the meaning "by means of bodily action.
This same principle applies to the phrases "he worships with speech" and "he worships with the mind. And this being so, [the meaning is]: "I worship by means of bodily action."
It is established that the primary statement is precisely this: "I pay homage with verbal action, I pay homage with mental action, I pay homage with all three types of action.
All of this has been stated because it appears in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) in the section on the virtue of restraint of the sense faculties (*indriyasaṃvara-sīla*).
However, in the phrase "with the eye," only the primary sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) is possible. Why? Because of the eye, which is defined as seeing...

This is because the eye-consciousness possesses the specific condition of a pre-arisen faculty (purejātindriya-paccaya) as its physical basis (vatthu). This same method applies to such phrases as "having heard a sound with the ear," and so forth.

Regarding the expressions "he salutes with the body" and "he salutes with speech": although these two types of material form—the bodily intimation (kāya-viññatti) and the vocal intimation (vacī-viññatti)—are produced by the co-nascent volitional action (sahajāta-cetanā-kamma), that volitional action is not produced by the two intimations. Even so...
That pair of material qualities is a specific condition of decisive support (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for the accomplishment of the bodily act of homage and the verbal act of homage of that volition.
Just as a son born of a mother, having reached maturity, becomes a source of strength and support for his mother in various tasks,
so too, having established it thus, that pair of material qualities is called "door-matter" (*dvāra-rūpa*) in the Abhidhamma.
Therefore, it should be understood that the expressions "by body" and "by speech" are also primarily terms denoting the instrument (*karaṇa*).
If it is argued that when "by body" means "by bodily action," an identity between that action and the act of salutation would follow, this is not the case.
Why? Because the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, I say that volition (*cetanā*) is action; having willed, one performs action by body... [and so forth].
Regarding "by speech" and "by mind" in this sutta: just as in the phrase "having intended," one has intended by means of prior volitions;
and "one performs an action" means that the subsequent volition of determination performs the action—so too here, both prior and subsequent volitions are possible.
For in this context, "by bodily action" refers to the prior volition as the action, while "he pays homage" refers to the subsequent [volition].
“Volition that brings about determination” (*sanniṭṭhāpanacetanākamma*). 9. “Arranging” (*racayanto*) means distributing.

“Will arrange” (*racayissati*) is a future tense used for the past when it is not directly perceived. “Ascended to the manuscript” (*potthakāruḷhaṃ*) means ascended by way of being written upon the leaves of the manuscript.
10. Regarding the words “in the *Abhidhammattha*”: “In the *Abhidhamma*” (*abhidhamme*) means in the treatises of the *Abhidhamma*. By the words “here” (*ettha*) and “by this” (*etenā*),...
The application of the grammatical rule of *ekasesa* (retaining one from a group) is also understood for the word *saṅgaha*.
It is said: "Two other versions of the text are spoken of. Why is that two-fold text called *Abhidhamma*? This is stated by the words beginning with "And that... (*tañca*).

"In accordance with its own conditions" (*yathāpavatte*) means occurring in conformity with its own causal conditions. "Only in ultimate phenomena" (*paramatthadhamme evā*) refers to such passages as: "Monks, there are these two persons," and "Monks, there are these three persons," and so forth.
Although the teaching proceeds by way of conventional designation (*paññatti-vohāra*), it does not proceed without the ultimate phenomena (*paramattha-dhamma*).
This is because the diversity of persons arises solely through the diversity of ultimate phenomena. Therefore, [the Buddha] illuminates only the ultimate phenomena;

he does not illuminate the formulation of commands. In the phrase “in two phenomena,” the locative case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*). “Whosoever from among these” [refers to those who have attained the path].

[The word] *niddhāraṇīyaṃ* [means] that which is to be singled out. "Who" (*yo*) refers to whichever phenomenon (*dhamma*). "From the other" (*itarato*) means from the other phenomena, that is, from the phenomena of the discourses (*suttanta*).
"And having done thus" (*evaṃ ca katvā*) means by this reason; this is the connection with the phrase "stated in the commentaries" (*aṭṭhakathāsu vuttaṃ*).

Its "excessiveness" (*atirekatā*) is due to its being an exhaustive classification of the various modes of what ought to be taught; its "distinctiveness" (*visesatā*) is due to its proceeding as a teaching based on pure phenomena (*dhammadhiṭṭhāna*).
[The sections] should be joined. Regarding the word “yato” (since), it means “because of the analysis without remainder” and “due to the absence of an excessively prolix teaching”;
this is what is meant. As for the question “Why do they teach only among the devas?”, he says: “For humans [are not able],” and so forth. Therein, the connection is:
“For humans are not able to receive [the teaching]. “Suitable for circulation” means capable of being circulated.

“Discourse-path” (*kathāmagga*) means a continuous series of instructional discourses. “Following a single matrix” (*ekamātikānubandhā*) means following a single Abhidhamma matrix, such as “wholesome states, unwholesome states,” and so forth.
“Of that” (*tassa*) refers to the Abhidhamma. The connection is with the phrase “the exceedingly distinguished treatise” (*atirekavisesaṭanti*).
“Therein” (*tattha*) means in this *Aṭṭhasālinī*. Regarding the question “In what sense at the very beginning?”: [it is in the sense of] “the meaning of the word ‘beginning’.”
Having stated that *abhidhamma* means "that which exceeds the Dhamma" (*dhammātireka*) or "that which is distinguished from the Dhamma" (*dhammavisesa*), he explains its meaning in detail:
"For when reaching the Suttanta, the five aggregates are analyzed only partially (*ekadesena*), not exhaustively (*nippadesena*); but when reaching the Abhidhamma, they are analyzed exhaustively.
Therefore, he says, "of those named 'Dhamma,'" and so forth. "But the Dhamma," he says, referring to the two-fold Pāḷi. Thus...
"Even though it exists"—this is how it is analyzed in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*. "The most senior of all" means the most senior among the three Piṭakas.
To the question, "Why is it the most senior of all? he says: "For one who disparages the Vinaya," and so forth.
In that context, "disparaging" (*vivaṇṇentassa*) means censuring. It moves and proceeds, thus it is called a "wheel" (*cakkam*). By anyone in the world...
The "Wheel of Authority" (āṇācakkam) is the method of command that cannot be turned back by anyone—a recluse, a brahmin, a deva, Māra, or even Brahmā.
Likewise, the "Wheel of Dhamma" (dhammacakkam) is the method of teaching that cannot be turned back in such a way.
In this regard, [it is stated]: "Whosoever, O bhikkhu, engages in sexual intercourse, he is defeated and no longer in communion," and so forth.

The method of issuing commands as they occur is called the Wheel of Command (*āṇācakkam*). The method of teaching beginning with "Monks, there are these four Noble Truths" is called the Wheel of Dhamma (*dhammacakkam*).

Neither of these two can be broken by anyone; nor can one turn a monk who has committed a *pārājika* offense into one who has not, or turn the Dhamma of the Four Truths into something that is not the Truth. Indeed, it is only while one is actually attempting to do so...
Like Devadatta, he becomes one bound for the states of misery. And a bhikkhu who has committed a *pārājika* offense, failing to purify himself, likewise goes only to the states of misery.
This is the case with all the training rules (*vinaya-sikkhāpada*) of the Discipline.
Thus, because it is impossible for anyone to turn back from them, both of these are called the "irreversible wheel. Regarding the Discipline, it is said: "The Discipline is the root of the Teaching."

When the Saṅgha of bhikkhus is established, the Saṅgha is manifested. When the Saṅgha of bhikkhus is manifested, the True Dhamma in its three aspects is manifested, and the Teacher’s Dispensation in its three aspects endures.
Thus, the Vinaya is the root of the Dispensation in its three aspects.
And how is it that when the True Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyatti) is manifested, the Dispensation in its three aspects endures? It is said: therein—
"As for 'the Dispensation remains'—for how long does it remain? The ancient commentaries have declared that it remains for five thousand years.
Those who hold wrong views criticize this, saying: 'In the Cullavagga of the Vinaya, in the Bhikkhunī-kkhandhaka, it was said:
"If, Ānanda, women had not received the going-forth in my Dispensation, the True Dhamma would have remained for a thousand years. Now that women have received the going-forth..."'"
It was permitted [to women] because of Gotamī’s repeated entreaties. It has been said: "Ānanda, the True Dhamma will endure for five hundred years.
Therefore, the Buddha's dispensation lasts for only five hundred years; beyond that, it does not endure even for a single day.
To say, "Now there remains only a mere semblance of the dispensation," is merely their false statement.
“Five hundred years”—this, however, is not a definitive statement; it is merely a statement intended to illustrate the dangers for women.
And that danger was warded off by the Teacher himself by establishing the eight *garudhammas*.
Subsequently, the phrase “a thousand years” arose as the definitive statement. Regarding this, some say that it is indeed a thousand years.
"The Dispensation remains; after that, it does not remain for even a single day, but vanishes. At that time, even the *sīmā* boundaries become non-*sīmā*.
Those who have received full ordination (*upasampadā*) later on would also be unordained. Nowadays, there is merely a semblance of the Dispensation.
This too is a mere false statement, because it was spoken without seeing or knowing their purpose and reason.

This is the meaning here: “The true Dhamma might endure for a thousand years” means that the true Dhamma would remain for exactly a thousand years without declining. Beyond that, however, it would not remain;
rather, it would gradually go into decline. But how does it remain without declining, and how does it go into decline?
It is said: Five assemblies are to be known, within which the true Dhamma remains. Which five?

The assembly of those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsavasaṅgha), the assembly of non-returners (anāgāmisaṅgha), the assembly of once-returners (sakadāgāmisaṅgha), the assembly of stream-enterers (sotāpannasaṅgha), and the assembly of virtuous worldlings (puthujjanakalyāṇakasaṅgha).
Therein, all five assemblies are found within the interval of a thousand years. Thus, for a thousand years, the true Dhamma does not decline.
It remains. Beyond that point, the Saṅgha of those whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava) is no longer discerned.
The remaining four thousand years are successively produced as the fields for the other four types of Saṅgha. Thus, it proceeds by declining beyond that point—this is the meaning here.
The reason is stated: regarding the phrase "the True Dhamma (saddhamma) shall remain," the True Dhamma is threefold.

“The True Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyatti-saddhamma), the True Dhamma of practice (paṭipatti-saddhamma), and the True Dhamma of realization (paṭivedha-saddhamma). This very [Dhamma] is also called the threefold Dispensation (sāsana). Therein, the True Dhamma of the scriptures refers to the Three Piṭakas together with their commentaries;
and that remains complete even now. How could the scripture of the Dispensation be merely a counterfeit? And the monks...”
There appear to be many hundreds of thousands of those engaged in the study of the scriptures (*pariyatti*). Otherwise, this Dispensation would not endure for even a single day beyond that point.
And there will remain many hundreds of thousands of monks at present who are established in the practice of virtue (*sīla*).
Otherwise, how could the practice of the Dispensation not endure beyond that point? And as for the study of the scriptures...
It cannot be said that while the practice (paṭipatti) remains, the true Dhamma of penetration (paṭivedha-saddhamma) does not remain.

For example, there was once a certain eminent treasurer who, for the sake of his lineage of sons and daughters, buried great treasures of precious gems in many places in the earth and left them there. Furthermore, he recorded their full details in writing in books.

He deposits it. In that case, as long as the caves, the books, and the letters endure, it cannot be said at all that these treasures are lost or disappear. This is how this Dispensation (sāsana) should be viewed.

For therein, the word of the Buddha in the Three Pitakas is like the ground where treasures are stored, and the jewels of the Dhamma are like the wealth and gems themselves. And just as one born into a lineage of wealthy merchants...
A man endowed with strength, having seen the book and digging well, will certainly obtain those jewels.
Likewise here, a bhikkhu endowed with strength, having heard the Dhamma of the teaching and practicing it well, will certainly obtain those jewels of the Dhamma.
And since they are being obtained, how could those jewels of the Dhamma have disappeared? And as for the boundaries...
Whether it be the process of arising or the process of cessation, this is the domain of the Wheel of Authority (*āṇācakkam*) alone, not the Wheel of Dhamma (*dhammacakkam*).

As for what was said—that the True Dhamma will endure for five hundred years, and that the True Dhamma might endure for a thousand years—this statement refers only to the Wheel of Dhamma, not the Wheel of Authority.
Furthermore, when the established boundaries (*sīmā*) recede, they recede and disappear for two reasons.
It ceases either by the abolition of the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*), which constitutes the wheel of authority, or by the disappearance of the Dispensation (*sāsana*).

In that regard, at the end of a thousand years, there is no abolition of the formal proclamation. As for the disappearance of the Dispensation, it is delimited by the final extinction of the relics (*dhātuparinibbāna*) in the future.
Once the final extinction of the relics has occurred, the entire wheel of authority is gone and disappears.
Furthermore, the Wheel of Dhamma will continue to turn even among the deva worlds until the time of future Buddhas, just like the verses of Āḷavaka’s questions.
Moreover, it was said: "Ānanda, the Dhamma and Vinaya taught and laid down by me shall be your teacher after my passing.
Thus, the Dhamma and Vinaya, which constitute the Pitakas, are the Teacher; they are the threefold Dispensation that exists at present.

He stands illuminating and making manifest the world. From that time forth, a great light of knowledge—unshared by various outsiders—shines and prevails among gods and humans who speak the Buddha’s word.
Having heard the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dhamma currently existing, which were taught by him through his omniscient wisdom throughout the beginningless cycle of saṃsāra...
In infinite world-systems, they know the entire operation of the three worlds and the entire operation of all phenomena through the knowledge consisting of what has been heard (*sutamaya-ñāṇa*),
which follows after omniscience. Furthermore, for the sake of heaven in the future, and for the sake of the paths, fruits, and *nibbāna*, they undertake various bases for the performance of merit,
go forth into homelessness, master the scriptures (*pariyatti*), fulfill the practice (*paṭipatti*), and cultivate meditation (*bhāvanā*).
All of this is not merely a semblance of the Dispensation; it is the Dispensation itself. Why? Because it proceeds in accordance with the Dhamma and in accordance with the Vinaya.
And because through this practice, there is the attainment in the future of the path to heaven, the fruits [of the spiritual life], and Nibbāna.
To this extent, all the false speech of those who hold wrong views has been dispelled and destroyed.
Commentary on the Verses of Homage. 11.
In the commentary on the second verse: “Of the first verse” means by the statement of the first verse. “Accompanied by this or that purpose” means accompanied by such and such a purpose.
“The five meanings” refers to the five types of alms-food (piṇḍa). “Those meanings of the Abhidhamma” refers to the term *abhidhammattha*.

“The meaning of the Abhidhamma has been illuminated. Regarding the phrase “therein,” it refers to that second verse. As for the expression “it was not stated,” even the act of denying [that it was stated] implies that it was indeed stated previously.
The construction is: “From where were the meanings of the Abhidhamma stated previously?

Having thus shown the contradiction regarding time in the first of these alternative interpretations of the meaning, he now says “nor” and so forth, in order to state the contradiction regarding the words themselves in the second and third [alternatives].
In this context, by the phrase “at the very beginning,” he shows that a reference made at any time whatsoever is secondary (*appadhāna*).
Regarding the term “secondary words,” these are the preceding qualifying words within this single compound word, namely *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha*.
When it is construed as “stated in every respect therein,” it means: in that treatise, the *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha*, and in that *Abhidhammattha*...
The meaning "that which was spoken by me in every respect" does not fit. The meaning "that which was spoken by the Buddha, the Blessed One, in that Abhidhamma in every respect" fits.
Furthermore, if one refers to [the word] as a subordinate term (*appadhānapada*), a fault indeed arises.
Therefore, he said: "For it being thus," and so forth. In that context, "for it being thus" refers here to the term *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha*, just as it does in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*.
When there is the word *paccāmasante*. The sound *hi* indicates the result (*phala*) or the completion of the sentence (*vākya-jotaka*).

It is also appropriate to take it as indicating the attainment of a quality (*laddha-guṇa-jotaka*), because the meaning "it has been rejected" (*paṭikkhittā hoti*) occurs in that phrase from the *Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha* as stated by me in every respect.
To show that not only that fault follows, but there is another fault as well, he said "for she," and so forth. In the *Dhātukathā*...
The connection is to be made with the modes of inclusion and non-inclusion already described. 12.
In the commentary on the *Paramatthapada*, a qualifying term (*visesanapada*) is employed in some instances for the purpose of stating a fact, as in “the crow is black” or “the crane is white.
In other instances, it is employed for the purpose of excluding something else, as in “a blue cloth” or “a blue flower.”

But here, in order to exclude other [types of] conventions, he says, “For truths are of two kinds,” and so forth. It is called a *paññatti* (concept/designation) because it is made known (*paññāpiyati*).
And the making known is accomplished through two factors: the common usage of people acting in concert and their acceptance [of that usage].
Therefore, he says, “And those people...,” and so forth. The connection [of the sentence] is: “Therefore, they are called conventional truths (*sammuti-sacca*).”
“Because of being agreed upon” means because of being expressed and because of being accepted. Regarding the phrase “of the truth of speech and the truth of abstinence”:
here, the “truth of speech” refers to truthful speech free from false speech. The “truth of abstinence” refers to the abstinence from wrong speech (right speech).
For that is called the “truth of speech” merely by virtue of abstaining from verbal misconduct such as false speech and so forth. “Because of being the basis” means...

Because it serves as a basis for resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna*), it is called conventional truth (*sammutisacca*). It is "convention" (*sammuti*) because it is agreed upon, and it is "truth" (*sacca*) because it is the foundation for truths;
thus, it is termed conventional truth. Alternatively, it is also appropriate to call it conventional truth in the sense that it is a truth established by convention (*sammutiyā siddhaṃ saccaṃ*).
"Practicing rightly" means practicing correctly by such means as not killing living beings and wishing that all sentient beings be free from enmity.

“*Sabbalokiyasampattiyo*”: all worldly successes that have arisen as the fruit and result (*phala-vipāka*) of the bases for meritorious action (*puññakiriyavatthu*), such as generosity (*dāna*), virtue (*sīla*), and so forth.

“*Sabbe bodhisambhāradhamme*”: all the qualities that are requisites for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra-dhamma*), such as the perfections (*pāramī*) beginning with the perfection of generosity and the perfection of virtue.
“*Ārādhentī*”: they accomplish or fulfill. “*Micchāpaṭipajjantā*”: practicing wrongly by way of misconduct (*duccarita*), wrong livelihood (*durājīva*), false livelihood (*micchājīva*), and so forth.

By the statement, “Such is the great conventional truth,” he shows that one should not reject conventional truth with the thought, “I accept only ultimate truth. For one who rejects it would be excluded from all success.
And how does one reject it? [One might say: “There is no such thing as a ‘being’; there is no such thing as the transition of a being from one existence to another; that which produces existence...”
One who holds that there is no such thing as wholesome or unwholesome kamma stands in the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*).

Such a person is excluded from all prosperity and becomes a filler of the states of misery. The phrase "he causes one to grasp at what actually exists" means that perception, consciousness, and views cause one to grasp by way of being the objective basis for the perversions.
Therefore, he says "personality-view" (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), and so forth. For it is thus perverted...
Regarding the phrase “conventional truth” (*sammutisacca*): by firmly grasping conventional truth alone, one must not reject ultimate truth (*paramatthasacca*).

For by rejecting it through such views, one is overcome by them. And how does one reject it? By grasping at the aggregates (*khandha*) or what is apart from the aggregates as a self or a life-principle (*attajīva*), and then grasping that those selves or life-principles are annihilated after death—one falls into the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*).

Thus he stands. And those who, being self-sustaining, having become eternal in various states of existence, wander and run from one state of becoming to another—by grasping this, he stands in the view of eternalism (*sassatadiṭṭhi*).
"Not deceiving" means they do not bring about a perversion [of the truth]. "But that," however, refers to the reality of intrinsic nature (*sabhāvasacca*).
It is only by taking into account the mere distinction in experience that feeling is called "pleasure. In every respect...
Feeling is not called "pleasure" because it is actually pleasure; rather, the intended meaning is that "all feeling is indeed suffering.
In this regard, the classification of experience is threefold: experiencing as pleasant, or as unpleasant, or as neutral.

The phrase "indeed suffering" means suffering in the sense of being fearful. And "in the sense of being fearful" means in the sense of being something to be feared by those who see the terror of *saṃsāra*.
“Those whose result is pleasant” means they have a pleasant ripening; these are the wholesome states of the three planes.

By the phrase “regarded as wholesome,” he shows that even though these possess the truth of their own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva-sacca*), they are nevertheless conventional designations based on worldly consensus (*loka-sammuti*). “Possessing taints” (*sāsava*) means the state of being accompanied by taints (*āsava*).

“Defiled” (*saṃkilesika*) means the state of being conjoined with defilements (*saṃkilesa-dhamma*). It is the state to be reached through the floods (*ogha*), the yokes (*yoga*), and the clingings (*upādāna*).
“[The state of] being subject to the flood, subject to the yoke, and subject to clinging. The internal [factors] are the self.
External material phenomena are the self of the tree in the sense of its core (sāra). The material phenomena in the branches are the self of the branch in the sense of its core.
However, the material and immaterial phenomena included within the continuity of a sentient being are the self, more so than those external [to it], in the sense of being firmly grasped by craving.

The term *ajjhatta* (internal) is a worldly convention used in the sense of "one's own. Therefore, he said: “And that which has the internal as its basis,” and so forth. The connection [of the sentence] is:
“The state of being the cessation of suffering and the path—this tetrad is called a Noble Truth (*ariyasacca*). “This very same” refers to this tetrad alone.
By the word “unshakable” (*acalamāna*), he illuminates the meaning of the word *ariya*. The so-called “pleasantness” of phenomena belonging to the three planes [of existence]—

It is moving. Why? Because it is of an impermanent nature (*anicca-dhamma*). By grasping those phenomena as "pleasure" and making them their own internal constituent, they very soon encounter suffering.
But once they have known those phenomena as "suffering" and are liberated from them, there is no returning to suffering again.
This same method applies to the remaining Noble Truths. In the passage beginning with "In these," the Truths are twofold.
Regarding the two truths that have been stated: “Therefore it was said,” and so forth, is a statement of the qualities acquired.

In the phrase, “That which exists without recourse to another designation,” here “recourse to another designation” (aññāpadesa) means that, depending on the combination of eight factors, the shape of a jar is perceived and the shape of a cloth is perceived;
that shape is established without its own intrinsic nature, by recourse to another designation. [This refers to] the concern for subsistence.

There is indeed such a thing as activity (kiriyā), which is called "mind" (citta). It is not established by means of another designation; it is established solely by its own intrinsic nature (sabhāva).

This same principle applies to the activity of touching (phusana-kiriyā) and the activity of feeling (vedayita-kiriyā). To demonstrate this point, he said: "Even without another designation," and so forth.
"Having conceptualized with the mind" means having made a non-existent shape (saṇṭhāna) existent by means of the mental consciousness (manoviññāṇa-citta).
“Having made it with vigour” means having made it with physical effort; what is meant is that one has made the basis together with the material substance.

“Made of mind, fashioned by mind” means produced by the mind and fashioned by the mind, like the forms seen in a dream. To the question, “Why is it called an ultimate reality established by its own nature?
he says, “For it,” and so forth. By the word “exists” (*santi*), it is stated that the meaning is established by way of the verbal root *as* (to be).

They say that it is called "attha" (meaning/purpose) because it is to be sought after and approached by means of words and cognitions. "Itarato" (from the other) means from what is established through supposition.
"Paramo" (supreme) means superior. Therefore he said, "reached the pinnacle. By this, he states the meaning of the word *parama* as "superior.
Now, in order to show its meaning of "ultimate," the passage beginning with "Furthermore" (*apicā*) was stated. In that regard, within this teaching of the Buddha—
There are five great duties of the Dispensation: the direct knowledge of phenomena to be directly known; the full understanding of phenomena to be fully understood;
the abandoning of phenomena to be abandoned; the realization of phenomena to be realized;

and the development of phenomena to be developed. In this context, all ultimate phenomena (paramattha-dhammā) are called "to be directly known. Phenomena belonging to the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca) are "to be fully understood."

[They are] called "the truths. The phenomena of the truth of origination (*samudayasacca*) are called "to be abandoned" (*pahātabba*). The fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*) and Nibbāna are called "to be realized" (*sacchikātabba*).
The phenomena of the truth of the path (*maggasacca*) are called "to be developed" (*bhāvetabba*).

Through the accomplishment of those duties regarding those phenomena, the duty of the Dispensation (*sāsanakicca*) is accomplished within this Teaching; it reaches its conclusion. And those very phenomena are the essence of the Dispensation.

In order to show that these are called "ultimate realities" (paramatthā) in the sense of being supreme because they do not fail in their functions and are non-deceptive, he said, "Moreover," and so forth.
Therein, "which" (ye) refers to those persons. "This" (ayaṃ) refers to this Dhamma.
"Of that" (tassa) refers to that which is to be directly known, that which is to be fully understood, that which is to be abandoned, that which is to be realized, and that which is to be developed.
The connection [is thus]. The *Paramatthavaṇṇanā* is finished. “That is not beautiful”:
it is not beautiful in terms of the phrasing (*byañjana*). It is not beautiful not only in terms of the phrasing, but also in terms of the meaning (*attha*).
For the phenomena of the Four Truths are also the objective domain of the knowledge of the Paccekabuddhas. [This applies] to the five knowable things (*pañcañeyya*).
But *dhammas* belong only to omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). In that context, "dhammas of the four truths" refers exclusively to ultimate realities (*paramattha-dhammas*).
However, "dhammas to be known" (*aññeyya-dhammas*) include all conventional designations (*paññatti*) along with all ultimate realities.
The full awakening to the four truths by the Omniscient Buddhas is accomplished together with the designation of those *dhammas*. [The same applies to] the four truths of the Paccekabuddhas.

Full awakening does not occur apart from the designation of the Dhamma. Therefore, those who have themselves realized the Four Truths are unable to teach others by extracting the designation called "Dhamma.
It is stated in the commentaries that for them, the full awakening to the Four Truths is like a mute person seeing a dream.
Therefore, together with the designation, there are five objects of knowledge (*ñeyya*).
"Only phenomena (dhammā) are the domain of omniscient knowledge"—this could be said.
The commentary on the ultimate meaning of the words is finished. 13.
Regarding the meaning of the word "citta": for it is not obtained without an object (ārammaṇa). When it is said, "it thinks," what does it think?
"One contemplates the object" (*ārammaṇaṃ cinteti*)—this is because it would be impossible [to say this] without a verbal noun (*kammappada*) functioning as the object.
Therefore, here "contemplation" (*cintanā*) is to be understood; thus, the connection is that its name is established.

In the case of "knowledge consisting of what is heard" (*suta-maya-ñāṇa*) and "knowledge consisting of reflection" (*cintā-maya-ñāṇa*), there is also a "reflection" (*cintā*) which has the nature of being an object, and that too is wisdom (*paññā*). Thus, that [is wisdom].
It is said, “The object... up to ... non-apprehension,” in order to turn [the mind] back. “Citta, mano, mānasa, viññāṇa”—all these are names for consciousness. The object is bound to its condition;
it is not bound to any other condition, nor is its name obtained through any other condition. This [term] indicates a distinct meaning consisting of the cognition of such an object.
The phrase beginning with “santesu ca” was stated to show that [the object] does not exist.

The phrase “etena” is stated to show that this expresses the instrument (*karaṇa*) as a means of accomplishing the action (*kiriyāsādhana*) which provides an excessive assistance to the agent (*kattū*). Regarding the term “cintanamattaṃ,” the word *matta* has the sense of excluding a qualification;
he shows the meaning excluded by it with the words beginning with “sabbepi hi. The analysis (*viggaha*)...
“Or” (*vā*) means the body. “Dependent on conditions” (*paccayāyattā*) means dependent upon conditions. “Dependent” (*āyattā*) means connected.

“Functioning” (*vatti*) means activity; it is either arising or persisting. Those whose functioning is dependent on conditions are “those whose functioning is dependent on conditions” (*paccayāyatta-vuttino*). “By power” (*thāmena*) and so forth are mutual synonyms.
“Only one [term] is obtained as a primary noun-derivative (*bhāvasādhana*)” refers to these phenomena (*dhammānaṃ*).
This was stated with reference to each respective state of mere activity (*kiriyā-mattabhāva*).
However, even though those phenomena consist of mere activity, they may abide in a basis produced by various conditions, or they may abide in a basis arisen from various conditions.

Therefore, even in the context of ultimate reality (*paramattha*), the acquisition of other means as appropriate is not precluded. Otherwise, [the distinction between] cause (*hetu*) and condition (*paccaya*)...

Regarding [the question] such as "How can the analysis of the abstract noun (bhāvasādhana) be appropriate in cases like 'object-condition' (ārammaṇa-paccaya), 'co-nascent condition' (sahajāta-paccaya), and 'support-condition' (nissaya-paccaya)?":
"From the primary standpoint" means from the perspective of the principal factor.

The phrase "making a distinction in that which is being considered without distinction" is stated with reference to the analysis of the agent (kattusādhana) in the sense of "that which thinks" (cinteti). "Of the stone-child" refers to the child of the grinding-stone used for medicinal roots.
There is no separate limb called "body" (sarīra). Even though it is not distinct [from the rock], it is spoken of by making a distinction, saying, "the body of a stone statue" (silāputtakasarīraṃ).

This is what is called "creating a distinction where there is no distinction," and it is an unreal form (abhūtarūpa). He said, "and acting in such a way," etc., to show that it may be spoken when there is a purpose, but it should not be spoken when there is none.
In that context, "of what is imagined by others" refers to those of other sects (aññatitthiya).

Regarding that which is thoroughly considered by means of modes of conduct: if one were to say, “Because of mindfulness... [and so on]... because of conceptualization,” and if there were a self (*ātman*), then it would have to be stated that “the self thinks;
therefore, the self is called consciousness (*citta*),” and so forth. However, it cannot be said that “consciousness is that which thinks,” because consciousness is merely an activity.
Furthermore, there is no such thing as an agent, such as a self. Therefore, taking the mere activity itself as the agent, it is said: “It thinks.”
It is said, "the mind. By this it is understood that in the world there is no such thing as a self or a single entity.
This is what is meant by the statement that the purpose of conceiving a distinction where there is no distinction is [to show this].

"Predominant with respect to a self" means being oneself the principal and oneself the chief among many factors of action (kārakas) in the accomplishment of an activity. "The state of being its agent" refers to the status of being an agent established in the world.
"Once again, the state of being a cause" means once again the state of being a cause established in the world.
Having thus shown the meaning of the word *citta*, he now says "Furthermore, in this context," etc., in order to show its referential meaning (*abhidhānattha*).

"Just as these animals that exist in the world are variegated (*citta*) and non-variegated (*avicitta*); so too, there is nothing else that is variegated (*citta*) and non-variegated (*vicitta*) that we do not perceive as belonging to another single class."
The construction [is as follows]: “*Nikāya*” means a collection of the classes of beings (*sattajātisamūha*).

“*Nissakke karaṇavacanan*” means that the instrumental case (*karaṇavacana*) is used in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*). By this, he states the meaning: “from that conduct, from that mind. In the verse, “that respective nature” refers to the nature consisting of cognizing, touching, and so forth, just as heat is the nature of fire. “The excellence of function” means by means of those respective phenomena.

The function of the instrument (*karaṇakicca*), the quality of excellence obtained after performing that function, and the quality of illumination—just as in the case of fire, there is the function of maturing its fuel and the quality of illumination.
"A form to be grasped" (*gayhākāra*) means a form serving as the banner of each respective phenomenon, which is to be apprehended by knowledge.
"Excellence" (*sampatti*) is said to be the very essence (*rasa*). "Or even the fruit" (*phalaṃ vāpi*) refers to the fruit of the effect, just like smoke is to fire.
“Proximate cause” (*āsannakāraṇa*) refers to the cause that produces its own fruit immediately following itself, like a person who makes a fire for a fire.
“Able” (*ala*) means capable. “Of one possessing awakened intelligence” (*vibuddhino*) refers to a wise person endowed with distinguished understanding.

“The function of being the precursor” (*pubbaṅgamarasa*) is the primary activity in the grasping of an object. “Manifestation as continuity” (*sandhānapaccupaṭṭhāna*) means manifestation in the mode of uninterrupted occurrence.
“Name-and-form as the proximate cause”: name, consisting of contact and so forth, and form, the physical basis, are the proximate cause for consciousness.
The commentary on consciousness is finished. 14.
“Existing in the mind” means manifested within the mind. “By this they are established” is the connection. “That...”
In this way, the birth of contact and the rest [should be applied]; that which is the aging of consciousness is itself the aging of contact and the rest—thus it should be joined.

“Tied together by a single stalk” means tied together by one stalk-staff. “Tied together by the discourse on a single birth, etc. means tied together by way of the discussion concerning a single birth.
“Ce” (and) is equivalent to “ceva” (and indeed). “Nā” (not) is not to be stated. In the verse.
“Phenomena” (dhammā) refers to the mental-data aggregate (nāmakkhandha). “By mind alone” means by the mind acting as the agent.
“Produced” (pakatā) means set in motion. “Fashioned” (nimmitā) means brought about.

“Being merely the activity of consciousness” means that consciousness, in cognizing an object, cognizes only after generating a mode of contact; that mode of contact is called “contact” (phassa). The remainder...
However, all mental concomitants (cetasika-dhammas) arise dependent upon contact (phassa).

It is said: "Contact is the cause, contact is the condition, for the arising of the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-khandha), the aggregate of perception (saññā-khandha), and the aggregate of formations (saṅkhāra-khandha).
Even so, because they are rooted in consciousness and dependent on consciousness, these three aggregates are indeed nothing other than the activity of consciousness itself.
“By this” means by this line of verse. In the *Vibhāvanī*, however, it is explained merely by the state of having a single object (*ekālambanatā*).
The intention is that the mental factors (*cetasikāṅga*) are complete because the Elder himself will explain them further on.

But here, since this is the section for explaining the meaning of the words (*padatthavibhāvana*), it is appropriate to explain them by means of all the factors in their completeness; therefore he said, “that is not good. “In the physical basis” (*vatthumhi*) means in the cloth, the wall, and so forth.
“Various mental activities” refers to the forms of elephants, horses, and so forth. Consciousness (*citta*) is merely that which cognizes;
it cannot be described as either wholesome or unwholesome. It is only because of its association with various mental factors (*cetasika*) that it can be so described.
For this was said by the Blessed One: “Bhikkhus, this mind is luminous, but it is defiled by adventitious defilements.”
Therefore he said, "Water, space, and consciousness," and so forth.
The commentary on the mental factors (cetasika) is finished.

Regarding the word "ruppati" (it is affected), it is established as a passive construction with the agent as the subject. To show that "being affected" (ruppana) is indeed the undergoing of change, [he says...]

“By cold, heat, and so forth,” etc., was said. Therein, “by way of uneven occurrence” means by way of the uneven occurrence of the elements; what is meant is “by way of the disturbance of the elements.

Regarding the phrase “by what is it afflicted?,” here the word “by what” (kena) should be understood as expressing either the sense of a cause (*hetu*), or the sense of an agent (*kartr*), or the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*).
The same applies to the cases of “by cold,” and so on. “Gnats and mosquitoes” refers to those with needle-like mouths.
Small flies and large flies; winds refers to east winds and so forth; heat refers to the heat of the sun;
reptiles refers to snakes, scorpions, centipedes, and so forth. It is affected even by contact with these.
It either undergoes death or experiences suffering equal to death. "Those phenomena" refers to the twelve kinds of material phenomena that possess resistance (*sappaṭigha-rūpa-dhammā*).
“Of others” means of the sixteen types of non-reactive (appaṭigha) material phenomena and of immaterial (arūpa) phenomena. “Among them” is the locative case used for selection (*niddhāraṇa*).
Now, correlating the primary meaning of “being struck” with the canonical text, he says: “And ‘coming together’,” etc. The connection is as follows:
“Coming together” is said to be mutual impact. And there is both “coming into range” and “making into an object.”
“Setting aside” is the construction [of the sentence]. “Or of the great elements themselves” means of the three great elements excluding the water element.
Having stated, “It undergoes a transformation,” he says “At whatever moment,” etc., in order to explain that very point.
“They themselves also reach a state of transformation” means that those three great elements themselves abandon their natural state and attain a condition of deficiency or excess.
The meaning [of the term *ruppa*] is as follows: “And of material continua that are weak or intense”—this was said with reference to material continua arising in succession.
Having thus explained, according to the method of the Pāḷi, deformation (*ruppana*) by way of misfortune (*vipatti*), it is now stated:

whether there be misfortune or prosperity, even a change (*vikāra*) consisting in a dissimilar occurrence of preceding and succeeding continua is, by one way of explanation, called deformation (*ruppana*).

Having stated this, he spoke the passage beginning with “Furthermore, here” (*apicettha*) in order to demonstrate that very same process of deformation (*ruppana*). The question, “Is it only by way of striking (*ghaṭṭana*) that material phenomena (*rūpa-dhamma*) are subject to deformation?

is asked because it is established that material phenomena possess the intrinsic nature of being deformed through striking alone—even in the absence of those phenomena subject to deformation [such as] by way of coming into contact (*āpāta*), etc.
“They are ‘with a grasp’ (*saviggaha*)” means they are accompanied by a mode of substance and shape (*saṇṭhāna-ākāra*).
Why? Because their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) is gross. This is because many material groups (*rūpa-kalāpa*) arise simultaneously as a single, unified mass.

Furthermore, immaterial phenomena (*arūpa-dhamma*) possess a subtle and refined nature; even if hundreds of thousands of them were to arise together, they would never assume a physical shape or form like a mountain.
Moreover, within the continuum (*santāna*) of a single being, only one material group can exist at any given moment.
It occurs. Why? Because it occurs by way of immediate condition (*anantara-paccaya*). Therefore, they possess a physical structure (*saviggaha*).
However, material phenomena (*rūpa-dhamma*) have a coarse nature; when there is an accumulation of many [atoms], they serve as the basis for the shape of the substance.
Furthermore, even many groups (*kalāpa*) occur at a single moment as if bound together. Therefore, they possess a physical structure.
“By the power of the terms ‘cold’ and so forth” means by the power of such terms as “it is affected by cold” and “it is affected by heat,” which are evident to the world through direct perception.

The intention is that this expression indicates that what is intended here is the “being affected” (ruppana) of non-material phenomena, which is not evident to the world. “A conventional term” means it is stated that it is a name or designation.
It exists. “By way of worldly convention” means by way of the practice, the usage, or the speech of the majority of people.
“Precisely by way of the manifest cause for the occurrence of sound” means precisely by way of the manifest cause for the arising of the word-sound.

By the word “also” (*pi*), he indicates that it is so even by the power of the inclusion of “cold,” etc. Even though this is so, it is not possible to establish the canonical text (*pāḷi*) in every instance.
It should be understood that the statement regarding the "manifest sign" (*pākaṭanimitta*) is common to all instances.

"The cessation of the suspicion regarding that" means the cessation of the suspicion that those immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhammā*) possess the nature of form (*rūpatā*). "Proceeding by way of the transformation of psychic power" (*iddhivikubbanāvasappavattā*):

here, "transformation of psychic power" (*iddhivikubbanā*) refers to the attainment of various modes through psychic power (*iddhi*). "The accomplishment of the state of form" (*rūpatā siddhī*): this is the accomplishment of the perception (*saññāsiddhi*) known as "form."
“But this,” he says, meaning “this material form. Regarding the phrase “by way of non-afflictive cold and so forth”:

although the mention of cold and so forth in the text was stated by way of afflictive cold and so forth—since those do not exist in the Brahma-world, and only non-afflictive [sensations] exist there—the intended meaning is “by way of those [latter].
“They are specified in the text”: “It is called ‘perception,’ monks; therefore...”
It is called "perception" (saññā). And what does it perceive? It perceives blue, it perceives yellow, and so forth—as stated in the Pāli:
"Monks, because it cognizes, therefore it is called 'consciousness' (viññāṇa). And what does it cognize?
It cognizes sweet, it cognizes sour, and so forth—as specified in the Canon.
The commentary on the word *rūpa* is finished.
16. On the word *nibbāna*: “*Khandhāvā*” means the aggregates (*khandha*) that will exist in another becoming within the realms of misery (*apāya*) and so forth.
For past phenomena do not “extinguish” (*nibbāyanti*), because they have already ceased after having oppressed sentient beings; this is the intended meaning. [As for] present [phenomena]...

Since present phenomena are currently afflicting [beings], and future phenomena that will inevitably arise will afflict them in the future, how can it be said that they "extinguish"? To this he replied: "Regarding present...
[there is] nothing at all to be said. "The locative of the object" (*visayebhumma*) means the locative based on the object.
A "primary locus" (*mukhyādhāra*) refers to cases such as "people go on the earth," where the earth is the primary support for the action.
It does not exist. Yet, without that [space], one is unable to perform that action elsewhere.
Therefore, it is said "as in space" and so forth, in order to show that space is conceptually designated as a support (*ādhāra*).
Just as the action of flying for birds cannot be accomplished elsewhere without space, so too is the action of extinguishing (*nibbāna*) the phenomena of the suffering of saṃsāra.
In order to show that [the cessation of suffering] cannot be established elsewhere apart from *nibbāna*, he said, “*Yehi te*,” and so forth.

Therein, “*ye*” refers to those phenomena characterized by the burning heat of the twenty-one-fold suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*). “*hi*” is a particle used for emphasis. The word “*te*” is a rhetorical ornament. “*Tabbinimuttam*” means separated from *nibbāna*.
There is no place called a “site of extinction. Therefore, the intention is that *nibbāna* serves as the objective domain and the support for their act of extinguishing.
Just as this lamp goes out, so too do the wise go out—this is the construction [of the verse]. “Of those various defilements” means of those existing defilements.
“Or of the aggregates” means of the aggregates in future existences.

“The state of being without further rebirth-linking” means that noble persons reach the state where there is no further linking of the continuum. Just as the word for the instrument (*karaṇavacana*) is used in the case of the Path.
[The instrumental case] is seen in such instances as, "Surely by this practice I shall be liberated from aging and death," and so forth.
It is not so [used] regarding *nibbāna*; thus he said, "as in the case of the path," and so on.

Regarding *nibbāna*, only the locative expression is seen, as in "where name-and-form ceases without remainder," and so forth. Therefore, the instrumental expression is not seen for *nibbāna*, because it possesses only the characteristic of an instrument (*karaṇa-lakkhaṇa*).
In order to show that it is not [a cause] by way of non-existence (*abhāva*), it was said: "And not Nibbāna," and so forth. An instrument (*karaṇa*) is a characteristic mark;

it is the state of being a cooperative condition for the agent (*kattū*) and the action (*nāma*). [Objection: Is it not seen that they "attain Nibbāna" (*nibbāyanti*) in the element of Nibbāna without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu*)?

[Reply: True; however, in that context, the mention of the instrument is for the sake of specification (*visesana*). It is not [used] in the sense of the instrumental case-factor (*karaṇa-kāraka*). For that [mention] was stated for the purpose of excluding [the attainment of Nibbāna] from the element of Nibbāna with residue (*saupādisesa-nibbānadhātu*).
Commentary on the State of Nibbāna.
The commentary on the second verse is finished. 18.
Regarding the term *kāmāvacara*: "It is desired" (*kāmīyati*) means it is wished for. [The basis for the gratification of signs] is explained in the *Majjhima-aṭṭhakathā*.
“Has arrived. “*Tekāmīyantī*”: those [realms] such as the Avīci hell are desired. “*Tattha uppannānampi*”: even for those beings who have arisen there in the Avīci hell and so forth.

“*Bhavanikanti nāma hotī*”: craving that grasps at one’s own aggregates—designated as ‘existence’—thinking, “This is mine,” “I am this,” or “This is my self,” is called *bhavanikanti*. That [craving] exists even for beings in the hells.
It certainly exists. “It moves within the sense-sphere (kāma)” means it is included within the sense-sphere; it is contained within the sense-sphere.
Even that which has arisen in the realms of form and formlessness does not enter into the reckoning of form or formlessness; it enters only into the reckoning of the sense-sphere.

The meaning is that it enters into the enumeration of the sense-sphere. “Even those arisen among the three types of beings” means even those arisen in the mental continuums of beings in the sense-sphere, form-sphere, and formless-sphere do not [enter] into the reckoning therein.
They are indeed *apariyāpanna* (unincluded). The intended meaning here is that they are exclusively *apariyāpanna*. Regarding the phrase "the fault of falling into the state of being *kāmāvacara*":
it is the fault of falling into the state of having to be called "states belonging to the sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacara-dhamma*).

Regarding the phrase "the fault of falling into [being] exempt from the state of being *rūpāvacara*, etc.": it is the fault of falling into the state of having to be called "these are not states belonging to the fine-material sphere, not states belonging to the immaterial sphere, and not supramundane states."

"What is stated" means "it is called a fault. This same method applies to the phrases: "The attainment of the fine-material and immaterial realms is a fault; the emergence from the sense-sphere realm is a fault.

Even if the word *avacara* is taken in the sense of "arisen," these faults do not follow. Why? Because the methods of "generality" (*yebhūyya*), "statement," and "abundance" (*tabbahula*) also exist in the world.
Stating this point, he said: "Is it not also by way of what is stated as general? and so forth. In that context, "of some" (*kesañci*)...
It refers to certain individuals or phenomena. Just as a deer-hunter is called a "forest-dweller" because he frequents the forest even though he wanders about in the village;

or as a royal elephant is called a "war-elephant" because it frequents battlefields even though it wanders elsewhere—this is what is called the method of majority (yebhūyyanaya). It is like a forest where mango trees also exist.

There are other trees as well; however, because of the abundance of mango trees (*amba-rukkha*), that forest receives the name "Mango Grove" (*ambavana*). The same applies to the *simbali* grove and others.

This is the method based on predominance (*tabbahulanaya*). But here, the planes receive the names "Sense-sphere," "Fine-material," and "Immaterial" by way of predominance, whereas phenomena receive the names "belonging to the sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacara*) and so forth by way of the majority (*yebhūyyanaya*). When it is understood in this way...
In order to show the meaning that "when there is [craving], those faults follow," he said: "Therefore, here too... [there is] fault. "No" means that there is no fault whatsoever;
the intention is that it certainly exists. Regarding "tasmāssā," the word *assā* refers to the term *avacara*.
"Without grasping the meaning as such" means without grasping the sense of its arising. "Produced by the craving for sensual pleasure (*kāmataṇhā*) which is possessive" [is the meaning].

Likewise, how can there be a "sphere" (*gocara*) for craving (*taṇhā*) that is not within the range of possessive craving for sensual pleasures? That which one desires by means of this is "sensual pleasure" (*kāma*);

thus it is craving for sensual pleasure (*kāmataṇhā*). That wherein one moves about is a "sphere" (*avacara*). That which moves within the sphere of sensual pleasure is "belonging to the sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacara*).
Furthermore, the meaning is also established as "belonging to the sense-sphere" because it is the range and object of craving for sensual pleasure.
It ranges in the realm of form, thus it is "form-sphere" (*rūpāvacara*). "In form" refers to the sixteenfold plane of form.

"Ranges" means it occurs there by way of being included within that [plane]. It ranges in the formless, thus it is "formless-sphere" (*arūpāvacara*). "In the formless" refers to the fourfold plane of the formless.
"Ranges" means it occurs there by way of being included within that; this is the meaning he expresses.
"This same method should be applied to the fine-material and immaterial spheres as well. Existence in the fine-material realm is "form" (rūpa); craving for form is "craving for form.

Existence in the immaterial realm is "the immaterial" (arūpa); craving for the immaterial is "craving for the immaterial. The sphere of form is the "fine-material sphere" (rūpāvacara); the sphere of the immaterial is the "immaterial sphere" (arūpāvacara).
He clarifies this meaning with the words beginning "But among those... "In this place" means in this context. Even though it is greed, passion...

“Kāma,” “taṇhā,” and “all this” are synonyms for greed (*lobha*). However, because “lust for the fine-material realm” (*rūparāga*) and “lust for the immaterial realm” (*arūparāga*) are analyzed separately, here the word “kāma” includes that other kind of greed.
By the phrase “all greed whatsoever,” it should be understood that even the views associated with eternalism and annihilationism are included.
19. “Form and formless sounds are established in those planes”—the intended meaning is that they are established as being signless (*animitta*).

Now, he explains the method with signs (*sanimitta*) by means of the phrase beginning with “Furthermore. “Metaphorical application based on support” (*nissayopacāra*) refers to metaphorical application based on location (*ṭhānūpacāra*), such as when one says, “The whole village has arrived.

“Metaphorical application dependent [on something else]” (*nissito pacāro*) refers to metaphorical application based on the object (*ṭhānyūpacāra*), such as when one says, “The banners are arriving. “Whatever in this... [and so forth].

“In the interval” means those aggregates, elements, and bases that exist within this interval. The construction is: “whatever form, whatever feeling, whatever perception, whatever formations, whatever consciousness.
“Well-purified” means thoroughly cleansed because of its lack of confusion through methods such as the *yebhuyya* (majority) approach.
“What is the use of distraction? means: what purpose is served by mental distraction?
20. “In the sense of crumbling and disintegrating”: in the sense of breaking and falling apart. “Wherein”: in that collection of phenomena belonging to the three planes.
“It settles”: it constantly dwells upon or approaches.
“Of that”: of that wrong grasp. “Of those”: of supramundane phenomena (*lokuttara-dhamma*). “Of which”: of mundane phenomena (*lokiya-dhamma*). “Crumbling”: by way of momentary dissolution.
“Breaking up” (*bhijjana*) means breaking apart in various ways through the dissolution of shape and the severance of the continuity [of the aggregates].
However, the intention here is that *nibbāna* is not included, because this context concerns the collection of states of consciousness.
And that state of being "unincluded" (*apariyāpanna*) is a distinct fourth stage; thus, the construction is: “[these] are the names for the stages (*bhūmi*).”
The commentary on the analysis of the four planes is finished.
21. “Inferior” (*hīna*) means inferior because it is not endowed with the qualities that beautify, such as faith, mindfulness, and so forth.

“Entirely inferior” (*sabbahīna*) means more inferior than all other types of consciousness because it is associated with evil states such as greed and the like. “For the sake of that” (*tadattha*) means for the purpose of making the subsequent types of consciousness easy to recognize as beautiful.

Regarding the phrase beginning with “From the outset”: “By way of process-consciousness” means by way of the impulsion-process consciousness that occurs as the craving for existence (*bhavanikanti*), thinking, “This is mine, this I am, this is my self.
Since this is the case, one asks, “What is the reason for mentioning the greed-rooted consciousness first?
and thus says, “But among the unwholesome [states],” and so forth. “By two roots of the round” means by the two roots of the round known as greed and delusion.
22. “*Siniddhacittam*” (affectionate mind): the intention is that it is not a coarse mind because it is associated with pleasant feeling (*sātavedanā*).

When “the state of being well-minded” (*sumanassabhāva*) is mentioned, there might be the implication that this includes even bodily pleasant feeling; therefore, it is said: “mental... [etc.]... called. “*Sumanābhidhānassā*” means “of that which is named *sumana*.
“*Pavattinimittan*” means the immediate cause for its occurrence. But how is a state (*bhāva*) the cause for occurrence?

He said, "It does not exist... [omission] ...having done," thus: the locative case is used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta*). For it has been stated that "existence" (*bhāva*) is indeed the cause for the occurrence of a word.
Now, showing the characteristic mark (*lakkhaṇa*) as a cause, he said "just as it is said," and so forth. "In that case" (*tattha*) means in that particular application.
"The cause of the teeth" (*dantanimittaṃ*) means for the sake of the teeth. "That cause of feeling" (*taṃ vedanānimittaṃ*) means for the sake of that feeling. Here, it might be asked:

Regarding the statement, “In this [expression] ‘etasmim’ (in this), it is the locative case,” one might ask: since a *nimitta* (sign/cause) is by definition non-agential (*akāraka*) and non-instrumental (*asādhana*), how can it be logically consistent with an analysis based on the instrumental case (*sādhanaviggaha*)?
It should be understood that the cause for the occurrence of a word is in accordance with the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) as its instrument.

Furthermore, they say that both forms—“etena” (by this) and “etasmā” (from this)—are used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*). This is because the nature of the signified cause is proximate to the form of the instrumental case.
Such is their intended meaning (*adhippāya*). It performs well; it brings about, by its own power, an action not yet accomplished through a primary suffix (*pakatipaccaya*), thus it is a *saṅkhāra*.
"Prior formation" (*pubbābhisaṅkhāra*) means a formation in the prior stage. It instigates, it directs, thus it is an *payoga*.
That by which a goal consisting of a fruit is approached is an *upāya*. "Or by command" (*āṇattiya vā*) means by sending forth.

“By entreaty” means by means of a request. “Or by threatening” means by showing [them] fear. “Others explain various means”—to the question of how they explain them, he says “in not doing,” and so forth.

The construction is: “Because it is applied to this or that action, it is here called ‘volitional formation’ (saṅkhāra). “The group of suffixes” refers to the group of primary suffixes. “By that” means by that volitional formation.
“Common” means common to the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate [states]. “By means of two kinds of formations” means by way of application (*payoga*) or by way of method (*upāya*).
With the words “But he who is accompanied by that,” etc., the meaning already stated previously is made clear through another mode of explanation by saying “When he,” etc.
“Thus,” etc., is a statement regarding the qualities acquired. “The name for the cultivation of the collection of conditions.”
What is meant is that it is specifically the group of conditions (*paccayagaṇa*) itself that is being named. To explain how the suffix *-ika* is understood in the sense of "having arisen," he says:
"At whatever time," and so forth. "In the Pāḷi" refers to the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī-pāḷi*. "Without having observed" means "without having reflected.
All of this is indeed appropriate. Why? Because it does not conflict with the Pāḷi and its commentaries, and because it accords with both the logic of the meaning and the logic of the phrasing.
“Given by one who is not wise” is the intended meaning. “That” refers to the mind. “By this” means by the prior application.
“In the manner already stated” means by way of the specific excellence of adornment characterized by sharpness.
“But that” refers to the prior application. “Thus” means therefore. “Produced by that” means produced by that prior application. “Having missed” means having fallen into an improper course.
The connection is: "she is one who has rejected food. In the verse, "born from the mind" (*cittasambhavī*) means arisen within the mind.
The construction is: "a specific formation is called [volition]. It was stated that this applies to such cases as "with hair" (*salomako*) and "with wings" (*sapakkhako*).

However, it would be more appropriate when stated in such contexts as "dhammas subject to taints" (*sāsavā dhammā*) or "dhammas with an object" (*sārammaṇā dhammā*). The phrase "established by the Pāḷi and the Commentary" means from the Pāḷi and the Commentary.
It is established. Furthermore, in such works as the *Visuddhimagga*, the terms "unprompted consciousness" (*asaṅkhāra-citta*) and "prompted consciousness" (*sasaṅkhāra-citta*) appear.
Therein, this latter method is appropriate. Because many hundreds of [variations] arise from that which is produced by means, it is said: "And this is merely a demonstration of the method.
"By way of equanimity" (*udāsinabhāvena*) means by way of neutrality (*majjhattabhāvena*). "Since" (*yato*) means because. It reaches a state of change (*vikāra*). Therefore...
The construction is: “excessive contemplation is discerned.
Now, while examining the terms *sahagata* (accompanied) and *sampayutta* (associated), he began with the words “And here,” etc.
Why was it said, “But they do not possess differentiation”? Is it not the case that those too are eye-contact, ear-contact, and so forth?

And because [of the phrases] beginning with "sensual thought" (*kāmavitakka*), "thought of ill-will" (*byāpādavitakka*), and so forth, as well as "ignorance regarding suffering" (*dukkhe aññāṇa*), "ignorance regarding the origin of suffering" (*dukkhasamudaye aññāṇa*), and so forth, they possess divisions.
This is true. However, those divisions do not make this consciousness divided.
Therefore, it is said that they "possess divisions. And yet, this conceptual differentiation does not exist within them.
The connection [is as follows]: “In this consciousness” means in a consciousness rooted in greed (*lobhamūlacitta*). “In some” means in any consciousness whatsoever.
When “inclusionary terms” (*yevāpanaka*) are mentioned, it refers to those inclusionary terms that have been handed down in the *Sudhamma* [recension].

“By others” means by those rooted in hatred (*dosamūla*) and delusion (*mohamūla*). The connection is: “Are these not also to be included here? “No” means they are not to be included. Why? He says: “Because of them,” and so forth. Those too...

Here, they may be included; yet it is not that they should not be included. Why? Because feeling itself possesses the quality of being subject to dissolution (*bhedavanta*), and because of the presence of conceptualization (*vikappa*) within the formations of views (*diṭṭhi-saṅkhāra*);
this is the intended meaning. 24. "The cause of joy" means the cause for the arising of joy. When the cause for the arising of joy has been stated...
Since it is established that the cause for the arising of the consciousness associated with that [feeling] is also present, it should be understood that this very [cause] has been stated.
Therefore, he said: “One who has a rebirth-linking with joy,” and so forth. Or rather, it should be stated: “The conjunction with an inferior... object;
and the consciousness of one thus conjoined arises,” and so on. The same applies to the *Byasanamutti* (Section on Adversity). Regarding the causes of equanimity (*upekkhā*):

“Deliverance from calamity” (*byasanamuttī*) is a statement regarding the avoidance of attachment to mental distress (*domanassa*). “Inclination” (*ajjhāsaya*) refers to a dwelling (*geha*) that has been occupied;
one whose inclination consists of views is called “one with a view-inclination” (*diṭṭhajjhāsayo*). The state of being such is “the condition of having a view-inclination” (*diṭṭhajjhāsayatā*).

“Emerging in a base manner” (*ayoniso ummujjana*) means directing oneself or attending [to objects] by way of what is not a proper method (*anupāya*). “By way of being intent on reflection” (*cintā pasutavasena*)—
