Regarding profound teachings, it is by way of the flow of reflection (*cintā*) and by way of the increase of investigation (*vīmaṃsā*).
“Only the semblance of what has been seen” means that which is merely a counterfeit of what has been seen as a reason. Therefore he said: “Emerging from [the perspective of] essence and truth.

“By the opposite of that” means by that which is contrary to it. These are: having an inclination toward what has not yet been seen, avoiding persons whose views are corrupted, and hearing the true Dhamma.
It should be stated that an abundance of right thought (*sammā-vitakka*) and wise emergence (*yoniso ummujjana*) are the causes for dissociation from wrong view (*diṭṭhi-vippayoga*).

Furthermore, regarding the statement, "The method for the arising of these consciousnesses should be understood from the *Visuddhimagga*," it should be taken from the Exposition of the Aggregates (*khandha-niddesa*) in the *Visuddhimagga*.
For it is said therein: "When, by way of such a method as 'the danger in inferior things and sensual pleasures,' one [sees] wrong view..."

Having placed [wrong view] foremost, he either enjoys sensual pleasures with a mind that is joyful and satisfied, or he regards [erroneous things such as] "seeing good omens" (*diṭṭha-maṅgala*) and so forth as essential, with a mind that is by nature sharp and incited. At that time, the first unwholesome consciousness arises.
When it is with a mind that is dull and incited, then the second [unwholesome consciousness arises]. When, without placing wrong view foremost, [he acts] merely...

When one, elated and joyful, engages in sexual intercourse, covets the prosperity of others, or steals another’s property with a mind that is naturally sharp and uninstigated [by external factors], then it is the third [unwholesome root].
When it occurs with a dull mind that has been instigated [by external factors], then it is the fourth.
However, when it arises due to the non-attainment of sensual pleasures or other causes for joy...
In the absence [of joy], they are devoid of mental joy (*somanassa*) in all four alternatives; at that time, the remaining four arise accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā*).
The commentary on the mind-sets rooted in greed (*lobhamūlacitta*) is finished.

25. Regarding the mind-sets rooted in hatred (*dosamūlacitta*): "Ugly" (*virūpa*) means corrupted or cruel. When it is said, "the state of one who is dejected," this refers even to bodily painful feeling (*kāyikadukkhavedanā*).
"It may be a consequence" is what was stated as "mental... [etc.]... called. It strikes back; it afflicts. "Heated" means made to burn.
(26) "Causing division" means causing mutual distinction. "They are causes of division for this mind" means they are factors that produce mutual distinctions in this consciousness.

The inclusion of "mental distress" (*domanassa*) is understood as being taken for the purpose of excluding other possible consequences. "Consequence" (*pasaṅga*) refers to the various different types.

“Attachment to good people. To explain how this constitutes a connection (*pasaṅga*), he says, “When [one says],” and so forth. “Proclaiming their satisfaction” means they speak of the nature of their satisfaction, such as, “By their death,” and so on.

Having thus dispelled the connection associated with co-existence (*sahagata-pasaṅga*), he says, “The mention of aversion (*paṭighaggahaṇa*) also,” and so forth, in order to dispel the connection with association (*sampayutta-pasaṅga*).
In the killing of animal life, there is indeed demerit (*apuñña*).

There is none. The intention is that [the world] was created by the Lord of the World, who abides as the sovereign of the world, for the sake of human beings enjoying it according to their desire from the beginning of the eon.
"Relaxed" (*vissaṭṭhā*) means free from apprehension. "Or others" (*aññeva*) means other people. "Doubt" (*vimati*) itself is "doubtful" (*vematikaṃ*).
Those in whom doubt has arisen are "those who have become doubtful" (*vematikajātā*). The state of being accompanied by greed in the preceding consciousness—
The construction is as follows: "These eight [types of] consciousness are accompanied by greed" is established by this very minor conclusion (*cūḷanigamana*).

Since the state of being associated with aversion (*paṭighasampayutta*) is established by the minor conclusion, the state of being accompanied by mental displeasure (*domanassasahagata*) is also thereby established;
taking this into account, it is said, "the inclusion of those. "Of those" refers to the two types of consciousness not associated with aversion. In this consciousness...
Envy, stinginess, worry, restlessness, and torpor are indeed factors associated with the indeterminate (aniyata) and are also classed as "occasional" (yevāpanaka).
Therefore, he said, "In the preceding consciousness," and so forth. Mental grief (domanassa) exists in this consciousness but not in other types of consciousness;
therefore, it is called an "unshared" (asādhāraṇa) factor. It is also called an "exclusive" (anaññasādhāraṇa) factor. The phrase "as is the case" (yathātaṃ) serves as an illustration.
An example of that is as follows: the meaning of *katamaṃ* is "which one? "He characterizes" (*upalakkheti*) means he makes known.
"It protects against the heat" (*ātapaṃ tāyati rakkhati*) is *ātapattaṃ*; it is a white parasol (*setacchattaṃ*). One by whom the white parasol has been obtained is *laddhātapatto*, a prince.
When it is said that he has obtained the white parasol, it is understood that he has obtained all the royal prosperity. Therefore, this is a figurative expression (*upalakkhaṇavacanaṃ*).
It should be understood as "arisen. "Of both" refers to the two: mental grief (*domanassa*) and aversion (*paṭigha*).
Since it was previously stated that [the mind] is accompanied by mental grief, and at the conclusion it is stated that they are "states of consciousness associated with aversion," it is said:
"Because of the establishment of this... [and so on]. 27. "By undesirable worldly conditions" means by the four undesirable worldly conditions: loss, disrepute, blame, and suffering.
“*Taṃ kutettha labbhā*”: even for one who aspires, thinking, “May I not encounter non-gain and so forth for a month,” the meaning is:
“How can this aspiration be fulfilled here in this world at all times? Furthermore, the word *labbhā* is a primary form (*pāṭipadika*) indicating the object of the action.

The manner of their arising has been stated in brief in the *Visuddhimagga*; it should be understood that they occur during the periods when the [perception] functions either sharply or sluggishly with respect to killing living beings and so forth.
The commentary on the states of consciousness rooted in hatred is finished.
28. Regarding the states of consciousness rooted in delusion: “By being devoid of another root” means by being devoid of any other root.

“Crawls about” (*saṃsappati*) means crawling about. “‘Is it thus? or ‘Is it otherwise? means that it wavers and trembles in these two ways; this is the meaning. “Is distracted” (*vikkhipati*) means being distracted.
“‘For the purpose of restriction’ means that this is designated as associated with doubt; it is for the sake of restricting [the classification].

For this is not established by a concluding summary in the same way as that which is associated with aversion (paṭigha). ‘Having found its place here’ means having found its place here precisely because of the absence of any other root.
‘Intrinsic nature’ means being of the essential character (sabhāva); thus, the construction is: ‘therefore, it does not exist. ‘Without receding’...”
"Not turning back" means not retreating from behind. "Not sinking" means not falling downward; by both [terms], it is said that there is no interruption.
"Due to extreme delusion" means due to delusion that is utterly bewildered because it lacks any other root.
"Due to extreme restlessness" means due to extreme restlessness caused by creeping, wavering, doubt, and agitation. "In all respects" means in all cases whatsoever.
Regarding objects: in the Commentary, ignorance is stated to be twofold by way of its division into formations (*saṅkhāra*).
How is it so stated? Ignorance is twofold as non-practice and wrong practice; likewise, it is stated to be "with formations" and "without formations.
Or, it is "threefold": in this context, there is a threefold state including ignorance that is free from mental formations (*cittasaṅkhāra*).

The manner of the arising of these two types of consciousness has been stated briefly in the *Visuddhimagga*; it should be understood that their occurrence takes place at times when there is neither finality nor distraction.
29. Whether the phrase “sabbathāpi” (in every way) is a collection of particles, or a synonym for one another, or a separate particle—it means “in all such modes.
In the word *akusala*, the letter *a* has the sense of opposition (*viruddhattha*), as in the examples *amitta* (non-friend), *asura* (non-god), and *atithi* (non-guest); this is to show that.

He said, “unwholesome,” and so forth. “The state of being opposed” means the state of being opposed to unwholesome states such as delusion (*moha*). “Not worthy of cultivation” means those that do not deserve to be cultivated.
But how are they not worthy of cultivation? He said, “again and again,” and so forth.

“Even those entering the fixed course” refers even to those entering the fixed course by way of the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantariya-kamma*) and by way of fixed wrong view (*niyatamicchādiṭṭhi*).

"Partakers of the states of loss" (apāyabhāgin) means those who resort to the states of misery (apāya). "Kamma-makers": their state; by that [state]. "Fixed in the stream of the round" (vaṭṭasotaniyata):
fixed within the stream of the cycle of existence (saṃsāra). "Attained a more stable state" (thiratarapatta): attained a state of greater stability by way of concentration (samādhi).
Now, in order to clarify this same meaning by another method, he said "Moreover" (apica), and so forth. The word "might be" (siyuṃ) [is formed] from verbal roots and suffixes.
A *siddha* word is not called a "completed word" (*nipphannapada*). Why? Because here, the meaning of a derivative formation (*parikappa*) is impossible.

It is a particle-word (*nipātapada*). Why? Because the occurrence of multiple meanings is possible. However, in this context, it has the same meaning as the word *bhavanti*. Therefore he said: "In this case, it should be understood as a particle-word."

Commentary on the Unwholesome (Akusalavaṇṇanā). 30. Regarding the rootless consciousnesses (*ahetukacitta*): “The most base of all” means it is inferior to all [other] consciousnesses. Again, “the most base of all” means it is inferior to all rootless [consciousnesses]. “That” refers to the unwholesome resultant (*akusalavipāka*).
31. In the Sutta Canon, “a log” (*kaṭṭha*) means dry wood; “a splinter” (*sakalika*) means a small piece of wood that has been cut and split.
“Thus” means rice-tax. “Refuse” means rubbish. It should be applied in this way:
“That consciousness which arises dependent on the eye and forms is called eye-consciousness,” and so forth. In that context, “forms” refers to objects consisting of form.
The same method applies to “sounds” and the rest. Furthermore, in this case, the consciousnesses are supported by a single physical basis; therefore, [the term] “basis”...
The singular number is used for the doors. However, many objects are grasped by even a single consciousness;
therefore, the plural number is used for the objects. "Dukkhayati" means it causes suffering (*dukkha*); this is a nominal root (*nāmadhātu*). As those learned in grammar say, for example:

"He pleases himself" (*sukheti*) or "he plays the lute" (*vīṇeti*). In the lists of verbal roots (*dhātupāṭha*), however, it is stated that [the root *dukkh*] is used in the sense of the act of making happy or causing suffering.
“Takkiriyā” means the performance of pleasure and the performance of pain; it is said to be the performance of satisfaction and the performance of gratification.
Taking the word “ca” (and) in the sense of “opportunity,” it is said: “the granting of an opportunity is difficult. 32.
“The non-disruption of the eye” means the non-separation of the material form that is the clarity of the eye. For when that [clarity] is disrupted—
"Forms do not appear to one who is blind. This same method applies to the phrases "the non-deficiency of the ear," and so forth.
Regarding "the acquisition of dependence upon light": the eye performs its function when there is light; it does not exist [in that sense] when there is none. The same holds true for visible form.
Therefore, light is the dependence for their entering into the relationship of object and subject. Of that dependence upon light...
This is the method for [understanding] those things based on space and so forth. The exposition of the logical connection between these factors will appear later in the *Rūpasamāsa*.
Regarding the phrase "in the Commentary," it refers to the *Aṭṭhasālinī*.
Therein, not accepting the statement, "But even when that [object] comes into range, if there is no basis in light, eye-consciousness does not arise," [the author] says: "Without that..."
He said, "By light," and so forth. "Primarily the vision of non-existence" means that which has the vision of non-existence as its predominant factor.
33. Regarding the meaning of the term *vipāka* (ripening): it is called *vipāka* because it ripens (*vipaccati*). And "it ripens" means it reaches the state of having ripened.
What is meant is that the karma performed in the past now attains its manifestation. Now, this meaning is made clear:
While doing so, he said, "And this is the meaning," and so forth. In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, possession (*samaṅgitā*) through the accumulation of karma (*āyūhana*) is also mentioned.
However, here, since volition (*cetanā*) is included within possession, it is stated as "the four kinds of possession.

Possession (*samaṅgitā*) means being endowed with. "At the time of accumulating such and such karma" refers to [karma] such as killing living beings and so forth, and the abstention from that, and so forth.
"At the time of the accumulation of each respective action of misconduct or good conduct" means at the time of its selection (*samuccayana*).
"Having reached total non-existence, it ceases": the intention is that it does not cease in the same manner as indeterminate (*abyākata*) phenomena, which cease having reached total non-existence;
rather, it does not cease in that way. "Complete in all aspects" refers to [the perfection of] killing living beings.

While performing [the action], many bodily, verbal, and mental transformations corresponding to that karma become manifest. This same method applies to the taking of what is not given (*adinnādāna*) and so forth.
It is "complete" through all such modes and transformations. "Having deposited" (*nidahitvā*) means having established.
"With reference to which" (*yaṃsandhāya*) means with reference to that specific qualification of the action which constitutes the depositing.

In this verse: “*Sajjū*,” on this very day; “*khīraṃ vamuccatī*,” just as milk is called that which is released on this very day—it abandons its original nature and undergoes transformation—so too is the application: “the evil deed committed does not [disappear] in such a way.
But how does it come to be? He says: “it follows the fool while burning,” like “a fire covered by ashes.”
“Like a fire covered by ashes. As for the phrase “but that,” it refers to a specific kind of activity (*kriyā-viśeṣa*).

The statement “it does not even attain the status of a separate ultimate phenomenon (*paramattha-dhamma*)” means that it does not attain the status of being reckoned as a separate associated phenomenon (*sampayutta-dhamma*); this is the intended meaning.

For it should not be said that it is not an ultimate phenomenon because it is a phenomenon conditioned by karma (*kammapaccaya*). Therefore he says: “the latent dispositions (*anusaya*) and the elements (*dhātu*).”
“Viya” means “like. “So” refers to a specific action. “Taṃ” refers to either the kamma, the sign of the kamma, or the sign of the destination.
“Then it finds an opportunity” means it finds an opportunity for the purpose of ripening. The intended meaning is that having found the opportunity, it manifests.
“Therein” means among those states of being endowed with the faculties. “Iti” is a term denoting a quality already obtained. And “evaṃ”...
The phrase beginning with “having made” is a restatement of the qualities already obtained. “In the Pāḷi” means in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* Pāḷi.

“From the continuity of kamma” refers specifically to the immaterial (arūpa) continuity. “But those who” refers to the authors of the treatises (*ganthakārā*). “Of them” refers to the authors of the treatises. It should be connected as “he incurs [the fault].
Alternatively, it should be construed as “or the doctrine of them. The construction is: “and they show a simile for that.”
“In that” means in that statement. The construction is: “and they do not obtain it. “Then” means at that time of ripening.
“Stalk” means the stem of the flowers and fruits. 34.
“Origin” (sambhava) means the cause of occurrence. “Sorcery” (abhicāra) means movement or activity characterized by distinction. Distinction...
*Vutti*. *Abhicāro* means deviation (*byabhicāro*). It is common occurrence (*sāmañña-vutti*). What is meant is that it is shared with another alternative position.
"Shared with another alternative position" means that it is merely attached to, or merely connected with, the various modes of that other position;

this is what is meant by the term "deviation" (*byabhicāra*), which refers to the contingency (*pasaṅga*). By the words "herein" (*ettha ca*) and so forth, [the author] addresses the possibilities and deviations.
He speaks of non-existence alone. And the connection is that there is no arising with a cause by way of unwholesome causes.
“Of those” refers to the unwholesome results. “Invariably indeed” means precisely without deviation. 35.

“Arising in the five doors” is said because it arises in dependence upon the transformation of the five doors. Therefore he says, “For that,” and so forth. This same method applies to mind-door adverting as well.
For if this meaning were so, then—this being the case—the following consequence would follow; such is the connection. “Of those” refers to the process-consciousnesses (*vīthicitta*).
Since the word *uppāda* (arising) is necessarily masculine, it is said: “But in the commentaries... [it is] indicated.

“By the method stated” means by the method stated as “due to the absence of associated causes. The function of ripening (*vipaccanakicca*) is the function of the resultant states (*vipāka*). It is the function of producing the result.

This is the function of the wholesome and unwholesome [states]. As for the phrase "consisting merely of various functional (kiriyā) states," the adverting consciousness consists merely of the functional state of adverting, and the laughing consciousness consists merely of the functional state of laughter.
The rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death-consciousnesses have weak functions because they are merely fallen into the continuum by being projected solely by the force of kamma.
And the five sense-cognitions depend upon the sensitive bases, which are insubstantial and powerless.
Because they have arisen, their bases are weak. Furthermore, the functions of receiving and so forth are weak because they merely follow upon the fivefold sense-consciousnesses.
Therefore, all of them proceed by the mere process of ripening alone, without any exertion of their own.

"From the stream of resultant [consciousness]" refers to the five-door adverting consciousness and the mind-door adverting consciousness, which arise from the stream of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) resultant.

It has obtained its conditions. The determining consciousness (*voṭṭhabbana*) and the fivefold sense-consciousnesses have obtained their conditions from the stream of resultant states (*vipākasantāna*).

"But the others" refers to the consciousnesses that arouse laughter, the great functional consciousnesses (*mahākiriyacitta*), and so forth. "In a stream devoid of underlying tendencies" means in the stream of one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), which is free from underlying tendencies (*anusaya*).
"They are indeed devoid of effort" is like how there are such things as wind-blossoms on trees.

Because they lack the moisture that produces fruit, they do not produce fruit. Likewise, because they lack the moisture of craving that produces a result, they are indeed devoid of effort and activity. 36.
In this investigation of feeling: “Like two balls of cotton wool” refers to the mutual friction of two balls of cotton wool.
The construction is as follows: the mutual impact of the derived material phenomena (*upādārūpa*) is likewise weak.

"Of those which have become objects" refers to the three great primary elements (*mahābhūta*). "In those which are the support of the body" refers to the great primary elements that serve as the support for the body. "By them" refers to the fivefold sense-consciousnesses (*pañcaviññāṇa*).

"By the preceding mind" refers to the mind of reception (*sampaṭicchana-citta*). "That" refers to the unwholesome-resultant investigating consciousness (*akusala-vipāka-santīraṇa*). [This occurs] through repulsion (*paṭigha*).
It does not proceed without [them]. To the question "Why does it not proceed?", he says: "Because it is exclusively unwholesome," and so forth.
"Because of its impossibility among the indeterminate" means because it is impossible for it to be applicable within indeterminate (abyākata) states of consciousness.

And having been released from the influence of karma, the continuity of fruition (vipākasantāna) proceeds by the power of karma just as before. The intended meaning is that it does not proceed in such a manner [as it did previously].

“By some” means by some state of consciousness (*citta*). “By way of turning back toward a dissimilar stream of consciousness” means by way of turning back toward a subsequent stream of impulsion consciousness (*javana-citta*)—such as wholesome and so forth—that is dissimilar to the preceding stream of resultant consciousness (*vipāka-citta*).

For thus these two types of consciousness are defined in the Canon as “turning back” (*āvaṭṭanā*), “following after turning back” (*anvāvaṭṭanā*), “mental advertence” (*ābhoga*), and “attention” (*samannāhāra*).
“In all cases” means both in the case of a desirable object and an undesirable object.
“By way of one’s own subsequent consciousness” means that it cannot be said [to exist] in dependence upon one’s own subsequently occurring consciousness; this is the intended meaning.
“It can be said to exist by its own conditions alone” means that when its own conditions are strong, it becomes strong.
"If it is weak when [the preceding] is weak, it becomes weak"—the intention is that it is capable of recurring.

"A dissimilar mental continuum" refers to the mental continuum of the functional consciousness (*voṭṭhabbanakiriyacitta*). 37. In the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, within the discussion on formations (*saṅkhāra*) and investigation (*vicāraṇā*), under the section on the exposition of resultants (*vipākuddhāra*), it says: "Also by both kinds of kamma."
“By means of both volitional (sasaṅkhārika) karma and non-volitional (asaṅkhārika) karma. “By the Elder” refers to Mahādatta Thera.
“The absence of the state of both” means the absence of the states of being volitional and non-volitional. Regarding the phrase “for even those [two] have indistinct functions”:

here, let it be granted that the two types of adverting (āvajjana) have indistinct functions because their function is to precede the impulsive moments (javana). As for the consciousness that arouses laughter (hasituppāda-citta):
"But since it has the function of impulsion (*javana*), how could its function be indistinct?
To this it is said: "That too is called 'indistinct in function' because it merely accompanies [the primary consciousnesses] such as the knowledge of omniscience.

Regarding the statement, "It should be explained just like the eight great resultants (*mahāvipāka*)," the state of being prompted (*sasankhārika*) or unprompted (*asankhārika*) in the case of the great resultants refers to the objects [perceived] at the time of death in a previous existence.
The intention is that it should be stated as such, referring to the presence [of consciousness] either together with or without application (payoga).
38. "In the production of weak kamma" is said with reference to the functions of rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, and death.
"In the places of weak bases and functions" refers to those having weak bases such as the eye, etc., and to those having weak functions such as adverting, etc.
He explains that meaning with the words beginning “Tatthā. Therein, “associated with distraction” means being associated with restlessness through its function of causing distraction.
What is called “lasting for an eon” (kappaṭṭhitika) refers to the formal act of schism in the Saṅgha.
Among the six types of physical bases, only the heart-base is the essential core, like gold or silver; the others are without essence, being merely translucent, like crystals.
It is said, "in the weak bases such as the eye," meaning that seeing and the other functions are minor functions because they precede the function of impulsion (*javana*).
Therefore, he said, "in seeing and so forth," and so on. 39.
Here, in the exposition, the phrase "it is indeed" is understood as a qualification of the eighteen terms; thus, he says, "in every way."
It is stated: “[... should be understood as such. However, in the *Vibhāvanī*, taking the word "sabbathāpi" (in every way) as an adjective for that [word], it says:
"[... in every way, by way of the division into wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional [states].
The commentary on rootless consciousness is finished.
40. Regarding "in beautiful states of consciousness" (*sobhaṇacittesu*): even though not explicitly stated, it is established [that this applies].

Just as when it is said, "the eight supramundane states of consciousness," the remaining mundane states of consciousness are also understood even without being mentioned; such is the intended meaning. "One possessed of self" (*attasamaṅgīno*) means one who is endowed with an evil deed by way of oneself.
"Even while not desiring" (*anicchante yeva*) means even if there is an object of delight in the signs of the Avīci hell.

Let some desire it as they wish. However, the intention is that for those who do not know, their desire is not authoritative. Regarding the phrase “for the attainment of good fortune” (*sobhagga-pattiyā*):
the analysis (*viggaha*) is that the state of being fortunate (*subhaga*) is “good fortune” (*sobhagga*). And “of the fortunate one” (*subhagassa*) means “of the one possessing great splendor.

(41) Regarding “in accordance with reality” (*yāthāvato*): it means “according to its own nature. Here, it may be asked: since it was stated that “knowledge is that which knows,” does it know everything?

"Knowledge knows things as they truly are. What does this mean? If all knowledge knows things as they truly are, then it follows that for those who deliberate with knowledge, there is no such thing as not knowing, nor is there any failure to hit the mark.
On the other hand, if all knowledge does not know things as they truly are—knowing some things and not knowing others—then, in that case:
"Where one knows, there alone that knowledge exists; where one does not know, there that very knowledge does not exist"—this is what follows [from your position].

To this it is replied: Even for those who think, "I shall reflect by means of knowledge," in whatever instance there is no knowing according to reality, in that instance the mind is dissociated from knowledge (*ñāṇavippayutta-citta*). Furthermore, there are phenomena that are counterparts to knowledge.
There is mind, and applied thought (*vitakka*), and sustained thought (*vicāra*), and view (*diṭṭhi*). While thinking by means of these, they imagine, "I think with knowledge.
Regarding the phrase "the excellence of the gift, the object, and the recipient": this refers to the excellence of the material object to be given and the excellence of the person who receives it.
Regarding the phrase "rebirth in a world free from affliction" (*abyāpajja*): here, a "world free from affliction" refers to the absence of bodily suffering.
The world of higher deities or the Brahma-world is free from mental suffering (*cetasika-dukkha*). "Arising" (*upapatti*) means the act of arising;

the meaning is "approaching by way of rebirth-linking" (*paṭisandhi*). One whose arising is in a world free from affliction is "one whose arising is in an unafflicted world" (*abyāpajja-lokūpapatti*).

This is the analysis of the compound. "Remoteness from defilements" (*kilesa-dūratā*) occurs either through the power of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) or through a particular practice (*paṭipatti*).
Either the state of having suppressed defilements or the state of having eradicated defilements by means of the Noble Path.
Their arising, method, and purification are stated thus in the *Khandha-niddesa* of the *Visuddhimagga*:

"For when, having encountered the excellence of the gift, the recipient, and so forth, or some other cause for joy, one is glad and delighted, and [the thought] 'it exists,' 'it has been given,' and so on, occurs in such a manner..."
When, having placed right view foremost, one performs meritorious deeds such as giving without sinking and without being urged by others,
then his consciousness is accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, and without volitional effort (*asaṅkhāra*). But when, being glad and elated in the manner described,
one places right view foremost while sinking due to being unrestrained in conduct and so forth, or [being urged] by others...
Or when one acts having been urged on, then that very mind of his is "with volitional formation" (*sasaṅkhāra*).
For in this context, "volitional formation" (*saṅkhāra*) is a designation for the prior application that proceeds either by one's own impulse or through others.
However, when young children—who have developed familiarity from seeing the conduct of their kinsmen—suddenly feel joy upon seeing monks...
When someone gives or pays homage to what has come into their hands, O King, then the third consciousness arises.
But when they act in this way because they have been urged by relatives saying, "Give! Pay homage!", then the fourth consciousness arises.
However, when there is a deficiency in the gift or the recipient, or an absence of other causes for joy—
Having approached [these states], they are devoid of joy in all four alternatives. At that time, the remaining four arise accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā*).
42. Regarding the word "eight" (*aṭṭha*) in the phrase *aṭṭhapīti*: by the particle *pi*, it is shown that these consciousnesses are not only eight, but rather more than that, even much more;
this is stated with the words "Therefore... and so forth, in order to illustrate this sense of inclusion (*sampiṇḍana*).

Among the ten bases for meritorious action (*puññakiriyavatthu*), "straightening one's view" (*diṭṭhujuka*) is an act of knowledge (*ñāṇakicca*). How, then, can they perform it with consciousnesses dissociated from knowledge (*ñāṇavippayuttacitta*)?

It is said: Those who straighten their view by means of consciousness associated with knowledge (*ñāṇasampayuttacitta*) also perform it by means of consciousness dissociated from knowledge, because these [moments of dissociated consciousness] fall into the stream of knowledge at intervals.
[This is done] by such means as, "All beings have their own karma as their own property," and so forth.
It should be understood by such passages as: "The Buddha is the Blessed One; that Dhamma is well-expounded;

that Saṅgha is practicing rightly," and so forth. Therefore, he said: "These are the eight types of consciousness," and so on. In that context, the ten bases of meritorious action (*dasapuññakiriyavatthu*) are:

giving (*dāna*), virtue (*sīla*), mental development (*bhāvanā*), honoring (*apacāyana*), service (*veyyāvacca*), dedication of merit (*pattidāna*), rejoicing in merit (*pattānumodana*), hearing the Dhamma (*dhammassavana*), and teaching the Dhamma (*dhammadesanā*).
The kamma has been seen. It is multiplied and increased by those [factors]. And these arise with respect to the eight objects.
While performing three types of kamma, they perform them by means of those same eight.
And all of these are indeed inferior, middling, and superior. Therefore, once again, he performs the increase by means of the objects and so forth in successive order.
In this context, the connection is: "those [factors] are to be set aside. "Pure" means unmixed with predominants (*adhipati*).
"Having done so" means having brought it thus to mind. The construction is: "likewise, those dissociated from knowledge amount to two thousand one hundred and sixty.
"Excluding those with investigation as the predominant factor" means excluding those for which investigation is the predominant factor. "Multiplied in that way" means...
All [these] are multiplied equally by the performance of meritorious deeds and so forth. “By skill” means by that which is reckoned as skill.

“In the cognitive process with various adverting” means in the cognitive process associated with adverting that is distinct from the processes dissociated from knowledge. “By that very same” means by that very same supporting knowledge (upanissaya-ñāṇa) which has investigation (vīmaṃsā) as its dominant factor.
Even though this is so, the connection is: “it is not possible to become.”
43. Regarding the meaning of the terms: “in the sense of breaking” means in the sense of piercing. “In the sense of being harmful” means in the sense of being opposed to what is beneficial (*ahita*).
“In the sense of being unrefined” means in the sense of being harsh, not subtle. “In the sense of having an undesirable result” (*aniṭṭhavipākaṭṭhena*):

those whose result (*vipāka*) is undesirable are “those with undesirable results. The state of being such is “the sense of having an undesirable result. [It is] by that sense of having an undesirable result.

“Because they are the opposites (*paṭipakkhattā*) of lust and so forth. Having thus shown the meaning of the designation as understood through its etymological derivation (*pariyāyattha*), he now shows the literal meaning (*vacanattha*) as it appears in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), beginning with the words “in what is vile,” and so on. Therein, “in what is vile” means in that which is to be loathed or censured.
They “shake” by way of abandoning through substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgappahāna*), and they “cause to tremble” by way of abandoning through suppression (*vikkhambhanappahāna*).
“They destroy” means by way of eradication through complete cutting off (*samuccheda-pahāna*). “In the sense of thinning out” means in the sense of scraping away.

“In the sense of bringing to an end” means in the sense of making a final conclusion. “Moreover,” etc., shows the method of illustration. “In the sense of being produced by skill” is the method of the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*.
Therein, the state of one who is skilled (*kusala*) and wise is “one-pointedness. It is knowledge. By that, it is produced.
A dispute has arisen concerning what has been produced through skill.
44. “By powerful karma”: by karma of the three-rooted type that is of the quality of a cock (kukkaṭṭha). “By weak karma”:
by either weak three-rooted karma or two-rooted wholesome karma. “By some teachers”: [referring to] the Elder Mahādatta, who resided at Moravāpi.
This was said with intentional meaning. “By the compiler” means by the Venerable Bhadanta Buddhaghosa Thera.
“By way of proximate conditions” means by way of conditions that stand nearby; what is meant is: by way of present conditions. Kamma and so forth are the established objects;
the great resultant [consciousnesses] are those that have occurred. “Because of having a non-resultant nature” means because of having a nature that does not ripen as a result.

"Of the nature of producing non-resultant [consciousness]" means this is what is stated. "In the commentary" refers to the commentary on the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*. "Here" refers to the great resultant consciousnesses.
"And because it does not occur in that way" means because it does not occur by way of giving and so forth. 45. In the great functional consciousness.
"Above" refers to the determination of the object at that time in the *Vīthi-saṅgaha*. "By himself alone" means by the Elder Anuruddha himself.

“Vakkhati” means it will be spoken. “Yathārahaṃ” means in accordance with what is appropriate for the great functional consciousnesses (*mahākriyā*) that arise within the mental continuum of one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*).
The intention is that this is a qualification of the speaking of reality (*bhūtakathana*), because there is no other meaning to be excluded by it.

“Taṃ” refers to the inclusion of those [consciousnesses] accompanied by roots (*sahetuka*). It is called a “delimiting qualification” (*byavacchedaka-visesana*) because it excludes the rootless resultant (*vipāka*) and functional (*kiriya*) consciousnesses.
The qualification serves to delimit the connection with the actual state (*sabbhāva*).

Just as in the statement, "He sees pebbles and gravel, and schools of fish, whether stationary or moving," the construction is such that one sees the pebbles and gravel stationary, and the schools of fish both stationary and moving; so it is here as well.
46. “Yadidam” means this capacity for illumination; the construction is “this is the capacity.

The meaning is: “this is the state of being capable. It is connected with the phrase “in the statement of the classification” and “in the objection. In this verse of composition, “these” refers to the beautiful sense-sphere consciousnesses (*kāmāvacara-citta*).
“By way of the classification of meritorious, demeritorious, and functional actions” means by way of the distinction between meritorious, demeritorious, and functional deeds.

47. Which phenomena belong to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara)? Since it is defined in the Canon as extending downward to the Avīci hell and upward to include the Paranimmitavasavatti devas, it is said here that by the word "sense-desires" (kāma), the entire sense-sphere plane (kāmabhūmi) is meant.
The word "included" (pariyāpanna) is to be supplied as a remainder of the text. Regarding the phrase "and action" (kriyā ca):
The word *ca* has the sense of "and. The word *iti* has the sense of "thus. The connection is with the phrase "are excluded by this.

"Here" (*idha*) means in this Compendium of Consciousness (*cittasaṅgahe*). "Of that" (*tassā*) refers to the word *sabbattha*. What is called "existence" (*bhava*) is said to be a collection of phenomena (*dhamma-samūha*) occurring within a continuum bound by the faculties (*indriya*).
However, here in the phrase "phenomena of the sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacarā dhammā*), it is the word *kāma* [that is intended]. And that is earth...
It is said that "the entire realm of sense-desires (kāmabhūmi), together with mountains and so forth," refers to this; thus it is stated, "and the enumeration of planes (bhūmipariyāyo)," and so on.

Regarding the phrase "the collection of phenomena bound by faculties and unbound by faculties": the collection of phenomena bound by faculties pertains to the continuity of sentient beings (sattasantāna);

the collection of phenomena unbound by faculties pertains to earth, mountains, and so forth. Among these, that which is not bound by and not dependent upon the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) is "unbound by faculties."
The Sub-commentary (Anudīpanā) to the Elucidation of the Compendium of Mind-States Concerning Sensual Desire (Itikāmacittasaṅgahadīpanī) is finished. 48.
Regarding the fine-material-sphere consciousness (*rūpāvacaracitta*): "By the combined" means by the five factors combined. The meaning is: by the five factors being together in harmony.
For absorption (*appanā*) occurs only when there is the harmony of the five factors together, not when it is absent.
“Sāmaggiyaṃ” means “because it brings about a state of complete harmony through its great strength.

“Because it is to be practiced” (paṭipajjitabbattā) means because it is to be attained. There are two kinds of jhāna: contemplation directed toward the object (ārammaṇūpanijjhāna) and contemplation directed toward the characteristics (lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna). Therefore, he said “of the kasiṇa and so forth,” and so on.
But here, contemplation directed toward the object is intended. And “contemplation” (upanijjhāna) refers to the object such as the kasiṇa-sign.

Having approached with the mind, it is the non-contemplative observation [of the object]. It is stated, “because of the burning away of opposing states,” since the meaning of the word *jhāna* can also be "burning.
The sense is that, like fire to wood, it burns away the defilements (*kilesa*).
The intention is that one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*) alone is particularly appropriate at the time of attaining absorption (*appanā*). However, in the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*),...
In the first jhāna, the state of strength in *vitakka* (initial application) is required. He explains this meaning with the words beginning “For that...”:
“For that is called one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*)”—this is the grammatical connection. That which has a single self-nature is *ekatva* (oneness).
That which has oneness as its object is *ekattārammaṇā*. This is *ekaggatā*. The analysis of the compound is: the state of that [oneness].
The word *agga* has the sense of "peak" (*koṭi*) or it has the sense of "portion" (*koṭṭhāsa*). "In its occurrence as such" means in the mind's occurrence by way of one-pointedness.

"By way of connection with the quality of predominance" means by way of connection with the quality of being the dominant factor (*adhipati*). What is meant is: "by way of connection with the quality of being a faculty and a condition.
That very one-pointedness is called both "one-pointedness" (*ekaggatā*) and "concentration" (*samādhi*); this is the syntactical connection. "Concentration" (*samādhī*)... [text ends].
The compound *samādhi* can be analyzed in two ways: as *pada-saṃ-ādhī* or as *sama-ādhī*. In this context, the prefix *saṃ-* has the meaning of the word *sammā* (rightly).
As for the word *sama*, it is a noun, as seen in expressions such as "he rules the kingdom righteously and justly" (*dhammena samena rajjaṃ kāreti*).
Showing these two alternative interpretations, he says: "That very mind... and so forth. That very mind is called *samādhi* because it is "rightly placed" (*sammā ca ādhiyati*). That very [mind]...
“Concentration” (*samādhi*) is analyzed in two ways: it is so called because it “concentrates the mind” (*cittam samañca ādhiyati*).
In this context, “properly” (*sammā*) means beautifully; “concentrates” (*ādhiyati*) means it places [the mind]. And since placing is itself fixing, it is said that “it fixes.

“Evenly” (*samañca*) means without unevenness. “Right there” (*tattheva*) means right upon that very object. “By way of removing laxity and agitation” (*līnuddhaccābhāvapādanena*) refers to the absence of both laxity and agitation.
And "non-existence" (abhāva) is the non-existence of sluggishness and agitation. The analysis of the compound is: "causing to attain" (āpajjāpana) is the act of making one attain that [state].

"Distractedness" (visāhāra) is the drawing away of the mind in various ways. "Non-distractedness" (avisāhāra) is the absence of distractedness; and that very state is what has been indicated [by the term *ekaggatā*].

Thus, in these two senses, it should be understood that one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*) alone is appropriately endowed with the specific quality [of concentration]. When this is so, one-pointedness alone is jhāna.
Anticipating the objection that [only] concentration should be mentioned and not applied thought (*vitakka*) and the rest, he says, "Applied thought and the rest are also [included]," and so forth.
The word *api* has the sense of inclusion; the word *pana* has the sense of an alternative position. "Of that one-pointedness" means of that concentration.

"Together with its excellence" means together with its pre-eminence (*atisaya*). "To sink back" means to become despondent. "It" refers to the mind. "To crawl away" means [to think], "Is it thus? Or is it otherwise? etc.
“*Kha*” means to waver in two ways. “*Ukkaṇṭhitun*” means to become oriented toward something else; what is meant is to be diverted.
“*Laddhassātan*” means that by which pleasure (*sāta*) has been obtained. “*Sātan*” means impassioned (*sāratta*). “*Upabrūhitan*” means greatly increased.
“*Because of its peaceful nature*” means because of its naturally tranquil nature. “*Thus assisted*” means by way of making it face toward the object and so forth.
“Favored. Because concentration is the antidote to the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*), it is said: “Having himself... having warded off...
By saying “having remained motionless,” he states the function of absorption (*appanā*).
Having thus shown the purpose of close contemplation (*upanijjhāna*), he says “And among those... and so forth, showing the purpose of burning (*jhāpana*). “Their opposites...”
They are the adversaries and opposites of those factors that constitute the jhāna-factors. “In the mind as well” means even in the mind-door;
the word *api* here has the sense of inclusion, implying “how much more so in the doors of body and speech. The word *api* is also appropriate [in this context].
“They are called ‘consumed’” means they are, as it were, burnt by the fires of the jhāna-factors. “Even though this is so, in their combination...”

The construction is: "Thus the designation 'jhāna' is established. Regarding the phrase "the exertion for the harmony of factors": in the place of jhāna, it is the exertion for the harmonious state of the factors that are jhāna-constituents;

in the place of the path, it is the exertion for the harmonious state of the factors that are path-constituents; and in the place of enlightenment, it is the exertion for the harmonious state of the factors that are enlightenment-constituents.
Having thus explained jhāna according to the opinion of the compilers, he now says "others," etc., in order to show it according to the opinion of others.
"But others say," is the connection [of the sentence]. Therein, "as their own functions" (*sakaṃkiccāni*): *sakaṃ* means "one's own"; *assa* means "of oneself.
*Idaṃ* means "that which belongs to. The meaning is: "those things which belong to oneself. "Thus" (*iti*) means "therefore.

"Having reached the condition of jhāna in the *Paṭṭhāna*... it indeed accomplishes [its function]. For it is said there: "The condition of jhāna" (*jhānapaccayo*) refers to the jhāna-factors [for those things] associated with jhāna.
It is a condition for those mental states and for the material phenomena co-arising with them by way of the jhāna-condition. Regarding the "path-condition":
the path-factors are a condition for the mental states associated with the path and for the material phenomena co-arising with them by way of the path-condition.
"The pentads, decads, etc. refers to the pentads and decads [of materiality]. "And precisely for the state of being the first jhāna, etc. refers to the first jhāna and so forth.
The intention is that it is merely the acquisition of the name [of jhāna]. “Of the state of jhāna” means of the acquisition of the name ‘jhāna.
“Due to the absence of such specific functions” means due to the absence of specific functions such as the fixing of the mind upon the object (ārammaṇābhiniropana) and so forth. 49.
“There might be here” refers to a question at this point. “Difference in factors” means that in the first jhāna there are five factors.
The classification of factors begins with "four factors in the second jhāna," and so forth. "By the inclination of the individual" means by the specific desire of that person.
Such is the answer. "He" refers to that person. "Hi" indicates expansion. "Vitakkasahāyo" means one for whom applied thought (vitakka) is a companion.
"He becomes disenchanted with applied thought" because this applied thought is coarse and close to the hindrances.
"Established" means that having seen the danger in applied thought (*vitakka*), one becomes disenchanted with it. "His inclination" is the connection [to the following].

"Fading away from applied thought" (*vitakkavirāga*) means he causes applied thought to fade away, to disappear, or to be transcended. It is a compound meaning "fading away from applied thought" (*vitakkavirāga*) and "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*).
"In the attainment of successively higher jhānas" means in the acquisition of ever-higher jhānas. By the power of his inclination...

The connection is that it is not like the access-concentration (*pādakajjhāna*). The connection is that the mental aspiration (*cetopaṇidhi*) succeeds. "Because of purity" means because of purity of virtue (*sīlavisuddhi*).

50. In this investigation of the analysis of formations (*saṅkhāra*): "The analysis of formations was not stated"—the intention is that it was not stated by way of [classifying] the wholesome consciousness of the first jhāna as "one without prompting" (*asaṅkhārika*) and "one with prompting" (*sasaṅkhārika*), and so forth. "That" refers to the formation (*saṅkhāra*).
“Breaking up” (bhedo). “Because it is established” means because the breaking up of formations is established. To the question “How is it established?”, he says “For thus,” and so forth.
“Those whose practice is pleasant” (sukhappaṭipadāni) refers to those for whom the practice is pleasant; the analysis [of the compound] is: the state of those [persons].

“Who” (yo) refers to the individual practitioner. “From the beginning” (ādito) refers to the start. “Suppressing” (vikkhambhento) means liberating or effecting a separation. “He suppresses with difficulty” (dukkhena vikkhambheti).

The connection [is as follows]: “By seeing the danger in sensual pleasures, etc. means having seen the danger in sensual pleasures by means of the simile of the pit of glowing embers—that sensual pleasures are full of suffering, full of despair, and that the danger therein is even greater—and so forth.

By the word “etc.,” the seeing of the danger in applied thought (*vitakka*) and the rest is included. “By that very same [means]” means precisely by the seeing of the danger in sensual pleasures, etc.
Here, one should not speak of a differentiation of formations (*saṅkhāra*) based on a differentiation of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).
In order to show that it must be stated precisely according to the distinction of the *paṭipadā* (modes of progress), the passage beginning with “*khippābhiññajjhānānaṃpī*” was spoken.

Therein, *abhijānanaṃ* means direct knowledge (*abhiññā*). Those for whom the direct knowledges are swift and rapid are “those with swift direct knowledge” (*khippābhiññāni*). Those for whom the direct knowledges are sluggish and not rapid are “those with sluggish direct knowledge” (*dandhābhiññāni*).
[This refers to] the jhānas. “If it were so”—thus, by way of the distinction of the *paṭipadā*, the [volitional] formations (*saṅkhāra*)...
"If there were a distinction" is the meaning. "At the time of practicing" means at the time of entering into meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
"Obstructive" means those that create an impediment. "By way of being present or absent" means by way of being situated nearby or not.
Those for whom the vehicle is pure insight are "pure-insight-vehicle practitioners. "Pure" means unmixed with calm-abiding jhāna (*samatha-jhāna*).
"Having struck with a weapon" means not by others striking or cutting with a weapon. "Violently" means more swiftly.
"Arising in those who are dying" means arising at the time close to death; this is the intended meaning.

For even non-returners (anāgāmins) who follow the vehicle of pure insight (suddhavipassanāyānika) are indeed called "perfected in concentration" (paripūrakārino). When they desire, they can attain anything.
Jhāna succeeds even by means of mere attention directed toward a sign (*nimitta*). Therefore, he said: "That too has its course established through the Path.
The phrase "in the world of form-brahmās" (*rūpībrahmaloke*) is stated with reference to the fact that even the eight attainments (*samāpatti*) are natural there.
However, in the formless world of brahmās (*arūpībrahmaloke*), only one attainment can possibly be natural. [This refers to] the jhānas established by rebirth (*upapattisiddhajjhāna*).

The differentiation of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) has been explained according to the difference in conditions present in another existence; how that [differentiation] is to be understood is stated:

"Even in a single existence... they are applicable. Because there is the possibility of doubt—namely, that at the time of actual occurrence, the very same differentiation of volitional formations might apply due to its proximity to the differentiation of volitional formations obtained at the very first moment of a single existence—the text provides this clarification.

This has been said. By this, he shows that for those who have attained jhāna through rebirth in another existence, there is no need to speak of a difference in formations (*saṅkhāra*) due to a difference in proximate conditions.

Now, as for those jhānas accomplished through the Path and those accomplished through rebirth, their arising occurs at the moment of the Path and the moment of rebirth respectively, at the time they are established, without depending on proximate conditions.
Having taken the complete absence of the path as the primary meaning, the phrase "or because the arising of jhāna is devoid of the path," etc., is stated in order to show another alternative.
Having thus explained the analysis of formations established by means of the commentaries regarding sublime jhānas,
the passage beginning with "Furthermore" is commenced to show that this is indeed established even by means of the canonical texts (pāḷi).
[This refers] to the two kinds of concentration—those with sluggish direct knowledge and those with quick direct knowledge—which are preceded by the painful way of practice (*dukkhappaṭipadā*).
"To this extent" (*ettāvatā*): that which has this measure is "to this extent" (*ettāvaṃ*); [the meaning is] by this much. Here it may be asked:
why is the classification of formations (*saṅkhāra*) not stated here? By such a sequence of words, [the answer] is established; this is the connection. The rest is easy to understand.

51. In the *Vibhāvanī* recension: "Preparation" (*parikamma*) refers to [the preliminary exercises] such as "earth, earth," "water, water," and so forth, as well as the preparatory meditation (*bhāvanā-parikamma*) such as "form is impermanent," "form is suffering," "form is non-self," and so forth.

"Requisite" (*adhikāra*) refers to the kamma of meditation performed in a previous existence, and also the meritorious kamma such as giving and virtue performed while aspiring for the jhānas, paths, and fruits in a previous existence. "This, first of all, is not appropriate."
Here, the word *tāva* is a particle used in anticipation of what is yet to be said; it indicates that there is something further to be stated.
Prior kamma-formations (*pubbābhisaṅkhāra*) are twofold: natural prior kamma-formations and functional prior kamma-formations.
Among these, the preparatory prior kamma-formations are called "natural prior kamma-formations"; this is the group of natural conditions.
Thus it is. What was stated previously is called the "prior application" (*pubbappayoga*) or "prior volitional formation of application" (*payogapubbābhisaṅkhāra*).

To show that this very [volition] is intended here, he said, "Not indeed," and so forth. "At least" (*antamaso*) means by way of a final limit. "A morsel of alms-food" (*ālopabhikkhā*) refers to a single morsel of alms-food;
that is the prior volitional formation consisting of preliminary preparation (*parikamma*). And all the jhānas that have arisen are indeed [included].
The connection is with the word "there is not. "Thus" means therefore. "That" refers to the volitional formation of meditation (*bhāvanābhisaṅkhāra*).

"Of them" refers to all meditative absorptions (*jhāna*). For there are no such things as mundane absorptions... [omission] ...because even throughout all eons, including the time of the destruction of an eon, it is possible for these beings to develop absorptions and have the Brahma-world as their destination; this is the intended meaning. "Previously, in the practices of serenity..."
The phrase "one who has performed the preliminary service" (*katādhikārassa*) is said with reference to one who has performed the service in a proximate existence.

However, in the case of a distant existence, there is no one whatsoever who has not performed the service regarding the formal acts of the Saṅgha (*samathakamma*). "In this very way" (*evameva*) means exactly so.

Because [the state] must be described in terms of past karma prior to the dissolution of the formations (*saṅkhāra*) within the resultant jhānas (*vipākajjhāna*), it is stated as "in wholesome functional jhānas" (*kusala-kriyājjhānesu*). The passage beginning with "Or else" (*athavā*) is the latter [explanation].

"An alternative interpretation (vikappa) is as follows: Alternatively, since for that which arises solely through prior volitional formation (pubbābhisaṅkhāra), a state of being unprompted (asaṅkhārika) can never possibly occur, the term 'unprompted' is not stated; and because there is no deviation [from this rule], the term 'prompted' (sasaṅkhārika) is also not stated—this is the alternative interpretation.
In this context, the connection is: 'the term "unprompted" is not stated because there is no deviation.'"
Because there is no possibility [of it being otherwise] due to its unconditioned nature (*asaṅkhārika*), the term "with effort" (*sasaṅkhārika*) is not stated.
If it were stated, it would be entirely purposeless. Why? Because there is an absence of both possibility and deviation.
For it has been said: "A qualification is meaningful when there is possibility and deviation. And the wise do not utter purposeless speech. Why?
Because it is a characteristic of the unwise. However, when both existence and deviation are present, it can be stated in that way.
Why? Because it is purposeful. The wise speak only what is purposeful. Why? Because it is a characteristic of the wise; this is the intended meaning. 52.
In the determination of direct knowledge regarding the path: "From the arising of the sign" means from the arising of the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*).
The application of the terms is as follows: the "pleasant way of practice" (*sukhāpana-paṭipadā*) refers to the fact that jhāna which has arisen either slowly or quickly makes the path pleasant.
Regarding the phrase "in a previous existence," it means in a proximate previous existence. As for "obstructive states" (*antarāyika-dhammā*), they are:

those obstructive by way of defilement (*kilesa-antarāyika*), those obstructive by way of kamma (*kamma-antarāyika*), those obstructive by way of result (*vipāka-antarāyika*), those obstructive by way of transgressing the formal rules (*paññatti-vītikkama-antarāyika*), and those obstructive by way of reviling the Noble Ones (*ariya-upavāda-antarāyika*).

In this context, there are three [types of obstacles]: that which is called the obstacle of defilement (*kilesantarāyika*), consisting of the three fixed wrong views; that which is called the obstacle of karma (*kammantarāyika*), consisting of the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantariya-kamma*);
and that which is called the obstacle of result (*vipākantarāyika*), consisting of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) as a result of being without roots or with two roots.

Furthermore, for those established in the state of a monk, the transgression of the Vinaya rules (*paññatti*) without having performed amends is the obstacle of the transgression of rules (*paññattivītikkamantarāyika*).

[This is] the name. When a counteraction has been performed, it does not constitute an obstacle. Reviling and abusing noble persons (*ariyapuggala*) by way of their birth and so forth, and failing to perform a counteraction—this is called "an obstacle consisting in reviling the noble ones" (*ariyūpavādantarāyika*). Here too, when a counteraction has been performed, it does not constitute an obstacle.
Regarding the remaining three, there is no such thing as a counteraction. These phenomena [exist] in this present existence.

They are called "obstructive" (*antarāyika*) because they create an obstacle to the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and the paths (*magga*). One who is liberated from them is called "liberated from obstructive states" (*antarāyika-dhamma-vimutta*).
"Established in beautiful practice" means established by way of fulfilling the beautiful practice beginning with the purification of virtue (*sīla-visuddhi*).
"With impediments severed" refers to the ten kinds of impediments (*palibodha-kamma*), such as the impediment of the dwelling place (*āvāsa-palibodha*).
Having cut [the fetters], he stands firm. “Resolute” (*pahitatto*) means:

endowed with the energy of right exertion (*sammappadhāna*) that functions thus: “There shall be no halting of my effort until I have attained that which is to be reached by human strength and human prowess.
For he is called “resolute” because his selfhood (*attabhāva*) has been sent forth, dispatched, and made independent.
“‘Non-possession’ means it does not exist. The intended meaning is: “if one is endowed with the five factors of striving. The five factors of striving are:
perfection of faith, absence of deceit, health, non-slackness of energy, and possession of wisdom. 52. In the case of resultant jhāna:
“‘Become supple’” means become weak due to the deficiency in the power of development (*bhāvanā*). Because of being weak—

And it is weak. “In various places of activity” means in seeing, hearing, and so forth. “Even in inferior personal existences” means even in persons who are rootless (*ahetuka*) or possess two roots (*dvihetuka*).
“Even dissimilar” means that even a karma of three roots (*tihetuka*) produces a fruit of the highest grade, and even a rootless (*ahetuka*) result is produced;
thus, it produces even dissimilar results. “Only in the places of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*)”—here, *bhavaṅga*...
By the term "sound," the points of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and the points of death (*cuti*) are also included. Regarding the phrase "exactly like the wholesome":
the wholesome first jhāna produces only the resultant (vipāka) of the first jhāna; the wholesome second jhāna produces only the resultant of the second jhāna, and so forth.
Thus, it produces a resultant that is exactly like the wholesome. Regarding the statement "only the wholesome... is called kamma-jhāna," this is said because there is no distinction [between them].

The intended meaning is "by way of figurative usage" (*pacārena*). Figurative usage (*upacāro*) is conventional expression (*vohāro*); it is called "figurative usage by non-distinction" (*abheda-upacāro*) when one treats even a distinction as non-distinction.

[This is explained] in the commentary on the summary verse (*saṅgahagāthā*). "Distinction of jhānas" (*jhānabhedo*) means the differentiation of the jhānas. However, in terms of actual meaning, what is called "distinction of jhānas" refers to the distinction in association with the jhānas;
thus he says, "by way of the distinction in association with the jhānas. This is shown by the passage beginning with "a consciousness associated with the first jhāna" (*pathamajjhānikaṃ cittaṃ*).
It should be applied. “That very same” means the mind of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) itself.

However, in the *Vibhāvani*, having seen the statement in the subsequent summary verse, “Having made each one fivefold by way of the distinction of jhāna-factors and yoga,” it is stated here that [the classification] is “by way of the distinction of jhāna” and “by way of the distinction of association with jhāna-factors.
Even so, because the distinction of jhāna is intended here as something separate, [it is treated thus].
“Another classification of jhāna,” and so forth, was stated.
The sub-commentary (*anudīpanā*) on the exposition of fine-material-sphere consciousness (*rūpāvacaracitta*) is finished. 55.

In the exposition of immaterial-sphere consciousness (*arūpacittadīpanī*): “Excessively” (*bhuso*) means more than usual. “In its own nature” (*sarūpato*) means by way of its ultimate intrinsic nature (*paramatthasabhāva*).
That which has no matted locks (*jaṭā*) is "without matted locks" (*ajaṭa*). That which is without matted locks is "space without matted locks" (*ajaṭākāsa*).
"Circumscribed space" refers to spaces such as door-openings, window-openings, and so forth, wherein one acquires the space-kasina sign (*ākāsakasiṇanimitta*).

Space obtained after removing the kasina sign is "space resulting from the removal of the kasina" (*kasiṇugghāṭimākāsa*), because it is produced by the removal of the kasina. [This refers to] the groups of material phenomena (*rūpakalāpa*).
Space that consists merely of delimitation is "space as the delimitation of form. Regarding the phrase "it is pervaded by way of its infinite nature":

even something the size of four finger-breadths is called "infinite" and is pervaded through the mental attention of meditation (*bhāvanā-manasikāra*). Regarding the phrase "the basis for the resolve of the gods":
this refers to the place where powerful gods receive offerings from villages and towns; it is there that people, at the proper time, [make offerings] to their family deities.
“They offer an oblation (*bali*). "Oblation" refers to an object worthy of worship. "In that" means in the space cleared by the *kasiṇa*.

"That very same" means that very same object. This should be applied in three ways: for one who has attained a wholesome *jhāna*, or for one reborn through a resultant (*vipāka*) *jhāna*, or for one dwelling in happiness in the present life through a functional (*kiriya*) *jhāna*. It is called "infinite," just as in the case of the earth-*kasiṇa*.
Because it proceeds [from that basis], the jhāna is called the "earth-kasiṇa. "In one part" means at the moment of arising, or during its persistence, or at the moment of dissolution.
It is called "infinite" (ananta) because it has disappeared [from that specific location]. "In what is known as infinite" means in that which is named infinite.

"Because it proceeds through meditation on 'infinite'"—this refers to the fact that the first consciousness of the form realm proceeds through such preliminary meditation (pubbabhāga-bhāvanā) as "infinite."
“By way of the mode of suffusing oneself”: the intention is that this does not depend upon preliminary-stage meditation (*pubbabhāgabhāvanā*).

“By way of etymology (*nirutti*)”: having applied the suffix *-ya* in its own sense (*sakatthe*), the letter *n* is elided. “It does not accord with the text (*pāḷi*)”: it does not accord with the text of the *Vibhaṅga*.
“It suffuses the infinite”: it suffuses the infinite as “infinite, infinite. “The first is the absence of materiality and consciousness”: [this refers to the first base].
It is a mere designation for its absence. "Neither exists" means it is not present. "Of it" refers to the fourth absorption of the form realm (*rūpajjhāna*).
Regarding the phrase "of the function of sharp perception" (*paṭusaññā kiccassa*) in the passage beginning with "Or else," it means of the function of clear perception.

To explain the meaning of the phrase "because it exists in a subtle state as a residual formation" (*saṅkhārāvasesa-sukhumabhāvena vijjamānattā*), he says "And here... and so forth. "Reached the summit" (*muddhabhūtaṃ*) means having attained the peak.
“Merely the heading of the exposition”: this means merely the principal statement, as in the case of [the phrase] “The king is coming,” and so forth.

“Of that very same”: of the first immaterial-sphere consciousness itself. The wholesome first immaterial-sphere consciousness becomes the object of the second immaterial-sphere consciousness, whether it be wholesome in ordinary persons (puthujjana) or in those in training (sekkha). However, the arahant is threefold.
In this regard, one who has attained Arahantship while abiding in the first immaterial state (*arūpa*) produces the second immaterial state without having previously entered it.
For that person, the wholesome first immaterial state becomes the object (*ārammaṇa*) of the functional second immaterial state.
Furthermore, one who has attained Arahantship while abiding in the first immaterial state may again enter that same first immaterial state.
The second [consciousness] produces form. One, having established the second formless state, attains arahantship.
For these two, the first form-consciousness—which is an act—becomes the object of the second formless state, which is likewise an act. Therefore he said:
"Consciousness is called... and so forth.

The Elucidation of Formless Consciousness. 57. Regarding supramundane consciousness: "A flow of water" refers to a collection of streams of water. "From its source" means from the place of its initial arising.
"As it says" means how it is stated in the Canon. "That is to say" asks: which one? "And this too" refers to this Noble Path as well.
The noble path lasts for only a single moment of consciousness; how then does it flow and stream on until the element of Nibbāna without residue?
To this he says: "By way of the pervasion of its power. In the text, the names of the five great rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā are given.
"Sloping toward the ocean" means they incline and lean toward the great ocean. "Inclined" means they have descended toward it. "Tending downward" means they flow down toward it.

“Of the defilements” (*kilesānaṃ*) is the functional term for non-approaching. In the text, “a jar” (*ghaṭo*) refers to a water-jar filled with water. “Upside down” (*nikujjo*) means placed with its mouth facing downwards.
“Does not swallow back” (*nopaccāvamati*) means it does not swallow again. “Does not come back” (*na puneti*) means it does not return or approach;
the noble disciple (*ariyasāvako*) [does not return]. “Does not go back” (*na pacceti*) means he does not return. To explain that meaning, it says: “he does not return. Thus...

Having demonstrated that non-retrogression through those who establish it by means of the scriptures (*pāḷi*), he now spoke the passage beginning with "And just as" in order to clarify it through those who establish it by means of reasoning (*yutti*).
"From which" (*yato*) means for what reason. "They" (*te*) refers to worldlings (*puthujjana*). "Immoral" (*dussīla*) means lacking virtue. "Insane" (*ummattaka*) means insane from bile (*pitta*).
"Deranged in mind" (*khittacitta*) means those whose natural state of mind has been scattered by demons. "Lacking wisdom" (*duppañña*) means devoid of wisdom. "Mute and dull" (*eḷamūga*) means...
“Mutes with mouths dripping saliva due to very poor wisdom. “On that very path” means on the Noble Eightfold Path itself.
That path, moreover, is fourfold: the first path, the second path, the third path, and the fourth path.
“Setting out from the beginning” means the setting out, the proceeding, of the stream of the first path at the beginning among the four paths.
"Acquisition" (paṭilābha) is what is meant. "Of stream-entry" (sotāpattiya) means by the entering of the stream. "Being attained" (adhigammamāna) means being acquired. The connection is as follows:
all the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma), proceeding in a non-retrogressive course, are called the "stream.

Perfect enlightenment (sambodhi) is said to be the knowledge in the four paths. Those for whom the higher enlightenment itself is the final goal (parāyana) are "those whose higher enlightenment is their final goal."
"Final resort" (*parāyana*). "Final resort" means a refuge. How is the term "stream-entry" (*sotāpatti*) a grammatical coreferent (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the "path"?
To this it is said: "Of the stream-entry consisting of the first path," and so forth. "It searches" (*maggeti*) means it seeks.
It is established as "path" (*magga*) according to the etymological method of "going while killing" (*mārento gamana*); thus it is said: "It is a path because it goes while killing the defilements."
58. Regarding the path of the once-returner (*sakadāgāmi-magga*): "He comes once" means that having gone from here, he returns again to this world.

"By nature" means by way of his natural disposition (*pakatisabhāva*). They are called "those who come to the sense-sphere world" (*kāmalokāgamana*) because they come to the sense-sphere world by means of these [factors]; these are the defilements (*kilesa*).
By their presence—that is, by their state of existing—the phrase in the text, "of a certain person" (*ekaccassa puggalassa*), is used in the genitive case to denote the agent.
The connection is: "by a certain person, [craving] has not been abandoned. "Companionship" (*sahabyataṃ*) means the state of being a companion.
Having said "he becomes one who comes back," he states that same meaning as: "having come to this state" (*āgantvā itthattaṃ*). One who comes by habit is "having come" (*āgantvā*).
The state of being thus is "this state" (*itthattaṃ*). The construction is: having come to this sensual existence (*kāmattabhāvaṃ*), therefore he is called "one who comes back" (*āgāmī*). And this...
The meaning [of "attha"] is that one comes to this world once by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), and so forth.

Regarding "by way of the defilements and the course of existence" (*kilesa-gati-vasena*): it refers to the course of existence through the defilements of going from the sense-sphere world (*kāmaloka*). Defilements suppressed by jhāna acting as an ally to the Path are completely eradicated by the Path;
this is what is called "the power of jhāna acting as an ally to the Path. Therefore, he said "not indeed," and so forth.
"In 'from the world of the gods' (devalokato), the world of Brahmā is also included. However, the construction is "if there is a subsequent meaning" (pacchimasmiṃ pana atthe sati).
"One who has the habit of coming" means having come. "Not having come" means not having arrived. "By that" refers to the non-coming.

Regarding the phrase "because of the arising of different meanings," among the two instances of the word *itthatta*, in one case it means "this sensual-sphere world" (*kāmāvacara-loka*), and in the other, "this human world" (*manussaloka*).
Thus, because various [other] meanings are impossible. In the Pāḷi, “*sabyābajjho*” means accompanied by the affliction of mental disease, which is reckoned as mental suffering.
Therefore he said: “*tehi paṭighānusayassā*,” and so forth. Therein, “*te*” refers to the worldlings (*puthujjana*), stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*), and once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*).
The connection is with the phrase “of those who are *sabyābajjha*. Regarding the phrase “of the latter sentence,” having come to this state of existence...

Regarding the statement, "The stream-enterer and once-returner are to be seen by him": because it is said that [the once-returner] comes "to this state" (*itthatta*) among the two types of once-returners, it refers, in that sense, to the stream-enterer and once-returner among the two who bear the name of once-returner.
"Of the former" refers to the stream-enterer. "Not even in common with another" means not in common with those established in the second fruit and so forth.

For those stream-enterers (sotāpanna) dwelling in the Brahma-world, there is no state of being limited to seven more births (*sattakkhattu-paramatā*), just as for those established in the second fruit, there is no state of being a once-returner (*sakadāgāmī*).
Therefore he said, "those established in the first and second fruits," and so forth. The phrase "therefore" and so on is a statement of the qualities already acquired.
"By this reason" refers to the aforementioned cause. "By way of rebirth in the lower [realms] or higher [realms]" means:
“By way of rebirth from above to below and rebirth from below to above”—this refers to rebirth in the manner of ascending and descending.
“And having done thus,” etc., is the second statement of the qualities obtained. “The five reach their end here”:
this means that for these five types of persons, the end here in the sense-sphere world (kāmaloka) is the attainment of Nibbāna without residue (anupādisesa-nibbāna). “But that,” etc.

As for the once-returner (sakadāgāmi) person: however, for those whose meaning is according to the commentaries on the *Cariyāpiṭaka*, the construction is that this once-returner person is stated to be only fivefold, and not a sixth person.
But for those whose meaning is "this world," it is shown that even a sixth [type] is obtainable; thus he says: "In the *Mahāparinibbāna*... [etc. ...he has indeed come."
It has been said. In that context, “he has indeed come in the sense of coming once” means he has come among the *sakadāgāmins* (once-returners) in the sense of returning only once.
The construction is: even the omniscient Buddhas, having attained the first fruit (*sotāpatti*), appear as if they remain within the state of being limited to seven more births.
And here, “in the state of being limited to seven births” refers to the condition of having at most seven births remaining. Furthermore, this...
This is merely an illustrative statement. Even the omniscient Buddhas, having attained the second fruit, remain established in their nature of returning only once.
Why? Because at that moment, they abide in the manifestation of that specific natural disposition; this is the intended meaning.
All six types of persons mentioned here should be understood [in this way]. By this, that which was stated in the *Vibhāvanī* regarding the five types of *sakadāgāmis* [is clarified].
"The fifth alone is intended here"—this is rejected. Why? Because if only the fifth were intended here by the term *sakadāgāmi*, one would have to state where the other four would be intended.

Being a productive cause, [the lineage] is "only that which has come through the proper method" (*ñāyāgatā*), meaning it has been handed down through tradition. Therefore he said "just as," and so forth. "Unopposed" means unopposed by the proper method.

59. "The lower part" (*orambhāga*) refers to the lower portion, namely the sense-sphere world (*kāmaloka*). "Leading to the lower part" (*orambhāgiyāni*) refers to the fetters such as sensual lust (*kāmarāga*), ill will (*byāpāda*), and so forth. "He" (*so*) refers to the person who is a non-returner (*anāgāmi*). 60.
