He states "stiffness (thinaṃ), the act of stiffening (thiyanā)," and so forth, because the term is established according to the Pāli tradition.
"Having made it unworkable" means having made the body and so forth incapable of action and extremely weak. [It is as if striking with a mallet; this is what is meant.
"Them" refers to the mind and mental factors associated with it. "Having made them sluggish" means having made them sluggish, sinking down. Therefore he said:
“*Iriyāpathan*,” and so forth. *Thina* (sloth) overcomes the mind because sloth is a malady for the function of cognizing.
*Middha* (torpor) overcomes mental factors because torpor is a malady for the functions of contact and so forth; this is the intended meaning. 96.
Regarding the meaning of the word *vicikicchā*: the term *cikicchana* is established by way of the root *kit*, in the sense of removing disease.

He said, "It is called the 'conditioned functional state' (saṅkhata-kiriyā-pada), meaning it is a 'counteraction of knowledge' (ñāṇappaṭikāra). And "counteraction" (paṭikāra) refers to an action that is the opposite of a disease.
"By this" (etāya) is an ablative expression. They investigate the Dhamma; thus, they are "investigators" (vicino). They are "examiners of the Dhamma" (dhamma-vīmaṃsakā).
One suffers and is distressed by this; thus, it is "suffering" (kicchā). Showing this meaning [of the term], he says: "Investigation (vicinaṃ) and suffering (kicchā) is doubt (vicikicchā)."
He said, “‘Sabhāvan’” and so forth. “‘Vicikicchati’” is a term for the conditioned element (*saṅkhata-dhātu*).
To show that this refers to doubt (*kaṅkhā*), he said, “‘Or it doubts’” and so forth. It is called *dveḷaka* because it wavers or trembles in two ways;

thus, it is a mind that functions in such a manner. The analysis of the compound is: “the state of being *dveḷaka*. “‘In the eight [objects] beginning with the Buddha’” means one doubts regarding the Buddha.

“He doubts the Dhamma, he doubts the Saṅgha, he doubts the training, he doubts the past, he doubts the future, he doubts both the past and the future, and he doubts the specific conditionality and dependently arisen phenomena”—these are the eight objects of faith mentioned in this way.
Regarding these, there is also the expression: “he doubts the Buddha.”
One who lacks faith in the qualities of the Buddha as stated in the passage beginning "The Blessed One is an Arhat," is said to have doubt regarding the Buddha.
One who lacks faith in the qualities of the Dhamma as stated in the passage beginning "The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One" is said to have doubt regarding the Dhamma.

One who lacks faith in the qualities of the Saṅgha as stated in the passage beginning "The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way" is said to have doubt regarding the Saṅgha.
One who lacks faith in the three trainings regarding the cycle of existence, suffering, and the goal of deliverance is said to "doubt the training.
One who doubts whether one's own past existence did or did not exist is said to "doubt the prior limit.
One who doubts whether one's own future existence after death will or will not exist is said to "doubt the subsequent limit."
One who is doubtful as to whether both [the past and the future] exist or do not exist is said to be "doubting about the past and the future.

One who is doubtful regarding the dependent origination and the state of being dependently originated of one's own aggregates in this present existence is said to be "doubting about the specific conditionality of dependently originated phenomena. "By way of perplexity" means by way of a state of being in doubt.
Doubt that is currently occurring. It is said that "doubt-like states" do not exist even for the omniscient Buddhas, whose intelligence is unimpeded regarding all phenomena;
thus it is stated, "of those who are not omniscient," and so forth.
The exposition on the mass of unwholesome states is concluded.
97. Regarding the meaning of the word *saddhā* (faith): “Well-seated” means unmoving. “Firmly” means having made it non-forgetful and unshakable.
“Bears” means one bears it by way of observation, thinking, “It is exactly thus. Likewise, “places it. Or, beings endowed with faith (*saddhā*) have faith.
Things worthy of being believed are “objects of faith” (*saddheyyāni*). “Clarity” is said to be the absence of turbidity.
Citta. *Akālussiya* means the absence of turbidity (*akālussa*). The analysis of the compound is: "the state of that [absence].
"Conviction" (*okappanā*) refers to thinking by way of resolving, [thinking] "it was well," "it was good. "Just wrong resolve" means just the resolve associated with views.
"When there is no wealth" means when there is no property; for property is called "wealth" (*vitta*). Whatever one desires, that very thing—
[It is called *sati*] because they find [it] by means of this. "Of them" refers to human beings.
(98) Regarding the sense of the word *sati*: "remembers" means recollects. "Done" means previously done.
"To be done" means what is to be done now or later. A wholesome deed (*kalyāṇa-kamma*) is not, by its very nature, a place of delight for the mind.
It exists. Evil action alone becomes the basis for the mind’s delight. Therefore, mindfulness by a specific name must be sought only for the sake of not being negligent regarding wholesome action;
there is no need for separate mindfulness regarding evil action. All mental states and mental factors (citta-cetasika-dhammā) are of an un-negligent nature.
Hence he said, "the others also," and so forth. [The phrase] "mindfulness itself does not exist" is stated separately.
That which is called *sati* is not merely a single mental factor (*cetasika*). To explain what it is, he says: "Of what [is there non-forgetfulness]? and so forth.
In this context, "non-forgetfulness of what has been done" means non-forgetfulness by way of either rejoicing in some things or by way of grieving for others.
"Non-forgetfulness of what ought to be done" means the state of being intent upon performing it at all times. "Of what... [refers to the object].
Or, the genitive case (*sāmivacana*) is used here in the sense of the locative (*bhummatthe*). The same applies to the remaining two phrases.

One who is appointed to all royal duties is a "general officer" (*sabbakammiko*). "Appointed" (*niyutto*) means one whose mind is engaged and diligent. They are called "beneficial in all respects" (*sabbatthikā*) because they are desired in all situations;
for that [mindfulness] performs the function of guarding the mind at the six doors, owing to its nature as the restraint of the sense faculties (*indriya-saṃvaraṇa*).
Therefore, that [mindfulness] should be cultivated so that a mind rooted in greed does not arise toward a desirable object among the six sense doors;
a mind rooted in hatred toward an undesirable object; and a mind rooted in delusion toward a neutral object.

Furthermore, this scriptural passage was spoken in reference to the stages for the development of the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga). Therefore, it should also be cultivated when the mind is in a state of lethargy.
This [verse] is to be connected with the passage beginning: "It is to be desired for the purpose of warding off the mind from the side of despondency.
(99–100) Regarding the meanings of the terms *hiri* and *ottappa*: "He feels shame because of bodily misconduct, etc. means he feels shame regarding the performance of those [actions].
Having despised those base and inferior actions as being lowly deeds, he desires to protect himself from them. Therefore, it says: "he feels disgust."
“*Ukkaṇṭhatī*” means he is repelled; he desires dissociation. “*Tehi yeva*” means by those very things, namely, bodily misconduct and so forth.
“*Ubbijjatī*” means he is terrified; it presents itself as fear. Regarding the verses:
“*Alajjiyesū*” refers to wholesome deeds that ought not to cause shame. “*Lajjare*” means they feel shame. “*Abhaye*” refers to wholesome deeds that ought not to cause fear. Because...
The connection is: "But the true persons preserve themselves. Regarding the phrase "having generated self-respect through a sense of shame":
having held one's own birth, qualities, and so forth, or one's virtue, qualities of character, and so forth, in high esteem, one thinks, "An evil deed is unbecoming for someone like me to do.
If I were to do it, I would later realize that I am impure and become sorrowful and dejected."
Thus, having generated self-respect (*hirī*) toward oneself, and "having generated respect for others through moral dread (*ottappa*)," the intended meaning is:
having feared the dread of being censured by others. In this context, "the dread of being censured by others" refers to the fear of reproach from other virtuous people;
it also includes the fear of the states of misery (*apāya*) and the fear of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra-vatta*). They protect the world, thus they are "world-protectors" (*lokapālā*).
“World” (loka) means the world of sentient beings (sattaloka). “Protecting” (pāleti) means guarding [them] from the fear of the states of misery (apāya).

Regarding the meaning of the word “non-greed” (alobha): he says “the opposite of greed” (lobhappaṭipakkho), because the letter *a* has the sense of opposition. The meaning is that it is opposed to greed.
To show that this state of opposition should be understood as the relationship between the abandoner and the object to be abandoned, he says “for he,” and so forth.
The connection there is: "Having become [the mind] by way of the element of renunciation (*nekkhammadhātu*), it proceeds. Regarding the phrase "in those things perceived as beneficial":
this means in those things perceived thus, "This is for my welfare, for my benefit, for my happiness. "By way of attachment" means by way of the desire not to let go.
The connection is: "It proceeds toward those very things. "Having despised the success of existence and enjoyments as if they were a heap of excrement."
This is an illustrative statement made with reference to the Bodhisattvas. In this context, "having despised" means having censured. That by which one goes forth is "renunciation" (*nekkhamma*);
that very thing is the "element" (*dhātu*), hence "the element of renunciation" (*nekkhammadhātu*).
This same method should be applied to such expressions as "the opposite of hatred," "the opposite of delusion," and so forth.

103. Regarding equanimity (*majjhattatā*): "Of sinking and agitation" means that the state of mental sinking (*līnatā*) is one side of imbalance, and the state of agitation (*uddhaṭatā*) is the second side of imbalance.
A sunken mind falls into the side of imbalance that is indolence (*kosajja*); an agitated mind falls into the side of imbalance that is restlessness (*uddhacca*).
Both of these belong to the unwholesome side. Likewise, excessive dryness of the mind...
One side is uneven. By means of the passage beginning with "excessive elation is one [extreme]," the entire exposition of the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) should be expanded upon.
In that context, however, equanimity (*majjhattatā*), not allowing the associated states to fall toward either of the two extremes, itself stands firmly upon the Middle Way.
104. Regarding tranquility (*passaddhi*) and the others: "'Therein they experience that' means they obtain that mental happiness within those meritorious deeds."
105. Lightness (*lahutā*) is twofold. “On a heated stone” means on the surface of a stone that has been made red-hot. “Therein” refers to meritorious deeds. 106–110.
Regarding malleability (*mudutā*) and the following [qualities], everything is easy to understand.
111. Regarding the three abstinences (*virati*): “By way of talk, volition, and abstinence” means right speech as talk, right speech as volition, and...
It is by way of right speech as abstinence (*virati*). It gives rise to that talk, thus it is "that which gives rise to it" (*taṃ-samuṭṭhāpikā*).
The construction is: "but that which is the occurrence of the mind in the mode of abstaining from evil.

Or, "of one undertaking [it]" means of one who makes a vocal utterance such as "I abstain from false speech," and so forth. Or, "of one resolving [it]" means by the mind alone, without making a vocal utterance.
Or for one who so resolves. With these two phrases, he speaks of the occurrence of the undertaking and the abstinence.
By the phrase “or for one who does not transgress,” he speaks of the occurrence of the abstinence from what has been reached. “By this” means by the abstinence of right speech.
That [abstinence], however, being co-existent with both the agent and the action, brings about the act of undertaking even more effectively. Therefore...
That is what is called an instrument (karaṇa) as a means of accomplishment (sādhana). Therefore he said: "The word *karaṇa* is used in the sense of the instrument.

When many sequences of impulsion (javana-vāra) are occurring, right speech included in each preceding sequence of impulsion becomes a condition for the act of undertaking (samādāna-kriyā) arising from each succeeding sequence of impulsion.
However, because that [right speech] does not coexist with that act, it possesses the characteristic of an instrument.
It does not succeed. The cause (hetu) resides in the characteristic (lakkhaṇa). Therefore he said:

"The word for cause is indeed a term for the instrument (karaṇa). And this is stated because it is obtainable by way of its meaning. However, the word *sammāvācā* (right speech) is established only in the sense of the instrument when it functions as a noun (kitasādhana).
For a causal sense that is not an agent cannot possibly be called an instrument. [Regarding the phrase] "words of undertaking":
The words of undertaking originate from right speech (*sammāvācā*). "From that" means after that. "Of them" refers to those who are conversing.
And all this has been stated by making the vocal expression (*vacībhedavāca*) primary in the term "right speech.

However, for right speech that consists of the abstinence of attainment (*sampattavirati*) and the abstinence of eradication (*samucchedavirati*), there is no function (*kicca*) by way of vocal expression. This is the function of abstinence (*viratikicca*).

The phrase beginning with “Furthermore” (*apicā*) was stated in order to show that it is a basis for exertion (*padhāna*). “While occurring” (*pavattamānā*) means because of its state of occurring; this is a qualifying causal term. 112–113.
There is nothing further to be said regarding right action (*sammākammanta*) or right livelihood (*sammāājīva*). 114.

“The object that has arrived” (*sampattaṃ vatthuṃ*) refers to the object of the act of killing living beings and so forth. That [consciousness] has only the present as its object (*paccuppannārammaṇa*).
Why? Because the basis possesses its own characteristic by way of being present to one’s own direct experience.

Regarding the phrase, “Or it arises for one who undertakes [the precept]”: this refers to the abstinence that arises at the very moment of undertaking, such as when one undertakes the training by saying, “I shall abstain from taking life,” and so forth.
But as for the statement, “That, moreover, has a present object”—how is it that it has a present object?
When one says, "I shall abstain from taking life," the mind gradually proceeds by making the meaning of the words "life" and so forth its object.
In this context, "life" (pāṇo) is, in conventional usage, a living being; in the ultimate sense, it is the life-faculty (jīvitindriya).
And that living being, as well as that life-faculty, exists at all times in the world. Such a life-faculty...
It is stated that they have present objects with reference to the commonality [of all beings]. The same principle applies to such passages as, "I abstain from taking what is not given," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "having future objects," for one who undertakes the precept by fixing upon a single day, there are beings existing on that very day, and there are also beings yet to arise; both of these are included in the term "living beings" (*pāṇa*).

It is indeed included. For one who undertakes it for as long as life lasts (*pāṇupetaṃ*), there is nothing further to be said. Moreover, there is indeed an undertaking even with respect to the future:
"From such-and-such a day onwards, I shall abstain from taking life for as long as I live," and so forth.
Thus, an undertaking of abstinence regarding the future is also effective. Regarding the phrase "by way of cutting off the conditions": each respective...
By way of the total eradication of the condition known as the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) of the defilements (*kilesa*). The rest here is easy to understand.

115–116. Regarding the pair of *appamaññā* (immeasurables): in the passage beginning with "Furthermore" (*apica*), the phrase "in existence, which is the source of the Kali age" refers to the existence of *saṃsāra*, which is the condition for the arising of suffering.
Regarding "in the defeat of the evil Kali," the meaning is that the word *kali* applies both to evil and to defeat.

Compassion (*karuṇā*) is so called because by means of it one protects beings from misfortune (*kali*). In the phrase "from beings" (*sattehi*), the ablative case (*apādāna*) is used for the sense of protection when that sense is intended;
as in the expression, "They protect the rice from the crows. Alternatively, compassion is so called because by means of it one protects beings who have fallen into misfortune.
In the word "fallen into misfortune" (*kalito*), the ablative case is used for the sense of protection even when that sense is not intended; as in the expression, "from evil thoughts."
"Restrain [the mind]. Even when the immeasurables (appamaññā) are occurring toward a single being, they are still called "immeasurables.
This is just as omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa), even when it occurs with respect to a single object, remains omniscient knowledge itself. 117.
There is nothing further to be said regarding the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya).
The illumination of the beautiful heap is finished.
118. *Ettāvaṃ* means "having this much as its measure. By the phrase "*ettāvatā*" (by this much), it refers to the sequence of terms beginning with "contact, feeling, perception," and so forth.
Regarding the expression "*cittuppādesu*" (in the arising of consciousness): "Which states are to be abandoned by vision? The four [types of] views associated with wrong view..."

Regarding the phrase "arising of consciousness" (*cittuppāda*) and so forth: a collection of consciousness and mental factors is called an "arising of consciousness. However, in this context, it is said that "consciousnesses themselves are called 'arisings of consciousness,'" which is why he explains:
"'In the arisings of consciousness' means simply 'in consciousnesses. Regarding the phrase "because of being the weakest of all":

because it is weaker than all other consciousnesses. Regarding the phrase "by the power of development": by access concentration (*upacāra*) joined with the weapon of the fading away of applied thought (*vitakka-virāga-satti*).
“By the power of development” means by the power of insight-development leading to emergence. “Because it is the leader of the powers” means because it leads the factors that are powers;
because it is the eldest among them. 119. Regarding the unwholesome mental concomitants:
“The last one” refers to the statement [applying] to all twelve wholesome types of consciousness as well.
“Of the former” means: [it refers] to the statement that all [mental factors] are common to the wholesome.
Why is it said that they are common to all unwholesome [states]? Because they are found in all [unwholesome] minds, etc.;
therefore, the statement is a proof that they are common to all wholesome [states]. Furthermore, because these [factors] do not arise without these four [roots], [they are established as such].
Therefore, the construction is: "they are found in all of those. To the question "Why do they not arise without [them]? he says: "Because they are not beneficial," and so forth.

"By them" means by the evils; the meaning is "from all evil states. "Having touched them in such and such a way" means one touches the aggregates with views such as "they are permanent, stable, eternal," and so on.
Or, pride touches them with thoughts such as "I am," or "I am superior," "equal," and so forth.
Having touched [them] in such and such a way. “Among them” (tesu) refers to those possessing views and conceit; this is the locative case used for selection (*niddhāraṇa*).
The construction is: “view proceeds by misapprehending. “That apprehended mode” means that sign-mode which is apprehended as “I am.

Those for whom personality-view (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) alone is their destination are called “those whose destination is view”; they are those in whom personality-view has not been suppressed. “Apprehending ‘I am’” means...

They grasp through conceit (*māna*). The construction is as follows: "Not indeed like conceit" means that while conceit has an activity in the grasping of a self (*attasampaggahaṇa*), such an activity in the grasping of a self does not exist for view (*diṭṭhi*).
And here, "grasping of a self" refers to the thorough grasping of oneself as superior and so forth in relation to others. "And not like view" [is the further comparison].
The construction is: "Just as there is an activity in the conceptualization of a side that is not in accordance with reality regarding phenomena through [wrong] view.
In this context, "a side that is not in accordance with reality" refers to such views as "the self is eternal" or "it is annihilated," and so forth.

Anticipating the objection that "miserliness (macchariya) must be associated with greed (lobha) because it arises from a greed characterized by attachment to one's own excellences," he says, "But as for miserliness... and so on. In this regard:
“Of those” means of one’s own attainments. The rest here is easy to understand. 120.

Regarding the beautiful mental factors (*sobhana-cetasika*): “In the three aggregates” refers to the aggregate of virtue (*sīla-kkhandha*), the aggregate of concentration (*samādhi-kkhandha*), and the aggregate of wisdom (*paññā-kkhandha*).
“Right view is the last” means that it follows after [the others], being subsequent to right view. Regarding right view...
The meaning is that it is accompanied by its retinue. “Even when that is absent” means even when that right intention is absent in the paths and so forth belonging to the second jhāna.
“But among the factors of the aggregates of virtue and concentration”: the three factors—right speech, right action, and right livelihood—are called the factors of the aggregate of virtue;
right effort, right mindfulness, [and right concentration are the factors of the aggregate of concentration].
Right concentration—these three factors are called the aggregate of concentration. Regarding these aggregates of virtue and concentration:
"One does not accomplish the function of another. Thus, right speech does not accomplish the function of right action;
it does not accomplish the function of right livelihood; and right action does not accomplish the function of right speech, and so forth.

Everything should be stated. Regarding the phrase "by way of practicing the precepts in their entirety," the intended meaning is "by way of completely severing those states that are opposed to the precepts.
The construction is as follows: one is able to abandon false speech itself through the abstention from false speech, but not the others, such as malicious speech and so forth.
Here, it might be argued: "Abstention from false speech is indeed a wholesome state (*kusala-dhamma*), and a wholesome state..."
It is the antidote to every unwholesome state (*akusala-dhamma*). One might say that when even a single wholesome state arises, all unwholesome states can be abandoned within that continuum.
Nevertheless, it is stated that the abstention from false speech (*musāvāda-virati*) is able to abandon only false speech, and not the others. How is this to be understood?
It is said: "He is able to abandon"—this refers to abandonment by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgappahāna*) among the five types of abandonment.

Abandonment by substitution of opposites means the abandoning of each respective unwholesome factor by means of its corresponding wholesome factor; this is called abandonment by substitution of opposites.
What is meant here is that a person of integrity [undertakes] the training rules individually, such as: "I shall abstain from taking life," and so forth.
Having undertaken it, one abandons the unwholesome factor known as the taking of life by means of the wholesome factor known as abstention from the taking of life.
One abandons the unwholesome factor known as taking what is not given by means of the wholesome factor known as abstention from taking what is not given;
in this manner, it should be elaborated. Even when a single wholesome state arises within that continuum...

Regarding the statement "all unwholesome states do not arise," they do not arise here simply because there is no opportunity for them to do so, not because they have been abandoned. For it is not the case that only those unwholesome states fail to arise in that continuum at that moment;
rather, all other wholesome consciousnesses also do not arise, and all indeterminate consciousnesses likewise do not arise.
Those states do not arise simply because they are non-existent; they do not arise because they have been abandoned.
However, with reference to abandonment by way of "abandonment by substitution of opposites" (*tadaṅgappahāna*) and so forth, it is said here that one "is able to abandon" or "is not able to abandon.
To this extent, what is called "abandonment by substitution of opposites" becomes clearly manifest. Regarding the abstention from false speech, one is able to abandon false speech itself.

"Not others" means that this is also well-established. Regarding the passage beginning with "And here," those [factors] occurring for the purpose of moving a limb of the body or a limb of speech are called "bodily and vocal intimation.

The abstinences (virati) are seen only among the wholesome states of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara). In the phrase "among the wholesome states of the sense-sphere," the locative case is used in the sense of selection (niddhāraṇa). Within the plane of the sense-sphere...
These are indeed seen only among those wholesome states of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).
Furthermore, the three bases of hypocrisy (*kuhana*) are situated within the category of things to be abstained from. Here, "hypocrisy" (*kuhana*) means deceiving;

it is said to be the performance of various acts of guile and fraud toward people in order to obtain gain, honor, and fame, thereby creating a state of wonder and amazement. That, moreover, is threefold: "hypocrisy regarding the use of requisites," and...

Deceit consists of whispering to neighbors and deceit regarding the maintenance of deportment. In that regard, while being one who actually has great desire, one displays the appearance of having few desires;
having initially refused the four requisites when they arrived or were departing, one later accepts them in great abundance once they have arrived.
This is called "deceit regarding the use of requisites. While being one who actually has evil desires...

Desiring honor—thinking, "May people esteem me as one who has attained meditative absorption (jhāna), or as one who has attained direct knowledge (abhiññā), or as an Arahant"—one deceives others by placing oneself near those who possess superhuman qualities (uttarimanussadhamma) or by placing them near oneself.
This is called the hypocrisy of "borderland chatter" (sāmantajappana-kuhana). Being possessed of evil desires, one [claims]: "This person is of peaceful conduct, concentrated, and energetic."
Desiring to be esteemed by others, thinking "May people hold me in high regard," one performs various deceptions based on one's deportment.
This is called the hypocrisy of maintaining a formal posture (*iriyāpatha-ṭhapanā-kuhana*).

"Subjects of the training rules" refers to drinking fermented liquor, eating at improper times, watching or listening to dancing, singing, and instrumental music, and so forth. For one undertaking the vow, "I shall abstain from drinking fermented liquor and spirits":
The volition regarding the drinking of fermented liquor and spirits is called the "object to be abstained from.

For one undertaking the vow, "I abstain from eating at improper times," the volition of consuming an item that is permissible only during the proper time at an improper time is called the "object to be abstained from.

The same principle applies to the remaining [precepts] as well. Regarding supramundane consciousnesses (*lokuttara-citta*), there are three [terms]: "in every respect" (*sabbathāpi*), "fixed" (*niyata*), and "either/or" (*ekato vā*).
These are the qualifications. Regarding the mundane [attainments], however, there are two pairs of qualifications: "at times" and "separately.

Therein, among the supramundane attainments, "in every way" refers to the vision of abandonment by eradication (*samucchedappahāna*); whereas among the mundane attainments, its opposite—the vision of abandonment by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgappahāna*)—is intended.
Having taken this into account, it is said: "or by way of the abandonment of each respective type of misconduct."
121. Regarding the *Appamaññā* (Immeasurables): “In the *Vibhaṅga*” means in the analysis of the immeasurables.

“Of one whose nature is compassion” means of one whose essential character is compassion. “Free from envy” means devoid of the quality of jealousy. Established compassion abandons cruelty (*vihiṃsā*) arising from hatred.
Established sympathetic joy (*muditā*) abandons discontent (*arati*) arising from hatred; thus it is said: “The escape from cruelty and discontent.”
"Beings. Herein, "discontent" (*arati*) refers to weariness with secluded dwellings and with meditative practices.

When there is an escape from aversion (*dosa*), the escape from mental distress (*domanassa*) is also necessarily established. And this "escape" occurs by way of the stabilization of the opposing state.
Therefore, it is with the underlying intention that one should understand the constant stabilization of joy (*somanassa*) within the immeasurables (*appamaññā*) even during the preliminary stage.
He said, “And as the opposite of mental distress,” and so forth. Regarding the phrase “contradictory even with the Commentary”:

in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, it is stated that in the case of sense-sphere wholesome consciousnesses accompanied by equanimity, the arising of compassion (*karuṇā*) and gladness (*muditā*) is indeed permitted by the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* even at the time of the preliminary stage (*parikamma*). Therefore, [this view] is contradictory even with that Commentary.
The rest here is easy to understand. As for the statement, "But regarding repulsive objects...
there is nothing at all to be said," this means that repulsive objects are far removed from joy (*somanassa*); likewise, suffering beings are also far removed from it.

Therefore, at the beginning, both the mind in the development of foulness (*asubha-bhāvanā*) and the mind in the development of compassion (*karuṇā-bhāvanā*) are accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā-sahagata*). They are neither [joyful nor sorrowful].

There is nothing at all that needs to be said. By the phrase “equanimity of feeling pertaining to the sense sphere,” the equanimity of feeling belonging to the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara*) is meant.
In the reading of the *Vibhāvanī*, the phrase “even for one whose mind is directed elsewhere” means even for one who is attending to another object. The ellipsis of the text is “recitation succeeds;
comprehension succeeds. Thus, for that reason. Here it might be argued: “That has been rejected.”

Why was it said? [Is it not the case that] even in minds accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā-sahagata-citta*), the arising of compassion (*karuṇā*) and sympathetic joy (*muditā*) is indeed established?
True, it is indeed established. However, by means of that [equanimity], he illustrates their arising in those [minds] through the power of familiarity (*paricaya*).
But here, by the phrases beginning with "and herein" (*ettha ca*) and "in repulsive and delightful objects" (*paṭikūla-rammaṇesu*), he shows that they arise naturally, without such familiarity.

It is said that for them, the predominance of occurrence is only together with the feeling of equanimity (*upekkhā-vedanā*). "By the power of the application of yoga" means by the power of the effort (*vīriya*) of one who is engaged in practice.
"Of those whose minds are yoked" refers to the mind and mental factors (*citta-cetasika*). Regarding the phrases beginning with "And here," it was stated previously: "Sometimes..."
“They appear individually; sometimes they arise having become distinct. And he will say further on:
“In this context, however, the five immeasurables and the abstinences should each be applied separately.

Regarding envy and the others, their occasional conjunction as distinct factors will be stated further on: “Envy, stinginess, and worry, however, should each be applied separately in this context. [Regarding] conceit and sloth...

However, regarding the various types of sloth (*middha*), a specific application must here be stated. Having said "sometimes" (*kadāci*), he explains that meaning with the words beginning "of those" (*tesaṃ*).
"Of those" refers to those dissociated from wrong view. "By way of being overcome by sleep" is an illustrative statement;
by this, it should be understood that indolence (*kosajja*) and so forth are also included. "By way of unwieldiness" means by way of the state of being unworkable.
By means of those [states of] envy, avarice, and worry, and by that conceit—there is diversity when there is opposition in function or opposition in object;
there is coexistence when there is no opposition. 123.
“By way of delimiting the bases of conjunction”: first, regarding those common to all consciousness, in all ninety-eight types of consciousness-arising, [they are present].

[The first type is] by way of the enumeration, number, and delimitation of those consciousnesses that constitute the appropriate instances, such as "there are fifty-five kinds of wisdom in the states with consciousness.
[The second type is] "by way of the delimitation of the heaps of associated phenomena," such as "there are thirty-six in the supramundane, thirty-five in the sublime," and so on;
this is by way of the enumeration, number, and delimitation of the heaps of associated phenomena. The rest is easy to understand. "In the Pāḷi" means...
In the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* Pāḷi: “Of those methods” means of the fourfold and fivefold methods.
(124) “With the function of purifying body and speech” means with the function of purifying the door of the body and the door of speech.
(125) Because the supramundane abstinences arise even in the supramundane resultants, it says: “And this... should be seen.”

Of those immeasurables (*appamaññā*). Of those great resultant states (*mahāvipāka*). The analysis of the compound is: that which has "the seven designations" (*sattapaññatti*) and so forth as its object.
"By that" means by the wholesome state (*kusala*). "Because it is devoid of conceptualization" (*vikappa-rahitattā*) means because it is devoid of thinking in various modes.
"Produced by specific kammic states that have reached absorption" (*appanāpatta-kamma-visesa-nibbattā*). These are called "specific designations."
The earth-kasiṇa sign and so forth. Regarding the phrase “Api ca” (but also) and so on: there is no designation (paññatti) that exists apart from the phenomena (dhammas).
And this being the case, even designations—which are the objects of sensual craving and have the result of sensuality—would also become cognitive objects (ālambana).

[The phrase] “those which effect the classification according to the method of inclusion” refers to those which effect the classification according to the method of inclusion, such as: thirty-six in the first-jhāna consciousnesses, thirty-five in the second-jhāna consciousnesses, and so forth.

126. Regarding the passage beginning with “And here,” etc.: “In the five unprompted [consciousnesses]” is a locative expression used for specification (*niddhāraṇa*). Likewise for “in the five prompted [consciousnesses]. The rest here is easy to understand. 128.

“By way of distinction of plane, class, association, and so forth”: Contact itself is fourfold—belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), and the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*).
This is the distinction of plane. There are twelve unwholesome contacts and twenty-one wholesome ones.
There are thirty-six resultant [consciousnesses] and twenty functional;

such is the classification by way of birth (jāti). The classification by way of association and so forth should be stated as follows: "accompanied by joy," "associated with views," "unprompted," "prompted," and so on.
"Classification equal to that of consciousness" means either by itself or by what is associated with it.
"By way of the division of consciousness" means a division equal [to the number of] the sixty-nine types of consciousness.
Herein, doubt is associated with only one mental factor in a single type of consciousness, thus it is one alone.
Hatred, envy, avarice, and worry—these four are associated with two types of consciousness each, thus they are two each separately. Likewise, wrong view and conceit are each fourfold.
"Stiffness and torpor are each fivefold," and so forth—all should be stated accordingly.
The sub-commentary (*Anudīpanā*) to the *Cetasikasaṅgahadīpanī* is finished.
3. Sub-commentary to the *Pakiṇṇakasaṅgaha*.

129. In the Compendium of Miscellaneous Items (*Pakiṇṇaka-saṅgaha*): Regarding both consciousness (*citta*) and mental factors (*cetasika*), "thirty-five" means thirty-fivefold. "State" (*bhāva*) refers to an existing activity;
that which is called the "characteristic" (*lakkhaṇa*) among the characteristic, function (*rasa*), and so forth. Therefore, he said "of phenomena" (*dhammānaṃ*) and so on.

The word "occurrence" (*pavatta*) is a supplementary term [to be supplied]. By this, it is also understood in such passages as: "The compendium of consciousness and mental factors by way of feeling," and so forth.
By the phrase "the grouping of mind and mental factors occurs through the division of feeling," he shows the connection.
Regarding the statement, "The meaning of the words has been shown," he asks how it is shown and replies with "the grouping of mind and mental factors through the division of feeling," and so forth.
In the phrase "Now, of these as appropriate," "of these" refers to mind and mental factors; the connection is that this is what is called "grouping."
By this, it is established that this "compendium" (*saṅgaha*) is indeed a compendium of consciousness (*citta*) and mental factors (*cetasika*). The connection is as follows:
"From the perspective of feeling" (*vedanā-hetuto*), etc., up to "from the perspective of the object and the basis" (*ārammaṇa-vatthuto*), it is called a "compilation" (*saṅgaho*).

By this, it is established that in the subsequent sections such as "the compendium of feeling" (*vedanā-saṅgaho*) and so forth, "compilation from the perspective of feeling" means "feeling-compilation" (*vedanā-saṅgaho*), and likewise, up to "compilation from the perspective of the basis" means "basis-compilation" (*vatthu-saṅgaho*). This applies to the terms beginning with "from the perspective of feeling."
And the phrase "by way of the division of feeling" and so forth is established in meaning. Thus, the literal meaning of the six miscellaneous groupings has been shown.
Therefore, he said, "by way of the division of feeling," and so on; the connection is that [the grouping] is "shown by means of" [that phrase].
Because it was stated, "what is called a 'grouping' is led forth," it was said, "there is what is called 'led forth'. And the meaning of "is led forth" is "is set in motion."
[Objection: "But surely, since it is said that 'this inclusion is led forth,' this inclusion must be led forth by the two—consciousness and mental factors alone.

[Reply: No. This is because it is stated, beginning with "But when consciousness is established," in order to show that once consciousness has been led forth, there is no separate function for the mental factors to perform.

130. Regarding "feeling" (*vedanā*) in the context of inclusion (*saṅgaha*): because this inclusion occurs based on the classification of feeling, it is stated as "for the purpose of grasping the supporting phenomena" (*nissaya-dhamma-pariggahatthaṃ*). "In the *Saṃyutta*" means in the *Vedanā-saṃyutta*.

"They experience the object" means they experience the flavor of the object. "They" refers to those who feel. "That" refers to that object. "From the pleasant" means from the mode of pleasure (*sukhākārato*).

“From what is afflicted” means from that which causes suffering. There is no other assistance than that; therefore, the construction is that feeling is indeed threefold by way of its characteristic of experiencing.
“Two” refers to two feelings. Alternatively, the construction is that two feelings are stated by including equanimity within happiness, namely, happiness and suffering.
“While this sublime happiness exists” refers to that which is associated with meditative absorption (*jhāna*) and is not suffering.
This was said with reference to pleasure (*sukha*). The detailed explanation regarding the five types of feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth should be taken from the *Vedanā-saṃyutta*.
"To be felt" (*vedayita*) and "feeling" (*vedanā*) are one in meaning. "All that is within suffering" means that all that is to be felt is indeed included within suffering.
"It was with reference to the suffering inherent in formations (*saṅkhāra-dukkhatā*) and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-dukkhatā*), Ānanda, that I spoke."
"Whatever is felt, all that is included in suffering"—this is the Pāḷi. "By way of the distinction of faculties" means:
accompanied by joy, accompanied by equanimity, accompanied by grief, accompanied by pleasure, and accompanied by pain—thus, by way of the distinction of faculties.
"In which phenomena" means: in the associated phenomena. "Of those" refers to the associated [phenomena].
Of phenomena (*dhammā*). Therein, phenomena associated with pleasure are twofold: by way of being associated with bodily pleasure and associated with mental pleasure.

Thus, because the associated phenomena that occupy the position of sovereignty are twofold, one divides the single feeling of pleasure among the three feelings according to their specific modes of experience, [establishing] the faculty of pleasure (*sukhindriya*) and the faculty of mental joy (*somanassindriya*).
It has been stated. This same method applies to those phenomena associated with suffering (*dukkha*) as well. “Moreover” (*api ca*) means that there is something further to be said.

“Those too” (*te pi*) refers even to those phenomena associated with equanimity (*upekkhā*). The “sensitive bodies of the eye and so forth” (*cakkhādi-pasāda-kāyā*) are the sensitive bodies of the eye, ear, nose, and tongue.
“Dependent upon them” (*tesu nissitā*) refers to the arising of consciousness such as eye-consciousness and the like. “Because of their existence” (*sabbhāvā*)—

The construction is: they are twofold by way of their state of peace (*santabhāva*) and their state of being manifest (*saṃvijjamānabhāva*). “Because of having a single flavor” means because of having a single flavor through the state of neutrality (*majjhattabhāva*).
“The others” refers to the faculties of joy, grief, and equanimity. The rest here is easy to understand. 131. In the *Hetusaṅgaha*:
“The accomplishment of the state of being well-established” means they are well-established (*suppatiṭṭhita*) because they establish themselves firmly.

The construction is: "The function of the cause (hetu-kicca) is called the 'accomplishment of the state of being well-established' (suppatiṭṭhita-bhāva-sādhana). "'These states as well' (imepi dhammā)" refers to these six causal states.
"'Therein' (tattha)" means among those objects; they accomplish [the result]. Therefore, it is said: "The function of the cause is called the 'accomplishment of the state of being well-established'.
"'But others,' however," refers to the Elder Revata, who appeared in the discussion on the meaning of *paṭṭhāna*.

The doctrine: "The establishment of the wholesome and other states of phenomena" means the establishment of the wholesome nature, the unwholesome nature, and the indeterminate nature of co-nascent phenomena. "If this were so," and so forth, is the statement of refutation by those who reject that doctrine.
"Of which" refers to delusion in the two types of consciousness rooted in delusion, as well as delusion in rootless consciousness-arising and matter.

And regarding the *nibbānas*: “It would not succeed” means that, due to the absence of a co-nascent cause (*sahajāta-hetu*), the state of unwholesomeness (*akusala-bhāva*) of that delusion (*moha*) would not be established, nor would the states of wholesomeness or indeterminate-ness (*abyākata-bhāva*) of the other [associated] factors be established.

This is what is meant: it has been stated that a cause indeed establishes the wholesome and other qualities of co-nascent phenomena. This being so, that delusion [would not establish] the unwholesome nature of the associated phenomena.
One would have to establish its state as unwholesome. However, for that which establishes its own unwholesome state, there is no other co-nascent cause.

Therefore, its state as unwholesome would not be established. Likewise, since there is no such thing as a co-nascent cause for establishing the indeterminate state of rootless consciousness-arising, matter, and Nibbāna, their state as indeterminate would also not be established.
And it is not the case that it does not succeed. Therefore, that doctrine of the Elders is not logical. Herein, it might be argued:
"That delusion is unwholesome by its own nature; and those rootless consciousness-arising, matter, and Nibbāna are indeterminate by their own nature.
This being so, just as those phenomena are, so too other phenomena [would be] by their own nature.
In this way, they would become wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.

And there is no reason here by which those same phenomena, by their own intrinsic nature (*dhammatā*), are unwholesome or indeterminate, while other phenomena, by their own intrinsic nature, are not wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate, but [only] by means of causes.
Therefore, for all of them, whether wholesome and so forth—
There is no purpose in [postulating] causes for the sake of an existing state. Therefore, that Theravāda position is indeed not tenable.
Furthermore, there is not only this much fault in that Theravāda; rather, to show that there is yet another fault as well, he said, "And those which...
and so forth. Herein, this is the intended meaning: if the state of phenomena—such as being wholesome and so on—were dependent upon co-nascent causes, [then...]
This being the case, material phenomena (rūpa) obtained from a wholesome cause (hetu) through its conditions would themselves be wholesome;
material phenomena obtained from an unwholesome cause would themselves be unwholesome. But they are not so. Therefore, that position is indeed untenable.
Now, in order to reaffirm that same Theravāda position, he says: "Just as... and so forth.
“In phenomena” means among the phenomena of the Four Noble Truths. The activity of delusion is called the activity of darkness.
“Desire for the Dhamma” refers to the desire that arises through such thoughts as wishing to give a gift, wishing to fulfill ethical discipline, or wishing to develop meditation.
“Intolerance” means not enduring, not finding pleasure in, or being displeased with. Evil states are opposed to evil objects.

The mind’s opposition to the sevenfold sexual intercourse and other evil states that serve as bases for sensual lust, as well as to the delightful objects of the five strands of sense pleasure, is loathsome and repulsive.
However, the act of delusion itself is exclusively of an unwholesome nature. To this extent, in the two types of consciousness rooted in delusion, delusion is unwholesome by its own inherent nature.
This establishes the point. The passage beginning with "If this were so" dispels the attribution of fault to that [position].

Now, in order to establish the point that mind-moments arising without roots (ahetuka-cittuppāda), material phenomena (rūpa), and Nibbāna are indeterminate (abyākata) by their own inherent nature (dhammatā), he says, "And whatever phenomenon...
and so forth. By saying "only this much," he indicates that there is no other difficult-to-understand reason.
The intention [is as follows]: “Of rootless consciousnesses” means of those consciousness-arising-moments that are without roots. Established by its own intrinsic nature (*attano dhammatāya*) alone.
By this much—“rootless,” etc.—it establishes this point: that the *nibbānas* are indeterminate (*abyākata*) by their own intrinsic nature.
The passage beginning with “This being so” removes the attribution of faults therein. Now, all delusion (*moha*) itself...
By way of the nature of things (*dhammatā*), it is established that unwholesome states exist;

and in order to demonstrate that even those factors such as desire (*icchā*) and impatience (*akkhanti*)—which are mentioned in the sense that "others have desire" and "others have impatience"—are indeed unwholesome, he says, "In this context, delusion (*moha*)," and so forth.
"They are simply the outflows (*nissanda*) of delusion" means they are merely the resultant fruits of the activity of deluding. Not only [is this true] for greed (*lobha*) and the rest...

It establishes the unwholesome nature [of greed and hatred]; however, it is stated, "And of non-greed, etc.," in order to show that he likewise establishes the wholesome nature of non-greed and the others.

"Established together with the underlying tendency of ignorance" means that those [states] are wholesome as long as the underlying tendency of ignorance has not been abandoned within the continuum of a being;
the intention is that when it is abandoned, they become functional (kiriya). Now, regarding greed and hatred, and non-greed and the others...
In order to show the function of the cause (*hetu-kicca*), it was said: “But those [states], greed and so forth,” and so on.

“Outflows of lust, hatred, and delusion” (*rajanādi-nissandāni*) means the outflows resulting from lust, hatred, and delusion. “Views, conceit, and so forth” refers to views, conceit, envy, avarice, and so on.

“Outflows of non-lust, non-hatred, and non-delusion” (*arajjanādi-nissandāni*) means the outflows resulting from non-lust, non-hatred, and non-delusion. “Faith and so forth” refers to faith, mindfulness, and so on.

[This refers to] shame (hiri), fear of wrongdoing (ottappa), and so forth. Regarding the phrase "also by way of cause": it is stated that the indeterminate (abyākata) nature of rootless (ahetuka) consciousness-arising, material phenomena (rūpa), and Nibbāna is established by their own intrinsic nature (attano dhammatāya).

However, the intention is that while the indeterminate nature of resultant (vipāka) and functional (kriyā) states accompanied by roots (sahetuka) is established by their own intrinsic nature, it is also appropriate to say it is established by the causal function (hetu-kicca) of the co-nascent roots (sahajāta-hetu).
In the *Vibhāvanī* commentary: “To be sought” (*maggitabbo*) means to be investigated. Then, the construction is as follows:

“the state of those [factors], such as wholesomeness (*kusala*), etc., might be bound by other associated causes. “Unbound” (*appaṭibaddha*) means not bound by a cause. “The state of wholesomeness, etc.
(*kusalādibhāvo*) means it would be the state of wholesomeness, etc. “Of those without a cause” (*ahetukānaṃ*) refers to mind-moments and matter that are without a root-cause (*ahetuka*).
Regarding the [two] types of *nibbāna*: now, rejecting the statement beginning with “those conditions which have obtained their causes,” he says “*yathāca*” and so forth.

In the phrase “among material and immaterial phenomena” (*rūpārūpa-dhammesu*), the locative case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*). “Only among immaterial phenomena” is the object being selected.
They do not pervade material phenomena. This being the case, why are those material phenomena mentioned among those things arisen through the condition of *jhāna*?
He said, beginning with “But those,” and so forth. The rest here is easy to understand.
“But that of theirs” refers to that specific color of those [beings], such as the swans and others. “Bases” (*yoniyo*) means the births from mother and father.

“But for the indeterminate, all” means that for indeterminate states, the state of being indeterminate is bound to the continuum (*santāna*), bound to karma, and bound to the state of non-resultantness.
"All this should be understood as 'bound' (baddho ca)"—the intention is that this is entirely included within that aforementioned position. 132. In the *Kiccasaṅgaha*:
"In that [state] which is completely exhausted" is the connection. "'Of karma'" means of another karma. "'The rebirth of a deceased being'" is the connection.
"'By way of the linking together of another existence and so forth'" refers to another existence (*bhavantara*).
“By way of rebirth-linking from the very beginning” means by way of the continuity of existence (*bhavasantāna*).
To the question “How does it proceed?”, he says: “As long as that karma,” and so forth.

“By way of being a factor through uninterrupted proceeding as a condition” means by way of being a factor designated as the primary condition for uninterrupted proceeding. By this, he explains the meaning of the word *aṅga* (factor) in the term *bhavaṅga* (life-continuum).

Therefore he said, “Of that,” and so forth. “Of that” means of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). “Adverting” (āvajjana) and “turning toward” (āvaṭṭana) have one meaning. Or, it is one [explanation]: “it adverts to that.
“That” refers to the mental continuum (cittasantāna). Or, it is one: “it turns toward that herein.

Or, it is one: “it turns toward that by means of this. “That” refers to the mental continuum. Or, it is one: “it causes to advert. “Determining” (voṭṭhabbana) is the prefix *vi-* plus *ava-* plus *ṭhapana* (placing).
Word-breakdown: *Vibhāvani* means investigation. Regarding the phrase “from the adverting consciousness and the preliminary consciousness (*ekāvajjana-parikamma-cittato*”), the analysis is:

that which has a single, identical adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*)—whether by way of the Path (*magga*) or direct knowledge (*abhiññā*)—is [the compound]. In that cognitive process (*vīthi*), there are:

adverting, preliminary (*parikamma*), access (*upacāra*), conformity (*anuloma*), and change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*). Here, the preliminary impulsion-consciousness (*javana-citta*) is what is meant by “preliminary consciousness.”
It has been said: “Those” refers to the path-moments and the moments of direct knowledge (*abhiññā-javana*). “Therein” means in that explanatory text.
“For a long duration” means for a long time, by way of falling asleep either throughout the entire night or throughout the entire day.
The rest here is easy to understand. “The place of rebirth-linking” means the locus of the function of rebirth-linking. By way of time...
By the statement, "Name is a single conceptual phenomenon (*paññatti-dhamma*) that has become an object for consciousness separately," this doubt is cleared away:
"Since time does not exist by way of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), how can it be possible for it to be the locus of the occurrence of activities?
The phrase "otherwise" means: if one were not to grasp it in that way, but rather grasp it differently, such that there is no distinction between the various loci of activity. "Itself..."
“Associated with joy” means that sometimes it is itself associated with joy. “That” refers to the investigation (santīraṇa) of joy.

“By way of having obtained a condition” means by way of having obtained the immediately preceding condition (anantara-paccaya). “Even though devoid of the state of repetition” means even though lacking the quality of repetition (āsevana-guṇa);
for that [investigation] is neither a condition in the sense of a repetition-condition (āsevana-paccaya), nor is it an arisen-from-a-condition (paccayuppanna).

"It does not exist. Regarding the statement, "Because it proceeds by the power of preparatory development (*parikamma-bhāvanā*)," this is evident in the sequence of the attainment of fruition (*phala-samāpatti*) within the fruition-impulsions (*phala-javana*). The rest here is easily understood. 133.
In the Compendium of Doors (*Dvāra-saṅgaha*): "Made of a mirror-surface" means fashioned from a mirror-surface. "Only two" means there are only two doors.

“Because they resemble gates” means because they resemble city gates. Regarding the phrase “established by the distinction of kamma and the distinction of the great primary elements,” the analysis (*viggaha*) is:
“that which is established by both the distinction of kamma and the distinction of the great primary elements.

Furthermore, the [mental states] beginning with adverting (*āvajjana*) include the consciousnesses of the cognitive process (*vīthi-citta*). “In which” means in which eye; the connection is that that very eye is called the “eye-door” (*cakkhudvāra*).
“Of those two” refers to the material signs and the process-consciousnesses such as adverting. Regarding the phrase “of the attainment of the state of object and subject”:
here, the attainment of the state of being an object by the material signs is said to be their arrival within the range of the eye-socket;
the attainment of the state of being a subject by the adverting consciousness and the others is said to be their taking those signs as an object.

“Because it has become the path to the face” means because it has become the route to the face. Having thus shown the grammatical construction of the word *dvāra* (door) as an instrument (*karaṇa-sādhana*), he now shows the construction as a locus (*adhikaraṇa-sādhana*) with the words beginning “Alternatively,” etc. “Of forms” means of the signs of form.
By the phrase “the eye itself is the door to the eye,” [it is shown that] the eye itself is the door, [and thus] the “eye-door.”

This demonstrates a restrictive compound (*avadhāraṇa-samāsa*). “The cause has already been stated” means it was stated below, in the section on the mind-door adverting consciousness within the *Cittasaṅgaha*.
All eighty-nine types of consciousness are called the mind-door alone. For it is said in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*:
“It should not be said that this ‘name-mind’ is not the mind-door. “The rebirth-linking [consciousness] is the door alone” means...
The existence at rebirth (*upapattibhava*) is comprised solely of the door produced by kamma (*kammaja-dvāra*).
“And here” means in this *Saṅgaha* treatise. The connection is: “and that corroborative statement. “Therein” refers to the *Vibhāvanī*.
“That is appropriate right there” means that very corroborative statement is appropriate in that specific passage of the Pāḷi. The connection is: “the other two conditions.”
“*Manaṃ cā’ti etthā”ti means: in the sentence “Dependent on mind and mental objects, mind-consciousness arises,” it refers to the word *manaṃ cā*.
In that context, for the arising of impulsive (javana) mind-consciousness, among the four conditions, two conditions are obtained under the phrase *manaṃ cā*:
the life-continuum mind (*bhavaṅga-mano*) which serves as the door, and the advertence mind (*āvajjana-mano*). In the phrase *dhamme cā*, [it refers to] the mental object (*dhammārammaṇa*).
One condition is obtained by way of its classification. By the word *ca* (and), the aggregates associated with mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇa*) are included.

Thus, there are four conditions. Regarding the phrase “*ettha ca*” (and here) in this commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), it is because, by the inherent force of the word *paṭicca* (dependent upon), only those conditions that are present and immediate are intended therein.

Because that is what is intended in the Pāli sentence. Regarding the phrase "of that which is fit to be a door": this refers to that which is fit to serve as the gateway for the occurrence of the object and the subject, according to the method already stated.
By this, it is established that whether objects enter the field of perception or not, and whether consciousnesses proceed through their respective pathways or not, it is immaterial;
rather, the very fitness to serve as a door by virtue of its luminous and clear nature is the essential criterion.
It illuminates. “A conclusion must be reached here” means that a definitive resolution (*sanniṭṭhāna*) must be reached in this matter.

Those [mental states] which have such functions rooted in the transformation of the doors are "possessors of those functions. "They are accomplished by way of kamma" means they proceed within the continuum of a sentient being;
this is the intended meaning. Those minds possess those functions. In the *Vibhāvani* text, [it says] "designated as the mind-door..."

"From the state of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga)" means from the state of the life-continuum known as the mind-door. "Because of not proceeding by way of grasping another object" means that at the time of its occurrence,
having abandoned the object— such as the kamma or the sign of kamma— as it was grasped by the rebirth-linking consciousness,
it does not proceed by way of grasping another object that has come into range at the six doors.

Furthermore, even below [the level of the sense-sphere], it is described by way of its specific functions—namely, adverting, eye-consciousness, receiving, investigating, determining, sense-sphere impulsion, registration, and so forth—as stated in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.
For in this context, "adverting," "receiving," and so on, are names for specific functions (*kicca-visesa*). If one were to say, "No," that should not be said.
“Because it has not been heard thus”: nineteen are called door-freed (*dvāra-vimutta*); six are both door-based and door-freed;
and the sublime resultant states are called door-freed—this has been heard. But it has not been heard that they are door-based and freed.
134. In the Compendium of Objects (*Ārammaṇa-saṅgaha*): “By a weak man” means because he is overcome by illness or overcome by old age.
Or, by a weak man who is unable to stand up, to steady himself, or to move from one place to another without a staff or a rope, a staff or a rope is grasped.
Having grasped it, he stands up; he steadies himself; he moves from one place to another. It is just like this.
The phrase "having become free from conceits" (*amucca mānehi hutvā*) is a textual supplement (*pāṭhaseso*). "Having come" (*āgantvā*) refers to the object (*ārammaṇa*).

In the sense of "having come from here and there by way of being the instrument," if the meaning is "it is taken as an object because it is established separately," then *ālambana* is established, but *ārammaṇa* is not.
If the meaning is "they delight in coming to these," then *ārammaṇa* is established, but *ālambana* is not. And this being so, [the two] are one word.
"Seeing [them] with two kinds of statements is not proper. "Other objects" means objects other than visible forms, such as sound-objects and so forth.
"It comes" means it goes to manifestation; by way of its arising and occurrence, it reaches the state of being directly perceived (*paccakkha*).
"It has come" means it has gone to manifestation; by way of its arising and occurrence, it has reached the state of being directly perceived.
Regarding the term “anāgata” (not-yet-come): here, the negative particle (*na*) does not function as a negation of a state.
Any phenomenon (*dhamma*) which, when the conditions are assembled, is of a nature to come, has the habit of arising—that very same thing is now coming, or it came just now;
it stands within the process of its future arrival. By this sense—that it neither comes nor has come—it is called “anāgata. [This refers to] Nibbāna.
Designations (*paññatti*), however, do not have arising as their nature. Therefore, because there is no possibility of their coming [into being], they are not said to be "not yet come.
For this reason, he said: "They have arising as their nature," and so forth. Having stated, "That must be investigated," he shows the manner of investigation with the words, "All of them," and so on.
The connection is: "When those stand on the side of being subject to expression... [Arising...]
[This refers] to conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhammā*) that are of the same nature. Regarding those designations of Nibbāna:

the construction is that "not so for these"—that is, the object of these [states] liberated from the doors does not exist in that way. "Therein" (*tattha*) means in that particular state of existence (*bhava-visesa*).
In the reading of the *Vibhāvanī*, "like the object of adverting consciousness" (*āvajjanassaviyā*) means like the object of adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*). It is simply not grasped.
Having offered [the oblation]: "The state of not being included in the single-moment cognitive process (*ekavajjana-vīthi*) is not the criterion here";
thus, "being included in the six doors" is the criterion here. This is because what was grasped in another existence is intended [as the object].
"A generality independent of time"—the intention is that it is not something that is independent of any time whatsoever. The conventional designation established by scripture is called "kamma."
The terms "sign of the deed" (*kammanimitta*) or "sign of destiny" (*gatinimitta*) refer to well-known conventional designations.
King Ajātasattu killed his own father even in the *Saṅkicca-jātaka*. Therefore, it is said, "in two states of existence.

The phrase "by means of six doors" refers to the six doors, such as the eye, which function as instruments (*karaṇabhūta*). The phrase "by means of death-proximate impulsion-moments" refers to those acting as agents (*kattubhūta*) at the moment of death.
[This occurs] through the six active door-impulsions. “A manifold nature” means a state of non-uniformity (*anekantabhāva*).

The connection is: “whatever object [there may be]. Regarding the phrase “it remains ungrasped by any door whatsoever,” it is logical that for beings passing away from the non-percipient realm (*asaññī-bhava*), the karma and so forth that serve as the object for rebirth-linking in the sense-sphere (*kāma-paṭisandhi*) remain ungrasped by any door in the subsequent existence.
Why? Because in that existence (arūpabhava), there is an absence of any sense-door whatsoever.

To clear away this objection—namely, how an object recognized as the sign of destiny for those passing away from the formless realm could have been grasped by any door in another existence when it is destined to be the object of a sense-sphere rebirth-linking, and thus must have been grasped solely by the mind-door—the text states: "And here, because in the *Paṭṭhāna*... and so forth.
It has been said. Regarding the phrase "of the rebirth-linking of sense-desire (*kāmapaṭisandhi*) for beings who have passed away from there":

the analysis of the compound is "that which has the sign of the destination (*gatinimitta*) of the present as its object. Thus it is "rebirth-linking of sense-desire. It should be connected with such statements as:
"The manifestation of karma and so forth occurs even by the power of another's application. [Regarding] "well-cultivated" (*suṭṭhu āsevitānaṃ*), it means for a long period of time.

“Of those [deeds] well-practiced through the performance of various duties toward the Saṅgha and the Cetiya, and through the practice of various meditative exercises”—it is indeed the case that “there is the appearance” of those deeds and so forth.
“Having come” means that having come to this human world, they seize [the person]. Even then, that particular destiny shown by the wardens of hell—
They pass away making that sign their object. "Her" refers to the woman named Revatī. [Objection:
But surely those called hell-wardens would not be able to go to the Tāvatiṃsa realm? [Reply: They would indeed be able to. Why?
To show that this is because they are of the class of powerful *yakkhas*, the words beginning with "by them" were spoken. "Messengers of Vessavaṇa" refers to the Great King Vessavaṇa.
The messengers say: “Abiding in access concentration” means abiding in sense-sphere jhāna, which constitutes access development because full absorption (appanā) has not yet been reached.
“Those very signs” refers to the counterpart signs, such as the earth-kasiṇa sign and so forth.
“The object for the rebirth-linking of sensual desire” refers to anything suitable other than those sign-objects, such as the kamma of access development.

Or [it is] the sign of the destiny (*gati-nimitta*). By the statement, “Having grasped those very signs,” it is shown that those signs were grasped by the impulsion moments (*javana*) occurring near death.
And because they are conceptual phenomena (*paññatti-dhamma*), they do not become objects for the rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) of the sense-sphere (*kāma*).
“When the sign of the destiny of the present is established, it is indeed established”—[this refers to] one who has gone to that existence; therein...

An object that must be experienced for as long as life lasts exists both as something present, insofar as it is existing at that very moment, and as something future, insofar as it is increasing from there.
Among these, when the present is manifest, it becomes the object of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
However, although the future is not manifest, it is as if included within the present.
This is the intended meaning (*adhippāyo*). According to the reading in the *Vibhāvani*, it appears as if it were a present objective sign (*paccuppanna-gatinimitta*);
why? Because the task is accomplished by the present objective sign alone—this is the intended meaning.

The rest here is easily understood. Regarding the passage beginning with “*Tāni hi*,” some say: [the phrase] “*anejosan”* refers to the Muni, because it is stated that “at whatever time the Muni passed away.”
The death-consciousness (*cuti-citta*) of the Omniscient Buddhas and others takes Nibbāna—characterized by peace—as its object.
To show that this [death-consciousness] must be excluded in every respect from those [states] whose objects belong to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*), it is said:

"Even though those have arisen in the Omniscient Buddhas," and so forth. In the passage beginning with "supramundane states" (*lokuttara-dhammā*), the word "those" (*tāni*) refers to the twelve [types of consciousness].
The wholesome consciousnesses consist of the eight wholesome functional impulsion-moments dissociated from knowledge (*ñāṇa-vippayutta-kusala-kiriya-javanāni*).

It is stated that “together with concepts (*paññatti*), the sense-sphere objects (*kāmāvacara-rāmmaṇāni*)” because ordinary worldlings who have not attained meditative absorption (*ajjhāna-lābhin*) are unable even to take sublime absorptions (*mahaggata-jjhāna*) as their cognitive object.

“Those very ones” refers specifically to the sense-sphere wholesome states associated with knowledge (*ñāṇa-sampayutta-kāma-kusalāni*). For those who have attained meditative absorption, it is only these [states] associated with knowledge that are [the objects].
They are wholesome. The lower fruit-states have as their objects the very paths, fruits, and Nibbāna attained by themselves.
"Aspiring for jhānas" means they make an aspiration, thinking, "May we become attainers of jhāna in the future.
"Of them" means even of those worldlings (puthujjana). "They" refers to those supramundane states. "Experience" means they reach [them].
“In the Navanipāta”: in the Navanipāta of the Aṅguttara Nikāya. The rest is all easily understood. 135. In the *Vatthusangaha*:
“*Vatthu*” refers to a specific basis (*nissaya*). Those [phenomena] which have those as their bases are called “*tabbatthuka*.
Regarding the phrase “the word ‘and’ is not appropriate for them”: the word ‘and’ is not appropriate in their doctrine.
For there is no such thing as a compound word (*dvanda*) that lacks the elision of the case ending (*alutta*).

As for the phrase "it should be brought forward from the preceding words," it means it should be brought forward by way of [stating] "the eye-base and the ear-base," and so forth; however, a compound word (*samāsa-pada*) is not applicable here.
For it is not appropriate to bring a single part of a compound word elsewhere. The mention without a case ending (*avibhattika-niddesa*) is as follows: "eye, ear, nose..."
When it should have been stated as "the tongue, the body, the heart, and the basis" (*vatthu*), there is an indication in the preceding sections without case endings.
This being so, it is permissible to bring both the word *vatthu* and the word *sadda* into the preceding sections.

"Produced by karma dependent on craving for sense-pleasures" means produced by karma that is subject to and reliant upon craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*). "The enjoyment of visible forms and so forth."
The enjoyment of the five strands of sensual pleasure, beginning with visible forms. “Limited karma” refers to all karma belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).
“Fulfilling” means bringing to completion. The eye is called the unsurpassed excellence of seeing; the ear is called the unsurpassed excellence of hearing.
Among all functions of seeing, the vision of the Buddha is the unsurpassed seeing by way of its day.
"Janeti" (begets) refers to the unsurpassed vision. Likewise, regarding the unsurpassed hearing, it should be stated that it consists in the hearing of the Dhamma of the Four Truths.
"In those internal and external continuities" means in both the internal continuity and the external continuity.
"Pure" means devoid of any light and darkness; for light is simply a particular kind of visible form. Similarly...
And there is darkness; yet these do not exist there. "In this compendium" refers to the compendium of bases (*vatthu-saṅgaha*). Discernment (*vijānana*) is distinguished knowing.
And that discernment does not exist in the three mind-elements (*manodhātu*), hence it is said: "due to the absence of the function of discernment.
What is the function of adverting (*āvajjana*)? It is merely attention (*manasikāra*). And the function of receiving (*sampaṭicchana*) [belongs] to the fivefold sense-consciousnesses.
Just as there is merely the reception of the five objects exactly as they are grasped, he said: "The functions of discerning specific distinctions do not exist.
Seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching—these functions involve a slight discernment of specific distinctions;
therefore, it was said: "By means of seeing and so forth through direct perception," and so on. Slight...

The functions of knowing with distinction are [the specific tasks] of these [consciousnesses]. Therefore, they are called the five sense-consciousnesses (*pañcaviññāṇa*). However, the remaining ones, such as investigation (*santīraṇa*) and so forth, are named the mind-consciousness elements (*manoviññāṇadhātu*);

this is the connection [of the sentence]. [Objection: But even if it were said that "mind" (*mano*) is so called in the sense of thinking (*manana*), and "consciousness" (*viññāṇa*) is so called in the sense of cognizing (*vijānana*), there would still be no distinction from the five sense-consciousnesses.
[Reply: He says: "They are elements (*dhātu*) because they know with an exceeding distinction. (*atissaya-visesa-jānana-dhātuyo*)
"the meaning. Even though this is the case, that meaning is not established by grammatical propriety (*saddayutti*); it is stated according to one's own whim.

Therefore, he says "of synonymous terms" (*pariyāya-padānaṃ*) and so forth. By this, he shows that the meaning is established precisely by grammatical propriety, and is not stated according to one's whim.
In the case of a descriptive compound (*visesana-samāsa*), such as "mind-consciousness" (*manoviññāṇaṃ*), where [it is analyzed as] "the mind and that consciousness."
In the *kammadhāraya* compound: regarding the term “*padaṭṭhānaṃ*,” both *pada* and *ṭhāna* are words expressing the sense of a cause;
therefore, they are synonymous terms (*pariyāyasaddā*). When it is said, “that which is both a *pada* and a *ṭhāna*,” the meaning understood is “a preeminent cause.
Likewise, there are such expressions as *dukkhadukkhaṃ*, *rūparūpaṃ*, *rājarājā*, and *devadevo*. In some instances...
"It is neither seen nor is it logical" means that it is not seen anywhere; even if it were seen somewhere, it would still not be logical—this is the meaning.

Regarding the phrase "consciousness of the mind," here the entire continuum of consciousness, from the moment of rebirth-linking up until the moment of death, is explained by dividing it according to the seven elements of consciousness.

It should be stated as follows: the five doors, the adverting consciousness, and the two types of receiving consciousness are called "mind" (*mano*) because they are merely mind-element (*manodhātu*).

The five sense-consciousnesses are called "mere consciousness" (*viññāṇamatta*) because they are merely consciousness. All remaining consciousnesses are called "mental consciousness" (*manoviññāṇa*) in the sense that they are the consciousness of the mind.
In this context, the phrase "consciousness of the mind" refers to that which has become the immediate condition (*anantara-paccaya*).
Or, it is consciousness (viññāṇa) that has arisen conditioned by the mind (mano). Herein, the pair of receiving consciousnesses (sampaticchana) is called "conditioned mind.

From the moment of investigating (santīraṇa) until it reaches the five-sense-door adverting (pañcadvārāvajjana) at another door, the entire continuum of mental consciousness (manoviññāṇa) in that interval is called "consciousness arisen conditioned by [the preceding] consciousness" (paccayuppanna-viññāṇa). Again, [it is said]: "Consciousness of the mind."

Consciousness (*viññāṇa*) is the condition for the mind (*mano*) that has arisen by way of conditions. Herein, the five-door adverting consciousness is called "the mind that has arisen by way of conditions.
Prior to that, the entire continuum of mental consciousness (*manoviññāṇa-santāna*) is called "the mind that is the condition.
The rest is easy to understand. Regarding the phrase "and the remaining ones," etc., the "remaining" refers to [the statement]: "The mind-consciousness element brings about existence."
