Furthermore, these states are called the mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*), and they function only in dependence upon the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*).
Thus, he ascertains and praises the nature of those states as being the mind-consciousness element; the meaning is that he clearly elucidates them.
Regarding the phrase "But here," and so forth: "In the Pāḷi" refers to the Pāḷi of the *Indriya Saṃyutta*. It is precisely in the second jhāna.

The statement regarding "cessation without remainder" would be contradictory. How so? If aversion (*paṭigha*) were not a basis (*vatthu*) for the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), it would have to have ceased even prior to the first jhāna.

If, on the other hand, it were to arise even in the access concentration (*upacāra*) of the second jhāna, then the first jhāna would have been lost. If that [first jhāna] has been lost, the second jhāna as well—

It would not arise. Thus it would be contradictory. "The very first cause" refers to the cause itself, namely the absence of obstruction and the absence of resistance in the material basis (*vatthu*).
What is called "the voice of another" is a primary condition for disciples to attain right view;
however, that does not exist in the formless realm (*arūpabhava*). What is called "the breakthrough to the Dhamma" (*dhammābhisamaya*) is the penetration of the Dhamma of the Four Truths.
The Buddhas and the Paccekabuddhas, being self-enlightened, penetrate the Dhamma without the voice of another;
yet they do not arise there [in the form realm]. “By the development of dispassion toward form” means by the power of the development of dispassion toward form.
“Of those fine-material-sphere consciousnesses”: because of having thoroughly transcended them by way of abandoning attachment to them.
The rest is all easily understood.
The sub-commentary (*anudīpanā*) to the *Pakiṇṇakasaṅgahadīpanī* is finished. 4. Sub-commentary on the Compendium of the Cognitive Process (*Vīthisaṅgaha*).
136. In the *Vīthisaṅgaha*: “Of those very [two]” refers to mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*cetasika*) alone.
“In the manner already stated” means in the manner stated thus: “Therein, first, consciousness is fourfold: sense-sphere, fine-material-sphere,” and so forth.

“Arranged with the former preceding the latter” means arranged with the former preceding the latter according to the method beginning with “Thirty-two [types of] happiness arise from merit. “Of the introductory verse.”
Thus has the compendium of the process of existence been explained by way of the cognitive series during the course of existence;
now, the compendium of the process of existence at the moment of rebirth-linking will be discussed.
In this way, the compendium of the process of existence is established for both the period of the course of existence and the period of rebirth-linking. Some...
In the discourse, when "in rebirth-linking and in the course of existence" (*paṭisandhi pavattiyaṃ*) is taken as a selection (*niddhāraṇa*), the meaning is:

"Of these two—rebirth-linking and the course of existence—I shall now explain the compendium of the course of existence (*pavatti-saṅgaha*), and afterwards I shall explain the compendium of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi-saṅgaha*).
Therein, "compendium of rebirth-linking" refers to the compendium at the time of rebirth-linking; "compendium of the course of existence" refers to [the compendium] during the course of existence.
At the time of its occurrence, there is inclusion (*saṅgaha*). To show that this does not accord with the following verse, he says, "This being so," and so forth.
"Those three hexads have been set down" means that only the hexads have been set down, not the whole [of the Abhidhamma].

The intended meaning is that there is inclusion by way of basis (*vatthu*), door (*dvāra*), and object (*ārammaṇa*). "But that" refers to the occurrence within its specific domain. "Any [occurrence] most rapid" refers to the swiftest [cognition].
Some [consciousness] is exceedingly swift. "Slow" means sluggish or delayed. "Unarisen" means incomplete;
what is meant is that a fault arises because it is incomplete. "Analysis of elements" (*dhātubheda*) refers to the differentiation of the seven consciousness-elements.

"Variety of elements" (*dhātunānatta*) refers to the variety of their respective functions of maintaining [their objects]. Thus, the connection is: therefore, the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is mentioned separately. "Minding" (*manana*) refers to the state of cognizing.
It has not yet been attained. It is merely advertence, merely reception, and merely knowing.
By the phrase “whatever mentation,” even down to mere advertence and mere reception, joy is intended.

But by the phrase “the pure stream of mind-consciousness,” it refers to the stream of mind-consciousness that proceeds in dependence upon a transformation of the mind-door; it does not refer to the stream of mind-consciousness of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
For it is because of being outside the cognitive process (*vīthimutta*) that there is little occasion for this here. However, the connection is "but in the mind-door (*manodvāra*), it is twofold.
The time of the Blessed Buddha’s first resolution (*pathamābhinīhāra*) refers to the time during the era of the ascetic Sumedha when he resolved his body and mind toward Buddhahood.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), one includes the taking of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) in his final existence and so forth. "Birth..."
The intention is that because they are completely pervaded by that radiance, they become like blocks of crystal.
"But for the gods and Brahmās who are born [there]" means for those gods and Brahmās who are of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*) and possess rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
"Of the primary elements that are the support for the sensitive matter" refers to the sensitive bases of the eye and so forth.
“Dependent on the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Regarding the passage beginning with “But those which...”: the construction is that they arrive at the range of impact after having passed through two or three mind-moments (*cittakkhaṇa*).

The same applies elsewhere. As for the terms “of the manifest” (*vibhūta*) and “of the unmanifest” (*avibhūta*), this [refers to] the manifest in the case of the mind-door (*manodvāra*) at the outset.

"And of the unmanifested" (*ca avibhūtassa*) is the extraction of the words. "Of forms, of forms" (*rūpā rūpānaṃ*) refers to both material phenomena (*rūpa-dhamma*) and immaterial phenomena (*arūpa-dhamma*).

"So long" (*tāva*) means that it occurs even earlier than the manifestation of the cognitive process (*vīthi-citta*). "The delimitation of duration" (*addhāna-paricchedaṃ*) means the delimitation of the time of a moment (*khaṇa-kāla*).
In the *Vibhāvanī* commentary, it says: "By means of a day, the determination of the object becomes too vast."

In the beginning, by the statement "six bases, six doors, six objects, six consciousnesses, six cognitive paths, and six occurrences in the objective sphere," among these six sets of six that were thus mentioned, [the author] includes only the phrase "six occurrences in the objective sphere. That is untenable.
Therefore he said, "If this were so," and so forth. [It would be] for the purpose of defining the objective sphere.
It cannot be said that the phrase "measure" (*mā*) was stated solely for the purpose of defining the scope of objects such as "excessively large" and so forth.
In the Abhidhamma, the delimitation of the duration (*addhāna-pariccheda*) of material phenomena (*rūpa-dhammānaṃ*) is intended everywhere.

Therefore, it should be understood that this [term] was also stated for the purpose of demonstrating that. Regarding the phrase "the acquisition of intrinsic nature" (*sabhāvappaṭilābho*), [it refers to] reflection, touching, and so forth.
“Manifestation” (pātubhāvo) is said [to mean appearance]. “Non-retrogression” (anivatti) is said to mean non-disappearance. “Having declined” (parihāyitvā) refers to the function of aging.

“At the moment of snapping the fingers” (accharāsaṅghāṭakkhaṇassa) means at the moment of the clashing of the fingers. The Elder Ācariya Ānanda is said to be the author of the Abhidhamma commentaries.
“The duration of that lightning-flash is not perceived separately” (assā vijjuyā ṭhiti nāma visuṃ na paññāyati) refers to the arising of the lightning-flash.

It is not perceived by those passing [through it]. Likewise, the mind also breaks up immediately after its expansion; such is the construction of the sentence. Therefore he said, “That too,” and so forth.
The "portion of arising" (udayabhāga) refers to the portion of expansion, while the "portion of passing away" (vayabhāga) refers to the portion of disappearance.
“Having done thus” is a statement expressing an acquired quality. “Does one single mind last for a day? is the interrogative statement. “Yes,” [is the reply].
“Paṭiññā” means a statement. “‘Vayakkhaṇo’” is the question. “‘Na hevaṃ vattabbe’” is the negation. The singular ending of the personal pronoun [is used].
The meaning is: “It should not be stated thus. “‘By the Mahāthera’” refers to the Mahāthera Moggaliputta Tissa.
The connection is: “Is it not stated in the Suttantas? “‘Nā’” means it is not found. “‘Because this has been stated’” means...
Because these words have been spoken. Those whose objects are the characteristics of the conditioned are "those whose objects are the characteristics of the conditioned" (*saṅkhatavisayalakkhaṇāni*).
It stands by striking against only conditioned phenomena; this is the intended meaning of "the nature of things (*dhammatā*) in the Abhidhamma.
By the phrase "by the author of the *Saṅgaha*," he refers to the Elder Master Buddhaghosa. "The moment of existence" (*atthikkhaṇaṃ*) refers to only two moments.
The connection is: "Having said this, she establishes that meaning. In the verse, the phrase "of that very" (*tasseva*) refers to the destruction of that very state of existence.

The construction is: "Death is said to be the [end] of all living beings at all times. The phrase "that meaning" (*tam-atthaṃ*) means the meaning that is obtained starting from those moments of existence (*atthi-khaṇa*).
"Or else" (*athavā*) indicates one tradition of the Elders (*theravāda*). "Abiding by way of continuity" (*santati-vasena ṭhānaṃ*) refers to that which has stood.

Regarding the phrase "changeability is discerned," they say that here "standing" (ṭhāna)—which is defined as the state of remaining—should be understood by way of continuity (santati) and duration (ṭhiti).

As for the statement, "In this sutta, however," it refers to this sutta which says: "The arising of feeling is discerned, its passing away is discerned, and the changeability of that which has stood is discerned.
"Without obstructing" means without preventing. [This applies] to the extent of its increase.
There is indeed such a thing as cessation (*nivatti*). That very cessation consists solely in the limit of arising (*udaya-pariyanta-matta*). Regarding the phrase "by two aggregates":

the aging of matter is included within the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*), while the aging of the immaterial is included within the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*); thus it is "by two aggregates. This is the connection with the words "and what was stated therein.
The arising of matter is taught by dividing it into two types. How so? [It is] accumulation (*upacaya*).
The continuum (*santati*) extends for three *yojanas*. Regarding the phrase "the divisions are secret": arising (*uppāda*) is so called because it arises and then perishes;
it is the same single factor that exists during the period of the increase of material phenomena. It is called accumulation (*upacaya*) in the sense of further increasing above that.
It is called continuity (*santati*) in the sense of proceeding for a long time according to the manner in which it has arisen, remaining without further increase. Thus are the divisions.
* Rahassa: “Teaching in accordance with [the disposition]” (*yathānuloma-sāsana*) means a teaching that accords with the inclinations of those persons to be trained.
Regarding the terms “formless” (*arūpa*) and so forth: “Formless” (*arūpa*) refers to mind and mental factors (*nāma*), because they are entirely devoid of the configuration of form (*rūpa*).
“Because it has the nature of the formless” (*arūpi-sabhāvattā*) means precisely because it has the nature of formless phenomena (*dhamma*). In that context, formless phenomena...
Intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) refers to the quality of being extremely swift and subtle by a hundredfold or even a thousandfold degree compared to material phenomena (*rūpa-dhamma*).

Regarding the term *vibhāva* in the recension: in the passage, “Because the state of the grasper (*gāhaka*) and the graspable (*gahetabba*) is produced according to each respective moment,” here, within the cognitive processes of the five doors, the relationship between the subject and the object—the state of the grasper and the graspable—refers to the relationship between the consciousnesses of the cognitive process (*vīthi-citta*) and their respective objects.

[This is] the name. Because they are produced according to their respective moments, the path-consciousnesses (*vīthi-citta*) fulfill the function of apprehension precisely by grasping even a single object through various functions such as adverting (*āvajjana*), and so forth.
These various functions are accomplished by means of the various consciousnesses.
And the objects, having arisen prior [to the consciousness], persist until those functions are accomplished.
Thus, they accomplish their grasping only while existing in the state of the present.
This being so, because the apprehending path-minds have a duration of three moments, the function of apprehending is accomplished and fulfilled.
And because the objects to be apprehended have a duration of seventeen mind-moments, the function of being apprehended is accomplished and fulfilled.
Thus, because they are produced according to their respective moments, the two types of intimation (viññatti) last for only a single consciousness-moment (cittakkhaṇa).
Why? Because they are phenomena that follow the movement of consciousness. "Merely arising" (uppādamatta) refers to the mere arising of produced material phenomena (nipphanna-rūpa).

"Merely ceasing" (bhaṅgamatta) refers to the mere cessation of those same [phenomena]. "Of material phenomena" (rūpadhammānaṃ) refers to produced material phenomena. "Arising and cessation" (uppādanirodha)...
The connection is: "because the doctrine of the Great Commentary (Mahā-aṭṭhakathā), which consists of the exposition of arising and cessation, has been rejected.
"That" refers to that statement of the Great Commentary. "In that doctrine" means in that doctrine of the Great Commentary.
"Contained therein" means contained in that doctrine. The connection is: "but as for the reason stated in the Vibhāvani..."
“*Taṃ ṭīkānayan*” means that root-commentary method which illustrates the lifespan of sixteen consciousness-moments (*cittakkhaṇa*).
The connection [of the sentence] is: “It was spoken by the commentator of the *Vibhāvanī*, who established its meaning. Regarding the commentator of the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
“*Upacarīyatī*” means it is designated by way of conventional usage (*upacāra*). In the reading of the *Vibhāvanī*: “*Etānī*” refers to the objects (*ārammaṇa*); “*taṃ*” refers to that one...

“Mind-moment” (*cittakkhaṇaṃ*). “And those” (*te ca*) refers to material phenomena (*rūpadhammā*). “Having obtained complete conditions” (*paripuṇṇapaccayūpaladdhā*) means having obtained complete conditions.
“He” (*so*) refers to the author of the commentary (*ṭīkākāro*). “The others” (*itarāni*) refers to odors, tastes, and tangibles.

“The state of being an object” (*gocarabhāvaṃ*) refers to the state of being an object for the five-door consciousnesses. “The first two” (*purimāni dve*) refers to the objects of visible form and sound. “The sign” (*nimitta*).
"By way of [the object], they strike [the sense-faculties]"—when one looks at a mirror, an image of the face, a sign of the face resembling the face itself, appears in the mirror.
In this way, the visible-object object strikes the visual sensitivity, and the sound-object strikes the auditory sensitivity, by way of a sign similar to that [object].
They strike by way of a new basis; they do not strike by going there themselves.

This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). "Of objects not yet reached" means of those objects that have not been attained. "By way of the sign's appearance" means by way of the sign’s manifestation.

"By way of the sign’s absorption" means by way of the sign’s entry [into the mind]. In the case of the mind-door, however, there is an elliptical addition (*pāṭhaseso*) stating "having remained un-reached.
In such passages as "the entering into the range," etc., the term "of sealers" refers to those who perform sealing.
“Branded pillar” means a pillar made of iron used for branding. And that branded pillar, having been struck against a palm leaf, makes the characters appear.
In this context, “having struck” means having covered or overlaid it.
“Within the range of the eyes and so forth” means within the field of objects of the eyes and other senses. Not only do they come within range at one’s own sense-doors; rather—

They also enter the range [of perception] at the mind-door (*manodvāra*). The construction is: "It is not only at the mind-door that they enter the range [of perception] during the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).
Regarding the phrase "But among those," it means "but among those objects. Those objects which belong to them are "those objects" (*tadārammaṇāni*).
Path-consciousnesses (*vīthicitta*) do not proceed toward five objects simultaneously; rather, they proceed toward each object individually.
Because it has been so stated, it cannot be said that [the five objects] exist in two, three, or four moments of consciousness.

The construction is: "The five objects that have passed through many moments of consciousness [are received] by the five doors that have passed through many moments of consciousness. And "in the five doors" (*pañcadvāre*) means "in the five door-faculties" (*pañcadvāresu*). "If this were so" (*evaṃ sati*) means:

if there were the simultaneous arising of those [five] sensitive faculties together with the adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*). "The initial characteristic" (*ādi-lakkhaṇaṃ*) refers to the five objects.
In the five doors, "impact" (āpāta) is defined as the initial characteristic of the manifestation of the object, which is reckoned as its arrival; it should be understood as "movement.
The connection [of the sentence] is thus: "as it was grasped" means in the manner it was grasped starting from the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi).
In the reading of the *Vibhāvanī*, "by way of abiding in a suitable place" means by way of reaching a place fit for impact and a fixed location. And "joining" (yujjana),...
The construction is as follows: "churning," "agitating," "striking," and "going to the place of impact" are what is meant.

This "going to the place of impact" and so forth has already been explained below by the passage beginning with "And here... The phrase "in those situated in various places" means in those standing in different locations.
"A single fixed law of nature" refers to how, for example, when the Bodhisatta takes rebirth in his mother's womb, there is a fixed law of nature.
By virtue of that, there was a shaking of the earth throughout the entire field of birth.

Likewise, here too, when an object impinges upon each of the five sense-doors, there occurs a vibration of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) by virtue of the fixed order of phenomena (dhammaniyāma). This is what is called the "fixed order of phenomena.
Regarding the phrase "simultaneously" (sahevā), it means at one and the same time. How could there be a vibration of the life-continuum, which is supported by the heart-base?
The interpretation (*yojanā*). And herein, it should not be said that "there may be movement of the fivefold sensory consciousness.

Why? Because at that time, the fivefold sensory consciousness is non-existent. And when it exists, it should not be said that "it does not move," for indeed, every process-consciousness (*vīthicitta*) moves.
What is called "continuity" (*santati*) is a succession of preceding and succeeding moments. What is called "configuration" (*saṇṭhāna*)...
“Co-existence” means their remaining together in one place. Here, “configuration” (saṇṭhāna) is intended.
By “having the heart-base as their support along with the five supporting great elements,” it is meant that they are bound together by way of having a single configuration.
Therefore he said, “but it should be stated ‘by way of configuration. [This refers to] “such a sequential movement.”

The sequence of vibration as described thus—namely, that when the sensitive matter (pasāda) is struck by a form or other object, comparable to the striking of a drum, the great elements (mahābhūta) dependent upon it vibrate;
subsequently, through the vibration of the remaining material qualities connected to them, the heart-base (hadayavatthu) vibrates;
and by means of that vibration, the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) supported by it is set in motion—is to be understood through the analogy of the drum and the sound.
“Flowing as the life-continuum (bhavaṅga)” means the continuity of the life-continuum. “Making” means performing. “Observing” means determining that “this is indeed it.
“By way of appropriate attention and so forth” means: appropriate attention is a condition for the arising of wholesome impulsion;
inappropriate attention is a condition for the arising of unwholesome impulsion. [Free from] underlying tendencies (niranusaya).

The state of continuity (*santānatā*) is the condition for the arising of functional consciousness-moments (*kriya-javana*). Furthermore, the conditions for the arising of joyous functional moments (*somanassa-javana*) and so forth among those [moments] should be understood according to the method explained below in the "Compendium of Consciousness" (*Citta-saṅgaha*), starting from the phrase "descent into the life-continuum" (*bhavaṅga-pāta*).
[This applies to moments] that have arisen starting from the moment of adverting (*āvajjana*), as well as from the continuum of kamma-result (*vipāka*).
Having released its object and, through a distinct functional activity (*kriyāmayabyāpāra*), having grasped another object, it has arisen and emerged.
Even the vibration of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) is the beginning of the emergence; therefore, including that too within the mental continuity that has emerged, it is said:
"starting from the very first vibration of the life-continuum. "In this place" refers to the cognitive process-moments (*vīthicittāni*).
In due course, [the mind] proceeds toward its objects in the place where its own functions operate. “The simile of the doorkeeper” refers to the simile of the deaf doorkeeper.
“The simile of the village boy” refers to the simile of the village children. “The simile of the mango” refers to the simile of the mango fruit. There are other similes as well:

the simile of the monkey’s rope, the simile of the sugar-cane press, and the simile of the man blind from birth. All of these are explained in the *Aṭṭhasālinī* under the section on the extraction of the result (*vipākuddhāra*).
It should be understood from the discourse, as in the passage beginning with "Wherein... and so forth. [The question is: "How is there the application of six sets of six?

[The answer is: the mention of the eye as the basis (*vatthu*), the mention of the eye as the door (*dvāra*), the mention of visible forms as the object (*ārammaṇa*), the mention of eye-consciousness (*viññāṇa*), the mention of the cognitive process (*vīthi*) of the eye-door and the cognitive process of eye-consciousness, and the mention of the very large object (*atimahantārammaṇa*).
These are the sixfold sets (*cha-chakka*). Having been brought together by those sixfold sets, they are displayed in this street.

They should likewise be displayed in the remaining streets according to their availability. Such is the application of the sixfold sets. Regarding the passage beginning with “And here, as many as...”:
“In the measure of forty-nine” refers to the forty-nine minor moments within a single produced material phenomenon (*rūpa-dhamma*).
Excluding the moment of arising (*uppādakkhaṇa*) and the moment of dissolution (*bhaṅgakkhaṇa*), there are forty-nine moments of the duration-phase (*ṭhitikkhaṇa*) in between.
During those moments, forty-nine instances of the eye-sensitivity (*cakkhu-pasāda*) arise in succession.

Regarding the phrase "in any one," it cannot be said that they do not strike [the object] in any particular one among those [moments]. As for the phrase "but among those," it is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇe*).
This is the locative case. "That which is the single eye" is the term to be singled out (*niddhāraṇīya*). But what is that?
It is the single eye that, having arisen together with the past life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), attains its connection at the moment the life-continuum vibrates after having passed beyond it.
Furthermore, that eye establishes for consciousness both the state of being a basis (*vatthu*) and the state of being a door (*dvāra*). [The same applies] to the remaining types of consciousness.
It accomplishes the state of being a door. Therefore, he says "accordingly. This very thing is called the accomplishment of the function of the eye;
for it accomplishes both the function of the basis and the function of the door for the arising of the cognitive process (*vīthi-citta*). Regarding the phrase "one of medium lifespan":
because it occurs in the middle between those of short lifespan and those of long lifespan, they call it "one of medium lifespan. That is the function.

The construction is: "the accomplishment of its function. Regarding the phrase "but the others," among the forty-nine sensitive organs (*pasāda*) mentioned as the eye-sensitivities, with the exception of one that accomplishes its function, the remaining forty-eight eyes are called "futile bases" (*moghavatthu*).

Even for those [eyes] that have obtained contact together with visible objects as their objects, the cognitive process (*vīthi*)— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.*
The basis for the arising of consciousness is devoid of function and door-function. Regarding those [bases], he says "But those...
and so forth, asking: which among them are called "short-lived"? Because they accomplish their function, the former ones are so named;
that is, from the moment of the dissolution of the first of the thirteen bhavaṅga-moments prior to the past bhavaṅga, thirty-seven [moments] arise moment by moment.
The eye-sensitivities. They say these have a short lifespan. Why? Because they accomplish their function while having a shorter duration of life.
Regarding the accomplishment of their function: the latter refers to the eleven eye-sensitivities that arise moment by moment starting from the subsistence-moment of the past *bhavaṅga*;
they say these have a long lifespan. Why? Because they accomplish their function [in that manner].
Because they have a longer lifespan. The connection is that both of these together should be understood as being forty-eight in number.
"From those" means from those forty-eight. "The earlier ones" refers to the thirty-seven [factors] belonging to those with a short lifespan;
for those are not included here because they are not apprehended by way of their presence at the moment of the arising of visual consciousness.
“Later than the last” means that they are later than the eleven [bases] which have a long life-span.
And although those [bases] have arisen at the moment of the arising of eye-consciousness, they are not included here because their state of presence (thiti-bhāva) is not perceived at that moment.
But why are both of these not perceived by way of the state of presence at the moment of the arising of eye-consciousness?

"Here they are not included. At the moment of the arising of visual consciousness (*cakkhu-viññāṇa*), among the forty-eight eye-moments existing by way of their state of presence, one must consider which specific eye performs the function of the basis (*vatthu*) and the function of the door (*dvāra*) for that visual consciousness.
And herein, the five bases (*vatthu*) [are so called] at their own moment of presence.

It should be understood that this is stated both because the five consciousnesses are not included here since they accomplish their functions through the basis and door at the moment of the arising of eye-consciousness,
and because [the bases] are existing by way of the state of persistence at the moment of the arising of eye-consciousness.
Regarding the phrases beginning with “In this case it might be”: “By this path” means by this exceedingly vast and delightful path.

“Grasping the aggregate” means grasping the collection of visible objects (*rūpa-ārammaṇa*). “Perception of color” means the determination of color. “Grasping the substance” means grasping the shape of the material object.
“Grasping the name” means grasping the designation of a name. “Grasping the fire-brand circle” [is mentioned].
"Having seen," means that in the darkness of night, one person takes a firebrand and whirls it around. Another, seeing it, imagines it to be a wheel.
Therein, in each place where the firebrand has passed, sense-door cognitive processes (*cakkhudvāra-vīthi*) arise based on the present form.
However, the mind-door cognitive processes (*manodvāra-vīthi*) [arise] regarding the past [forms] grasped by the preceding sense-door cognitive processes.
Without abandoning the individual forms, they grasp them by forming a single configuration and continuity;

at that time, it appears to the observer like a wheel. Thus, this should be understood as grasping a composite whole. Regarding the phrases "there is no arising of the registration [consciousness]" and so forth:
"of which" (*yassā*) refers to whichever object. "Consciousnesses" (*cittāni*) and "having various objects" (*nānārammaṇāni*) are the subject terms. As for the remainder...

“On that object. “By the compiler”: because he compiled the ancient commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) together into one, all the commentaries composed by the Elder Buddhaghosa are called the *Saṅgaha-aṭṭhakathā*;
and he is called the compiler. “Even here”: even in this *Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha*. “By the Elder”: by the Elder Anuruddha.
“He desires even one [object] alone. In such passages as “For him who has four,” etc., it should be construed as: “for which object there are four, five, or six,” and so forth.

In such passages as “Even without the arising of the impulsion (javana),” etc., following the word “without arising” (*anuppajjitvā*), there is the phrase “its own primary activity” (*attano padhānakriyā*) with the words “which occurs” (*yaṃ pavattati*).
The meaning is: "together with its own verbal form. Regarding the phrase "stated in some [texts]," it means stated in certain grammatical treatises (*saddagantha*).

Furthermore, it should be understood that the suffix *tvā* is stated in the sense of indicating a cause (*hetu*) and a characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), while the suffix ending in *-māna* is stated in the sense of indicating both a cause and a characteristic;
they are not stated in the sense of being something to be verbally expressed. By the phrase "by way of the natural rule" (*pakati-niyāmena*), he specifies the particular type of suffix.
It demonstrates that four or five feeble impulsions arise. Therefore, he said, “And here too,” and so forth.

Regarding the phrase “two or three times,” it is stated as a compound word with another word as its referent (*aññapadattha-samāsa*) in the sense of the particle *vā* (or), namely, “either twice or thrice.

“The repetition of the determining consciousness” refers either to its state as a condition through repetition (*āsevana-paccayatā*) or to its state as a resultant of such a condition (*paccayuppannatā*).
Regarding the phrase “of adverting,” here *adverting* includes the function of determining (*voṭṭhabbana*).
The construction here is: “In this case as well, due to the weakness of the object, the arising of four or five impulsion-moments (*javana*) is to be expected.

In that context, “in this case as well” means even in this series of limited objects (*paritta-ārammaṇa*). The construction is: “There are three series of determining and five series of limited objects. “The others” refers to...
"Small and great" refers to great objects. "In both ways" means both by way of entering [the range of the sense] and by way of making it an object.
This refers to the word [in the phrase] "But at the mind-door," etc. "Even for a moment of the limited" means that consciousness, contact, and so forth have fewer moments.
“Past and future as well”: this refers to past and future phenomena (*dhamma*) as well. “By means of impact”: by means of the impact of visible forms (*rūpa*) and so forth.
“Where”: in whichever *bhavaṅga* (life-continuum). “Following the five doors”: following the course of the five sense-doors. The connection is:
“it simply causes the past object to proceed. “Just as it had already entered the range”: in the very same manner as it had naturally entered the range.
“In such and such a way” means by this or that mode, such as through the connection [of cause and effect] and so forth. “Anything” refers to some object.
“Having seen” means having made it directly present; for an object apprehended by the five doors is called “seen” in the sense of being made directly present.
“Of one who is inferring” means: “It was thus,” “it will be thus,” or “it is thus.”
"For one who reflects with inferential knowledge" means for one who contemplates by means of the knowledge of inference. "An object similar to that" refers to an object resembling it.
"Faith in another" means having heard another's words, the conviction that "it is exactly as this person says. "View" (diṭṭhi) refers either to knowledge or to a settled opinion.
"Contemplation" (nijjhāna) means thorough observation. "Acceptance" (khanti) means forbearance or endurance; it is the state of not wavering from [one's position].
“Contemplation by means of views” is *diṭṭhinijjhāna*. “Acceptance of contemplation by means of views” is *diṭṭhinijjhānakkhanti*.

“The rest” refers to [the passage] beginning with “by the power of various kamma,” and so forth. “By way of presentation by a deity” means that sometimes a deity presents various objects to certain people in their dreams;
thus it is also “by way of presentation by a deity. “Subsequent awakening” (*anubodha*).

"Awakening" (*anubujjhana*) refers to the realization of the phenomena of the Four Truths by means of mundane knowledge (*lokiya-ñāṇa*). "Penetration" (*paṭivedha*) refers to the function of supramundane knowledge (*lokuttara-ñāṇa*).

By the inclusion of the condition of the immediately preceding materiality (*anantara-rūpa-upanissaya-paccaya*), the condition of natural decisive support (*pakati-upanissaya-paccaya*) is also implied.
The connection is as follows: [it refers to] the state of being the condition of immediate material support for the mental continuum (*citta-santāna*). Anantara-rūpa-upanissaya...
It is said that the power of conditions (*paccayasatti*) is of great scope by way of immediate succession, serial succession, and pervasion.
It is also appropriate to say it is the experience of the condition for infinite materiality as its support. To the question, "How is its pervasion great? he says, "Even once," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "having thoroughly cultivated," this refers to repeated cultivation after having made it such that it is not forgotten later.

"Thorough cultivation" means this. It is shown by the passage beginning with "And what is called consciousness," etc., to demonstrate that not only does the power of that decisive support-condition (upanissaya-paccaya) for the preceding stream of consciousness possess great amplitude, but also the function of thinking—characterized as the mind's inherent diversity—is likewise of great amplitude. How is it of great amplitude?
He said, “some sign,” and so forth. “Some sign” refers to some slight object, such as what has been seen, among various delightful objects of sight and so on.
“By those causes” means by those causes consisting of the acts of seeing and so on.
“Being urged” means being impelled. “Associated with intention” means conjoined with intention. *Bhavanga*.
The object of the mind is indeed unmanifest. The syntactical connection is: "having caused the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) to vibrate, it directs the adverting consciousness.
"In those who have obtained conditions" means in those possessing conditions obtained either by way of light and so forth, or by way of seeing and so forth.
"Tending toward that" means a state of being directed and inclined toward those objects at all times. Attention is that which proceeds by way of such a mode.

For that which is associated with it: by these statements, it is established that the arrival of objects at the pure door of the mind (manodvāra) and the vibration of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) occur not only by way of the conditions obtained for the objects,
but also by way of the mind itself— which possesses the function of investigating the path of consciousness— when it is joined with such attention (manasikāra).
For it cannot be said that there is no such thing as the "turning toward" (abhininnākāra) another object.

Why? Because even when cultivation and attention are occasionally applied by people whose minds are undeveloped and who are prone to negligence, the turning toward various external objects is still seen occurring within the stream of consciousness. "And just as in this case... [is said].

The construction is as follows: "Just as here in the mind-door (manodvāra), even when the object is vivid for beings—whether of the fine-material or immaterial realms—at that time there is no arising of an object.
However, in the *Ñāṇavibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā*, the stage of "determining" (voṭṭhabbana) is also mentioned. As it says:
"Even at the time of saying, 'It was as if seen by me in a dream,' or 'It was as if heard by me,' [the consciousness] is indeed indeterminate (abyākata). For in that context, "indeterminate..."
...is indeed indeterminate (*abyākata*) by way of the adverting consciousness that arises two or three times at the mind-door during a dream.
After that, there is a lapse into the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*). It is also stated in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*:

"But this section [of indeterminate consciousness] is obtained at the time of saying 'it was seen by me,' 'it was heard by me,' and so forth. However, that occurs at the five doors regarding limited objects (*parittārammaṇa*).
This is stated by way of the determining consciousness (voṭṭhabbana) that arises two or three times. "That too must be obtained here":
even that stage must indeed be obtained in this mind-door. "When the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) has vibrated, [there are] the stages of turning back":
having remained for just two vibrations of the life-continuum, without the path-consciousnesses (vīthicitta) arising, [it returns] by way of the subsidence of the life-continuum.

For those who turn back, even at the door of the mind, there will certainly be no opportunity (vāra). Now, if it is argued that since there is no occurrence of a cognitive process (vīthi-cittappavatti) in this instance, that "opportunity" should not be mentioned in this summary of processes, it must indeed be mentioned. Why?
To show that it is included within this group of six by the phrase "the sixfold occurrence of objects."
“*Visaye ca āpātāgate*,” etc., was said. The occurrence of objects (*visaya*) consists of those things that have become objective supports (*ārammaṇa*).

In each successive section: “The sections on the registration [consciousness], etc. refers to the section on registration (*tadārammaṇa*), the section on impulsion (*javana*), the section on determining (*voṭṭhabbana*), and the section on the futile (*mogha*).
Among these, however, the section on registration is not found in the apprehension of the physical basis (*vatthu*) nor in the apprehension of the name-base (*nāma*). “Physical basis” (*vatthu*)...

“Configuration” (*saṇṭhāna*) is a designation (*paññatti*). “Name” (*nāma*) is a designation of name. And it is not the case that because an object is designated as an object, it then becomes an actual object.
Therefore it was said: “accordingly. “Therein” (*tattha*) means among those six sections beginning with the section on what has been seen.
“But nowadays some teachers,” is the remainder of the text. “By way of past life-continuum” (*atīta-bhavaṅga-vasena*) means having passed over one life-continuum.

Regarding the phrase "by way of the object" (*ārammaṇa-vasena*): when the object has entered the avenue of the senses (*āpāta-gate*), there is one [moment of] advertence; after two life-continuum moments (*bhavaṅga*) have passed, when it has entered the avenue, there is one [moment of] advertence—and so on—according to the distinctions of the past life-continuum.
Regarding the phrase "by way of the object at that time" (*tadārammaṇa-vasena*): at that time, there is the occurrence of the object as either arisen or unarisen;
thus it is "by way of the object at that time. They fashion (*kappenti*), they think, or they arrange. The strength and weakness [of the consciousness] are according to the moment (*khaṇa-vasena*).

Regarding "arising": just as in the case of the five doors, even when objects are extremely large and attractive, once those objective phenomena have reached the stage of arising, they remain weak for the duration of a single consciousness-moment and are unable to enter their respective doors.
However, after that single consciousness-moment has passed, they become powerful and are able to enter their respective doors.
However, it should be stated that [the consciousnesses] in the case of great objects and so forth are weak for only two thought-moments (*cittakkhaṇa*).
Such a possibility of strength or weakness based on the duration of the object does not exist in the mind-door (*manodvāra*) in the same way.

To the question "Why does it not exist?", he says "At that time," and so forth. Therein, "at that time" means at the moment of the occurrence of the cognitive process (*vīthicitta*). "Therein" means in the mind-door.
Regarding the passage beginning with “*ettha siyā*”: “*siyā*” means that there might be an investigation by some. “*Ekāvajjanā*” means having a single adverting [consciousness].
“*Vīthī*” refers to a series (*pabandho*) of process-consciousnesses (*vīthicitta*). The grammatical analysis (*viggaha*) is: it is both a single adverting and a series.
“*Āvajjanaṃ*” refers to the adverting consciousness; the connection is: “it adverts” (*āvajjati*). “*Tena tena javanena*” means by this or that impulsion (*javana*).
The construction is: “or he adverts to another’s mind as it has arisen,” namely, “What is there [to be said] here?”—the meaning of this statement is that there is something to be said here.

If, first of all, the subject under discussion is both adverting and impulsion, then “that mind” refers to the other person’s mind. “Even so, it is indeed distinct”—it is indeed distinct from the perspective of the phenomena (dhamma) of the impulsions. Herein, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
"Vinicchitaṃ" (determined) is the connection [to the following]. The construction is: "Even though that consciousness has ceased, it is still present for the impulsion-moments as well.
"'Taken by way of duration' (addhāvasena)" means taken by way of the present duration. "'Taken by way of continuity' (santativasena)" means taken by way of the present continuity.
This is the opinion of Ācariya Ānanda. For all [these types of consciousness], adverting...
For the javanas, it is simply consciousness; therefore, they are non-different in terms of dhamma.

And since it is present, it is said to be non-different in terms of time. In the case of the proximity condition (*anantara-paccaya*), both the past and the present are appropriate by way of moment (*khaṇa*).
If it were appropriate by way of duration (*addhā*) or continuity (*santati*), then a present dhamma would [not] be the proximity of a present dhamma.

It would have to be called a "condition by way of condition. Why? Because in a single adverting (ekāvajjana) cognitive process, all the consciousnesses are indeed present by virtue of the duration of the continuity (addhāsantati).
138. In the section on absorption (appanāvāra): “Absorption impulsion” is the object of the action; “then the object” is the agent; “the faculty... [is the instrument].
"By means of evenness, etc. refers to the five faculties, such as faith and the rest, by way of their mutual non-excessiveness (anativattanavasena) through evenness and so forth.

"Completely" (parito) means all around. "Having approached" (upetvā) means having drawn near. "The state of being capable of bringing about absorption" (appanāvahasamatthabhāvo) is the quality of being able to carry or produce absorption.
"From the occurrence of which" (yassa pavattiya) means from the occurrence of that access-moment (upacāra-javana). "Not long" (aciraṃ)...
"At once" means after a short time. "Birth" refers to birth in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara*). "Lineage" is a term for the agent of karma.
"Is overcome" means it is being overcome by the power of meditation; the meaning is that it is being crushed.
"Is cut off," however, is the vision of the culmination of that overcoming. Until that lineage is severed...
It is said that [the mind] reaches [its object], is overcome, and is crushed. It is also appropriate to call it "gotrabhū" (change-of-lineage) because it overcomes the lineage.
"The fifth" refers to the fifth mental cycle. For at that time, the impulsion (javana) is said to have "fallen";
normally, the occurrence of impulsion is limited to seven times at most. And the fourth is the "head-reaching" (muddhapatta). From the fifth...
"Having fallen" means having fallen [from its position]. Therefore, in that fifth turn, the impulsion (javana) is said to have "fallen.
"By the second" means by the word "second" itself. "The second" refers to the second mental turn; at that time, the adaptation (anuloma) becomes the first impulsion, which is why it is stated:
"Adaptation is that which has not attained repetition. "By this very same" means by these two words themselves.
In the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, however, it appears as if it is permitted. For it is stated there:

"For one of dull wisdom, there are four conformities (*anuloma*); the fifth is the change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*); the sixth is the path-consciousness (*maggacitta*); and the seventh is the fruition (*phala*).

Regarding the phrase "in other commentaries," this refers to the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā* and so forth. Regarding the phrase "because it is prohibited," this means because the arising of the fifth [moment], the change-of-lineage, is prohibited.
Since it was stated in the beginning that [the term] applies "to eight [factors] except for another," it is said here that the word "ceased" (*niruddhe*) must necessarily be supplied;

thus it is said: "The analysis of the phrase is ‘in the ceased, immediately after’ (*niruddhe anantarameva*). And because the word *anantara* (immediately) always requires a correlative, that same word is added by changing its case-ending;
thus he says: "‘Of the ceased’ (*niruddhassa*) is already obtained by implication."
“Even though they have become masters (vasibhūtāpi)” means even while being masters. “Having impelled [the mind] once” is said with reference to mundane absorption (lokīyappanā).
In the case of supramundane absorption (lokuttara-appanā), it arises for a seventh time as well. In the reading of the *Mūlaṭīkā*:

“Upon reaching another plane (bhūmantarapattiyā),” the change-of-lineage consciousness (gotrabhu-citta) belongs to the sense-sphere plane (kāmabhūmi); the absorption consciousness belongs either to the sublime plane (mahaggatabhūmi) or the supramundane plane (lokuttarabhūmi).

Thus it is by way of reaching another plane. Regarding the phrase "by way of obtaining another object," this is said with reference to the fruition-impulsion (*phala-javana*) within the path of attainment of fruition (*phala-samāpatti*).
For therein, the preceding conformable impulsions (*anuloma-javana*) have conditioned phenomena as their object, whereas the fruition-impulsion has Nibbāna as its object.
This, however, is merely a reason; the previously mentioned simile of the clod of earth is what is truly appropriate here.
"It should be seen. "But this should not be seen in that way"—this class of things should not be viewed in such a manner.

"Not lasting" (*anaddhaniyā*): they do not endure for a long period of time (*addhāna*), thus they are "not lasting. They are without core (*asārā*). Precisely because they lack a core, they grow more quickly;
they more rapidly reach growth and increase. But those possessing a core, by means of that core—
Because they grow together, they do not sprout more quickly; they do not reach growth and development more rapidly.

Therefore he said, "living for one year," and so forth. Regarding the phrases beginning with "evameva" (in the same way), "in the fifth, sixth, and seventh impulsions" refers to the fallen impulsions.
Regarding the phrases beginning with "ettha ca" (and here), "resembling well-cooked rice" means just as the rice dishes...
Because they are so fully ripened, they become very soft, weak, and short-lived; even on that very day, they undergo putrefaction.

Such are the moments of absorption and impulsion (*appanā-javana*). Regarding the phrase "And because," etc.: "Of the two-fold restriction" refers to the restriction of the impulsion and the restriction of time.
"Arising as the immediate condition for rebirth-linking" refers to the volition of the seventh impulsion.
The proximity condition (*anantara-paccaya*): the resultant continuum that has arisen immediately following [the kamma] is the "arisen-by-condition" (*paccayuppanna*);

and that very same [continuum], having become the death-consciousness (*cuti-citta*) at the end, serves as the proximity condition for the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhi-citta*) in the next existence. Thus, the meaning is: "that which will necessarily come to be by way of being the proximity condition for the rebirth-linking consciousness. And this is the reason.

This alone [is sufficient]. However, the statement from the *Mahāṭīkā*—“Is there anything further to be said regarding material form?”—is not rejected. Regarding the phrase “of those occurring without interval,” etc.:
those which have distinct (bhinna) or dissimilar feelings (*vedanā*) are called “distinct-feeling” (*bhinnavedana*). Regarding the phrase “of those opposed to repetition” (*āsevanapaccanīkānaṃ*):

it refers to those that are counter-opposites to the condition of repetition (*āsevanapaccaya*). The analysis of the compound is: “those whose feeling is non-distinct” (*abhinnā vedanā yesaṃ*). Immediately after the functional impulsion (*kriya-javana*),...
The fruit of arahantship and the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) are to be seen within the cognitive process (vīthi). The rest here is easily understood.

139. Regarding the passage beginning with “In every way”: there may be some object desired by the common people in the world that is not desired by those who are most exalted, such as King Mandhātā and others;
likewise, there may be something not desired by those common people [that is desired by them].

Some object is desired even by those who are extremely destitute and dwell in remote regions. Therefore, having established the desirable and undesirable nature of objects, the classification does not proceed on the basis of the extremely exalted or the extremely destitute;
it proceeds only on the basis of the middling. Thus he says, "And therein," and so forth. "Object" is the subject (agent) term. "Resultant consciousness" is...
The section on action (*kammapada*). “Anything whatsoever” means any form. “In anything whatsoever” means in a certain flower.
“Or by that” means by that cloth of pleasant touch. The rest here is easy to understand.

Regarding the phrases beginning with “for the purpose of establishing the determination of feeling,” [it is said]: “Just as of the reflection of a face in a mirror”—just as, in a mirror, of the reflection of a face...

The connection with movement, falling away, and so forth, as well as the connection with various colors, is established exactly according to the object [of experience]. Likewise for the resultants (*vipāka*).

However, the connection with feeling (*vedanā*) is established precisely according to the objective field (*ārammaṇa*); this is the construction [of the meaning]. In that context, "the connection with feeling" means the connection with various feelings.
"Having fashioned" (*kappetvā*) means having reflected. "Having planned" (*pakappetvā*) means having reflected in various ways. And it is not only for the resultants...
The construction is: "In this way, feeling is a bond (yoga) according to its object. Regarding the passage beginning with "And this," etc.:

"Also in the Commentary" means also in the *Paṭṭhāna-aṭṭhakathā*. "By way of that object" (*tadārammaṇavasena*) is an elliptical expression meaning "of those [consciousnesses] occurring by way of that object.
"Of the five" refers to [the five types of consciousness] together with the investigating consciousness accompanied by joy (*somanassa-santīraṇa*).
This was said with reference to the four great resultant states of mental joy (*somanassa*). "In the natural course" means in the manner that occurs at all times by way of one's ordinary nature.
In the scriptural text: "One by whom the faculties have been cultivated" is *bhāvitindriyo*.
"Pleasant" means delightful; "unpleasant" means not delightful. "He might dwell" is to be connected with "if he has doubt. "Repulsive" means...

"In the disagreeable": "perceiving it as non-repulsive" means perceiving it as agreeable; the same applies to the remaining cases. "Of them": of those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*). In the text of the Canon:
"Joyful" means one who possesses joy (*somanassita*); "dejected" means one who possesses dejection (*domanassita*). In the text of the Canon:

"He pervades with loving-kindness" means he pervades with a mind of loving-kindness (*mettācitta*), thinking, "May this being be free from enmity," and so forth. "He brings [them] together by way of elements" means, as follows:
“Friend, even this body is a compound of the four elements. Therein, not even a single element is either repulsive or non-repulsive;
it is merely empty, void, and of the nature of its own essence. In the same way, this body of a living being [is likewise],” and so on—thus he applies the analysis of the elements.
“Or by means of foulness” means by means of the meditation on foulness (*asubha-bhāvanā*). The meditation on foulness is performed with the mind...
It is said [in this way]. Or, "for the sake of the foul" (*asubhāya*) means for the purpose of its state of foulness.
"Divine dancers" refers to celestial nymphs (*devaccharā*). "Those with festering sores" means those whose sores are festering.
"Bodies" refers to the limbs of the physical frame. One whose body has festering sores is "one with a body of festering sores. "Festering" means oozing. Feeling (*vedanā*).
The construction is: "Others say they are connected. Therefore, the connection is: "it becomes a condition.
To the question "How does it become a condition? he says: "By seeing the benefits," and so forth. Therein, "in the commentary" refers to the Visuddhimagga commentary.
"By seeing the state of the Buddha being well-awakened" refers to one's own Teacher, the Buddha.

“Through seeing the well-understood” means through seeing [the truth]. “Through seeing one’s own excellence,” however, we mean through seeing one’s own success in this way: “We have been freed from such suffering.
“In the form of a skeleton and a peta” refers to a heap of bones and the body of a hungry ghost (peta), devoid of flesh and blood. “Of a leper” refers to the body of one afflicted by leprosy.
“In the commentary” refers to the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā*. “Ati-iṭṭhe” means in that which is exceedingly desirable.

Regarding the color and so forth of celestial nymphs (*devaccharā*): [it refers to] that which is extremely undesirable, such as the body of one suffering from putrid leprosy. “Becoming the object” (*vatthu-bhūto*) means becoming the locus of arising.

“Of those various beings” (*tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ*) is a genitive used in the sense of the agent. “Both of these” (*tadubhayaṃ pi*) means both that and the grasping. “Of them” (*tesaṃ*) refers to those worldly people.
“It occurs precisely through the influence of perversion” (*vipallāsa-vasenaiva hoti*) [refers to] regarding the color of celestial nymphs and so forth.

Even the grasping of things as excessively desirable occurs by way of perversion (*vipallāsa*) alone. Why? Because, regarding the beauty and other qualities of celestial nymphs, there is no perception of perversion due to the presence of a perception of them as excessively desirable.

In the *Vibhāvanī* commentary, the word "pavattiya" means "because of occurring. Since it was stated while standing on the intended meaning of the *Aṭṭhakathā*, [it was said] out of respect for the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "That..."
“It must be investigated” is what was said; however, in terms of its meaning, it is stated that this is indeed inappropriate. This same method applies elsewhere as well.
“Devoid of the eye of Dhamma” means devoid of the eye of knowledge that discerns the Dhamma.

“Only wholesome and unwholesome states” refers to the wholesome and unwholesome states that have arisen for those who are devoid of the eye of Dhamma. In the verse, “forms” (rūpā) refers to them by way of form.
The connection is with the word “do not quiver. The same method applies to the terms “sounds” and so forth.
“Do not quiver” means they do not move, do not shake, and do not undergo a change of state in the mind.

Likewise, the construction is that even immediately after the functional javana of equanimity, the registration moments (*tadārammaṇa*) would indeed be associated with the feeling of joy and equanimity. In the reading of the *Mūlaṭīkā*, it says: “the state of being a registration [moment]” (*tadārammaṇatā*).
"By way of having that as its object" means by virtue of having that [preceding javana] as its objective support (*ālambana*). "In some cases" refers to certain passages in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka.
"And when that exists" means when that registration (*tadārammaṇa*) which follows the functional javana (*kriya-javana*) is present.
The connection is: "it follows this, namely, the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*). The construction is: "just as the current of a river follows a boat going against the stream."

“‘The impulsive consciousness (javana) is indeed expansive’—it is logical that only the wholesome or unwholesome impulsive consciousness follows immediately [after the registration], accompanied by a force of pervasion in manifold ways across even hundreds of objects for a mere moment, by way of the defilements and the perversions.
However, it is not logical that the functional impulsive consciousness follows; such is the construction. ‘Because of his looking with the six factors...’”

[This refers to] one endowed with equanimity possessing six factors, as stated by way of the six doors in such passages as: "Having seen a form with the eye, he is neither glad nor sad; he dwells in equanimity," and so forth. *Vattana* means conduct (*vutti*).
One whose conduct is peaceful is "one of peaceful conduct" (*santavutti*). Examining that, he said, "But in the *Paṭṭhāna*... and so on. "If this were stated... [he says].
Here, the phrase beginning with “‘This’ is the verbal expression of the action” refers to this statement. “In that” means in that statement.
“By such a method as this” means by a method beginning in this way. In the *Vibhāvanī* recension, “the answer” means the resolution.
“By way of the practice of insight” means by way of the occurrence of insight. “Of those” refers to joy and grief. “Mutual immediate conditionality” means...
The meaning is "mutual immediate condition" (*aññamaññānantara-paccayatā*). "By the Elder" refers to the Elder Anuruddha.
"All were delightful" means all the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) moments. "They proceeded for a long time" means they continued for a long duration.

By the words "by these," etc., [the author] states the logical reason for the indefinite occurrence of registration consciousnesses (*tadārammaṇa*) immediately following those eighteen impulsion moments (*javana*).

It shows [this]. It is called *sambhava* because by means of it there arises (*sambhavati*) or originates (*uppajjati*). Thus, "the arising of the delightful object at that time" is *tadā-rammaṇa-sambhavo*.
Alternatively, the phrase "the arising of the delightful object at that time" and so forth was stated to show these two meanings: "arising" (*sambhavanaṃ*) and "origination" (*uppajjanaṃ*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "But for those who," etc.: "for those" (*yesaṃ*) refers to those persons; "the others" (*itarāni*)...
Equanimity and investigation are other than the two [previously mentioned]. It was stated, "It should not be said that they do not exist.
If this is so, why were they not mentioned here by the Elder? They were not mentioned here because they were not mentioned in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*.
But why were they not mentioned in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*? They were not mentioned because they fell under the stream of the general rule (*yebhūyya-niyama*), and not because they were unobtainable.
Showing the meaning of the phrase "they are not stated," he said, "But in the Aṭṭhakathā... and so forth.
The statement, "Only two types of investigation accompanied by equanimity are mentioned," is made because they function as adventitious *bhavaṅga*. As it was said:
"Then, for one who has a rebirth-linking accompanied by joy, having produced a jhāna during the course of existence and subsequently fallen away from that jhāna through negligence..."
When one reflects, "The sublime Dhamma has been lost to me," mental distress (*domanassa*) arises by way of remorse (*vippaṭisāra*).
At that time, what [feeling] arises? For it is prohibited in the *Paṭṭhāna* that mental distress follows immediately after joy (*somanassa*), and that joy follows immediately after mental distress.
When a consciousness process (*javana*) occurs with reference to a sublime object, at that very moment the object also [arises] right there.
"As to 'prohibited': either a wholesome resultant or an unwholesome resultant mind-consciousness element accompanied by equanimity arises.
What is its object? Any one among the limited phenomena such as visible forms and so forth.
For it should be understood that this consciousness arises having as its object whichever among these has come into range at that time."

Thus, it is stated in the Commentary that only the two types of investigation (*santīraṇa*) accompanied by equanimity—which correspond to the impulsion (*javana*) accompanied by mental grief—arise as adventitious life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*). "This too is indeed logical":

at the conclusion of an unwholesome impulsion, this adventitious life-continuum accompanied by roots is indeed logical. [The text continues: "After an impulsion accompanied by mental grief, the life-continuum..."
"‘It occurs at dawn’ means that the root life-continuum (bhavaṅga) accompanied by equanimity occurs at dawn. There is no function for the adventitious life-continuum. Why?
Because equanimity is the nature of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi). Nor is there the possibility of registration (tadārammaṇa). Why?
Because registration is impossible with respect to those objects. For it is not possible [for registration to occur] with respect to great objects or indistinct objects."
And thus, the sequence of that object (tadārammaṇa) is possible; however, there is no possibility of a root life-continuum (mūlabhavaṅga). Why?
Because the root life-continuum, which is of the nature of joy (somanassa), is incompatible with a javana of grief (domanassa).
"Having done so" means for this reason. "One" refers to one resultant [consciousness] accompanied by equanimity (upekkhā). Likewise, for one who arouses that same grief...
There is no possibility of registration (tadārammaṇa) [of that object], nor is there a possibility of the root-life-continuum (mūlabhavaṅga).

Therefore, having considered this, the construction is: "Immediately after [the consciousness associated with] grief, [it] proceeds in the six [sense-spheres]," and so forth. In that context, "of that very person" refers specifically to one whose rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) was accompanied by joy (somanassa).
There is no possibility of registration. Why? Because even when objects are extremely vast or extremely vivid, if there is joy...
Because registration (tadārammaṇa) is incompatible with the impulsion (javana); and because equanimity (upekkhā) is incompatible with its object (ārammaṇa).

For registration does not occur with equanimity toward an extremely desirable object. However, in the case of sublime (mahaggata) and conceptualized (paññatti) objects, neither [equanimity nor registration] arises at all as registration.
Nor is there the possibility of a root-life-continuum (mūla-bhavanga).
It exists. Why? Because it is incompatible with the impulsion (javana).
Regarding the phrases beginning with "And here": "In all phenomena" means in all objective phenomena (ārammaṇa-dhamma).

"The first application of attention" refers to the function of adverting (āvajjana). In the Suttanta text: "Arising from that" means arising from the arrival [of the object] within the range of those objects.
“*Tajjo*” means “corresponding to that,” they say. “*Viññāṇabhāgassā*” means of the portion of consciousness pertaining to the eye-door.
“*Yato*” means at which time. To explain how it does not arise without adverting, he says:
“If by adverting,” and so forth. Regarding the phrases beginning with “*Ettha siyā*”: however, just as it is without adverting and with a broken object, so too is it here.
The construction [of the sentence] is as follows: “Even for one” means that there is no fault even for a single adventitious *bhavaṅga*.
This is not found in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, but it is indeed found in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*.

Regarding the phrase “because of its vibrancy,” the meaning here should be understood according to the method explained under the term “savipphārika. “And the others are all” refers to sublime (*mahaggata*) and supramundane (*lokuttara*) impulsion (*javana*) moments. Which ones?

Are they not all equally limited in their objects? If, however, there is no sense-sphere life-continuum (*kāmabhavaṅga*) that could have those [fine-material or immaterial realms] as its object, then the registration consciousnesses (*tadārammaṇa*) do not arise for those in the fine-material and immaterial Brahma-worlds. This being the case, one might ask whether eye- and ear-door consciousnesses would also not arise for those in the fine-material Brahma-worlds;
therefore, he says: "But as for eye- and ear-consciousnesses," and so forth. [The passage continues: "The functioning of the faculties..."

Regarding the phrase "by way of influence": because the bases of the faculties—namely the eye-base and ear-base—are present within the continuum of the form-brahmās, it is said "receiving and investigating" and so forth in order to show that the eye- and ear-consciousnesses arise through the influence of those [bases] as the form-brahmās proceed.
Regarding the phrase "by the power of conceptualization," this refers to the wholesome [states] of the desire realm.
Mindfulness is the capacity for grasping an object after having fashioned and prepared it in various ways, just as one does with wholesome states (*kusala*).

Regarding the phrase "or in the specific work of cultivation that has attained absorption," it should be stated that this refers to the super-knowledge impulsions (*abhiññā-javana*) as well as the sublime resultant (*mahaggata-vipāka*) and supramundane resultant (*lokuttara-vipāka*) states. The phrase "in the commentary" refers to the commentary on the *Paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅga*.

“The reasons stated in the *Vibhāvanī*”: having extracted these from the *Aṭṭhakathā*, these are the reasons stated in the *Vibhāvanī*, such as “because it does not produce [the result], because it is similar to that which produces,” and so forth. 140.
Regarding the determination of the impulsion (*javana*). In the *Aṭṭhakathā* as well, a sixfold occurrence is stated. As it is said: “But if...”
A powerful object comes into range. When the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is arrested by the functional mind-element (kriyamanodhātu), eye-consciousness and the others arise.

At the stage of impulsion (javana), however, the first sense-sphere wholesome consciousness acts as an impulsion and, having impelled for six or seven moments, yields its turn to the registration consciousness (tadārammaṇa).
By the phrase "in a state of greater softness," it refers to the time when [the embryo] is still within the mother's womb.
"At the time of birth" refers to the extreme softness of the physical basis (*vatthu*).

"By being afflicted by something" refers to the state of being afflicted by wind, bile, phlegm, or other humors at the time of contracting a severe illness. "By being overwhelmed" is merely a synonym for that same state.
Those whose force has become slackened are called "slackened-force. "By means of unbearable forms" means by means of things whose intrinsic nature is suffering.
“Of beings who are overcome. And that statement was indeed spoken with reference to ordinary beings, not with reference to specific types of beings.
This being so, he said “But those who... and so forth, in order to show how it should be understood with reference to specific types of beings.
“Above” means at the place where death occurs. “For it is said” refers to what was stated in the *Visuddhimagga*. “The Twin Miracle” (yamakappaṭihāriyaṃ).
It is a marvelous feat occurring simultaneously in both members of a pair. “Two jhāna factors” refers to equanimity and one-pointedness as the jhāna factors.

“Through the accomplishment of the task of yoga” means [the state] of one who has accomplished the task of yoga through cultivation (*bhāvanā*). “Supernormal power of transformation” (*iddhi-vikubbana*) means the performance of various deeds by means of supernormal power (*iddhi*).
“Only for the sake of accomplishment” means solely for the purpose of achieving success. It arises immediately following oneself.
"Having this as its fruit" means having immediate fruition (*ānantariya-phala*). It refers to the volition of the Path (*magga-cetanā*). "Thus" (*iti*) means for that reason.
"Of the dull-witted" (*mandassa*) means of a person who is dull. "Of the sharp-witted" (*tikkhassa*) means of a person who is sharp. There are three resultant consciousnesses (*phala-citta*).

"Of the preparation and formation" (*payoga-abhisaṅkhārassa*) refers to the prior preparation and formation consisting of the concurrent practice of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), beginning from the first jhāna.
“Of one who has not performed the preliminary work” means: of a person who, in a previous existence close at hand, has not performed the preparatory exercises for meditative absorption (*jhāna*).
The construction is: “For all those established in the fruits [of the path], mastery has indeed been attained.
The determination of the impulsion (*javana*) is concluded.

141. Regarding those with two roots (*duhetuka*) and so forth: since it is intended that birth (*jāti*) consists only of those with two roots and so on, it is said, "accompanied by rebirth-linking consciousness" (*paṭisandhiviññāṇasahagatā*), etc.
"Of these two" means of both those with two roots and those without roots (*ahetuka*). They obstruct or hinder the sublime jhānas, paths, and fruits;
thus they are "obstructions" (*āvaraṇa*). The analysis (*vigga-ha*) is: "they are results (*vipāka*) and they are obstructions. "Results" refers to those without roots.
These are results of two-rooted rebirth-linking. For those who have taken rebirth-linking with those [two roots], there is no attainment of jhāna, path, or fruit in this existence.
Therefore he said, "Because of the presence of the obstruction of result," and so forth. "Of them" refers to persons of miserable destiny who are rootless;
"of persons" is what is meant. "Are not obtained" is the connection. "Of the others" refers to those other than them—persons of happy destiny who are rootless.
Regarding the phrases beginning with “It might be here”: [this refers to] those included in the miserable destinies (*duggati*) and those that are rootless (*ahetuka*).

In the passage beginning with “In the root-life-continuum” (*mūlabhavaṅge*), it means in the root-life-continuum that has arrived having become the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*). “Whatever” (*yaṃ kiñci*) means any life-continuum whatsoever. “Is said” (*vuccate*) means the answer is being stated.
“Rejected in all the commentaries” (*sabba-aṭṭhakathāsu paṭikkhitto*): first, in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, in the discussion on the extraction of resultant states (*vipākuddhārakathā*).

Among the sixteen wholesome and resultant states of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), it shows the arising [of consciousness] only for the eight rootless resultants (*ahetuka-vipāka*) among beings in the woeful states, and not for the eight root-possessing resultants (*sahetuka-vipāka*).

Likewise, it is rejected in the commentaries on dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), in the expositions of the term "consciousness" (*viññāṇa-pada*), and in other works such as the *Abhidhammāvatāra*; thus, it is rejected in all the Aṭṭhakathās.
It is so called because it is to be accomplished through the application of effort, as in the phrase “due to being strengthened by yoga.
For when an application is made to increase or diminish wholesome or unwholesome states, they indeed increase or diminish. It is appropriate to take [the state] that is dissociated from knowledge.
Why? Because the root life-continuum (*mūla-bhavanga*), which was referred to as "of the rootless life-continuum" (*ahetukassa bhavaṅgassa*), is itself rootless. [This applies] to both...

"Of those without roots" means of those without roots in an unhappy destination and of those without roots in a happy destination. Regarding the phrase "Furthermore," and so forth, this is another theory found in the *Vibhāvanī*. For it is stated there:

"Others, however, explain that just as for those without roots the object-of-perception (tadārammaṇa) is accompanied by roots, so too for those with two roots the object-of-perception is accompanied by three roots. And in accordance with their view:
Regarding the statement, "Here too, the rejection of resultant [consciousness] associated with knowledge refers only to those that are rootless," they say this is what is intended.

However, that does not accord with what appears in the discussion on the exclusion of resultants, where it says, "In this very [category], there are twelve paths of action," and "In this very [category], there are ten paths of action.
For in that context, among the sixteen wholesome resultants, two are produced by double-rooted karma.

For individuals who possess two roots or are rootless, there are twelve types of consciousness known as the "sense-sphere path," excluding the four resultant states associated with knowledge. Furthermore, among the remaining twelve resultants, there are two—
resultants dissociated from knowledge produced by unprompted (asaṅkhārika) karma— and two— resultants dissociated from knowledge produced by prompted (sasaṅkhārika) karma.
Excluding the results of kamma, according to the doctrine of the Second Elder, there exists what is called the "tenfold path.

In this context, even a person endowed with two roots, being possessed of a predominant zeal, energy, or consciousness, may extensively learn, hear, retain, recite, and contemplate either the scriptural Dhamma or various branches of knowledge and crafts. Then, for such a person, there arises impulsion associated with knowledge.

One should practice frequently. Then, it is stated that for such a person, it is not impossible for a consciousness associated with knowledge (*ñāṇasampayutta*) to arise as a registration (*tadārammaṇa*) following a swift impulsion (*javana*) through various karmic actions. That appears to be logical. As for the statement, “It is also said in the Commentary...

how was it said?”—it was said thus: for among humans and among the gods of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), these [consciousnesses] belong to those possessing merit and are endowed with two roots (*dvihetuka*).
It is stated [in the text] that they mature as rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) at the time of rebirth-linking for those [kamma-formations] that have [rebirth-linking] as their cause, and so forth.
They are threefold and ninefold—this is the connection. "Their state of being such" means the state of being wholesome for the wholesome, and the state of being unwholesome for the unwholesome.
"Devoted to training in the Dhamma" refers to the necessity of training because of the presence of defilements that are to be abandoned by the three trainings.
The intended meaning is "abiding in their natural state. "And of the lower ones" means of the lower fruits. "Respective" means according to each one's own.
"Of the higher ones" means of the higher individuals. "Because the duty of training has been completed":
the duty of training exists solely for the purpose of abandoning defiled states; therefore, when these have been entirely abandoned...
The duty of training has been brought to completion. Because the duty of training has thus been completed, one is "well-capable," which is the meaning of *sambhava*.
He said "according to possibility" (*yathāsambhavam*), indicating that *sambhava* is a qualifying term. 142.
"Right here" means in this very world of sense-desire (*kāmaloka*). "Of those devoid of this or that faculty" means [devoid] of this or that sensory faculty (*pasāda*).

Of those [consciousnesses] devoid [of the five doors]. Those that arise at this or that door are "door-related" (*dvārika*). There are sixty-four types of consciousness belonging to the cognitive process (*vīthi-citta*).
There are forty-two types of consciousness belonging to the cognitive process. Regarding the phrases "or in the Brahma-world," etc., this is a statement from the *Aṭṭhakathā*. As it has been said:

"In the fine-material existence (*rūpa-bhava*), there is a condition for four kinds of consciousness; likewise, it is a condition during the course of existence (*pavatta*), not at rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). And that indeed...
