In the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara*), there is undesirable seeing of forms and hearing of sounds; however, in the Brahma-world, there are no such things as undesirable forms and so forth.
The same applies to the sense-sphere divine worlds (*devaloka*). These are the four types of consciousness. Regarding the phrase “therein”:
it refers to that world of form (*rūpaloka*). Regarding the reading in the *Vibhāvanī*: “here” means in this statement. “Included within each respective plane” means...
Included within each respective plane. The rest here is easy to understand.
The sub-commentary (*Anudīpanā*) on the *Vīthisaṅgahadīpanī* is finished.
5. The Sub-commentary on the *Vīthimuttasaṅgaha*.
143. In the *Vīthimuttasaṅgaha*: “The compendium of occurrence” (*pavattisaṅgaha*) is the compendium explaining the manner in which the arising of consciousnesses occurs.
“In rebirth-linking” (*paṭisandhiyam*) means at the time of rebirth-linking. “Of these” (*tesam*) refers to the consciousness and mental factors. In the reading of the *Vibhāvanī*:

“By its proximity” (*tadāsannatāya*) means by the proximity to that rebirth-linking. “Or by the inclusion of that” (*taṃ gahaṇeneva*) means precisely by the inclusion of the womb (*sandhi*), that is, by the mention of the womb.
“‘The occurrence of the object’ means the occurrence by way of the objects—namely, the kamma, the sign of kamma, and so forth—entering the doors.
‘Established only at the moment of death’ means it is established only in the impulsion (javana) moments at the moment of death.
By this, he illustrates that the process of death is dominated by the impulsion, not by the actual falling away (cuti).”
For in that process [of death], there is no mention of the occurrence of objects in that falling away (cuti); such occurs only in the javanas.
Furthermore, that death-moment is established as occurring at the beginning of that existence, once the occurrence of the rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) has been established.
"Of them" refers to those [processes] outside the cognitive series (vīthimutta). "Arise" means they become manifest. "From that" means from this [present existence]. "To be gone to" means...
They are to be reborn by way of taking rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). "Going" means they proceed. "Across" (*tiro*) means transversely.
"Drawn out" (*añchitā*) means gone, proceeding, or extended. "By way of common birth" (*samānajātitāya*) means by virtue of being of the same species as those born among animals.
"Mixing" (*yuvanti*) means they become intermingled. "From a mass of pleasure" (*sukhasamussayato*) means from a collection of pleasure.
“*Dibbanti*” means they shine. “*Iti katvā*” means having established this meaning of the words; the construction is: “the higher deities (*uparideva*) are called *surā*.
“*Vepacittipahārādādayo*” refers to Vepacitti the lord of the asuras, Pahārāda the lord of the asuras, and so forth, among the gods and asuras.
“*Surappaṭipakkhā*” means those who are adversaries of the Tāvatiṃsa gods. “*Surasadisā*” means similar to the Tāvatiṃsa gods.
“Vemānikapetā” means ghosts (petas) named Vemānikas. “Vinipātikā” means those of a wretched divine class named Vinipātikas;
their conduct will be clarified later in the phrase “and of the Asuras who are Vinipātikas.
“Tepi” means even the beings of the Lokantarika hell. “Kālakañcikāpetā” means ghosts named Kālakañcikās. Thus it is stated in the Kathāvatthu Pāḷi.
The connection is that Vessabhu and the others have arrived as the messengers of Yama, the King of Death. Vessabhū, Notti, Soma, Yama, and Vessavaṇa—these are the kings of the *petas*.
"Sovereignty" (*rajja*) refers to the state of being a king and the duties of a king.
And the connection is that those known as *yakkhas* and *rakkhasas* wander about performing [their tasks]. "Performers of cruel deeds" means performers of violent deeds. "Revatī... [text fragment]
"In the celestial mansion" refers to the Revatī-vimāna-vatthu. "From here" means from the human world, or from a happy state of existence.

Among them, those called *yakkhas* and *rakkhasas* exist both as dwellers on earth and as dwellers in the sky. "Performing various types of tasks" refers to thirty-two kinds of duties involving the performance of work.
This is to be connected with the phrase "of those hell-wardens" (*tesampi nirayapālānam*). "Of the three" means of the three.
Regarding the planes of misery (*apāyabhūmi*): *apāyabhūmi*. There is a twofold analysis:
either "those whose minds are elevated" (*ussita*) or "those whose minds are swollen" (*ussanna*). "Elevated" (*ussita*) means risen up; "swollen" (*ussanna*) means extensive.
To the question, "Why is it said that their minds are sharper? he says, "Because they are fulfilled," and so forth.
Because it was stated in the introductory passage by way of being common to infinite world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*), the words “in this [world]” and so forth were spoken again;
there is nothing further to be said. The intention is that it is precisely here that the Omniscient Buddhas and others have arisen.

“They grasp” means they grasp having made it superior. “Valiant” means those whose minds are courageous regarding both evil and wholesome kamma. “Possessing mindfulness” means those who have vast mindfulness.
“‘The dwelling of the holy life here’ means the existence of the dwelling of the holy life, which consists in the fulfillment of the three trainings, right here.
‘Regarding the laws of boundaries’ means regarding the customs of worldly conduct. ‘Dhataraṭṭha’ refers to King Dhataraṭṭha;
likewise for Virūḷhaka and the others. ‘Residing upon fragrant trees’ means those who dwell upon fragrant trees. ‘Kumbhaṇḍas’...”
What is called "earth" (*pathavī*)? The grammatical analysis is: "those for whom there are treasures and goods that have gone into the earth.
"Danava-rakshasas" means rakshasas named Danavas, in the sense of being the offspring of the goddess named Danu. "Avaruddhakas" means those who obstruct or create obstacles.
"Vigaccharūpa" means one whose complexion has deteriorated. "Nihīnakammakatā" refers to base or evil deeds.
Having done so, they have come. The connection is: "some are born as Gandhapiyā. They are called *yāgandhapiyā* and *joginī*, and they are also called *juṇhā*;
such is the connection. "On the specially distinguished nights" means on well-known nights; that is to say, on the uposatha nights.
"At the time when they are intent upon their range" means at the time when they wander about for the sake of their range. "In the sense of radiance" means in the sense of shining forth.
They are called *vasundharā* because they bear (*dhārenti*) treasures (*vasūni*). The analysis of the compound is: "those who are both earth-deities (*vasundharā*) and *yakkhas*.
The phrase "they are indeed called *nāgas*" means that, according to the Pāli text, they are included among the *nāgas*.
"Those which" refers to those species of earth-deity *yakkhas*. "Of those which" refers to those species of earth-deity *yakkhas*. "By way of sport and delight" [refers] to the Bodhisattas and...
And it was at the time when the Buddhas were born that they proclaimed [the Dhamma] by way of increasing their playful activities.
“And the mantra-words of which”: those mantra-words which proceed by way of censure, praise, honoring, and so forth.
“In them”: in those four types of persons who have fallen into ruin. “By way of being addicted to play”: by way of being a gambler. “By way of being addicted to food.”
"By way of eating and consuming like a rogue. *Soṇa* means a dog. "Beings" refers to those in the hells or the *petas*.

"'And although it may be' (*kāmañca hoti*)" has the sense of "even though it may be so. "'A place of constant connection' (*nibandhanokāsa*)" means a place of perpetual association. "'In those that have come down through tradition' (*samudāgatesu*)" means in those that have been handed down from one to another.
"'In the places of the king of gods' (*devarājaṭṭhānesu*)" means in the abodes of the Thirty-three (*Tāvatiṃsa*) within this world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), which are the stations of the king of gods.
The intention [is as follows]. “In the Pāḷi itself” means in the Pāḷi of the Janavasabha Sutta in the Dīgha Nikāya.

“Yāmo” (the watch) means that which they go to (*yanti*) or settle into (*niyacchanti*). “They settle into” (*niyacchanti*) means that they depart from mutual strife, quarreling, and so forth, rooted in envy and avarice.
“Because of its association with that” means because of its constant association with that class of deities known by the name Yāma.
Because they arise together. "Exercising control" means fulfilling one's desires;
this is what is meant. "In front" means in a place directly before one. Since that place is called a high position, he said "in a high position.
Regarding the phrase "the Brahmā Sahassa," and so forth: because he illuminates a thousand world-systems (cakkavāḷa) with the radiance of his own body, he is named "Sahassa."
This is the intended meaning in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*). "Family deities" (*kuladevatā*) means deities worshipped through successive generations of a family.

Regarding the phrase "they wait upon": in appropriate places, having constructed shrines for the deities (*devavatthu*) and *devamālakas*, they go there from time to time and worship with perfumes, garlands, and so forth;
they pay homage, offer praise, and make aspirations for boons—this is the meaning. "They indeed become attendants."
The intended meaning is that they serve merely as attendants. "Of anyone" means of any lower [being]. "Therein" refers to those Brahma-world planes.
Again, "therein" refers to that second level. "Radiance" means bodily radiance. "They issue forth" means they emerge from the limbs and members of the body.
"Immovably established" means that, unlike on the second level, it does not waver.
Then they became immovable. The construction is as follows: “of them” refers to those speakers; [the phrase] “the name ‘Brahmapārisajjā’ and so forth is not established” is the connection.
“By those of a trembling nature” means by those of a moving nature. “There is the trembling of the lower planes, which is the fruit of merit”—this is the connection.
“By that of an unshakable nature” means by the equanimity-jhāna of an immovable nature, for those reborn therein.
“Of the fourth levels. “By some obstacle” means by an obstacle such as the conflagration at the end of an eon (*tejosaṃvaṭṭa*).
“Even here” means even on this fourth level. “Due to diversity of lifespan” refers to the variety in the measure of life-span.
“Of the gross” is said because they are gross by nature; it is not because of the existence of subtle [beings]. There is no affliction.

These are the Avihas. What is meant by "not being disturbed"? It is said: "The attainment of non-distraction in the tasks of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). This means that there is no reaching of distraction for the mind.

"By the eyes of clarity, the divine, the Dhamma, and wisdom"—that is, the eye of clarity (pasādacakkhu), the divine eye (dibbacakkhu), the Dhamma-eye (dhammacakkhu), and the eye of wisdom (paññācakkhu).
Indeed. Therein, it is the eye of clarity (*pasādacakkhu*) alone that is here called the "divine eye" (*dibbacakkhu*). "The eye of Dhamma" (*dhammacakkhu*) refers to the knowledge of the lower paths.
"The eye of wisdom" (*paññācakkhu*) refers to all remaining knowledge together with the knowledge of insight (*vipassanā*) and the knowledge of reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇā*).
"Of beings possessing form" (*rūpīnaṃ sattānaṃ*) means of beings possessing a physical body (*rūpakāya*). "The state of being younger" (*kaniṭṭhabhāvo*) means the state of being inferior.

"The rejection [of the path] even for one standing on the path of non-returning" means that the path of non-returning arises only for one who is developing [the path] while established in the state of a once-returner, and not otherwise;
thus he said, "by the rejection of the once-returners," and so forth.
The tetrad of planes is concluded.
144. It is called *okkantī* because they descend (*okkamanti*) into it during another existence. “Devoid of the ear” means devoid of the ear of faith;
the same applies to the remaining [faculties]. “By way of being an *āsittaka* paṇḍaka, etc. means by way of being an *āsittaka* paṇḍaka and so forth. “With two sexual organs” means with two marks.
“One whose speech is impaired” means one whose speech is defective. Regarding the phrase “of one whose basis is impaired,” here “basis” (*vatthu*) refers to—
The "eye" refers to the equipment (sambhāra). Because it has failed from the very beginning, a person endowed with it is said to be "one whose basis has failed" (vatthuvipanna).
"Of this and that" means of such an eye. "At the very time of birth" means at the very moment of delivery. Regarding the phrase "of the state of proficiency in wisdom" (paññāveyyattiyabhāva):
here, the state of one who is proficient (byatta) is "proficiency" (veyyattiya). "Of one who is proficient" means of one possessing pervasive knowledge (pharaṇaññāṇa).

“Of a person”: the analysis is “one who possesses discernment (paññā) known as proficiency (veyyattiya). The connection is: “it is not possible to determine [the presence of faculties] even for those with two or three roots.
To the question “How is it not possible? he says: “In the mother’s womb, there is no such thing as impairment (vipatti).
Of what things is there impairment? Of the eye and ear that have already arisen. For what reason is there impairment?
The construction is: "ruin" [occurs] either through the efforts of another, or through the mother's improper conduct, or through various afflictions.
Because the root *yakkha* is listed in the *Dhātupāṭha* as meaning "to worship," it is said [here] in the sense of "worthy of worship.

By this, he shows that *yakkhas* are so called because they are to be approached (*yak-khitabba*) and worshipped (*pūjitabba*). However, those who wander about having fallen into a life of hardship are known as "earth-dwellers" (*bhūmasita*).

The construction [of the commentary] is as follows: regarding the reading “bhūmissitā,” in order to show the meaning “situated on, or dependent upon, the earth,” it is said “produced by merit,” and so forth.
“Having become deformed” means they are ugly in color; they are misshapen in form;
and they are miserable in their livelihood—thus, having become ruined in appearance. “Falling down helpless” also means being fallen into the lower realms (*vinipātika*).
They say this. *Vivasāti* means that one dwells (*vasati*) according to one’s own will or desire. “In secluded places” means in places devoid of people.
They maintain their lives by seeking [food], or they maintain their lives by afflicting [others], or they maintain their lives by both terrifying and afflicting—such is the construction.
“Ghosts belonging to celestial mansions” (*vemānika-peta*) refers to those who possess divine celestial mansions produced by their own merit.
Those who possess [such a state] are the *vemānika* (intermediate beings).

Because they are produced by karma that is a mixture of merit and demerit, some experience divine bliss by day and the suffering of a *peta* (hungry ghost) by night; others experience divine bliss by night and the suffering of a *peta* by day.
They are called "those who subsist on what is given by others" because they live depending upon the fruit of merit bestowed and offered by others.
“The fruit of merit given by others”: this refers to the fruit of merit given when relatives, having performed a meritorious deed, say, “Give this merit to our deceased kinsmen who have passed away.
“Included within the entire world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) and belonging to the same plane”:
just as the so-called Tāvatiṃsa plane exists in all world-systems, so too does every [heaven] last for a thousand celestial years.
There is a single limit to the lifespan. This cannot be said regarding this Cakkavāḷa [world-system].

Likewise, there is no such thing as a single uniform limit for the lifespan in the hells, the animal realm, the sphere of hungry ghosts, the host of asuras, among humans, or among the earth-dwelling devas.
It has been stated that there is no fixed rule for the calculation of the measure of the lifespan in the four states of misery; but is it not the case with Brahmā?
In the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*, it was stated by the Blessed One concerning the monk Kokālika that there are ten separate hells.
This is true. However, those ten hells are included within the Avīci hell and constitute merely its sections.
It cannot be said that the entire Avīci hell has a fixed lifespan and a definite measure based on those individual sections.
Moreover, even that limit of their lifespan is not established as a fixed rule for the Avīci realm; rather, it is established by specific differences in karma.
Therefore, what was stated—"because there, for the most part, the measure is determined by karma"—is well said.
Thus he says, "In those hells," and so forth. "This being so" refers to the fact that there is no increase in the lifespan of the inhabitants of the other continents.

When it is said, "there is also descent," the meaning is "when this exists. "Good conduct" refers to the ten courses of wholesome action (*dasasu-caritāni*). "Bad conduct" refers to the ten courses of unwholesome action (*dasadu-caritāni*).
The connection is that prosperity and adversity are the respective outflows (*nissanda*) of those two. The phrase "of them too" means "of the inhabitants of the other continents as well.

[If one were to argue that] "he [the Buddha] is limited in that way," it would follow [that he is not omniscient]; however, it is not possible for it to be so. At the time of the first eon (*ādikappa-kāla*)...
"It might be argued that for all inhabitants of the four continents, an incalculable lifespan (*asaṅkhyeyya-āyuka*) is possible.

Furthermore, for the inhabitants of the other continents as well, there is an increase and decrease of their life-span. This being the case, even now, their life-span might be of the same order as the life-span of the inhabitants of Jambudvīpa.
The response begins with "It is merely a residual effect" (*nissandamattattā*), and so forth. [The opponent says: "This is not mine."

“Amamā” (without "mine") means those for whom the craving directed toward personal possession (*pāṭipuggalikataṇhā*) expressed as "this is mine" has ceased. “Apariggahā” (without possessions) means being devoid of the possession of children, wives, and so forth.
“In the upper realm of the Four Great Kings” refers to the Four Great Kings who dwell in the sky. “Celestial” (*dibba*) means perfected in the divine world (*devaloka*).
“As far back as the time of King Nimi” means as far back as the period when we were born as the Bodhisattva King Nimi. Of whom?
Pabuddha appeared in a previous intermediate aeon (*antarakappa*), whereas King Nimi appeared in this present intermediate aeon.

The statement, “Fifty human years constitute a single night and day for the Cātumahārājika [devas],” and so forth, is spoken according to the method found in the *Dhammahadaya-vibhaṅga* of the Abhidhamma.
Regarding the expression “of the higher ones,” it refers to those who are higher.
Of the gods. The connection is: "The measure of their lifespan is one thousand years. "Two" means two thousand years. "Eight" means eight thousand years.
"Of the lower" refers to the lower gods. "Of the upper" refers to the upper gods.
This should be applied starting from the phrase "In the Yāma [heaven], one day and night... "Four" refers to [the lifespan] in the human world.
Four hundred years. The same applies to the remaining [deities]. Regarding the phrase "by way of showing the beginning and the end":
the calculation of human years among the Cātumahārājika devas is called "showing the beginning. Now, the calculation of human years among the Vasavatti devas is called "showing the end.

"Not too weak" means not excessively weak. "That" refers to that jhāna consisting of non-initial application and non-sustained application (*avitakka-avicāra-matta*). "In another plane" (*bhūmantare*)...
From the plane of the first jhāna to another, namely the plane of the second jhāna. Regarding the term *kappa*:
it is called *kappa* because it is reckoned (*kappīyati*)—that is, it is delimited by years, seasons, months, fortnights, nights, days, or daytime.

Alternatively, it is called *kappa* because various occurrences of phenomena (*dhamma*) are reckoned (*kappīyanti*) by it, being delimited by the past day. It means time. A great *kappa* is a *mahākappa*. [This refers to] years...
"Immeasurable" (*asaṅkhyeyya*) means that which cannot be calculated even by a hundredth part, a thousandth part, or a hundred-thousandth part.
A *kappa* (eon) appearing within one such immeasurable period is an "intermediate eon" (*antarakappa*). The "life-eon" (*āyukappa*) refers to the specific limit of the lifespan of sentient beings;
for humans, when their lifespan is ten years, it is delimited by those ten years. [The term] *nevasaññā-*...
The period of the gods is delimited by eighty-four thousand *kappas*. The connection is that what is called an "intermediate *kappa*" (*antarakappa*) refers to minor *kappas* (*cūḷakappa*).
Some say that minor *kappas* are said to be divided into twenty types; such is the construction [of the sentence].
"Those" refers to the intermediate *kappas* divided into sixty-four and so forth. "As destroyed" means according to the manner of destruction, that is, by way of the nature of being destroyed.
The eon is expanding; it has evolved. "In the manner of evolution" means by way of the mode of evolution and the nature of evolution.
"With the passing" means with the elapsing. "By the taking away" means by the removal. "Therein" refers to that statement regarding the eon.
The connection is: "because it is stated in the commentary. "By its heat" means by fire. "It contracts" means it perishes at that time. "Below" means...
"Below is the light. In the phrase "in sixty-four instances," the locative case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*).

[It refers to] "in the verses. Regarding the phrase "seven times seven by fire": they are destroyed by fire seven times over seven cycles. Alternatively, it is the nominative case used in the sense of the locative.
The construction is: "In seven times seven cycles, the world is destroyed by fire. Therefore, he said: "In the eighth..."
"In the eighth" means "by water. The construction is: in the eighth and indeed the eighth aeon, the world will be destroyed by water.
When sixty-four aeons have been completed, there may then be one wind-aeon. In that context, "then" refers to that sixty-fourth aeon.
"Expanding" (vivaṭṭamānaṃ) means forming [the world-system]. "It expands" (vivaṭṭati) means it forms. "Contracting" (saṃvaṭṭamānaṃ) means being destroyed.

“*Saṃvaṭṭati*” means it perishes. “*Two asaṅkhyeyyas*” is stated figuratively by taking one and a half asaṅkhyeyyas as two asaṅkhyeyyas, just as it is said that there are eight kappas for the Ābhassara devas. Regarding “*by a half*”:

during the water-cycle, while the lower planes are being destroyed by water, the plane of the second jhāna is not yet destroyed. This remains so for a long time even during the period of dissolution (*saṃvaṭṭakappa*).
It remains just as it is. This was said with reference to this. All of this was stated because it is obtainable.
It was stated with reference to an incalculable eon (*asaṅkhyeyyakappa*); this alone is the measure.
The tetrad on rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhicatukka*) is finished.
145. In the tetrad on kamma: “Produces” means it produces what has not yet been produced; it makes manifest.
“Supports” means it supports what has already been produced; it makes it long-lasting. “Oppresses” means it oppresses what has already been produced;
it causes it to decline. “Destroys” means it cuts it off. “Of material phenomena produced by kamma” means of those material phenomena born of kamma, which are termed “produced by kamma.”
Regarding the phrase “having reached the path of action”: here, it should be understood that when rebirth-linking occurs, all karma whatsoever is said to have reached the path of action.
“Vipakkavipāka” means that which has ripened (*vipakka*) is its result (*vipāka*).
It continues by being supported. The intention is that it does so even when [the karma] itself obtains conditions. “Of one who has not obtained an opportunity” means:
This is merely an illustration. Even for one who has gained an opportunity, support (upatthambhana) must indeed be sought.
The construction is: "another unwholesome kamma gains an opportunity. “Cāyaṃ” means “this person. “Kālaṅkariyā” means “he might die.
“Assā” means “of this individual. “Pasāditaṃ” means “serene. “Padūsitaṃ” means “corrupted. [Previously...]
Because it was stated [elsewhere] as "at the time near death," it is stated here as "even during the course of existence.
"This" refers to the support for another kamma. "Requisites for life" means the conditions that surround life. "Having acquired" means having brought together.
"In this" refers to the supporting kamma-object. The connection is with "the nourishing of the continuity of the aggregates."

“By the method already stated” means by the method stated as “having removed [it] from the obstacle to life,” and so forth. The connection is with “the continued flow of the continuity of the aggregates for a longer period.
“Of the kind already mentioned” means of the kind thus mentioned: “all wholesome or unwholesome volitions that have not found an opportunity to ripen, or whose ripening has already occurred.
“Either making it weaker or obstructing it” refers to the *upapīḷaka* (obstructive kamma).
The function of karma has been explained. “At the time of the accumulation of weak generative karma” refers to the time of its integration.
“With its power struck down” means its efficacy has been destroyed. “Among those of great influence” means among those of great majesty.
“The supportive [karma] should also be understood as the opposite of that” means it should be understood as the reverse of the obstructive karma. “The higher plane...”
The intended meaning is that in such passages as "even while producing [a result] in a lower plane,
it produces [it] in a higher plane," one should state it as "even while producing [a result] in a lower plane, it produces [it] in a higher plane.
In the case of King Ajātasattu, although his act of patricide was destined to produce rebirth in the Great Avīci Hell, later— due to the Buddha’s...
Being obstructed by *paṭṭhāna-kamma* (foundational karma), its power being destroyed, it causes rebirth in that specific hell.
The connection is this: the obstruction of the continuity of the aggregates (*khandha-santāna*) is what constitutes the arising of suffering for a sentient being.

How is it that causing the misfortune of cattle, buffaloes, and so forth, as well as children, wives, relatives, and friends, constitutes the function of that being’s *upapīḷaka-kamma* (obstructive karma)?
[It] would be [so]. That person is one thing, while the cattle, buffalo, and so forth are another.
And it is objected that a deed performed by one should not cause the arising of suffering or the arising of happiness for other beings. He answers this with the words "of two kinds," and so on.
In the story of the merchant Ānanda: the merchant Soṇa was extremely stingy; he even prevented others from giving gifts.
Having passed away from there, he was born in a certain village in the womb of a woman.
It is stated in the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā* that from the time of his birth, suffering arose for all the people of that village, beginning with his mother, due to his evil karma.
Therefore, by way of the result of outflow (*nissandaphala*), karma performed by one person [produces effects] for others.
It should be understood that it indeed brings about either the arising of suffering or the arising of happiness for sentient beings. Regarding the phrase “the continuity born of kamma is the head”:
from the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) onwards, there exists a single continuity of material phenomena born of kamma;
because this serves as the head for the subsequent successive occurrence of similar continuities of material phenomena born of kamma, it is called a “continuity” (santati).
It is called the "head. Any single stream of vocal-kamma is one head; two streams of vocal-kamma are two heads. [This is according to] the *Visuddhimagga* text:
“Tadeva” means that very same obstructive kamma. “Idha ca” means in this *Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha*.
“Imassapi” means even of this obstructive kamma. And in the story of King Duṭṭhagāmaṇi and the Elder Soṇa...
In the case of their father, at the time of his approaching death, the signs of an unfortunate rebirth first appeared. However,
as the king recollected a single previous meritorious deed and the elder’s father performed a single meritorious deed at that very moment,
those signs of an unfortunate rebirth vanished, and the signs of heaven appeared.
They manifest. Both, having passed away, are reborn in the heavenly realms.

Because he brings about the exhaustion of wholesome and unwholesome kamma, he is called "the one who effects the exhaustion of wholesome and unwholesome kamma. Regarding the phrase "while life-span and kamma still exist":
for that being, the limit of his life-span has not yet reached its end, nor has the power of his kamma been fully exhausted. Thus...
"While the life-span and kamma still exist": this refers to an "offensive kamma" (*aparādha-kamma*) committed by way of offending one's parents or righteous recluses and brahmins.
"But that" (*so panā*): this is the position of the *Majjhima-aṭṭhakathā*. "As if not being desired": as if it were not wanted. "That" (*so*):
this is the position of the *Majjhima-aṭṭhakathā*. "In that regard... (*tattha*)...
“*Panā*” refers to the *Madhyma-aṭṭhakathā*. The connection is: “All this” means that all these words of the Sutta were spoken by way of [this method].

By those who do not accept it, [it is said] by the *Carīya-ṭīkā*. “*Vipākaṃ paṭiicchitabbo*” means it should be desired depending upon the result (*vipāka*). Here, “result” (*vipāka*) refers to the continuity of the aggregates produced by karma. Of that...
Productive karma is called "productive karma. The intention is that karma which supports that very same continuum of aggregates, which oppresses it, and which harms it, is called "injurious karma.
"In the Sāketa Questions" refers to the Sāketa questions found in the *Vipākuddhāra*. [It concerns] Queen Dhammadinnā and King Uggasena.

In a previous life, Queen Sādevī killed a goat; by that kamma, she fell into the states of misery, and subsequently, as the ripening of her continued existence, she experienced the suffering of having her head cut off for as many times as there are hairs on the body of a goat throughout many births.
As for the phrase "But that": it refers to that single volition of taking life. (The Story of Mahāmoggallāna)
The story of the execution of five hundred thieves by the Elder:
Having obtained his execution at the hands of the thieves due to a kamma of interruption performed by himself in a previous life, the Elder attained final Nibbāna.

Likewise, Queen Sāmāvatī and the five hundred bhikkhus dwelling on the banks of the Vaggumudā River encountered such an assault from others due to kamma of interruption performed by themselves in previous lives.
Having attained [merit], they were reborn in the heavens. He who was called Dussimāra is said to have been the son of the Māra deity during the time of Buddha Kakusandha.
He who was called King Kalābu is said to have been the slayer of the Teacher who preached patience.
However, at that very moment, due to the obstructive karma they themselves had committed, they passed away instantly and were reborn in Avīci. In those previous instances...
Cutting-off karma merely effects the cutting off [of the flow of other karma]; it does not yield its own result.
However, in the case of the final existences, it both effects the cutting off and yields its result—this is the reading in the *Vibhāvanī*.
Regarding the phrase “preceded by cutting off,” the construction is: it generates a result preceded by cutting off. Having indeed cut off the result of another karma...

The intention is that it produces its own result (*vipāka*). Regarding the phrase "it produces its own result," it is said that this is not excellent because no distinction is made here as to whether it sometimes produces [the result] and sometimes does not.
Therefore, he says: "In this case, by what was done previously," and so forth.
"Because it is found only in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*)" means that in those instances, the piercing is the interrupter.
Because it was stated, "They die by means of kamma," [it is so called]. That which produces a result is "result-producing" (*vipākanibbattaka*).
The state of that is "result-producing-ness" (*vipākanibbattakatta*). The analysis is: "the absence of result-producing-ness.
The section on the fourfold productive [kamma] is finished.

136. “If it is being resisted by force, attachment does not yield its result”: the intention is that even for one who has attained meditative absorption (*jhāna*), if there is attachment at the time of death to being reborn [in a certain plane], that absorption does not yield its result.

“Of one” means of a single person. “Of those” refers to sublime deeds (*mahaggata-kamma*) and deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantariya-kamma*). That which was performed in the final cognitive process (*javana-vīthi*)...
Because the basis (vatthu) is weak, [the mind] itself becomes weak; it does not produce rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi). Therefore, he said:
"Performed in the proximate period prior to the final javana-process. And this was stated by way of the general nature of kamma.
However, to show that when there is a specific kind of kamma, one cannot say that it does not give [a result], he said: "But as for the kamma of wrong view," and so forth.
The construction is: "It should be understood that what is called 'proximate karma' is to be grasped. In the sequence of the text (*pāḷipāṭhe*):
for a person at the time of death, right view has been undertaken and adopted, or wrong view has been undertaken and adopted—this is the construction. What follows will come forth in full.
That which produces joy does so by way of the occurrence of another's volition; that which produces torment does so by way of the occurrence of remorse and regret.
This is called the "heavy tetrad" (*garuka-catukka*); it is stated with reference to those karmas that ripen in the immediately following existence.
Thus he said: "only karmas to be experienced upon rebirth" (*upapajjavedanīya-kammāni*). Karma may be either wholesome (*kusala*) or unwholesome (*akusala*).

When there is repeated cultivation after having acquired it, it yields its result (*vipāka*); when there is not, it does not yield it. This applies to wholesome karma of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).

It is stated in the Canon: "Eye-consciousness has arisen as a result of what has been done and accumulated," and "Eye-consciousness has arisen as a result of unwholesome kamma that has been done and accumulated.

For here, after saying "because it has been done" (*katattā*), the further statement "because it has been accumulated" (*upacitattā*) is used to indicate the repeated practice (*āsevanā*) characterized by constant increase.
This makes it known that [kamma] gives its result in this very way. Therefore, although it is said, "What kind of kamma?

Kamma that has been performed (kaṭattā kammaṃ)," since here only that kamma which ripens in the immediately following existence is intended, the *Aṭṭhakathā* states, "having repeatedly obtained the opportunity for practice," in order to show that only such repeated practice is to be understood here.

Regarding the passage beginning with “And having done so”: “Where it is stated as ‘that previously performed kamma’” means that in that section of the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), that *kaṭattā-kamma* is stated as “previously performed kamma. Regarding the passage beginning with “Why here?”:
“Here” means in this *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha*. In the canonical text (Pāḷi): “That which is heavy gives its result; in its absence,” [the next lightest gives its result].
That which is most frequent; in its absence, that which is proximate; in its absence, it is the meaning that whatever karma has been performed (*kaṭattā*) gives its result.
The rest here is easy to understand. In the Suttanta reading:
"It produces a pleasant feeling" means "to be experienced as pleasant" (*sukhavedanīya*). "Fully undertaken" (*samattā*) means well-grasped. "Adopted" (*samādinnā*)...
This is the explanation of its meaning. "Sufficient" means capable. Throughout his life, Tambadādhika habitually performed many evil deeds;
however, on the day of his death, having heard the Dhamma teaching of the Elder Sāriputta, he passed away and, due to that proximate kamma, was reborn in heaven.
Throughout his life, Vātakāla habitually performed many wholesome deeds.
On the day of his death, however, having formed a perverted perception regarding the Buddha’s teaching, he was reborn in a state of misery (apāya) due to that proximate kamma.
The Section on the Four Heavy [Kammas] is concluded. 147.

Regarding the Section on the Four [Kinds of Kamma] to be Seen in This Very Life (*diṭṭhadhammacatukka*): "To be seen" means perceived. "Dhamma" refers to the collection of phenomena consisting of the aggregates (*khandha*) and the sense bases (*āyatana*).
“Diṭṭhadhammo” means the seen phenomenon (*diṭṭhadhamma*). It is the present collection of phenomena which is called the personal existence (*attabhāva*).

By taking the state, the occurrence, and the cause of that which is designated as a self—the essence of which is imagined through views—he says, “the seen phenomenon is spoken of,” and so forth, in order to show this meaning.
By the phrase “experiences the result (*vipākaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti*),” he shows how it functions as a karmic instrument (*kamma-sādhana*).
In the phrase "experiencing" (*paṭisaṃvedana*), when the word for action is seen as "result" (*vipāka*), that which is called the result is to be understood as "to be experienced" (*vedanīya*).
It is "to be experienced" (*paṭisaṃvedanīya*) because it is to be known (*viññātattā*). "Having approached" (*upetvā*) means having gone near.

"Having been reborn" (*upapajjitvā*) means having approached and then being born; the meaning is "having reached. In the reading of the *Vibhāvanī*: "from the present life" (*diṭṭhadhammato*) means "of the present life" (*diṭṭhadhammassa*).
The fifth case (pañcamī) is used in the sense of the source (sāmi-atthe). This is stated in the Pāḷi: “*Ettha hī*” and so forth, according to the method already explained in the preceding passage.
The word *apara* always requires an ablative (apādāna). And that ablative is [to be understood] from the words mentioned immediately prior:
“from the present life (*diṭṭhadhammā*) and from the subsequent future life (*anāgatānantarabhavā*); such is the meaning. “*Parivatto*” means a continuous succession.
"Aparāpariya" means either "one after another" (*aparo ca aparo ca*) or "that which proceeds from one to another" (*aparāpare pavatto*). The meaning is "that which occurs in succession.

"Rebirth-existence" (*upapajjabhavaṃ*) refers to the immediately future existence. Regarding the word "Ahosi-kamma," he says it is "called 'Ahosi'" because it is a conventional name (*ruḷhīnāma*), like the word "Koṇḍañña. But from where does that conventional term originate?
He said: “There was karma,” and so forth. Regarding the phrase “by way of the reading thus spoken,” the reading spoken here is abbreviated;
however, the complete reading is: there was karma, there was the result of that karma; there was karma, there was no result of that karma;
there was karma, there is the result of that karma; there was karma, there is no result of that karma; there was karma, there will be [the result].
“Kamma and its result,” “there was kamma, but there will be no [further] kamma-result,” and so forth, appear in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*.

“Sā” (that) refers to the volition of the first impulsion (*javana*). Regarding the phrase “with less result” (*appatara-vipākā*), the word “iti” here is a particle used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*);
therefore, because it has a short duration, it disappears after giving its fruit in this very life (*diṭṭhadhamma*), and thus it is “less.”
The construction is: "Because it is a result of maturation (*vipāka*), it ceases after giving its fruit as mere rootless [consciousness].
"And 'condition' (*paccayo*)" means that which is called a condition because it has been obtained as a condition. "'That'" refers to the condition mentioned as being great.
"'Like that of Kākavalī and others'" means like the karma to be experienced in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*) of persons such as Kākavalī. "'Giving a more manifest fruit'" means...
A specific type of karma that yields its fruit more manifestly by way of attaining the status of a merchant prince and so forth within seven days itself. The construction is:
either the volition of the first impulsion occurring in the continuum of the path-of-action impulsion, or even other [volitions] of the first impulsion.
"Any" means certain volitions of the first impulsion. The remaining ones are karmas to be experienced in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*).

Regarding "kamma to be experienced upon rebirth" (*upapajjavedanīyakamma*): "accomplishing eight" means accomplishing the purpose of final determination (*sanniṭṭhāna*). What is meant is that it accomplishes the tasks such as the killing of living beings.
It is called "determinative" (*sanniṭṭhāpika*) because it brings [the matter] to a complete conclusion. "The rest as well" refers to the remaining types of kamma to be experienced upon rebirth.
"In this world" refers to this human world. "Mixed kamma" refers to wholesome [kamma] mixed with unwholesome [kamma].
[The stories of] kamma. The *Vimānavatthu* (Stories of Celestial Mansions) are included in the *Vimānavatthu-pāḷi*.

Regarding the phrase "stories of those experiencing misfortune in a happy destination" (*sugatīyaṃ vipattiṃ anubhavantāni vatthūni*), "misfortune" (*vipatti*) here refers to the impairment of the eyes, ears, and other limbs or members [of the body], or it refers to misfortune consisting in the arising of various forms of suffering.
Regarding "prosperity in an unhappy destination" (*duggatiyaṃ sampattiṃ*), this refers to [the prosperity of] highly powerful beings such as nāgas, supaṇṇas, and so forth.
Prosperity. "By the aforementioned bases" means by the various bases for ghosts (*petavatthu*) and so forth.
In the reading of the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), "there is no shifting of them" means that there is no shifting of those karmic actions at the time they ripen.
"They remain in their very own place" means that they abide precisely in the places described by the Blessed One according to the present life (*diṭṭhadhamma*) and other such categories.
"Thus it was said" means it was stated in the manner beginning with "there is no transition for them," and so forth. Regarding "or because of the absence of logical consistency":
here, this refers to the absence of logical consistency for a result to be experienced in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*) to have rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) as its fruition, and so on.
This concludes the tetrad on the present life.
148. In the tetrad on the manifesting place (*pākaṭṭhānacatukka*): “Of the body, etc. refers to the movable body, etc.; that is to say, of bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*), etc.
“They cause to fall beyond” means they cause [the object] to fall by overstepping [the boundary] through an application of effort. Therefore he said: “And here, causing to fall beyond,” and so forth.
“What is not given” (*adinnam*) means the property of another not given by the owner. “Places not to be approached” (*agamanīyavatthūni*) are for the purpose of non-transgression.
The bodies of women and men, such as those protected by their mothers and so forth, are not to be approached. “Of her” means of another living being.
“From that” means from the state of being possessed by another. “The intention of one who seizes” means the intense intention of seizing the property of another as if it were one’s own;
it is what is called the intention of plundering. “By way of the path... [text continues]
“Of one who establishes others on the path” means of one who joins others with the supreme path by means of his own path.
“In this case too”: just as in the case of taking what is not given, the second factor-word “perceiving it as belonging to another” was stated; so it is here too.
Here they say that instead of saying “the mind by way of an object not to be approached,” it is stated as “the mind intent on indulgence therein. Therefore...
"Perceiving it as an object not to be approached" means that even if it is not explicitly stated, it is equivalent to what has been stated.
This is not so; for the expression "not in that" does not express a meaning accompanied by a specific designation (*saññā*).

And in such instances, if the designation were predominant, then just as "perceiving it as a living being" (*pāṇasaññitā*) and "perceiving it as belonging to another" (*parapariggahitasaññitā*) are constituent factors (*aṅgapada*), here too [the phrase] "perceiving it as an object not to be approached" [would be a constituent factor].
The second factor-phrase, "perceiving [it as such]," must necessarily be stated. Why? Because it serves to define the factors. Therefore he said, "By this," and so forth.
"It is described as having four factors": its four constituent parts are:
an unsuitable object, the mind that engages with it, the application of engagement, and the acceptance of the path as the path. "That" refers to...
“Bhikkhunī. “Included among those who are protected” means included among those protected by their mother, protected by their father, and so forth.
“But in the commentaries (*ṭīkā*)” refers to the commentaries on the Suttantas. “She” refers to the bhikkhunī. “Heretics (*pāsaṇḍa*)” refers to the sixty-two types of views and so on.
Those who advocate such views are called heretics (*pāsaṇḍika*). Their doctrine is called the heretical doctrine (*pāsaṇḍiya-dhamma*). Immoral conduct also [applies] to one who is immoral.
The transgression against a woman is slightly blameworthy. More blameworthy than that is [the violation] against one who has the nature of a cow.

More blameworthy than that is [the violation] against one who has gone for refuge, against one who observes the five training rules, against a female novice, and against an ordinary nun, and so forth—according to the text of the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
Regarding the word “herein,” it refers to this unwholesome bodily action. Regarding the phrase “not included,” it was not [included] by the Elder or by the masters of the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
Or it is not grasped. It is called *surāmerayapāna* because one drinks *surā* (fermented liquor) and *meraya* (distilled spirits) by means of this;

the volition of swallowing that is the kamma. "The lightest of all" means that among all the results of the kamma of drinking *surā*, that which is the lightest result—namely, merely a result occurring in the course of existence—is what is meant. "Leading to madness" means the state of being insane.
“Leading to” (*saṃvattaniko*). “Even the five” (*pañcapī*) means even all five together with the action of drinking liquor (*surāpāna-kamma*).

This is according to the statement in the *Mūlaṭīkā*. “Of that” (*tassā*) refers to the action of drinking liquor. The connection is that this was stated in the commentary on this passage in the *Paṭisambhidāmaggaṭīkā*.
Therein, “and the abstaining from that, etc. (*tabbiramaṇādayo cā*) means the abstaining from that drinking of liquor, and so forth. “From intoxication” (*madassā*)—
“Of intoxicants”: of the path of demerit, that is, of unwholesome courses of action (*akusala-kamma-patha*). “Abstention from that as well”: abstention from that drinking of liquor as well.
“The state of being free from pride”: the condition of being devoid of intoxication. “That”: the state of being free from pride. “Of the path of merit”:

of the wholesome course of action (*kusala-kamma-patha*). “Thus”: therefore. “Those”: the actions of drinking liquor and the action of abstaining from it. “Not... [The sentence continues: ...not... [the rest of the passage].
The phrase "the other" refers to that which is not connected with the courses of action (*kammapatha*). The construction is: "Drinking intoxicants does not, by itself, give rise to rebirth.

However, regarding the abstention from that, if one understands that this so-called drinking of intoxicants is an evil deed and misconduct, and guards that training rule through the attainment of both formal undertaking and natural abstinence, then that virtue [is included] among the other paths of merit.
It should not be said that even if it is unrelated, it does not separately produce rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). The construction is as follows:

“In this way too”—meaning that this action of drinking liquor, being an accessory (*parivāra*) to an action that has reached the level of a course of action (*kamma-patha*), likewise produces rebirth-linking.
“Therein” refers to the discourses on the courses of action (*kammapatha-sutta*). And it can be maintained that it was not stated in its own form; such is the connection.

“*Yaṃ*” means that action which is the drinking of liquor. “*Tatthā*” means among those suttas on the courses of action (*kamma-patha*). “*Kamma-jananaṃ nāma*” means the production of actions consisting of misconduct.
The connection is that by Sakka, the lord of the gods, its leading to states of misery (*apāya*) was stated.
“*Tassā asurāya puṇṇaṃ imaṃ surākumbhaṃ kiṇātha. Mūlaṃ detha gaṇhāthā*” means: “Buy this jar of liquor filled for that goddess; pay the price and take it. “*Tassā*” refers to her.
"Leading to the states of misery" (*apāyagāmī*) means that it causes one to go to, or reach, the states of misery (*apāya*), such as drinking intoxicants.

"Namely this" (*yadidaṃ*) refers to the application [of the term] according to whatever is available. In the *Mūlaṭīkā*, regarding the statement "conascent with karma," it means craving conascent with unwholesome karma.
"Of these" (*tesaṃ*) refers to those five types of karma. "By way of categories" (*koṭṭhāsato*) refers to how it is stated in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*: "There is contact, there is feeling," and so forth.
In the section on the summary of the Dhamma (*dhammuddesavāra*) that has been recited, the categories beginning with *jhāna* have come down.

Among those, the five training rules (*sikkhāpada*) belong exclusively to the category of courses of action (*kammappatha*). The meaning is that they are included within the category of courses of action.
"Of the four preceding" refers to the four actions beginning with the taking of life. "Prohibited" means that their status as courses of action is prohibited [in the case of the training rules].
“Third”: this refers to the third sutta. And in these commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) regarding bodily action (*kāyakamma*) and so forth:
the "body with its material basis" (*sasambhārakāya*) is the entire physical body (*rūpakāya*). The "body of sensitivity" (*pasādakāya*) is simply the sensitivity of the body (*kāyapasāda*).

The "informative body" (*copanakāya*) is the intimation of the body (*kāyaviññatti*). "Informative" (*copana*) is said to mean movement (*calana*). "That very same" refers to the informative body itself.
The construction is as follows: bodily action (kāyakamma) is indeed a means of acquisition; therefore, it is called the "gateway for the manifestation of karmas.
Regarding the phrase "to distinguish the karmas," this means to distinguish and determine them such that "this is called bodily action" and "this is called verbal action" (vacīkamma).
"Are able" means they are able to distinguish the karmas. Therefore, [it is said] "that which exists at the door of the body" and "that which exists at the door of speech."
And this is the intended meaning of what was stated. Because sexual misconduct does not occur through the door of speech, it is said, "the first two.
"The middle four" refers to the four verbal actions beginning with false speech.
"'Those faults are of six kinds'" refers to those six kinds of faults beginning with "one should abandon bodily action. How is it that each one is associated with the word *bāhulla* (abundance)?
"He avoids those sixfold [courses of action]" means that he avoids them both through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative exclusion (*vyatireka*). How so?
The act of taking life, even if it sometimes arises slightly at the door of speech, occurs predominantly at the door of the body; because of its abundance, it becomes purely a bodily action.
It does not count as a verbal action, nor does it receive two names. However, at the door of speech...
Because it occurs only rarely, it is not called "vocal action" (*vacīkamma*); it does not lose its name as "bodily action" (*kāyakamma*). Or rather, it does not come to have two names.
Thus, by stating that [the action] occurs predominantly through the single door of the body, one avoids the six kinds of faults in the act of taking life.
The same applies to the remaining [courses of action]. A "forest-wanderer" (*vanacāraka*) is a forest hunter. Furthermore, he...
Sometimes, even if one moves about little in the village, because of frequent movement in the forest, one is simply a "forest-roamer" (*vanacāraka*);
one does not receive the name "village-roamer" (*gāmacāraka*). Nor do both names apply to him simultaneously. The same applies to those who move about in battle.

An "elephant who moves about in battle" (*saṅgāmāvacara*) is called such because it frequently moves within the battle. Here, the mind-door (*manodvāra*) is mentioned because it is common to all types of action.

It was stated that one cannot distinguish between [types of] kamma. This being the case, one might object: "Since covetousness, ill will, and wrong view are said to reside in the mind, they should not be called 'mental kamma'. It should not be said that this is incorrect.
For, depending on the establishment of kamma, they are unique to their own specific doors. Therefore he said: "But as for mental kammas," and so forth. "Established" means...

It has arisen. Regarding the phrase "the door of bodily action" (*kāyakammadvāra*): therein, because the occurrence of bodily actions is frequent in the body of contact (*copanakāya*), it is called the "door of bodily action.
Because the occurrence of verbal actions is frequent in the speech of contact (*copanavācā*), it is called the "door of verbal action.

However, as for wholesome or unwholesome impulsion-consciousness (*javana-citta*), it is [called] the "door of mental action" (*manokamma*) because the performance of the function of action (*kamma-kicca*) is accomplished right there.
"Mind-door" means that the definition of the door by way of action should be understood in this manner.
"To break the name of that door" means to break the name "body. "Or to give its own name" means to give it the name "speech.
"Just as the status of a brahmin village and so forth [belongs] to the brahmin village and so forth" refers to that [status] among other families.
Even though it is springtime, because of the abundance of brahmin families, it is called a "brahmin village.

Even though there are other trees in that forest, because of the abundance of *khadira* trees, it should be called a "khadira forest. Thus, bodily action (*kāyakamma*) is concluded. 149. Verbal Action (*vacīkamma*).
"Speaking falsely" means speaking what is untrue. That by which one grinds [others] is "slanderous" (*pisuṇā*). [This is a term for] etymology (*nirutti*).
Regarding the phrase "by this method" (*nayenā*): here, where one should say "making dear-emptiness" (*piyasuñña-karaṇā*), the elision of syllables is called the *nirutti-naya* (etymological method).
"By whom" (*yenā*) means by which person. Regarding "frivolous talk" (*samphaṃ*): here, the prefix *sam-* signifies "that by which suffering is stilled" (*sammati dukkham etenā*);

thus, it functions in the sense of happiness and welfare. Therefore, he said: "‘Sam’ means happiness and welfare. To the question "What kind of happiness and welfare? he replied: "By virtuous people..."
"to be attained. By this, he rejects the welfare and happiness that ought to be attained by evil people.
He says, "he breaks the path to welfare and happiness," because the destruction of welfare and happiness means cutting off the path by which it arrives.
Regarding the phrase "or that," here "that" refers to welfare and happiness. "The eight things of one who has departed" [means] in terms of both meaning (*attha*) and doctrine (*dhamma*).

And for one who has departed [from the world]. “Of eloquence in mind”: for the purpose of increasing the delight and joy of the minds of those listening, it is that which is esteemed by the mind through the knowledge of eloquence.
“Wherein”: in whichever path of discourse. “The word of meaning, the Dhamma, and the Vinaya”:

the word of meaning (*atthapada*), the word of Dhamma (*dhammapada*), and the word of Vinaya (*vinayapada*). Therein, “meaning” (*attha*) refers to the attainment of health and the attainment of friends.
The perfection of wisdom, the perfection of wealth, and the perfections of enjoyments.
Among these, a phrase or sentence that generates skill regarding them—such as "This is called good conduct; it leads to heaven," and "This is called misconduct;
it leads to the states of loss"—is called a *dhammapada* (word of Dhamma), because it generates skill regarding phenomena (*dhamma*) in their essential nature (*sabhāva*). Thus, the mind...

The term *vinayapada* refers to a sentence or phrase that generates skill regarding the discipline (*vinaya*) concerning those things to be disciplined, such as: "It must be subdued; in this way the faculties are to be subdued; in this way lust is to be removed; in this way hatred is to be removed.

That which contains none of such phrases of meaning (*atthapada*), phrases of Dhamma (*dhammapada*), or phrases of discipline (*vinayapada*), but consists merely of the substance of speech—that is what this name [refers to].
The construction is: "it occurs. "Frivolous talk" (*samphaṃ*) refers to the aforementioned kind of meaningless speech. "Therein" (*tattha*) means among those verbal actions.
"Deceiver" (*visaṃvādaka*) means one who causes another to be deceived. "One who destroys the purpose" (*atthabhañjanaka*) means one who breaks up or ruins the goal.
"A specific path of kamma" (*kammapathabheda*) refers to a particular type of kamma that produces rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
“Other” means a false speech other than the eight types of breaking [friendship]. “Merely action” means verbal action alone that produces the result of the process [of existence].
“Dust” means particles of soil. “Arising therein” means those things which arise in those happy and miserable destinies.
“Because they are the path” means because they are the path of arising. “With the priority of breaking” means with the priority of breaking friendship.

"One who breaks a friendship" means a breaker. "Defiled volition" means a defiled volition that is devoid of priority given to the Dhamma, priority given to the Vinaya, priority given to discipline, or priority given to instruction;
rather, it is simply a volition that has the breaking [of friendships] as its priority.
"Only when others have been broken" means only when other people have been split by other people through the act of creating enmity.
“Whatever” means any basis for abuse. “This too” means this harsh speech as well.
Thus, the construction is that even an act of reviling succeeds against one who stands at a distance or who is dead.
It is called “making known what is harmful” because it makes known merely the basis for useless speech. “Only when they take it as true” means as he...
He speaks thus, taking that object as truly real because it has arisen in the past.
Some, having grasped it as true, place some object in a venerable spot and preserve it by praising it, worshipping it, and bowing down to it;
they go for refuge to it for the sake of future lives. All of this is useless. [The phrase] "by way of its gratification" means...
If one speaks there on such topics as talk of kings, having found delight in them and speaking with a sense of relish, that becomes karma.

However, the intention is that for one who speaks for the purpose of discerning the characteristic of impermanence, or for the purpose of discerning the qualities of the Triple Gem, or for the purpose of censuring evil and honoring the good, it is merely a weapon [of wisdom]. Therefore he said: "Attha..."
“Dependent upon the Dhamma and the Vinaya,” and so forth. The rest here has already been explained under the door of the body (kāyadvāra).
150. Regarding mental action (manokamma): “They covet” means they meditate excessively, think, or look upon [objects].

Showing this meaning, he said, “without remaining satisfied with mere gratification,” and so forth. “They become ill-willed” means they bring about a state of being devoid [of virtue], or they cause it to be attained.
And that accomplishment is not by means of body or speech; rather, it is by mind alone—thus it is said, "thinking.

"By way of its limited nature" means by way of what is contrary to the designation of a true person (*sappurisa*). "In that regard" refers to those mental actions. "This would be mine" is to be construed as:
"this property would become my own; oh, how excellent! "Having made it one's own" means having made it one's own.
Having made it one's own. Regarding the phrase "They are gainful" (*lābhāvatime*): here, "gains" (*lābhā*) refers to those who obtain what is easily gained.
"I would make it my own" means I would make it my property. "Based on another's goods" (*parabhaṇḍavatthuko*): that which has another's goods as its object;

"object" (*vatthu*) here means the objective basis (*ārammaṇa*). The construction is: as long as one does not transfer [the ownership], so long there is no breach of the path of action (*kammapatha*).
The phrase “For this has been stated in the commentaries (aṭṭhakathā)” serves as the heading. “This one” refers to this sentient being.
“Of him” means of that sentient being. “Wrong view with ten bases” refers to wrong view such as ‘there is no gift, there is no offering, there is no oblation,’ and so forth.
Among the sixty-two types of speculative views, some views have the nature of nihilism and so on; however, here it is according to the method of what is most prevalent.
“It is action alone” is what was stated. The connection is with the phrase “as previously described. Of the person who is going.
“Arising of consciousness” refers to the arising of the path-consciousness. “Seeing” means seeing the three characteristics. The connection is with the word “stated.

“Certainty” (niyāma) means the certainty of rightness; the meaning is the certainty that is non-perverted. Again, “certainty” refers to the certainty of wrongness; [the meaning is] the perverted [certainty].
“Niyāmanti” means they lead [one] away. “Atekiñcho” means incapable of being cured; the meaning is that one goes exclusively to the states of misery (apāya).
“Having failed to see” means having failed to see the points of view (diṭṭhiṭṭhāna). “By mere wrong resolve” means by mere faith in the practices of the various sects (titthācariya);
this is the intended meaning. “One’s own teacher’s doctrine” (sakaṃ ācariyakaṃ) means that which belongs to one’s own teacher.
The person who is established. As stated in the Commentary: they are "states of falsehood" (*micchattā*) because their intrinsic nature is false.

Because they give rise to their result immediately after the breaking up of the aggregates when the opportunity for ripening exists, they are "fixed. Being both states of falsehood and fixed, they are "fixed in falsehood" (*micchattaniyatā*).
They are "states of rightness" (*sammattā*) because their intrinsic nature is right. Being both states of rightness and fixed, [they are fixed] immediately thereafter.
“By way of certainty in the giving of fruit” means by way of being fixed in the rightness [of the path] (*sammattaniyata*). “Of that” refers to wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*).
“Without displacing” means without moving. “By this” means by this word as well. “Of these” refers to mental actions (*manokamma*).

“By this” refers to the statement “only in the mind. “Fulfilled” means complete. “By way of characterization and so forth” means by way of the method of characterization (*upalakkhaṇa-naya*), the method of illustration (*nidassana-naya*), the method of the primary factor (*padhāna-naya*), and so on.

“How does it become ‘there is the consequence of a different meaning’? Without the word *eva*, when it is stated that ‘killing is called bodily action because it occurs predominantly through the door of the body,’ this becomes a mere illustrative method (*upalakkhaṇanaya*), like saying ‘this is a prince who has received his inheritance.
By that, one would observe its predominant occurrence in the other doors as well; thus there would be the consequence of a different meaning. Thus.
"In the remaining methods as well": this indicates that there is something further to be said with the words "Moreover" (*apicā*).

"In those": in the cases of killing living beings and so forth. "One factor": the effort (*upakkama*), which is the fourth factor. "And co-nascent with that": and co-nascent with that volition (*cetanā*).
Volition is on the side [of the action], thus it is "volitional" (*pakkhikā*). It is stated that they attain the status of bodily action just like volition.
It exists. “Going towards non-verbal status” means going towards a state where it is not sufficient to be designated as mental action (*manokamma*).
Those for whom the self (*attā*) is primary are “self-primaries. [This refers to] covetousness and so forth.
They are not self-primaries; volition (*cetanā*) is what is primary. The meaning is that here, these very things become self-primaries. “In such and such a way” means “O, how indeed!”
“By this or that way” means by such modes as “May this be mine,” and so forth. “Therein” refers to those mental actions.
“In every way” is a term meaning “entirely”; the sense is “in all its aspects. “Here” refers to the subject of mental action.
“By a specific function of mental action” means by a specific function such as “Oh, may this be mine,” and so forth. The exposition of mental action is concluded.
151. Regarding the passage beginning with “And here, even of ten,” etc.: “Even those” (*tāpi*) refers to those preceding and succeeding volitions (*cetanā*).
The connection is that they are the volitions proceeding from the very beginning. Regarding the passage beginning with “And those which,” etc.: One person says to another, “I will kill this being;
you kill such-and-such a being. Having spoken thus, both undertake the means. However, as for the kamma, it belongs to both.

It does not succeed. In that case, if the act of commanding—namely, "You, kill such-and-such a being"—is carried out by the commander, it is called bodily action (kāyakamma) occurring through the door of speech.
However, because it is not actually accomplished here, what is seen at the door of speech is called verbal action (vacīkamma);
that is to say, it is merely a verbal transgression (vacīduccarita). This same method applies to the remaining cases as well.

Regarding the phrases beginning with “rooted in hatred” (*dosamūlena*): hatred itself is the root, thus it is “hatred-root” (*dosamūla*). Alternatively, hatred is the root of this [state], thus it is “hatred-root. Its meaning is twofold:

either it is the consciousness associated with that [root], or it is the state itself. What is called “ill-will” (*byāpāda*) is indeed hatred; how then could it arise from hatred as its root? To answer this, it is said:
“the preceding [states] are free from the fault of ill-will. This same method applies to covetousness (*abhijjhā*) as well. This is according to the reading in the *Vibhāvanī*.

“Treasure-readers” (*nidhipāṭhakā*) refers to those who determine royal treasures. Since it is stated therein that “the fierce one must be restrained,” it is said [here] for the purpose of restraining the wicked.
The construction is: “The taking of what is not given by kings arises from the root of delusion.

“And of the brahmins” refers both to brahmins who take whatever they please under the perception that it is their own property, and to those who deny the connection between action and its fruit. “Taking” (*āharaṇaṃ*).
“Taking by way of taking what is not given” means stealing; this is what is intended.

The connection is as follows: that delusion which has arisen among kings, that which has arisen among brahmins, and that which has arisen among those who deny the relationship between action and its fruit.
“Greed is the source for the origination of karmas”: greed is the source, the cause, for the thorough increase of karmas.

The construction is: "it occurs" (*hoti*). Those in whom doubt has arisen are "those with arisen doubt" (*sañjātakaṅkhā*). That which arises completely (*parito*) within something is an "obsession" (*pariyuṭṭhāna*).
An obsession consisting of doubt is "doubt-obsession" (*kaṅkhāpariyuṭṭhāna*). The connection is: "those are the actions of people.
The explanation of unwholesome kamma is concluded.
157. Regarding "wholesome action" (*kusalakamma*): the connection is that this [term] appears in such scriptural passages as these.

"Loving bodily action" (*mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ*) means bodily action accompanied by loving-kindness (*mettā*). The same applies to verbal action (*vacīkamma*). Here, "action" (*kamma*) is intended to mean volition (*cetanā*).

In the case of mental action (*manokamma*), however, both volition and non-ill-will (*abyāpāda*) are applicable. "Knowledge follows along with it" (*ñāṇaṃ anuparivatti*) means that knowledge accompanies it (*ñāṇānuparivattaṃ*).
“Accompanied by knowledge” (ñāṇānuparivatti) is also a reading; it has the same meaning. “Skilful” (padakkhiṇaṃ) means increased. He shows another method with the words “But in which...,” etc.
The state of being immoral is immorality (dussilyaṃ). It is the action of killing living beings and so forth.

“While occurring” means while occurring at the door of the body. “But that which is wholesome” refers to the wholesome [state] consisting of abstention from killing living beings and so forth. “Occurring” means...
"Occurring in the mind": "By way of the function as the primary factor" means that the function is made the principal element; this is the intended meaning.
The rest here regarding bodily action is easy to understand.
"The same method applies to verbal action as well" refers to that instance of misconduct in which speech becomes impure. Verbal...
It should be stated beginning with, “The restraint is broken,” and so forth. Regarding the phrase, “But the remainder”:

this refers to what remains after the three bodily actions and the four verbal actions. Therein, “by the three bodily actions” means by the three actions consisting of abstention from bodily misconduct;
“by the four verbal actions” means by the four actions consisting of abstention from verbal misconduct. “All wholesome action” means all [such action].

The application is as follows: the work of giving, all work of mental development (*bhāvanā-kamma*), the work of honoring (*apacāyana-kamma*), the work of service (*veyyāvaccakamma*), the work of transferring merit (*pattidāna-kamma*), the work of rejoicing in merit (*pattānumodanā-kamma*), the work of hearing the Dhamma, the work of teaching the Dhamma, and all work of rectifying views—even when occurring through the three doors—is called "mental action" (*manokamma*).
Of these two methods [of classification], however, only the latter...
The connection is with "exertion" (*padhāna*). The particle "as far as the gods" (*yāva devā*) indicates the final limit;

the meaning is "by way of the highest limit. Regarding the word "virtue" (*sīla*): the meaning is twofold—"it makes firm" (*sīlayati*), meaning it correctly establishes and maintains [the mind]. "Well-composed" (*susamāhitāni*) means well-established.
"Higher wholesome states" (*uparime kusala-dhamme*) refers to sublime and supramundane wholesome states. [This applies] to the seven [limbs of enlightenment].

"In the purifications" refers to the wholesome states beginning with the purification of mind (*cittavisuddhi*) and so forth. "Superior wholesome states" refers to the superior wholesome states that are factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya*).
"Given by others" means that very same merit (*patti*). All those [deeds] such as giving and the rest are wholesome.
"Noble persons cleanse them" means that those very merits are each a basis for the performance of merit (*puññakriyavatthu*). "By this condition" means...
“By means of requisites such as robes,” “by means of requisites such as food and drink,” or “by means of requisites such as wealth and grain.

“All this” means all this tenfold merit. “By inferior desire” means by inferior desire in the form of longing for fame and so forth, by inferior intention, by inferior energy, and by inferior inquiry. “By middling” means...
By means of the middling [degree of desire], such as through the wish for the fruit of merit (*puññaphala*). Regarding the phrase "by the excellent" (*paṇītena*):

the application is that it is "excellent" because it proceeds by way of an excellent desire (*chanda*) and so forth, in the sense of cultivating the noble lineages (*ariyavaṃsa*), which are understood as things that ought to be performed.

"Through the wish for fame" (*yasakāmatāya*) means through the wish for reputation, renown, or praise; or through the wish for a retinue. "Through the wish for the fruit of merit" means through the wish for success in existence (*bhavasampatti*).
“Out of a desire for the attainment of enjoyments. Regarding the phrase “relying on the state of an Ariya”: this so-called giving is the lineage of the Ariyas. Thinking, “I too am an Ariya;
therefore, this must also be performed by me,” such is the meaning of “relying on the state of an Ariya.
And here, the term “Ariya” applies both to one who is noble in conduct and to one who is noble in vision. In that regard, one who is noble in conduct is a true person (*sappurisa*).
One who is virtuous is called a *puthujjana-kalyāṇaka*. A noble one (*ariya*) by way of vision is a noble one in the ultimate sense.
"Perfection is giving" refers to that which has reached the pinnacle among all forms of giving—the giving that carries sentient beings to the further shore (*pāraṅgata*) toward Great Enlightenment.
For it is the pinnacle because it proceeds for the sake of the liberation of all sentient beings, and it has gone to the further shore because there exists no gift superior to it.
Regarding the remaining bases for meritorious action: "The two triads" refers to the two triads of the first [set] and so forth, and the inferior and so forth.
"By the last basis" means by the transgression of the last basis. "One called immoral" refers to an immoral bhikkhu;
for as long as he has not relinquished his recognition as a bhikkhu, he remains a bhikkhu indeed—not a novice, nor a layman. That...
If another monk defames him with a groundless charge of the ultimate offense (antimavatthu), there is a *saṅghādisesa* for the one who defames him.
In the case of verbal abuse, it is a *pācittiya*. Regarding the rule on sharing a sleeping place (*sahaseyya*), even if he sleeps with him for more than one night, there is no offense.
Therefore, he should simply be called a "monk of bad character" (*dussīla-bhikkhu*). "Furthermore, it must be undertaken through the formal ritual procedure (*kammavācā*)."
Just as for one who renounces the training, the entire undertaking is broken;
and since one desiring the state of a monk again must undertake it through a formal act (*kammavācā*), there is no such thing as having to undertake it again through a formal act.
"But in other cases" refers to those disciplinary measures (*daṇḍakamma*) other than the loss of the characteristic mark (*liṅga*), and to the constant precepts (*niccasīla*) and so forth.
“Whatever is always appropriate”: the virtue of abstaining from taking life is what ought to be guarded at all times;
that which is inconstant is not appropriate. Why? Because for one who commits the killing of living beings and so forth, misconduct occurs at every moment.
Therefore he said, “That which is inconstant is blameworthy. The meaning is that it constitutes misconduct. “Whatever is always appropriate”... [and so on].
For householders by nature, the virtue consisting of abstaining from eating at improper times and so forth is always appropriate.

The intention [of the phrase] “it is also appropriate even for a limited time” is that there is neither the fault of transgression nor the fault of misconduct for one who eats at an improper time and so forth after having passed the day on which the undertaking was made. Therefore he said: “It is not blameworthy. It is not misconduct...

The meaning is "it becomes. Likewise, the construction is: "And the tenfold precept (dasasīla) is the 'inconstant precept' (aniccasīla) for householders by nature. Regarding the phrase "it becomes merely an inconstant precept":

even for those householders who, having undertaken that tenfold precept by making it constant for as long as they live, protect it, it does not become what is called a "constant precept" (niccasīla)—a status established by the very nature of birth among those who have gone forth—because they have not gone forth. [This applies] for as long as life lasts.

The intention is that it becomes constant precisely by way of having undertaken the formal commitment (*samādāna*). Regarding the phrase "because it is accomplished together with the wearing of the robes":
how is it accomplished by the wearing of the robes? "Wearing of the robes" means discarding the clothing of a householder and wearing saffron-colored garments (*kāṣāya*).
And the saffron-colored garment is indeed the banner of *arhatship*. Furthermore, for one who wears the banner of *arhatship*...
It is permissible even for one who has not formally undertaken the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) to eat at an improper time;
likewise, it is permissible to watch dancing and the like, to wear garlands and the like, to dwell on high beds and the like, and to accept gold and silver.
If one asks why, the reason is that for them, it is only necessary to constantly maintain and protect their respective individual virtue (*sīla*) in its purity. Thus is the cause.
