"It is just as stated below" means that the intention is that those who have not yet attained absorption (*appanā*) are intended here, because the sublime meditations (*mahaggata-bhāvanā*) that have reached absorption will be explained separately further on.
"In this very [context]" means in this very work on meditation.
"Those very perceptions" refers specifically to the Triple Gem and so forth. One who has begun to go is a traveler; one who is going along a long path is a wayfarer.

“A traveler. “With a pure mind” means with a mind that is pure due to being free from expectation of gain, honor, and so forth, and due to being devoid of self-exaltation, disparagement of others, and the like.
“With a mind suffused with welfare” means with a mind that suffuses them with welfare and happiness, thinking:
“While I am practicing this, such and such welfare and happiness will come to him. This is what is meant by “with a mind of loving-kindness.”
[The phrase] “as if in one’s own duties” indicates that one takes all their duties upon oneself as a burden.
“Sharing in the performance” means giving one’s own merit to others. “Making a verbal expression such as ‘well done, well done! to make known one’s appreciation” refers to the act of speaking.
The connection [of the sentence] is: “For that which is both given and rejoiced in becomes manifest in this very life.”
“Standing in appropriate attention” means: having abandoned inappropriate attention (ayoniso-manasikāra) such as that which sides with worldly praise and the like,
one stands in appropriate attention while listening with the thought, “Having heard this Dhamma,
may I experience its flavor of meaning and its flavor of Dhamma,” and while teaching with the thought, “While teaching this, may I provide assistance to both the Dhamma and those who listen.”

Attention directed toward gain, honor, and so forth is called improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*). Attention directed toward the goal of deliverance and the goal of renunciation is called proper attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*).
Faultless deeds (*niravajja-kamma*) refer to such activities as agriculture and cattle-rearing.

Faultless crafts (*niravajja-sippa*) refer to the crafts of carpentry and the like, as well as the medical arts and so forth. Faultless branches of knowledge (*niravajja-vijjāṭhāna*) refer to the memorization of others' works.
“Beneficial” refers to the sciences of bodily marks (*aṅgavijjā*), the Vedas, spells (*mantavijjā*), and so forth. “The making of purification” means the making of specific purity.
“Because it is its own nature” means because giving is its own nature. “Because of the conduct and virtue of the good” means because the natural conduct and virtue of noble persons [is such].
Again, “because it is its own nature” means because meditation (*bhāvanā*) is its own nature. For it is thus for both the one teaching and the one listening.
Furthermore, because the cultivation of the mind through following the stream of the teaching brings about the cultivation of knowledge, the hearing of the teaching possesses its own inherent nature.
For one who straightens out their own view by themselves, the cultivation of knowledge is indeed the action;
likewise for one who straightens it out after hearing the Dhamma-teaching from another. "There is no such thing as Dhamma"—this is a teaching that says there is no such thing as Dhamma. Why?

Even when teaching generosity and virtue, because the three characteristics must be made manifest at the conclusion through the proclamation of truth, this demonstrates that teaching and hearing are of the same nature as the meditation subject, since they are established in the meditation subject through the contemplation of the three characteristics at the end.
The phrase "mental action alone" is extracted from the text. "In the mind alone" means precisely in the mind-door. "From the accomplishment of its function" means...

"Because the function of absorption is accomplished. "Because of the possibility of being a factor" means because of the possibility of being a factor for the accomplishment of the function of absorption.
"And that consists in cultivation" is the extraction of the phrase. "By way of giving and so forth" means by way of giving and virtue.
First, it is logical that non-arising occurs by way of giving; however, as for the statement that non-arising occurs by way of virtue, this is not [supported] by the text.

[The opponent] objects: "In the Pāḷi, even regarding sublime meditative absorptions (*mahaggata-jjhāna*), it is stated that 'abandonment is virtue' (*pahāna-sīla*) and 'the virtue of abstinence' (*veramaṇi-sīla*), and so forth.
In order to resolve this, he says, "But as for that... and so on. [The opponent asks: "By what figurative method (*pariyāya*) was it stated? [The reply:
"By the method where natural conduct (*pakati-cāritta*) is called 'virtue' (*sīla*); and when the first absorption has arisen, there is the abandonment of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*)."
The term *nāma* refers to natural conduct (*pakaticāritta*) itself, which occurs according to its own natural law (*niyāma*). Thus, because it is natural conduct, it is called "virtue" (*sīla*).

Furthermore, the very abandonment of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) is called "abstinence" (*veramaṇī*) in the sense of departing from them, "restraint" (*saṃvara*) in the sense of closing them off, and "non-transgression" (*avītikkama*) in the sense of not abandoning the duty of abandonment. This is what is meant by "virtue as volition" (*cetanāsīla*).
Here, however, it is volition associated with jhāna that is spoken of. It should be understood that this is called "virtue" because it is born of virtue and because it acts as virtue.
The phrase "attained to absorption" (*appanāpatta*) is an extraction of the term; however, it should rather be stated as "by way of the distinction of jhāna.
For the wholesome [kamma] of the fine-material sphere is fivefold by way of the distinction of jhāna, while jhāna itself is fivefold by way of the distinction of its factors (*jhānaṅga*).
The Elucidation of Wholesome Karma is finished. 153.

Regarding the passage beginning with “In this”: “In the Dhammasaṅgahe” means in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* of the Canon. “By seeing” means by the knowledge of the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga-ñāṇa*).
“That” refers to the volition of restlessness (*uddhacca-cetanā*). “By cultivation” means by the cultivation consisting of the three higher paths.
In the Pāli text: “Cittuppādā” means mind and mental factors (citta-cetasika). “Siyā” is a particle used in the sense of “some.

The meaning is that among these six types of consciousness-arising, some six types of consciousness-arising are to be abandoned by the stream-entry path (sotāpatti-magga), while other six types of consciousness-arising are to be abandoned by the three higher paths. In that regard, in the first phrase, “some... [is used].
"Six types of consciousness-arising" refers to the six types of consciousness-arising that coexist with kamma that has reached the state of a path of action (*kammappatha*).

In the second phrase, "certain six types of consciousness-arising" refers to the six types of consciousness-arising that do not reach the state of a path of action, which occur in wholesome states by way of gratification, delight, and so forth.
"Therein" means in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*. "In the other" means in the others, [namely] in the section on development (*bhāvanā*).
Regarding those things to be abandoned: "Of that" refers to asynchronous kamma-condition (*nānakkhaṇika-kammapaccaya*).
In the textual reading, "conascent" (*sahajāta*) means conascent with its own conditionally arisen states.

"Asynchronous" (*nānakkhaṇika*) means not conascent with its own conditionally arisen states, but volitions such as killing that occur at a different time in the past. "If it were so" means if it should be thus; if...
It should be understood that restlessness (*uddhacca*) does not project rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) because it is not mentioned in the section on volition (*cetanā*).
The phrase "if this were so" (*evaṃ sati*) is an elliptical remainder [of the sentence]. If one were to say "it does," one could not say "no.

Regarding the phrase "of its result" (*tassā vipākassa*), this refers to the result of that volition of restlessness. In the reading of the canonical text (*pāḷipāṭhe*): "knowledge regarding these states" (*imesu dhammesu ñāṇaṃ*) refers to these states...
“Knowledge arisen by making that [result] its object. Regarding the phrase “in their result”: it refers to the result of those states accompanied by restlessness.
“Knowledge” means knowledge arisen by making that result its object. The connection is: “And it can be said that all [such knowledge] is weak.
“Because of being exceedingly dark-natured” means that it creates an obstacle for the jewel of faith toward great objects such as the Buddha and so forth.

Because it proceeds by having performed [the act of doubting], it is an exceedingly dark state. The construction is: "It should be understood that even the drawing forth of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) by that volition of doubt is [impossible].
"Precisely because their intrinsic natures (*sabhāva*) are opposed": doubt has the intrinsic nature of non-ascertainment, whereas resolve (*adhimokkha*) has the intrinsic nature of ascertainment;
thus, it is precisely because their intrinsic natures are opposed [that they cannot coexist].

Regarding the passage beginning with “In all places” (*sabbattha*): they say that “it ripens” (*vipaccati*) means “it causes to ripen” (*vipāceti*). However, since that does not fit the form of the word, he stated another meaning, beginning with “Or else, all...”.

“Having brought forth great successes” (*mahāsampattiyo samuṭṭhāpetvā*) means having brought forth great successes such as divine palaces and the like, which are similar to the divine success found in the world of the gods. This is what is meant by “having made room.”

This is an adjective qualifying the word "state" (*pada*). Therein, the phrase "having a pleasant result" (*sukha-vipāka*) is said with reference to the eight rootless resultant states (*ahetuka-vipāka*).

In the form realm (*rūpaloka*), the physical body (*rūpakāya*) of the Brahmās is produced by form-sphere karma (*rūpāvacara-kamma*); yet that [body] is indeed merely an aggregate of sense-sphere phenomena (*kāmāvacara-dhamma*).
This being so, even the five rootless resultant states produced in that world are produced by form-sphere karma.
“May they be” is the objection. In order to refute that, he said, “Wholesome [kamma] of the fine-material sphere,” and so forth.
“Those” refers to the eight rootless resultants (ahetuka-vipāka) arising in the plane of misery. “In the entire sensual world” means in the elevenfold sensual world.
“And among those” means among those eight rootless resultants. “To another object” means other than the kasiṇa-sign and so forth.
“On the object”: “The signs on the object” means on the objects designated as signs, such as the kasiṇa sign and so forth.

“Those five are resultant”: the construction is that the five beginning with eye-consciousness are rootless resultants, being the resultants specifically of wholesome kamma belonging to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara).
“The sixteenfold path” means the path consisting of a series of sixteen discourses. Thus...

The twelve sense-bases (*dvādasāyatana*). "The group of eight rootless" (*ahetukaṭṭhaka*) refers to the group of eight rootless resultant states (*vipāka*). "One who understands thoroughly" (*sampajāna*) means one who knows in the correct manner;

it is knowledge (*ñāṇa*). The grammatical analysis (*viggha*) is: "that which is done by one who is thoroughly understanding. "That which is not done with thorough understanding" (*asampajānakata*) is that which is done without thorough understanding.

By the word "having believed" (*saddahitvā*), he illustrates the perfection of the knowledge of action and its results (*kamma-ñāṇa-sampatti*) for one of right view; for one is not [qualified] unless endowed with that knowledge.
"He has faith in both karma and the fruit of karma. Alternatively, the reading may be "having known" (*jānitvā*).

"Each one" (*ekamekaṃ*) refers to each individual wholesome deed (*kusalakamma*). "At the time of the wholesome" (*kusala samaye*) means at the time of performing a wholesome deed, or at the moment when the wholesome arises.
For whomever such merit is abundant, for that person there is the attainment of existence, the attainment of wealth, the attainment of friends—all attainments are, without exception, certain.
“Easily gained” (sulābhā) is the meaning. “Well-gained” (suladdhaṃ): this merit is well-gained. “Having wandered among gods and humans”—this is the remainder of the text.
“By the rest”: by the remainder of the ripening of that kamma. This is according to the reading in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. “In a single alms-offering” (ekapiṇḍapātasmiṃ):
in the giving of alms-food on one occasion; this is stated in the *Saṃyutta-aṭṭhakathā*. Therefore, as for what was said: “a single volition... [the rest follows].
The intention is that it is well said: "It gives only a single rebirth-linking. "By opposites" means by opposite unwholesome states. "Especially deluded" means thoroughly confused.
"Exceedingly deluded" means utterly confused. The analysis of the compound is: "serving as a condition for the state of being exceedingly deluded.
The meaning is: "serving as a condition for extreme lack of wisdom. For that is what the Elder says.
The connection: “Having done thus” means having brought it to mind in this way.
“By the mere presence of a condition” means by the mere fact of a condition being situated nearby; what is meant is “by the mere condition of prior application.
Because it arises through the power of strong karma, the result is more intense. When it arises through a collection of conditions devoid of such application, then it is *asaṅkhārika* (unprompted).
When it is accompanied by effort, then it is called "prompted" (*sasaṅkhārika*). In this context, the unprompted is called "sharp" (*tikkha*), while the prompted is called "dull" (*manda*).
Likewise, this should be applied even to dull results arising from weak karma.
Thus, there might be a case where sharpness and dullness attain the state of being dull and sharp respectively; however, the intention is that such a thing cannot actually occur.

Here it might be argued: "If the distinction between the eight great resultant [consciousnesses] by way of volitional effort (*saṅkhāra*) is established, then that same distinction by volitional effort should also be established for the eight rootless resultants (*ahetuka-vipāka*).
For some of those too are produced by effortless karma, while others are produced by karma with volitional effort. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Of the rootless resultants..."
He said, beginning with the words, “...both,” etc. Regarding the phrase “arising from both types of kamma”:

because they are devoid of the differentiation of formations (*saṅkhāra*), there is no contradiction with *asaṅkhārika* (unprompted) kamma, nor is there any contradiction with *sasaṅkhārika* (prompted) kamma.
They arise through *asaṅkhārika* kamma, and they also arise through *sasaṅkhārika* kamma. Thus, it is logical that they are produced by both types of kamma.
“Such is the intention” means the intention of that Elder.

“Not by way of the arrival of karma” means not by way of the condition consisting in the arrival of what is termed karma from a long period of time. The analysis of the compound *āgamana* is: it is called *āgamana* because one arrives (*āgacchati*) by means of it.
“In a kamma-existence” means in a past existence characterized by the performance of kamma. “Some” means certain ones. However, in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*:
And [the phrase] "it has come" [is used]. However, in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, it is stated that [the path] possesses two roots; such is the connection.
Stating that at this point the commentary on the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* should also be cited, he says, "In that regard, however," and so forth.
"At three moments" means at the three moments: the moment of the kamma, the moment of attachment, and the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). "The author of the *Ṭīkā*" refers to...
The author of the Abhidhamma-ṭīkā says: "With remainder" (*sāvasesapāṭha*) means that in the Pāḷi, by means of three-rooted kamma, a two-rooted rebirth-linking remains;
and by means of two-rooted kamma, a rootless rebirth-linking remains. Thus, it is a reading accompanied by such remaining statements. *Sarikkhaka* means "similar.
That which is similar to kamma—like kamma—is "kamma-sarikkhaka. [This refers to] the result (*vipāka*).
“By the Great Elder” means by the Great Elder Sāriputta. With the words “And having done thus,” etc., he supports the statement of the commentators.
The section on sense-sphere karma is finished.
154. Regarding form-sphere karma: “Due to lack of proficiency” means due to lack of familiarity; due to non-development. “By inferior zeal and so forth” means—
“By means of inferior zeal and so forth” refers to being dependent on gain, honor, fame, and the like. “Those states” refers to the states of zeal and so forth;
these are not intended here. Why? Because they do not establish the various distinctions of rebirth—this is the intended meaning.
“These very ones” refers to these very jhānas. “In the threefold [planes]” means in the threefold planes within a single level, by way of the Brahmā-pārisajja and the other classes.

“Having analyzed by way of eighteen divisions”: among the three—inferior, medium, and superior—each one is divided into nine types through such categories as the inferior-inferior, the inferior-medium, and the inferior-superior.
Then, among those [nine], the three medium ones are further divided into nine types through such categories as the medium-inferior and the medium-medium. Thus, there are eighteen divisions.
"Having analyzed": "The doors of action" means the gateways for the occurrence of karma. "Because they are manifested by these":

because they are manifested—that is, set in motion—by these manifestations, which are the root causes. "The eighteen kṣatriyas": eighteen kṣatriyas according to the divisions of inferior, middling, and so forth.
Likewise, there are eighteen brāhmaṇas and so on. There are forty-eight clans (gotta), namely the inferior, middling, and so forth.
The forty-eight clans, such as the Gotama clan and others, are distinguished by their respective days. Their "feet" (*caraṇa*), which consist of conduct and practice, are likewise forty-eight.
Here, it might be objected: "In the former statement, the 'low' and so forth refer to the Brahma-world, whereas in the commentarial statements, the 'low' and so forth refer to the human world;
thus, the thing to be established (*sādhyam*) is one thing, while the establishing proof (*sādhakam*) is another. This is the objection.

He addresses that [objection] with the words beginning, “By this... “Discerns” (upalakkheti) means that by showing one part that is evident through direct perception, he makes known even that which is not evident, though it is of the same nature.
“Able or the state of being able” (samatthā samatthaṃ vā) means either the capable ones or the state of capability.
“Thus by this” (tathā hānena) means indeed by this teacher; it is said, “by the practice of Anuruddha. [This is] the name.

The connection is that this was stated in the *Rūpapariccheda*. When an equal (*samāna*) repetition is obtained, and a powerful [kamma] exists, a sublime (*mahaggata*) kamma produces its result. The construction is:
"Failing to obtain—that is, not finding—such a cause, the volition of direct knowledge (*abhiññā-cetanā*) does not ripen as a result.
In that context, "equal repetition" refers to an equal repetition by way of equality of plane (*bhūmi*).

It should be understood that sense-sphere impulsion has equal adverting and reviewing with sense-sphere impulsion; fine-material-sphere impulsion with fine-material-sphere impulsion; and immaterial-sphere impulsion with immaterial-sphere impulsion.
Therefore it is said: “from the perspective of having the same plane,” and so forth.
In that context, “due to the absence of that” means due to the absence of such a state of strength. And sublime volition occurs only once. “All being first” means—

This was stated with reference to sublime (mahaggata) javana occurring immediately after the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) consciousness within the sequences of meditative attainments (samāpatti-vīthi).
Supramundane path-intention (lokuttara-magga-cetanā), even when it is similar [to the fruition], never receives "cultivation" (sevana).

Nevertheless, starting from its own immediate successor, it indeed produces the noble fruit (ariyaphala) for as long as life lasts and even in future existences. It is said: "In this very way. This is the "fruition of occurrence" (pavattiphala).
If it is argued: "In that [previous] case there was craving, whereas here rebirth-linking is considered the fruit; therefore, this illustration is inconsistent," we reply:

Volition associated with the Path is not karma leading to the round of existence when accompanied by craving; rather, it is karma leading to the cessation of the round when not accompanied by craving.
Therefore, it does not give rise to rebirth-linking. However, if that [volition] were accompanied by craving—

It would be an action leading to rebirth in the round (*vaṭṭagāmikamma*). It would also yield its fruit at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). The fact that they are dissimilar would not serve as a criterion for [distinguishing] the practice.
Thus, because of these other reasons, it is an illustration of what is dissimilar. It should not be understood as "because the practice is dissimilar.
"Because of being accumulated" means because it has been increased through repeated acquisition of practice. "That volition," etc., refers to the sublime [volition] of a beginner.

And volition (*cetanā*). "No" is a negation; the meaning is that it should not be so. Nor does that [volition] constitute practice obtained through factors belonging to the same plane (*samānabhūmika*).

Even though this is the case, it is stated [in the texts] as "because of having been done" and "because of having been developed. And "because of having been developed" means precisely because it has increased through the attainment of repeated practice.
Therefore, it is understood [that this refers to volition] associated with those belonging to different planes (*asamānabhūmika*) that occurred in the prior stage.
It is said that [the kamma] has been accumulated here precisely through repeated indulgence, having been obtained again and again through the impulses of sensual desire.
Therefore it was said: “But in both cases,” and so forth. In that context, “in both cases” refers to the two readings mentioned:

“because of being done” and “because of being accumulated,” as well as “because of being done” and “because of being developed. “Starting from the first mental application” refers to the sublime jhāna.
Prior to the path of absorption (appanāvīthi), during the two stages of preliminary development— namely, preliminary development (parikamma-bhāvanā) and access development (upacāra-bhāvanā)—
for one who is developing preliminary development by means of the first mental application (pathama-samanāhāra) such as "earth, earth," and so forth; and in the supramundane path,

for one who is developing comprehension-knowledge (sammasana-ñāṇa) as the very first among the ten insight-knowledges (vipassanā-ñāṇa) by means of [the contemplation] "form is impermanent, feeling is impermanent," and so forth.
The meaning is: "starting from the first act of attention. "Having accumulated" (*upacinitvā*) and "having developed" (*bhāvetvā*) have the same meaning as "having increased.
"'Abbuṇhā' means 'quite new,' so it is said. "'This discourse' (*ayaṃ vādo*)" refers to the discourse on conduct by Anuruddha.

If this is so, then in the commentaries, within the explanations of the phrase "with volitional formations as condition, consciousness [arises]" (*saṅkhāra-paccayā viññāṇa*), there is indeed "supernormal volition" (*abhiññā-cetanā*).
It is said that the condition for consciousness from another [source] was not included; regarding this, another appropriate reason should be stated, and in stating it, he says:
"But as for the concentration of the fourth jhāna," and so forth. "The commentators" refers to the commentators on the Abhidhamma.
"But as for that," and so forth, is a statement of self-admonition. [This refers to] the volition of direct knowledge (abhiññā) while it is being accomplished.
The connection is that perception (saññā) is fading away (virāga) together with the aspiration for the state of non-consciousness (acittakabhava). “Here” (idha) means in the human world.

Regarding the passage beginning with “And as for the non-returner” (anāgāmino pana), etc., “by this” (etena) means by this statement of meaning. “One who has faith as predominant” (saddhādhiko) means one who has the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) as predominant.

The same applies to those who have energy (vīriya) as predominant, and so forth. “Of the attainments obtained by oneself” (attanā laddhasamāpattīnaṃ) refers to even a single individual having many [attainments].

Of the attainments acquired by oneself. Among those—ordinary persons (*puthujjana*), stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*), and once-returners (*sakadāgāmī*)—"ordinary person" refers to an ordinary person who has attained *jhāna*.
"When there is attachment" means when there is attachment to the realm of sense-desire (*kāmabhava*).
"But the others," however, refers to the stream-enterers and once-returners; they are reborn there only after having fallen away from their *jhāna*, and not by the power of attachment.

This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). In the reading of the *Vibhāvanī*, the phrase "of them too" refers even to stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*) and once-returners (*sakadāgāmī*) who have attained meditative absorption (*jhāna*).

This is according to the desire of the commentator (*ṭīkācariya*). Likewise, when there is attachment (*nikanti*), ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*) and others are reborn in the sensual realm (*kāmabhava*) by the power of sensual-sphere karma;
such is the construction [of the sentence]. The mental aspiration (*cetopaṇidhi*) succeeds. Why? Because of its purity. That is to say, because of the purity of virtue (*sīlavisuddhi*).
The intention [is as follows]. “Those” refers to stream-enterers (sotāpanna) and once-returners (sakadāgāmin) who have attained jhāna, according to the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* reading.

“With the arising of vision”: here, “vision” (dassana) refers to the knowledge of the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga-ñāṇa). It means together with the moment of the arising of that vision. There is also a reading: “There is no such fetter for him.
“This world” refers to this sense-world (kāmaloka). “Insight-attachment” (vipassanā-nikanti).
“Craving”—thus, by that very passion for the Dhamma and that delight in the Dhamma, insight is described as craving which is an attachment to pleasure.
Because they arise and perish when conditions exist, they are "subject to change" (*kuppa*). Those for whom these are subject-to-change states are "those with subject-to-change states.
"States" (*dhammā*) refers here to exalted states. These two—the stream-enterer and the once-returner—are those who fulfill their conduct in the precepts.
[This is] the name. Because the defilements opposed to virtue have been abandoned in every respect, they are called "those whose nature is unshakable regarding virtue.
However, regarding concentration, they are indeed "those whose nature is shakable. The phrase "they are not reborn among the Mahābrahmās" means that they do not attain the state of a Mahābrahmā.
Regarding the phrase "because their inclinations are inferior," women are by nature inferior in their inclinations.
They have low aspirations, low minds, weak energy, and weak wisdom. Why? Because they possess inferior characteristics (*hīnaliṅga*).
And why do they possess inferior characteristics? Because they are produced by weak karma. "Weak karma" is said in comparison to the karma that produces manhood.
It should be understood that this includes the Brahmapurohitas as well. Why? Because [the text] says "of the Brahmapārisajjas."
This is because the statement in the *Aṭṭhakathā* is made in a general sense (*yebhūyyavacanattā*). Therefore, he said, "not [the realm] of Mahābrahmās.
Otherwise, it would have had to be stated as "neither of the Brahmapurohitas nor of the Mahābrahmās.
Nor can it be stated in that way, because it would contradict the expression, "Brahmahood means Mahābrahmahood. And this meaning is not established by the method of generality alone.
[The word] *siddho* [is established]. Now, in order to show that it is also established by the power of the phrasing (*byañjana*), he said “by them,” and so forth.
Therein, “them” refers to the Brahmapurohitas. In the reading of the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*, regarding the phrase “let it occur to you” (*paṭibhātu taṃ*):
here, “it” (*taṃ*) means “to you. “Let a discourse on the Dhamma occur to you”; let it manifest. What is meant is simply: “speak. “The brahmins” refers to Abhibhū.
He addresses the bhikkhu: “For Brahmā” means for the sake of Mahābrahmā. The same applies to the other two.

“Of them” refers to the Brahmapurohitas. In the reading of the *Vibhāvanī*, it says, “the meaning should be understood thus,” and because the word is in the masculine gender—as in “among the Brahmapārisajjas”—it emphasizes the individual (puggalappadhāna) rather than the plane (nabhūmippadhāna). Therefore, this meaning is established by way of logical consistency.

"It should be seen. Regarding the phrase "in the three planes of existence": in the realm of form (*rūpaloka*), there is the plane of the *vehapphala* [deities], which is called the "plane of existence for worldlings" (*puthujjana-bhavagga*), because beyond that, there is no further plane for worldlings.

The *akaniṭṭha* plane is called the "plane of existence for noble ones" (*ariya-bhavagga*), because for the noble ones established there, their final goal (*niṭṭhā*) is reached right then and there. The plane of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññābhūmi*) is called the "plane of existence for the world" (*loka-bhavagga*). Beyond that—
“Because of the very non-existence of the world.
The elucidation of the fourfold cycle of kamma is finished.
155. Regarding the occurrence of death: “Of the measure of life” means of a lifespan. “Of both” means of the lifespan...
And [the phrase] "of the karma": "by destructive karma" means by powerful karma such as the taking of life.
"Like those of Dussīma, Rājā Kalābu, and others" means like their deaths. The analysis of the compound is: "the continuity of the aggregates (khandhasantāna) has been obstructed.
"Obstructed" (uparodhita) means having approached and caused to cease. The karma is simply exhausted. This being so, all...
Death is accomplished by the destruction of a single [specific] kamma; therefore, it is said that only one kind of death—namely, death through the destruction of kamma—should be mentioned.
The objection, “The others are also mentioned,” means that the other three types of death are also spoken of. The response is stated:
“By way of their own inherent nature (sarasavasena)” means by way of their own natural law. They “dispose” or “construct” various lifespans and aeons.
They are the arrangers of various life-spans. "In the collection of beings" means in the multitude of sentient beings. They are called "stabilizers" because they cause stability at all times.
They are called "causers of increase" and "causers of decrease" because they sometimes bring about growth and sometimes bring about diminution.
"By way of these" means by way of those temperature and nutriment factors. "And these three as well" refers to these three, beginning with the stabilizers.
The connection is: "Kamma, while ripening, gives [its fruit] and then exhausts. By this, he illustrates that in such a situation, kamma is subordinate.
"Just as appropriate to that" means just as appropriate to that ten-year period. "And the enjoyment of wealth, grain, and so forth" refers to the use of riches and crops.

"Those whose course is that of these" (taggatikā) means those whose course follows that of those seasons and foods. "They follow the course of those seasons and foods" means they conform to their patterns.
Thus it has been said. Therefore he says, "following after that. The connection is with "except by those who know conditioned phenomena" (*saṅkhāravidūhi*).

The meaning is: "excluding those who know conditioned phenomena. "Produced by psychic power" (*iddhimaya*) means produced by means of psychic power (*iddhi*); "by psychic power" refers either to divine psychic power or to psychic power consisting of mental cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya-iddhi*).
"Produced by knowledge" (*vijjāmaya*) means produced by means of knowledge; "by knowledge" refers to the knowledge of the Gandharva. [The components are] bone, sinew, flesh, blood, and so forth.

They are called *rasāyana* because the bodily constituents (*rasa-dhātu*) go toward or increase by means of them. They are called *rasāyana-vidhi* because they bring about those [constituents] by means of these methods;
they are instructions on the principles. They are called *jīvita-saṅkhāra* because they sustain life for the sake of its long duration by means of them.
This refers both to the *jīvita-saṅkhāra* consisting of supernormal power (*iddhimaya*) and knowledge (*vijjāmaya*), and to the *jīvita-saṅkhāra* designated as the *rasāyana-vidhi*.

And the compound *vidunoti* [is explained as follows]. Regarding the phrase “in material phenomena arising from two,” this refers to material phenomena arising from temperature (*utu*) and material phenomena arising from nutriment (*āhāra*).
Regarding the phrase “while they are changing,” this means while they are undergoing transformation. Therefore he said, “while they are decaying,” and so forth.
The phrase “as great as the joy” refers to the extent of the fruit attained, like the activity of the Omniscient Buddhas.
"Even though it is very great": this refers to the karma. "It may be led away even by death that interrupts":
when a powerful interrupting karma arrives, even a very great productive karma is exhausted by the failure of its own basis for fruition.
And that exhaustion does not occur through its own inherent power, but rather through the power of the interrupting karma; thus, here [the term] "interrupting" is used.
"Death is mentioned separately"—this should be understood in the same way regarding death by interruption (*upacchedaka-maraṇa*). "Untimely death" (*akāla-maraṇa*):
the three types of death, such as death through the exhaustion of the life-span (*āyukkhaya*), are called "timely deaths" (*kāla-maraṇa*);

that is to say, they are deaths occurring at the proper time for dying. Any death other than those is called "untimely death. Therefore he said: "For that which is occurring," and so forth. "By way of the breaking of the root" (*mūlabhedato*).
"By way of the classification of their primary causes. Furthermore, the connection is: "because it was stated in the *Milindapañha*.
"Sannipātā" means those that assemble. It is said "of those assembled" (*sannipatitānaṃ*) with reference to the meaning of "arisen from assemblages" (*sannipātikā*).
Alternatively, "assembling" (*sannipatanaṃ*) is "assemblage" (*sannipāto*). It is the state of mixture of two or three humors (*doṣa*). By means of such an assemblage...
It is also appropriate to say that they have arisen from a combination [of humors]. “Of those who act without reflection” means those whose habit is to act without having reflected or deliberated.
The construction is: “Diseases arise for those who have engaged in improper conduct.
“Of their own undertakings” refers to those performed by means of using weapons, consuming poison, throwing oneself into water, and so forth. “Destroying” means [by means of] a rain of weapons.
Having caused rains of sand and the like to fall, or having raised waves upon the ocean, they bring about destruction by creating such great terrors and calamities.
"On the path of men" means in human regions. "They" refers to the fierce *yakkhas*.
"They bring about the end of life" means that for the sake of drinking the fat and blood of humans or of cattle and buffaloes, they [inflict] various diseases upon them.
The meaning is that they bring about the end of life after producing [calamities] for eons (*kappa*).
Regarding the phrase "there is nothing at all to be said," the intention is that when it is stated that they destroy an entire kingdom, a realm, or an island,
there is no need to separately state that they destroy an entire province, a city, a market town, a village, or such-and-such an individual.
“‘The aeons of sword, famine, and disease’: the meaning is that these three intermediate aeons—the aeon of swords, the aeon of famine, and the aeon of disease—are also to be mentioned here.
Among them, the aeon of disease occurs when *yakkhas* release wild non-human beings; by this means, many people die—this is one aspect [of it].”
It has already been stated: “The *upapīḷaka* [kamma] is so called by way of the ripening of destructive (*paghātaka*) kamma.

Herein, it should be understood that by means of gaining an opportunity for those kamma-formations, they afflict the continuum of happiness within the personal continuity (*sattasantāna*) of a being, bringing about either death or suffering amounting to death;
this process of afflicting and destroying is what is expressed here by the term “ripening” (*vipaccana*).
"Whether it produces a result or not, it is called 'immeasurable' here. Herein, one might ask:
among the eight causes, in the context of the "volitional" (opakkamika), it is stated that "angry deities destroy everything, including the entire kingdom, leaving nothing behind.
In that case, do the people who have been destroyed perish by means of afflictions or punishments born from their own individual kamma-vipāka, or rather...
Or they perish through various afflictions or punishments inflicted by others.

As for what was stated here—that "untimely death occurs either through a life-terminating karma (*upacchedaka-kamma*) or through many thousands of other causes"—in that regard, for one who has no such thing as a life-terminating karma, how could there be what is called untimely death through any other cause? In this context:
If they were to say this, there would be no such thing as untimely death for anyone else. For it has been said:
"All beings are owners of their karma, heirs to their karma, born of their karma, bound by their karma, and have karma as their refuge. Refuting their argument, [the Blessed One] said:
"Whatever beings are seen in the world," and so forth. Furthermore, strengthening that point, he said: "As it has been said," and so forth.
It speaks. In this context, the fruit of karma is twofold: the fruition fruit (*vipāka-phala*) and the outflow fruit (*nissanda-phala*).
Therein, the "fruition fruit" refers to the aggregates of fruition (*vipākakkhandhā*) and the material forms produced by past karma (*kaṭattā-rūpa*), such as the eye, ear, and so forth.
That belongs exclusively to the one who performed the previous karma; it occurs only within that person's own continuum. The "outflow fruit," however, is...
For the arising of his pleasure or the arising of his pain, there are desirable or undesirable objects that have arisen externally through the power of his own karma.
However, that [power] is common to others as well. With reference to this, it was said: "They arise solely from one's own karma...
they are indeed common to others. In the world, there are eight worldly conditions (*loka-dhammā*).

It cannot be said that all [phenomena] are born solely from the ripening of kamma (*vipākaja*). Furthermore, as these beings wander through *saṃsāra*, they drift and transmigrate while submerged in the eight worldly conditions;
therefore, even without the pressure-inducing kamma (*upapīḷaka-kamma*), they certainly experience various forms of suffering due to other causes.
Likewise, even without the interrupting kamma (*upacchedaka-kamma*), they certainly encounter the suffering of death.
Therefore it was said: “Arising from anywhere without [the influence of] karma,” and so forth.
“They arise” means those various diseases and so on arise. “Nor skilled in means” means they are not skilled in the methods for liberating themselves from that.
“Nor skilled in remedies” refers to the fear of arisen diseases and so on.
They are not skilled in the formal act of reconciliation (*paṭikāra-kamma*) for the purpose of removing or pacifying [the offense].
"Nor are they skilled in the means of release (*parihāra*)" means they are not skilled in releasing [the offender] from that [offense] by going to another region.
The rest here is easy to understand. As for the statement, "It is only diseases and so forth that continue to exist while consuming it," how is that?
“They exhaust previous karma”: they exhaust it by destroying the continuum of life that has become its result.
When the continuum of life is destroyed, that which produced that existence is indeed exhausted. Therefore he said, “Just as,” and so forth.
“In the same way for karma too”: in this very same way, the extreme weakness of previous karma is established, just like a drop of dew on the tip of a blade of grass.
It exists. When life is exhausted, because the prior karma that produces that existence has also been exhausted.
"And this being so"—this statement from the *Kammappatisaṃyutta* should be accepted here according to the method we have explained.
The entire view that all [experience] is caused by what was done in the past (*pubbekatahetudiṭṭhi*) means that all pleasure or pain, or good conduct or misconduct, [occurs] in a previous existence.
The view that arises thus: "It arises solely due to the cause of past karma performed by oneself. Regarding the phrase "whatever this may be," it means "whatever this [being] may be.
For those who are intent upon the state of a Great Bodhisatta, there is no need here for the task of fulfilling the perfections (*pāramī*) while remaining for a long time;
I shall now, having passed away from here, arise in the human world—let [this life] cease.
“Having resolved, ‘This is my life,’ and having applied the mind firmly, one should pass away.
“Bringing the knife oneself” means: having struck one’s own neck with a knife oneself. “Right here” means: precisely in the case of untimely death. Regarding the phrase “and likewise,” etc.:

“Of those who have attained meditative absorption” is a locative case used for specification (*niddhāraṇa*). “Of those for whom life and the head are equal” means: [of those who regard their life and their head as being of equal value].

Having attained the path of arahantship, they enter the final cognitive process (vīthi) at the moment of death by means of the very same path-reviewing process; because they attain final nibbāna (parinibbāna) through this, they are called *samasīsino*—those who have a common head.
"A common head" (*samaṃ sīsaṃ*) refers to the fact that the limit of the continuity of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*) is the same as the limit of the continuity of life.
"Of all" (*sabbesaṃ pi*) means of all those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*).
“The passage from this sutta” refers to the passage found in the *Mahāparinibbāna Sutta*. “They” refers to those disputants. “By that” means by that statement of their doctrine.

The functional mind-element (*kriyamanodhātu*) is the five-door adverting consciousness. The functional root-cause mind-consciousness-element (*kriyāhetukamano-viññāṇadhātu*) is the smile-producing consciousness.
“Of him” refers to the Buddha who was attaining final nibbāna. “It certainly does not coincide” means it is not consistent.

Regarding the phrase "making the peace of *nibbāna* without residue (*anupādisesa*) the object," even if one were to say "making it the object by means of the *parinibbāna*-impulsions (*javana*),” it would still not be consistent.

Therefore, he said, "For thus... and so forth. In the passage, "Having descended into the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), he attains final *nibbāna*," it is the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*) itself that is called the "life-continuum. And the term "death-consciousness" applies only to one who is going to another state of existence.
It is said. However, here it should be understood as being merely conventional usage. In the reading of the *Vibhāvanī*:

"of the death-proximate consciousnesses ending with the moment of death. Just as the great life-continuum consciousness (*mahābhavaṅga-citta*) that has arisen for the Blessed Buddhas throughout their lives takes only kamma, the sign of kamma, and so forth as its object, so too does the death-consciousness at the moment of final Nibbāna; thus he said.

“‘Not indeed,’ and so forth. [Objection: Is it not the case that at the time of death, the grasping of kamma, the sign of kamma, and so on, is for the purpose of going to another existence (*bhavantara*), yet Buddhas do not go to another existence? Therefore, this statement ‘Not indeed... he does not perform [it]’ is not logical.
[Response: It is not illogical. The phrase “for the purpose of going to another existence” should be understood as referring to the grasping [of objects] by way of the impulsion-moments (*javana*).

Furthermore, showing that they are grasped by the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*), he says: "They are not grasped by the death [consciousness]," and so forth. "For the accomplishment of karma" means for the sake of the fulfillment of karma.
Regarding the phrases beginning with "And here," etc.: "Of that" refers to the father of the Elder Soṇa. Regarding the phrases beginning with "By the power of karma," etc.:
"By the power of another cause" means by the power of causes such as habitual tendencies (*āciṇṇabhāva*). However, the sign of the destination (*gatinimitta*) is indeed by the power of karma alone.
It would be appropriate [to say]: “Established in such a manner” means having been established in many mental moments prior to the final moment.
Among those belonging to the side of evil, there are signs of an unhappy rebirth; among those belonging to the side of goodness, there are signs of a heavenly rebirth.
The appearance of signs belonging to the side of evil at the time of King Dhammāsoka’s death is mentioned in certain Sinhalese texts.
Having taken possession of the entire earth and given away hundreds of millions of treasures,
one may in the end find not even so much as half a myrobalan fruit.
“Asoko” means one who has attained sovereignty;
“Ti ca. “Asoko soka māgato” means one who has not come to sorrow;
“Ti ca. “Taṃ” refers to the ripening karma. Regarding the phrase “niyāmaka-sahakāri-paccayabhūtā,” it is like [the conditions] for a boat.
A pilot (niyāmaka) steers a ship toward the desired direction; that is, he directs it.
Likewise, this craving (taṇhā), having become an attachment to existence (bhava-nikanti), steers the continuum of consciousness toward the existence to be reached; that is, it directs it.

It should be understood that it also serves as a cooperative condition (sahakārī-paccaya) by acting as a companion to karma through its own persistence. “Or the signs of wholesome and unwholesome kamma,” etc.
Or other wholesome signs of wholesome kamma. “Supporting it” means supporting that kamma.
“Attached to the gratification in the sign” means finding gratification in, or craving, the facial features and so forth.

“While standing, it stands” means it stands having become established; what is meant is that it stands without letting go. A “secondary characteristic” (anubyañjana) is a form that is dear and pleasant.
“Speaking, talking, and so forth” refers to specific types of actions. “Of that person” means of a person whose death is imminent.
In the commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), “distorted by the power of the defilements” means distorted by the power of the defilements such as ignorance and craving.

The analysis of the compound is: “that which has concealment and so forth as its own. “That” refers to the continuum of consciousness. “In that” refers to the object, such as karma and so forth. [End of] the commentary.
It does not agree. It is said there, "in that object" (*tasmiṃ visaye*); it is not said, "in that existence" (*tasmiṃ bhave*).

Regarding the phrase "stated therein" (*tasmiṃ vuttānaṃ*), this refers to those things stated in the commentaries (*ṭīkā*) at the point where it says, "for the most part, [the mind] is grasped by the six doors in another existence.
That which is called the "arising of similar impulsion" (*sadisa-javanuppatti*) refers to the present impulsions that are similar to the impulsions that occurred at the time of performing the kamma.
The meaning is that karma concealed by existence (*bhavappaṭicchanna*) and karma that is not manifest (*apākaṭa*) does not appear in that way;
rather, it appears only by having reached the gateway through the process of one’s own new making.

“‘Fallen into despair’ (*visīda pattā*)” means having fallen into a state of despair by becoming disoriented (*visaṃñībhāva*). “By the opposite of that, those who abound in evil karma should also be described.”
It should be stated as follows: "In the meantime, those with weapons in hand, striking at living beings and shouting, 'Seize him!
Bind him! were possessed of evil intent," and so forth, according to the readings in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. "One by whom a sword has been raised" is *ukkhitāsiko*.
That by which they strike or pierce is *patodanaṃ*; it is a goad-stick. A needle made at its tip is a *patodanasūci*. "The goad... [End of fragment].
“Suffering” refers to the suffering of piercing. But how is it that its manifestation in the form of one with a raised sword and so forth is called the "manifestation of karma" (kammupaṭṭhāna)?
And how does it become the object-condition for rebirth-linking? To this he says, beginning with “And that,” etc., referring to beings who are being reborn.
“But for others” means for those being reborn in the realms of form and formlessness. “Having made complete” means...
Having thus completed [the process] as ending with the registration-moment (*tadārammaṇa*) or with the pure impulsion-series (*javanavīthi*);
furthermore, this so-called "arising of the death-consciousness at the conclusion of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*)" does not exist in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).

As for what is stated here and there, such as "having descended into the life-continuum, one attains final Nibbāna," even in those cases, the term "life-continuum" refers in the sub-commentaries (*ṭīkā*) specifically to the death-consciousness itself.
They praise [this]. Therefore, in order to explain how the statement "only upon the destruction of the life-continuum" (*bhavaṅgakkhaye*) is appropriate, he says "And here," and so forth.

It lies down in accordance [with its object], thus it is a latent tendency (*anusaya*). It lies down as a continuous follower, thus it is a latent tendency. Or, it lies down repeatedly, thus it is a latent tendency.
And here, what is called a latent tendency is not co-nascent with the impulsive moment (*javana*). And here, it is spoken of by the name "latent tendency. Various impulsions...
Co-nascent ignorance (*avijjā*) and craving (*taṇhā*) are indeed specific conditions for rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). To the question, "How then are these included here?

he says, "And herein," and so forth. This being the case, it is very appropriate when it is stated [in the *Visuddhimagga*] that [the kamma-formations] are "encircled by ignorance and rooted in craving," because the impulsions co-nascent with the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) are also included. Therefore, the underlying tendencies are included here.
The objection is that the statement is not logical. Showing that it is indeed logical, he says, “Moreover,” and so forth. “Complete” means finished.
“That too” refers to the collection of phenomena such as contact and the rest. “Only such forms” means only those forms not yet abandoned by the supreme path;
what is meant is that they exist as latent tendencies (*anusaya*). “That” refers to the continuum of consciousness. “Therein” means in both of those.
To explain how they are cast off there, he said, “In that,” and so forth. “By the consciousness-element” means by the *viññāṇa*-dhātu. There is no such thing as “transmigration.
The intention is that wherever they arise, right there they perish.
How could there be any transmigration existing at the time of death? This is the construction of the sentence. Such being the case, this statement [is] from the *Anamataggiya* [Sutta].
"It might be in contradiction with the Sutta. It is not in contradiction.
For this is an Abhidhamma statement, a primary (mukhya) statement, whereas the *Anamatagga-sutta* is a Suttanta statement, a figurative (pariyāya) statement;

showing this, he said "And that which... and so forth. Having stated that it was spoken figuratively, he demonstrates that figurative mode with the words "For those who... and so forth. "He" refers to that person.
“Of these”: [it refers] to ignorance, craving, and volitional formations, as well as the phenomena of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) and name-and-form.

“By way of the connection between cause and fruit, one runs on and wanders through another existence”—thus, even at the time of performing karma in the past, it is those very things—ignorance, craving, and volitional formations—that are called “that being.
Subsequently, even at the time of the manifestation of this rebirth-linking which is their fruit, [they are likewise so called].
That being is called a "being" precisely because of its rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). In the interim, even that continuity of phenomena (*dhammappabandha*) is called a "being.
Thus, for one who unifies the causal phenomena together with the resultant phenomena into a single being, there exists a connection between cause and fruit.
Through this connection between cause and fruit, that very same [being] performs the karma; by means of that karma, that very same [being] enters another existence (*bhavantara*).

"It runs on, it wanders about"—thus it is said. And herein, because it is stated by way of the conventional designation for "beings" in the passage, "Bhikkhus, this has no known beginning... of beings hindered by ignorance," it is a teaching of common characteristics (*sādhamma*) and a figurative teaching (*pariyāyadesanā*).

And because it is a figurative teaching, the expression "running on, wandering about" is also established as figurative. However, in that teaching of the Dhamma where there is a teaching of the Dhamma [in its true sense]—
He teaches only the Dhamma in accordance with his words, not a "being" (satta) nor a "person" (puggala). This teaching of the Dhamma alone is called the primary teaching.
Furthermore, regarding the phenomena taught therein, there are none that have migrated from one place to another, from one time to another, or from one moment to another.
Wherever they arise, right there they perish. [This is] their destruction and passing away.
They go. Therefore it was said: “For there are no phenomena that have arisen and then transmigrated.

Echoes, lamps, and cryptography; by the word “and so forth,” the commentary lists reflections, shadows, seeds, conditioned formations, sureties, and the spells, weapons, and medicinal herbs employed upon the bodies of young boys. Thus these are what has come down in the commentary.
Illustrations are summarized here. "Illustrations" refers to similes.
In this context, "an echo" means that when someone standing at the entrance of a deep cave makes a sound, an echo arises within the cave.
Therein, the original sound produced at the entrance does not enter the interior of the cave; it ceases right where it was produced. The echo—

And yet, it does not come from that [sound]. Nor does it proceed from anywhere else without the condition of the original sound; it proceeds there solely by means of the condition of the original sound.
In this context, past karma is like the original sound, and rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) in the immediately following moment is like the echo.
This same method applies to the lamp, the cipher, and the reflection and shadow. Therein, "the lamp" refers first to one...
Having lit one lamp, he lights another hundred lamps or even a thousand lamps with it. “Calculation” (*muddā*) refers to the lines of marking.
Therein, by means of one set of marks, he produces a hundred or even a thousand lines of marking.
“Reflected shadow” (*paṭibimbacchāyā*) refers to the bodily shadow that arises upon clear mirror-sheets or in water.
By these illustrations, it is shown that what is called a "fruit" does not come from the cause; yet, without the cause, it cannot be accomplished—this much is the point demonstrated.

Regarding the phrase "seed-conditioning": at the time of planting mango seeds and the like, for the sake of the manifestation of the desired color, fragrance, and taste in the flowers and fruits that will arise at a later time, [one prepares] the elements of the desired color, fragrance, and taste within those seeds.
*Paribhāvanā*: In that regard, when flowers and fruits arise at a later time due to those conditions, their respective color, fragrance, and taste become manifest.
*Pāṭibhoga*: This refers to one who, in order to accomplish some purpose, takes a loan from another person and says:
"I will give you this amount of wealth together with interest after a year, even if I do not have it. [He then pledges: "Such-and-such a field of mine..."

Or, the establishment of a promise such as, "Let the property be yours," is the setting forth of a condition. In that case, having obtained wealth by means of that [promise], one accomplishes that purpose.
When the time arrives, one clears the debt along with the interest. Regarding "knowledge, craft, and medicine":
in the world, for the sake of the lifelong welfare of their children, they teach them some knowledge or craft during their childhood.
In order to prevent harsh diseases for as long as they live, people in their youth consume some potent medicinal herb.
In that case, by reason of that, there is indeed either the attainment of benefit for the children for as long as they live, or the non-arising of such diseases.
Just as by these means, even when the original undertakings—such as surety-bonds and the like—are no longer present at a later time, [the result persists] due to what preceded them.
It is only because of prior performance that the eight accomplishments and so forth are later achieved.

Likewise, it demonstrates that after performing wholesome or unwholesome kamma, even though those actions no longer exist at a later time, the results such as rebirth-linking manifest later precisely because they were performed previously.
Therefore it was said: "And here, echoes, lamps, seals, and so forth are the illustrations. [The phrase] "by way of the weakness of the kamma" means:
This was stated with the understanding that because the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) is weak at that time, the kamma is likewise weak.

Although this has been explained and demonstrated in the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), the connection [of the present passage] is that it is nonetheless possible. In that context, "that too" refers to the sign of the destination (*gatinimitta*).
"Of those passing away thus" means of those passing away having made the celestial chariot and so forth the sign of their destination. "With a burning body" means...

The instrumental case here expresses the characteristic of having reached such a state (*itthambhūtalakkhaṇe*). In this verse, the construction is: "In the five doors, rebirth-linking may occur in the two objective spheres even without kamma.
Therein, "in the two objective spheres" means in the two objective spheres consisting of the sign of the kamma (*kammanimitta*) and the sign of the destination (*gatinimitta*).
Therein, what is called "rebirth-linking in the five doors" occurs at the end of the process-faculties (*vīthicitta*) that are proximate to death in the five doors.

Rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). When it is stated that this [rebirth-linking] may also occur with respect to an object that serves as the sign of the destination (*gatinimitta*), it is thereby established that the five-door process-consciousnesses take as their object the five sense-objects which serve as the signs of the destination.

And this being so, it follows that at the conclusion of those process-consciousnesses, without deviating, there can sometimes arise for some individuals a forest [or similar scene] even through the mind-door process-consciousnesses that follow upon them.

It can indeed be said. However, among those [objects], even past objects of motion (*gatinimitta*) are obtained for those [consciousnesses] that have already vomited out [the object] through the apprehension of the past and the apprehension of the aggregate within the continuous sequences (*vīthi*).

Furthermore, for those [consciousnesses] that have vomited out [the object] through the apprehension of the physical basis (*vatthu*) and the apprehension of the name (*nāma*), the mental phenomena (*dhamma*) are certainly still obtainable as the object (*ārammaṇa*).
Therefore, as stated by the Teacher: "In the sense-sphere rebirth-linking, six types of objects are apprehended by the doors."
It should be understood that it is well said: "The sign of the kamma and the sign of the destination are apprehended as objects in the present and the past.

Furthermore, regarding the Master’s statement that "the stream of consciousness frequently proceeds by taking that very object which has thus appeared," this refers to the occurrence of many series of cognitive processes (vīthi) prior to the final process.
It has been stated. It is also appropriate to understand that this refers to having taken as an object the sign of motion (gatinimitta) thus established.
And this being so, in order to show that the sign of motion can also be past, the passage beginning with “yadā panā” was stated.
“By way of continuity” means by way of present continuity. “Of that” refers to the sign of motion. This is stated in a general sense, not as an exhaustive inclusion of all cases.

The intended meaning is "stated. Regarding the phrase "because it must be accepted even for the death-proximate impulsions (javana) of the mind-door," the intended meaning is that it must be accepted by way of being a pre-arising condition (purejāta-paccaya).
Regarding the phrase "following upon those," it means following those death-proximate impulsions of the mind-door.
Regarding the phrase "because it is possible even for rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi)," it refers to that same pre-arising condition being possible even for rebirth-linking.
[This is] due to the existence of the conditionality of pre-arising (*purejāta-paccayatā*). If it is argued:
"Is it not the case that, since the Elder [Buddhaghosa] has analyzed [the matter] and stated that even when something is to be broken, breaking itself is what is appropriate?"—this is not correct.

Why? Because they share the same destiny as the object-sign (*kamma-nimitta*). Therefore he said, "Not this," and so forth. Having stated in the *Vibhāvanī* that it should be applied according to what is possible, others, however, [apply it] without distinction.
“They praise” is stated as another opinion. In that context, “they praise without distinction” means they praise without making any differentiation.
Not accepting that other opinion, he said, “But in the Aṭṭhakathā...,” and so forth.
However, here, supporting that other opinion, he again said, “And whatever therein...,” and so forth. In that context, “having that as its object” (tadārammaṇāya) means:
“Those [words] are for the purpose of indicating the destination. “The words of those others” refers to the words of other [commentators].
Why was it said, “except for the investigation”? Is it not the case that everything beginning with “But in the Aṭṭhakathā...

is indeed a statement of investigation? True, according to the reading as it has been seen; however, it does not investigate the state of the reading being incomplete. Therefore, “except for... [is said].
"...because of non-investigation. Here it might be asked: "Let the reading of the *Aṭṭhakathā* be incomplete;
but since the reading of the *Mūlaṭīkā* states it as a restriction, namely 'only at the mind-door,' how can it be incomplete?
Even when stated as a restriction, it remains incomplete here because the intended meaning is not fully expressed. Therefore it was said: "There is no other reason except..."

“Because of non-investigation,” as in the passages beginning with “the present and the past. The construction is: “There is a lapse for the five-door cognitive process (pañcadvārika-javanavīthi) ending with the registration consciousness (tadārammaṇa).
The same applies elsewhere. “Even though it is powerful” means even when it is strong.

“Only for the process ending with registration” refers to that specific sequence. “But because it is stated” means because it is stated in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) itself. “Only in the prior portion” refers to the five-door [process].
“Only prior to the final path. “By means of those” means by means of the objects that are the gifts. “According to that” means the sense is: what kind of thing is that category?
“From here” means from the human state. The connection is: they describe a sound similar to a sign.

“With the letter *ca* lost” means with the letter *ca* fallen away. In the reading of the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), it says that relatives, such as mothers and so forth, bring [the child] near at the five doors.
The connection [is as follows]: “For your sake” means for the purpose of you.
“By way of Chinese cloth, Somāra cloth, and so forth”: cloth produced in the kingdom of Cīna is *cīnapaṭa*; likewise for *somārapaṭa*. “Those” refers to tastes and tangibles;

however, other types of tangibles are also certainly appropriate. “They exist now” is said because they have become present through being brought to mind (*manasikata*). “Of the formless ones” (*arūpīnaṃ*).

“Of the formless Brahmas. “They” refers to the formless beings. “Those” refers to the lower jhānas. “Those who have relinquished jhāna” (*vissaṭṭhajjhānā*) means those by whom the jhāna they had attained has been let go.
“And for that very reason” means precisely because they have relinquished the jhāna. The analysis of the compound is: “those whose minds (*mānasa*) or consciousness (*citta*) have been drawn back.
This is a qualifying phrase for the cause. Because their minds have been drawn back, [they do not fall] into the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*).
This explains that [the result] arises for them. "Of those immaterial beings":

"another weak kamma" refers to a kamma of three-rooted inferiority, distinct from the kamma of access concentration. "Of them": of those who have vomited out the realm of form. "Being present": being existing or remaining.
"There is no cause for support": this is because the kamma of access concentration follows the destiny of a heavy kamma.

It has been said. However, even karma consisting of exclusively weighty actions, if it is the karma of sublime jhāna, does not produce rebirth-linking when it is warded off by the power of various inclinations (*nānānikanti*).
It should be understood that there is nothing further to be said regarding the karma of access concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*).
“Of such a kind” means that those types of inferior two-rooted (*duhetuka*) karmas find no opportunity [to arise]. Regarding the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*):
“Precisely because they have been thoroughly suppressed. “By which”: by that cause for the occurrence of desire (*chanda*) and so forth.
“Various karmas as well”: other than the karma of access concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*), there are also present-karma and past-lives karma (*aparapariyāya-kamma*) performed in previous existences.
“And by which”: and by that cause for obtaining the opportunity even for various karmas. “They”: the form-possessing (*rūpin*) Brahmās.

“Or by the method already stated” means: because their mental continuum has been cultivated by the specific jhāna attainment reached through those hindrances being thoroughly suppressed—this is according to the method stated [by the passage beginning with] “But because...”.

“That reason” refers to the reason for the absence of rootless rebirth-linking (ahetuka-paṭisandhi). Furthermore, it refers to the mode of occurrence of path-excluded consciousnesses (vīthimutta-citta) during successive existences.
The connection is: "to show. Regarding the phrase "just as those very medicines": suppose someone in the world, having obtained a certain medicine, consumes it daily.
Seeing him consuming it on the first day, [another] asks, "What medicine are you consuming?
He replies, "I am consuming this medicine. Then, seeing him consuming the medicine on subsequent days as well...
He asked the same question again. He replied, "I am taking that very same medicine. In this context, "that very same medicine" means:
that which was the medicine on the first day, which you asked about and which I described—that very one I am taking today.
However, the medicine taken on the first day was one thing, and the one taken today is another; yet it is another that is similar to it.
In the world, they speak of it in this very way: "I am eating those very same medicines. Thus, here too, one should understand that there is a figurative designation for what is similar to that.
"In that" refers to the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*). When it does not occur, rebirth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) is cut off;
when it occurs, it is not cut off. Therefore, because it serves as the cause for the non-interruption of that rebirth-existence, it is called the "life-continuum" (*bhavaṅga*).
This is the intended meaning of the word "is said. Furthermore, "existence as rebirth" refers to the continuity of the aggregates born of karma.
"In other systems" refers to the doctrines of those holding annihilationist views. "Roots of the round" refers to ignorance and craving; the analysis [of the compound] is:
that wherein the roots of the round are thoroughly cut off. "For the sake of which" means for the sake of attaining Nibbāna with residue remaining, and so forth.
“Paṭṭhapīyantī” means they are set in motion. It is called a “pada” (footing) because noble persons (*ariya-janā*) go to it and reach it there.

Since the state without remainder (*anupādisesa*) is understood from the subsequent word *santi*, it is stated here as “with remainder” (*saupādisesa*). They awaken, thus they are “awakened ones” (*budhā*).
Those by whom the bond of affection (*sinehabandhana*) has been thoroughly and completely cut off are “those who have thoroughly cut off the bond of affection. And how?
He says, "It is thoroughly eradicated," and "along with even the mere latent tendencies (*anusaya*)," etc., to explain with whom it has been eradicated.
"By the remaining defilements" means by those defilements other than the bond of craving and attachment.
"Lying prostrate" means lying excessively so as to become impossible even to suppress. "Bringing attainment" refers to the ninefold supramundane attainment.
The Dhamma. That which brings this about is "conducive to attainment" (*adhigamāvaha*). "Virtue" (*sīla*) refers to the virtue of the fourfold purification.
"Ascetic practice" (*dhutaṅga*) refers to the thirteen ascetic practices. The rest here is easy to understand.
The sub-commentary to the *Vīthimuttasaṅgahadīpanī* is finished.
6. The Elucidation of the Compendium of Matter (Rūpasaṅgaha-anudīpanā) 156.
Regarding the compendium of matter (*rūpasaṅgahe*): “Mind and mental factors” (*cittacetasike*) refers to the phenomena (*dhamma*) that are mind and mental factors.

“By way of two modes of differentiation and occurrence” (*dvīhi pabhedappavattīhi*) means by way of two modes of occurrence through differentiation and compendium. “Those which proceed” (*ye vattanti*) refers to those phenomena which proceed and occur.
“*Ettāvatā*” means by this much—that is, by the sequence of words beginning with “the Abhidhamma topics mentioned therein.
Those who prefer the use of the particle (*nipāta*) explain it as being by these five chapters.

It is also appropriate to take it as a transposition of the word order (*vacanavipallāsa*). “*Samuṭṭhātī*” means it arises well, it manifests, it comes into existence. “*Kammādī*” means [starting] from kamma.
The condition of karma and so forth. "Mass" (*piṇḍī*) refers to a state of being a single compact whole. The connection is: "having become truly great by depending [on them].
The continuum bound to the faculties is the continuum of a sentient being; it is also called the internal continuum. "In the sense of being deceptive" means in the sense of being contradictory.
It is in the sense of showing what has been made real as unreal, and what has been made unreal as real.
This has been said. The act of concealing what is true and blameworthy is called "Great Illusion" (mahāmāyā). Those who practice such illusion are called "illusionists" (māyākārā).
"Possession" means entering into the bodies of sentient beings. "Seizing" means bringing sentient beings under one's own control.
Where do those who perform both of these things stand when they do so? They do so either standing inside [the body] or standing outside [the body].
It is called an "inconceivable state" because it is impossible for ordinary people to know or see. Regarding the phrase "in the sense of being deceptive":
they deceive by transforming their own naturally very ugly bodies into the form of celestial nymphs;

they also deceive by turning a thicket of trees where they dwell into a divine mansion. It is in such a sense of being deceptive. "In that very sense" refers to the sense of being non-factual, and so forth.
It is by way of these three meanings alone. For even though they are not a self, they deceive [beings] by representing that non-self as "self";
they deceive them by representing what is not a tree as "tree"; and they deceive them by representing what is undesirable, unlovely, and disagreeable as "desirable, lovely, and agreeable.
Likewise, among those co-nascent [aggregates], they either stand within one another, or they stand outside of one another. Thus it is said: "They stand either inside or outside."

"It is a state that cannot be known or seen. "In both cases" means in the case of the great elements such as the illusionist and so forth, and in the case of the great elements such as earth and so forth.
"Non-existent" (*abhūtāni*) means non-being, unreal. "Marvelous" (*abbhutāni*) means extraordinary deeds.
"In this reading" refers to the reading containing the connected words "of the four great elements. Elsewhere...

The intention is that in such cases as "derived matter" (*upādārūpa*) and "non-derived matter" (*anupādārūpa*), the absence of the letter *y* is observed. Because roots have multiple meanings, it is stated: "it extends" (*pathayati*) and "it manifests" (*pakkhāyati*).

"Puthu" is the original word form (*pāṭipadika-pada*). To show that this very term is established as "earth" (*pathavī*) by way of etymological derivation (*niruttinaya*) in the sense of "that which has arisen," it is stated:
"it expands greatly" (*puthumahantī*), and so forth. In the sense of "it is praised in various ways" (*pakārena thavīyati*).
“Pathavī” (earth) is straightforward. “Āpeti” means it pervades. “Appāyati” means it causes to grow greatly; it increases.
Therefore he said, “It thoroughly expands,” and so forth. Since the sense of ripening is also obtained through the very sense of sharpening, he said, “or it ripens.
“Samīreti” means it thoroughly moves or shakes. It is called “vāyo” because it blows or carries; this is the etymological derivation (*atthātissaya*).
By way of method: "Expansion" (*vitthambhana*) means the propping up, supporting, and projecting of the aggregates of primary elements (*bhūta-saṅghāṭa*) in various ways.
"Hardness" (*kakkhaḷatā*) means roughness and harshness. It is the stiffness and bulkiness for the purpose of providing a foundation for the co-nascent material phenomena.
Since this does not exist in the other primary elements, he says: "in relation to the remaining three primary elements. Regarding the term "instability" (*anavaṭṭhānatā*): here...
“Fixedness” (avaṭṭhāna) means a state of being immovable. “Not fixedness” (anavaṭṭhāna) means the absence of fixedness; it is synonymous with “wavering.
Therefore he said, “Even when they have become supple,” and so forth. Regarding “binding”: when the object to be bound is supple, it does not bind firmly;
but when it is rigid, it binds firmly. Since this is established by common worldly experience, he said, “Of that which is to be bound,” and so forth.

“*Tabbhāvan*” means the state of being digested. “‘Because it is seen to be that which ripens’” means they say it is because it is seen to be the excellent ripener of foods swallowed during the winter. It burns and consumes, thus it is *uṇhaṃ* (heat).
Regarding “it burns”: the heat-element (*tejo*) burns by way of its hot nature, and the cold-element also burns by way of its cold nature. An object touched by heat is “hotness” (*uṇhattaṃ*).
When it moves, the object touched by coldness undergoes coldness.
That which undergoes heat is said to "burn" by means of the quality of heat; that which undergoes coldness is said to "burn" by means of the quality of cold.
Thus, even the fire of coldness "burns" in the sense of "scorching," and therefore it possesses the characteristic of heat (*uṇhatta-lakkhaṇa*). This being so—
An object touched by a blue color becomes blue; touched by yellow, it becomes yellow.
If it is argued that both the blue and the yellow burn that object, [the answer is] no, because there is no such thing as being "touched" by a blue color, nor likewise by yellow. Why?
Because derivative material phenomena (upādārūpa) such as blue and so forth lack the functional capacity for contact. What occurs is merely a mixture; and yet, by mere mixing alone—
It burns. It burns only by touching. Even for earth and wind that are in contact, there is no function of burning;

the intention is that there is no function of maturing. If there were expansion in a solid, rigid stone pillar, the entire stone pillar would become loose and light, like a tuft of cotton wool; yet it does not so happen. Therefore, there is no expansion therein.
With the intention that [the quality] does not exist, he challenges [the opponent] by saying, "But that is not found in solid and rigid things such as stone pillars.

In this context, however, while expansion (*vitthambhana*) is found, it is not found in an excessive degree; rather, it is found merely as a support for the co-nascent primary elements (*sahajātabhūta*).
