Demonstrating this, he says "no" and then states "for there... and so forth. In that passage, "it carries" means it carries out the function of being rigid and hard.

Regarding the pasāda-rūpas: "Even and uneven" refers to even places and uneven places, even locations and uneven locations, even paths and uneven paths, and so forth—this is what is meant by "even and uneven.

"Explains" means that it performs the function of knowing that [object] as if it were explaining it. Therefore he said: "Because it is the root cause for the knowledge of the even and the uneven. "Because of not rejecting" means...
Because it is not rejected. “That or” means form or. People hear it; it is heard by people. The same applies in cases such as “they smell it,” and so forth.

“The cause for the maintenance of life” means that which serves as the reason for the occurrence of life. “By way of inclination” means by way of inclination through the process of becoming object and subject.
“Because of accomplishing the functioning of life” is the intended meaning, referring to the setting in motion of various vocal distinctions and vocal actions.
The connection is: "These, moreover, are the five [faculties] beginning with the sensitive eye. "Desire to see" refers to craving for visible forms (*rūpa-taṇhā*).
By the word "etc.," desire to hear, desire to smell, desire to taste, and desire to touch are included.
In terms of meaning, these are simply craving for sounds, craving for odors, craving for flavors, and craving for tangibles. "Source" means the cause. [This refers to] the desire to see and so forth.

The analysis of the compound is *nidāna-massa*. "Wholesome" (*kusala*) refers to wholesome kamma. That by which something originates is an "origin" (*samuṭṭhāna*); this is simply kamma. The compound means:
those for whom kamma—having as its origin such things as the desire to see—is the "origin. The "elements" (*bhūta*) are earth and so forth. The analysis of the compound is:
those whose characteristic is the sensitivity (*pasāda*) of these [elements]. In the second alternative, there is the impact of the five objects, beginning with visible form (*rūpa*).

"Arahāti" means it is worthy of being struck by visible forms and so forth. "Bhūtappasādo" is the clarity of the primary elements (*bhūta*). The analysis of the compound is: "that which has these as its characteristic.
The connection is that the eye resides within the visible circle (*maṇḍala*) the size of a louse's head.
"'In the visible circle' (*diṭṭhamaṇḍale*)" refers to the clear circle seen by the common people with their ordinary eyes. The oil, having spread through the seven layers of membranes...
The construction is: "It stands apart" (*tiṭṭhati viyā*). "The ear-cavity" (*sotabila*) means the hollow of the ear. "Finger-rings" (*aṅguliveṭhanā*) means finger-rings.
"Thick, thin, and copper-colored hair" (*upacitatanutambaloma*): it refers to hair that is gathered into a mass, sparse, and copper-red in color.

The analysis of the compound is: "that which has thick, thin, copper-colored hair gathered into a mass. "Shaped like a goat's hoof-print" (*ajapadasaṇṭhāna*) means possessing the shape of a footprint made by a goat's foot.
“Uppaladalaṃ” means a lotus petal. It has the shape of the tip of a lotus petal.
“Vaṭṭi” here refers to a long, rounded mass shaped like the body of a human being. This is connected with the phrase “except for the dried skins.
Those, moreover, are the five types of sensitive matter (pañcappasāda). “Samudīraṇaṃ” means moving or shaking. “Yathātaṃ” means “like what? These—
The faiths are diverse; as to how they are diverse, he says: "They are dissimilar to one another. As to how they are dissimilar, he says: "By those," and so forth.
This refers to the visible forms that serve as their objects. "A distinction of color" means for the sake of a distinction of color; what is meant is a transformation of color.
"State reached in the heart" (*hadayaṅgatabhāvo*) is a state that has gone to and proceeded within the heart. Furthermore, "state" (*bhāvo*) is said to mean intention. He makes that manifest.
Because of being a condition for knowing thus: "Having seen a change in the complexion on the face, this person is pleased with me;

this person likes me; this person is angry with me; this person is joyful; this person is sorrowful. The phrase "even by nature" (pakatiyā pi) means even without undergoing a specific change in complexion.
"Whatever object" (yaṃ kiñci abbaṃ) refers to a sentient being. Previously, [the text mentioned] the even and uneven.
It is explained. One declares this or that meaning, because by hearing it, one comes to know that respective meaning.
Or, one declares one's own basis, because by hearing it, one also comes to know that basis.
"He makes his own basis known" means here he proclaims: "This is what exists. "It is touched" means it is cognized through being touched. "That" refers to the touching.
“Of that” means of the water element (*āpodhātu*). “Fluidity” means the state of being moist or liquid. [The opponent] objects: “It is perceived by touch, and that might be the water element.
The following response is stated: But this is not possible; therefore, that is indeed fire (*tejo*), not water.
Here, even though such fluidity cannot be established [as water], it is indeed water, not fire. Why? Because of the coldness of water as well.

“Twofoldness by way of occurrence”: for if it were argued that in that liquid metal the heat is hot water, and in cold things the coldness is cold water, then the consequence would be that there is no such thing as fire;
this is the rebuttal. “Because of not occurring together” means because of not occurring in one place.
“Like the near and far shores” means: on a river, this bank is called the near shore, and this...
There is no fixed rule regarding the "further shore" (*pārima*). That wherein one stands oneself is the "near shore" (*orima*), while the other is conventionally designated as the "further shore.
Thus, there is no fixed status for the near and further shores.
And here, by the phrase "because cold and heat do not occur together," it is meant that if they were to occur together, then in that case coldness would have to be called "water" and heat "fire."
It may be so. However, he shows that they do not arise simultaneously, and therefore it is not appropriate to speak of them in that way;
yet, it is not that they cannot be so spoken. Why? Because water joined with the heat of fire attains the state of heat itself.
Just as earth and air, when joined with the heat of fire, also attain the state of heat. Therefore, they do not arise simultaneously. Simultaneously.
The objection is as follows: even when those [qualities] are not manifested, since coldness exists elsewhere in cold objects, it must indeed be called "water.
This being the case, all material phenomena (rūpadhammā) in that liquid metal would become heat;
thus, they would all attain the state of fire. For it has been said: "Fire is characterized by heat. And if there were such a thing as "coldness" in cold objects...
It may be so. Even there, all material phenomena (rūpadhammā) associated with it indeed become cold.
Even there, according to your view, they all reach the state of water. But it is not possible for them to become so;
for such a change in characteristic (lakkhaṇaññathatta) does not exist in them. There is only a change in state (bhāvaññathatta). In this context, "change in characteristic" refers to earth—
It goes to the state of water; it goes to the state of earth, and so forth.
"Alteration of state" means that earth is sometimes hard and sometimes soft; water is sometimes merely cohesive and sometimes flowing;
fire is sometimes hot and sometimes cold; wind is sometimes merely distending and sometimes moving.
Thus, for each individual element, there is indeed what is called a "transformation of activity" (kriyā-saṅkanti) according to its being sharp,
dull, slight, or excessive. Therefore, as for what was said— that water joined with the heat-element becomes hot itself,
just as earth or air joined with the heat-element also become hot themselves— that is a statement concerning a change in characteristic (lakkhaṇa-ññathatta).
This is not tenable. For it is not the case that all these phenomena, when joined with the heat of fire, undergo the state of heat;
they do not abandon their own respective intrinsic natures (*sabhāva*). Thus, for example, when molten iron is heated and glowing, its substantiality (*bhāva*) does not become heat;
it does not abandon its intrinsic nature of cohesion or its intrinsic nature of flowing. If [it were] heat...
It would depart; it would abandon its own nature. This being so, in that metallic essence, neither the mode of cohesion nor the mode of flowing would be discerned.
All material phenomena would disperse; having dispersed, they would vanish.
Yet, it is not the case that they are not discerned, nor do they disperse. Nor does the mode of cohesion therein undergo heating. For it is another...
The mode of cohesion is water; heat is fire. This same method applies to the elements of earth and air as well.

Therefore, as it was said: "If they were to function together, then coldness could be called 'water' and heat could be called 'fire. But since they do not function together, they cannot be described in that way."
"This has been well said" is how it should be understood. Regarding the phrase "because they are not fixed":
if cold and heat were fixed, then one could say that at all times what is cold is called water and what is hot is called fire.
However, these are not fixed; they are indeed unfixed. Therefore, they cannot be described in such a manner.
This is what he shows. Furthermore, if those who hold that things are not fixed were to say that coolness is "water" and heat is "fire," then it would follow that water and fire are also not fixed.
For they would have to admit that what is now water becomes fire in another moment, or that what is now fire becomes water in another moment. And it is not possible for that to be so.
Because when there is no difference in characteristic, a difference in conventional designation is impossible. Therefore it was said:
“And it is known from their non-abiding, like that of this shore and the far shore. In that context, “it is known” means it is known that coolness is fire itself, not water.

Regarding the passage beginning with “Atha panā”: that which was previously stated by the opponent—“Is it not the case that fluidity is apprehended through contact?”—was stated as “Atha panā” and so forth in order to examine that point. Therein, “Atha panā” means “but if it is apprehended”;
“evaṃ sati” means “this being so. The connection is: “And this being so, it would necessarily be an object [of consciousness]. This, however, is the intended meaning here: if...

If water, having become liquid in nature, could be touched and grasped, then likewise, even water that exists merely as cohesion within a lump of iron and the like should be touchable and graspable. Why? Because of its identity with the element of water (*āpa*).

And if this were the case, then in those lumps of iron and so forth, that water—while one is touching or striking them with the hand or foot—would exist without the other great elements (*mahābhūta*).
It may be an object-condition for bodily pleasure and pain separately.

Just as, among those very same iron balls and so forth, the earth-element exists as a separate object-condition for bodily pleasure and pain without the other great elements, so too it is with the fire and air elements.
However, that [earth-element] is not a separate object-condition for bodily pleasure and pain [independently].

Therefore, it does not have the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of tangibility (*phoṭṭhabba*). And just as it does not have the intrinsic nature of tangibility, so too, although water and other elements possess the state of fluidity by their very nature, that water-element does not become an objective condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) for bodily pleasure or pain for one who touches or strikes them;
nor does it have the intrinsic nature of tangibility. This being the case, how [could there be tangibility] in iron balls and the like?
When it has become merely a state of cohesion, water does not serve as a condition for bodily pleasure and pain.
And how do the other great elements, each individually, serve as conditions for bodily pleasure and pain? To show this, he said, "For when...
and so forth. In that context, "by way of softness and hardness" refers to the earth element present within those [elements] by way of its softness and hardness.
Or rather, it is said that for a pleasant sensation of soft earth, the hard earth is a condition as an object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*).
The same applies to the remaining cases. Regarding the phrase "of the internal support," this refers to the nature of expansion existing within those iron balls and so forth.
"Not otherwise" means that apart from those three causes, there is no act of binding.
The intended meaning is that there is no arising of bodily pleasure or pain dependent [upon it].
Now, the common people imagine that one perceives even the water element—which consists of the state of fluidity within natural water and so forth—by touching it.

In order to demonstrate the quality obtained along with the refutation of that [view], he says "Therefore," and so forth. Therein, the phrase "First, together with fluidity... they perceive" refers to this.

This is the statement of the primary argument. In the world, people who know shape—such as "this is short," "this is long," "this is round," or "this is circular"—after touching with the hand or seeing with the eye, imagine that they know it simultaneously through either the touch of the hand or the sight of the eye.
However, in that case, the process of the body-door occurs first.

Either by contacting the three present elements with the mind, or by seeing a present visible form with a sense-door process-consciousness (cakkhudvāra-vīthicitta), they subsequently know the shape through the process that has arisen at the apprehension of the physical basis (vatthu).

This same method applies even to one who knows the shape of a fire-brand circle (alātacakkasaṇṭhāna) at night; for in that case, there are many successions of preceding and succeeding process-consciousnesses.

These things are to be desired. Likewise, in the world, those who perceive the holes and openings of doors, windows, and so forth by means of the eye, imagine that they know them simultaneously with the seeing by the eye.

However, in that process, after the door-slab-forms and wall-forms—which are present—have been seen repeatedly by the consciousness of the eye-door process occurring in the preceding stage, subsequently, like a circle of fire...
Even though they know the opening in the middle, they perceive that space— which consists of a gap or fissure— exclusively through the mental-door process of consciousness that arises separately.
Likewise, for one touching water with the hand, first the three great elements of tangible objects (phoṭṭhabba-mahābhūta)—
which are moist, liquefied, and soft— are perceived individually by the mind-continua of the body-door process.
Having taken the object by means of the function of touching, they subsequently know the fluid element— which is characterized as a state of liquidity and flows—
exclusively through the pure mind-door process. Even though this is so, the intention is that they imagine they know that state of liquidity simultaneously with the touching by the hand.

"Because cows graze here," he says, "it is the place for cows to graze. However, since those learned in phonology maintain that the word *go* (cow) can also signify the sense-faculties (*indriya*), he says, "or 'the senses' (*go*)," and so forth.

Those [faculties], such as the eye and the rest, operate upon these [objects], such as visible forms and the rest; or else, these [objects], such as visible forms and the rest, operate within those [faculties], such as the eye and the rest.
In this regard, according to the former [explanation]: "The cows, which are the sense-faculties, graze upon these [objects]."

This shows that they are "spheres" (*gocara*). By the latter [explanation], they are called "spheres" because they move among the sense-faculties of cattle. These, moreover, are the five [objects] beginning with visible form.
In the two genders, a woman is so called in the sense of desiring, in the sense of standing, and in the sense of placing.
For she, for the sake of sensual pleasure, desires another who possesses desire; she herself is desired by one who possesses desire; and another man possessing desire [desires] the household life.
He approaches that place for the sake of happiness and establishes himself there;

and for the sake of establishing his family lineage in the future, he plants the seed of the family lineage there. He is called a "man" (purisa) in the sense of filling (pūraṇa) and in the sense of desiring (icchana).
For he fills his own welfare and desires the welfare of others; he fills his welfare in this world and desires his welfare in the next world; and [he fills] his welfare in both worlds.
It fills, it desires, seeks, and searches for supramundane welfare; thus it is *puṃsaka*. It is that which possesses the male (*puṃs*).

It consists of the masculine gender and so forth. That which has no male aspect is the neuter (*napuṃsaka*). "Of whatever phenomenon" refers to a phenomenon in the sense of its essential nature (*bhāva*).
"That" refers to the pentad of aggregates. It is called a "gender mark" (*liṅga*) because it marks—that is, makes known—the great configuration and the specific class of beings.

“Readers of marks” (lakkhaṇapāṭhakā) are so called because they indicate or recognize the results of good and evil kamma by means of them; thus, it is a “sign” (nimitta). “Action” (kiriyā) is what is performed.

That which is measured out or fashioned according to one’s lifespan is “demeanor” (ākappa). All these, beginning with the “characteristics” (liṅga), as well as that state of being unobtrusive and so forth, are included.
“And in words” (vacanesu ca) refers to such terms as “woman” (itthi) and “man” (purisa). “And in the meanings of words” (vacanatthesu ca) refers to the same.

Regarding the meanings such as "female shape" (*itthi-saṇṭhāna*) and "male shape" (*purisa-saṇṭhāna*): the phrase "like the word *nimitta*" means that the word *nimitta* is well-known (*pākaṭa*) in the sense of the genitals (*aṅgajāta*).
It is not seen [in that sense] as being unknown. However, the intention is that it is seen in some instances as being unknown.

The phrase "verbal cognitions arise" (*saddabuddhiyo bhavanti*) is according to the method of the science of grammar (*saddasattha*). The phrase "gender and so forth arise" (*liṅgādīni bhavanti*) is according to the method of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), for therein...

It is said that the characteristic [of the female faculty] is its state as the cause for the female gender and so forth. And the phrase "when this exists" means that when birth exists, aging-and-death occurs;
"when it does not exist, it does not occur"—this too is stated here for the purpose of making manifest the relationship between cause and fruit.

Regarding the materiality of the physical basis (*vatthurūpa*): meanings of words arise according to the method of etymological derivation (*nirutti*). The pair of elements refers to the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*).
"Two": "without depending on" means without depending on the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*). "That": the material form of the heart-base. "Five": the five bases. "Of those":
of those [states] such as the wholesome and so forth. "Stated therein": stated in the *Paṭṭhāna*. "'Depending on which material form'":
this refers to the statement that the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*) proceed depending on which material form.
He explains the reading: "In places not shared with others" means in wholesome and unwholesome states that are not shared with other bases, such as the eye-base and so forth.
"In the materiality of life.
"By way of the condition of predominance" means by way of the state of being predominant (*adhipatibhāva*). And "the state of being predominant" refers to the faculty-condition (*indriya-paccaya*).
"Function" (kicca) is what is being spoken of. It is not the function of the predominance condition.

"Living" means they do not abandon their green state; for it is not the case that they are exclusively called "living. This is because life-force matter (jīvitarūpa), which is exclusively born of kamma, is not found externally.
The connection is: "the kamma-born material phenomena are indeed living. "Even when kamma is absent," etc.
This was stated because the volitional action (*kamma-cetanā*) had ceased previously. To make that meaning clear through contrast, he said, "For it is thus," and so forth.

"The other material phenomena" refers to mind-born matter (*cittaja-rūpa*) and the rest. The "occurrence of a single cognitive process" (*ekavīthivāra*) refers to the occurrence of a process in the five sense doors. The "occurrence of a single impulsion" (*ekajavana-vāra*) is what is called the occurrence of a process in the mind door.
It becomes delimited. Why? Because when each individual occurrence of a cognitive process has ceased, the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) [returns].
The intention is that it is because of the manifestation of an incomparable continuity of material form (*rūpasantāna*) at that moment.
Furthermore, this specific distinction of material form becomes manifest only to one who knows it; however, to one who does not know it, it remains unmanifest for that very instant. Why?

Because even such a continuity of material form produced by the seasonal elements (*utujarūpa*) persists only briefly. For indeed, by means of the continuity of material form arisen from a fault (*dosa*), the facial form— [...is affected... (as the sentence continues).

It becomes discolored. Even when the fault has ceased, that material form still appears somewhat discolored. The governing principle here is: "The continuity of those born of temperature and born of nutriment is the present.
It is stated that there is only one kind of present, namely, the present by way of duration (*addhā-paccuppanna*).
But are not the eye, ear, and so forth—being continuities of material form born of kamma—at times very clear and at other times clear during their course?
"Sometimes they are seen to be non-existent. This is true; however, such occurrence does not happen through the interruption of the continuity (*santāna*).
Furthermore, once a particular continuity has been severed, there is no rejoining of those [faculties] within that same continuity. The intention is that once one is blind, one remains blind;
and once one is deaf, one remains deaf. "If it were thus"—the meaning is, "if it should be so. "Arūpa..."
“The continuity of phenomena (*dhammānaṃ santati*) is the present”—this is the governing context. “Resultants (*vipākānī*)” refers to resultants that have become the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).
They proceed solely by way of a single continuity; therefore, it cannot be said that their various continuities constitute the present. Why?
Because they are produced by a single kamma for as long as one lives—this is the intended meaning. “But the others,” however...

Furthermore, wholesome and unwholesome functional consciousnesses (kriyacitta) have ceased objects as their "object" (*tadārammaṇa*). By virtue of their power to pervade the duration [of existence], they continue to proceed.
However, unlike mind-born materiality (*cittaja-rūpa*) and so forth, they do not cease when their own productive conditions have ceased.
This is the intended meaning: this is the distinction regarding the living nature of immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*). "This point must be stated" refers to the immaterial phenomena.

The distinction regarding the state of being living must be stated. Just as in the continuity of material form (*rūpa-santati*) there is no such thing as an "immediate condition" (*anantara-paccaya*), so at the time of death, the continuity of material form belonging to another existence ceases without having attained the status of a condition for that other existence.

Therefore, for those [material phenomena], there is no manifestation in another existence. It is not so with the continuity of the immaterial (*arūpa-santati*). In that case, even the consciousness at the moment of death—
Having functioned as the condition immediately preceding rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), it ceases. Thus, for them, there is indeed what is called the manifestation of another existence (bhavantara).
This too is a distinction regarding the living state of immaterial phenomena (arūpadhamma).

Therefore, one should not raise the objection that because immaterial phenomena—like kamma-born material phenomena—are always associated with life-force (jīvita) and thus possess a living state, their continuity (santati) could not be called "present."

Wholesome and unwholesome functional consciousnesses (kriyā-citta) are not born of karma. Like mind-born matter and so forth, they arise through various concurrent conditions at that very moment, without depending on past karma.
Therefore, for those who are living as well as for those who are not, there exists a present continuity (santati), just like mind-born matter and so forth; this is what is meant by "livingness."
The intention is that there is indeed a distinction. On this point, some say:
"Even in trees and such things, there is what is called 'life,' because their greenness and non-greenness, as well as their growth and lack of growth, are observed. It is replied:
If they possess what is called life, it must be either immaterial life or material life. In that regard, if it were immaterial life...

It exists. Just as a sentient being endowed with such [life] dies again and again and reappears in successive existences, so too would trees die and reappear in successive existences; thus, there would be a material life-force (*rūpajīvita*).
Furthermore, just as when the continuity of life in the limbs of sentient beings—such as the eyes—is severed, those limbs cannot be made to live again.
Likewise, even when the trunks or branches of trees are cut and the continuity of life is severed, it might be thought that those trunks or branches could not be planted elsewhere again;

yet they certainly can. Therefore, it should be understood that both of these lack what is called "life. In the *Vibhāvanī* commentary, it is stated: "For in their case, karma alone is not the cause of their persistence."

Regarding the phrase "it does not," it should be construed as: "here, karma is not at all a cause for stability. Therefore, he said: "of those born of nutriment, etc. The analysis [of the compound] is:
"co-nascent conditions" (sahajāta-paccayā) refers to those that have gone into and function within a single group (kalāpa); "dependent on them" (tehi āyattā) means bound by them.

The generative power of the productive conditions—such as karma and so forth—for the production of matter exerts its influence only at the moment of the arising (uppādakkhaṇa) of the material groups, and not [at the moment of their presence].
At the moment of subsistence (*ṭhitikkhaṇe*). The continuities of accumulation (*upacaya-santati*) are obtained at the moment of arising (*uppādakkhaṇe*), not at the moment of subsistence.
Therefore, because they are obtained at the moment of the efficacy of the producing conditions (*janaka-paccaya*), they receive the name "born from something" (*kutoci-jāta*).

However, decay (*jaratā*) is obtained only at the moment of subsistence, not at the moment of arising. Therefore, it does not receive the name "born from something. But if [the case of] nutriment-born (*āhāraja*) and so forth...

The persistence of material phenomena would have to depend on productive conditions such as nutriment; likewise, aging too would have to be found at the very moment when the power of the productive conditions is present.
This being the case, it too would have to be called "born from something.
But it is not so called. Therefore, showing that their persistence does not depend on productive conditions, he said, "Otherwise," and so forth.
“Supporting” means supporting by standing within the [material] group. “Not for the sake of the occurrence of momentary stability” is to be construed as:
they support it—that is, they sustain it—for the purpose of its occurrence in the state of momentary stability.
This applies to all material and immaterial phenomena. “That” is a term referring back [to what has been said]. “But this,” however, refers to the life-faculty materiality (*jīvitarūpa*).
Regarding the phrase "in the case of nutriment-form" (*āhārarūpe*): "A statement together with its basis" (*savatthukavacanaṃ*) means that it occurs along with its physical basis, such as food;
thus it is "with-basis" (*savatthuka*). It is a "statement" (*vacanaṃ*). For indeed, once nutriment-form has been produced, it cannot be made into a morsel.

"Separated" (*vivecitāni*) means divided by the function of digestion; they are made distinct from one another. "They undergo a fivefold division" (*pañcadhā vibhāgaṃ gacchantī*) refers to one [nutriment].
One portion is consumed by worms; one portion is burnt by the digestive fire (*udaraggi*); one portion becomes urine; one portion becomes feces;

and one portion, having attained the state of nutritional essence (*rasabhāva*), nourishes the blood, flesh, and other tissues. In this manner, according to the method described, they undergo a fivefold division.
"In the world" (*loke*) means in worldly treatises. "From that" (*tato*) means from the stomach (*āmāsaya*). "Digesting" (*anupharanto*)...

“Having offered. “Of that” means of the portion of flavor. “In the elements” means in the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*). “Possessing faculties” (*sendriya*) means that which functions together with the sense-faculties;
it refers to the body. “It arises” refers to nutritive essence (*ojā*); here the letter *da* has been changed to *ja*. It protects and generates, thus it is “nutritive essence” (*ojā*);
here the vowel *a* of the word *ava* has been changed to *o*. “One’s own basis” means the material body (*rūpakāya*) which serves as the support for oneself.

“Designation by another” (aññāpadeso) means the designation of one material phenomenon by way of the mere activity of another material phenomenon, as in the case of the lightness of matter and so forth.
“Produced directly” (ujukatova nipphāditaṃ) means produced primarily.

For just as all non-produced material phenomena, being of the nature of non-arising (ajāti-dhamma), are not said to be born from kamma and so forth directly; whereas produced material phenomena are born from kamma and so forth.
Because it is seen as dependent [on the body], the two types of intimation (viññatti) are called "mind-born" (cittaja) and so forth by way of their location and vicinity.
This derived matter (nipphanna-rūpa), however, is not like that. Rather, because it is subject to birth (jātidhamma), it is said to be produced and generated directly by conditions such as kamma;

this is what is meant. When the term "matter" (rūpa) is used alone, non-derived matter (anipphanna-rūpa) is also included; therefore, for the purpose of distinguishing it from that, [the term "derived" is added].
Because it is said that "it is called 'form' (rūpa) because it is affected (ruppati)," he stated, "endowed with the characteristic of being affected," and so forth.

In this context, the "characteristic of being affected" means the characteristic of undergoing transformation due to cold, heat, and other such factors. This [characteristic] is not primarily found in unformed (anipphanna) matter; it is found only in formed (nipphanna) matter.
Why? Because the various transformations of formed matter are themselves called "transformative matter" (vikāra-rūpa).
A characteristic is called a "characteristic-form" (*lakkhaṇa-rūpa*). However, there is no such thing as a "change of change," nor is there a "characteristic of a characteristic.
If one were to say that there is, then for a change there would be a change, and for that change another, and for that yet another—there would be no end to it. The same applies to characteristics.
In the space element (*ākāsadhātu*). “They appear” means they are known as “this is one, this is one.
He says “delimits” with the words beginning “all around” (*parito*). Having stated “unmixed,” he explains its meaning as “not attaining unity.
He says “delimitation” (*paricchedo*) because it is that which is delimited; thus he says “or by those,” etc. “By those” refers to those belonging to other groups (*kalāpa*).
"Or: 'Without making it for oneself or for others'" means without making it for one's own side or for the side of others.
"Limitation" (*pariccheda*) refers merely to the act of delimiting; thus he says "of those," and so forth. "'Of those' (*tesaṃ vā*)" means of those that constitute other groups (*kalāpa*).
"'But this' (*ayaṃ panā*)" means but this limitation. "'Of that' (*tassā*)" means of the limitation. That [explanation] is stated in the Canon (*pāḷi*).
“Connection”: “Having thus attended to it” means having reflected in this way. “By these” means by these great elements (*mahābhūta*).
“Mutual non-pervasion” means that when two or three groups of material form (*rūpakalāpa*) come together to form a single group, that is called mutual pervasion;
the failure to do so is called mutual non-pervasion. Therefore he said “oneness,” and so forth. “Therein” means—
In that text: by the phrase “of beings belonging to various groups,” it is precisely the limit of the group that is stated.
Regarding the two types of intimation (*viññatti*): “and itself” refers to that which is reckoned as intimation itself.

“By that” refers to the moving bodily member. “By them” refers to people standing within direct range. In the passages beginning with “therein,” etc.: “of one performing a modification of a bodily member” refers to advancing and so forth.
For one who produces a modification consisting of the movement of body parts such as the hands and feet for the sake of some purpose;
and all those groups of mind-born [material] qualities (*cittaja-rūpakalāpa*) arise facing precisely the intended direction—this is the construction.
"Without arising either thus or otherwise" means it is stated without restriction that they do not arise. And for whom... [the rest of the sentence follows].
“Of the body. “By those” means by the groups of mental-velocity factors (*cittajavātakalāpa*). “The pilot” is the one who steers the ship.
“And those” refers to the collection of those groups of mental-velocity factors; by this, he indicates the entire limb of the body. What is meant is that the entire limb of the body is like a ship.
“Having moved” means having shifted. But how is it like a pilot? To this he says, “Just as,” and so forth. “That which it is able to do”—this refers to what follows.
The connection is that the word has been spoken. “For a few turns of the impulsion” means for two or three turns of the impulsion.
“From that” means from that turn of impulsion in which the movement known as the reaching of another location arises.
From that turn of movement, only stiffening and supporting occur; there is no reaching of another location known as movement. “In this” means in this [state].
In the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*): "In various cognitive series of impulsion (*javana-vīthi*). ... It is indeed appropriate [to say that the life-continuum] is supported;
the intention is that it is not appropriate [for this support] to occur within a single cognitive series of impulsion alone.

If such support were admitted to occur in various cognitive series of impulsion, then since there are many instances of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) occurring in between, how could there be support for it therein?"
He said, "It would be possible," and so forth, beginning with "for thus.
In that context, "assemblages of temperature-produced matter" refers to the clusters of temperature-produced material aggregates that occur during the moment of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).

"Possessing its form" means possessing the form of that stream of consciousness-born matter. This is because successive assemblages of material aggregates arise one after another in a continuous sequence.
[This is] the connection. There would be no momentary nature for those preceding aggregates of material groups, yet they are not non-momentary phenomena.
Otherwise, there could be no movement, which is defined as the transition to another location.
Movement is said to be the manifestation of various actions; and "various actions" refers to various phenomena.
Thus it is. And because the movement of the limbs and members at every moment is directly perceived in the world, their state of momentariness must also be seen.
By this, he shows their momentary death, which is called the characteristic of impermanence (*anicca-lakkhaṇa*) of material and immaterial phenomena.
Furthermore, there is the state of non-agency (*abyāpāra-dhammatā*) and the lack of mastery (*avasavattitā*).
It would not be so for them. Nor would those phenomena (dhammas) be non-active, nor would they be phenomena that do not come under one's own control.
Otherwise, their very existence dependent upon conditions would not be possible.

And as for "existence dependent upon conditions," this means that when a condition is present, they proceed, and when it is absent, they do not proceed; such is their mode of occurrence dependent upon conditions, because in the completeness of the conditions...
When the conditions are present, they simply proceed; there is no need for any effort on one's part for their proceeding.

Nor is there any need for effort to prevent them from proceeding, for they proceed according to their own nature. When the conditions are absent, they simply do not proceed; there is no need for any effort on one's part for their non-proceeding.
Nor is there any need for effort to prevent them from proceeding, for they do not proceed according to their own nature. And because their proceeding is dependent upon conditions...
"Existence" (vutti) is indeed seen by the wise in the world as a direct experience. Therefore, their state of non-agency and lack of mastery must be observed.
By this, he demonstrates that [the aggregates] are entirely empty of all modes of selfhood and persons;
this is what is called the characteristic of non-self (anattalakkhaṇa) of material and immaterial phenomena.
“Vaci-bheda” means a variety of vocal sound consisting of speech that has reached the state of syllables and phrases.
“Upādinnaka-pathavī-dhātuyo” refers to the earth elements born of karma (*kammaja*). The connection [of the sentence] is: “the striking together within them. It is connected as follows:

it approaches by means of a modification of form co-nascent with itself, and it is perceived by means of that. [The term] “internal” refers to that which has entered the personal continuum (*santāna*).
Since all fourfold material phenomena are in some instances called "clung-to" (*upādinnaka*), he said, "or indeed of the fourfold primary elements.

Regarding the two positions—the position of the instrument and the position of the locus: on the side of the instrument, the mind-born earth element, which functions in a mobile mode, strikes only the karma-born earth while it is in contact with the earth element on the side of the locus. On the other earth...
It is stated that "it cannot be said that it does not strike" (*na ghaṭṭeti*), and for this reason, the term "only here" (*idha eva*) is employed.

Regarding the phrase "the two types of transformation" (*vikāradvayañca*), this refers to the two transformations: bodily transformation and verbal transformation. To the question of how these are to be understood as unmixed, he says "and here" (*ettha ca*) and so forth;
the connection is that there exists a method for the manner of their striking. "Of them" (*tāsaṃ*) refers to the mind-born earth and so on.
“‘For the sake of attaining various phonemes’ means for the purpose of reaching various phonemes such as *ka*, *khā*, and so on.

As for what was said regarding the position of bodily intimation—that ‘this matter will become clear in the subsequent investigation into the arising of syllables’—he says ‘And here,’ etc., making it clear in this context.
For that very reason, the connection is: ‘...as stated in the Mūlaṭīkā. ‘Here’...”
And so it is in the reading of the *Mūlaṭīkā*. "In the prior stage" means in the stage preceding the path of the clear manifestation of syllables.
"By various cognitive-series of impulsion" means by various types of rounds of cognitive-series of impulsion.
"Even of the first impulsion-consciousness" means even of the first impulsion-consciousness that has arisen in the path of the clear manifestation of syllables. And its repetition (*āsevana*).
The intention is that [the name] would have been obtained from the preceding street-sections (*vīthivāra*) themselves.

Furthermore, it has already been stated below that the term "cultivation" (*āsevana*) should be understood as a figurative expression (*upacāra*). Regarding the word "of that" (*tassā*), it refers to the clearly articulated syllable.
And it is said in the *Saddasattha*: "When pronouncing long [vowels]," five long vowels are spoken. In the *Mithindapañhāpāṭha*: "In more than a hundred measures of rice" (*vīhivāhasata*).
A cart filled with rice grain is called a "rice-cart" (*vīhivāha*). "In a hundred carts that exceed [the number] of rice-carts. "Conceit" (*abhimāna*) is the act of overestimating (*abhimaññana*).

"The rest here is according to the method stated regarding bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*). This means it is according to the method stated as follows: "They proceed in a continuity of derived matter born of a moving mind," and so forth. But here, it is according to the method beginning:
"They proceed in a continuity of sound born of speech-producing mind, which is a composite of temperature-born matter," and so forth.
It should be stated. Therefore he said, "according to possibility. "The sense of causing to proceed" means the sense of setting into motion such things as approaching, reciting, and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "And here," etc.: in cases such as approaching and returning, there is no bodily intimation (kāyaviññatti) devoid of the desire to inform another;
and in cases such as reciting the Suttantas, there is no vocal intimation (vacīviññatti) devoid of the desire to inform another.

They are to be seen. Regarding the phrase "in the two types of informative intimation that awaken": this refers to the bodily informative intimation that awakens and the verbal informative intimation that awakens.
The former is bodily informative intimation, and the latter is verbal informative intimation. The construction is as follows:

subsequently, it is understood solely by means of a pure mind-door impulsion (*javana*), and not by a five-door impulsion. Having been grasped by the visual consciousness process (*cakkhuviññāṇa-vīthi*)...

The connection: Regarding the phrase “in the process of body-consciousness,” this process of body-consciousness should be understood as the making known of one’s intention by means of grasping the hand and so forth, without uttering a vocal expression.
As for why the alternative definition “it is called *viññatti* because it is itself made known” was stated, he says:
“For that [intention] makes itself known,” and so forth. The word “in between” refers to the process of apprehending the intimation (*viññatti*) and the process of apprehending the intention.
"In the middle. How does one communicate intention (*adhippāya*) through the manifesting intimation (*viññatti*) of movement?
He says "But in the two," and so forth, because two meanings are obtained: that one communicates the intention oneself, and that it is understood by oneself.

Those who know "this one is advancing" and "this one is retreating" know both the application of the act of advancing and the consciousness that generates that application. "Another's speech" refers even to that which is devoid of the desire to inform.
The word *parassa* means "of another. They also know the mind of lust (*rāgacitta*). Therefore, it is stated in the *Mūlaṭīkā*:

"Even without the performance of approaching and so forth, out of a desire to inform another, there is a modification (*vikāra*) co-arising with that mind; this is the intention (*adhippāya*). Thus, in both ways, it is indeed intimation (*viññatti*).

Regarding the material phenomena of modification (*vikārarūpa*), "suitable for action" (*kammayogga*) means fit to be employed in actions such as approaching and so forth. "Unstiffness" (*adaṇḍhatā*) is what is meant.

"Quick occurrence" (*sīghappavatti*): the analysis of the compound is "that which has this as its characteristic" (*lakkhaṇaṃ assa*). The compound means "that which has as its characteristic a state of wieldiness (*kammaññabhāva*) conducive to bodily action.
"Elements" (*dhātuyo*) refers either to the great primary elements (*mahābhūtadhātuyo*) or to the elements such as bile, phlegm, and so forth.
The sentence is: "the manifestation of water, known as the putrid-mouthed snake. "An unbearable burden" (*asayhabhāro*) means a burden that is impossible to carry. "That occurs" (*sā pavattati*).
Lightness of the body occurs. The context is that the elements within the body cause it to become rigid.
An *āmarika* is one who kills excessively; the letter *ā* is an augment. A band of thieves who plunder villages and market towns. Overwhelmed by fear of them.
"Rolling about" means turning about in a distorted manner. "Becomes the root" means when there is the indulgence in what is unwholesome.

That [disturbance] first obsesses [the body]. Whether it be an excess of cold or an excess of heat—it is said that when this one is obsessed, all other forms of obsession proceed from it. "These three types of matter are the specific characteristics of the material body;
therefore, the construction is: 'it is called changeable matter.'"

Regarding the material phenomena of characteristics (*lakkhaṇa-rūpa*): “Accumulation” (*caya*) means the process of becoming accumulated. “From the beginning” (*ādito*) means at the start. “From above” (*uparito*) means in the upper part.
“Accumulation” (*ācaya*) means accumulation at the beginning. “Sub-accumulation” (*upacaya*) means accumulation upon accumulation.

“By way of filling out the duration” (*addhāna-pūraṇa-vasena*) means by way of filling out the personal existence (*attabhāva*) for a long period, such as a hundred years or even a thousand years. “In that manner” (*tena pariyāyena*) refers to the prefix *upa*.
This is according to that method stated by not considering the diversity of objects, but by including within "origination" (nibbatti) and "growth" (vaḍḍhi).
And for each of those [material phenomena], there is a continuity (santati) in the present.

In that regard, among the material phenomena born of consciousness, the origination, growth, and occurrence of inhalation and exhalation, or of the strokes of words and hands, or of syllables, are indeed clearly seen.
Likewise, there is joy (*pīti*) regarding the various successions of material form (*rūpa-santati*) arisen from diverse states of mind.

Among the material phenomena born of the primary elements (*utu-rūpa*), the production, increase, and occurrence of various successions of material form—which give rise to pleasure and pain—are indeed observed in dependence on the diversity of postures (*iriyāpatha*).
Similarly, externally, [these are observed] through contact with stumps, thorns, and so forth; through contact with cold, heat, and so forth; and through contact with wind, sun, and so forth.
Or [it refers to] the various successions of material forms arisen in the body, such as the material forms of eye-disease and so forth.
Regarding "the various successions of even and uneven material forms arisen in the body in dependence on the diversity of nutriment" among the material forms born of nutriment:

"This method" refers to the method of illustration by way of the external continuity. By that, [it is shown] also in the internal continuity, regarding the continuities of beings and the continuities of hands, feet, and so forth.
It demonstrates the arising, growth, and occurrence of the continuity of hair, body-hair, and so forth. "Decaying" (*jīraṇa*) means the diminution from a state of novelty.
In the textual reading, "change of state in what persists" (*ṭhitassa aññathattaṃ*): "otherwise" (*aññathā*) means another mode. The state of being otherwise is "change of state" (*aññathatta*).
By this, transformation is described either by way of aging or by way of various diseases, afflictions, and so on. "Likewise, due to the connection with the distinction of states."
At the very beginning, there is the arising of birth-form (*jātirūpa*). Following that, there is its growth. Following that, there is its occurrence;
thus it is through connection with the distinctions of these stages. Therefore he said, "For it," and so forth. "It binds" means it creates a continuity.
Furthermore, [these terms] are easily understood in the summary verses (*saṅgahagāthā*) and elsewhere. Regarding the passage beginning, "And here, the latter ones," and so on.
Regarding the phrase “the mere existence established by conventional usage,” designations such as “person,” “being,” “self,” and “life-principle” are merely established by conventional usage;

they are not established by intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). This is because they are called “established by convention” since they are accepted and expressed by the common people as “there is a thing called a person” based upon the five aggregates.
However, they are not established by intrinsic nature. Therefore...
It is established that in the terminology of the Noble Ones (ariya), there is no such thing as a "person" (puggala).

However, these material phenomena (rūpa), because they are established by way of their own intrinsic nature (sabhāva), are established as existing even in the terminology of the Noble Ones. Therefore, he said, "by such [a person]," and so forth.
"Established by way of the course of pure phenomena": the earth element (pathavīdhātu), for instance, is a pure phenomenon; it undergoes arising and it undergoes aging.
It also undergoes dissolution. Therefore, its arising, aging, and dissolution are established as being within the course of pure phenomena (*suddhadhammagati*).
Thus, the ultimate characteristic (*paramatthalakkhaṇa*) of the material phenomena of characteristics should be understood as being established within the course of pure phenomena.
Likewise, it applies to the two types of intimation, the three types of mutable matter, and delimiting matter. And just as with these...
Of forms. Likewise, Nibbāna also possesses the characteristic of the ultimate meaning (paramattha-lakkhaṇa) established by the nature of pure phenomena (suddha-dhamma-gati).
Indeed, when the noble path (ariya-magga) has not been developed, defiled phenomena (kilesa-dhamma) proceed toward arising through the succession of existence (bhava-paramparā);
but when it has been developed, they proceed toward non-arising and cessation (nirodha). Therefore, the non-arising and cessation of defiled phenomena also [constitutes] the nature of pure phenomena.
It is established by name. In this same way, it should be understood that the ultimate characteristic of Nibbāna is established as the mode of existence of pure phenomena (suddhadhammagati).
This Sutta—“There exists, monks, that which is unborn, that which has not become”—should also be cited here.

By this, the Blessed One has stated that Nibbāna absolutely exists according to the terminology of the Noble Ones (ariyavohāra). Therefore, he said: “Otherwise,” and so forth. “Not by way of intrinsic nature (nasabhāvato)...”

By the statement, "Because they are not apprehended, they are called unconditioned," it is also demonstrated that it cannot be said of these [factors] that they are "form lacking intrinsic nature" (*asabhāva-rūpa*), "form without characteristics" (*alakkhaṇa-rūpa*), or "form not subject to comprehension" (*asammasana-rūpa*). Why?

Because they possess their own intrinsic nature through their respective intrinsic natures, and because they possess their own specific characteristics through their respective characteristics; for in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, [they are included] under the knowledge of comprehension (*sammasana-ñāṇa*).
In the *Vibhaṅga*, birth, aging, and death are also included among the phenomena to be comprehended (*sammasitabba-dhammā*).
This same point is stated in the *Aṭṭhasālinī* as well. As it says: "Regarding 'fully accomplished' (*parinipphanna*): fifteen types of form are called 'fully accomplished.
Ten types of form are called 'not fully accomplished' (*aparinipphanna*). If they are called 'not fully accomplished,' then they would have to be 'unconditioned' (*asaṅkhata*)."

Furthermore, the bodily modification of those very forms is called bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*). The verbal modification is called verbal intimation (*vacīviññatti*). A fissure, an aperture, is called the space element (*ākāsadhātu*).
The state of lightness is called lightness (*lahutā*). The state of malleability is called malleability (*mudutā*). The state of wieldiness is called wieldiness (*kammaññatā*).
Arising is called accumulation (*upacaya*). Continued occurrence is called continuity (*santati*). The mode of decaying is called aging (*jaratā*).
"Having been burned, its mode of non-existence is called impermanence"—thus, all [this] is indeed fully accomplished and conditioned (*saṅkhata*).
In that context, "of those very forms" uses the locative case in the sense of selection; the meaning is: "in the midst of those very ten kinds of form.
"All this" means: all this tenfold form is indeed fully accomplished and indeed conditioned. This is also stated in the *Khandhavibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā*.
It has already been stated. As it was said: "The five aggregates of the final existence are indeed fully accomplished (*pariniṣpanna*), not unaccomplished;

they are indeed conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); moreover, they are indeed accomplished. Furthermore, among all phenomena that possess intrinsic nature (*sabhāva-dharma*), only *nirvāṇa* alone is unaccomplished and unproduced.
And how can it be said that the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and designations (*prajñapti*) [are likewise]? Regarding the attainment of cessation:
It cannot be described as mundane or supramundane, conditioned or unconditioned, or produced or unproduced.

However, it is indeed produced, because it is to be attained by one who enters into attainment. Likewise, the designation "name" (nāma-paññatti) does not admit such classifications as mundane and so forth;
yet it is produced, not unproduced. For even while one is grasping the term "name,"...
And it is said, "it grasps. By this, the fact that even characteristic-forms (*lakkhaṇarūpa*) are produced (*nipphanna*) is established.
Furthermore, in the *Visuddhimagga*, in the exposition of the dyad of the produced and the unproduced, it is stated:

"The eighteenfold form is 'produced' because it must be discerned by its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), having transcended the states of delimitation, transformation, and characteristic; the remainder is 'unproduced' due to being the opposite of that."
Furthermore, "produced matter" (nipphanna-rūpa) is called "material matter" (rūpa-rūpa). That which is born from the four [causes], such as karma and so forth, is called "four-born" (catuja).
This refers to all remaining matter, excluding the characteristic matter (lakkhaṇa-rūpa). It is stated that characteristic matter, however, is not born from anything.
All of this is merely a terminology adopted by teachers and follows their own preference. Whatever one finds agreeable [is what should be used].
"Having grasped that, it should be explained.
The exposition on the enumeration of matter is finished. 197.
Regarding the classification of matter: "In order to show first the method of the singlefold," means in order to show it first by way of the classification of matter.

By this, he shows that the method of the singlefold [classification] is not yet the "analysis of matter" (*rūpavibhāga*). That does not accord [with the definition]. To the question "In what way does it not accord?", he says: "The wise analyze by way of the internal and so forth," and so on.
By this, the method of the twofold [classification]—beginning with "all matter is twofold by way of internal and external"—is indeed the method for the analysis of matter.

The name is cognized. Therefore, what is meant is that it does not coincide with that [consciousness]. Furthermore, regarding the Pāḷi passage beginning, "States with roots, states without roots," and so forth:

one should understand that such a statement was made because even the formulation of a restriction—such as "all matter is exclusively without roots, not with roots"—is considered to be merely a classification of matter (*rūpavibhāga*).
As for the phrase "the others, however," this refers to [matter] belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) and so forth.
However, the phrase “by way of a producing condition” (*janaka-paccaya*) is a primary statement; nevertheless, supporting conditions (*upatthambhaka*) and others must also certainly be included.
“Having come together” (*saṅgamma*) means having assembled. “Is produced” (*karīyati*) means it is brought forth. Regarding the passage beginning with “whatever phenomenon,” etc.:

“even though abandoned” (*pahīno pi*) means even though abandoned by means of cutting, breaking, and so forth. “When that exists” (*tasmiṃ sati*) means when there is the abandoning of the origin (*samudaya*). Of the functional conditions...

In order to show the two-fold meaning by way of illustrating both the sense of "arahant" (one who has attained) and the sense of "sakka" (one who has been reached), the phrase beginning with "because of its non-existence" (*aṭṭhānattā*) was stated.
"Of that object" (*tabbisayassa*) means of the object which is form (*rūpa*). "Thus being so" (*evaṃsante*) means when it is thus the case.

"'It will be abandoned' (*pahīnaṃ bhavissatī*)" means that for the sake of its non-arising again in a future existence, it will be abandoned right here; therefore he said, "with its root cut off," and so forth.
“Rendered like the stump of a palmyra tree” means it will be made like the trunk of a cut-down palmyra tree.

“Reduced to non-existence” means rendered into a state of non-being once again. “Manifest” means known through specific functions such as seeing and so forth. “With reference to that” means having that as a basis.
In the reading of the *Vibhāvanī*, “internal matter” is the extraction of the term; it refers to that which pertains to the self (*attānam adhikicca*).
“Occurrence internally” means that which is internal. By the phrase “consisting of the personal existence,” etc., he shows that it is precisely the internal [that is meant by] “internal-organ.

That is not correct. Why? Because, as will be explained later, it would result in there being no distinction between internal phenomena (*ajjhattadhamma*) and internal-organ phenomena (*ajjhattikadhamma*).
The phrase “so-called door-matter” is a term extracted from the compound. Why is it called “door-matter”?
He said, “In due order,” and so forth. This same method applies from the subsequent [section] as well.

“For the sake of preserving the distinction in the teaching” means for the sake of preserving the distinction in the teaching regarding the aggregates (duka). Therein, what is called the “distinction in the teaching” is as follows:

in the *Rūpakaṇḍa*, having stated that for the five types of sensory consciousness there is both a material basis (*vatthu-rūpa*) and no material basis, and both an object (*ārammaṇa-rūpa*) and no object, but for mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇa*)... [it is not stated].

It has been stated. If it were said that in the dyad of objects (*ārammaṇaduka*), the object of mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇa*) is material form (*rūpa*), then the phrase "not an object, material form" would not be found in that dyad.
This is what is called a difference in teaching. Among the dyads of bases (*vatthuduka*), the mind-consciousness dyad—which is obtained by way of the heart-base—is not mentioned.
[The phrase] "because of its gross nature" is said with reference to subtle material form. "Far..."
“Even though it occurs [within one’s own body]”: just as subtle matter, even while occurring within one’s own body, cannot be quickly grasped by knowledge, so too is this [case].
Furthermore, “even though it occurs at a distance”: the intended meaning is that it has reached the state of being graspable by knowledge.
In the *Vibhāvanī* reading: “And by way of its own basis,” where “itself” (sayaṃ) refers to...
And by way of the dependence on the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*). In this context, the tangible elements (*phoṭṭhabba-dhātu*) are said to be "reached" (*sampatta*) in their own right;
odors and tastes are said to be "reached" by way of dependence; and both eyes and visible forms, as well as ears and sounds, are said to be "not reached" (*asampatta*). The construction is:
that which has the quality of being face-to-face, and that which has mutual contact (*aññamañña-patana*). And these are not of any other kind.
The connection is: "it is possible to become thus. "By way of favoring and harming" means: by way of favoring for the sake of increase, and by way of harming for the sake of decrease and so forth.

"Whatever" refers to matter arisen from the four causes. "Because it has been taken up and clung to" means: because it has been taken up by craving and conceit as "this is mine," "I am this," and so on;
and because it has been clung to by views as "this is my self."
“By way of constant occurrence” means by way of its continuous operation from the moment of rebirth-linking onwards, due to a single productive kamma.
“Is designated” means it is conventionally expressed. “Discernment of a specific object” means the discernment of the specific function of a visible-form object.
“By way of non-arrival” means by way of not itself reaching the location of the sense-object. Its own location—
Or [it occurs] by way of the non-arrival at the object. Therein, showing the non-arrival at the object, he says “tatthā” (therein), and so forth.
Likewise, when sounds are being produced in the ear having struck one another. “Sampattiyā evā” means precisely for the sake of arrival.
Likewise, the construction is that water is a condition only through arrival. Weak earth alone is the support.
The analysis of the compound is *yassa*. “*Assā*” means of the eye. “*Sotassa pana kathañ*”—how is it evident that the ear grasps what has not reached [the sense-organ]?
He demonstrates that it is precisely the grasping of what has reached [the object] that is evident. Therefore he says, “*Tattha hī*,” and so forth. The intention is:
it is heard from the right side [of the speaker], by those standing in the eastern direction relative to the shrine (*cetiya*) and so on. “*Paṭighaṭṭanānighaṃso*” (the sound of impact).
The force of impact upon the sense-bases. “Of them” means of those standing either near or far.
Let there be the conceit that for those standing far away, it is heard after a long time. But why would one not hear directly, but rather hear from the right side or the left side?
Why would it be unheard? This is the question. In explaining that, he said “Moreover,” and so forth. [This occurs] in the *Vibhāvanī* commentary.

“If you say that having gone to that region of the object, it pervades and grasps it”—the meaning of this is that those two, the eye and the ear, would have to pervade and grasp the location where objects situated at a distance arise.
Yet, while seeing and hearing from a distance, one sees even a massive mountain in a single moment and hears even the great sound of thunderclouds in a single moment. Therefore...
It is understood that both [the eye and the ear] have a range that does not reach [their objects].
Standing upon this statement, he shows this hypothetical explanation: having gone to the location of the object, those two grasp even a great mountain or the sound of a cloud by pervading it.
Therefore, one sees and hears even what is great. It is not because their range does not reach [the object] that one sees what is great.
"Someone might say they hear"—this is what is meant. "Even in the act of resolving, that would be within its range.

This being the case, even in the act of resolving for the supernormal powers of the divine eye and divine ear, that visible form and sound—which are the objects of those sensitive faculties of the eye and ear—would already be within the range of those [faculties];
thus, there would be no such thing as the function of resolving for the supernormal powers. [This applies to] the eye and the ear.
Even if it were to go to the world of the gods, it might take on divine forms or divine sounds; yet it does not do so.
Therefore, it is said that one should not contemplate its traveling to the realm of objects nor its pervading of a vast area.
The exposition of the analysis of visible form is concluded.
158. Regarding the arising of matter (*rūpasamuṭṭhāne*). In the Suttantas, even covetousness (*abhijjhā*) and so forth, when associated with volition (*cetanā*), are stated to be "kamma.
However, in the *Paṭṭhāna*, these do not fulfill the function of that condition once they have reached the status of a kamma-condition; rather, it is volition alone that fulfills it.
Thus he says, “That [volition] alone,” and so forth. And regarding “the matter arisen from that”: by means of the roots (*hetu*) and the phenomena associated with the roots.

And by the phrase "of the origins of material phenomena," the fact that mental states (*cetasika-dhamma*) are also originators of matter is established by way of their functional purpose (*atthavasena*).

For the connection is: "it arises (*udayati*), it brings forth (*pasavati*). "By way of establishing the world-cycle" (*kappa-ṣaṇṭhāpanavasena*) means by way of maintaining the world-cycle (*kappa-patiṭṭhāpanavasena*).
The term "internal" (*ajjhattika*) applies only to the six internal bases (*āyatana*), beginning with the eye; however, here [the term] refers to the whole.
"Internal continuity" is intended; thus he said, "But it should be stated as 'in internal continuity. "Moment by moment" is a distributive expression.
And since "distributive" means pervading over many moments, he said, "in thirty-three moments. Regarding the *Yamakapāṭha* passages:
or else, for whichever person [it is], "ceases" expresses the state of being possessed of the moment of dissolution (*bhaṅgakkhaṇa*).

“Arises” means being endowed with the moment of arising (*uppādakkhaṇa*). “Thus” (*iti*) refers to this question. “No” is a negation. What is meant is that at the moment of dissolution (*bhaṅgakkhaṇa*) of the truth of origination (*samudayasacca*), there is no such thing as the arising of form or mind which constitutes the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*).
Two readings should be accepted: “for whom wholesome states arise” and “for whom unwholesome states arise.”
"No" means that at the moment of arising of wholesome or unwholesome states, there is no such thing as the cessation of indeterminate (abyākata) matter or mind;
this is what is being said. In those passages, the phrase "the immaterial existence" (*arūpabhava*) and so forth is stated to provide an opportunity for certain proponents to speak.
"If" (*ce*) means if some proponent were to say: "No" (*nā*), it should not be said. "It arises" (*uppajjati*).
"And they would be extracted"—this is the connection. "And in the other case" means in the other reading, namely, "those wholesome states," and so forth.
"That too is not" means that statement also should not be said. "In the first section" refers to the intention regarding this first position:
"of those non-percipient beings, there [is no consciousness] therein. "In the last section" refers to all those who are passing away.
Regarding the phrase "during the process at the moment of the mind's dissolution," this refers to the latter alternative.
It might have been stated simply as "for those passing away" rather than "during the process at the moment of the mind's dissolution," yet it was not so stated;
therefore, it is understood that even the material life-faculty does not arise during the moment of the mind's dissolution during the process. And while the material life-faculty is not arising...

The intention is that it should be understood that, when there is [a consciousness], all kamma-born material phenomena, temperature-born material phenomena, and nutriment-born material phenomena do not arise at the moment of the dissolution of the mind.

Regarding the phrase "in the final portion": this refers to the latter alternative—that is, for all those passing away, at the moment of the dissolution of the mind during the course of existence (*pavatta*). And therein, regarding "at the moment of the dissolution of the mind during the course of existence":
This is what is intended. Having thus shown the proof based on the canonical text (*pāḷi*), he now says "And because... and so forth, in order to show the proof based on reasoning (*yutti*).

"Of that" refers to the commentator on the *Mūlaṭīkā*, Ānanda. In the *Vibhāvanī*: "There is no arising of matter at the moment of dissolution (*bhaṅga*), or [it is said] by way of those things born of mind;
for it was spoken with reference to the formless (*āruppa*) in the *Yamaka*. It is not the stability of mind (*cittatthiti*).

And it is said: "Even at the moment of dissolution, there is no non-occurrence of form. In this context, "for there is no non-abiding of consciousness" means that there is indeed no such thing as the non-abiding of consciousness.
"And at the moment of dissolution" refers to the moment of the dissolution of consciousness. One who does not accept this says, "But as for the Yamaka-pāḷi," and so forth.
By the phrase "neither different in meaning nor different in phrasing," he indicates that the reconciliation of the textual passages (*pāḷisaṃsandana*) is indeed to be treated with weight.

He illuminates [the meaning]. By the phrase “The Teacher’s intention is profound,” he shows that having made himself one who knows what is approved by the Teacher, it is difficult to say, “This refers to this;
that refers to that. “Purely immaterial alone” means purely an immaterial rebirth-linking (*arūpapaṭisandhi*).
The forty-six types of consciousness are not able to produce material form. This being so—
As to why it is said, "excluding the immaterial resultant," he says: "the removal of the immaterial resultant," and so forth. In the reading of the *Vibhāvanī*:
"Of the cause" means of the cause consisting of the cultivation of dispassion toward the material. "Because of its being the antidote thereto" means because of its opposition to the material.

The path consists of the cultivation of dispassion toward both the material and the immaterial. [It is] of that which is produced by that [path]. "The sphere of the material" refers to existence in the sense-sphere and the fine-material sphere.
In the *Vibhāvanī* commentary: “Of the seventy-nine bhavaṅgas” means of the seventy-nine bhavaṅga consciousnesses that produce matter during the period of occurrence (*pavatti*).
However, since even during the period of occurrence, immaterial resultant consciousness does not produce matter, he says “therein,” and so forth.
Some, however, [hold that] matter is produced at the moment of arising of the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*).

It does not receive a postnascence condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya*). Some say that at the moment of its own subsistence, matter receives a postnascence condition from the subsequent life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*);
however, this should not be accepted. To show that it is not to be accepted, the passage beginning with "for not by itself" was stated.

A condition that is beneficial while being present is an existence-condition (*atthi-paccaya*). And the postnascent [condition] is one part of that. Regarding the phrase "of the life-formations" (*āyu-saṅkhārānaṃ*)...
“Of those such as Ussada,” etc. “That” refers to the death-consciousness of those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*).

“As it was said”: what did that elder say? “It is stated”: it is stated in the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*). However, from the statement “but thus,” it is understood that the death-consciousness of others also does not produce matter;
this is the primary meaning. The word *pana* indicates a lack of approval. It clarifies the phrase “even though it is stated thus. Vocal formation (*vacī-saṅkhāra*).
"Name" refers to applied thought and sustained thought. "Bodily formation" refers to the wind of inhalation and exhalation.

By the statement that this does not cease for any sensual beings at the moment of the arising of the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*) nor at the moment of the arising of the consciousness immediately preceding it, [the text] makes known the absence of inhalation and exhalation precisely prior to the death-consciousness. Is this not so?
The text states that at the time of death there is an absence of inhalation and exhalation; it does not state that there is an absence of other types of mind-born materiality.
Therefore, by this passage, it is understood that the death-consciousness of all beings does not produce inhalation and exhalation, but not other mind-born materialities.
Anticipating this objection, he says, "No," and so forth. For [it is not the case that] the consciousness that originates materiality...
The connection is: "there is the arousal of bodily formations. Regarding the phrase "in the absence of being bound by entering the womb, etc.":
for one who has entered the mother's womb, inhalation and exhalation do not arise;

likewise for one submerged in water, for one who has become deeply unconscious, for one attaining the fourth jhāna, for one attaining the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), and in the fine-material and immaterial realms (rūpa- and arūpa-bhava).

"Of one who stands": therefore, these factors such as conception and so forth are "bound to" or "restricted by" inhalation and exhalation; thus, they are "bound to conception and so forth. The analysis of the compound is: "the absence of those.
What is meant is that without these causes, there would be no distinction between inhalation and exhalation on the one hand and material phenomena born of other states of consciousness on the other.
He shows another logical connection with the words "and having passed away," and so forth. And he has passed away...
The construction is: "And it is not logical that mind-originated matter (cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa) should continue [to exist].
And that is a very gross material phenomenon (rūpadhamma). Thus, the connection is: "Therefore, it is not possible to say [that].
Having stated "of this meaning," he explains that meaning with the words beginning "of the gross" (oḷārikassa), etc. "For only a few moments" means for only fifteen or sixteen moments.
“Due to the occurrence of mind-born matter” means because of the arising of matter born of mind. They are weak;
at that time, even the five objects do not enter the range of the five doors.

“Or due to the deficiency of conditions” is said because of the non-attainment of the postnascent condition (*pacchājātapaccaya*) at that time. They are weak. Precisely because of that weakness, the five objects [do not enter] the range of the five doors.
They do not arise. Even at the conclusion, they last for only a single moment of consciousness. They depend on the beginning and end of the physical basis (*vatthu*):
at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), they depend on the beginning; at the time near death, they depend on the end. Thus, they are indeed equally weak.
Therefore, just as every rebirth-linking consciousness does not produce matter, so too every death-consciousness (*cuticitta*) does not produce matter.
“It can be known. Regarding “contradiction with the text,” this refers to the contradiction with the previously shown *Saṅkhāra-yamaka-pāḷi*. “The reason has already been stated”:
for it has already been stated that consciousness becomes powerful precisely at the moment of its arising when it receives a complete set of conditions.
“That” refers to the absorption (*appanā*) impulsion. “Without wavering. “In uninterrupted succession” means by way of the sequence of cognitive process-moments (*vīthicitta*).
“Unmixed”: when proceeding in such a manner, the factors do not sink down;
rather, they proceed as if they were fixed in their positions. “Nothing further than that”: it does not produce any further distinction of material form beyond that.
“Any [consciousness] whatsoever”: any kind of consciousness. “Subsequent function”: successive functions. “Eight for worldlings”: the eight joyous impulsion-moments (*javana*) also produce laughter.
The heading is "six impulsions" or "five impulsions. The connection is with "of those Buddhas. "Smiling act" (sitakamma) means an act of smiling.

As for the phrase "the reason has already been stated": the reason has indeed been stated thus: "But temperature and nutriment, which serve as supports for matter, and states that are postnascent conditions, pervade [matter] only at the moment of its duration (ṭhitikkhaṇe)."

"The state of being strong in the utu (physical temperature)" means the state of being strong for the purpose of producing material form (*rūpa*). However, the state of being strong for the persistence of the continuity (*santati*) depends upon the postnascent condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya*).
[If it were so dependent,] the material form would not be produced. To show that it is not the case that it does not produce it, he says "And he will say," and so forth.
The connection is: "Nutriment is twofold, consisting of that which pertains to the internal continuum and that which pertains to the external continuum."

Regarding the phrase "In this case" (*ettha ca*) and so forth: temperature (*utu*) is fivefold. It is fourfold within the internal continuum by way of the four [great] primaries, and onefold within the external continuum by way of temperature itself. Likewise, nutriment (*āhāra*) is also fivefold.

Among these, with the exception of external nutriment, there is no dispute concerning the production of material form within the internal continuum for the remaining [types of nutriment]. However, regarding external nutriment within the internal continuum...
He said, "And here," and so forth, in order to show that there is a dispute regarding the production of material form (*rūpasamuṭṭhāpana*).
