"As in the case of temperature and nutriment" means as in the production of material form within one's own internal continuum by temperature and nutriment. In the reading of the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
"But what is crushed by the teeth" means what has been chewed and reduced to powder by the teeth. "Grain-particles" (*sittha*) means particles of rice-powder from cooked food.
In the *Ṭīkā* reading: “That” refers to external nutritive essence (*ojā*). “Not well-chewed” means not thoroughly masticated.

“Even by that much alone” means even by the mere act of placing it in the mouth. “Of the internal” refers to internal nutriment. “It arouses eight or eight material phenomena” means it arouses them by way of support;
however, by way of actual production, it is internal nutriment alone that arouses them.
The intention [is as follows]: “Clung-to” (*upādinnaka*) refers to those produced internally. The connection is that even external nutritive essence (*ojā*) indeed generates material form.

“By that internal temperature” (*tenautunā*) means by the internal temperature. “Being heated” (*sediyamānā*) means being warmed by heat. “And by that nutritive essence” (*tāya ca ojāyā*) means by the internal nutritive essence.
“By way of the accumulation of fat and moisture” (*medasinehupacayavasena*) refers to the portions of fat and the portions of the moisture of the nutrient-fluid.

By way of increase. The other three, however, originate from material form (*rūpasamuṭṭhāna*). In the textual recitation (*pāḷipāṭha*), "faculties" (*indriyāni*) refers to the material faculties such as the eye and so forth.
"Abiding" (*vihāra*) is said to be meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) itself.

He asks why it is stated that those faculties are "serene" (*vippasanna*) because they are produced by the mind (*citta*). [The answer is: "Because of metaphorical application" (*upacaritattā*), by way of proximity (*ṭhānūpacāra*).

Because it is so designated. “Their color” refers to the material forms of the sense faculties (*indriya-rūpa*). In the *Nidhikaṇḍa* discourse: that which has a beautiful color is “golden” (*suvaṇṇa*);
the state of being golden is “goldenness” (*suvaṇṇatā*). Likewise for “exquisite voice” (*sussaratā*). And by “voice” (*sara*), sound is meant.

“Goodly shape” (*susaṇṭhāna*) means the excellent configuration of the limbs and members. “Beauty of form” (*surūpatā*) means the state of having a beautiful physical body. “In what manner” (*yathā*) means by whatever mode.
When it is "established" (saṇṭhita). The construction is: "It is established in such a way, in that manner.

Regarding the triad beginning with lightness (lahutā): the analysis (*viggaha*) is "it arises from conditions that are the opposites of the disturbances of the elements which cause heaviness and so forth.
"Of this" refers to what was stated regarding the triad beginning with lightness. Therefore, this triad beginning with lightness is "originated by kamma" (*kamma-samutthāna*).

The intended meaning is that it should be stated thus. Regarding the statement, "In the Yamaka [treatise] as well, only the present duration (addhā-paccuppanna) is taken," this refers to such passages as:

"For one whose eye-base arises, does the ear-base arise? In the case of those being reborn who possess eyes but lack ears, the phrase "their eye-base arises" and so forth refers to the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) in the section on arising (uppādavāra), and to the moment of death (cuti) in the section on cessation (nirodhavāra).

The intention is that it is indeed the present duration (*addhā-paccuppanna*) that is spoken of. The distinction of time is stated in reference to the period of occurrence for those [diseases] not born of karma (*akammaja*).

Regarding the statement, "It is said that diseases are born of the ripening of karma (*kamma-vipākajā*)," this is stated in the *Vīthimuttasaṅgaha*, in the section explaining the interrupting karma (*upacchedaka-kamma*), where it says:
"There are diseases arisen from wind (*vāta*). ... There are diseases born of the ripening of karma. These are [the types of diseases] that cause oppression and injury.
The connection is that even kamma-factors, upon encountering failures, cause disturbances and give rise to various diseases. "Abiding in the body" means they remain within the body;
"they follow that [disturbance]" means that even those factors born of kamma and so forth become disturbed—this is the intended meaning.
By this, it is shown that among the eight causes, by whichever cause a disease such as eye-disease arises, [it occurs].
When that [kamma-born] factor arises, all disease-originated material phenomena occurring in the body necessarily attain the state of affliction (*ābādha*).

Even so, it is shown that the kamma-born material phenomena included within that [body] attain the state of affliction by way of following along with it, and not directly through the power of kamma itself.
There is no such thing as an affliction originated by kamma. Nevertheless, in the eight...

Just as in such passages as "there are afflictions arising from wind," etc., it is not said "there are afflictions arising from karma," but rather "there are afflictions born of the ripening of karma" (*kammavipākaja*).

In that context, any disturbance of the elements whatsoever that arises by way of oppressive or destructive kamma is indeed called "the ripening of karma" (*kammavipāka*) in the discourse of the Suttas;
[the affliction] born from that [disturbance] is what is meant here.
It is said that "there is no affliction whatsoever that is not born of the ripening of kamma. This point is very profound; it must be explained after thorough investigation.

The word "yato" means "because," referring to the fact that the conditions for affliction arise from kamma. "Labbhamāno siyā" means "it might be found. The construction is: "There is simply no such thing as an affliction that is not born of kamma.
"Non-harming (avihiṃsā) is produced by kamma" means it is produced by the kamma of loving-kindness (mettā) and compassion (karuṇā).
The connection is that they are "unassailable" precisely because of their extreme remoteness. "By way of stability" (*saṇṭhitiyā*) is a qualifying term for what is difficult to disturb;
or it should be regarded as a causal phrase. "Difficult to disturb" means hard to shake. "Granted" (*kāmaṃ*) is a particle used in the sense of "even though" or "although.
The rest here is easily understood.

In the passage beginning with “It is said,” etc., the conditional function of material phenomena (*rūpapaccayadhamma*) is threefold: producing (*janana*), supporting (*upatthambhana*), and maintaining (*anupālana*).
Among these, the function of producing is obtained only at the moment of birth (*jātikkhaṇa*) for those things that are to be produced.
However, the other two are obtained even at the moment of presence (*ṭhitikkhaṇa*). At the moment of dissolution (*bhaṅgakkhaṇa*), however, no conditional function whatsoever exists. Therein—
While investigating by way of the function of producing, he said, “of those that produce material form,” and so forth. Regarding the passage beginning with “Moreover”:

“Of these” refers to the [material] accumulations (*upacaya*) and continuities (*santati*), as well as aging (*jaratā*) and impermanence (*aniccatā*). “In these” refers to those things arising from various sources; however, here it refers to the *Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha*.
“Even though this is so” means even though there is no visible distinction due to the specific condition. “More essential” means being exceedingly essential. “Better” means superior.
The exposition on the origination of matter is concluded.

169. This is the application of the group [of terms]. Regarding the word “reckoning” (*saṅkhāna*), it means counting. The connection is that he shows by means of the word “one” (*eka*) in the sense of reckoning.

“A mass” (*piṇḍi*) means a single solid body. In the reading of the *Mūlaṭīkā*, the phrase “from the occurrence of arising and so forth” (*uppādādippavattito*) refers to [the process] by way of arising and so forth.
Because they proceed [together]. "Thus" means for that reason. They are indeed called derived material phenomena (*upādārūpa*).

"In this way, the material phenomena of change and delimitation should also be combined"—this refers to the five types of material phenomena of change; they possess the nature of being brought together as a single group (*kalāpa*), not as each individual phenomenon.
Therefore, they exist only as single units within each respective group. However, the material phenomenon of delimitation (*paricchedarūpa*) is included within the group.
There is no [separate] matter. Therefore, it should be understood that between each pair of groups, that too exists as a single unit.

Regarding the phrase, "Because of the arising through the support of the four great elements," here, although there is a distinction among the four great elements by way of their individual characteristics, they must indeed be called a "single support" in the sense of being reckoned as one, due to their being a single solid mass by way of their occurrence.
For this being so, there is no movement in the meaning of the word *eka*. By the phrase "by that sound," it means by the sound born of mind (*cittaja-sadda*).
Saying "by intention" (*adhippāyena*), he indicates his own purpose; what is meant is: "by the Elder’s intention. Showing his own intention, he said "But here... and so forth.
In that context, "by sound" means by the sound born of mind. "By that speech" means...
The meaning is: by means of sound consisting of speech. “Intimation” (*viññatti*) has the sense of making known. One makes known, thus it is “intimated” (*viññāpita*).
The state of being that is “the state of having been intimated” (*viññāvitatta*).

What is called the “sound of the diffusion of applied thought” (*vitakkavipphārasaddo*) occurs when, for someone contemplating a great matter, a powerful applied thought proceeds either due to sorrow or due to joy. That [sound] sustains either the sorrow or the joy.
Being unable [to speak clearly], he utters an indistinct sound from his own mouth as if conversing with a second person.
Ordinary people may or may not hear that mere sound; even if they hear it, they do not know the syllables, the meaning, or the intention.
One who hears it through the divine ear (*dibbasota*) or the ear of knowledge (*vijjāsota*) [perceives] even the syllables...
He knows both the meaning and the intention. Having known them, he reflects: "Such is your mind, and such is your mind," and so forth.

This is what is called the sound produced by the diffusion of thought (*vitakkavipphāra-sadda*). It is stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* that this sound is devoid of intimation (*viññatti*) and is cognizable by the ear.
However, the author of the *Saṅgaha* maintains that there is no such thing as a sound consisting of speech that is devoid of intimation or not cognizable by the ear.

“He rejects. “In the *Aṭṭhakathās*” means as they appear in the commentaries. “To be accepted” means to be believed. “In the two *Ṭīkās* on it” refers to the two sub-commentaries (*ṭīkā*) on the *Assasacca-saṅkhepa*.
“Letters, phrases, phonemes, and meanings” is a *dvanda* compound. The analysis (*viggaha*) is: that whose letters, phrases, phonemes, and meanings are not well-known.
“Of the Andhas, Damilas, and so forth” means of those belonging to the Andha race, the Damila race, and others.
“Of the foreigners (*milakkhūnaṃ*). ‘The sound of clearing the throat, the sound of spitting, the sound of vomiting, and the sound of discarding’ is a *dvanda* compound.
By the word ‘etcetera’ (*ādi*), such things as belching, hiccupping, laughing, and weeping are included. The rest here is easy to understand.
The exposition of the application of the *kalāpa* is finished.”

161. Regarding the sequence of the occurrence of form (*rūpappavatti*). There is no qualification by way of the individual (*puggala*); there is a qualification by way of the plane (*bhūmi*), and the intention is that this is indeed by way of the time of occurrence. Regarding the phrases "among these" (*ettha cā*) and so forth:
the connection is that [the distinction] should be understood according to the method of the Canon (*pāḷinaya*) in respect of the first two modes of birth (*yoni*).
Because they have "gone out" (*nikkhantā*), they are therefore called "egg-born" (*aṇḍaja*) and "womb-born" (*jalābuja*). How is it that this method is called the "method of the Canon"?

By the statement in the *Pāḷi*, "They are born having repeatedly broken through the egg-shell and the membrane," the meaning is understood to be that they are born, produced, or emerged from the egg (*aṇḍaja*).
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is stated: "born from an egg" (*aṇḍejātā*) and "born from a water-bag" (*jalābumhijātā*).
Regarding the "womb-enclosing membrane" (*gabbhapaliveṭhanāsayo*): it is that by which the embryo remains enveloped. In the reading of the *Vibhaṅga*:
“By way of the limit of the highest attainment” means by way of determining the occurrence of the most excellent. What is meant is: “by way of the superior method.

In the phrase “a maiden should be given to one who is handsome,” although it is stated in general terms as “a maiden should be given,” because it is specified as “to a handsome man,” it is understood that the maiden must also be a beautiful maiden. This is the superior method (*ukkaṭṭhanaya*).

[This refers to] the phrase "all those therein," and so forth. The meaning is that even all those—namely, the eye, ear, nose, and the pair of [female and male] faculties—are not obtained through inferior kamma; they are obtained only through superior kamma.

In the *Vibhaṅga* recitation, it is stated that "the sound base" (*saddāyatana*) is not obtained at the time of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), as in the passage "eleven bases. This is because one who is deficient in the eye...
Ten [types of beings], those lacking the ear as another ten, and nine for those lacking both eye and ear; by way of those born from a womb, there are seven bases (*sattāyatana*).
Because it is stated in the Canon (*pāḷi*) that only those born spontaneously (*opapātika*) and those born from a womb (*gabbhaseyyaka*) [are included], it is said:
"Even though not mentioned in the Canon. This refers to the lack of eye and so forth, even though it was not mentioned. How is it that "their existence is described as being mutually inseparable"?

It was stated [in the *Peṭakopadesa*] by way of a formulaic expansion (*peyyālamukha*) as follows: "For whom the nose-base arises, for him the tongue-base arises?"—"Yes. Or again: "For whom the tongue-base arises, for him the nose-base arises?"—"Yes," and so forth.
However, this is not accepted by the teacher, the Venerable Ānanda Thera; such is the connection [of the argument]. [The phrase] "on account of the state of being solely tongue" [is used].
There is no such thing as a deficiency of the tongue.

Regarding the statement, "It is logical that there is also a deficiency of the nose," this passage from the Pāḷi—referring to "women and men who are noseless"—is said with reference to women and men whose nasal faculty had not yet arisen in the womb or who had previously vomited it out.
Some also say that it is not because of the actual existence of those deficient in the nose [that they are so described].
They lie in the womb, thus they are "womb-layers" (*gabbhasaya*). Womb-layers themselves are "womb-dwellers" (*gabbhaseyyā*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "at the time of the process," this is from the reading in the *Mūlaṭīkā*. "From that point on" is said with reference to rebirth-linking;
it means not having arrived for eleven days. The visible-object base will not arise, but the eye-base will not necessarily not arise.

This is stated by way of the present continuum (*addhā-paccuppanna*). Therefore, the visible-object base (*rūpāyatana*) that has arisen from the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) is said to be "arisen" for as long as life lasts;
it is not said to be "about to arise. However, for one who remains prior to the eleventh week [of gestation], the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*) is not yet arisen.
Because it has not arisen at that time, it is said to be "about to arise" when the eleventh week is reached.
This must be said. However, because they are in their final existence (*pacchimabhavika*), neither of these two will arise in another becoming.
"Produces the nose-base" means the production of the nose-base; this refers to the karma.

For those who have taken rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) by that karma—provided, however, that they would take rebirth-linking through the very karma that produces it. [This applies] when the nose-base has not yet arisen.

It was said [in the text] with the intention that "they might not die in the interval. Even for those taking rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) by means of the karma that produces that [existence], there is no such thing as not dying in the interval before reaching the moment of the arising of the sense-base of the nose, provided that a more powerful obstructive karma (*upacchedaka-kamma*) has arrived.
This is stated in the *Ṭīkā* regarding the mention of the eye and the nose: "Established in meaning" (*atthato siddhā*).
“Thus it is”: these [states] arise on the eleventh day of the fortnight; thus they are indeed established.

“In such places” means in difficult situations when investigating the intrinsic nature [of things]. The intention is that it is appropriate to take the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) itself as the authority.

In the reading of the commentary: “The prior wheel of existence” refers to the wheel of existence rooted in ignorance and ending with feeling. “Because of illustrating the successive occurrence” means...

Just as in the latter craving-rooted wheel of existence (*bhavacakra*), when explaining the process of rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*), it is stated by combining [the factors] together as "with existence as condition, birth" (*bhavapaccayā jāti*);
it is not so in the former wheel of existence. For there, the sequential progression is illustrated by such statements as "with volitional formations as condition, consciousness;
with consciousness as condition, name-and-form," and so forth. "That [combined statement] is indeed rejected."
Having stated that in the section on the determination of the order of the sense bases (*āyatana*), the sequence of teaching alone is appropriate, the sequence of arising is thereby rejected.
In the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*, in the *Yakkha-saṃyutta* of the Pāḷi, among the verses: "From *kalala*" means from the *kalala* stage; "from *abbuda*" means from the *abbuda* stage;
"from *pesī*" means from the *pesī* stage; "from *ghana*" means from the *ghana* stage; and "with the woolly hairs of birth" refers to the woolly hair of a pure-bred ram.
“With hair and flesh”: “A mass that has fully matured” means that after the stage of *kalala*, it has become slightly matured and takes on a clustered form.
“Turning away from that state” means existing while abandoning the state of *kalala*.
“It melts like ghee in fire” means it is like ghee melting in a fire. “It is released” means it does not stick to the skull. “These are born” is stated thus in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).
It is said: "In forty-two days. This means after nine months have passed, on the twentieth day.
If that is so, then the five limbs are produced in the fifth week, and the four sense-bases (*āyatana*) are produced in the eleventh week;
however, there are five weeks in between. To address how this occurs, he says "And here," and so forth. "Six weeks," etc.
Together with the eleventh [day], there are six days and seven nights. For even on the eleventh day, because it was born on the final day, six days remain.
"The time of ripening" means the time of full maturation. Indeed, only when the great primary elements born of karma have reached full maturation do they become clear.
And the qualities of clarity in those [elements] are the sensitive matter (*pasādarūpa*). "Of that" refers to the *kalala*. "A color has arisen."
The connection is with the words "or its shape. "Situated in a portion of space" means placed by humans in a portion of space.
"Having been" is a supplement to the text. To the question, "How could it be smaller than an atom? he says, "For that," and so forth. "That" refers to the atom.
At the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), the embryonic matter (*kalalarūpa*) has the dimension of three groups (*kalāpa*). An atom, however, has the dimension of forty-nine groups.
Therefore, it is said that this [kamma] is limited compared to that. However, after the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), even that [kamma] becomes accumulated from moment to moment.
"Of the elements" (*dhātūnaṃ*) refers to the four great primary elements (*mahābhūta*) as they appear in the "Definition of the Four Elements" (*Catudhātuvavatthāna*).

It is also appropriate to understand this as being stated by taking the measure of accumulation at the stage of the *kalala*. "In the physical basis" (*vatthusmiṃ*) refers to the physical basis of the *abbuda* and so forth.
“By following the root of the water-born”: the intention is that [it was done] by following its root at the time it was born from water.
In this verse, where one should say “having gone beyond the mother’s womb,” it is stated as “gone beyond the mother’s womb” due to the requirements of the metrical composition.
Therefore he said, “gone beyond the mother’s womb. “Hollow” means endowed with subtle apertures. Or, having obtained...
“Food and drink. “From that point on” means from the seventeenth bhavaṅga consciousness onward.

“It has already been stated regarding the origination of matter” refers to what was stated in the investigation of the Mūlaṭīkā’s position on the origination of matter, beginning with the words, “That which was said there is not appropriate,” and so forth.
“Due to the absence of swallowed food” means due to the absence of external food; this is the intended meaning. “Therein” means in the world of the Rūpa-brahmās.
He praises non-existence. But why does he praise it? Would there not be a contradiction with the *Aṭṭhakathā* for one who praises it?
Whether there be a contradiction or no contradiction, he cites the text from the *Vibhaṅga* beginning with "of the form-element" (*rūpadhātuyā*) to show that the scripture itself is the authority.
Therein, "of the form-element" means of the world-element of form; "in the realm of form" (*rūpa-brahmaloke*) is what is meant. "At the moment of rebirth" (*upapattikkhaṇe*)...
"At the moment of rebirth-linking. Explaining the teacher’s intention, he says "And here," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "even when tangibles are excluded," this exclusion should be understood as the delimitation [of the object] into either the five bases (*pañcāyatana*) or the five elements (*pañcadhātu*).
"Because of the presence of another function" means that there exists another function distinct from the function of tangibles.

"What other function? It is the function of being the cause and condition for the occurrence of the material body. For it was said by the Blessed One: "The great elements are the causes, the great elements are the conditions, for the manifestation of the aggregate of form.
Therein, the function of being a cause is the function of generating matter; the function of being a condition is the function of supporting matter. Thus, there is no other function whatsoever.

The function of the nose and the other [senses] consists in their having the state of being the domain and object; there is no function for them other than that. "By which" means by another function. "Those" refers to odors and so forth.
Now, showing the doctrine followed by the Aṭṭhakathā, he says "yathāpana" (as indeed) and so on.
"By which specific function" means by the specific function of having the state of being the domain and object. [This refers to] the production of matter and the stabilization of matter.
And by way of a specific function: “Everywhere” means in every portion of the Pāḷi. “Of them” refers to the perfumes and so forth.
“Therein” means in the world of form (rūpaloka). Regarding the phrase “by way of the state of mere natural outflow (nissanda-dhammamattabhāva)”:
here, just as when a fire has been kindled, its natural outflows arise whether one desires them or not—so too, color arises, light arises, and fragrance arises.
Sapidity, smoke, and even blossoms sometimes arise; whether there is a specific function to be performed by those colors and so forth or not, they simply arise.
Likewise, when the great elements have arisen, their by-products (nissanda) arise—whether one desires them or not—and whether there is a specific function to be performed or not.
Thus, by virtue of being merely phenomena that are by-products, there is an entry [into the body].

The intended meaning is that it would be appropriate [to speak of] internal continuity (*santāna*). However, in the case of external continuity—such as in clothing, ornaments, celestial palaces (*vimāna*), and so forth—their existence [therein] might be desired.
Or, even regarding the internal, it refers to the time when the body has been made gross and fashioned.

And here, regarding the phrase "entry into the base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*) and the element of mental phenomena (*dhammadhātu*)," first, in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, those who have not arrived at the application [of the term]...
It was stated that even visible forms and so forth are called "dhammas as objects"; however, that [position] has been rejected there.
"Going where there is no access" (anāpātāgamana) refers to being devoid of the function of the range of the sense-sphere.

And this is intended to mean simply the non-going where there is no access among the sensitive forms of humans, devas, and Brahmas. That, moreover, should be discussed after investigating whether it exists or does not exist.
Furthermore, the so-called "outflow-forms" (*nissanda-rūpa*) may consist of various modes of the gross primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
However, the internal form of the Brahmas is exceedingly subtle, having arisen through the specific power of kamma attained in absorption (*appanā*).
Therefore, just as in the continuity of beings in the sense-sphere realm, one must certainly investigate whether the outflow-form is fully present there. And the object of the mind...
It is stated in the Pāḷi that there is no such thing as an "anuloma-dhammāyatana" having the primary dhammas as its object.

Regarding the phrase "and the life-decad," it should be stated [as applying] to the fine-material world (rūpaloka). The word "therein" (tattha) refers to the non-percipient beings (asaññasatta). Why is the life-nonad not mentioned separately in the sense-sphere world (kāmaloka)?
Why is it not mentioned at the moment of rebirth-linking? It is likewise not mentioned separately during the course of existence (pavatti-kāla).
“Of that which is supported by nutriment” means of that materiality designated as nutriment which supports [the body].
“Of the life-force pervading the entire body and protecting it” refers to the life-faculty included within the body-decad and the sex-decad. “Just this, O gods” refers to the life-nonad alone.
“Therein” means in the world of form (rūpaloka). “Of that which has come to be arisen” means of that which has come to be increased. “In two fires” means...
In the digestive fire (*pācaka-ggi*) and the bodily fire (*kāya-ggi*). "Affliction" (*ātaṅka*) is said to mean disease. The analysis of the compound is: "one who has much affliction.
"By the irregularly digesting" means by that which digests unevenly. "By the stomach-fire" (*gahaṇī*) means by the digestive heat of the abdomen.

"Capable of exertion" (*padhānakkhamā*) means capable of the task of undertaking meditation, which is termed "exertion" (*padhāna*). "This" refers to the ninefold life-force (*jīvitanavaka*). By the Elder...
"And by" refers to the Elder Anuruddha. "This" refers to the group of nine [factors] beginning with life. "The sequence of cessation" refers to the sequence of cessation at the time near death.
"In this" refers to the world of form (*rūpaloka*). "Corpse" (*kaḷevara*) means a dead body. The "deposition of the corpse" (*kaḷevaranikkhepa*) is its laying down.
Furthermore, there is no such thing as the deposition of a corpse for other beings of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*). Why, then, is there no deposition of their corpses?
He said, "There is no [such thing]," beginning with the words "For of them," and so forth. In the *Vibhāvanī* reading:

because of the absence of nutriment-originated matter for all the fine-material Brahmās, it is stated that they possess three types of origination. Because of the absence of even mind-originated matter among the non-percipient beings (*asaññasatta*), it is stated that they possess two types of origination.
"Those" refers to the mind-originated [matter] produced at the moment near death. That which has this as its measure is...
"To that extent" means: "The transformation of lightness, heaviness, and so forth" refers to the transformation of the entire material body (rūpakāya) into states such as lightness or heaviness.

Furthermore, because there is a total absence of conditions that cause rigidity and so on—such as disturbances of the elements—the qualities of lightness and so forth always prevail throughout the whole body.
What need is there to consider the occurrence of opposing factors therein? The same applies to non-percipient beings (asaññasatta).
"Regarding the contemplation of the transformation of deformation":
the exposition on the sequence of the occurrence of form is concluded. 161.
In the Compendium of Nibbāna: Of the two terms for Nibbāna, the first term has its meaning unknown; it is a general term.
The second [term] is a specific word for one who understands that state. One who calms the defilements (*kilesa*) is a *samaṇa*; he is a noble person (*ariyapuggala*).
The state of being a *samaṇa* is *sāmañña*. The Noble Path is *sāmañña*. The fruits of *sāmañña* are the *sāmaññaphalāni*.
That which transcends and surpasses the world is *lokuttara*. With reference to the meaning that it is not made known in the world, he said, "No," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "the knowledge of the four paths" (*cattārimaggaññāṇāni catumaggaññāṇaṃ*): he says "by means of the four noble-path knowledges" (*catūhi ariyamaggaññāṇehi*) because, when such a compound word or sentence ending in the singular reaches the plural state through the force of contraction, it becomes plural. "Of such a kind" (*tādisamhā*) means similar to the Noble Path.
"With their faces turned away" (*vimukhānaṃ*) means with their backs turned. "Like those born blind" (*jaccandhānaṃ viyā*) refers to those born blind [not seeing] the lunar disk.
It is like the state of being outside one's range. “Of that” refers to Nibbāna. In this context, “of those born blind” is the possessive term (*sāmipada*) for the word “object” (*avisaya*);
“of that” is the abstract noun (*bhāvapada*). “Whatever” refers to any kind of object. The connection is: “the establishment of that which is Nibbāna.
For a phenomenon (*dhamma*) that is not manifest, there is not even an effort; how much less its realization?
The intention is "it will come to be. "By which" means by effort. "Without Nibbāna" means without having obtained the object of Nibbāna; this is what is meant.
"Failure to accomplish their task" means the failure to accomplish the task of abandoning the defilements. "Therefore" means for that reason. "For the sake of slaying" means in order to kill.
"Striving" means making an effort. In the verse, "internal tangle" refers to the tangle of craving within the internal continuum.

“Entangled by craving” (*taṇhāvinaddhā*). “External tangle” (*bahijaṭā*): the tangle of craving within the external continuum; they are entangled by craving. “Of that” (*tassā*): of craving. “From the standpoint of the basis” (*vatthuto*):
from the perspective of their individual, distinct natures as they arise. They have attained final Nibbāna, are attaining final Nibbāna, and will attain final Nibbāna;
thus they are “those who have attained Nibbāna” (*parinibbutā*). This is because the suffix *-ta-* functions across all three times. Just as [they are] seen, heard, or sensed.
"Viññātā" means that which is to be known by making it distinguished; thus, it is consciousness (*viññāṇa*).
"Anidassana" means that which cannot be pointed out. "Ananta" means that which has no end. "Sabbatopabhaṃ" means that from which the radiance of qualities flows forth in every direction.
"It was spoken by the Blessed One" refers to what was spoken in the *Kevaṭṭa Sutta* of the *Dīgha Nikāya*. "The flowing rivers" refers to the great rivers.
"Or mountain streams. "Enter" means they flow into [the ocean]. "Showers" refers to the showers of rain from clouds.

The statement, "When Buddhas do not arise, not even a single being is able to attain final Nibbāna," is said with the understanding that Pacceka-Buddhas also arise only during eons in which a Buddha has appeared.
However, in the *Apadāna* text, it is stated that there are Pacceka-Buddhas even in eons empty of Buddhas.
The origin [of this] has already been explained. Alternatively, "even a single being" should be understood as a disciple-being (*sāvaka-satta*).
For it is in this way that there is no contradiction with the Apadāna text. "Accomplishing" (*ārādhenti*) means they achieve or obtain.

It is said, "endowed with radiance on all sides" (*sabbatopabhā-sampannaṃ*), with reference to the meaning: "one whose light of qualities proceeds from every side. "Like a tree possessing light" (*jotivanta-taro vā*) means like a tree possessing radiance.
Or: it prevails and is found everywhere; with reference to this meaning of "all-pervading" (sabbatopabhaṃ), it is said that "it is indeed abundant from every side.
Therefore he says: "It is not absent anywhere. "Even though this is so" means even though it exists in a single way according to the manner just described.
"To employ metaphorically" means to express by way of figurative usage (upacāra). "As it has been said" refers to...

What does it say again in that same sutta? "Leading to existence" (*bhavanetti*) means that which leads to becoming; it is craving for existence itself. "Pertaining to the future life" (*samparāyikā*) means that which is to be attained immediately after death.
The connection is that the state of being without residue (*anupādisesa*) has been stated for two types of those whose taints are destroyed.
Here, "state of being without residue" refers to *nibbāna* without residue. Among those in training (*sekkha*), [this applies] to the trainee who stands at the path of Arahatship.

The state of being "without remainder" (*anupādisesa*) is stated by way of the absence of a remainder of defilements (*kilesūpādisesa*). "A remainder of defilements" (*kilesūpādisesa*) refers to a remainder consisting of defilements;

likewise for a remainder of aggregates (*khandhūpādisesa*). In such terms as "one who attains final nibbāna in the interval" (*antarāparinibbāyī*), what is called "final nibbāna" (*parinibbāna*) is said to be the nibbāna of defilements.
The meaning of terms such as "liberated in both ways" (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*) will be explained in the ninth chapter. "By the destruction of defilements" (*kilesakkhayena*)...

"Along with [the exhaustion of defilements], they are exhausted": in the present existence, at the moment of the path of Arahatship, they are exhausted together with the exhaustion of the defilements (kilesa).

They attain the state of non-arising (anuppāda-dhammatā). Likewise, for a person who is a Non-returner (anāgāmin), the aggregates of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi-kkhandha) pertaining to the sense-sphere are [exhausted] at the moment of the Non-returner path;
and for a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna), the remaining aggregates of rebirth-linking pertaining to the sense-sphere, excluding those within seven existences, are likewise [exhausted].

At the moment of the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*), those respective defilements do not perish simultaneously with it; however, the present aggregates (*paccuppannakkhandhā*) do perish together with the destruction of the defilements.
Existing as what is called "the remainder of the aggregates" (*khandhupādisesa*), they continue to occur even for those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*) until the time of death.
To the question "Why do they occur?", he says: "occurring until death," and so forth. [This refers to] the continuity of the present aggregates.

The connection is with the phrase "established by the nature of things" (*dhammatāsiddha*). "Being the outflow of the fruit" means being both the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*) and the fruit of outflow (*nissandaphala*).
"By that very same [means]" means together with the destruction of the defilements (*kilesakkhaya*). Regarding the passage beginning with "But because," etc.: they bind and obstruct on all sides;
they create obstacles to the happiness of peace, thus they are called *palibodhā* (obstacles). They are the functions of the formative activity of the defilements (*kilesābhisaṅkhāra*).
They have the function of forming kamma and the function of forming the aggregates. They are "with impediments" (sapalibodhā) because they exist together with impediments.
They are "with signs" (sanimittā) because they exist together with the signs of formations. They are "with aspirations" (sapaṇihitā) because they exist together with the aspirations of craving.
"Tato" means from evil kamma and from the suffering of the woeful states. "Koci" refers to some phenomenon. "To cease" (nirodhetuṃ)...
"They can cease" means that when the view of a personal body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) has ceased, those [obstacles] cease; they do not cease as long as it has not ceased.
Therefore, although the cessation of the view of a personal body is itself a state devoid of activity, it is said to "cease those obstacles.
Furthermore, the phrase "it is able to cease them" should be understood as a conceptualization of activity within that which is inactive. It is simply the cessation of the view of a personal body.
Regarding the statement "he is able to suppress those obstacles," here the suppression of both is one and the same.

Even so, there is a conceptualization of difference where there is no difference, as in such expressions as "from the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations" (*avijjā-nirodhā saṅkhāra-nirodho*). "Arising and occurrence" (*uppāda-pavatta*) refers to arising and occurrence;
the analysis of the compound is "that which has these two as its root. They are called "Māras" because they kill by means of a coarse mode of being.
"Murderers and enemies" is what is meant. [This refers to] the defilement-Māra and the others. They are "Māra's realms" (*māradheyya*) because Māras dwell and persist within them.
It is called "Death" (*maccu*) because it kills and causes one to fall away; it is death itself. They are "Death's realms" (*maccudheyya*) because Death dwells and persists within them.
When it is said, "There is no sign in that," even regarding phenomena that are mere designations (*paññatti*), there is a sign which is the root of their arising and occurrence.
There is no such name. If this were so, it would follow that there is no distinction between those [arahants] and Nibbāna;

this is the objection. In order to resolve this, he said, "For that," and so forth. The expressions "having destroyed" and "establishing" are merely figurative attributions of activity to what is inactive, for the purpose of making the specific meaning clear.
Regarding the distinctions such as "excellent" and so on: "This Nibbāna of the Buddhas is excellent; this [Nibbāna] of the Paccekabuddhas..."
Nibbāna is the middle [state]. This should be construed as follows: "This nibbāna of the Buddha’s disciples is not divided by being inferior.

That by which one deposits the mind in various ways is "directed" (*paṇihita*). "Deposits" (*nidheti*) means that one establishes [the mind] by making it inclined, sloping, and leaning toward the objects. It is the same for *paṇidhāna* and *paṇidhi*. In meaning, they are one: a longing through craving.
“Name. “Even though they are obtainable” means even though the attainments of existence and the attainments of wealth are obtainable.
“Because it is a state that removes thirst”: thirst is the desire to drink or to consume; that which removes (vineti) or dispels (vigameti) thirst is the “remover of thirst.
“The pleasure of what is felt” means the pleasure of feeling. “What is that, friend?”—in the reading of the Pāḷi, “that” (taṃ) means “therefore” (tasmā). “That which here...”
"Because there is no feeling (*vedayita*) here," means that since there is no feeling here, the construction is: "Therefore, what is called 'happiness' (*sukha*) is [defined] in Nibbāna.
"In this" (*ettha*) means in this Nibbāna. Regarding the phrase "This very thing here" (*etadevettha*), etc., it means "this very thing" (*eta deva*).
Because there is no feeling here, the construction is: "Therefore, this very absence of feeling is happiness in this Nibbāna."
Regarding the passage beginning with “And here,” etc.: the connection is that this very cessation and stopping exists.

However, some say that this cessation and stopping is not merely an activity (*kriyāmatta*)—namely, *nibbāna*—but is merely a conceptualization of non-existence (*abhāvapaññattimatta*). Refuting that, he says: “It is not so,” and so forth.
“The nature of a concept” (*paññattirūpaṃ*) means its essential characteristic as a concept. In the reading of the Pāḷi text: “He exerts himself” (*padahati*).
He makes his energy firm. One by whom the self (ātman) has been urged forward is "one whose self is urged forward" (*pahitatta*).

"Urged forward" (*pahita*) means "exerting oneself. It means established in the state of non-retrogression; they also explain it as "dispatched. "By the body" means by the mental body (*nāmakāya*). "Subject to craving" (*taṇhāvasika*) means those who proceed under the influence of craving.
"Of them too" means even in their doctrine. There are no so-called "infinite qualities" in that mere destruction and cessation; this—
The phrase beginning with “and of nibbāna” was stated in order to clarify the argument.

By the words “they are established by way of their opposites,” it is shown that those who perceive the great danger in the phenomena of saṃsāra (vaṭṭadhamma) likewise perceive the great benefit and excellence in their cessation.
However, as for those who do not know that the aforementioned destruction and cessation is ultimate-nibbāna (paramattha-nibbāna),...

There is simply nothing that can be said [against them]. Because the terms for these qualities are so profound, they imagine that the mere cessation of exhaustion cannot be the basis for infinite qualities.

Now, it has been stated that Nibbāna is the supreme happiness. To refute the objection as to how that mere cessation of exhaustion could be called "supreme happiness," the passage beginning with “It is called the bliss of peace” was spoken.
In the sutta beginning with "There being, monks... (*atthi bhikkhave*), the phrase "if this had not been" (*no cetaṃ abhavissa*) means:

if this [existence] had not arisen, or if it were not existing and present. "Not of this" (*nayimassa*) means "not of this. By saying "of this," he points to the five aggregates (*khandha-pañcaka*) as something directly perceived.
Furthermore, the genitive case is used here in the sense of the ablative. It is the escape for beings from that which has arisen, come to be, been made, and is conditioned.
The construction is: "the name would not be discerned. This same method of analysis applies to others as well. Regarding the phrase "this method applies to all," and so forth:

phenomena called misconduct arise when conditions are present; they do not arise when conditions are absent. Thus, even that which has not yet arisen exists for them, just like that which has already arisen.
And if there were no such thing as the "unarisen," then only the "arisen" would exist. This being the case, regarding one's own misconduct...
Even for those who practice rightly for the sake of the unborn, all phenomena of misconduct would have arisen within themselves, rather than being unborn.
Why? Because that which is called "unborn" does not exist; thus it should be connected [to the argument].
“To this extent,” refers to the scriptural statement beginning with: “There is, monks, the unborn. All conditioned formations subside and come to rest.
"Herein" means the stilling of all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*). "The noble ones relinquish all acquisitions (*upadhi*) herein" refers to the relinquishing of all acquisitions.

"'Is found' (*upalabbhamāno*)" means being found by means of knowledge characterized by peace (*santi*). "'They sought'" (*esiṃsu*)—this was stated as "they attained" in order to show the goal reached at the culmination of the act of seeking.
The explanatory notes on the Compendium of Nibbāna are finished.
The explanatory notes on the Compendium of Matter are finished.
7. Explanatory Notes on the Compendium of Categories.
162. In the *Samuccayasaṅgaha*, the connection is with the phrase "by means of its own specific common characteristic.
The intention is that by means of the designation "other," those which possess their own characteristics are called "salakkhaṇāni" (those with their own characteristics).

Regarding the statement, "Even for Nibbāna, there is the state of having an intrinsic nature obtainable in its own form," this refers to the state of having an intrinsic nature obtainable while being devoid of dependence on anything else. [Objection: Is it not the case that even Nibbāna...

There is indeed the demonstration of other supports through such phrases as "the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion," and so forth. This is merely a demonstration.
However, Nibbāna is not bound by lust and the other defilements; rather, it is far removed from them, its opposite, and its direct antithesis.
For that which is described as the destruction, passing away, breaking up, and impermanence of form—[that is Nibbāna].
In that context, the "destruction" of form is said to occur after it has arisen; thus, it is dependent upon form itself.
Here, however, the non-arising of lust and the other defilements even again is stated; thus, it is independent of lust and the rest. It is not merely independent;
rather, it is far removed from them and more diametrically opposed to them, because its establishment is achieved through qualities that are the direct opposites of those [defilements].

Even unproduced material phenomena (*anipphannarūpa*) are indeed intended here, because they too are included within the aggregates (*khandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), and truths (*sacca*).

Regarding the terms beginning with "outflows" (*āsava*): "in the sense of being subject to fermentation" means in the sense of undergoing the process of fermenting. "In the sense of intoxicating" means in the sense of producing intoxication.
"Undergoing fermentation" means it is said that they reach a state of full-blown corruption. Again, "fermentation" refers to the fermentation of foul odors and so forth.

“Filled with taints” (*āsava-bharita*) means indeed filled with taints. “Corrupting the six objects” (*chaḷārammaṇāni dūsentī*) intends to say that they bring those [objects] to a state of being subject to taints (*sāsava*), and so forth.
“From existence” (*bhavato*) has the meaning of “from the plane” (*bhūmito*). That from which something is delimited or defined is a limit (*avadhi*);
it is called the ablative case (*apādāna*). A boundary (*maryāda*) is a circumscribed limit. An object of action (*kriyā-visaya*) that consists merely of a boundary—
The domain of *maryādā* (limit). *Avadhi* means a mode of pervasion; the domain of the action of pervading is the domain of *abhividhi* (inclusive limit).

"Of whom" (*yassā*) refers to the basis of the limit. "Himself" (*attan*) refers to the basis of the limit. "Having placed outside" (*bahikatvā*) means having made [him] merely present; this is the intended meaning.
In this discussion of limits, "of the sound" (*saddassa*) refers to the sound of the Blessed One’s fame. "That" (*taṃ*)...
The object that serves as the limit. "Fame" means the sound of reputation. "The other" occurs having set aside the scope of non-inclusive extension.
"In the case of the taint of sensuality, etc. "By its name" means by the name of sensuality. "Having that as its object" means having sense-sphere phenomena as its object.
"Or this meaning" refers to the latter meaning stated by the words "it is desired," and so forth. "Exalted wholesome states" is what is intended here.

This was said with reference to *kamma-bhava* (existence as kamma). “Produced by that” means produced by that [craving]. “Having that as its object” means having the two kinds of existence (*bhava*) as its object.
“Craving alone” means craving for existence (*bhava-taṇhā*) alone. “Existence alone” means craving itself, which bears the name ‘existence’ because it has existence as its object.
“These alone” means craving, views, and ignorance alone. “When they are present” means when they have been stored up. “The sphere of sensual desire” means...

“Having the phenomena of sensual desire as their object. Regarding the word “in that,” it refers to the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*). One should apply the same logic to the statement that pride and the other [defilements] have existence (*bhava*) as their object and are thus excluded.
The same applies to the phrase “having views as their object.
“Having made it non-comfortable” means having made it devoid of inhalation and exhalation. “In the sense of sweeping away” means having overwhelmed it.

In the sense of killing. It is also appropriate [to say] "having looked down, in the sense of killing. "In the sense of being difficult to cross" means in the sense that it is difficult for one falling into it to cross over.
"By the method stated" means by the method stated regarding the taints (*āsava*).

"In the round" means in the threefold round of existence (*vaṭṭa*). "In the wheel of existence" means in the wheel of existence beginning with ignorance (*avijjā*) and volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*). "Touching" means...
It shows the meaning of the word as "grasping after having conceptualized in such and such ways.
"In the Dispensation" means in the Dispensation of the scriptures (pariyatti), that is, in this or that sutta. "'Views' are view-grasping":

views themselves are called view-grasping in the sense of being a firm grasping toward the bases of views. In the grasping of self-theory (*attavāda*), "conceptualizing intellect" is said to be wrong knowledge (*micchāñāṇa*).
“Created by a Supreme Lord” means created by Mahābrahmā, the lord of the entire world, at the beginning of the eon.
“Arisen fortuitously” means arisen without cause or condition. “Absolutely eternal” means eternal throughout the succession of existences.
“Partially eternal” means that after reaching a particular state of existence, certain beings are eternal. “Annihilated” means...

The meaning is that there is grasping [to the idea] that "the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) is purified" and so forth, [thinking]: "Wherever one may be after death, [existence] is cut off; old karma is exhausted, and new karma is not performed. A *sakkāya* is a "body of existence" (*kāya*) that "exists" (*santa*).

"Exists" means existing in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*). "Body" refers to the material body (*rūpakāya*) and the mental body (*nāmakāya*), or alternatively, the body of each individual self is the *sakkāya*.
“Individual body” means a body belonging to a specific person; it refers to the two types of bodies already mentioned.

“Personality-belief” (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) is the view regarding personality. In that context, “views regarding personality” means that, like those who speculate about the past and future, without considering the past and future, all beings [hold] toward their own aggregates:
“Form is my self,” or “The self is mine.”
"‘Possessing form’ (rūpavā) means ‘form is mine’ (attani me rūpaṃ), or ‘I am in form’ (rūpasmiṃ me attā),” and so forth;

what is meant is that such views are established by the very nature of things (dhammatā). “‘Unlearned’ (assutavā): because he has not previously heard the teachings concerning the aggregates and other doctrines associated with the principle of emptiness (suññatadhamma), there is nothing heard by him; thus he is "unlearned. “‘An ordinary person’ (puthujjano): this refers to the common worldling (lokika-mahājana).
In that context, even a single person who is included therein is called a worldling (*puthujjana*). Among them, there are both those who have heard the Dharma and those who have not.
Here, it is the one who has not heard the Dharma who is intended. A noble person (*ariya-puggala*), however, is not included therein.
Terms such as "I," "mine," "in me," or "my" are known as "clinging-terms. [The same applies to] "other phenomena," etc.
“Having grasped”: either having grasped the remaining mental aggregates (nāmakhandha) as “this is my self” from the perspective of form;
or “having grasped a self apart from the phenomena (dhamma)” means having grasped a self conceived as existing independently of the five aggregates.
“Caturāvatthikā” means that which has four states. Because feeling has the nature of enjoyment, it is said, “I enjoyed.”
“Happy one” (*sukhito*) refers to a person endowed with pleasant feeling (*sukhavedanā*). In terms of its constituent phenomena (*dhamma*), it is simply the five aggregates (*pañcakkhandha*).
However, because pleasant feeling is predominant therein, one who regards it in that way is said to regard feeling as the self (*attā*).
“Having grasped from the collection” means grasping from the collection [of factors] such as “I am,” “I am one,” or “I am a being. “Basis” (*vatthu*) refers to the five aggregates.

"Those whose objects are not fully understood" (*apariññātavatthukā*) means those for whom the bases have not been fully understood by way of the full understanding of the known (*ñātapariññā*) and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "sometimes as self," this was said with reference to the four modes beginning with "one regards form as self.
"With the sign of self" refers to [the conceit] in bodily, verbal, and mental activities such as approaching, thinking "I am approaching," "I..."
By the phrase "I am withdrawing," etc., that which appears in the mind is called one's own shadow (*attacchāyā*).
"In the sense of desiring" means in the sense of wishing. "In the sense of longing" means in the sense of aspiration.

"Languor" (*līnabhāva*) is the contraction of the mind and its mental factors. "Is taken up" (*āpādīyate*) means the act of taking up (*āpādana*). The analysis of the compound is: "the taking up of the state of languor" (*līnabhāvassa āpādanaṃ*).
“*Tandi*” means laziness. “*Vijambhitatā*” refers to the stretching and contracting of the limbs due to the influence of the defilements (*kilesa*).
The analysis of the compound is: that [state] itself is the condition for this. Regarding the sense of the word *anusaya*:
“*uppajjanti*” means they are able to arise; however, they do not necessarily arise.
When the aggregates have absolutely ceased, there are no such things as underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), because the very function of lying down has ceased.
Alternatively, "arise" means they are capable of arising, as in expressions such as "a *pattha* measure of rice is sufficient for many people.

For conceptual designations (*paññatti*)—being of the nature of non-substantial phenomena (*asabhāvadhamma*)—are not capable of arising even when the necessary conditions are met. However, these [underlying tendencies]...
Because they possess the nature of phenomena (dhamma) and their own specific characteristics, they are capable of arising when the necessary causes are present.

This being so, it is established that even those [defilements] which have not yet reached actual manifestation possess the nature of ultimate reality (paramattha-jātika). Regarding the phrase "they adhere together" (*saha anusenti*), this refers to what is said of them adhering as one;

namely, the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*), the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*), the underlying tendency to conceit (*mānānusaya*), the underlying tendency to views (*diṭṭhānusaya*), and the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*).

Furthermore, among these beings, there is no simultaneous arising [of all latent tendencies] within the continuum of a single being, except for the mere functional state of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*).
If they were to arise simultaneously, then the twelve unwholesome types of consciousness would arise together at all times within the continuum of a being;
yet they do not so arise. Therefore, it is understood that "arising" refers to the state of being liable to arise by virtue of not having been abandoned.
“Is said. Having stated that they “sense,” he demonstrates that meaning with the words beginning with “separately. “Not yet arisen” means not having reached the stage of arising.
“Proceeding in such a manner” means proceeding by way of movement. Again, “proceeding in such a manner” means proceeding by way of being co-nascent with impulsion (*javana*).
“Of which” refers to the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) such as sensual lust. “Adverting” refers to the adverting consciousness (*āvajjana-citta*). “Taming” refers to...
The state of being well-tamed. “Proceeding in such a manner” means proceeding in the mode of following along with the mental continuum (*cittasantāna*).

Those for whom those [states] are their condition are “those existing in that state. If they have not yet reached arising, one might object: “In that case, they would not even be called ultimate realities (*paramattha*”).
He dispels this objection with the words beginning “But those,” and so forth. If they also follow along with the mental continuum of wholesome and indeterminate states...
If this were so, he avoids the objection that "those [factors] would be called wholesome and indeterminate" by means of the words beginning with "And not.

Or else, they would be exclusively unwholesome. If this were so, he avoids the objection that "they would be opposed to the wholesome and the indeterminate" by means of the words beginning with "Nor also.
If they had not yet reached arising, then, if this were so, he says "nor also at the three times," [meaning] they would be independent of time.
"...are liberated," and so forth. "In the mental continuum containing latent tendencies" means in the mental continuum of those in training (sekkha) and worldlings (puthujjana).
"Simultaneously with the arising of the Path" means together with the very arising of the Path. "Stated here and there" means as stated in the commentaries (aṭṭhakathā) and sub-commentaries (ṭīkā).
"Similarity to the future" means resembling what is yet to come; they do not say it is exclusively the future. How are these of a conditioned nature?
He said, "They exist," and so forth, beginning with "by those paths. In the *Vibhāvanī* reading: "Not abandoned" means not abandoned by the path.

"In that state" means in the state ready to arise. "Because of having that nature" means because of having the nature of sensual lust and so forth. "They are called thus" means they are called "latent tendencies" (*anusaya*).
They are not called "future" [in the sense of being non-existent], because they are established as existing within the continuum of consciousness (*cittasantāna*).
“If he abandons” means if he indeed abandons. “Therefore” means for that very reason. “Lusting” means having become possessed of lust. “Hating” means having become possessed of hatred.
“Deluded” means having become possessed of delusion; the point being stated is that it would follow as a fault that he abandons [the defilements] while still possessing them.
“Of those who have reached the obsession” refers to lust and the other [defilements]. “To be destroyed by the Path” means to be slain by the Path.
“Arisen” (*uppanna*) means present. That which is both occurring and arisen is “arisen while occurring” (*vattamānuppanna*).

“Having been experienced” (*bhutvā*) means having made use of the object. “Disappeared” (*vigata*) means it has vanished. That which is both disappeared after being experienced and arisen is “arisen after having been experienced and disappeared” (*bhutvā vigatuppanna*).
“Making room” (*okāsakata*) means creating space for the purpose of ripening. And that which is [so] made room for...
"And arisen" (*uppanna*) means arisen by way of having made room [for its occurrence]. "Manifest activity" (*samudācāra*) is said to be frequent occurrence.

That which is both manifest activity and arisen is "arisen as manifest activity" (*samudācāruppanna*). It acquires a plane known as the pentad of aggregates; thus it is "plane-acquired" (*bhūmiladdha*).
That which is both plane-acquired and arisen is "arisen as plane-acquired" (*bhūmiladdhuppanna*). It grasps the object more intensely; thus it is...
"Seized by the object" means it is grasped by the object. "Seized by the object and arisen" means *ārammaṇādhiggahituppanna*.
"Not suppressed by sublime jhāna and arisen" means *avikkhambhituppanna*. "Not eradicated by the Path and arisen" means *asamugghāṭituppanna*.
Thus [are the characteristics] of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) that are to be abandoned by the Path.
Because they are described by way of their state of having arisen, their "presentness" should be stated only figuratively. "Learners" (*sekkhā*) refers to the seven types of persons in training.

"The lower portion" (*orambhāga*) refers to the sense-sphere world (*kāmaloka*) and the state of being a worldling (*puthujjana*). They are called "lower-fettering" (*orambhāgiyāni*) because they manifest in the lower portion.

"The higher portion" (*uddhaṃbhāga*) refers to the exalted state (*mahaggatabhāva*) and the noble state (*ariyabhāva*). They are called "higher-fettering" (*uddhaṃbhāgiyāni*) because they manifest in the higher portion.
In this context, sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and ill will (*byāpāda*)—these two fetters—are seen only in the lower realm, which is designated as the world of sense-desire (*kāmaloka*).
Views, doubt (*vicikicchā*), and adherence to rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*)—these three—are designated as the state of an ordinary person (*puthujjana*).
The remaining five, however, are designated both as the state of the sublime (*mahaggata*) and as the state of the noble (*ariya*), and thus belong to the higher realm as well.

They appear together. Alternatively, those first five fetters, when not abandoned by one, pull down toward the lower portion—known as the sense-sphere world—even that person who stands in the higher realms;
therefore, they are called "leading to the lower portion" (*orambhāgiya*).
Those last five, when not abandoned by one, [pull] even that person standing in the sense-sphere world toward the upper portion.
They draw [one] upward; therefore, they are called "factors conducive to the higher" (*uddhaṃbhāgiyāni*).

For among them, the two—attachment to form and attachment to the formless—draw one exclusively toward the sublime state (*mahaggatabhāva*). Furthermore, pride, restlessness, and ignorance, when accompanied by attachment to form and the formless, also draw one [upward].
They belong to the lower, the sensual world (*kāmaloka*); therefore, they are called "factors conducive to the lower" (*orambhāgiyāni*).
They are called "higher-fettering" (*uddhaṃbhāgiyāni*) because they lead one to resort to the higher worlds of form and formlessness; thus they are also described in this way.

"But the others," however, refers to the two fetters of envy (*issā-saṃyojana*) and stinginess (*macchariya-saṃyojana*). "What, then, is the sequence of the two? means: here, in this summary, what is the order of these two?
"Oppressing" (*vibādhenti*) means they cause harm. "And tormenting" (*upatāpenti*) means they approach and cause suffering. The rest here is easy to understand.
The elucidation of the inclusion of unwholesome states is finished.

163. In the Compendium of Mixed Categories: “The directing of the mind and the application of the mind toward what is reckoned as a happy destination, a miserable destination, and the turning away from the round.
This refers to existence in a happy destination, existence in a miserable destination, and that which is reckoned as Nibbāna. For Nibbāna is so called because it has gone away from the round (vaṭṭa).
“Turning away” (vivaṭṭanti) is what is said. “By means of seeing and so forth” means precisely by means of seeing, intention, and the rest.
“Straight course” (uju-gati) is said to be a process that leads to welfare and happiness. “Crooked course” (vaṅka-gati) is a process that leads to harm and suffering.

“Limbs of the path” (pathaṅgāni) refers to the limbs of the path, the way. Since “path” (magga) is said to mean a means (upāya), he says “limbs of the means” (upāyaṅgāni). “The others” refers to right view, right intention, and so forth.
The limbs (*aṅgāni*) are the means for proceeding in a straight course. These four factors of the path (*maggaṅga-dhammā*) are also mentioned as "factors" (*dhammā*).
“Proceeding in such and such a way” refers to proceeding by way of false speech and so forth. “The name-group of ‘nā’” refers to both the wrong path (*micchāmaggo*) and the right path (*sammāmaggo*).

“Those whose existence is dependent on themselves” means those whose occurrence is under one’s own control. One’s own course (*gati*) refers to the seeing and so forth of the eye-faculty and the rest.
“Function” (kicca) alone is what is being spoken of. The phrase “lords and masters” (issarā adhipatino) is stated for the purpose of making the sense of predominance (ādhipacca) clear;
however, the meaning should be understood by way of the predominance of the state (bhāva). For “faculty” (indriya), “lordship” (issariya), and “predominance” (ādhipacca) are synonymous.
“Feminine forms” refers to the feminine gender, masculine gender, and so forth. “Otherwise, there would be no occurrence” means in the case of the female form...

[This refers to] the non-occurrence of the male signs and so forth in what has the form of a man, and the female signs and so forth in what has the form of a woman. Therefore he said, “For thus,” and so on. The connection is:
the mind is the lord over associated states in their function of cognizing, because it proceeds by way of being unassailable by anything else.
Thus it is in the other [commentary]. “In the decisive resolve upon the object” means in the occurrence of the mind toward an object free from doubt. “In the manifestation of the object” means...
When an object superior in its Buddha-qualities appears to the mind: "The Dhamma of the Four Truths" refers to the Dhamma of the Four Truths previously unknown by that person;
or it refers to the Deathless State previously unknown. The compound means: the faculty (indriya) that functions as the thought, "I shall know what was not yet known.
The phrase "of one who has entered upon the path" is stated because it is established by implication. "By way of being incomplete" [is said].

By virtue of having reached the state of "no-more-learning" (*aśaikṣa*). Among the six trainees (*śaikṣa*) who are engaged in the function of knowing again and again—by this, he illuminates the meaning that "knowing" consists in the abandoning of all defilements (*kleśa*) right up to the end. They also explain it as "knowing without transgressing the boundary already known by the first path.
One who has fully understood the meaning is an "Aññātāvī. [This refers to] the Arhat whose taints (*āsrava*) are exhausted.
"Having done what was to be done, having lived the holy life. In order to show the meaning of "the faculty of one who has known" (*aññātāvindriya*), it is said:
"of one whose duty of understanding is fully accomplished," and so forth. "Liberation from that" means liberation from the grasping of a self (*attaggāha*).
"In that" means in that self. "Defiled" means corrupted by various defilements (*kilesa*). "Agitated" means...
“Shaken by various pleasures and pains. “For the sake of a purified attainment” (*vodānapattiyā*) means for the purpose of attaining purification.

“For the sake of that attainment” (*tāyapaṭipattiyā*): the instrumental case is used here in the sense of the instrument or the cause. “For the sake of a purified attainment” (*vodānapattiyā*): the genitive case is used here in the sense of the possessor. “They strengthen themselves” (*balīyantī*):
this is a designation of a nominal root. Therefore he said, “making it strong. “By strength” (*balasā*): by means of power. Completely.
They are called *parissayā* because they lie all around and surround one. The state of one who lacks faith is *assaddhiya*. By means of the opposing factor known as laziness (*kosajja*).
One whose mindfulness (*sati*) is lost or destroyed is *muṭṭhassati*. The state of one who is forgetful is *muṭṭhassacca*.
"The remaining two pairs" refers to the pair of shamelessness (*ahirika*) and the pair of moral dread (*hiri*).
In such cases as "householder" (*gahapati*) and "husband and wife" (*jāyampati*), the word *pati* is a synonym for "lord" (*sāmi*) or "master" (*issara*); thus he says, "‘Patī’ means lord or master.
"'Of others' (*paresaṃ*)" refers to other co-nascent faculties (*indriya*). "'By others' (*parehi*)" is the instrumental case used in the sense of the accusative.

The meaning is: "among other co-nascent faculty-phenomena. "'Superior' (*adhiko*)" means more excellent. "'Of those whose mode of existence is dependent on self' (*attādhīnavuttīnan*)" means of those whose way of being is under the control of the self.
Regarding the phrase “or by way of the arrival of desire (*chandāgamanavasena*): here, *āgamanaṃ* (arrival) means that by means of this, the fruit arrives;

it is the primary cause, the root cause, the originating cause. Desire itself is the arrival, thus it is “the arrival of desire. Therefore he said, “In former past existences,” and so forth. The connection is:
“having made the associated states dependent upon themselves. A great flood [sweeps away] grass, leaves, and reeds, making them dependent upon themselves.
“Acting as if” is the interpretation. In that context, “dependent on oneself” (*attaparādhīna*) means one who has another—namely, oneself—as supreme is “self-supreme” (*attapara*).

Those who are dependent on the self-supreme are “dependent on oneself” (*attaparādhīna*); this is the meaning. “In the remaining cases as well” refers to the remaining [factors] where energy (*vīriya*), mind (*citta*), or investigation (*vīmaṃsā*) are predominant.
By this it is shown: “Energy itself is the predominant factor, thus ‘energy-predominance’ (*vīriyādhipati*). For one possessed of energy, what task indeed would not be accomplished?”

In this way, he extends the method [of the preceding] by means of former volitional formations (*pubbābhisaṅkhāra*), or by means of having well-cultivated the application of energy (*vīriyārambha*) in previous past existences;

that is, energy which proceeds by constantly taking up its burden with firm resolve, as if a great flood were sweeping away grass, leaves, and straw—namely, the states associated with various wholesome and unwholesome kamma, which are dependent on oneself and subject to others. "The last three... [and so forth].
“States” (*dhammā*) refers to the states of energy (*vīriya*), consciousness (*citta*), and investigation (*vīmaṃsā*).

The objection is that even when they function under the control of another, they lack the status of predominance (*adhipatibhāva*) at that time. The connection is that the function of predominance is the carrying of the burden.

Regarding the phrase “without regard for this or that specific function,” it means that the eye-faculty is sovereign over the function of seeing, the ear-faculty over the function of hearing, and so forth.

It depends upon this or that specific function, and likewise upon not depending [on others]. "Functions such as cognizing" refers to all the functions of the sense faculties (indriya-kicca) as stated in such passages as, "The mind cognizes the object.
They are called *āhāra* because they carry or transport intensely (*bhuso*). "Intensely" means excessively. But how are they intense?
He says "co-nascent, etc. because they carry [the result]. The construction is: "these are the condition-dhammas" and "these are the conditioned-dhammas.
"In this" refers to this textual passage (pāḷi). Regarding "condition-food": here, every condition, such as the root-cause (hetu) or the object-condition (ārammaṇa), is called "condition-food";
however, "food-condition" is a specific condition distinct from the others. "By way of the meaning of condition" refers to the root-cause (hetu).
In the sense of being a condition by way of object and so forth. "Become food" means they constitute a specific function of support; this is what is meant.
"Of the sprouts and shoots" is a genitive case used in the sense of the accusative. "For growth" means for the purpose of increasing.
"For stability" means for the purpose of maintaining. The connection is: "These beings proceed in the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*). The rest here is easily understood. "On the side..."
“Having dispersed” means having shifted from one side; or alternatively, “on one side” means having dispersed the wind with the wings.
“Of that which has adhered to it” means of that which has adhered to that stream of resultant consciousness.
“Having made manifest” means having made it evident and clear through direct perception. “Not having obtained” means not having obtained it in the eye; that is to say, not having seen it.
“In that very place” means in the dwelling place itself. “Associated” means associated with consciousness.
“They have come to be” (*bhūtā*) means they have increased. “Seeking growth” (*sambhavesino*) means those who seek or search for the cause of growth (*sambhava*).
“In the manner stated” means in the manner stated by the passage beginning, “Just as in the case of barley seeds or rice seeds. “He nourishes” means he causes [them] to proceed.
“Mental volition as nutriment” refers to mental volition that constitutes wholesome and unwholesome kamma.

“The three realms of existence” refers to the three realms of rebirth, beginning with the sense-sphere realm (*kāmabhava*). It is stated [in the text] both “for the maintenance” and “for the assistance”;
the intention is that otherwise it might have been stated “for the arising.”

“Because of having weak functions, weak bases, and weak foundations”: this means because of having weak functions (*dubbalakicca*), weak bases (*dubbalaṭṭhāna*), and weak foundations (*dubbalavatthu*).
“They are mere occurrences”: the intended meaning is that they are mere instances of seeing, hearing, and so forth.
“Jhāna has applied thought as its final member”: the sense is that what are called jhānas follow after applied thought (*vitakka*). “Therein”: [refers to] therein.

Regarding those five types of consciousness: "They" refers to feeling and one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*); "that" refers to the function of *jhāna*. The connection is that one-pointedness is not powerful.
"For the sake of the state of strength of the path-faculties" means for the purpose of the state of strength of the path-faculties.

It is stated "belonging to the three planes," etc., because supramundane resultants and the functions of impulsion (*javana*) possess a dominant factor (*sādhipatika*). The rest here is easily understood.
The Elucidation of the Compendium of the Combined [Factors] is finished.
164. In the Compendium of the Requisites of Enlightenment: regarding the term “foundations of mindfulness” (*satipaṭṭhāna*), the word *pati* has the sense of being foremost or primary;
thus he says, “having become foremost and primary. The word *ṭhā* has the sense of the cessation of movement; thus he says, “having turned back the movement of the mind.”
“...occur. “Contemplation of the body” means contemplation occurring with respect to the body. It is called “contemplation” because by means of it, yogis see again and again.
To the question, “What do they see? he says, “of the in-breath, out-breath, and so forth,” and so on. To the question, “And how do they see that?
he says, “in the form of this or that part of the body,” and so forth. Now, showing the meaning of the word *punappunaṃ* (again and again):
He spoke the words beginning with “as much as. This same method applies to the contemplation of feeling (*vedanānupassanā*) and the others as well.
That is not correct. Why? Because the entire aggregate of form (*rūpakāya*) is intended here. The rest in this context is easy to understand. Regarding the phrases beginning with “If it is thus”:

“The other is also established” means that the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*) and the others are also established. Why? Because they are included within the contemplation of phenomena (*dhammānupassanā*). “For one who contemplates in such a manner...”

For one who contemplates from the perspective of the characteristic of materiality: “By way of this or that aggregate of material phenomena” means by way of the aggregate of material phenomena consisting of in-breath, out-breath, and so forth.
“Of the perversions such as beauty” means of the perversions of beauty, pleasure, and permanence.
“Of the gross” means of the gross [form] by way of its being well-manifested. “Bound up with a self” means bound up, or fettered, by a self.
“Kāmam” means “certainly. It is connected with “let it dry up. “Yantam” refers to the jhānas, the direct knowledges (abhiññā), the paths, the fruits, and Nibbāna.
“The steadying of energy” means the steadying of energy by way of its cessation—that is, the stopping of the movement and the proceeding of energy.
Since the word “arisen” includes both past defilements and present defilements, he said: “In such-and-such...”

Regarding the passage beginning with "At the proper time," etc.: "Arisen in me" refers to what has arisen at this present moment. Regarding "For the sake of abandoning," it is the abandonment by eradication (*samucchedappahāna*) that is intended here;
thus he says, "for the purpose of bringing about the state of non-arising. In that context, those for whom non-arising is their nature are "those whose nature is non-arising" (*anuppādadhammā*).
The analysis of the compound is: "the state of those things whose nature is non-arising," referring to unwholesome states (*akusaladhammā*) abandoned by the Path.

The compound "the bringing about of the nature of non-arising" (*anuppāda-dhammatā-āpādana*) means the act of causing that [nature]. "Having seen" (*disvā*) means having seen the basis for their arising.
