"For the purpose of cutting off conditions" (*paccaya-samucchindanatthaṃ*) means for the purpose of severing the underlying tendency (*anusaya*) which serves as the condition.

"Not yet reached" (*apattā*) means not having reached it now. "At the opportune time" (*samaye*) refers to the moment when a Buddha has appeared. "They do not enter into the fixed course" (*niyāmaṃ na okkamanti*).
They do not enter, they do not descend into, the certainty of rightness known as the Noble Path.

One whose nature is unshakable because it cannot be shaken by defilements is "one of unshakable nature" (*akuppa-dhamma*). This refers to one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*). The state of being one of unshakable nature is "the quality of having an unshakable nature" (*akuppa-dhammatā*);
this is the fruit of Arhatship. "Of those" refers to wholesome states (*kusalā dhammā*). [The phrase] "for the abandoning of arisen evil states" is understood.

For one who applies themselves to the states conducive to purification, when the work of meditation has gradually reached its culmination, even those evil qualities that have arisen from the very beginning are abandoned.
Those not yet arisen do not arise. Wholesome qualities not yet arisen do arise.

And those wholesome qualities already arisen reach full perfection through cultivation. This same method applies to the [four right strivings] beginning with "for the non-arising of unarisen evil states."
Thus, for one who exerts himself rightly even by means of each single door among the four doors, the right effort accomplishes its four functions.
Therefore he said, “But among these,” and so forth.

All ultimate phenomena (paramattha-dhammā) that are to be known by means of the knowledge of the discernment of phenomena (dhamma-vavatthāna-ñāṇa) in its most distinguished form are those to be directly known (abhiññeyya).
[The term] *abhiññā-siddhi* means the accomplishment of the task of direct knowledge (*abhijānana*).

The phenomena of the Four Noble Truths that must be known by discerning each one individually are called "the things to be fully understood" (*pariññeyya*). By means of these [knowledges], the phenomena of the truth of suffering are to be fully understood;
the phenomena of the truth of origin are to be abandoned; the phenomena of the truth of cessation are to be realized; and the truth of the path...
“Phenomena (dhammā) are to be known by way of being developed. “The accomplishment of development” means the accomplishment of the task of development.
The connection is that this accords with this passage in the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*. “But in the *Vibhaṅga*” refers to the *Iddhipāda Vibhaṅga*.
“The aggregate of mind and mental factors” refers to the higher-than-human states (uttari-manussa-dhamma) together with preliminary development.
“Wisdom is the aggregate of consciousness and mental factors. Regarding the phrase “therein, moreover,” it refers to that *Uttaracūḷabhājanīya* section in the *Vibhaṅga*.
“Herein” means in this compendium.
The so-called four factors of stream-entry are: being endowed with unwavering confidence in the Buddha, in the Dhamma, and in the Saṅgha.
"Endowed with the virtues dear to the Noble Ones"—thus are stated the factors of stream-entry. Therein, "dear to the Noble Ones" means desired or wished for by noble persons.
"Virtues" refers to the five precepts of constant virtue or the eightfold virtue including right livelihood.
"In the right efforts" refers to the functions of the right efforts.
“By sixteen functions”: this means by sixteen functions, four being assigned to each Truth.
It is said [also] by way of the sixteen meanings, such as the meaning of oppression (*pīḷana*), the meaning of the conditioned (*saṅkhata*), and so forth; these meanings will be explained later.
It is stated that mindfulness itself is a factor of enlightenment (*sambojjhaṅga*); but how does it instruct and give rise to full enlightenment? To this he says: “For it,” and so forth.
The same method applies to the remaining factors of enlightenment as well. Regarding the phrase “in those states,” it refers to states both internal and external.

“The side of lethargy, contraction, and indolence” means the side of lethargy, the side of contraction, and the side of indolence. “Exertion of the burden” (*dhurasampaggaha*) means that one properly takes up and lifts the burden.
“The burden” refers to the burden of serenity (*samatha*) and the burden of insight (*vipassanā*). “Discontent” (*arati*)...
“Discontent” (*ukkaṇṭha*) refers to the side of dissatisfaction (*arati*), the side of disenchantment (*nibbidā*). Delight in the Dhamma is *dhammarati*; joy in the Dhamma is *dhammanandī*;
delighting in the Dhamma is *dhammārāma*. “Aggression” (*sārambha*) means mental harassment; “distress” (*daratha*) means mental torment.
Because of the statement, “Monks, one who is concentrated understands and sees things as they truly are,” it is by means of wisdom (*paññā*).
It is said that the state of being a basis for concentration (*samādhipādakatā*) is evident; thus, the passage beginning with “of that” (*tassā*) and so forth was stated.
That which carries its own function evenly (*samaṃ*), without unevenness, by its very nature, is called *samavāhī*.
The state of being such is *samavāhitā*. The connection is that this [state] is fourfold. “Of that” (*tassā*) refers to right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*). “Visākhā” is a form of address.
The word *padaṃ*. To show the connection with the statement, "All [these] are supramundane," he said, "Those thirty-sevenfold divisions," and so forth.
"Possessing nine bases" (*navaṭṭhānika*) means that it has nine bases. "Supramundane" (*lokuttare*) refers to the supramundane consciousness.

"Of those opposed to self" (*attappaṭipakkhānaṃ*) means of those opposed to one's own [wrongful] rectitude. "Those" (*te*) refers to the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhammā*). The connection is: "By this, he shows."
“Kuṇḍaliya”: he addresses the brahmin of that name. “Vijjā” means the knowledge of the path (*magga-vijjā*). “Vimutti” means the liberation of the fruit (*phala-vimutti*).
The exposition on the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya*) is concluded.
165. In the *Sabbasaṅgaha*: “Five aggregates” means five groups. “Divided by the distinctions of past and so forth” means by way of the distinctions of past, future, and present.
Of those things divided by way of internal and external, coarse and subtle, inferior and superior, and distant and near.
"In the doors of rebirth" means in the doors of the eye and so forth. "In the doors of action" means in the doors of bodily action and so forth.
"Having come together" (*saṅgamma*) means having assembled. "Having met together" (*samāgamma*) means having gathered. "Or common functions" refers to all modes of conduct (*iriyāpatha*).
Regarding the common functions: in the Pāḷi text, “kiñcā” means “and why?”; “saṅkhāre vadethā” means “you should speak of the formations as ‘formations’”;

“kiñca saṅkhataṃ” means “and what is conditioned?”; “rūpaṃ rūpatthāyā” means that they construct the conditioned thing called “form” for the sake of the arising of the transformation of form—this is the meaning. [The word] “upabhogo” [means] enjoyment.
"Requisites" (*vatthu*) refers to internal enjoyments such as clothing and ornaments. "Appurtenances" (*paribhoga*) refers to external enjoyments such as beds and chairs.

The phrase "feeling pertaining to the future life" (*samparāyikañca vedanaṃ*) is the governing subject; this applies to the remaining factors as well—perception (*saññā*), formations (*saṅkhāra*), and consciousness (*viññāṇa*).

The expression "giving for the sake of giving" (*dānaṃ dānatthāya*) means for the purpose of generating the merit of giving. The meaning is that they form the conditioned thing known as giving. Alternatively:
The meaning of giving is "dānattha. "Meaning" (attha) refers here to the meaning of fruition, the meaning of result.

The sense is that they are fashioning the conditioned thing known as the merit of giving for the sake of the fruition of giving, for the sake of the result of giving. The same applies to the remaining [perfections].
"Devoting themselves" means devoting themselves to the work of insight (vipassanā). It was said: "They will weary themselves regarding three things. How will they weary themselves?

He said: “For it is thus,” and so forth. “In the objects that are the supports for what is called pleasure” means in the objects that serve as supports for the sake of attaining mental serenity (*cittasāta*) and mental delight (*cittarati*). “By them” means by those attainments. “Those” refers to the attainments.
There is a state called pleasure that has reached the ultimate excellence. Therefore, the knowledge of contemplation of suffering should be practiced even more intensely therein.
The intention is that for that purpose, the Blessed One has made that feeling a separate aggregate and thus teaches the exposition of the aggregates.
This same method applies elsewhere as well. Regarding the phrase "regarded by knowledge as [the self]," it means regarded as such by the knowledge of worldlings.
Regarding the phrase "making consciousness the supreme self," since discernment is considered supreme in the world, one makes this very discerning faculty the supreme self.
The rest here is quite clear. Regarding the phrases beginning with “where he eats”: “where he eats” means in whichever vessel he eats;
“and what he eats” means whichever food he eats; “and with what he eats” means with whichever condiment he eats;
“and whoever serves him” refers to the attendant standing nearby who distributes the food; and “and whoever is the eater” refers to the one who eats.
“‘Only those with taints’ (sāsavā eva): ‘with taints’ refers to mundane phenomena (lokiya-dhammā). ‘As if exerting themselves’:
this is said because they are phenomena characterized by non-exertion; for there is no such thing as exertion in phenomena that are non-exertive.
Rather, because they produce a fruit, they are ‘as if exerting themselves’ for the sake of that fruit. ‘Having scattered’: having spread out. The rest here is easily understood.”
In the *Dhātusaṅgaha*: “Its own individual essence” (*attano eva sabhāvaṃ*) can also be construed as “its very own individual essence” (*attano sabhāvaṃ eva*).
“Effort and activity” (*īhā ca byāpāro ca*): this refers to the exertion such as “I go forward” and “I go backward,” and the activity consisting of going forward and so forth.

“And not conjoined with a life-principle” (*na ca jīvayogā*): they are not conjoined with a life-principle as recognized by the common people of the world. In the reading of the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “it moves” (*yāyati*).
"Herein" means in this context. "Udukkhala" is a mortar. "Yantacakka-yaṭṭhi" refers to the lever-stick connected to the wheel of the machine;
"musalayaṭṭhi" is the pestle-stick. "Araṇī" refers to the two pieces of heartwood made for producing fire. "Adharāraṇī" is the lower piece of wood;
"Uttarāraṇī" is the upper piece of wood. "Like a dart" means like an arrowhead. "Like a stake" means like a piercing rod.

“Like those afflicted by disease”: like those who are ill, pierced by those arrows and spears. “The sign of what is not as it truly is” means the sign of beings, persons, and so forth, which is not real.
“Like a forest animal”: just as a forest animal perceives grass as a person, so too [the practitioner] perceives [the object].
“In a pit of embers” means in a pit of burning coals. “From the signs of various kinds of calamities” means from the signs of various types of...
The arising of calamities is due to their conditions. “Like a forest monkey” means like a wild monkey living in the forest.
“One who is difficult to tame” means one whose taming is done with great difficulty. “A wild colt” means a vicious horse.
“Falling wherever it pleases” means that in whichever object it desires or wishes to fall upon, there it falls; not remaining steady according to the person’s control, but [falling] among objects.
This means "falling according to one's wish. "Like a stage actor" means like a performer on a stage.

"Santo" (the peaceful) means that which exists by way of its own nature (*sabhāva*) and is found to be present. "Tathā" (thus) and "avitathā" (not otherwise) are identical in meaning. "Aññathā" (otherwise) means another mode;
"anaññathaṃ" (not otherwise) means that for which there is no other mode. "Dukkhadukkhaṃ" (the suffering of suffering) refers to bodily suffering and mental suffering.

“Born of kamma” means the material phenomena consisting of resultant aggregates and those produced by past deeds (*kaṭattā-rūpa*). “For arising” means for the purpose of production. “Even beforehand” means even prior to that.
“Even when arisen” refers to the eye that has already arisen. “For continuity” means for the sake of the persistence of the stream and for its maintenance.
“The suffering of maintenance” means the suffering of purification. “Deficiency of conditions” refers to such things as the interruption of nutriment. Is it not so?
It is true that, due to the fear of breaking, the very act of procuring requisites would indeed be suffering;
however, what is intended here is the procurement of requisites performed upon seeing a sign of imminent destruction.

Regarding the phrase "the suffering of providing protection, defense, and guarding," this refers to the making of arrangements for protection against various dangers, as well as for defense and concealment.

Suffering. “It is accomplished together with both of those”: for those performing activities such as plowing and tending cattle, or actions such as guarding, protecting, securing, and providing defenses, that suffering is accomplished together with that [other] suffering. “Of them”:
the connection is that it does not release those who indulge in the eye and so forth. “Arising and cessation...”
“Of what has come to be”: this refers to the cessation of the occurrence [of defilements] that have arisen. “He abandons that very thing”: he abandons that greed itself.
“Only so far as”: by way of the ultimate limit. The conceit that occurs as “I am” is the conceit “I am” (*asmimāna*).

Its eradication is its total cutting off. “When they are fully understood”: when those [defilements] have been fully understood by way of the abandoning of the underlying tendency (*anusaya*) of craving.
"But by the opposite of that" means: however, by the reverse of that. "Not being a basis for the conceit 'I am' (*asmimāna*)" and so forth is in terms of its meaning.
"Phenomena not bound to the faculties" refers to material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*) occurring in such things as the earth and mountains.
"He makes beings free from distress" is the connection [of the sentence]. "Thus" (*iti*) means: therefore. "Of those beings. "Difficult to abandon" is the name.
There is none [other]. Therefore, the construction is: greed alone is what is called the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering.

Wholesome states associated with the taints (*sāsava*) are called the Truth of Origin, because they are the origin, the cause of growth, and the condition for the resultant aggregates and the matter produced by kamma, which constitute the Truth of Suffering.
They are stated to be the root in such passages as "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise. "Like Nandana" means...
“In the world of the gods, like the Nandana grove. “The primary origin and source” means they are the beginning, the source, and the principal cause of suffering phenomena.
“Source” means the cause for their initial arising. “Of these” refers to suffering phenomena.
“In some place” means in some state of existence, such as the sense-sphere existence (kāma-bhava) and so forth. “At some time” means at some period, such as the past and so forth.
“Of some” means of certain beings among the classes of beings such as devas and humans. “From somewhere” means from some cause among many causes.
“In some way” means by some particular mode.
“Transformation” (pariṇāma) means the process of changing, that is, becoming otherwise. “Of those possessed thereof” means of those endowed with those [faculties] such as the eye.
Regarding the person (*puggala*). In the canonical text (*pāḷipāṭha*): “Blazing” (*āditta*) means set on fire, burning brightly. “By what?”—by what fire acting as the instrument?

Likewise, the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*) is subject to change (*vipariṇāmadhamma*). The construction is: that [Path], being subject to change, indeed oppresses the person intensely even through the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmadukkha*).
“Not” (*nā*) means it would not be so. “Calm” (*samana*) means the pacification, the tranquility of all sufferings.
The analysis (*viggaha*) is "they exist. The connection is "all the suffering of the cycle of existence" (*vaṭṭadukkha*). "Of that" refers to the Noble Path.
"And while occurring" means while proceeding by way of the persistence of the continuity (*santati*).
"Great suffering of fever" means great suffering of fever due to the occurrence of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. [This leads to] the non-arising of Nibbāna.

Because it is by its very nature a state of non-arising (*dhammatā*), there is no condition for its arising; likewise, because it is by its very nature a state of non-occurrence, there is no condition for its occurrence.
However, since it is something to be reached, there is a condition for reaching it; thus he said, "the mere trace of the formative activity of the conditions that bring about [realization].
The conditions that bring about [realization] are the Noble Path and its own conditions.
The connection is with "the mass of suffering known as existence and non-existence. "That very same" refers to that very mass of suffering.
"Successive giving" (*anuppadāna*) means it is given again and again. "The sense of bestowing" (*niyyātanaṭṭho*) means the sense of causing one to accept, saying, "Come, take it.
"From that" means from the suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*). "Of the means of liberation" refers to the means of liberation such as generosity, virtue, renunciation, and so forth.
“By way of deliverance through escape” means by way of deliverance known as escape (*nissaraṇa*). It is the sense of the non-existence of the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṅkhāra-dukkha*).

By the phrase “by way of the abandoning of delusion,” he shows that here, from this point onward, what is called “seeing” with respect to the four truths is precisely the attainment of non-delusion and the attainment of light. Therefore, he says: “the sense of penetration.”
A slave to craving is one who is a slave to craving (*taṇhādāsa*). The state of being a slave to craving is "slavery to craving" (*taṇhādāsabyaṃ*).
Independence from the power of others by way of liberation is called "the state of a free man" (*bhujissabhāva*).

One does not transcend slavery to craving through mundane paths. Filling the domain of craving, they produce a result that falls within the sphere of craving. This Noble Path alone [ensures] the absence of craving as an object.
Established [in this state], one transcends the servitude of craving. The intention is that, by shattering the power of craving, one generates a result that is outside the domain of craving.
“For the sake of liberation from suffering” means for the purpose of being freed from suffering. “For the increase of suffering” means for the purpose of increasing suffering.
The rest here is easily understood. Regarding the phrase “become destruction, fading away, and cessation,” it refers to the fading away (*virajjana*) of the defiled phenomena (*kilesadhamma*).
“Departing” means disappearance; it is dispassion (*virāga*). “Unwholesome terms” means terms for what is harmful, terms for fear and danger.
Regarding the phrase “by way of the division of the six doors and the six objects”: the six doors have mental phenomena (*dhamma*) as their object.
If this were so, one might say that it should not be called “the six objects,” because the object of mental phenomena has already been taken separately. [To this we reply: It should not be so stated.
Why? It is said, beginning with “And here,” in order to show that there is the existence of other objects of consciousness apart from the six doors.
The same method applies to the subsequent passages such as “and here too.
The Elucidation of the Compendium of All Categories is finished.
The *Anudīpanā* (Sub-commentary) to the *Dīpanī* on the Compendium of Categories (*Samuccayasaṅgaha*) is finished.
8. *Anudīpanā* on the Compendium of Relations (*Paccayasaṅgaha*) 166.
"In whatever ways" and "how"—their classification is that [classification]. And this exposition is an exposition by "single-remainder" (*ekasesa*).
In order to show that this is a partial exposition (*vicchālopaniddeso*), he said "of them" (*tesaṃ*) and so forth.
It does not coincide. For in the verse, the three meanings indicated by the three words beginning with *yesaṃ* are possible as the meanings of the word *ta-*;
and because the meanings of the word *ta-* must be stated by completing them in the connection (*anusandhi*). [The phrase] "arises well" (*samuppajjati*) has been made fully complete.

It arises; it manifests. “Inseparably” means having become inseparable. “With co-nascent phenomena” refers to the arising of volitional formations and so forth together with their co-nascent phenomena, as in such passages as “with ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]” and so on.
“By way of aggregates” means by way of pure aggregates of phenomena. “General characteristic” means a common characteristic. “The meaning” means...

“Conditionality by way of this” (*idappaccayatā*) is the meaning of the word. When it is said, “This meaning is rejected,” the sense of the abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*), namely “arising” (*samuppāda*)—meaning “the act of arising together”—is rejected.
“This very [meaning]” refers precisely to this sense of the abstract noun. The construction is: “old age and death come to be.
“Whether there is an arising of Tathāgatas” means whether there is the appearance of Perfectly Enlightened Ones. “Or whether there is no arising” means...

"Or rather, it is non-arising when there is existence. "The element remains established": when birth exists, the inherent nature (*pavatti-sabhāva*) of aging and death remains established in the world.

But what is that element? He says: "the stability of phenomena," and so forth. Therein, "stability of phenomena" (*dhammaṭṭhitatā*) means the stability of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) uncreated by anyone.
"Regularity of phenomena" (*dhammaniyāmatā*) means the regularity of intrinsic nature. "Suchness therein" (*tatra tathatā*)...

In that universal characteristic (sāmaññalakkhaṇa), there is the suchness (tathatā) of conditioned phenomena. This shows that the universal characteristic itself is what is called dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), and not the causal factors beginning with ignorance (avijjā).
Why? Because by those words, only the mere fact of the fixed nature of phenomena (dhammaniyāmatāmatta) is shown;
the actual nature of the phenomena beginning with ignorance is not shown. [The phrase used is] "the mere fact of the fixed nature of phenomena."

And it is precisely the aforementioned general characteristic that is being stated here. If one were to accept it as a noun denoting an abstract state (*bhāvasādhana*), then what is called a "denotation of an abstract state" would be devoid of an agent (*kattā*).
And when there is an absence of an agent, how can there be a shared agency (*samānakattukatā*) with respect to an action?
And if shared agency is not obtained, how could there be the possibility of the suffix *-tvā* [indicating] a prior time? This...
For one who maintains that [the term *paṭiccasamuppāda*] is a noun denoting a state (*bhāvasādhana*), there is a contradiction with the logic of the grammatical expression.
Anticipating this objection, he says: "But here... and so forth. For the Blessed One has stated: "O Ānanda, dependent origination is deep and appears deep.
Now, if it were a noun denoting a state, then "arising"—being merely an action—would not be a distinct, single dharma; how then could it be "deep"?
"Could it be?"—this constitutes a contradiction for one who maintains that [the term] is a noun denoting a state (*bhāvasādhana*). Avoiding that [contradiction], he says:
"And among conditioned phenomena," and so forth. Furthermore, what is called the characteristic of the conditioned is even more profound than the conditioned phenomenon itself.
For instance, that which is called "mind" is a conditioned phenomenon; yet it is well known to beings that "there indeed exists such a thing as mind."
However, its impermanence—the characteristic of the conditioned—is not apparent; it is well-concealed by the continuity [of the stream].
Likewise, that which is called feeling—whether pleasant or painful—is a conditioned phenomenon. And that [feeling] is apparent to beings as "I have this feeling.
However, its impermanence—the characteristic of the conditioned—is not apparent.
It is well concealed by continuity. The same applies to the remaining mental phenomena (*nāmadhamma*) and material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*).

Therefore, among the seven purifications, having first accomplished the knowledge of purification of view, which is defined as the discernment of conditioned phenomena, and the knowledge of purification by overcoming doubt, which is defined as the discernment of conditions such as ignorance, one subsequently [accomplishes] the tenfold...
The knowledges consisting in the contemplation of the characteristics of the conditioned must be accomplished. And just as impermanence—

the characteristic of the conditioned— is profound in relation to conditioned phenomena, so too this characteristic of the conditioned known as dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) should be understood as profound in relation to conditioned phenomena.

Regarding the phrase “the state of being dependent on that state” (*tabbhāvabhāvībhāvo*): here, *bhāvo* means that which exists or is found. That respective state, such as ignorance and so forth, is *tabbhāvo*.
Those things which by their nature exist or arise when that state is present are *tabbhāvabhāvino*; these are the formations (*saṅkhārā*) and so forth. *Bhāvo* means the cause of arising.
Demonstrating the meaning of “the state of those things dependent on that state,” he says “in each respective [state],” and so forth.
Furthermore, "existence" (*bhāva*) refers to the state of being present. The "existence of that" (*tabbhāva*) is the existence of each respective conditioning phenomenon.

Since phenomena arise and come into being through their own nature when that existence is present, they are called "those that exist when that exists" (*tabbhāvabhāvino*). It is also appropriate to speak of "the existence of those.

In such contexts as "the causal relation, the object relation, etc.," the phrase "the fixed order of the occurrence of conditions such as the cause" refers to the cause-condition (*hetu-paccaya*), the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*), and so forth.

The words "cause" (hetu), "object" (ārammaṇa), and so forth, indicate the specific particular powers of conditionality belonging to phenomena such as greed and so on, as well as visible forms and objects and so on.
And that respective particular power of conditionality for each of them constitutes a distinct determination of phenomena;

thus, [the text] excludes any other determination of the powers of conditions such as "cause" and so forth. The phrase "in this way and that way" refers to [the meanings of] root, basis, domain, object, and so on.
"In each respective mode of conditionality. For "he is so called" is the connection [of the sentence].

"Without remaining merely as an extraction of the conditioning phenomena"—the intention is that he does not perform a mere extraction by way of the designations for the phenomena that serve as conditions.
"Having struck" (*āhacca*) means having struck [them] and brought about the specific power of each respective condition; thus he said, "having brought them to their culmination."

For the specific power of conditions (*paccaya-satti-visesa*) is indeed the "culmination" (*matthaka*), because there is no further function to be described beyond that in the elucidation of cause and fruit.
"Not retreating" (*anosakkamānā*) means not turning back. "By this" (*etāya*) means by the power of conditions.
While the teachers are elaborating [on this], for this reason the fruit comes from the future side to the present side, depending precisely upon this.
"Condition" (*paccaya*) means that which causes something to manifest. It is both the cause of arising and the cause of occurrence.
Among these, the cause of arising is the generative condition (*janaka-paccaya*), while the cause of occurrence is the supporting condition (*upatthambhaka-paccaya*).

"By this" refers to the reason. Regarding the phrase "bodily, vocal, and mental action" (*kāya-vacī-manokamma*): here, "action" (*kamma*) denotes activity—namely, bodily activities such as walking, standing, sitting, and lying down; as well as speech and conversation.
“Vocal activity” refers to speaking, reciting, singing, and so forth.
“Mental activity” refers to cognizing, reflecting, investigating, and so forth. “They form” (*abhisaṅkharonti*) means they produce.

“By these” means by these mundane wholesome and unwholesome volitional states (*cetanā-dhammā*). Furthermore, beings form (*saṅkharonti*) by means of these, thus they are called formations (*saṅkhārā*). “They form” means...
"What do they construct? They construct a personal existence (*attabhāva*). They construct becoming and non-becoming.
They construct benefit or harm pertaining to the present life; they construct benefit or harm pertaining to future lives," and so forth.
"They construct the eye; they construct the ear," and so forth. "They construct seeing; they construct hearing..."
It is indeed appropriate to say "they construct" (saṅkharonti), and so forth. "It cognizes" (vijānāti) means it knows in various ways;

it knows by way of what is real (bhūta) and it knows by way of what is unreal (abhūta). "It inclines" (namati) means it inclines toward its range and object. "It is affected" (ruppati) means it is disturbed or agitated.
"It touches" (phusati) means it contacts. "It feels" (vedayati) means it makes known; that is, by way of clinging to this or that object.
It is also appropriate to call it *taṇhā* (craving) because it "cleanses thoroughly," "binds," and "does not allow one to be released.

"Grasps" (*upādiyatī*) means it takes hold firmly; thus he said, "it grasps with a grip that does not let go. "Becoming" (*bhava*) refers to existence. It is "existence by way of rebirth" (*upapattibhava*).

That by which things come into being is "existence"; this refers to "existence as kamma" (*kammabhava*). "Arising" (*janana*) is the manifestation of something new. "Decaying" (*jīraṇa*) [refers to the state] from its newly arisen condition...
“Hāyanaṃ” means wasting away. “Socanaṃ” means the tormenting of the mind. “Paridevanaṃ” means weeping. “Dukkhaṃ” means bodily affliction.
“Domanassaṃ” means mental affliction. “Visīdanaṃ” means the sinking of the mind, becoming deformed through intense mental exhaustion;
it is the wearing away of one’s fortitude and strength, from which the irregular occurrence of inhalation and exhalation arises.
"At that very moment, there is a complete cessation" means: "By some kind of happiness" means by some peace-happiness liberated from the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*).
"Concealing suffering" means concealing the state of suffering of the phenomena belonging to the three planes (*tebhūmika*), which are themselves suffering in the sense of being fearful.
“Concealer of the origin” means that craving conceals the state of being the origin of suffering.
“Concealer of cessation” means that craving conceals the state of being the cessation of suffering, which is precisely the cessation of craving.

“Concealer of the path” means that craving conceals the state of being the path to the cessation of suffering, which is precisely the Eightfold Path. “The past” refers to the succession of existences in the time gone by.
The "future limit" refers to the succession of existences in the future. Both of these together are called the "past and future limits.

"One who conceals dependent origination" means one who conceals the dependent origination of the aggregates within the present existence. "According to the method of the Suttantas" means that even in the Abhidhamma, there is what is known as the *suttanta-bhājanīya* (the Suttanta-style analysis) found in the *Vibhaṅga*;
it is by way of that *suttanta-bhājanīya* method [that this is explained]. [This refers to] wholesome states accompanied by taints (*sāsavā kusalā*).
The construction is: "Wholesome volition is called formations (*saṅkhārā*). "By the method of the Abhidhamma" means by the method of the *Abhidhammabhājanīya* in the *Vibhaṅga*.
In the reading of the Commentary: ignorance does not obtain the status of a decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for functional states (*kiriya-dhammā*).
The construction is: wholesome roots do not obtain the status of a decisive support condition for functional states. Functional...
It is said that mental phenomena (*dhammā*) do not receive the condition of decisive support (*upanissaya-paccaya*) from ignorance (*avijjā*) nor from wholesome roots (*kusala-mūla*).
"The mode of conditions" (*paccayākāra*) refers to dependent origination (*paṭicca-samuppāda*). "From the fading away of ignorance" (*avijjā-virāgā*) means from the disappearance of ignorance.

Of those same functional phenomena (*kiriya-dhammā*): in the case of consciousness and so forth, there is functional consciousness (*kiriya-viññāṇa*), functional mind (*kiriya-nāma*), the functional mind-base (*kiriya-manāyatana*), and functional contact (*kiriyaphassa*).
Because functional feeling exists, it is said: "The method of seeking [is applied] to consciousness and so forth as well. Regarding the phrase "wholesome, associated with wholesome result":
this refers to that which is associated with wholesome consciousness, unwholesome consciousness, and resultant consciousness.
"That is not applicable" means that for the triad of aggregates co-arising with the active resultant consciousness, that [method] does not apply to what is born simultaneously with them.
And because the mind-born matter (*cittaja-rūpa*) remains [unaccounted for], that [definition] is incomplete; this is the meaning.
For there, in the section on consciousness (*viññāṇa*), it is stated that the thirty-two types of resultant consciousness (*vipāka-citta*) in their mode of occurrence are called "consciousness.

This being so, in the sections on name (*nāma*) and form (*rūpa*) as well, both [mental factors and consciousness] must indeed be included in their mode of occurrence, accompanied by the consciousness that occurs therein. "That such-and-such consciousness..."
“Associated” means associated with the consciousness of rebirth-linking and the consciousness of the course of existence.
“Craving and clinging are manifest” means that the six types of craving are manifest by way of craving for forms, craving for sounds, and so forth;

and the four types of clinging are manifest by way of clinging to sense pleasures and so forth. “Mere characteristics” means they are merely the signs that mark the conditioned nature of conditioned phenomena.

“By the destruction of relatives, etc. means by the loss of relatives and so forth. “On account of the destruction of relatives, etc. means for the sake of the cause of the loss of relatives and so forth.
“In the suffering of the aggregates” refers to the truth of suffering consisting of the five aggregates. The occurrence of the aggregates is called the path, which is precisely the origin of craving.
The cessation of the aggregates is called the path, which is the Noble Eightfold Path. “Becoming the origin of the aggregates” refers to the arising of the aggregates.
“Acting as a cause. “For those enveloped by ignorance” means for those obstructed and shut in by ignorance.

“For those who have not abandoned the longing for existence” means for those whose aspiration for existence has not been abandoned by the Path; what is meant is: for those whose craving for existence (*bhava-taṇhā*) has not been abandoned.
“Obstruction” means an impediment. “For those that have arisen” means for those that have increased. “Support” means a basis. Specifically, pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*)...

It is said that it is a condition for craving; thus, "similar to pleasant feeling," and so forth, was stated. Furthermore, the fact that mental grief (*domanassa*) is a condition for that [craving] will become clear later in the section on the craving for further search (*pariyeṭṭhitanhā*).
Even neutral feeling (*upekkhā-vedanā*) occupies the place of pleasure for one who is oppressed by suffering;
thus, one longs for it as if it were pleasure. Having practiced and cultivated [it]. "Craving..."
“Evā” means craving for sensual pleasures (kāmataṇhā) alone. “And in oneself” (attani ca) means “and in views” (diṭṭhiyaṃ); this is the intended meaning.

“In one’s own objects” (attano ārammaṇesu) refers to the objects grasped by views, such as a self, a soul, the world, and so forth. “Consisting of relishing, acceptance, and approval” (assādana-khamana-rocanabhūtāya) means that it is a state of attachment, satisfaction, and longing, characterized by the perception of “mine” in what is good.
“Of what is to be clung to” (upādānīyassa) means of that which is to be firmly grasped.
“Of his own welfare” means of one’s own welfare, beginning with oneself. In the verse, “becoming” (*bhava*) means increasing; “decline” (*parābhava*) means perishing.

“Phenomena that endure through time” (*addhānavante dhamme*) refers to conditioned phenomena belonging to the three periods of time. The phrase “having made them not fall away” is an ellipsis (*pāṭhaseso*). Just as...

In the phrase "derived form" (*upādārūpa*), the word *upāda* is understood from the term *upādāna*. It is not the word *upa* with the prefix *na*. Otherwise, the term *upādāna* would not be established.
The same applies to the words *addhā*, *addhāna*, and *padesu*. Therefore he said: "the term *addhāna* is not established.

They are called *saṅkhepā* because twenty modes are condensed within them; they are the *saṅgahā*. "The phenomena of the round" (*vaṭṭadhammā*) refers to the phenomena such as volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*).
“In these”: in these [states of] ignorance and craving. To the question “How do they stand?”, he says:

“Because their existence is dependent upon them. “Bases” means well-established locations. “Origins” means the root causes and primary conditions for the continuous succession of the phenomena of the round of existence (*saṃsāra*).
In this regard, the reason must also be taught; otherwise, there would be room for the views of creation by a Supreme Lord (*issaranimmāna*) or the view of causelessness (*ahetuka*).
“*Siyā*” means that the fruit must also be taught; otherwise, there would be occasion for the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).
“*Addhuno*” means of long time. “*Nivatteti*” means he cuts off. “*Ahetū apaccayā sattā pavattantī*” means these beings proceed without a prior cause and without a prior condition.
“*Na hoti avijjādīhi sādhetabbo*” [refers to] the succession of existences (*bhavaparamparā*).
The intention is that for one who runs about as if permanent, there is no function to be performed by ignorance and the other [defilements].

The phrase "they simply do not arise for some" means they simply do not arise for non-returners (anāgāmin) and arahants. The construction is that the mention of sorrow and so forth is for the purpose of demonstrating the great disadvantage [of the defilements].
"Of those" refers to other conditions. "Having obtained" means, in terms of its sense, having acquired.

Regarding the phrase “by way of the characteristic of being inseparable from that”: here, the analysis is *tena tena paccayena avinābhāvīnaṃ bhāvo, so eva lakkhaṇaṃ*—the state of those things which are inseparable from their respective conditions;
that itself is the characteristic. “Also elsewhere” means in the subsequent passages such as “by way of the inclusion of craving, clinging, and becoming,” and so forth.

“At the beginning” refers to the beginning of the *Vibhāvanī* text. “By way of the commonality of the state of defilement” means because of the equality [of all factors] through their state of being defilements.
“Similarity of existence”: by means of the phenomena to be characterized, such as consciousness and so forth. “Of the first with the second”:
this should be construed as “there is one connection between the second compendium together with the first compendium,” and so on. “By way of the terminology familiar in the world”:
in the world, the phenomena of defilements and the phenomena of karma are well-known as causes; however, the phenomena of fruition are what bear fruit.
It is well-known. Thus, according to common worldly usage.

However, here, whether they be defiled phenomena (*kilesadhamma*), kamma-phenomena (*kammadhamma*), or fruition-phenomena (*vipākadhamma*), whatever stands on the side of conditions may indeed be called a "cause" (*hetu*). Showing that whatever stands on the side of the conditionally arisen is a "fruit" (*phala*), he said:
"The application of the terms 'cause' and 'fruit'," and so forth. In the text of the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*): "Of one who prepares... (*sajjantassa*)...
For one who possesses consciousness. From the beginning, starting with “Volitional formations are called *āyūhana*,” they are called *samuccaya-saṅkhāra*.
“*Dakkhiṇaṃ*” refers to the object of giving, or the water for the offering (*dakkhiṇodaka*). “And here” means in this third pentad.
“In the manner stated” means precisely in the manner stated in the first pentad. In the reading of the *Vibhāvanī*: “For future rebirth.”
The statement, “Volition as a condition is called *bhava*,” is stated in the recitation text (*uddesapāḷi*) according to the reading as it was seen [in the source].
Likewise, the statement, “In the previous existence (*purimakammabhava*), volition as a condition for rebirth-linking here is called *saṅkhāra*,” is also stated in that way.

However, since in this context the two types of *saṅkhāra* and *kammabhava* were already included within the two sets of five causes mentioned previously, they are not mentioned again in the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
In the manner already stated, the distinction between the two—volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) and kamma-existence (*kammabhava*)—is appropriate. Therefore he said:
"That is not applicable here. "Because it has already been included" means because it was already included previously. "This" refers to the statement in the *Vibhāvanī*.

"For the purpose of protecting the classification of phenomena" means that since rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*) is also analyzed within the section on existence (*bhavapada*) in the *Vibhaṅga*, [this is done] for the sake of preserving such an analysis of phenomena.

For the sake of protection. Although the existence at rebirth (*upapattibhava*) is not other than the fivefold fruit, it is described as "a portion of existence termed existence at rebirth" by treating it as if it were something else.

And that which is called existence at rebirth, because it is produced by present causes, is included within the fourth fivefold fruit itself. Therefore, by that term "existence at rebirth," it is precisely the fourth pentad [that is meant].
"Taken" is appropriate. Otherwise, if it were stated that "the two sets of five fruits constitute the resultant cycle," it would already be established [that the remaining ones do not].
This being the case, it should be understood that in the phrase "and the remainder," only the second set of five fruits remains.
[The statement] "Ignorance is delusion, and that is an unwholesome root," and so forth, is because it appears under the name "root" in the *Mūlayamaka* of the Abhidhamma.
It has been stated. Regarding the two wheels of existence (*bhavacakra*), ignorance (*avijjā*) is the beginning in the former wheel, while craving (*taṇhā*) is [the beginning] in the latter wheel.
Since it is appropriate to call the "beginning" by such terms as "root" (*mūla*) or "head" (*sīsa*), the phrase "or else" (*athavā*) and so forth was stated to show this synonymy.
In the phrase "in the requisites for coming" (*āgamanasambhāresu*), it refers to the requisites for coming from a past existence to this present existence; [it is] craving alone.
The construction is: "stated with ignorance as the head. Regarding the phrase "in between them," it means in between ignorance (*avijjā*) and volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*).
Why was it said that there is no room for craving (*taṇhā*)? Is it not the case that when ignorance exists, craving necessarily arises?

Moreover, that [craving] is a powerful condition for volitional formations. Therefore, [one might argue that] with ignorance as condition there is craving, and with craving as condition there are volitional formations.
"It might be said" refers to that [objection]. To resolve it, the passage beginning with "For this... was stated.

What is called "dependent origination in reverse order" (paṭiloma-paṭiccasamuppāda) is dependent origination proceeding in the manner: "With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations.
The statement "It might not be said: 'From the delusion of old age and death... and so forth, is connected to the forward order of dependent origination (anuloma-paṭiccasamuppāda).

It is stated having been made into a statement: “Of those things that establish the roots of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭamūla*)” means of those factors reckoned as ignorance and craving, which are the roots of the cycle and which impel [beings] toward the subsequent states such as future existence.

“Those too” refers even to sorrow and so forth, which are suffering-states (*dukkhadhamma*). “Arisen from the taints (*āsava*)” means produced or born from the taints. “Of them” refers to those suffering-states, sorrow and so forth.
“Grasping at the factor of aging-and-death”: this refers to the inclusion within the twelve factors of the factor of aging-and-death.
“Increases” means it grows intensely. “From the arising of the taints” means from the origination of the taints. “The arising of ignorance” means the origination of ignorance.
In the phrase “volitional formations conditioned by ignorance,” the word *iti* has the sense of “etcetera. “Of one touched by various calamities” refers to [calamities] such as the loss of relatives.
"Of one who is struck by various calamities and afflicted. "From which" (*yato*) means for what reason; it is for the reason of increasing ignorance and craving.

"The round" (*vaṭṭa*) refers to the wheel of existence beginning with volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*). "Delusion" (*sammoha*) is the state of being bewildered. "Seeking" (*pariyesana*) is the act of searching.
"It ripens" (*vipaccati*), thus it is "result" (*vipāka*). Result itself is "ripening" (*vepakka*). That which has delusion as its ripening is "having delusion as its ripening" (*sammohavepakka*).
The phrase "and likewise ripened through seeking" (pariyeṭṭhivepakkañca) shows this meaning by means of the words "both of these" (tadubhayaṃ), and so forth.
The construction is as follows: because both of these are its result (vipāka), suffering is called "ripened through delusion" (sammohavepakka) and "ripened through seeking" (pariyeṭṭhivepakka).
Furthermore, it is "ripened through delusion" (sammohavepakka) in the sense that it ripens—that is, generates—delusion. Likewise for "ripened through seeking" (pariyeṭṭhivepakka).
It is appropriate [to say this]. "Kicchaṃ" means having fallen into hardship and suffering. "Miyyati" means dies. "Ca vati" means transmigrates.
"Upapajjati" means enters another state of existence. "Atha ca pana" means even though he has become such [as described].
"Jarāmaraṇassa" is connected with "of this suffering known as aging-and-death. "Nissaraṇaṃ" means the exit. "Nappajānāti" means does not understand.
“This world does not understand. By “coming” (*āgati*) is meant the arrival by way of the arising of rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhi-viññāṇa*) in this present existence.

And by “going” (*gati*) is meant the departure by way of the manifestation of birth in a future existence. That which has a beginning (*ādi*) consisting of what is reckoned as the past limit is called “having a beginning” (*ādimanta*).
Not having a beginning is “beginningless” (*anādimanta*). “Of the process of the round” (*vaṭṭappavattassa*) refers to that which is reckoned as the threefold round.
“Of that which proceeds as a continuous bond. Since all the causes of birth have already been stated when birth itself was explained, it is said, “or of birth itself.
“Thus indeed” means *iti evam*. Therein, the connection is: “the Great Sage established [the sequence] by way of the formula beginning with ‘with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise.
According to the Teacher’s own system, however, “thus indeed” refers to the sequence beginning with “old age and death, delusion, and so forth.”
The connection is that [ignorance] is beginningless. Here too, having taken up that very same connection, he applies it thus: "In this way they bind... repeatedly binding.

Ignorance was mentioned at the beginning; therefore, the objection is raised: "How can it, being itself without cause or condition, serve as the primary condition for the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*)?
He resolves this with the words "of the cycle," and so forth. In the discourse on the cycle...
Because it is like the head [of a snake], there is no beginning to the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*). However, its progression and cessation do exist.
For those who know this, in order to explain these two, the discourse on dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), which is the discourse on the cycle of existence, must certainly be taught.
And when teaching it, among the phenomena of the cycle, one must determine the function of which phenomenon serves for the purpose of setting the cycle in motion.

It must be understood that one thing becomes more prominent. At that time, by way of its function, one particular dhamma should be made the root and the head for the exposition of the round of existence (*vaṭṭakathā*).
This is what is called the "head" of the exposition of the round. In this context, ignorance (*avijjā*) is delusion (*moha*);
it is the act of being deluded, and its function is to produce blindness. It is not the eye of wisdom (*paññā*).
There is no other primary function for the continuation of the round (*vaṭṭa*) comparable to that which causes blindness.

Therefore, because it possesses the most preeminent function here, ignorance (*avijjā*) alone is the head of the discourse on the round. Thus, because it is the head of the discourse on the round, it is mentioned at the beginning.
By this, its "beginningless nature" is shown; thus, the state of being without beginning is demonstrated.
Thus. The meaning is: it was not not shown. Thus, this collection of meanings is established through direct perception (*paccakkha*). “Here” means in this present existence.
“Of that” refers to ignorance (*avijjā*) included within past existences.

“Precisely by another ignorance” means precisely by another ignorance established even prior to the past existence, in a previous birth. “Of that too” refers to the ignorance in an even more distant previous existence.
“Selfhood” (*attabhāva*) refers to a prior selfhood.

“Because it is the primary condition” means that, according to the method explained previously, because its function is to produce blindness, it becomes the primary condition for the occurrence of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭappavatti*). Thus, “because it is the primary condition.
“‘Of this and that’—no conclusion at all would be discerned” means that a condition must be stated for that [prior] condition; and for that too...
If one were to state the condition for each condition, no conclusion would ever be reached even in a hundred years or a thousand years.
"It has indeed been stated" means that the condition for ignorance has already been stated. "'The five hindrances must be declared as its nutriment'":
it should be declared that the five hindrance-states are the nutriment for ignorance. In this context, "nutriment" refers to a powerful condition.
The exposition of the method of Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda) is concluded. 167.
In the method of the *Paṭṭhāna*: regarding the statement, “It is both a cause (*hetu*) and a condition (*paccaya*”), herein greed (*lobha*) is a cause because it belongs to the class of causes.

It is also a condition for another state by way of being an object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*), an immediate-condition (*anantara-paccaya*), and so forth; thus, since the meaning [of being both] is possible, it is called a “cause.”

He praises it as "having been a cause, [it is] a condition. Even though it has been praised thus, since the meaning "being a cause, it is a condition" implies that it is both a cause and a condition, and that very same meaning is possible, he praises it again as "a condition by way of being a cause.
Here it might be asked: in the phrase "it is a cause and it is a condition," these two words have a common substratum (*tulyādhikaraṇa*) because they refer to one and the same thing.
It exists. Regarding the phrase "a condition by way of being a cause" (*hetubhāvena paccayo*), however, these two terms do not share a common substratum (*tulyādhikaraṇa*).

For the first term emphasizes the state of the phenomenon (*dhamma-bhāva-pradhāna*), while the latter emphasizes the phenomenon itself (*dhamma-pradhāna*). This being the case, it is not appropriate to describe a sentence with a common substratum as having different substrata.
Is it not inappropriate? It is not inappropriate, for this is merely a matter of primary and figurative usage (*mukhya-upacāra-mātra*).
Because they have different meanings. For the latter statement is the primary (mukhya) expression, while the former statement is a figurative (upacāra) expression.

And in a figurative expression, a figurative meaning is appropriate; whereas in a primary expression, a primary meaning [is appropriate]. "As stated above" means exactly as it was stated in the *Pakiṇṇakasaṅgaha*.

It is called a cause (*hetu*) because things proceed (*hinonti*) therein, or because things proceed by means of it. In that context, "they proceed" (*hinonti*) means they are well-established (*suṭṭhu patiṭṭhahanti*).
"To what do they become established? he says: "Co-nascent phenomena. And "how do they become well-established? he says:
"By way of attaining growth, increase, and abundance. Why are they well-established?

To show that it is because the place of establishment, or the cause of establishment, is endowed with strength and power, he says: "By [the mind] which falls firmly upon the object and is endowed with strength and power."

This has been stated. Furthermore, this is a qualification of the cause (*hetu*). Here, one should also connect the word "dhamma" with "possessing strength and power" (*thāmabalasampanna*) when it is firmly established upon the object (*ārammaṇa*).

And the connection is that "the benefactor" (*upakāraka*) is indeed "perception" (*upaladdhi*). Regarding the phrase "by whatever intrinsic nature" (*yādisenasabhāvena*), it means by the intrinsic nature of being a cause and so forth.
Why was it said, "it is indeed perception"? Is it not the case that the word "benefactor" denotes either an agent (*kattāra*) or a causal agent (*kāretāra*)?

He speaks by way of mere conventional usage (*vohāramatta*). However, in order to show that from the perspective of ultimate reality (*dhammata*) there is neither an agent nor one who causes action, he says:

"For [there is no agent] among phenomena of intrinsic nature," and so forth. If, from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is neither an agent nor one who causes action, why is it called "the benefactor"?
To this he replies: "But in the case of such apprehension," and so forth.

Regarding the object condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*): "Hanging down" means hanging down by way of making an object. "By way of being an object" means by way of being a sphere of activity or a field of experience.
Regarding the predominance condition (*adhipatipaccaya*): "Treated as important" means treated as important either by way of relishing and delighting, or by way of confidence and clarity.
"Like slaves to a master" means like slaves who, under a master, act according to his will.
The co-nascent predominance (sahajātādhipati), however, was explained below in the *Samuccaya-saṅgaha*, and thus it is not mentioned here.
Regarding the two types of proximity-condition (*anantara-paccaya*): "Interval" (*antara*) means a gap or opening. "Continuity" (*santāna*) means the continuity of consciousness (*cittasantāna*).

"By way of binding the continuity" (*santānānubandhavasena*) means by way of repeatedly binding the continuity of consciousness. The connection is with the word "arising" (*uppādana*). "Of another state" (*dhammantarassa*)...
"Of another mental state" means of another dhamma. "Antecedent conditionality" means the function of the antecedent condition;

that is, any other dhamma whatsoever. "Of those occurring in the prior and posterior portions" means of those occurring in the prior portion and the posterior portion of cessation and the attainment of non-perception.
"Of the arising of consciousnesses" refers to the period prior to cessation.

[It is the condition] for wholesome and functional (kiriya) consciousness-moments of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; for the consciousness-moments of the fruit of non-returning and the fruit of arahantship occurring subsequently;
for the consciousness-moments of death in the sense-sphere existence occurring prior to rebirth in the non-percipient realm;

and for the consciousness-moments of rebirth-linking in the sense-sphere existence occurring subsequently. But among these, how can there be "immediacy" (anantara)? [Because it applies] to the preceding portions of each pair.

The objection is that there is an interval between the final portions [of the preceding consciousness] and the mindless period, as well as an interval between that mindless period and the subsequent stream of material form.
To resolve this, it is said: "For it is not non-existent," and so forth. "Of those" refers to the two successive occurrences of consciousness.
It is said that material phenomena do not create an interval, whereas immaterial phenomena are characterized by their lack of interval, and so on.
There is the following interpretation: “The capacity for such occurrence” means the capacity to produce another dhamma immediately after itself, as if they were unified.
Regarding the co-nascent condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*):
“But those dhammas” refers to the dhammas that have arisen by way of conditions; “in itself” refers to the conditioning dhamma.
“Mutually supporting like a tripod”: just as three sticks erected on the ground leaning against one another support each other mutually.
“By the former”: by the former co-nascent condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*). “Mutual propping”: mutual support.
“Cook” means one who prepares food. “Mortar” means a pot for cooking rice. “Showers of rain” means showers of rain from clouds.
“Supporting condition” (upanissaya) means the supporting condition for the arising of food. “When these are absent” means when the showers of rain upon the rice fields are absent.

“In the sense of being a more powerful support” means in the sense of being a stronger supporting condition. Regarding the term “natural supporting condition” (pakatūpanissaya), here “natural” (pakata) means—

It has been well done. Therefore he said, “well done. The connection [of the sentence] should be understood as follows: the act of doing, the thorough production within one’s own continuum, and the thorough cultivation [of the practice] are to be seen.
“In the manner stated” means in the manner stated by the passage beginning with “when it has been done thus,” and so forth.
“Only those phenomena which are supporting conditions and object conditions” means only those phenomena that are *nissaya-paccaya* (supporting conditions) and *ārammaṇa-paccaya* (object conditions).

Regarding the phrase “distinguished merely by prior-arising” (*purejātatāmattavisiṭṭhā*), here the word “merely” (*matta*) indicates that there is no distinct power of prior-arising separate from the powers of support (*nissaya*) and object (*ārammaṇa*).
However, some maintain that there is indeed a distinct power of prior-arising. To show that position, he says, “by the Elder Ācariya Ānanda,” and so forth.
Herein, the five bases (*vatthu*) and the five objects (*ārammaṇa*) [are distinguished] because of their prior-arising.
Thus, by virtue of their great strength, the five sense-consciousnesses accomplish the functions of their bases and objects.

Likewise, the heart-base accomplishes its function for the mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element. One might say that this is a specific distinction of the power of prior arising (*purejāta-satti*).
That is true. However, standing here at the door of the pure mind, one sees such forms of hell-fire in the hells.

They exist. Now, even for those who think that such divine forms exist among the devas, or who think that such forms have arisen among them in the past, or who think that such forms will arise among them in the future, those forms become indistinguishable and serve as objective conditions for mental consciousness (*manoviññāṇa*). Among these, those born in the past...

Having sacrificed, then those presently existing present material phenomena are the object-predominance condition (*ārammaṇa-purejāta-paccaya*). The others are merely the object condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*).
And herein, there is no distinction between the present material phenomena that are "pre-arisen" by virtue of their being pre-arisen;

nor is it the case that they do not function as the pre-arisen condition. If the pre-arisen condition were merely a specific power of pre-arising distinct [from the object], [then this distinction would be necessary].
One might say: "Those [objects] would not be called 'pre-nascence conditions' (purejāta-paccaya). Why? Because of the absence of such a specific distinction. But they do not fail to be so. Why?
Because of the presence of the specific distinction consisting merely in being pre-nascent. Here they might say:
"However, in the case of the five sense-doors, a distinct specific power of pre-nascence is seen according to the method previously stated. Granted it is seen; yet, that...
It is simply a specific capacity for support among the various conditions of support (nissaya), object (ārammaṇa), and so forth; it is simply a specific capacity as an object.

Furthermore, the statement that there is no such thing as a distinct, separate capacity for "prenascence" (purejāta) was made with reference to the absence of such a distinction in the aforementioned pure mental door (manodvāra). There is indeed no such thing as a distinct, separate capacity for prenascence.
The statement "it exists" (*atthi*) is said with reference to the existence of that specific [condition] within the five doors; one may accept whichever [interpretation] is preferred.

Regarding the postnascent condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya*): the construction is as follows—"like young saplings"—meaning it is like water poured later that assists by way of providing support, having caused the young saplings to reach a state of growth and flourishing. [He] poured food...
“Satī” means craving for nutriment (*āhārāsā*). It is hunger, thirst, and craving. The analysis of the compound is: volition associated with that [craving]. Furthermore, the connection is:
that volition which is craving for nutriment is indeed supported [by it].

“This is the meaning” refers to the meaning stated by the words beginning with “by being well-evident. All this investigation serves to exclude the possibility that the simile of the vulture is merely a simple comparison.
“They cultivate that condition-dhamma as the conditionally arisen dhammas”—this is *āsevana* (cultivation).
By this, it is shown that it is called *āsevana* because it must be cultivated intensely by means of the conditionally arisen dhammas. “That” (*taṃ*) refers to each preceding condition-dhamma.
“They resort to” (*bhajanti*) means they approach. Who resorts to them? He says: “dhammas arising one after another.”
“Phenomena” (*dhammā*) refers here to the mental states and mental factors that have arisen immediately prior. And how do they associate with it? To this he says:

“They proceed as if serving it well, as if associating with it. By the word “as if” (*viya*), he shows that in the world some people are as if serving some other person for some purpose. How is it that they are as if serving well?
He said, “Of that preceding,” and so forth. The meaning is: “of the immediately preceding arising of consciousness.

“The completely full mode” means a mode complete with all the qualities of impulsion—such as cognizing, touching, and so on—along with their speed and force, and including both the faulty and the faultless.
“It serves” means it is as if it were directing him, saying, “Serve me well! Therefore he said: “Of itself...”
“Vāsaṃ,” and so forth. Therein, “vāsaṃ” means dwelling. “Causes to grasp well” means he gives it completely; this is what is said.
By this, just as in the world one person gives others whatever they desire, those who receive it from such a giver simply associate with him;
there is no need for him to direct them, saying, “Associate with me. Even so here, the very act of giving a good dwelling is itself the causing of association.
He indicates this by the word "name. By the phrase "or increases," he expresses the synonymous meaning that cultivation (*bhāvanā*) through repeated practice (*āsevanā*) is "increase" (*vaḍḍhanā*).
"Initial application" (*purimābhiyoga*) refers to the performance of tasks such as recitation from the very beginning, according to one's capacity and strength, for a fixed period of time.
For one who acts in this way, that work of mastery attains a state of greater proficiency with each successive stage.

“By way of repetition” means by way of increasing; it is connected with the word “benefactor. “Of those of the same class” means of those that are of the same class by virtue of being wholesome (kusala) and so forth.
The formation of the bodily factor is the function of bodily volition (kāyasañcetanā). The formation of the vocal factor is the function of vocal volition (vacīsañcetanā).
The formation of the mental factor is the function of mental volition (manosañcetanā). “By way of activity” refers to the functions of seeing, hearing, and so forth.
[It is so] because of the absence of the activity of preparation for the functions of going, standing, sitting, and so forth. “In the basis” means in the basis of the womb (*gabbhavatthu*).
The aforementioned function of volitional formation (*abhisaṅkharaṇakicca*) refers to the function of volitional formation of the body-factor, the speech-factor, and the mind-factor.

The connection [of the sentence] is: “generated by the momentum of that volitional formation” means the specific activity which has the function of depositing [the embryo], generated by the momentum of that volitional formation of the body-factor and so forth.
"In the continuum" means in the mental continuum (*cittasantāna*).
The connection is that "arising" (*pātubhāva*) is indeed the state of ripening.

The state of being tranquil and devoid of effort refers to the lack of exertion in the functions of forming bodily and vocal formations—as in the case of wholesome and unwholesome states—and in the function of ripening in the future.
It is the state of being peaceful. It is not by way of the state of being calmed regarding the defilements.

However, regarding the function of mental formation, there is merely the capacity for the associated mental factors to come together as one with respect to the objects as they appear, by means of the associated volition.
Beyond that, even the function of seeing a dream does not exist. "In a very gentle manner" (*mandamandākārena*) means in an exceedingly gentle manner (*atimandākārena*).

“Cognizing something” (*kiñcijjānana*) refers to a process-consciousness (*vīthicitta*) that cognizes even a slight object such as karma. “In its occurrence” (*tassa pavattiya*). “Immaterial” (*arūpino*) means possessing the characteristic of being immaterial;

what is meant is that they possess the characteristic of name (*nāma*). “Even while producing” (*janayantāpi*) means even while producing co-nascent phenomena (*sahajāta-dhammā*). “For the persistence of the continuum” (*santānaṭṭhitiyā*) means for the establishment of the continuity. Regarding the passage beginning with “But why here...”:
“The pair of faculties of existence” (*bhāvindriya-dvayaṃ*) refers to the pair consisting of the female faculty (*itthindriya*) and the male faculty (*purisindriya*). “Here” (*idha*).
Regarding this condition of the faculties (*indriya-paccaya*): why is it not included? The intention [of the opponent] is:

"Since it is the cause for the manifestation of feminine gender and so forth, it ought indeed to be included here. "Productive-ness" (*janakatta*) means the function of producing. The same applies to the remaining [functions].

"Even this triad does not exist" means that even the triad of functions beginning with productive-ness does not exist. Such being the case, how can it be the cause for the manifestation of gender and so forth?
He said, "But only," and so forth. "The pair" refers to the pair consisting of the female state and the male state.
It does not become what is called a "faculty" by way of being a condition for the faculties.

For just as a king, while building houses in his own kingdom, establishes the design of the houses, thinking, "Let them be built thus," and all the people build exactly like that and not otherwise; therein—
The king performs no task whatsoever regarding the building or the maintenance of the house; rather, it is the owners of the house or the builders who do so.
And when they do so, they act without exceeding the structure established by the king. It is in this way that this should be understood.
The connection is with the phrase "in the sense of approaching and meditating. The prefix *upa-* is like the word *upanissaya* (support).
The meaning [of the term] is "above. Regarding the word "above," he says "or in that" and so forth, by way of the increase of strength and power. "In that" refers to the object (*ārammaṇa*).

It has been stated [that this occurs] "in the sense of leading to a happy destination, an unhappy destination, or Nibbāna. That specific meaning does not exist among the indeterminate path-factors (*abyākata-magganga*).
This being the case, he asks how those [indeterminate factors] can function as a condition for the path, and thus he says "And here" and so forth. [This occurs] "by means of right vision" and so on.
“By right view, intention, and so forth. “Of them” means of those possessing right view. “Of those too” means even of those right views that are indeterminate (*abyākata*).
“In that very sense” means in the sense of the characteristic of right vision and so forth.

Alternatively, “in that very sense” means in the sense of leading to a happy destination and Nibbāna. This being the case, even resultant and functional states that possess roots are determinate (*byākata*) phenomena.
In that sense, they might be entirely similar to wholesome states. They would not, however, because of the deficiency of conditions.

Since resultant indeterminate states have merely entered the continuum by the force of karma and possess a nature that is effortless and tranquil, the volition associated with them does not function as a "karma-condition" (kammapaccaya) at a different time.
Furthermore, functional indeterminate states arise in a continuum where no underlying tendencies (anusaya) exist.

The volition associated with them likewise does not become a condition for that [result]. Therefore, even though right view and the other factors are present among those resultant (vipāka), functional (kiriya), and indeterminate (abyākata) states, they do not accomplish the quality of leading to a happy destination (*sugati*).
Because they lack the function of abandoning the defilements (*kilesappahāna*), they also do not accomplish the quality of leading to Nibbāna.
This is due to the deficiency in their intrinsic characteristics (*sabhāvalakkhaṇa*). Regarding those factors such as right view:

It is simply non-existent. Therefore, those [factors] are included within the path-condition (*magga-paccaya*). Among the faculties (*indriya*), the dominant function (*ādhipacca-kicca*) of the immaterial faculties exercises its influence only upon immaterial phenomena.
As for material phenomena, they are said to be "arisen from that condition" simply because they have originated from it.
The same applies to the root-cause (*hetu*), kamma, path, and jhāna conditions. Hence it was said: "This method of investigation also applies to the kamma, faculty, and jhāna conditions."
In this context, by the word "kamma," the asynchronous (nānakkhaṇika) condition is to be understood.
The apprehension of association arises [as follows]: conascent mental states (nāmadhamma) [are associated] with the material phenomena they originate;
postnascent [mental states] with their own respective effect-produced material phenomena; and the basis-phenomena (vatthudhamma) with the mental states dependent upon them—[all] in terms of time.
Because they share a single basis and a single connection, there arises the suspicion that they might be associated with one another.

To show that "there is no contingency of being an association-condition (sampayutta-paccaya)," [it is said that] even conditions such as the object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya), the proximity-condition (anantara-paccaya), and so forth, are not associated with their own effect-arisings.
Therefore, these too could be described by way of the state of an association-condition; such is the contingency of being an association-condition.
The intended meaning is that [these] do not exist among those conditions such as the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*).
By the word "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "only in the types mentioned above," it is shown that there is no other condition.
If there is no other condition, then it certainly should not be stated. Why? Because it would result in the speaker being guilty of repetition and speaking what is meaningless.

"It is not to be said that it is 'from what has arisen. Why? Because one must abandon such a false adherence as: 'How can that which does not exist in the world, having ceased, be fit to be a condition for anything? By this, he makes known this meaning:
in the world, some phenomena are conditions for others only when they themselves exist, not when they do not exist. Some phenomena..."
This distinction must necessarily be accepted: that things serve as conditions for others only when they themselves are non-existent, and not when they exist.
Regarding the phrase "by way of making room," it means by way of making room for the arising of another state of consciousness.

In the Suttanta, "it exists" (*atthi*) is one extreme; this refers to a self (*attā*), which is the most excellent and essential core of sentient beings, existing at all times throughout the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
There is neither annihilation nor liberation whatsoever. This is called the doctrine of eternalism (*sassatavāda*); it is one side of the dispute, one extreme of the argument.
"It does not exist" (*natthi*) means that a so-called sentient being lasts for only a single existence; after death, nothing remains. It is absolute [non-existence].
"It is annihilated. This is called the second extreme of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*), the second limit of the uneven.
These two extremes are called "the pair of extremes" for those who do not understand dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).

However, for those who do understand it, there is no such thing as a "self" that could be said to either exist or not exist. There is only a continuity of pure phenomena (*suddhadhammappabandha*). Of that—
And as long as ignorance (*avijjā*) has not been abandoned, there is no such thing as annihilation (*uccheda*). But when ignorance has been abandoned, it does not proceed beyond that;
"it exists" no longer means "it is. This is called the Middle Way, liberated from the two extremes.
[The opponents] merely describe many various possibilities; the intention is that even for those who describe them, there is no real purpose whatsoever.
The exposition of the summary of conditions is finished.
168. In the description of conditions: “In five ways” means by five kinds of conditions. “In one way” means by a single kind of condition.
The same applies to the remaining cases. “For the sake of non-interruption” means for the purpose of continuity. “For the purpose of application” means for the purpose of coordination. Whoever...
The construction is as follows: no arising of consciousness whatsoever is not a condition for some other non-opposed arising of consciousness.

“Of those that have arisen again” means those that have arisen again after having ceased. Regarding the phrase “the preceding impulsion moments,” here the path receives the condition of repetition (*āsevana-paccaya*) from the change-of-lineage (*gotrabhu*).
However, for the fruition, that [change-of-lineage] is not a condition of repetition because it belongs to a different class.
It does not exist. However, the fruition (phala) is entirely free from repetition (āsevana). Therefore, both of these do not receive the designation of "prior impulsion" (purimajavana) here;
thus it is said: "excluding the path, fruition, and impulsions. This refers to the final impulsions among those excluding the fruition-impulsions.
Regarding the phrase "complete in all aspects," it is stated "even by way of mere genus" because the classes such as the wholesome (kusala) and so forth are also included therein.

They would indeed be non-distinct; they do not, however, become distinct. Sometimes some are indeed non-distinct. Therefore, [the phrase] "phenomena of distinct classes" (bhinnajātikā dhammā) is used.

The construction is: "they are not able to... The intention is that this refers to the continuum of consciousness (cittasantāna), namely, the attainment of the sublime (mahaggata) and unsurpassed (anuttara) states from the state of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara).
The mind belonging to the sense-sphere ground is the *gotrabhū* mind; the meditative (jhāna) mind is the sublime ground.
