Path-consciousness belongs to the supramundane plane. Even though the volition of the kamma has ceased, its mode of activity does not cease;
it persists within the continuum of consciousness. That very [volition] later manifests as a mass of phenomena destined for fruition.
Therefore, it is reckoned as the seed of the result. And as long as that [seed] has not yet matured, it continues to function within the process of saṃsāra.

When it exists, there is no such thing as being destroyed in the interim. Therefore, volitional action (*kamma-cetanā*), when arising, arises for the purpose of depositing its seed within the continuum of consciousness;
and when ceasing, it ceases only after having deposited that seed. Thus it is said: "and the depositing of the seed, which consists of its own mode of occurrence.
Regarding the phrase "it occurs through volition," this means it is common to volition.
It exists. The connection is: "The previously arisen *sāla* saplings are conditions. It should be connected as:
"material phenomena produced by the four [causes] that arose in preceding moments of consciousness. The phrase "the body born of nutriment" (*āhāraja-kāya*) is an elliptical expression.
There is no purpose for the "post-nascence condition" (*pacchājāta-paccaya*) in the case of "that which is born later," such as the watering of an old sapling.
The intended meaning is that it is as if it were so. “By which [factor]” means by which cause or constituent part.
“Basis-form” (vatthu-rūpa) refers to the heart-basis form that is proximate to cessation. “In this way, this too” means that this subsequent-arising condition (pacchājāta-paccaya) is likewise.
“Pervasion” (vipphāra) is the filling out in various modes, the reaching across different times and places. The compound means “that which has a great pervasion. “In the basis” (vatthusmiṃ).

In the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*). It is called the fivefold existence (*pañcavokāra*) because it is intermingled and mixed with the five aggregates (*pañcakkhandha*). This refers to existence in the sense-sphere and the fine-material sphere (*kāmarūpabhava*).
It is unable to arise without [the other factors]. The intention is that form has not been suppressed by the power of the cultivation of dispassion toward form (*rūpavirāgabhāvanābala*).
"Or pre-arisen" means pre-arisen at a point one mind-moment past. "Or situated on the side of increase" means from that...
"Subsequently, up to the eighth moment of consciousness, it remains on the side of increase. "The arisen basis" means the arisen *vatthu*-rūpa (heart-base).
"In this" refers to this pre-arisen condition (*purejāta-paccaya*). The connection is: "even though it is seen. "In the reverse" means in the section on the reverse order.
"That" refers to the object-pre-arisen condition (*ārammaṇa-purejāta*). The connection is: "because that object is not clearly manifest."

The commentators on the *Paṭṭhāna* state that the cause is the object. It is indeed stated in the commentaries (*Aṭṭhakathā*) that for some at the time of death in the immaterial realm (*arūpabhava*), a sign of the destination (*gatinimitta*) serves as the object-prenascence. This being so, a prenascence object must necessarily be obtainable there.
Yet, in the *Paṭṭhāna*, all prenascence conditions in that existence are rejected. If one asks why, it is because of the [absence of] a physical basis (*vatthu*).
With the intention that the pre-arisen condition (*purejāta-paccaya*) cannot be obtained there [in the formless realm], it is said, "as if in the formless [realm].
And here, in the *Paṭṭhāna*, both types of pre-arisen conditions are rejected for the formless existence (*arūpa-bhava*);
therefore, they also say that all formless persons do not take any material phenomenon (*rūpa-dhamma*) as an object (*ārammaṇa*). Having established it thus, the object—

In the *Saṅgahadīpanī*, it is stated: “Just as for those who have passed away from the non-percipient realm (*asaññībhava*), so too for those who have passed away from the formless realm (*arūpabhava*), the object of rebirth-linking in the sensual sphere—which serves as the sign of the destination—is not apprehended by any door in the intermediate existence; it is manifested solely through the power of kamma.

Regarding the phrase “excrement, corpses, and so forth”: this refers to excrement and the putrid bodies of the dead. Regarding the phrase “when these were spoken”: [it refers to the aforementioned objects].

[This is] because they were mentioned in the *Paṭṭhāna*. But how do those unwholesome states (*akusala-dhammā*) serve as decisive support conditions (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for the wholesome states of the four planes?
To this he said: "In that regard, one should exclude the immediate [kamma]" (*tattha ānantariyaṃ vajjāni*), and so forth.

Therein, it is stated that for those who have committed immediate kamma (*ānantariya-kamma*), there is no attainment of the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) or the paths (*magga*), because they are possessed of the hindrance of defilements (*kilesāvaraṇa*) and the hindrance of kamma (*kammāvaraṇa*).

“‘One should know the immediate (ānantariya) faults. The construction is as follows: “Those”—namely, unwholesome states such as lust and so forth—are powerful supports for the arising of wholesome states belonging to the four planes. “By way of transcendence”:

in the *Paṭṭhāna*, regarding the question, “An unwholesome state is a condition for a wholesome state by way of decisive support-condition (upanissaya-paccaya),” in the analysis of this [question], it says: “Having killed a living being, [one gives rise to] that...”
It is said: "One gives a gift for the sake of warding off [aversion], undertakes moral discipline, performs the Uposatha rites, arouses jhāna, arouses the Path, and arouses direct knowledge.
In this context, "for the sake of warding off that" means for the sake of counteracting, abandoning, and transcending that kamma of killing living beings.
If a person who has committed the destruction of life, having again attained a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*),
gives alms, undertakes moral discipline (*sīla*), and performs the Uposatha observance for the sake of transcending that kamma,
then that kamma of destroying life is said to "yoke" that person to the kamma of giving, as well as to the kamma of moral discipline and the kamma of the Uposatha. Just as a king...
One might say: "On this day, whoever does not observe the Uposatha, I shall have him executed.
At that time, all the citizens would observe the Uposatha. This is how it should be understood. For his act of taking life is like that of the king;
the slayer of living beings is like the citizens; and his acts of giving, virtue, and Uposatha are like the Uposatha observances.
“Wholesome kamma”: this same method applies even to such passages as, “He arouses jhāna, he arouses the path, he arouses direct knowledge.

Thus, it should be understood that by way of transcendence, even a single unwholesome [kamma] generates and sets in motion all wholesome kamma of the four planes through its power of decisive support (upanissaya).
“All those very ones” refers to all [unwholesome kamma] together with the deeds of immediate retribution (ānantariya-kamma).
The construction is as follows: unwholesome states alone serve as powerful supports for the arising of all unwholesome and indeterminate (abyākata) phenomena.
Wholesome phenomena consist of generosity, virtue, and so forth. What is intended here is a very powerful kamma, not a weak one, because it serves as a decisive support (upanissaya).
The connection is: "Are there not likewise powerful supports for those material phenomena? How so?
He said, "They exist," and so forth, beginning with "of external trees, grasses, and so on. Therein, the connection is as follows:

the essence of earth (*pathavī-rasa*), the essence of water (*āpo-rasa*), rainwater, and seeds are the powerful supports for trees, grasses, and so on; likewise, medicinal roots and the like are the powerful supports for the internal continuum (*santāna*).
"Of that which is natural" (*pakatasseva*) means precisely of the previously performed work of production and so forth. "Not thus... [is the conclusion].
Regarding the phrase "by means of the continuity of form" (*rūpasantānena*): there are no phenomena produced or cultivated by such a continuity of form.
"That" (*taṃ*) refers to the season, seeds, and so forth, as well as karma and so forth. "Prepared" (*pakataṃ*) means previously produced and cultivated. The connection is:

"the volition, the planning, and the preparation of one who possesses consciousness. The meaning is: "volition is what is called planning and preparation. Regarding the term "preparation" (*pakappanaṃ*):
And there is the arrangement. “Something” (*kiñci*) refers to some kind of action and so forth, as well as the weather, food, and so forth.
The construction is: one’s own arisen lust and so forth [are projected] into another’s continuum, and another’s arisen lust and so forth [are projected] into one’s own continuum.
“An illustration” (*nidassana*) means an example. The gods corrupted by mental malice (*manopadosika-deva*), upon seeing one another, corrupt their own minds. Intensely...
They give rise to the nature of envy. At that very moment, they pass away. For them, two states of envy become strong supports for one another;
thus it should be applied by saying, "they become strong supports for wholesome states of the sense-sphere," and so forth.
In the *Vibhāvanī* commentary, [it refers to] the object—distinguished as jhāna, path, fruit, insight, and so on—as well as reflection, relishing, and the rest.
The construction is: "He makes the Dhamma dependent upon himself. "Dependent upon oneself" (*attādhīne*) means under one's own control or bound to oneself.

This is because it is stated in the *Paṭṭhāna* (Conditional Relations), in the section on questions, that after giving a gift, undertaking moral discipline (*sīla*), and performing the Uposatha rite, one reflects upon them with reverence;
and likewise, "one reflects with reverence upon previously well-performed deeds," and so forth—referring to giving, moral discipline, and so on, up to Nibbāna.
"‘And so on’ (cevā) was stated. Because it is said that ‘they relish and delight in lust,’ and so forth, and because it is said that ‘they relish the eye,’ and so forth, it is stated:
‘lust, views, the eye, the ear, and so on. ‘Also elsewhere’ (parattha pi) means also in other [contexts], such as the condition of support (nissaya-paccaya) and so on.
‘That very same’ (so evā) means precisely that which provides the prop. ‘Anything at all’ (kiñci) means even a mere trifle."

The construction is: "They are unable to provide any support for the great primary elements (mahābhūta). [Objection: But does not nutriment-form (āhāra-rūpa) succeed in supporting the great primary elements, and does life-form (jīvita-rūpa) succeed in maintaining the great primary elements born of karma?
[Reply: True. However, what is intended here is the function of co-nascence-condition (sahajāta-paccaya).
And those two do not possess the function of co-nascence-condition. That will be made clear later.
"It will be. Regarding "the basis for the results" (*vatthu vipākānaṃ*): the physical basis (*vatthurūpa*) is [a condition] for the resultant states.

In the *Paṭṭhāna* text, when the six conditions—object (*ārammaṇa*), support (*nissaya*), pre-existence (*purejāta*), dissociation (*vippayutta*), presence (*atthi*), and non-disappearance (*avigata*)—are combined, three answers are obtained;
this is the construction. The three answers are as follows: the basis [is a condition] for wholesome aggregates...
The basis is a condition by way of six conditions: "the basis for unwholesome states" and "the basis for indeterminate states.

And herein, for one who, taking the internal basis as an object, comprehends it thus, "My basis is impermanent," and so forth, the materiality of the basis is a condition for the wholesome aggregates by way of six conditions.
But for one who clings [to it] with the notions, "This is mine, this I am, this is my self":
The physical basis (*vatthu-rūpa*) is for unwholesome states. In both cases, at the moment of adverting, it is for indeterminate states.

However, for an Arahant who contemplates that [basis] as impermanent and so forth, it is for the functional-indeterminate aggregates (*kriyā-byākatānaṃ khandhānaṃ*). Therefore, he said: "the present physical basis," and so on.
Therein, "the present physical basis" refers to one's own present physical basis. But in the section on the method of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna-vidhāna*),...

Just as the mind directed toward traveling through the air takes the physical body as its object, one should connect this with the fact that for one who resolves upon making the body light, the material basis included therein becomes the object for the two types of direct-knowledge consciousness (*abhiññā-citta*). Regarding the phrase "in an undesired place":

the arising of impulsion consciousness (*javana-citta*) without an act of adverting (*āvajjana*) is something that may be desired in some cases, but in other cases it is not desired. In that regard, from the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*)...

The "desired state" refers to emergence (*vuṭṭhāna*), the path-sequences (*maggavīthī*), the stages of change-of-lineage (*gotrabhu*) and cleansing (*vodāna*), and the adventitious life-continuum (*āgantuka-bhavanga*).

Any state other than these is the "undesired state. Thus, the meaning is "in such undesired states. "At the time of the natural state" means at a time other than the period immediately preceding death.
"Or those very [bases]" means their respective physical supports (*nissaya-vatthu*). "Another..."

“Or else” means another [object] such as visible form (*rūpa*) distinct from the physical basis (*vatthu*). “Having different objects” means that the object of the adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*) is one thing and the object of the impulsion (*javana*) moments is another;
thus, the impulsion moments have different objects from the adverting consciousness. Therefore it is said, “arising subsequently,” and so forth.
“Of them” refers to those process-consciousnesses (*vīthicitta*). “That very same” refers to that same physical basis, the matter (*rūpa*). “And the basis” means the support (*nissaya*).

“Of them” refers to the teachers of the *Aṭṭhakathā*. The connection is: “for they are not able to grasp it. The rest here is easily understood. Regarding the passage beginning with “Why was it said?”:
“Of that *yakkha*” means of that *yakkha* named Indaka. “And of the others” means also of those born of moisture (*saṃsedaja*) and those of apparitional birth (*upapātika*).
“In two ways” refers to the function of generating material form (*rūpa-janana-kicca*) and the function of supporting material form (*rūpūpatthambhana-kicca*).
Thus, it is by way of two kinds. Alternatively, "by way of two kinds" means by way of the support for internal nutriment and the support for external nutriment.
"And of such [states]" refers to those established through the distinction of kamma that has reached absorption (appanā).
By the word "also" (*pi*) in "internal nutriment also," one includes both the life-faculty as previously described and immaterial nutriment. "Of the bases and the resultants" (*vatthu-vipākānaṃ*).
“Basis-form (vatthurūpa) [is] for the resultants. “In every way” (*sabbathā*) is a distributive term (*abyāyapada*). And that is connected with all case-endings.
However, since here it is in the nominative singular, he said “in every way,” meaning “in every mode. The connection is: “and the mode should be understood.
To the question “How should it be understood? he says “threefold,” and so forth. “It should be included among the conascent” means by way of being a condition.
It should be included. "Co-nascence" (sahajana) means that which causes [other things] to arise together with itself.

And this does not have a separate function of producing, as in the case of karma, consciousness, and so forth. Rather, the function of production should be understood as follows: when the [primary] matter arises within itself, the other material phenomena arise;
when it does not arise, they do not arise. Thus, it is said: "even without a function of simultaneous arising."

The intention is that the nutriment has no function in the act of arising simultaneously with itself. For that very reason, even though it supports those things that arise together with it, it does not attain the status of a co-nascence condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*).
This same method applies to the material life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvitindriya*) as well; hence it is said, "Life too," and so forth. "In three" refers to these three:
objective support (*ārammaṇa*), decisive support (*upanissaya*), and presence (*atthi*). In the case of objective predominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*), [the condition] is pre-arisen (*purejāta*).

There is also the predominance of the object (*ārammaṇādhipati*). Since that is a pre-arisen presence condition (*purejāta-atthi-paccaya*), it is included within the presence condition (*atthi-paccaya*).
Regarding the phrase "when that has been done, for those proceeding": this means for those proceeding precisely because that action has been performed.

"The mode of the object" (*ārammaṇākāra*) refers to the mode of the field of experience and the objective domain. "Having made a distinction in the continuity" (*santānavisesaṃ katvā*): the intended meaning is "having made a deposit of seed. "Those" (*te*)...

The object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya) and the kamma-condition (kammapaccaya). "Timeless" (akālika): it is timeless by way of the volition of the Path (maggacetanā), for that indeed produces its own fruit immediately after itself.
Therefore, because there is no future time to wait for, it is called "timeless.
The remainder, the asynchronous condition (nānakkhaṇikapaccaya), is "timely" (kālika). "In the sense of a condition" means by way of the function of a condition. Of the process of the world...
The connection is with the phrase "because they have karma as their cause. Regarding the statement, "By way of the fruit and the cause," the construction is as follows:

having attributed the name of the cause—kamma, which is the cause of the entire course of worldly existence that constitutes the fruit—to the fruit itself, all twenty-three conditions, by way of conventional usage (*vohāra*), do not transcend the nature of kamma.
What is meant is that they come to be reckoned as kamma-conditions (*kammapaccaya*). [The word] "existing" (*vijjamānā*)...
"Only [those] that exist"—this means "only by way of the presence condition (atthipaccaya). Regarding the phrase "it is indeed contrary to the logic of the Teaching (sāsanayutti)":

here, "the logic of the Teaching" refers to the Three Pitakas. "It is indeed contrary" means that one who asserts that all earth, mountains, rivers, oceans, the cloudless sky, and so forth—which serve as objective conditions (ārammaṇapaccaya)—as well as all designations (paññatti) and even Nibbāna, fall under the category of kamma, is speaking in contradiction [to the Teaching].
Furthermore, one who asserts that all past and future phenomena (dhammas) exist as a condition by way of presence (*atthipaccaya*) contradicts even the Three Pitakas.
As for the *Paṭṭhāna-pāḷi*, there is simply nothing to be said [against this]. In the *Paṭṭhāna*, the term "exists" (*atthi*) signifies existing by way of being present;
it does not mean existing by way of ultimate reality (*paramattha*), nor by way of worldly convention (*loka-sammuti*). For [the term] does not refer to ultimate reality...
Even though they are phenomena (*dhamma*), past and future phenomena are included here under the category of "existence" (*atthi*);

yet they do not constitute a mere designation (*paññatti*). "In a location bound to one another" means in the locations of the sense-sphere existence (*kāma-bhava*) and fine-material existence (*rūpa-bhava*), which are not bound by a mutual relationship of support and supported.
"From which" means from that consciousness (*viññāṇa*) which is the rebirth-linking; or alternatively, "from which" means from that head [of the tree] or from that seed from which it is produced.

The construction [of the sentence] is as follows: “Like the great tree from its seed” means like the production of the continuum of a great tree, beginning with the sprout and so forth, by way of the condition of the seed.
In the reading of the Pāḷi: “You would not descend” (*na okkamissatha*) means if you were not to descend.

“You would accumulate” (*samuccissatha*) means would you indeed accumulate? Would you increase? “You would deviate” (*vokkamissatha*) means if you were to depart, if you were to perish. “You would be reborn” (*abhinibbattissatha*).
“Would it indeed arise?”—it would manifest. “Will it be cut off?”—if it were to be cut off. “Will you incur [fault]?”—would you indeed incur it?
“Yadidaṃ” means “that which is this. “Idaṃ” is a mere particle. “Viññāṇaṃ” means rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhiviññāṇa*). The construction is:
“That consciousness which exists, that very thing is the phenomenon of consciousness (*viññāṇadhamma*). “For the arising of form” means for the production of form.
"Conditioned by consciousness" (*viññāṇapaccayā*) means that consciousness is the condition for this; thus, there is the arising of matter.

"By the continuity of matter" (*rūpappaveṇiyā*) refers to the stream of matter born of kamma. "Also by temperature and nutriment" (*utu-āhārāpi*) refers to internal temperature and internal nutriment. This is stated by way of logical possibility.
However, in terms of actual fact, if the previously arisen continuity of matter does not exist, then those internal temperatures and nutriments do not exist either.
It should not be said that external temperature, even in the absence of a previously arisen continuity of matter, does not produce matter.
Regarding the reading in the *Ṭīkā*: “But as for the immaterial” (*arūpaṃ pana*) refers to the immaterial plane. “In whatever matter” (*yasmiṃ rūpe*) refers to matter born of kamma.

“The state of being a condition exists” (*paccayabhāvo atthi*) means there is the causal power for the subsequent arising of matter. If it is asked, “How is this known? he says, “Of the son,” and so forth.
“Designated as seed-state” means the seed-state of mango seeds and so forth. “Named determinate matter” refers to a specific temperature (utu).
“In this way or that way” means without restriction. “Designated as womb-state” means the birth-state of various lineages, clans, and castes.
“Determinate matter” refers to determinate matter designated as a specific temperature. These are similar in their material configuration.
“*Yesanti*” means conflict. “The power of rebirth-form alone” means the power of the rebirth-form that has arisen during the stages such as the *kalala*.
To show this same point again with greater detail, he says “*Apicā*,” etc. “*Samudāgataṃ*” means well-arrived or fully developed in succession. The connection is:
“It determines both the form of femininity, etc., and the seed-form. “*Niyāmakaṃ*” means determining.
It is the determiner of various colors, shapes, and so forth. Regarding the phrases beginning with “In this existence”:
the analysis of the compound is “wealth (dhana), grain (dhañña), and all other objects of enjoyment and utility (upabhogaparibhoga) remaining from that.

The dvanda compound is “knowledge (vijjā), craft (sippa), various extensive learning (nānābahussuta), and mastery of the scriptures (pariyatti). “Of those future ones” refers to those fresh acquisitions of wealth, grain, and so forth.
“*Upanissaya-paccayatā*” (the conditionality of decisive support) refers to the conditionality of decisive support for past preparatory action (*pubbayoga-kamma*).
In this context, “performing past preparatory action for the sake of obtaining wealth, grain, and enjoyments” means engaging in such activities as agriculture or commerce.
Regarding agriculture first: when performing agricultural work for the sake of obtaining wealth, grain, and enjoyments, [one obtains] wealth, grain, and enjoyments...
The condition of future decisive support (*anāgatūpanissaya-paccaya*). Now, the performance of agricultural work is its conditionally arisen result.
At the times of acquiring and enjoying wealth, grain, and possessions, the performance of agricultural work is the condition of past decisive support (*atītūpanissaya-paccaya*).
Both their acquisition and enjoyment are its conditionally arisen results. However, at the very moment of performing the agricultural work, the field—
The field, seeds, rain from clouds, farming implements such as ploughs, oxen and buffaloes, and laborers are the present decisive support (paccuppannūpanissaya).

The performance of the farming work is what arises conditioned by that. For one who accomplishes that work, his parents and ancestors are the past decisive support condition (atītūpanissaya-paccaya) for that work. That work [is the condition] for him...
"Conditionally arisen. The same applies to the remaining [terms]. The rest is easy to understand.

Regarding the passage beginning with "fivefold": "The state of configuration" (*saṇṭhānatta*) refers to the existence (*bhāva*) of all material configurations, starting from the atom (*aṇu*), the dust mote in a sunbeam (*tajjārī*), the chariot-dust (*rathareṇu*), the nit (*likkhā*), and so forth.
Furthermore, "existence" (*bhāva*) is said to be their occurrence (*pavatti*).
“‘The causes of occurrence’ refers only to ultimate material phenomena (*paramattha-rūpa-dhamma*).

Regarding the phrase ‘because of not following along,’ here ‘not following along’ is to be understood as [the mind’s] inability to follow due to the extreme subtlety of its own nature. The analysis of the compound is:

‘name’ (*nāma*) is what is called ‘designation’ (*adhivacana*). And ‘designation’ (*adhivacana*) is so called because it is a superior word (*adhika-vacana*) since it illuminates the meaning. ‘Name-designation’ (*nāmābhidhāna*)...”
And it is called "name-designation" (nāmapaññatti). Regarding the phrase "the state of being graspable":

having heard the designation of names from those who speak such things as, "This is called consciousness," or "This is called contact," it is the state of being graspable by knowledge through the process of knowing the corresponding essential nature (sabhāvattha). It is said that it is called "name" because it is to be known by following the name-designation.
It exists. It bends toward the object (*ārammaṇa*), thus it is "name" (*nāma*). Or, it is also appropriate to call it "name" because the objective phenomena (*ārammaṇika-dhammā*) bend toward it here.
Since designations (*paññatti*) are also included among the conditioning phenomena (*paccaya-dhamma*) in this compendium of conditions, the Elder has also placed the compendium of designations here.
In that context, regarding the phrase "that by which one is made known," "making known" (*paññāpana*) means the establishment of conventional usage (*vohāra*).
To show that this establishment is accomplished by two causes—namely, by the verbal expression of those who speak and by the acceptance of those who hear—it says, "And this," and so forth.
"It is accepted" means that it is expressed by successive generations of people just as it was expressed by previous persons.
It is also called "a designation" (paññatti) because it is made known in a specific manner.
It is appropriate. "The meaning of the phoneme" refers to the referent of a word, such as humans, deities, earth, mountains, and so forth.
"'Wisdom is established' means it is established in its various modes. The heading here is "he states the designation by means of words.

"The mode of preponderance" refers to the specific distinction of the preponderance of the earth-element in things such as earth and mountains; of the water-element in things such as river and ocean waters; and [of the fire-element] in masses of fire.
In the case of the fire element, it is the wind element within the masses of air; such is the distinction of their predominant state.
"Transformation" (*vipariṇāma*) means changing in various ways; thus he says, "the mode of transformation in this or that way.
The conventional designations "earth," "mountain," and so forth, do not occur based on a fixed shape. [One does not think: "Earth has such a shape," or "A mountain has such a..."

Regarding "shape" (*saṇṭhāna*): there is no fixed rule for shape. It is said that "shape is not the primary factor here" because the conventional designation is established merely by the occurrence of a heap or mass of dust and stones;
they are simply called "wood" and so forth. Depending on their various differences in shape, they are designated by various terms.
This is according to the specific mode of manifestation of the primary elements (*bhūta*), as in the cases of earth, mountains, rivers, oceans, and so on.

It is said: "For here, the collection is not the primary factor. "Designation based on clinging" (*upādāpaññatti*) means a designation made by taking the phenomena of the five aggregates as a basis, having rendered them non-different from those [aggregates] and unified with them.
It is not a designation that exists apart from those aggregates, like the designations of space, direction, or location.
"From which" (*yato*) means from whatever [source]. "Because of having obtained manifestation" (*laddhappakāsattā*) means because of having obtained illumination.

“*Ahassā*” means “of the day. Even for one who attends to the bloated corpse and so forth by way of their repulsiveness—thinking, for instance, “the bloated is repulsive”—the sign that arises is included among the signs of the primary elements (*bhūtanimitte*), because it appears in the form of a transformation of the primary elements.
“*In the commentary*” refers to the *Puggalapaññatti-aṭṭhakathā*. “*Of them*” refers to...
Of the eight designations, such as earth, mountains, and so forth. "In this way or that" means by various conventional expressions, such as "this is earth," "this is a mountain," and so on.
"Shadows of meanings" (*atthacchāyā*) means the shadows of ultimate meanings (*paramattha*). By "shadows," the shadows of signs (*nimitta*) are meant.
The "form of the shadows of meanings" (*atthacchāyākāra*) refers to the form of those shadows of meanings. By "form" (*ākāra*), a manifold collection is meant.

“Aspect” (ākāra) refers to various shapes and so forth. Alternatively, “object” (attha) means the referent of a word, the meaning of the expression. By the phrase “designated by words,” etc., he shows this meaning:
that very [referent] is called an “aspect of the shadow of the object” because it consists merely of signs such as the aspect of a collection.
“In the form of a reflection of substance” means in the form of a reflection designated as substance. “Hanging down” means having suspended itself.
“Having made it into something that conforms to counting” means having made it into a single unit, such as “this is one thing.
“These six” refers to the designations, expressions, and conventional terms known as name-kamma and so forth. “In the self” means in the self designated by the term “name.
The intention is that it functions for those who understand language only as an object of meaning. “When there is a name” refers to a collection of syllables.
When it is said that "a sentence is a word or a collection of words," this refers to the existence of nominal words (*nāmapada*).
"Of those learning them" means of people who learn each respective nominal word by way of bringing it to the tip of their tongue.
"Their meanings" means the meanings of each respective nominal word. "They indeed come forth" means they indeed come before the knowledge of those who understand the language.
By this, he shows that the "bending toward" (nāmana) of the meaning within itself is indeed the very function of illuminating the meaning (*atthajotana*).

In the phrase “knowledge for those who hear,” the word “knowledge” (*ñāṇa*) is a term used by way of illustration (*upalakkhaṇa*), because unwholesome consciousness (*akusalaviññāṇa*) is also intended there.
“It bends toward each respective meaning” means it bends by way of taking that as its object (*ārammaṇakaraṇavasena*). “By way of grasping the name” (*nāmaggahaṇavasena*)—this...
“Let it be named so-and-so”: this refers to the act of grasping a name in such a manner.
“It is maintained” means it is maintained by not forgetting it even for as long as life lasts. “Etāya” (by this): by means of this class of names functioning as the instrument (*karaṇa*).
“In the state of being unknown” (*aviditapakkhe*): in the state of not having heard the word for the name. “Having extracted from that” (*tato nīharitvā*): [having extracted the meaning] from that.

Having extracted it by means of knowledge from the side that was not yet understood: "It is spoken" (*kathīyati*) means that when one speaks at the time of hearing, it is explained and made known to the listener.
"Of its meaning" (*atthassa*) refers to the meaning situated on the side that was not understood.

"Or of this" (*etasse vā*) refers specifically to the nominal word (*nāmapada*). And a "nominal word" includes a verb (*kriyāpada*), a prepositional word (*upasaggapada*), a particle (*nipātapada*), and a primary derivative word (*pāṭipadikapada*).
Here, it is indeed called a "name-word" (*nāmapada*). Regarding the phrase "of those that have become qualifiers":

in a *aññapadattha-samāsa* (compound whose referent is external), the meanings of the compound words are called "qualifiers. Thus, "of those that have become qualifiers. Regarding the phrase "of the person":

this refers to the person who has attained direct knowledge (*abhiññālābhī*), who constitutes the external referent of the compound. The word "they say" (*vadanti*) is stated with reference to the teacher Ānanda; for he, in the *Paññattiduka-niddesa* of the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, [states as follows].

The *Mūlaṭīkā* speaks thus: “*Tabbhāvan*” means the state of letters, words, and phonemes (*akkhara-padabyañjana*). “*Assā*” refers to the designation by name (*nāmapaññatti*). The analysis (*viggaha*) is:
that which has letters, words, and phonemes as its range (*gocara*) and object (*ārammaṇa*). “*Anusārenā*” means by way of following after.
“*Lokasaṅketanimmitā*” means produced by the knowledge of worldly convention (*lokasaṅketaññāṇa*). And this [term] “knowledge of worldly convention” is as follows: [End of excerpt]
The knowledge that recognizes the conventional worldly designation (*lokasaññāṇa*) is such that it knows: "This is the name of this meaning; this is the meaning of this name.
"Taking as its object a past mere sound" means making a past mere sound—having ceased after serving as the object for the process of ear-consciousness—their objective referent.
"In the words spoken by him" refers to the monk who has renounced the training.

In the statement “I renounce the training,” the construction is as follows: the present sound [is grasped] by the auditory consciousness process, and the past sound [is grasped] by the mental consciousness process.
“Those syllables” refers to the constituent syllables within the sentence “I renounce the training.
“This collection of syllables” means that this is a nominal phrase (nāmapada). This is the meaning of this [passage].
“Vinicchayavīthim” means the process of discerning syllables and words. “Ekakkhare sadde” refers to the conventional sound consisting of a single syllable, such as ‘go’.
“Yā” refers to the designation (paññatti). “Vadantassa manasā” is the connection [of the phrase].
“Pubbabhāge” means that when one wishes to speak some meaning to others and speaks it, the name of that respective meaning—

Having first determined it through the mental-door process (*manodvāra-vīthi*), he speaks thus; that name, having been established by the mind while speaking in the prior stage, is called a "conceptual designation" (*nāmapaññatti*).
"The statement of sequence" means the statement of the order of occurrence. "'It is said' (*vuttaṃ*)" means as stated in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
Likewise, the connection is with the phrase "and 'half-brick' is also said. And "'It is said' (*vuttaṃ*)" refers to what is stated in the treatises on grammar (*saddasattha*).
In this verse: “*Matta*” refers to a single moment of the arising of consciousness (*vijjuppādakkhaṇa*). That which has one *matta* is “one-matta” (*ekamatto*).
“*Dīghamuccate*” means it is called “long” (*dīgho*). “*Pluto*” means that which is sung (*gāyito*) as various sounds (*ruto*) is “*paruto*.
By changing the letter *ra* to *la* and dropping the vowel *a* in the prefix *pa*, it is called “*pluto*”; thus, it is said to be “song” (*gīta*). “*Paramattha*... [The text continues].
“Of the sound-combinations” refers to the ultimate sets of sounds that have occurred in succession.

“Many hundreds of thousands of millions of consciousnesses” refers to many hundreds of thousands of millions of consciousnesses occurring between the impulsion-sequences (javana-vīthi) together with the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) consciousnesses.
The Elucidation of the Method of the Paṭṭhāna is finished.
The exposition on the Compendium of Conditions is finished.
9. Exposition on the Compendium of Meditation Subjects (Kammaṭṭhānasaṅgaha) 170.

Regarding the compendium of meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhānasaṅgahe*): the analysis of the compound is "one by whom the distinction between name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is known and understood. This refers to the individual who is a practitioner of yoga (*yogī*).
“*Sameti kilese*”: it pacifies the defilements of the hindrances, such as sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*). “*Tathā pavatto*”:
it proceeds by way of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), or it proceeds by way of complete stilling (*vūpasama*). “*Tāyā*”: by means of that wisdom of cultivation;
the connection is with the word “seeing. “*Passitaṃ*”: thoroughly seen. How is the practice of yoga, such as the cultivation of the *kasiṇas*, itself its own place?
It is said, “For [the sake of] the beginning, middle, and end,” and so forth.

In the *Vibhāvanī* commentary, by the phrase “by way of being the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhānatāya*),” it is indicated that the word *ṭhāna* (basis) is called *padaṭṭhāna* (proximate cause) in the sense that “it stands (*tiṭṭhati*)” or “it proceeds without turning back.

Regarding the phrase “of the specific kinds of happiness,” this refers to the happiness of jhāna, the happiness of the path, and the happiness of the fruit. Regarding the phrase “the ten kasiṇas,” and so forth...
The phrase beginning with “the ten kasiṇas” was stated in order to show the meaning in both ways: either primarily or figuratively.
“The rest” refers to the remaining meditation subjects, such as the illimitables (appamaññā) and so forth. “In accordance with what is suitable” means according to what is appropriate for each case.
“Practice” means repeated and intensive engagement. “Distinction through association” refers to the two types of conduct found in any given individual.
The classification [of the types of persons] is mixed [with others], such as "for some it is 'Tissa'" and so forth. "In the commentary" refers to the *Visuddhimagga-aṭṭhakathā*.
"Of all absorption" refers to absorption of jhāna, absorption of the path, and absorption of the fruit.
"That which occurs near or occurs far" is the governing topic. "But the other" refers to absorption occurring at a distance. "But of those" refers to...
Regarding the three kinds of development: "of those two" refers to the two signs. "A span and four finger-breadths" means a measure of one span with an additional four finger-breadths in width.
It is also appropriate to take it as either the measure of a span or the measure of four finger-breadths;
for instance, in the Visuddhimagga, in the section on the air-kasina, the head is described as being four finger-breadths in measure.
"It was seen being struck by the wind" is what was said. A "threshing-floor circle" (*khalamaṇḍala*) is a circular area of ground where farmers thresh grain.

Regarding the phrase "or made": they take a lump of clay devoid of specific colors such as blue and so forth, which has the color of dawn, knead it with water, and fashion it into a circular patch of earth with a well-polished surface, like a wheel-circle. Thus it is made.
Or: “*Akataṃ vā* (or unmade)” means that on some portion of ground it has not been made by anyone, or has grown spontaneously.

Regarding the phrase “*Kasiṇena jambudīpassā* (by the whole of Jambudīpa)”: for one who praises [the Buddha] as “Buddha,” whatever rapture (*pīti*) arises in the body, that rapture is indeed better than even the whole of Jambudīpa.
The remainder of the verse. Herein, the construction is: "From the entirety of Jambudīpa, [it is] even more excellent than that.
"From the entirety" (*kasiṇato*) means from the whole circle. What is meant is: by virtue of sovereignty and overlordship over the entire circle of Jambudīpa.
"Situated" (*sanniviṭṭhā*) means evenly established. "Manifested as a shape" (*saṇṭhānapaññatti*) means appearing in the form of a circle.
It is called a designation by way of a sign (*nimittapaññatti*). "In the place touched" means in the body or in places such as the tops of trees that have been struck by the wind.
"A whirlwind" (*vāyuvaṭṭī*) means a circular mass of wind. "Distinguished by the light of the moon, the sun, and fire" is a compound;
"distinguished" (*visiṭṭhā*) means differentiated.
“Smoking” (*dhūmātaṃ*) means fuming. It is said to be like a cloth filled with smoke; therefore he says, “having reached a state of putrefaction.
The letter *ka* at the end indicates censure; thus it is said, “because of its loathsomeness,” meaning because it is to be loathed.
“Of a corpse” (*chavasarīrassa*) means of a wretched body. “That very same” (*tadeva*) refers to the corpse itself. “Putrid” (*vipubbakaṃ*).
The connection is with the term "vicchinnakaṃ" (the severed). In that context, *vinīlaṃ* means "distinctly blue. That very same thing, because it is loathsome, is called *vinīlakaṃ*.
"That very same [body] having boiled again" means that the very body which was *vinīlaka* boils again after the lapse of time;
the meaning is that it has reached the state of being fully cooked as putrid blood. "From here and there" means from the openings of the apertures. That very same [thing] is appropriate.
The connection is with the word "body" (*sarīra*). "Fragmented" (*vicchinnaka*)—some also read it as *vicchiddaka*.

"Having pulled out" means having detached pieces from the body and dragged them to various locations. "A body with trickling blood" means a body from which blood is trickling from the openings of wounds at the places where it was cut or pierced.
Regarding the term “*buddhānussatī*,” here the word *buddha* is a figurative expression (*guṇyūpacāra-vacana*) for the qualities [of a Buddha].

Since the qualities are to be grasped by means of the name of the possessor of those qualities, it is said: “*buddhānussatī* is the recollection of the qualities of a Buddha. This same method applies to the recollection of the Dhamma (*dhammānussatī*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase “arahant and so forth,” this refers to the qualities of an arahant and so forth.
That from which stains such as immorality (*dussilya*) and stinginess (*macchariya*) have departed is [the state of] an arahant.

“Free from the stain of stinginess. The analysis of the compound is: “the state of that [stinginess]. By the phrase “and the Nibbāna attained by oneself,” the absolute pacification of the defilements of noble persons (ariyapuggala) is stated. “Having as one’s object” means having a particular person as one’s object.

“Bestowing of welfare” refers to the bestowal of welfare and happiness upon that person through such thoughts as, “May this person be free from enmity, may they be free from affliction,” and so forth.
The directing of the mind toward a person. Compassion (*karuṇā*) and appreciative joy (*muditā*) have meanings already explained below in the compendium of mental factors (*cetasika-saṅgaha*).

"Bestowing benefit" (*hitūpasaṃhāra*), "rejoicing in benefit" (*hitamodanā*), and "removing harm" (*ahitāpanayana*) form a copulative compound (*dvanda*). Among these, bestowing benefit is the function of loving-kindness (*mettā*);

rejoicing in benefit is the function of appreciative joy; and removing harm is the function of compassion. In that context, [one directs the mind] toward another who is endowed with benefit and happiness.
Seeing [the benefit], the increase of joy and gladness within oneself through that benefit for others is called "rejoicing in the welfare" (*hitamodanā*).

Seeing another who is suffering, thinking with the mind, "May this person be freed from this suffering; may they not suffer," and thus removing the harm and suffering from the other, is called "removing what is harmful" (*ahitāpanayana*).
"Of them" (*tesaṃ*) refers to other beings. "One's own" (*sakaṃ*) means that which belongs to oneself (*attano idaṃ*).
“This” refers to the cause of pleasure and pain. Those for whom their own karma—meaning karma performed by oneself—is their own are "owners of their karma" (*kammassaka*).
They are simply other beings. The state of being that is their nature; the analysis of the compound is: "the intensification of that. “Breaking down of boundaries” (*sīmasambheda*):
There are four boundaries—the self, the beloved person, the neutral person, and the hostile person. Breaking them down is *sambheda*; it is the mixing together.
The meaning is "making no distinction. The breaking down of boundaries is "boundary-breaking" (*sīmasambheda*).

Pervasion by way of specific delimitation, such as "all women" or "all men," is called "specific pervasion" (*odhisopharaṇa*). Pervasion by way of non-delimitation and without restriction, such as "all beings" (*sabbe sattā*), "all living things" (*sabbe pāṇā*), or "all creatures" (*sabbe bhūtā*), is called "non-specific pervasion" (*anodhisopharaṇa*). [For example: "All beings in the eastern direction..."
"Pervading the directions" (*disāpharaṇa*) refers to the pervasion by way of the divisions of the directions, beginning with the thought, "May they be free from enmity.

"Those who possess that" refers to persons who are endowed with those immeasurables (*appamaññā*). "By means of a state of heart that is constantly serene and cool" means at all times by means of a peaceful and cooling state of heart.
Alternatively, the word *brahma* is a synonym for "excellent," as in such expressions as "he produces brahma-merit."
That which is to be eaten or consumed is "eaten" (*asita*). This refers to the five kinds of solid food. That which is to be drunk is "drunk" (*pīta*).
This refers to the eight kinds of beverages. That which is to be chewed with the teeth is "chewed" (*khāyita*). This refers to various kinds of snacks, such as cakes and fruit.
That which is to be tasted or licked even by taking it with the fingers is "tasted" (*sāyita*). This refers to things to be relished, such as honey and molasses.
Repulsiveness due to its own nature (*sarasappaṭikūlatā*) means repulsiveness by way of its intrinsic characteristic.
For all four kinds of nutriment, wherever they smear, adhere, or coat—whether in bowls or on the hands, mouth, and so forth—they must be washed away with water.
If not washed, even that [vessel] becomes disgusting. Repulsiveness due to its receptacle (*āsayapaṭikūlatā*) refers to that [nutriment] while it is being swallowed.
Repulsiveness by way of its location refers to the repulsiveness resulting from its mixture with the receptacles of bile, phlegm, and so forth, which reside in the throat and other parts.
Repulsiveness by way of its storage (*nidhānato*) means repulsiveness by way of being stored; "storage" (*nidhāna*) here refers to the stomach.

Repulsiveness by way of its digestion (*pakkato*) means the repulsiveness arising when that which has entered storage reaches the state of feces, urine, and so forth at the time of full digestion. Repulsiveness by way of its non-digestion (*apakkato*)...
Repulsiveness by way of its state (*paṭikūlatā*) refers to the repulsiveness that arises in the body through the occurrence of various diseases when that [food] is undigested and not yet decomposed.

Repulsiveness by way of its result (*phalato*) refers to the repulsiveness that arises from the time of its digestion onwards, through the growth of repulsive masses such as head-hair, body-hair, and so forth, within the body.
Repulsiveness by way of its excretion (*nissandato*) refers to [the repulsiveness] of that [food] as it exits through the bodily orifices or the pores of the skin.
The repulsiveness [of food] consists in its oozing and trickling out through various other openings. “Therein” means in that fourfold food.

“Perception of the abandoning of craving” is the perception that arises by way of abandoning craving for flavors, even toward most delicious food, just as one might eat the flesh of one’s own son on a desert road in order to enable one’s parents to cross the desert.
“By way of their specific characteristics (*salakkhaṇa*), etc. means by way of their specific characteristics, their constituent parts (*sasambhāra*), and so forth.

Regarding the phrase “he conducts himself with lust (*rāgena carati*”), here the word “with lust” (*rāgena*) is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇatthe*), or it is an instrumental expression denoting a characteristic of a state (*itthambhūtalakkhaṇe*). In that regard, first, in the sense of the instrument:

“he conducts himself with lust” means that for the most part he conducts himself among the four postures (*iriyāpatha*) with a mind characterized by lust; he wanders about being led by a mind of lust.

This has been stated. However, in the sense of a characteristic of a state already attained (*itthambhūtalakkhaṇa*), in the phrase “he conducts himself with lust,” it means that he conducts himself having made lust his banner and lust his standard.
“Of him” refers to that person. “Exalted” means risen up, more manifest; they also say it means more abundant.
Regarding the word “for the abandoning,” the particle *iti* here has the sense of “and so forth. By this, compassion is to be cultivated.
It includes this textual remainder: "Loving-kindness should be developed for the abandoning of ill will; sympathetic joy should be developed for the abandoning of aversion.
Regarding the phrase "because it is a statement of escape": loving-kindness as liberation of mind is indeed the escape from ill will;
compassion as liberation of mind is the escape from cruelty; and sympathetic joy as liberation of mind is the escape from aversion.

Likewise, it is because they express the state of transcendence (*nissaraṇa-bhāva*). There are four immeasurables (*appamaññā*). It is said, "For one of a temperament characterized by hatred (*dosa-carita*).

And it is said, "Because of the absence of the state of being a basis for hatred (*dosa-vatthu-ttābhāvato*)," which means because of the absence of the state of acting as a basis for the arising of hatred.
The four kasiṇas, beginning with the blue, are said to be for one of a temperament characterized by hatred. Why, however, is this so for one of a temperament characterized by hatred?
Equanimity (*upekkhā*) is not mentioned separately as a suitable cause. Showing that it is not mentioned because it is a different kind of cause, he says:
"And here," and so forth. "Three" refers to the three immeasurables (*appamaññā*). "Pleasant forms" means pleasant colors.
The context is that one whose mind is distracted (*vikkhittacitta*). "Of him" refers to a person who is full of negligence and whose mind is distracted. It has been said:

It might be so. However, the intention [of the author] is that this is not stated thus in the *Visuddhimagga*. In the reading of the *Vibhāvanī*, it is said: "By way of being an object of the intellect (*buddhivisaya*).

If, because they are objects of the intellect, [the perceptions of death, peace, and discernment] are suitable for one of deluded temperament (*mohacarita*), then the discernments of death, peace, and discernment—which have become objects of the intellect—might also be suitable for one of deluded temperament; therefore, he says: "For if this were the case," and so forth.
“‘The kasiṇas of the primary elements’ (bhūtakasiṇāni) refers to the kasiṇas of the great primaries, beginning with the earth kasiṇa. ‘There too’ means even among those forty meditation subjects.
When it is said thus, the broadness and smallness of the color kasiṇas are also included here.
‘Large’ means larger than a span and four finger-breadths. If the word *eva* were to be taken according to its literal sense [in this context], it would be appropriate.”

If this were so, one might take the meaning to be that "only what is small is suitable for one whose temperament is dominated by applied thought (vitakkacarita), and not for those whose temperaments are dominated by intelligence (buddhicarita) and so forth.
However, this would contradict the statement in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) that "there is nothing whatsoever unsuitable for one whose temperament is dominated by intelligence.
It is with this intention that it was said: "The word 'small' is applied [to the object]. Alternatively, "vast" refers to the deluded temperament (*mohacarita*).

It should be understood that while a small [object] is permitted only for one whose temperament is dominated by applied thought (*vitakkacarita*)—and not for one whose temperament is dominated by faith (*saddhācarita*)—for those whose temperaments are dominated by wisdom (*buddhicarita*) and so forth, both large and small objects are permitted. "All this" refers to all these statements concerning the classification of temperaments.
Regarding the three types of persons with unwholesome temperaments, in the case of one whose temperament is dominated by applied thought, because of its extreme suitability...
The intended meaning is "in faith, wisdom, and conduct. Therefore, he said: "But [it is] not a suppressor of lust and so forth," and so on.

Regarding the phrase "the qualities of the Buddha... of the Dhamma... of the qualities," the word *guṇa* (quality) should be applied to the preceding terms, such as "of the qualities of the Buddha" (*buddhaguṇānaṃ*) and "of the qualities of the Dhamma" (*dhammaguṇānaṃ*), and so forth.
"Therein" (*tattha*) means in that word "quality" (*guṇapade*). It does not satisfy, thus it is "unsatisfying" (*atappanīyo*). Satisfying (*tappanaṃ*)...
The meaning is that it does not produce contentment. It is "arousing" (*saṃvejaniya*) because it produces arousal (*saṃvega*).
"Dhamma" means intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). That which has an arousing nature is "possessing an arousing nature" (*saṃvejaniya-dhamma*); [this refers to] death.
"Of the fifth jhāna concentration" means of the fine-material-sphere (*rūpāvacara*) fifth jhāna concentration. "Merely arisen" means merely increased. "Therein" means...
Regarding "on repulsive objects": "of an old cesspool" means of an ancient cesspool;
that is to say, one that has discharged excrement and urine. Therefore he said, "as if seeing a heap of dung.
These [meditations] never reach absorption (appanā) without mental joy (somanassa), because it is extremely easy for joy to arise through the distancing of ill-will, cruelty, and discontent.
And because pleasure and joy have not been suppressed, as in the fifth jhāna. "On the side of equanimity" means on the side of neutral observation (*ajjhupekkhanā*).
"Firmly" means intensely. "Clearly" means manifestly. Grasping the sign after making it firm and clear is "grasping the sign firmly and clearly.
"Of some object" refers to an object such as the qualities of the Buddha. "Counterpart sign" (*paṭibhāganimitta*)...
Here, because the word "counterpart" (paṭibhāga) occurs in the sense of being similar to that, he says "like that" (tādise), and so forth.

By the phrase "in its shape" (taṃsaṇṭhāne), he shows that the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta) is established only as a heap of intrinsic-nature phenomena (sabhāvadhamma) existing in the form of a shape, such as the earth-circle and so on.
The word "thus" (eva) refers, first of all, to the ten kasiṇas in the compendium of serenity (samatha).
“Skill in learning” (uggahakosallaṃ) refers to the learning of the entire procedure for the meditation subject from a teacher by a bhikkhu who wishes to begin the work of development.
Skill in that learning is “skill in learning. Furthermore, in this context, it means that one who is unable to learn everything should learn whatever he intends to undertake himself.
The complete procedure for that one [method] should be mastered. Regarding the phrase "of one who masters" (*uggaṇhantassa*), the vowel *u* has the sense of "subsequent.

And regarding the term "grasping" (*gahaṇaṃ*), the words "successively" (*uparūpari*) and so forth are stated to show that it is a grasping by the mind performed in such a way that it remains undestroyed within the mind.
Regarding the phrase "of one who contemplates" (*samanupassantassa*), [it means] correctly and repeatedly.
"For one who acts as if seeing with the eye. "Preparation" (*parikamma*) means performing [the action] all around, on every side.
What is meant is that, having completed whatever procedure is to be done regarding that work of grasping the sign, there is grasping.
By saying "repeatedly," etc., he shows the meaning of "development" (*bhāvanā*) as "increasing. "For one who strives without interruption."

For one who practices continuously day and night, even when grasping the configuration (*saṇṭhāna*) in the learning sign (*uggaha-nimitta*), he grasps it together with the essential nature (*sabhāva-dhamma*) consisting of color-form and so forth.

However, in the case of the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*), having let go of the essential nature, he grasps only the pure configuration, which is designated as the direction and sign. Here, it might be asked: even in the counterpart sign...
"It is true that what is called 'color' (vaṇṇa) is indeed visible. However, that is merely a counterpart (paṭibhāgamatta); it is not exclusively color. Therefore he said:
'The object which is its counterpart, liberated from [the concept of] phenomena (dhamma-vimuccita). 'Seated' (sannisinnaṃ) means immovable.
'Entered' (pavesitaṃ) means that it is as if placed within the mind of meditation; this is the intended meaning. It shines forth, thus it is 'illumination' (obhāsa). Illumination..."
“Having become manifest” (*obhāsajātaṃ*) means having become luminous. Alternatively, *obhāsa* is the act of shining; that which has produced such a shine is “having become manifest.

“They cause to fall back” (*pātentī*) means they cause them to fall away. They do not allow them to arise again by way of re-emergence. “By this” (*etāya*) is the instrumental case used in the sense of the agent.
“The method for guarding the sign” (*nimittarakkhaṇavidhānaṃ*) refers to the sevenfold [method] for the purpose of preventing the loss of the sign that has arisen.
For the purpose of guarding against obstructive conditions (*palibodha-dhamma*). But what are these seven kinds of obstructive conditions? We have nothing further to say on this matter here;
rather, to show that they have already been explained in the *Visuddhimagga*, he recited the verse:

"‘Habitat’ (*āvāsa*) means an unsuitable dwelling. ‘Range’ (*gocara*) means an unsuitable village for one’s range. ‘Speech’ (*bhassa*) means unsuitable talk. The same applies to persons (*puggala*) and so forth."
“Sevethā” means one should practice. “Evañhi paṭipajjato” means for one who practices by way of avoiding what is to be avoided and practicing what is to be practiced in this manner.

“Having transcended the state of being an object for sensual craving” by this is stated the transcendence of the sensual plane and sensual existence, as well as the descent from the form plane and form existence. “Vasanaṃ” means mastery (vasī). It means power (satti). It means capability (sāmatthiyaṃ).
*Attha*: "Vasibhūta" means having become masterful (*vasiṃ bhūtaṃ pattanti*). "Vasitā" means simply one who is masterful (*vasī eva vasitā*), just as in the term "pāramitā.
In the phrase "tato vicāranti," the word *iti* has the sense of "beginning" (*ādiattho*); by this, it includes the subsequent phrases such as "tato pītiṃ" and so forth.

"Icchantānaṃ tesaṃ sabbaññubuddhānaṃ" refers to those All-Knowing Buddhas who desire [to investigate]. "Yatthā" means "in which" two constituent parts of existence (*bhavaṅga*). "Bhavaṅgacāre" means during the occurrence of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅgappavattiyaṃ*).
“Slowness” (*dandhāyitatta*): it is called *dandhāyita* because it proceeds or functions slowly; the state of that is *dandhāyitatta*.
“To set aside” means to set aside having made a formal resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna*). “Not to exceed beyond that. “Wherever one wishes,” etc., are adverbial phrases.
“Wherever one wishes” means in whatever place according to one’s wish. “As one wishes” means in whatever [place].
"At whatever moment it accords with one's wish. "To the extent desired" means to whatever measure it accords with one's wish.

Regarding the phrase "for the abandoning of gross factors such as applied thought (*vitakka*)": by whose power does that abandoning occur? That abandoning occurs by the power of the cultivation of fading away (*virāga-bhāvanā*).
What, then, is this so-called cultivation of fading away? It is that which is embraced by a particular underlying intention (*ajjhāsaya-visesa*).
In order to show this meaning—that it is indeed the development of the preliminary stage (*upacāra-bhāvanā*)—the passage beginning with “First, as for the first jhāna” was stated.
Regarding “ardent energy” (*ātāpa-vīriya*): that energy by which the practitioner either exerts or torments himself, or exerts or torments the defilements, is called ardent energy.
Even when being opened up, it is simply space; having that as its object, there is the development [of the mind] for the arising of the subsequent jhānas.
Even as he practices again and again, that very fifth jhāna arises. And since the object has not been transcended, the jhāna itself likewise remains untranscended.
“Therein” means in that space-kasiṇa. “The possibility of transcending that” means the possibility of transcending the kasiṇa sign.
“As seen” means in the manner seen by the eye of jhāna. “Having considered” means...
"Having praised. "Right recollection" means thorough recollection. "Or of others as well" refers to wise worldlings (*puthujjana*).
The construction is: "In the determination of the perception of death, both the preliminary work (*parikamma*) becomes concentrated and access concentration (*upacāra*) is achieved.
Furthermore, according to the Commentary, even for worldlings of sharp wisdom, the attainment of access concentration is possible regarding the qualities of the Buddha and so forth.

It has already been stated. The phrase "in the jhānas of serenity" (samathajjhānesu) is spoken by way of topical reference (adhikāra). It should be understood that the work of insight (vipassanā-kamma) must also be included.

Some say that even one who has come after giving gifts previously and making a resolution, thinking, "By this merit, may I attain the jhānas and direct knowledges (abhiññā), or the paths and fruits (maggaphala), in the future," has indeed performed the preliminary service (katādhikāra). But which [is it]?
Regarding the phrase "one who has performed the preliminary work," he says "in a proximate existence" and so forth.

This is the supporting statement for those proponents who maintain that [the attainment occurs] among the eight types by way of the fourfold method, and among the nine types by way of the fivefold method; however, it must be accepted after due investigation.

Furthermore, even when one has attained the formless jhānas without the space-kasiṇa and subsequently performs the preparatory work for the sake of direct knowledge (abhiññā) regarding the space-kasiṇa...

Because it is possible for that [supernormal power] to be a basis for direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) since it is something that must be accomplished, it is said to be "possible" (*sambhava*) on account of the possibility of that meaning.

Furthermore, "one who has not previously developed meditation" and "one who has not performed the preliminary task" are identical in meaning. "A beginner" (*ādikammika*) means a beginner in the work of direct knowledge.
"Of such persons" refers to those who have not performed the preliminary task and have not developed meditation, thinking, "Now I shall perform a transformation by psychic power."

The connection is with "noble sons who are beginners in the work of direct knowledge (abhiññā) as they undertake it. Furthermore, the phrase "transformation by supernormal power" is an indicative term;
one should also include such things as "I shall hear sounds with the divine ear-element," and so forth.
This is stated because the present context concerns the procedure for beginners. For those who have attained mastery in the direct knowledges, that fifth jhāna—
It should simply be applied to whichever of the six sense objects is appropriate.

"It should be resolved" means it should be directed by the mind with the thought, "May there be a hundred! May there be a thousand! for the sake of accomplishing what is desired; that is to say, it should be brought forth.
This refers to the act of creating oneself as a hundred or a thousand, by way of resolving, "May I become a hundred," or "May I become a thousand."

This has been stated. As for the remainder, however, it is by way of creating something otherwise: either to hear a sound, or to see a visible form, or to know another’s mind, or to recollect a former existence.
In the reading of the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “He resolves (adhiṭṭhāti)” means he resolves by means of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).
It is said that he “resolves” in the sense of pervading or producing. For resolution is of two kinds: by way of preliminary work (*parikamma*)...
“Resolution through direct knowledge” means resolution by means of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*). Here, however, it is stated as resolution through direct knowledge.

By the phrase “resolution with the mind,” it is meant “with the mind of direct knowledge. “Of the preliminary-work mind” refers to the mind of the preliminary work (*parikamma*) consisting of adverting, the preliminary work, and the resolution-preliminary work at the prior stage.
The latter, however, is the attainment of the foundational jhāna (*pādakajjhāna*).
"It is said: 'For the purpose of concentrating the preliminary consciousness. To the question, 'What is the purpose when the preliminary consciousness is concentrated?

he says: 'For thus,' and so forth. "The remaining direct knowledges should also be explained as appropriate" means that regarding the preliminary work for the divine ear, it should be explained by saying:
"By means of that very preliminary concentration-knowledge of the ear, one hears even distant sounds belonging to the divine domain," and so on. "Having done thus" means:
Having reflected thus: “That” refers to the attainment of the final foundational jhāna (*pādakajjhāna*).
“It should be understood as not included here”—this is the intended meaning according to the Elder’s opinion.

However, since this section primarily concerns the procedure for a beginner, the attainment of the final foundational jhāna must indeed be mentioned. “Having resolved upon the body as the basis” means this body...
Having resolved by means of making the mind conform to the body’s movement, thinking, "May this mind also move slowly like this [body]," [one contemplates].
"By the visible body" means by the physical body that is seen by many people because it moves slowly.
By contrast, the fast movement should be understood. "It becomes a mere object" refers to unformed (non-material) form (*anipphanna-rūpa*).

It is said: “The object is pre-arisen. This refers to derived matter (*nipphanna-rūpa*). However, it should be understood that the other statement was made with reference to the heart-base matter (*hadaya-vatthu-rūpa*).

Since there is an investigation by the teachers of the *Aṭṭhakathā-ṭīkā* regarding the point of discerning the minds of others, the passage beginning with “And here, first, in the Aṭṭhakathā... was stated to show that. “In the Aṭṭhakathā” refers to the *Dhammasaṅgaṇi-aṭṭhakathā*.
In the *Aṭṭhakathā* as well, and in the *Visuddhimagga-aṭṭhakathā* as well: “By way of the momentary” means by way of the momentary present.
The connection is with the phrase “when the adverting [consciousness] has ceased. “One consciousness” refers to another person’s consciousness; they grasp that very same past consciousness.
“Those” refers to the impulsion moments (*javana*). “Of them” refers to the impulsion moments. “By that” refers to the adverting consciousness. “Otherwise” means...
If it were understood as being stated by way of continuity (*santati*) and duration (*addhā*), then it would be so stated. Why?

Because when the present is grasped by way of continuity and duration, all [moments] within a single cognitive series (*javana-vīthi*) constitute a single present. "All consciousnesses" refers to the impulsion-consciousnesses (*javana-citta*).
"Arising together" is said because of the co-existence even of those [factors] such as adverting (*āvajjana*) that arise simultaneously.
However, they do not grasp at a difference in time; they grasp every other's mind as if it were a single moment of consciousness.
Therefore, it should be understood that there is no difference in time either. It was said, "And Nibbāna"—how could Nibbāna be called "formerly dwelt in"?
When one recollects the paths and fruits of those who have attained final Nibbāna in the past, Nibbāna is also their object (ārammaṇa).
He simply recollects. In that context, because those paths and fruits have passed away, even Nibbāna is called "formerly lived.
"Whatever he resolves upon" means whatever quality, such as mindfulness and so forth, he prepares.
"In whatever way he resolves" means in whichever manner, such as by making himself visible and so forth, he prepares it. "Natural appearance" means the natural shape. "Of that very [person]" means...
Of the natural color itself. The connection is: "the ear of the devas' clarity. "Capable of receiving the object" means capable of receiving the manifestation of the object. The connection is:
that very same [ear] is also called "knowledge of others' minds" (*cetopariya-ñāṇa*).
"Mind" (*ceto*) means consciousness (*citta*). "Having discerned" means: "This is a mind with lust," "This is a mind free from lust," and so forth.
Having delimited [the time]. “By way of range and dwelling” means by way of making it one’s range and by way of dwelling there.
The intention is that this is the future cognition of the omniscient Buddhas, which falls within the scope of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).

Since mental states and mental factors (*cittacetasika-dhamma*) occurring within seven days of the future are the object (*visaya*) of the knowledge of others’ minds (*cetopariyaññāṇa*), it is stated as “within seven days of the future. Starting from...

The words "occurring" (*pavattamānā*) are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. Since all objects on this day and throughout the future fortnight are the domain of natural knowledge (*pakatiñāṇa*), it is said, "starting from the second day. "This" (*etaṃ*) refers to this future sign (*saññāṇa*).
"And just as this" (*yathā cetaṃ*) means just as this [knowledge] knows future phenomena in this present existence. "By way of uncommon time" (*asādhāraṇakālavasena*).
It is uncommon due to the factor of time, because the present existence is not shared by other forms of knowledge.
The exposition of the meditation subject for serenity (samatha-kammaṭṭhāna) is concluded. 171.

Regarding the meditation subject for insight (vipassanā-kammaṭṭhāna): “As it has been seen” means as it has been seen by the view of personal identity (sakkāyadiṭṭhi); [namely] the sign of permanence.

The name is merely a sign for the seven types of persons and so forth. For the sign of a "being" (satta-nimitta), because it is a mere designation (*paññatti*) and lacks destruction or change at every moment, it is established in a permanent form through such expressions as "he goes," "he stands," and so on. "A stable sign" (*dhuvanimitta*) means a firm sign.
This too is established in a firm form through such expressions as "even when he goes, he does not lose mindfulness; even when he stands, he does not lose mindfulness."

It is precisely the sign of a being (*sattanimitta*). “The sign of pleasure” (*sukhanimitta*) refers to the very sign of a being established in the mode of pleasure, such as by thinking, “I am happy, free from suffering, and fearless,” due to the absence of suffering characterized by destruction, decline, and dissolution at every moment.
“The sign of self” (*attanimitta*) refers to that which is established in the mode of exercising mastery, such as by thinking, “When desiring to go, I go; when desiring to stand, I stand.”
It is simply the sign of beings. “Action” (*kiriyā*) means the action of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
It is called purification (*visuddhi*) because it is purified, or because it purifies; thus, virtue itself is purification, which is “purity of virtue” (*sīlavisuddhi*).
Demonstrating this meaning, he said, “Virtue that is constant,” and so forth. Therein, virtue that is constant is the basis for the subsequent distinctions such as jhāna and the rest.

Because it accomplishes the task of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*), it is intended here; thus it is said, "only the perpetual precept" (*niccasīla*). Concentration (*samādhi*) is what is intended. For he will say:
"Both kinds of concentration are called purification of mind (*cittavisuddhi*). By this [concentration], one is purified; thus it is "purification.
Purification of the mind is "mind-purification. This also indicates that it is indeed concentration. Alternatively, purification is the act of being purified (*visujjhana*).
"Purification of mind" (*cittavisuddhi*) means the purification of the mind. However, it is also appropriate to say that, in terms of its actual meaning, it is simply the purified mind itself.
For when the word "purification" (*visuddhi*) is attached [to the end], it is called "purification of mind. It is not "purification by concentration" (*samādhivisuddhi*).
Regarding the phrase "sixteenfold doubt," this refers to what has come down in the Suttas, beginning with: "Was I indeed in the past? and so forth.
The sixteenfold doubt (*vicikicchā*). Or, "the eightfold perplexity" refers to the eightfold doubt as it appears in the Abhidhamma, beginning with "one is perplexed regarding the Teacher.
The "view of an uneven cause" is the view that grasps what is not a cause for the arising of beings as being the cause.
The "method of attention" refers to the method of attending to the characteristics of impermanence and so forth.
“Attention that is not a means” (anupāyabhūto manasikāro) refers to attention by way of [perceiving things as] permanent and so forth.

“Bases for overestimation” (adhimānavatthu) refers to the [meditative] illuminations and so forth. “As the path” (maggato) means by way of being the path; “not as the path” (amaggato) means by way of not being the path. “And the vision” (dassanañca) refers to the vision of impermanence and so forth regarding those bases for overestimation.
The connection is: “that very thing is called purification. “From the stain of delusion” (sammohamalato) refers to that which obscures the Four Noble Truths.

“From the stain of delusion. Is it not the case that “seeing” (*dassana*) is simply knowledge (*ñāṇa*)? This being so, he says “And here,” etc., because although the term “knowledge” is already established by itself, the phrase “knowledge-and-seeing” (*ñāṇadassana*) is used together with the word “seeing.
“By way of what consists of hearing and so forth” means by way of what consists of hearing (*sutamaya*) and what consists of reflection (*cintāmaya*).
Therein, the mere understanding of the meaning of the Dhamma of the scriptures as it has been heard is called “knowledge consisting of hearing. Having understood the meaning...

Knowledge that arises by way of reflecting upon the characteristic of the intrinsic nature (sabhāva-lakkhaṇa) corresponding to the meaning is called "knowledge consisting of reflection" (cintāmaya-ñāṇa).

Regarding the phrase "also knowledge such as inference," this refers to the knowledge of inferring the intrinsic nature and the knowledge of cognizing the intrinsic nature within the phenomena of name-and-form (nāmarūpa).

Regarding the phrase "only knowledge made manifest by oneself," this means only the knowledge that makes it manifest for oneself. Regarding the phrase "in all instances," this refers to [knowledges] such as the knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path (maggāmagga-ñāṇadassana), and so forth.

"In all instances. Here, it should be understood that the inclusion of the term "all" (*sabbattha*) is made because, even among the ten knowledges of insight (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*), by the word "insight" (*vipassanā*), only direct seeing (*paccakkha-dassana*) is intended.
For from the knowledge of comprehension (*sammasana-ñāṇa*) onwards, only seeing is intended, not merely the knowing of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
This is because [the object] is clearly seen only by one who sees with the eye.
In that regard, repeated cultivation (bhāvanā) must be undertaken as the work for the purpose of direct seeing (paccakkha-dassana).
"Dhammas" refers to conditioned phenomena (saṅkhata-dhammas). Impermanence itself is the characteristic; thus it is the "characteristic of impermanence" (anicca-lakkhaṇa).

Alternatively, it is also appropriate to call it the "characteristic of impermanent conditioned phenomena" (aniccānaṃ saṅkhata-dhammānaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ). "The mode of constant oppression" (abhiṇhasampaṭippīḷanākāra).
Just as a boat going upstream in this swift-flowing river is constantly and intensely oppressed by the suffering of volitional effort (*abhisaṅkhāra*), why?
Because in the absence of volitional effort, it would be swept downstream at that very moment.
For being swept downstream is the natural function of the boat; going upstream is accomplished only through volitional effort. In the same way...
In this swift-flowing saṃsāra, this personal existence (attabhāva) constantly and thoroughly oppresses the person who is being worn away moment by moment and day by day;
why? Because even when there is no volitional formation (abhisaṅkhāra) and the necessary conditions are deficient, it undergoes transformation at that very moment. For transformation—

The natural function of the personal existence (*attabhāva*) is downward movement; upward movement is accomplished through volitional formation (*abhisaṅkhāra*). In this way, the constant oppression should be understood.
