And here, the "rapidity of the stream" of saṃsāra refers to the swiftness of the arising and passing away of the material and mental phenomena included within the personal existence.
Furthermore, death here is twofold: conventional death and ultimate death.
And there is death. In this context, conventional death (*sammuti-maraṇa*) is the death of a being who exists as a conventional truth;

it is observed at the conclusion of a single existence (*ekabhava*). Ultimate death (*paramattha-maraṇa*) is the death of the phenomena of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-dhammā*) which exist as ultimate truths.
This alone is absolute death, true death, and death according to their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). In this regard...

In the context of insight (vipassanā), this ultimate death itself is called impermanence (aniccatā). It is also called the charnel ground of phenomena (dhammānaṃ susānakkhetta) and the cemetery site (susānabhūmi).
And that which is called the cemetery site follows the continuity of beings from the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) onwards.
Because it follows them, from the moment of beings' rebirth-linking, it is indeed...

There is no time when beings do not die. Furthermore, this constant following [of death] is itself a frequent oppression of beings, because they encounter confinement in all postures, as well as in their life, their limbs and members, and their bodily, verbal, and mental kamma.
However, for those who repeatedly experience the suffering of volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra-dukkha*) in the form of a lack of mastery over themselves—
This is indeed evident. When there is mastery (vasavattana), there is no opportunity for the function of volitional formation (abhisaṅkharaṇa-kicca).

This is because that function is accomplished exactly as desired through mastery alone. For in the world, all functions of volitional formation—even down to the function of inhaling and exhaling—are called such only because they perform their tasks by exercising mastery over phenomena.
The connection is: "the contemplation of the impermanent nature of phenomena" (*aniccassa dhammassa anuanupassanā*).
"Contemplation" (*anuanupassanā*) means repeated reflection and observation with the eye of wisdom. "Of phenomena" (*dhammānaṃ*) refers to the phenomena of the five aggregates.
"In whatever place" (*yattha yatthā*) means in whichever part of the body. "Of ancient phenomena" (*purāṇa-dhammānaṃ*) means of those that have long been manifest and have increased.
The disappearance of the constituent parts of phenomena (*dhamma*) is called their "passing away.

Having reached the task of insight (*vipassanā-kamma*), there is no further function of contemplation (*anupassanā*) by way of moments or by way of the analysis of individual phenomena; thus he said, "But by way of the mass and the continuity.
However, even the contemplation by way of the analysis of individual phenomena occurs in the case of consciousness, feeling, and so forth, which are naturally well-manifested.
It is indeed to be desired. "The ultimate limit of impermanence" means that there is no such thing as impermanence beyond that; this is the intended meaning.

The manner in which phenomena are to be feared in their various aspects refers to the manner of fearing taught regarding the five aggregates by way of "as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a tumor, as an arrow, as a misfortune, as an affliction," and so forth. The knowledge of contemplation (*samanupassanā-ñāṇa*) is the knowledge of that [fear].

Knowledge of fear (*bhayañāṇa*). By this it is shown that "fear" (*bhaya*) refers to that which people who are afraid of the suffering of the states of woe (*apāya*) and the suffering of *saṃsāra* ought to fear;
or, it is "fear" because they fear it. "Knowledge of the contemplation of fear" means knowledge that contemplates fear—this is the meaning shown.
"'Any object of fear' (*kiñci bhayavatthu*)" refers to objects of fear such as lions, tigers, and so forth. "'In a refuge' (*paṭissaraṇe*)" refers to caves, rock shelters, and so forth.
Regarding "refuge": "Of them" refers to those phenomena whose intrinsic nature is to break up; "by them" refers to those things whose intrinsic nature is to break up.
"Discontent" means a state of aversion in the mind, a tendency toward renunciation. "By way of forty aspects" refers to the five aggregates as:
impermanent, suffering, a disease, a tumor, a dart, a calamity, an affliction, alien, and subject to disintegration.
As subject to affliction, as a calamity, as fear, as a misfortune, as unstable, as fragile, as impermanent, as offering no refuge,
as providing no shelter, as affording no protection, as empty, as vain, as void, as non-self, as fraught with peril,
as subject to change, as pithless, as the root of suffering, as a murderer, as dissolution, as accompanied by taints, as conditioned, and as the bait of Māra.
"Seeing [them] as subject to birth, subject to aging, subject to sickness, subject to death, subject to sorrow,
lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, subject to vexation, and subject to defilement, one contemplates the world as empty"—
thus it is said in the *Mahāniddesa*, in the *Moghapañha-niddesa*, by way of these forty modes.
In this context, the passage beginning with "seeing the five aggregates as impermanent" and so forth should be applied accordingly.
"As impermanent" means by way of their impermanent nature; what is meant is that one sees all five aggregates as indeed impermanent.
But how is it that one who sees them as impermanent regards the world as empty? Because it is empty of the quality of permanence, one regards the world—which consists of the five aggregates—as empty.
He contemplates the world. The same method applies to the remaining phrases as well.

In that context, “only impermanent” means they are indeed impermanent because they are subject to death at any time from the moment of rebirth-linking onwards. “Only suffering” means they are indeed suffering precisely because they are impermanent phenomena;
for it has been said, “Whatever is impermanent, that is suffering. Or, it is because they are phenomena characterized by the truth of suffering. “Only diseases” means...

Because they are of the nature of disease, they are indeed diseases. Whatever various thousands of diseases known as "eye-disease" and so forth are seen in the world, all these are nothing other than these five aggregates (*pañcakkhandhā*).
There is no such thing as a "disease" apart from this. Therefore, they are exclusively of the nature of disease.
Furthermore, because they constantly afflict one with the three types of suffering inherent in the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*) and the four aspects of suffering, [they are called diseases].
In the sense of afflicting, they are simply diseases. Therein, "by three kinds of suffering" refers to these three kinds of suffering:
the suffering of suffering (*dukkha-dukkhatā*), the suffering of formations (*saṅkhāra-dukkhatā*), and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-dukkhatā*).

"By four meanings of suffering" refers to these four meanings of suffering: the meaning of oppression, the meaning of being conditioned, the meaning of burning, and the meaning of change. "By the functions of suffering" means...
This is the meaning. This method of analysis applies to the terms "boil" (gaṇḍa) and so forth. In this context, a "boil" refers to the disease of a carbuncle.
An "arrow" (salla) refers both to the arrow of defilement and the arrow of suffering, in the sense of piercing. "Misfortune" (agha) means that which is useless.
And these aggregates are indeed useless because they end in misfortune; for it has been said: "All successes end in misfortune. In the sense of being unreliable...

They are indeed other. For they do not deserve such confidence as: "This is mine, this am I, this is my self. Because for one who places such confidence in them, they constantly afflict with various forms of suffering.
From the moment of rebirth-linking onwards, because they are by nature subject to disintegration at any time, they are indeed of a disintegrating nature (*palokadhamma*).
"Calamity" (*ītī*) is said to mean an obstacle. [These refer to] the aggregates (*khandhā*).
It is said that they are indeed "obstacles" (*antarāya*). Because they have entered into the internal state, they are "calamities" (*upaddava*) due to their distressing and oppressive nature;

they are "fears" (*bhaya*) because they are things to be feared; and being themselves non-self (*anattā*), yet having entered into the internal state, they are "afflictions" (*upasagga*) because of their association with, clinging to, and causing of distress.
This is because they cause one to waver at all times through the worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*).
Because of their flickering nature, they are indeed unstable. Because they are subject to breaking apart in various ways, they are indeed fragile.
Because they do not remain steady for even a moment, they are indeed impermanent.

It is called a "refuge" (tāṇa) because it protects and guards one from fear, such as aging and death, or falling into the states of loss and ruin. Yet those aggregates are not a refuge for anyone, nor is there any refuge whatsoever in them. Therefore...
They are indeed without protection. A *leṇa* (refuge) is that wherein fearful people, being afraid, hide and take shelter;

yet they are not a refuge for anyone, nor do they possess anything called a refuge. Therefore, they are truly without refuge (*aleṇā*). That which one remembers in fear and which protects is a *saraṇa* (protection);
yet they are not a protection for anyone, nor do they possess anything called a protection. Therefore, they are without protection (*assaraṇā*).
It is exactly so. Because it is entirely devoid of all beautiful qualities such as permanence and the like, because it is hollow, empty, and void, it is indeed hollow;
it is indeed empty. "Self" (attā) is said to be that which is of the nature of an essence or a refuge for anyone whatsoever.
Those [aggregates] themselves do not belong to anyone as a self, nor does anything called a "self" exist for itself. Therefore, they are indeed non-self (anattā).
Because they are filled with defects such as impermanence and other dangers, they are indeed dangers (*ādīnavā*).

Because their intrinsic nature is subject to change, they are indeed subject to change (*vipariṇāmā*). Because there is no foundation whatsoever that constitutes a core, they are indeed coreless (*asārā*).

Because they are the basis for all that is useless and miserable, they are indeed the root of misery (*aghamūlā*). Being themselves possessed of the nature of death, by means of that sword of death...
Because they are constantly subject to Māra through the weapon of death, because they sever the life-faculty, they are indeed murderers.

Because they are devoid of constant happiness, welfare, and growth, they are indeed non-existences (*vibhava*). Because they are encompassed by the taints (*āsava*), they are indeed with-taints (*sāsrava*).
Because their existence at all times depends upon conditions, they are indeed conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Because they are the food and sustenance for the defilement-Māra and the death-Māra...

They are indeed the bait of Māra. Because they possess the inherent nature of being born as eye-disease and so forth, or as states of existence in the realms of misery (apāya-bhava) and so forth, even while one is unwilling [for them], they are indeed subject to birth (jāti-dhamma).
Because they possess the inherent nature of decay and death, even while one is unwilling [for them], they are indeed subject to aging and death (jarā-maraṇa-dhamma).

Because they maintain themselves as the objective basis for sorrow and so forth, they are indeed subject to sorrow and so forth (soka-ādi-dhamma). [They are also] the defilement of craving (taṇhā-saṃkilesa) and the defilement of views (diṭṭhi-saṃkilesa).
Because they are associated with the defilements of misconduct, these are called "defiled phenomena" (*saṃkilesika-dhammā*). Therefore it was said: "by way of forty modes.

"By way of reflection" (*paṭisaṅkhānavasena*) means by way of thorough investigation. "Of attachment" (*nikantiyā*) means of craving for attachment. "Being exhausted" (*pariyādinnāyā*) means having reached a state of dryness [or cessation].
"And fear" (*bhayañca*) refers to both the fear arising from the knowledge of danger (*bhayañāṇa*) and the dread of wrongdoing (*ottappa-bhaya*).
In the world, "self-life" (*attajīva*) refers to those things among the internal phenomena of sentient beings that are considered essential.
When these have departed, the remaining phenomena—having attained a state devoid of being and life—are regarded by the world as mere pithless wood or refuse.
Yet, since these so-called "self-lives" do not exist at all, the perception of the aggregates as mere refuse is the emptiness of self-life (*attajīva-suññatā*).
“Seeing” (dassana) is the name [of this knowledge]. By the phrase “being liberated” (vimuccamāno), it shows the meaning that “it liberates, therefore it is liberation” (vimokkho).
It is also appropriate to explain it as: “that by which they are liberated is liberation. “Signs” (nimittāni) refers to the signs constructed by the distorted states (vipallāsa-dhamma):
the sign of permanence, the sign of pleasure, the sign of self, and the sign of life; as well as the seven persons, woman, man, hand, foot, and head.

And there are the signs such as the neck and so forth. In this context, because formations are momentary phenomena, their very impermanence—due to the continuity of what is indeed impermanent being concealed by compactness—is the appearance in the form of permanence, such as "He was the same yesterday; he is the same today," and so on;
this is called the sign of permanence. Because they are enveloped by the stains of the defilements, it is precisely the impure things themselves that are concealed by ignorance.
The appearance of things in a beautiful aspect— such as "this is desirable, lovely, pleasing, dear"— is called the sign of beauty (*subhanimitta*).
Because it is concealed by that very [sign] even while there are sufferings in the sense of fear and insecurity, the appearance of things in a pleasant aspect—
such as "this is happiness, fearless, secure, agreeable"— is called the sign of pleasure (*sukhanimitta*).

Because they exist under the control of conditions, and because they exist solely by their own power in the absence of a condition, those things which are actually non-self appear in the mode of exercising mastery—such as acting, speaking, thinking, going when wishing to go, and standing when wishing to stand—according to one's own desire;
this appearance characterized by a self-sign (*attanimitta*) is what is meant. Likewise...
The appearance [of an object] in the mode of living—such as "this being lives for seven days," "it lives for a month," or "it lives for a year"—is called the sign of life (*jīvanimitta*).
Now, in such cases as "one acts according to one's own desire," what is this "desire"?
It is either craving (*taṇhā*) or volition (*chanda*). Both of these are associated with consciousness. Furthermore, "acting" refers to those things that constitute bodily activity.
It is a specific mode of occurrence of the groups of material phenomena born of mind (*cittaja-rūpa-kalāpa*).
This being so, because they occur by way of the mind, the statement "one acts according to one's own desire" is not contrary to the Abhidhamma. It is not that it is not contrary;

for the words "one's own" (*attan*) and "acts" (*karoti*) have been used. Indeed, there is no such thing as a "self" (*attā*) that could be called "one's own. Nor is there a so-called "agent" (*kattā*).

There is that which might be called "the one who acts. However, in this context, it is the pentad of aggregates (khandhapañcaka) occurring at that moment which is grasped as "self" and "agent," and thus it is said to be "the self" and "to act.
"Becomes a support" means it becomes a foundation. "Having dispelled" means having made them disappear through knowledge.
It is by means of the knowledge of vision (*dassana-ñāṇa*) that [one sees] they do not exist by way of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
"Having brought it to a definitive conclusion" is what is meant. "The vision of non-existence" means the vision of the absence of sorrow, suffering, and so forth.
"By way of resolving each respective compactness" means by way of breaking up and cutting through the compactness, continuity, and so on of the aggregates.
Among these, the breaking up of the compactness of the aggregate is the function of the knowledge of the definition of phenomena at the outset. At that time, the view of self is suppressed.
It exists. Furthermore, the view of a living soul (*jīvadiṭṭhi*) is said to be nothing other than a more subtle form of the view of self (*attadiṭṭhi*).

It should be understood that upon reaching the moment of the Path (*magga-kkhaṇa*), both of these are completely eradicated. "Of one whose virtue is directed" (*paṇihitaguṇassa*) means of one whose virtue is aspired to.
Regarding the term "Pātimokkha": here, "pati" refers to the elder or the preeminent; "mukhaṃ" refers to the primary cause. And "pati" [also implies]...
"Facing toward" (*patimukha*) means "facing toward" (*abhimukha*). Showing that the meaning of *pātimokkha* is precisely "facing toward," he said, "For that... and so forth.

The "all-worldly virtues" (*sabbalokiyasīla*) are the fourfold pure virtues (*catupārisuddhisīla*). "In their midst" means among those. "Because of being the eldest" (*jeṭṭhakattā*) means because it is the eldest virtue.
"That very same" refers to the virtue of the Vinaya formulation itself. "Of which phenomena" refers to restlessness, forgetfulness, and so on.
“Of phenomena. “They are called ‘fluctuations’ (vipphanditāni)” means they are scattered; this is the intended meaning. Therefore he said, “they are called ‘restless’ (lolāni).

“Following after those” means following after those very fluctuations of the sense faculties. “By what is censured by the Buddha” means by what has been rejected and forbidden by the Blessed One, the Buddha.
“By wrong applications” means by the acts of defiling the eight families and by the twenty-one kinds of improper search (anesanā).

“By the three bases of hypocrisy”: by these three bases of hypocrisy, namely, the seeking of requisites (*paccayappaṭisevana*), indirect hinting (*sāmantajappana*), and behavior based on deportment (*iriyāpathasannissita*). What is meant is: “by the three kinds of methods of astonishing acts.
It is purified; thus it is *parisuddhi*. *Pārisuddhi* is simply purification. “Of delusion” (*sammohassa*).
For one who is confused regarding the attention to the elements (*dhātumanasikāra*) and so forth:

"Of greed" means, due to that very confusion, of the greed of one who has cast food [into the bowl] among the conditions, of one who longs for it. "Of intoxication" means of the intoxication of pride rooted in gain, honor, and so forth.
"Of negligence" means of negligence and forgetfulness regarding wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*). Its respective purpose is the limit.
Regarding the requisite of robes (*cīvarapaccaya*), first, the purpose (*payojana*) is the warding off of cold and so forth; this is the "limit" (*ariyāda*).
The term "limit" refers to the boundary for the use of robes, such as warding off cold, which is indicated by the phrase "only to that extent.

And this limit is established so that one does not fall into the side of the blameworthy, such as delusion (*sammoha*) and greed (*gedha*) regarding the requisite of robes. Therefore it was said: "of delusion and greed..."
"For the purpose of abandoning intoxication and negligence. This same method applies to the requisites such as alms-food and so forth.

By this, the meaning is shown in the formulas of reflection (*paccavekkhanā*). Here, when it is said that "a bhikkhu uses a robe only for warding off cold, for warding off heat," and so on—it is only for the purpose of warding off cold that he uses it; not beyond that, for the sake of delusion.

"He uses it for the sake of greed, for the sake of intoxication, and for the sake of negligence," and so forth. This being the case, whatever robe, when used by one, gives rise to delusion, greed, intoxication, or negligence—that should not be used;
the other [type] is shown to be what should be used. "Individual nature" (*paccattasabhāvo*) means its specific, distinct nature.
"Designated as an effect" (*kāriyasaṅkhātaṃ*) means that which is to be done, that which is to be accomplished.
It is the effect. It has its fruit near at hand. Therefore he said, "Just as smoke is to fire. The proximate cause is called the *padatthāna* (footing). It is like the maker of the fire.
That by which the fruit proceeds, goes, or occurs is the *pada*.
That wherein the fruit stands is the *ṭhāna*. Both are merely synonyms for the cause. Because of this, even the sense of "excess" (*atisaya*) is established; thus he said:
“Proximate cause”: the intention is that this refers to those associated with views, [as stated] in the phrase “together with the perversions of perception and mind.
However, it cannot be said that perceptions and mental perversions dissociated from views are capable of being suppressed.
“In the teachings of the Dispensation” means in the teaching-dharma connected with the phenomena of emptiness, such as the *Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta* and others.
“‘The perversion of view has been suppressed’: having heard such a teaching on the Dhamma, and having gained faith in the Teacher who expounded it and in the Dhamma so taught, one realizes:
‘The Blessed One spoke the truth; however, I grasp at this as “this is mine,” “I am this,” and “this is my self”;
this grasping of a self is a wrong practice. In this way, [the perversion] is suppressed. From that point onward...”
Even when one says, "This is my self," one does not say so with a consciousness associated with wrong view (*diṭṭhi-sampayutta-citta*);
the intention is that one says it only with a consciousness dissociated from wrong view (*diṭṭhi-vippayutta-citta*). Furthermore, this [insight] is merely the suppression of firm grasping;

it is not the suppression of the vision of a self. They also say that this is accomplished only when the knowledge of the discernment of phenomena (*dhamma-vavatthāna-ñāṇa*) has been established. Of the four...
Name-and-form should indeed be comprehended by way of the four kinds of nutriment. Why?

Because the intention is that for one who, having comprehended the four nutriments, contemplates the three characteristics within them, the task of attaining supramundane knowledge and vision at the end is accomplished.
This same method applies to the sections beginning with "fivefold," and so on. It is not the domain of beginners; [it must be done] separately, separately.
Because it is impossible to comprehend [the aggregates] by way of their characteristics, functions, and so forth;

and even for one capable of such comprehension, because it is impossible to discern them individually during the work of insight (vipassanā). For he will say later: "having condensed them by way of groups.
"Of anything else" means of such things as a self or a soul. He performs wholesome and unwholesome kamma. He experiences [the result].
Having reached another existence, one experiences its result; one wanders from one state of becoming to another, hurled by the force of karma. The construction is:
"It is for the purpose of showing the absence of striving and activity in either name alone or form alone.

The analysis (*viggaha*) is: "The designation of the activity of persons and beings. "The view that occurs as 'self'" refers to the agent-view (*kāraka-diṭṭhi*). "By way of adherence to that [view] as its object" refers to the following.

Because conventional designations such as "being" (satta) and "person" (puggala) do exist, that which constitutes their referent—namely, the being, the person, and so forth—also exists by way of its own-nature (sabhāva).
It is not non-existent; this is [the meaning] by way of firmly establishing [this view] in the heart.

"And 'overreaching' (atidhāvana)" means that, instead of remaining within the mere conceptual designation of conventional usage, one goes beyond it and grasps the five aggregates as being a "being" and so forth; this is the intended sense.
In the phrase “by way of kamma, consciousness, temperature, and nutriment,” the letter *ka* is an augment (*āgama*) due to euphonic combination (*sandhi*).

The meaning is: by way of kamma, by way of consciousness, by way of temperature, and by way of nutriment. The analysis (*viggaha*) is: “the concurrence of appropriate conditions. “By way of occurrence in another manner” means by way of proceeding in a different mode. “By causes, requisites, and conditions” refers to the condition of cause (*hetupaccaya*).

By means of the conditions of equipment (*sambhāra-paccaya*). Those which are productive conditions (*janaka-paccaya*) are called root conditions (*hetu-paccaya*). Those which are accompanying conditions (*parivāra-paccaya*) are called conditions of equipment (*sambhāra-paccaya*).
"Of the occurrence of kamma" means from the occurrence of kamma. "Of the occurrence of fruition" means from the occurrence of fruition.
For a single being wandering through the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), there is both a material body (*rūpa-kāya*) and a mental body (*nāma-kāya*).
Apart from these, there is no other such entity called a "self. Furthermore, for one wandering in saṃsāra within the five-aggregate realm, both bodies (the material and the mental) function together.
For one wandering among the non-percipient beings (*asaññasatta*), only the material body functions; that alone is reckoned there as "one being.
For one wandering in the formless realm (*arūpa*), only the mental body functions; that alone is reckoned there as "one being."
It "goes into reckoning. The intended meaning of "it goes into reckoning" is that it becomes a mere designation (*paññatti*).
Furthermore, among those bodies, there is no mutual immediate conditionality (*anantara-paccayatā*) between death and rebirth-linking within the material body (*rūpa-kāya*).
Having existed as a single unit in each respective birth, it disintegrates at the time of death; the continuity of matter (*rūpa-santati*) is severed. By means of the rebirth-linking form...
The continuity of the relationship between condition and conditioned state does not proceed together [with the body].

However, in the case of the mental aggregate (*nāmakāya*), there exists a mutual immediate-condition relationship between death and rebirth-linking. Even at the moment of death, the mental continuum (*nāmasantati*) is not severed.

Rebirth-linking proceeds precisely as a continuity of the relationship between condition and conditioned state together with the mental aggregate. In this regard, it is dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
A skilled bhikkhu, standing in the knowledge of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), while observing the process of a single being within a single existence, does not perceive a "being.
He does not perceive a "person" (*puggala*). He does not perceive an "I," nor does he perceive a "you.
He does not perceive that "I was" in past existences, nor does he perceive "I am" in this present existence.

He does not see [them] as "I shall be" regarding the future. Rather, he sees only their uninterrupted occurrence by way of the succession of cause and effect among the phenomena of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), according to the method beginning with: "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) proceed; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness (*viññāṇa*) proceeds in another existence," and so forth.
When there is the seeing of the process within a single existence,
In this beginningless saṃsāra, amidst infinite states of existence, the course of that being’s wandering has indeed been seen:
"there too it was exactly thus; there too it was exactly thus. At that time, his sixteenfold doubt is abandoned. Showing this meaning, [the Blessed One] said:
"In this beginningless saṃsāra," and so forth. Therein, what is the sixteenfold doubt? It is: "I existed..."
"Was I indeed in the past? Was I not indeed in the past? What was I indeed in the past? How was I indeed in the past?
Having been what, what was I indeed in the past?"—thus is the fivefold doubt expressed regarding the prior limit (*pubbanta*).
"Shall I indeed exist in the future? Shall I not indeed exist? What shall I indeed be?"
"How indeed shall I be? Having been what, what indeed shall I become in the future time?"—thus the fivefold doubt regarding the future has been stated. "Do I exist? Do I not exist?
What indeed am I? How indeed am I? From where have I come as this being? Where will I go?"
Thus, six kinds of doubt regarding the present have been stated. These constitute the sixteen kinds of doubt. In this context, by means of the two phrases "Did I exist?
and "Did I not exist?", one doubts whether or not there was a state of being or non-being for oneself in the past.
If it did exist, one then doubts: "In what way did I exist?"—whether I existed through some cause or condition. Or [did I exist] through some...
The meaning is: "I was either created by one possessing psychic power (*iddhimant*), or I was born of myself, uncreated and without cause or condition.
If I existed through any one of those benefactors, how indeed did I exist?
Was I footless, or two-footed, or four-footed, or many-footed? Was I material (*rūpin*) or immaterial (*arūpin*)? Was I percipient (*saññin*) or non-percipient (*asaññin*), and so forth?
Then, among those such as the footless and so forth, I was one of them. Having been what, did I become what?
Having been what in the first existence, did I become what in the second existence and so on? This is stated by way of the succession of existences (*bhavaparamparā*).
This same method applies to the future as well. Regarding the present: "Do I exist, or do I not exist?"—as in the *Khuddakavatthuvibhaṅga* among the eight hundred modes of craving's wandering.
It is said: "I am eternal" and "I am annihilated. In this context, "I am eternal" means "I exist eternally," and "I am annihilated" means "I exist as one who has been cut off.
Furthermore, it is said: "To say 'it exists' is one extreme; to say 'it does not exist' is the second extreme.
In this context, "it exists" means that what is called the self exists at all times throughout various states of existence.
“‘It does not exist’ (natthi): it is thus non-existent; it is annihilated. The meaning is that ‘it does not exist after death.
Likewise here too, one wavers, thinking: ‘Do I indeed exist? Or do I not indeed exist? In that context, ‘Do I indeed exist? means:
‘Does this one called “I” always exist throughout successive states of becoming? Does my so-called self exist for all time, having been eternal? Thus it is said.”
“Do I not exist? means: “Do I not exist in such a way? The meaning is: “Does my self not exist in such a way?

And here, in the phrase “in various states of existence,” it should be understood that even though this refers to the present continuity (*pavatta*), the present self currently existing is included within the present.
“What indeed am I? means: having been born as one called “I,” what am I?

"Am I now? Is it by some cause or condition that I am? Or am I perhaps created by some possessor of psychic power (*iddhimant*)? Or rather, am I without cause or condition, or uncreated by anyone, or do I exist of my own accord?"—this is the meaning.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "How indeed am I?", this is not to be construed with [the categories] such as the footless (*apada*), but rather: "What indeed am I?"
"I shall belong to the Gotama clan," or "I am of the Gotama clan or the Vāseṭṭha clan"—thus it should be connected. At the beginning of the eon, those clans were distinct;
nowadays they have become intermingled. Therefore, one who doubts regarding them merely continues to doubt.
"From where have I come? means: from what state of existence did I come in the past? "To where will I go? means: to what destination will I go? Thus, he [reflects].
He doubts: "Where will I go in a future existence? Regarding the phrase "the overcoming of doubt":
that bhikkhu, seeing the five past causes beginning with ignorance within dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), sees the entire dependent origination in that very existence.
Seeing it thus, he realizes: "There is no such thing as 'I' there, depending upon which [a self] would relate to the past objects."
Fivefold doubt arises. By seeing the non-existence of the basis [of self] in the past through the thought, "There was only mere phenomena there," one transcends this fivefold doubt.
But surely, even for one who sees in that way, this doubt still exists: "How indeed was I? Having been what, what was I? Even for one who sees in that way...

For indeed, without the knowledge of past abodes (*pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa*), one neither knows nor sees whether, in a past existence, "I was bipedal" or "I was quadrupedal," or that "having passed away from there, I was reborn in such-and-such a state. It is said in reply:

however, once the mere manifestation of the phenomenon (*dhammamattappavatti*) has been seen, that doubt (*kaṅkhā*) is no longer an obstructive doubt; it is merely a semblance of doubt (*vicikicchā-paṭirūpikā*).

Indeed, for that [knowledge] is indeed obtained by the Noble Ones as well. Likewise, seeing the fivefold fruit in the future, one transcends the fivefold doubt regarding the future limit (*aparanta*).
Seeing both the fivefold fruit and the fivefold cause in the present, one transcends the sixfold doubt regarding the present.
All the rest is exactly according to the method already stated concerning the past limit (*pubbanta*). [End of] the eightfold...
Furthermore, upon transcending doubt, one who perceives dependent origination in both forward and reverse order transcends doubt regarding the teaching and regarding supramundane states.
Simultaneously with the transcendence of doubt regarding the Dhamma, one also transcends doubt regarding the Teacher while he is teaching,
regarding the Saṅgha as they practice according to the instructions, regarding the three trainings, and regarding the past limit as it has been described.
Furthermore, regarding the future, and both the past and the future, one transcends all doubt concerning dependent origination together with dependently originated phenomena.
Therefore, he said: "In the occurrence of phenomena according to their own nature," and so forth.
In that context, "in the occurrence of phenomena according to their own nature" means the successive occurrence of phenomena according to their own nature by way of a succession of conditions.
Furthermore, "the nature of things" (*dhammatā*) among phenomena refers to the beautiful nature of the Teaching by way of its being well-expounded and so forth;
it is the faultless nature of the Dhamma. "The perfect enlightenment of the Buddha" refers to the omniscient Buddhahood of the Buddha when teaching that Dhamma.
"The suppression of obsessed views and doubt" refers to [the suppression] by means of the aforementioned discernment of phenomena (*dhammavavatthāna*).

And it is accomplished by means of the discernment of conditions (*paccayapariggaha*). However, insight meditation (*vipassanā*) is practiced for the purpose of extracting the arrows of underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) consisting of views and doubt;
thus it is said, "and for the purpose of uprooting the underlying tendencies," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "But therein," it refers to that Path of Discrimination (*paṭisambhidā-magga*). The words "in the analyzed" (*vibhatteṣu*) are a supplement to the text. "Of whom" refers to the practitioner (*yogī*), the individual.
“Whether far or near”: the remainder of the reading is “whether form occurring at a distance, or form occurring nearby.
“But for the purpose of that”: for the purpose of extracting the phenomena already comprehended. “Having grasped firmly with knowledge”:

the intention is that one has made it well-manifest by means of the knowledge of the definition of phenomena (*dhammavavatthāna-ñāṇa*). Now, whatever is to be grasped firmly, that [should be stated] according to its specific nature.

He said “therein,” etc., in order to show this. Furthermore, he said “and that activity,” etc., in order to show the characteristic of impermanence (*aniccalakkhaṇa*) of matter that has been firmly grasped.
“They perish” means they break up; they go toward impermanence. Regarding the term “the activity of distension” (*vitthambhanakriyā*):
here, “distension” (*vitthambhana*) is a firming apart in various ways; it is a firming apart by way of facing toward various directions.
“Carry” is the meaning. “And of these” refers to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

Because they are stated separately and individually, it is possible for them to be included among the co-nascent factors (*sahajāta*) as mutual [supports]; thus it is said, “of water and so forth. The meaning is: “of water and so forth, and of the remaining great elements.
“Continuity-bodies” (*santati-sarīra*) means bodies that are a continuity. “Having fashioned in such and such ways” refers to material phenomena (*rūpa-dhamma*).

What is called "the turning of the continuity" (santati-parivatti) would occur thus for one walking forward, would occur thus for one walking backward, and likewise for one contracting or extending [the limbs], having thus imagined it.
Regarding the phrase "in the remaining aggregates too, there is such-and-such a diversity of continuity":
first, in the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-khandha), there is the diversity of the bodily-pleasure continuity and the bodily-pain continuity within the body.
In the mind, there are successions of joy and grief; however, the succession of equanimity remains unmanifested. One must infer it by means of conjecture:
when joy and grief do not appear in the mind, one should conjecture, "Now my feeling of equanimity is occurring";
and when they do appear, one should conjecture, "It has ceased. Thus one should reason.
"It should be rightly understood" is what is meant. In the case of the aggregate of perception (*saññā-khandha*), this is by way of the perception of forms, the perception of sounds, and so forth.

In the case of the aggregate of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra-khandha*), it is by way of volition regarding forms, volition regarding sounds, and so forth; by way of various types of applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), and so forth;

and by way of greed and non-greed, hatred and non-hatred, delusion and non-delusion, and so forth. In the case of the aggregate of consciousness (*viññāṇa-khandha*), it is by way of eye-consciousness and the rest, as well as wholesome and unwholesome consciousnesses, and so forth.
The diversity of continuity (santati-nānatta) is to be understood by way of this. Having stated, "He places his trust," he explains that meaning with the words, "This is mine," and so forth.
Therein, there are three kinds of trust: the trust of craving (taṇhā-vissāsa), the trust of conceit (māna-vissāsa), and the trust of views (diṭṭhi-vissāsa).
Among these, "This is mine" is the trust of craving; "I am this" is the trust of conceit; "This is my self" is the trust of views. "He maintains [it]"—
Having grasped them amidst various states of existence, it carries them away and bears them along.

“By way of the supreme internal state”: by way of the preeminent internal state; what is meant is, “by way of the essential internal state. “Grasped”: grasped by the grasp of views, thinking “this is my self.
For there are three kinds of grasping: the grasp of craving, the grasp of conceit, and the grasp of views.

Showing that what is called "existing entirely" would mean existing solely under the control of one's own will (*vasāyatta-vuttika*) and not under the control of conditions (*paccayāyatta-vuttika*), he says, "by those as previously stated," and so forth.
Therein, "as previously stated" refers to the formations of kamma and so on, in the manner described in the *Sabbasaṅgaha*.
"To be grasped in such a way" means to be grasped as "this is my self" by way of its supreme internal state (*paramajjhattabhāva*).
It must be comprehended as such. For indeed, one who acts according to his own will possesses no ownership over himself.
And regarding those phenomena such as form (rūpa) over which there is no ownership, to take oneself as the owner and grasp them with the thought "This is my self" is truly a misconception.
Likewise, whatever phenomenon is momentary and perishes moment by moment—
Taking that pentad of aggregates beginning with form as one’s own essence, such grasping is likewise indeed wrong.
And here, the phrase “indeed wrong” means it is wrong in relation to ultimate truth (*paramattha-sacca*); what is meant is that it is a perversion (*vipallāsa*).
“It destroys happiness” means it destroys both bodily happiness and mental happiness; it annihilates them. “Various sufferings... [The text continues:]... [it brings about] various sufferings.
It "generates" means it produces and gives rise to both bodily suffering and mental suffering. How is it that "this form becomes exactly like this"?
For beings established in a human existence, it destroys their human happiness as it occurs, reduces them to a state of decay and ruin, and generates manifold sufferings.
Having itself taken on an existence in the woeful states (*apāya*), [it causes others to do so].

It produces various sufferings of the states of misery for them. Likewise, it should be stated regarding those established in the state of a deity, the state of Sakka, the state of a Brahmā, and so forth.
Similarly, for those established in the human state, it destroys the happiness that occurs according to its course through various functions of transformation;
and through various functions of constructing conditions, it generates various sufferings. Therefore it was said: “And this...”

“Form is just like this. By the statement, “‘Essence’ (sāra) refers to a particular excellence of strength and power,” it includes the physical basis endowed with that particular excellence of strength and power.
Regarding the phrase “in the sense of being without essence” (asārakaṭṭhena): here, “essence” itself is “essenceness” (sārakaṃ);
“not having essenceness” is “without essence” (asāraka). With reference to this meaning, it is said: “But form itself is not such an essence.”
The meaning is that for beings, there is no essence consisting of a self (*attasāra*) or an essence consisting of a soul (*jīvasāra*).
With reference to the meaning "that which has no essence is 'essenceless' (*asāraka*)," it was said: "nor is it endowed with such an essence.
The meaning is that it is conjoined with an essence of self and an essence of soul. Therein, the former meaning was stated with reference to the passage: "one regards form as self."
This was said with reference to these three: "the self possessing form," "form within the self," or "the self within form.
By the phrase "in the sense of being without essence" (*asārakaṭṭhena*), it means by way of the state of lacking essence, or by way of being connected with what is without essence.

Regarding the term "non-self" (*anattā*), two meanings are established: either "that which is not a self is non-self," or "that in which there is no self is non-self. "And that which... (*yañcā*)... [text fragment].

And as for that form which "oppresses," it oppresses the person who possesses it. By this, he shows that once its lack of selfhood (*anattabhāva*) is established, its state of suffering (*dukkhabhāva*) is also established.
Regarding the statement, "The division of time should be applied by way of the three stages of life": form occurring in the first stage of life does not reach the second stage of life;
it ceases right within the first stage of life, and so forth—thus, in the case of the temporally present (*addhāpaccuppanna*).

The internal division should be applied [as follows]: “By way of a homogeneous and single continuity (*sabhāgekasantāna*)” means that the continuity of homogeneous phenomena, having become one in the sense of being homogeneous, is a “homogeneous and single continuity.

Regarding the phrase “of homogeneous phenomena,” those material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*) that arise simultaneously with a greed-associated consciousness proceeding without interruption among the mind-born [phenomena] are called “homogeneous material phenomena. The same applies to mental phenomena (*nāmadhamma*).

And so it is with those associated with hatred and the rest. Among the seasonal (utu) phenomena, those material phenomena produced by a cold season that occurs continuously are called "similar material phenomena" (*sabhāga-rūpa*).

Likewise for those produced by a hot season. This same method applies to those born of nutriment (*āhāraja*) as well; thus it is according to the continuity of similar classes. "To attain" means to attain through knowledge.
Regarding the phrase "by way of the continuity of time," here it refers to the continuity (*santati*).
Comprehension by way of reflection (*sammasana*) is specifically intended here.
By doing so, the method for analyzing the continuity of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) has been clearly demonstrated in the preceding passage on impermanence in the sense of destruction.

Furthermore, in this knowledge as well—as in the knowledge of arising and passing away (*udayabbaya-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of dissolution (*bhaṅga-ñāṇa*)—the perception of the characteristic of impermanence alone is paramount.
In the knowledge of fear, the knowledge of danger, and the knowledge of disenchantment, the vision of the characteristic of suffering is predominant.

In the four subsequent knowledges, the vision of the characteristic of non-self is predominant. Regarding the phrase "when arisen together": this refers to those things that have arisen together through mutual inseparability and association.
And herein, with the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of form; with the arising of craving, there is the arising of clinging.
"From the arising of nutriment comes the arising of form"—this is stated according to the canonical text (*pāḷi*). Regarding the phrase "by way of not having been abandoned":

in the canonical passage, it should be understood that the mere fact of ignorance, craving, and the underlying tendency to views existing within the continuum (*santāna*) by virtue of their being unabandoned is the criterion.
"They arise together" (*samudenti*) means they emerge from the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) as one; they come on top of one another. The meaning is that they arrive.
The intention is that they manifest by way of a single existence (*ekabhavabhāvena*). Therefore, he said: "until the time of death," and so forth.
"Flowing forth" (*pasavantī*) means increasing, flowing, proceeding, or streaming. "But among those" refers to ignorance, craving, clinging, and karma.
"Cease" means they cease within that very existence; cessation in that existence is [what is meant], not in another existence.
"Non-arising once again" is what is meant by the phrase "in another existence," and so forth. "In that continuity" means "in this present existence.
"Cessation known as non-arising once again" refers to what is called the cessation of the continuity (*santati-nirodha*), not the cessation that is *nibbāna*.
[The implication is: "If these conditions exist, they will certainly arise again in another existence. Now, as it has occurred...
When speaking of the meaning as the momentary cessation of all final instances of name-and-form included within the continuities, it is said:
"The continuities, as they have proceeded, are cut off and broken. Regarding the phrase, "And for one who contemplates rise and fall":
what is called "rise," what is called "fall," and how does he contemplate both of them?
He said: “Regarding ‘one who sees rise and fall,’ here [the meaning] is as follows,” and so forth. In that context, “a mass of darkness” (*tamo-khandho*) means a heap of darkness.
“It vanishes” (*veti*) means it disappears. “It fades away” (*antaradhāyati*). “Rise” (*udayo*) means both arising and increase. “Fall” (*vayo*) means passing away, disappearance.
“Or by way of various applications” (*nānāpayogavasena vā*) means by way of various applications such as contracting and extending. Of the factors belonging to the side of rise...

The construction is: "the arising of various successions from the perspective of arising, and the passing away of various successions belonging to the side of decay from the perspective of passing away.

Because he is endowed with the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*), he brings his own mind to fulfillment; thus it is "undertaken" (*āraddha*). The meaning is "one whose mind is joyful. One who sees clearly is a "clear-seeing one" (*vipassaka*).
Being undertaken and being a clear-seeing one is "one whose clear-seeing is undertaken" (*āraddhavipassaka*). For there are two kinds of clear-seeing ones.
There are two types: the one with nascent insight (*taruṇa-vipassaka*) and the one with established insight (*āraddha-vipassaka*).
Among these, the one who does not clearly perceive the arising and passing away of the aggregates is called "one with nascent insight," being weak in insight.

The one who clearly perceives the arising and passing away of the aggregates, whose mind has attained proficiency in the work of insight, and who is strong in insight, is called "one with established insight. It is with reference to this that it was said.
[Ka] “For a bhikkhu who has entered an empty dwelling, whose mind is peaceful,
there is a superhuman delight as he clearly sees the Dhamma. Thus it was said.
[Kha] And:
"Better than living for a hundred years without seeing rise and fall is a single day's life for one who sees rise and fall."
This is what is intended here. They defile by approaching insight (*vipassanā*); they cause it to reach a state of being soiled—thus they are "defilements of insight" (*vipassanūpakkilesa*).
They obstruct and hinder—thus they are "obstructions" (*paribandhaka*); this is precisely the name for the "states that are obstacles" (*antarāyika-dhamma*) mentioned below.
"Radiance of the body" (*sarīrobhāsa*) is the radiance issuing forth from the entire body. "Fivefold rapture" (*pañcavidhā pīti*) refers to minor rapture (*khuddikā pīti*), and so on.
Momentary joy (*khaṇikā pīti*), showering joy (*okkantikā pīti*), uplifting joy (*ubbegā pīti*), and pervading joy (*pharaṇā pīti*).

"Twofold tranquility" refers to the exceedingly powerful bodily tranquility (*kāyapassaddhi*) and mental tranquility (*cittapassaddhi*). Faith that functions in the mode of conviction regarding the work of insight (*vipassanā-kamma*) is itself resolution in the sense of being decisive;
thus it is "resolution through faith" (*saddhā-adhimokkha*). "Energy" (*vīriya*) [is applied] to that same work.
“Unrelenting energy” means energy that has taken up the burden and held fast at the head. “Happiness” refers to mental happiness; therefore, he says “joy.
“Insight-knowledge” refers to powerful insight-knowledge, like a thunderbolt hurled by Indra.
“Mindfulness” is the mindfulness that does not forget that task. “Equanimity regarding the middle” [refers to] the mind’s state free from the imbalances of dullness, agitation, and so forth.
“Liberated” refers to equanimity (upekkhā) characterized by mental neutrality. “Adverting-equanimity” (āvajjanupekkhā) refers to the equanimity characterized by adverting that has attained mastery.

“Attachment” (ālaya) means attachment consisting of craving (taṇhā). “Making” (kurumānā) means performing. “Subtle craving” (sukhumā taṇhā) refers to subtle craving that cannot even be recognized as unwholesome because it is mixed with wholesome states. “Indeed not mine” (na vata me) means [not mine].
The construction is: "never arisen before. "Accompanied by gratification" means accompanied by craving for gratification regarding the [meditative] illumination and so forth.
"By way of overestimation" means by way of conceiving it as something superior. "At that very moment" means at the very instant of the arising of attachment.
"The mode of longing" means the mode of desiring; the mode of finding gratification. "The basis for longing" means the object of attachment. "Certainly" means exclusively.
“Handā” is a particle used to express the relinquishing of the mind. It indicates this meaning: “I shall purify this very now; I will not allow it to continue for long.
“Tesveva” means “in those very [states],” namely, light and so forth. This does not agree with the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā).
The intention is that in the Commentary, “craving” (nikanti) is mentioned separately from suppression (vikkhambhana). This is the ripening of insight (vipassanā-paripāka).

In order to show that it is manifest through the occurrence of a specific distinction in its name, he said, "having reached the state of equanimity towards formations" (*saṅkhārupekkhābhāvaṃ pattā*), and so forth.
What is meant is: "having reached the state of insight leading to emergence" (*vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanābhāvaṃ pattā*). "Two insight-minds" refers to the access and conformity minds;

for that [emergence] is called "emergence" (*vuṭṭhāna*). The connection is: "it emerges either from the sign of formations" (*saṅkhāranimittato*) or "taking Nibbāna as its object" (*nibbānaṃ ārabbha*).
[It has] been set in motion. If that were so, then even the lineage-consciousness (*gotrabhū*) would be called "emergence" (*vuṭṭhāna*).
It would not be so, because it remains at the mere stage of adverting to the Path, and because it lacks the function of penetration—the function of utterly eradicating delusion.

"By itself" means by itself, which is to say, by the Path. "Or the person endowed with that" means the person endowed with that Path. "From the setting in motion of the round" [means from the turning of the cycle of existence].

"And" (cā) refers either to the occurrence of the cycle of the lower realms (*apāyavaṭṭa*) in future existences, or to the occurrence of the cycle of the happy destinies of the sense-sphere (*kāmasugati*) starting from the eighth existence.
"Leading to emergence" (*vuṭṭhānagāminī*) means that it causes one to go to, or to reach, emergence inevitably.
The intention [of the phrase] "going to emergence inevitably" is that for those established here, there is no turning back from emergence.
And this should be understood with reference to the Paccekabuddhas and the disciples of the Buddhas.

However, regarding omniscient Bodhisattas, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that after going forth in the dispensation of previous Buddhas and commencing the work of insight (*vipassanā*), they stop at the knowledge of conformity (*anuloma-ñāṇa*).
In that context, the word "having struck" (*āhacca*) is used for the purpose of showing the attainment of the culmination of the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa*).
It should be understood as "it is said. Regarding the phrase "in the place of adverting":
prior to that, when the object of Nibbāna has not been grasped by any other consciousness, it is the place of adverting. "That" refers to the knowledge of change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū-ñāṇa*).

It is called *gotrabhu* because it overcomes, surpasses, or cuts off the lineage (the mundane). Alternatively, the etymological meaning is that it reaches or attains the lineage; thus it is *gotrabhū*. How so?

However, it would be logical to say that the change-of-lineage consciousness (gotrabhū-citta) cuts off the lineage of the worldling (puthujjana-gotta) and attains the lineage of the noble ones (ariya-gotta), for at that moment, that person is still included within the lineage of the worldling. This is true.
Yet, because it has been cut off within oneself, it is said to "cut itself. And because Nibbāna is the domain of the noble ones, [the change-of-lineage consciousness] takes it as its object.
It should be understood that one "attains the lineage of the Noble Ones" (*ariyagotta*).

It is also appropriate to call it *gotrabhū* (change-of-lineage) because, through a specific power of the conditions, one develops and manifests the lineage of the Noble Ones immediately after oneself. "Having delimited" (*paricchijja*) means having cut off;
what is meant is that one has been released from all agitations such as wrong view and doubt. This should be seen simply as the abandoning of delusion. Not those...
Knowing by way of taking phenomena as an object. How does the Path thoroughly understand those phenomena without making them its object?

By way of the accomplishment of its task. For while abandoning delusion, even the preliminary knowledges that do take them as objects are said to "thoroughly understand the Truth of Suffering" because they do not accomplish the task of abandoning that [delusion].
They are not so called. However, although the Path does not take that [truth] as its object, it is said that "it fully understands that truth" because it accomplishes the function of abandoning it.
Why? Because from that point onward, for that person, the function of fully understanding that truth is established at all times.
For example, it is like a certain man whose eye is obstructed by defects such as bile or phlegm...
He is blind; he sees nothing at all. However, when he obtains a single potent ointment and applies it to his eyes, he sleeps throughout the entire night.
While he is sleeping, all defects in his eyes vanish, and his vision becomes perfectly clear. From that moment on, even while sleeping, he is said to see forms.
Why? Because the function of seeing is accomplished through the disappearance of blindness.
Thus it should be seen in this way. Or, [it is] partial in the lower paths, or complete in the path of Arahatship. Regarding the term "apacchāvattikaṃ":

here, *pacchāvattaṃ* means turning back again (*pacchato āvattanaṃ*). The analysis (*viggaha*) is: that which has no turning back again (*pacchāvattaṃ*) is "apacchāvattikaṃ. "Puna... [The rest of the passage follows].

“By way of reaching the state of non-arising, it is called cessation. At the very moment of the Path, those very rounds attain the nature of non-arising again; they cease. Thus it is called cessation.

By the phrase “by development consisting of arising,” this indicates that because the Path lasts for only a single moment of consciousness, there is no opportunity for development consisting of increase.

This was stated on the grounds that [the other types of development] do not exist [as such]. However, even preliminary development (pubbabhāgabhāvanā) undertaken for the sake of attaining the Noble Path is indeed development of the path; and having reached the Noble Path, it reaches its culmination.
Therefore, in this sense—that the Noble Path itself, having reached its culmination, is the supreme development—it is also called "development" in the sense of increasing (vaḍḍhanasaṅkhātā).
This indeed is appropriate. *Ānantarika* means that which occurs immediately after itself. The analysis (*viggaha*) is: "that which has an immediate fruit.
And this is connected with the statement: "And after that, two or three fruition-consciousnesses (*phalacitta*) occur.
*Apanītaggiko* means that from which the fire has been removed. By the phrase "as if extinguishing," [the text] refers to the function of pacification and abandoning.
It shows the occurrence in conformity with the path. “Of them” means of those eyes. The connection is: “that form does not yet become manifest to him. “To him” means to that person.
Regarding the phrase “in the sections on reviewing,” here the consecutive cognitive processes (*vīthi*) that follow upon what was seen by the physical eye (*pasādacakkhu*) are also included.
“Those to be slain by the higher paths” means those to be killed by the higher paths (*uparimaggavajjhā*). “In the classification of defilements” means in the classification of defilements such as:
“By this path, these specific defilements are abandoned. “In the text” refers to the *Paṭisambhidā* text on the paths. The connection is that it should be stated when [the text] is being recited.
The term “reviewing” (*paccavekkhaṇa*) refers to the reviewing of the factors of the path (*maggaṅga*), the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*), and so forth.
It is precisely the reviewing of the path. Thus, it is established that it occurs either subsequently.

Regarding the phrase "it is not contradictory," the intention is that even for those who do not practice according to the *Visuddhimagga*, such reviewing can occur in accordance with their own inclinations.

Regarding the phrase "in the commentaries on the exposition of overestimation (*adhimāna*)," this refers to the commentaries on the exposition of the term "overestimation" within the fourth *pārājika* rule of the Vinaya. "He" refers to...
“A noble bhikkhu”: the meaning is that it is not right for him not to obtain [the goal], or rather, the construction is “it is not right that he should not obtain.
Thus, the fourfold knowledge of the path is included, because it is stated as “purity by knowledge and vision.
“Adhering” means establishing oneself more firmly within. “As if on the visible slopes of Mount Sineru” means...

It is like its mere occurrence. By the phrase, "Because it is not seen as existing solely in dependence upon conditions," he states the reason for grasping the self by making the self the owner of the self, thinking, "This is my self, not another's self.

In that context, by the word "solely" (*kevala*), [it is implied] that because the self itself is non-existent even when reaching the ultimate truth (*paramattha-sacca*), [the self is merely a designation] of the five aggregates.

It turns back the notion that [the self] exists as something subject to one's own control. However, having reached conventional truth (*sammuti-sacca*), because a self is perceived to exist, the great mass of people—imagining their own five aggregates to have a mode of existence subject to their own control—grasp them, thinking, "This is my self.
By the phrase "because the momentary dissolution is not seen," it is meant: "This is my self in the sense of being an essence; this is my essence. This..."
"My body. As long as this pentad of aggregates does not break up or perish—even for a hundred years or a thousand years—I do not die.
When this breaks up and perishes, then I die.
"I and my pentad of aggregates are non-dual and not different"—thus he speaks the reason for his grasping. In that regard:
“Of momentary dissolution”: this refers to the breaking, the disintegration, and the death of mental and physical phenomena (nāma-rūpa-dhammā) at every single moment.
This death does not exist in conventional truth (sammuti-sacca); it exists only in ultimate truth (paramattha-sacca).
Therefore, failing to see this, the great mass of people, imagining their own five aggregates (pañca-khandhā) to be the core of the self, grasp them, thinking, “This is my self. “That...”
"Having clearly seen the two": having clearly seen with the eye of knowledge both the fact that the five aggregates function solely in dependence upon conditions and their momentary dissolution.

In that regard, one who clearly perceives the dependent origination of the five aggregates clearly sees both their functioning solely in dependence upon conditions and their functioning without a self (an-attā).
And he who does not live under the control of his own self, having reached the ultimate truth (paramatthasacca), is not even fit to say, "This is mine," let alone, "Who am I?
Moreover, what is called a "being" (satto) does not exist by way of intrinsic nature; it is a mere conceptual designation (paññatti).
It is that which would grasp at "I," "mine," or "for me. Since the self (attā) does not exist, what "my self" could there be?
"Could it be so? [The answer is: There is momentary dissolution. It breaks up moment by moment.
Yet that which is called a "being" (satta) is born only once at the beginning of a single existence and dies only once at the end.

In between, even for a hundred or a thousand years, there is no such thing as death. The course of other momentary phenomena is one thing; the course of the being is another. This being the case, how...
Momentary phenomena might be called "self" in the sense of being the essence of a being. Therefore, because they lack mastery and lack essence, they are indeed non-self (*anattā*).
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "in the sense of lacking mastery," here "mastery" (*vaso*) refers to a preeminent factor within the continuum of a being.
If there were such a thing as a self, that very self would have to be the master of that preeminent factor.
If this were so, that which is the master would be the self; and that which is the self would be the master.
And that being the case, one who grasps at form as the self would indeed be grasping at form, mastery, and the self as a single unity.
The same applies to feeling as the self, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as the self. And if this were so, the sentient being and the five aggregates would be identical.
The mastery (*vasa*) and the self (*attā*)—all this becomes one; it comes to be reckoned as "one being" (*eko satto*).
For in this sense of exercising mastery, it is impossible for a single being to have two selves, three selves, or many selves.
Thus, in whatever way the mastery of a being proceeds, so does its desire proceed; and in that same way, the pentad of aggregates (*khandhapañcaka*) also [proceeds].
One would follow the power of the being at all times. Why? Because there is no difference between the power of the being and the power of the five aggregates (*pañcakkhandha*).
If one were to follow [them] in this way, the grasping that "form is my self" or "feeling is my self," and so forth, would be possible;
it would not be contradictory to their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). However, one does not follow them in such a manner. For indeed, one who is ugly...
An ugly person is able, by his own power alone, to make his own physical body beautiful and handsome;
likewise, he can make a bad sound good, or a foul odor fragrant.
But he cannot make a blind man non-blind, a deaf man non-deaf, a sick man healthy, a leper non-leper, one with a tumor non-tumorous, an old man young, or one subject to decay immortal.
Nor can he prevent one from falling into the states of misery (*apāya*), nor can he liberate one who has already fallen there. Likewise, he cannot cause a god to fall from his divine state;
nor a Sakka from his status as Sakka, nor Māra from his status as Māra, nor Brahmā from his status as Brahmā. This same principle applies to the remaining aggregates (*khandha*).
Furthermore, by following the sequence of the ultimate truth (*paramattha-sacca*) upon reaching it within the five aggregates through the method of "going with the end" (*avasānugamana*):
It has no function as its own master, nor does it have the function of a lord; it is simply without a master and without a lord.
This being so, to treat the self as its master and lord and to grasp at form with the thought "form is my self" is indeed a false grasping.
Furthermore, the great masses of people in the world do not know and do not see the dependent origination of phenomena.

They do not penetrate [this]. Within the continuity of the aggregates (khandhasantāna) proceeding by way of mutual conditionality, there exist modes of differentiation according to conventional truth (sammutisacca).
Furthermore, various designations such as "owner," "lord," and "master" are seen in the world.
These are merely conventional expressions regarding those designations of owner, lord, and master that arise by way of conventional truth.
Not having understood the truth of its intrinsic nature, they grasp at false conceptions.
Here it might be argued: "Is not 'power' (vasa) indeed desire? And a being, desiring to go, goes; desiring to stand, stands.
This being so, his five aggregates must have a mode of existence dependent upon that power. It is not so. Why? Because their mode of existence is dependent upon conditions.
It is thus. For instance, the desire to go may arise for the sake of external wealth, or for the sake of various enjoyments, or for some other various reason.
In that regard, for those who lack wealth, whatever suffering—whether physical or mental—might arise, their desire for wealth arises on account of each such suffering. This is the desire for wealth.

From conditions such as the desire for travel, [other] desires arise. Likewise, there are no [separate] desires to be mentioned regarding the desire for various enjoyments or the desire for various karmic actions.

This is because they are rooted in various forms of suffering, fear, and calamity. The same applies to desires rooted in the suffering of being enticed by various objects, and to desires rooted in the agitation of various types of discursive thought (*vitakka*).
Thus, even one's dwelling is entirely dependent on conditions and functions according to them. "Going" [is likewise dependent].

The pentad of aggregates occurs in the mode of going. By whatever cause—such as wealth and so forth—a particular power arises, by that very same [cause] the going also arises, as well as through conditions such as nutriment and support.
However, power is merely one part of the condition for the going; for it is not able to arise by itself without other conditions.
How could one produce a going? It is the same with standing and the other postures.
This being so, it is right to say that this pentad of aggregates has its mode of existence dependent on conditions; it does not have its mode of existence dependent on a self (vasa).

Furthermore, when one who intends to go goes, it is merely a conventional designation (*paññatti*)—the "being" who goes; but the pentad of aggregates does not go, because it consists of momentary phenomena (*khaṇika-dhamma*).
"Whatever arises breaks up right there and then. Due to continuity, the sign of the mode of going appears.
Thus there is a lack of mastery. [Objection: "Let it be that it breaks up right there and then.
When there is an uninterrupted occurrence, the act of going is still accomplished. And when going is accomplished, there is no fault in its momentary breaking up."
It exists. For the momentary death of a being is what is called the "cemetery ground.
When there is stumbling or falling even while one is still on the way, a being who is traveling may at any time meet with death or experience suffering equal to death.

The etymological meaning of *nimitta* is that which "causes" (*nimināti*) or "produces" (*pavatteti*) defilements. And in the phrase "the sign of perversion" (*vipallāsanimitta*), it refers to perversion.
The sign is that which appears by way of phenomena as a task to be performed. The connection is: "craving itself is the aspiration. A great mass of dangers is a *mahā-ādīnava-rāsi*.
The characteristic of emptiness (*suññatā-lakkhaṇa*) among the aggregates is exceedingly profound;
it is an object of knowledge alone. And because the vision of emptiness is the direct antidote to views, he said: "regarding formations..."
“By way of seeing emptiness,” and so forth. Therein, “the accomplishment of the goal” (attha-siddhi) means the accomplishment of the goal consisting in the attainment of the path and its fruits.
“Self” (attā) is an adherence; thus, it is “adherence to a self” (attābhiniveso). It is called “grasping” (gāho) because one grasps; the meaning is that one takes up [it].
Grasping in the form of a view is “view-grasping” (diṭṭhiggāho). The analysis of the compound is: it is both an adherence to a goal and a grasping by way of a view.
The antidote to that is the knowledge of contemplation of non-self (*anattānupassanā-ñāṇa*). *Ānubhāvo* means successive becoming; the sense is "increasing by way of succession.
"Having thus contemplated" means having contemplated by way of emptiness (*suññatākāra*). Of the noble person who is being liberated:
"The characteristic of impermanence (*aniccalakkhaṇa*) is not very deep; it is even within the range of faith (*saddhā*). The characteristic of elevation..."

And he said, "By way of seeing impermanence," and so forth, because conceit (māna) regarding the aggregates is rooted in the perversion of permanence and stability, and is the opposite of faith (saddhā).

"Of that which has become a fixation on signs" means of that which has become a fixation on the signs of permanence and stability. "Of the grasping known as conceit" refers to the grasping termed conceit.
By the word "also" (pi) in the phrase "by faith also," he includes knowledge (ñāṇa). [The characteristic of suffering (dukkhalakkhaṇa):]
It is indeed a name that produces fear and a sense of urgency. It is the antidote for one who is greedy with craving and agitated by craving toward sense objects.
Specifically, because it is suitable for concentration (*samādhi*), he said, "by way of seeing suffering," and so forth.
"Of three things" refers to the three qualities consisting of the faculties (*indriya*) of wisdom (*paññā*), faith (*saddhā*), and concentration (*samādhi*). "Insight" (*vipassanā*)...
"Or by way of going"—this refers precisely to the cause of arrival known as insight leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminī vipassanā*).
Now, regarding what was stated previously: "And for the sake of becoming a condition for the classification of the seven noble persons (*ariyapuggala*).

In that context, in order to show the classification of the seven noble persons, the passage beginning with "Therein... was stated. Regarding the phrase "one who follows the Dhamma": [the following is said].
“Dhamma” here is said to mean wisdom (*paññā*), as in the passage: “Truth, Dhamma, steadfastness, and generosity.
One who recollects the Dhamma more keenly is a “follower by Dhamma” (*dhammānusārī*). What is meant is that one attains the Path at the beginning by means of following the power of wisdom.
Alternatively, “Dhamma” refers to the conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra-dhamma*) in the sense of being devoid of a sentient being or a soul; and it also refers to the vision of emptiness (*suññatā*).

Specifically, it is called "vision of the pure dhamma. Thus, one who recollects the pure dhamma and follows it by way of knowledge is a *dhammānusārī* (follower by dhamma). Regarding the term *diṭṭhippatto* (one attained through vision): here, "vision" (*diṭṭhi*) refers to the knowledge of seeing.
Because he is endowed with perfectly pure vision from the very beginning, by the power of that vision alone, he easily attains each respective path and fruit.

One who has attained [the fruit] is one who has attained through vision (*diṭṭhippatto*). Because he is liberated from the bonds of the defilements by that very power of the wisdom of seeing, he is one liberated by wisdom (*paññāvimutto*).
Firm conviction regarding the momentary nature of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāradhammā*) is called faith (*saddhā*), which is unwavering confidence (*aveccappasādo*).
In this context, "unwavering confidence" is confidence associated with knowledge (*ñāṇasampayutta*). And "knowledge" refers to the signs of the momentary nature of conditioned phenomena.
It is the knowledge of seeing. For when such knowledge exists, the kind of confidence known as *aveccappasāda* (unshakable confidence) arises therein, and not otherwise.
One who recollects faith is a "follower by faith" (*saddhānusārī*). What is meant is that one attains the noble path at the outset through the power of faith alone.
One who is liberated by the power of faith is "liberated by faith" (*saddhāvimutto*). Regarding the term "body-witness" (*kāyasakkhi*), here *sakkhaṃ* means what is directly seen (*sanditṭhaṃ*).
That which is called a "sādhaka" (one who accomplishes). One for whom what has been attained is directly evident within his own body is a "kāyasakkhī" (body-witness).
For a person who contemplates suffering is full of a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*). And spiritual urgency is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for exertion and vigor.
For it is said: "One who is stirred applies himself with wise effort. Therefore, applying himself to meditation by means of that spiritual urgency, whatever—
It is to be attained by human effort; one attains it. And while attaining it, one gains direct personal experience within one's own body.
What is meant is that one obtains the visible bliss of *jhāna* or the bliss of the paths and fruits (*magga-phala*).

One is called "liberated in both ways" (*ubhatobhāga-vimutta*) because one is liberated from the physical body by means of the formless *jhānas*, and from the mental body by means of the paths and fruits of *arahantship*; thus, by both [means].
He is liberated from bodily parts. And herein, there are three types of noble persons: those predominant in wisdom, those predominant in faith, and those predominant in energy.
Among them, the follower by Dhamma, the one who has attained vision, and the one liberated by wisdom are called "wisdom-predominant.
The follower by faith and the one liberated by faith are called "faith-predominant. The body-witness and the one liberated both ways are "energy-predominant."
"Name" (nāma) should be understood in this way. Furthermore, this method of classifying individuals (puggalavibhāga-naya) is stated according to the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*.

In the Abhidhamma, however, in the *Puggalapaññatti*, two individuals—the one liberated by faith (*saddhāvimutta*) and the body-witness (*kāyasakkhī*)—are stated only among those in training (*sekkha*).
But when these two have attained Arahatship, they should be understood as being "liberated by wisdom" (*paññāvimutta*) alone. Here it might be asked: [regarding] formations (*saṅkhāra*)...
It is said that "faith" (saddhā) is the unshakable confidence (aveccappasāda) consisting of firm conviction in the momentary nature of phenomena (dhamma).
But does one reach the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga) by such mere faith alone? Regarding this, there is nothing for us to say;
it has been stated by the Blessed One himself. As he said in the Mahāvagga, in the Okkantasaṃyutta: "Bhikkhus, the eye..."
"It is impermanent, subject to change, and subject to becoming otherwise"—he who has such faith and such conviction is called a follower by faith (*saddhānusārī*).
He has entered the plane of the noble ones; he has transcended the plane of the worldlings.

That karma by which one might be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, or a lower realm—that kind of karma he does not perform. "The ear, monks, is impermanent; it is subject to change."
The twelve sense bases (*dvādasāyatana*) should be explained in detail by means of the passage beginning with "subject to change" (*aññathābhāvī*).
In that context, "subject to change" (*vipariṇāmī*) means that which has change (*vipariṇāma*) is subject to change. "Change" refers to the state of decaying and breaking up moment by moment.
