"Subject to becoming otherwise" (*aññathābhāvī*) is a synonym for that same term. By the phrase "he resolves thus," [the text indicates] faith associated with knowledge.

It illuminates. That very [faith] is described among the factors of stream-entry as "being endowed with verified confidence in the Buddha, and being endowed with verified confidence in the Dhamma and the Saṅgha.

In that context, what is called "faith associated with knowledge" is the faith of conviction associated with the knowledge that perceives the sign of impermanence in the eye and so forth. And the "sign of impermanence" refers to material form (*rūpa*).

In the phrase "impermanence in the sense of destruction," according to the method already explained, it refers to the transformation of the continuity of the great elements that serve as the bases for the eye and so forth.
For one who sees this, faith arises and conviction is established regarding the impermanent nature of the eye and the other faculties.
The meaning is that one attains faith, conviction, and discernment through the realization that these too break up absolutely moment by moment.

Regarding the phrase “with unwavering confidence in the Buddha” (*buddhe aveccappasādena*): here, “unwavering confidence” (*aveccappasāda*) refers to the clarity of mind associated with the knowledge that perceives the qualities of a Buddha, such as his state of being an Arahant and a Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*).

The “noble plane” (*ariyabhūmi*) is said to be the stage of existence purified of the underlying tendencies of wrong view (*diṭṭhānusaya*) and doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*). The stage of existence accompanied by those [tendencies] is the “plane of the worldling” (*puthujjanabhūmi*).
[This is] the name. But how is it known that this person has transcended the plane of the worldlings (*puthujjana*) and entered the plane of the noble ones (*ariya*)?

To this he says: "He who... and so forth. He who, even for the sake of his own life, does not perform any action that has reached the level of a course of action (*kammappatha*) leading to the states of misery—he has, by necessity, transcended the plane of the worldlings and entered the plane of the noble ones.
"It is understood" is what is meant. This is the *Saddhānusāri-sutta*. Furthermore, it is said: "Bhikkhus, the eye is subject to change, it is subject to alteration.
He for whom even this much contemplation is acceptable—this one is called a *Dhammānusārī*," and so forth.
In that context, "contemplation is acceptable even to such an extent" means that, unlike the *Saddhānusārī*, he does not stop at mere faith.
Perceiving such impermanence in the eye and the other faculties, he indeed obtains vision little by little.
This being so, it is said that the eye and the other faculties are "tolerable" for that person—meaning they are sufficient for his contemplation and observation.
This is the *Dhammānusāri-sutta*. Furthermore, it is said: "Monks, the eye is impermanent, subject to change, and subject to alteration."
"He who understands thus sees. This is called "one who has entered the stream," and so forth.

In this context, "understands and sees" means that, unlike the follower by Dhamma (dhammānusārī) who remains at the mere level of reflective acceptance, he understands through wisdom and sees directly with the eye of knowledge (ñāṇacakkhu).
This is the discourse concerning those who have attained through vision (diṭṭhipatta), and so on.

Regarding the phrase “yathā sakaṃ phalaṃ”: here, *sakaṃ* means "one's own" (*attano idaṃ*). By the words "of the stream-enterer," etc., it shows the meaning of "whatever is one's own" as *yathāsakaṃ*.

However, in the process of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), it is only the conformable impulsions (*anulomajavana*) that are the proximate causes of the fruitions, not the path-impulsions;
thus he said, "not by way of proceeding on the path. "He" refers to...
The path (*magga*). It is the noble, existing reality. "Of it" means of the path.

Contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*) is signless (*animitta*) in terms of its function, but it possesses a sign (*sanimittā*) by way of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāvato*), for it is indeed accompanied by the sign of permanence.
This is because it apprehends the notion of "I am this. Furthermore, even this knowledge of insight (*vipassanāñāṇa*) is impermanent in the sense of destruction.
"And it must be regarded as such. In this context, having reached the Abhidhamma, there is a predominance of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), not a predominance of function (*kicca*).
Therefore, according to the method of the Abhidhamma, insight (*vipassanā*) is unable to give its own name to the path.
This is the intention of the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*). As for those defilement-phenomena (*kilesadhammā*) which arise in someone...
They fetter the person; they create confinement. Therefore, they are called "obstructors.
They cause that person to grasp at signs of permanence, signs of beauty, signs of pleasure, and signs of self. Therefore, they are called "sign-makers.
They cause that person to become intensely placed and settled upon sense objects. Therefore, they are called "wish-makers."
Furthermore, those [mental states] do not take the paths and fruits as their objects, nor do they associate with the paths and fruits.

Thus, by way of taking them as objects, the paths and fruits are absent for them. And because of that very absence, it is shown that those paths and fruits receive three names by virtue of their own intrinsic nature;
hence the words, "or by way of taking them as objects," and so forth.
“By their own nature” means by their own inherent character (*dhammatā*).
“They arise when the view of self has arisen” indicates the inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) of those views and doubts with the view of self;
however, it should not be understood that the view of self is inseparably concomitant with them. They “ripen” means...
They ripen in the states of misery (apāya). They produce rebirth-linking in the states of misery.

And for noble persons (ariyapuggala) who have seen the truths, unwholesome states associated with wrong view and doubt are already included by the mention of "wrong view" and "doubt"; therefore, he says, "dissociated from wrong view and doubt.
Or, as for the phrase "unwholesome states," it refers specifically to the ten unwholesome courses of action (akusalakammapatha) existing in the present. By the seven...
“*Bhavehi*” is an expression denoting the instrument in the context of the completion of an action, as in the phrase: “he completes the monastery in seven months.
Furthermore, the “completion of an action” refers to the swift finishing of that action. “Seven times” means seven occasions. The three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are:
the fetter of personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), doubt (*vicikicchā*), and the fetter of adherence to rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*). “Non-falling” (*avinipāta*)...
“*Dhamma*” means falling into a state of deformity; it is what is called a downfall (*vinipāta*). It is the falling into a state of ruin (*apāya*). The analysis of the compound is:
“that which has no *dhamma*—meaning intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*)—of downfall. “*Niyata*” means having a destiny fixed within the states of happy rebirth.
“*Sambodhi*” means one who awakens correctly; it is the knowledge of the Path. “*Parāyana*” refers to the destination to be reached in the future.
"One whose ultimate goal (*parāyaṇa*) is what is called full enlightenment (*sambodhi*)" means *sambodhiparāyano*. "The sense of indefiniteness" means that it is the sense of the particle *vā*;

among the meanings of the particle *vā*, it is the sense of indefiniteness, not the sense of alternative (*vikappa*). If it were in the sense of alternative, only two [types of persons]—those who are "seven times at most" (*sattakkhattuparama*)—would be obtained;
the mixed existence (*missakabhava*) would not be obtained. In the sense of indefiniteness, all three are obtained.
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, because the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*) is taken, only a single mixed existence (*missaka-bhava*) is obtained.

[Objection: But is it not the case that the word "and" (*ca*) is well-known in the sense of conjunction, not in the sense of non-restriction? Therefore, only the sense of conjunction is appropriate here.
[Response: It is not appropriate. Why? Because two [types] would not be included. However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, having taken the sense of conjunction...
It is said that those two types of persons are not included in this recitation.
If they are not included in this recitation, where else could they be included? For it is not reasonable to say that anyone called "one who has seven births at most" is not included here.
Regarding the phrase "of that scriptural recitation," and the passage beginning "And here, because... [omission] ...is called 'the highest'": this is what is meant.
In the subsequent sections, it should be joined with the phrases beginning with "those very in the realm of sense-desire" (*ye kāmabhave yeva*) and "either in this very life" (*yadiṭṭhadhamme vā*).
And he should be understood as either a dry-insight practitioner (*sukkha-vipassaka*) or one who has fallen away from jhāna; such is the connection.

"In the Pāḷi" refers to the *Puggalapaññatti* Pāḷi. "Finality here" means attaining the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya*) in this world of desire and reaching Parinibbāna regarding the aggregates.
The conclusion is by way of these [three]. "Conclusion" means the end. One who goes from family to family is a *kolaṅkolo*;
the meaning is that he goes from one existence to another existence. One who has only a single seed of existence, reckoned as rebirth-linking, remaining is a *ekabījī*.
And he who is an Arahant in this very life—his conclusion occurs right here; such is the construction. But by what [means] for the three?
What is the distinction among stream-enterers? First, the one who is "limited to seven more births" is distinguished solely by the faculties associated with the first path.
The other two are distinguished by the insight-faculties that have been set in motion for the sake of the higher paths.
Among them, the one limited to seven more births is entirely weak; the "one who goes from family to family" is sharp; and he is one who has six more existences remaining.

It is fivefold: one who has five more births, one who has four more births, one who has three more births, one who has two more births, and one who has one more birth. Among these, the one with five births is the sharpest;
the others should be understood as progressively sharper. However, the "one-seeded" (ekabījī), having only one birth remaining, is the sharpest of all.
Therein, the "one who returns seven times at most" (sattakkhattu-parama) is the weakest of all, because he is accomplished solely by the power of the first path.

The other two, having remained at the state of being limited to seven births by way of their natural disposition (*pakati*), establish the work of insight (*vipassanā*) for the sake of the higher paths.
At that time, their faculties (*indriya*) again reach a state of distinction and become sharp. Therefore, they are called "sharp" (tikkha) because they are limited to seven births at most.
The phrase "or fewer than seven times" refers to those who go from family to family (*kolaṅkola*) and those with a single seed remaining (*ekabījī*).
It has been said: "Insight governs the three higher paths. This was said with reference to the two types of stream-enterers (sotāpanna) mentioned above.
It should be understood that the state of being "one who has at most seven more births" is determined by the first path alone.

For it is that very person who is mentioned explicitly in the *Saṅgaha-pāṭha* as one who, having developed the path of stream-entry, goes no further into the states of misery through the abandoning of wrong views and doubt.
One is called a stream-enterer who has seven births at most. The other two [types] appear only in the Pāḷi in the sections classifying the persons who are stream-enterers.
Regarding the phrase "but those who": this refers to those persons who are stream-enterers.
In the verse, "seven here" means seven transmigrations in this human world; "seven there" means seven in that divine world. In the Aṅguttara reading, it says "by that clarity of mind."
Faith in the qualities of the Teacher arises in one who is capable of making himself understood by means of his voice throughout the great thousandfold world-system. By virtue of that faith:

"In that manner" means that if he continues to wander only among the devas, then after taking seven rebirths through spontaneous birth (*opapātika*), he will attain final Nibbāna right there. If he continues to wander only among human beings, [he will do the same].
"Having taken rebirths as seven embryos, he will attain final nibbāna right here.
This is the meaning of "having taught by way of fourteen sections" (*desanā-vāra*).
By stating "that must be investigated," the commentator (*ṭīkācariya*) indicates that he himself accepts only fourteen rebirths. Now, rejecting that doctrine of fourteen rebirths:
He said, “In the *Vibhaṅga*,” and so forth. “In the *Vibhaṅga*” means in the *Ñāṇavibhaṅga* (Analysis of Knowledge) within the Abhidhamma.
“Aṭṭhāna” means that for which there is no place (*ṭhāna*). “Place” (*ṭhāna*) means a root cause. “Anavakāsa” means that for which there is no opportunity (*avakāsa*).
“Opportunity” (*avakāsa*) means a conditional cause. “Yaṃ” is a reference to the action. That which might be produced—that production—is an impossibility (*aṭṭhāna*). That production...
The construction is: "Dhamma has no room. Regarding the phrase "of the consciousness that is volitional formation" (*abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇassa*):

this refers to the wholesome or unwholesome kamma-consciousness that produces rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) within the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*), beyond the seven [existences] of becoming. Regarding "by means of cessation" (*nirodhena*): it is by means of cessation at the very moment of the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*).
The connection is with the word "cease" (*nirujjhanti*). Regarding "name-and-form" (*nāmañca rūpañca*): these refer to those phenomena consisting of name and form.

[They] would arise. The construction is: "These material phenomena (rūpadhammā) indeed cease right here at this moment of the cessation of formative volition (abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa). "By the very method already stated" means by that same way, by the manner described.
"Of the delusion associated with that" means of the delusion that stands together with that greed and that hatred in a single consciousness.
[This does not apply] to the delusion associated with views and doubt, because that is abandoned precisely at the first path.
Nor [does it apply] to the delusion associated with restlessness, because that is to be abandoned precisely at the fourth path. Regarding the arising of lust, hatred, and delusion:
“In those who are righteous” means in those who have arisen through the Dhamma and through justice. “From which” means by which cause. “A powerful cause” means...
The meaning is as follows: “Of them” refers to stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*). “By way of scraping away” means by way of thoroughly scraping off the thick portion, the gross part.
“Occasional arising” (*adhiccuppatti*) means arising after the lapse of time, beyond the period during which [defilements] previously occurred.

This refers to the arising of lust, hatred, and delusion even in those who are [stream-enterers]. “Of them too” refers to once-returners (*sakadāgāmī*) as well. “Union with the basis for sexual intercourse is desired” [is said].

It is accepted that for *sakadāgāmins*, there exists what is called the union of sexual intercourse between husband and wife. The Elder, however, accepts it only as a spontaneous occurrence (*adhiccuppatti*);
he does not accept the presence of underlying obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*). He states that sons and daughters are even seen among *sakadāgāmins*.
As for the statement, "This is rejected in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*," it was rejected because it was merely the Elder’s own personal opinion.
All of this is stated in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*. “In the Chakkanipāta” means in the Chakkanipāta of the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*.
“In the Migāsāḷava case” means in the case concerning the female lay follower named Migāsāḷā. Seeing this case, some do not accept the position of the Great Commentary (*Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*);
they accept the position of the Elder Mahāsiva. “Non-practitioners of the holy life” refers to one who has not abstained from sexual intercourse.
“‘It was declared that he was a once-returner’: when he had passed away, that brahmin attained the state of a once-returner here and was reborn in the Tusita realm;
such was the state of a once-returner that was declared for him by the Blessed One. ‘By way of attainment’ means by way of the acquisition of the state of a once-returner.
The intended meaning is not, however, ‘by way of attainment while being one who does not lead the holy life.’”

For even at the time of death, it is not difficult for a noble disciple of sharp wisdom to attain the higher paths and fruits while maintaining the resolve upon the training rules (*sikkhāpada*). By this, the assertion of certain [who claim] that [this is impossible] according to the Theravāda is refuted.
By the phrase "having come to this world only once," [the possibility of] going from here to the other world and returning again from there to this one is [also addressed].
Because he is accomplished, this person is established as one who has at most two more births in the sensual realm (*kāmabhava*) by means of the pure path-process (*magganiyāma*). How so?
Having reached this world, being reborn there, and then attaining final Nibbāna here; or having reached that world, being reborn here, and then attaining final Nibbāna there.
As for the remaining four, they are established by means of the insight-process (*vipassanāniyāma*).
It is understood. Which four? One who, having reached this [world], attains final nibbāna here; one who, having reached there [the Brahma-world], attains final nibbāna there;
one who, having reached this [world], attains final nibbāna there; and one who, having reached there [the Brahma-world], attains final nibbāna here.

And herein, among the three types of stream-enterers, only the one who is "limited to seven more births" is established by way of the path-niyāma. However, the remaining two types of stream-enterers are established by way of insight-niyāma.
Established. Among the once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*), exactly two are established by way of the path; the remaining four, however, are established by way of insight (*vipassanā*).
In that regard, there is no confusion among the stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*) and once-returners who are established by the path. But among those established by insight, there is confusion.

It should be understood that when there is no contradiction in their actual meaning (*atthato*), there is no fault in the confusion [of terminology] as a mere conventional designation (*vohāramatta*).
"Having come" (*āgantvā*) is stated according to the reading; however, the reading "one who comes" (*āgantu*) is more appropriate. The meaning is:

one who has the nature of coming, being of a nature to come, is called a "once-returner" (*sakadāgāmī*). The same method applies here as well for the phrase "not coming to this state" (*anāgantvā itthattaṃ*).
The state of an *arahant* is *arahatta*; [it refers to] the path of *arahantship*. Those things which cause the failure of a gift are those that yield little fruit and little benefit.
"Bringing about success" means producing great fruit and great benefit.

"The qualities of the aggregate of virtue and so forth" refers to the qualities of the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation.

"Among those worthy of offerings" refers to persons who are deserving of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*). "The yoke" (*dhura*) is said to signify the primary burden or the foremost position. Faith itself is the yoke.
"Faith" means one whose vehicle is faith. Likewise for "wisdom. But why is "energy" not included here?

In the Canon it is said, "one who has faith as his vehicle develops the path," and "one who has wisdom as his vehicle develops the path," but it is not said, "one who has energy as his vehicle develops the path.
Therefore, it is not included. Why, then, was it not stated that "one who has energy as his vehicle develops the path"?
It is said: For one who is developing the path, the task at the outset for the abandoning of views and doubt is great.
Why? Because they are rooted in the states of deprivation (apāya). In this regard, faith and doubt are two direct opposites.
Wherever faith settles upon an object, there is no doubt; wherever doubt settles, [there is no faith].
In that [state], faith does not exist. Likewise, wisdom and views are direct opposites.
Where there is wisdom, there is no view; where there is a view, there is no wisdom. Moreover, faith dispels views within its own domain alone.
There is no need even to mention the dispelling of doubt by wisdom. Therefore, for one who has initiated insight into the impermanent and so forth—
By means of mere confident faith (*aveccappasāda*), having abandoned views and doubt, one attains the state of a follower by faith (*saddhānusārī*);

and by becoming even more firmly confident, one attains the state of one liberated by faith (*saddhāvimutta*). By means of wisdom, having made the contemplation of impermanence and so forth bearable, one attains the state of a follower of Dhamma (*dhammānusārī*);
and by seeing [the truth] even more clearly, one attains the state of one attained through vision and liberated by wisdom (*diṭṭhippatto paññāvimutto*).
Energy (*vīriya*), however, is not even a mere antidote to wrong view and doubt; rather, it is their companion and their leader.
For energy has the characteristic of exertion. It exerts faith, it exerts wisdom, it exerts wrong view, and it exerts doubt as well.
How then could it [be an antidote] by its own intrinsic nature?
He will be able to abandon views and doubt. Therefore, in this context, he is not described as "one who carries energy" (*vīriyavāhī*) or "one whose burden is energy" (*vīriyadhura*).
However, in the case of the body-witness (*kāyasakkhin*), faith and wisdom are of equal strength.
Energy itself, standing in the place of right effort (*sammappadhāna*), nurtures both of them. And that person, by the power of those two, [abandons] views, doubt, and so forth.
Having abandoned [the state of a body-witness], he attains the state of a body-witness; or, having produced the eight liberations, he attains the state of one liberated both ways.
In these two types of persons, however, the strength of their energy is very evident.

Therefore, these two should be described as "predominant in energy" (*vīriyādhika*), and not as "bearing the yoke of energy" (*vīriyadhura*). The four modes of practice (*catuppaṭipadā*) are: the painful practice with slow direct knowledge (*dukkhāpaṭipadā dandhābhiññā*).
The practice that is difficult with quick higher knowledge; the practice that is easy with sluggish higher knowledge; the practice that is easy with quick higher knowledge.
The threefold liberation consists of: the void liberation, the signless liberation, and the desireless liberation.
Regarding the phrase "three who attain final nibbāna in the interval," these are those who, without reaching the end of their lifespan, attain the final nibbāna of the defilements in the interim.
One who attains final nibbāna in the interval (antarā-parinibbāyī). He is of three kinds: one who attains final nibbāna in the first third of his lifespan, in the second third, or in the third third.
These three are called those who attain final nibbāna in the interval. One who attains final nibbāna upon arrival (upahacca-parinibbāyī) is one who attains final nibbāna at the end of his lifespan.
"Uddhaṃsoto" means one whose stream of existence flows upwards; he will certainly [reach] Akaniṭṭha.
"One who will go" means one bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm. One who attains final nibbāna by performing insight-work with effort and exertion is "one who attains nibbāna with exertion.
One who attains final nibbāna through insight-work accompanied by effortless ease is "one who attains nibbāna without exertion.
Regarding the phrase "twelve stream-enterers," there are three types of "single-seed" individuals; these same three, when multiplied by the four modes of progress, [make twelve].
Twelve. The twelve once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*) are exactly as described by the method previously stated.
[This applies] only to certain non-returners (*anāgāmin*) and arahants. “Of that which is clung to” (*ajjhosita*) means of that which has been adhered to.

Having reached a conclusion, it is established [with the thought], “It is mine alone. What is meant is: “of that which has been swallowed and established. By means of a thick and gross sensual lust (*kāmarāga*).
They are liberated; they are liberated from dense passion. And in the formless realms, they possess only the formless attainments, not the four form-sphere attainments.

Therefore, successive cessation is not possible there. "From the beginning" refers to the first jhāna attainment among the eight attainments, starting from that point. Successive cessation means [the cessation] in the first jhāna...
It is the cessation of perceptions of resistance and perceptions of diversity. "Perceptions of resistance" refers to the perceptions associated with the fivefold sensory consciousness.
"Perceptions of diversity" refers to the perceptions of mind-consciousness occurring toward various objects other than the sign of the *kasiṇa*.

There is successive cessation, beginning with the cessation of applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) in the second jhāna, and so forth. "Then the fifth jhāna" is according to the fivefold method.
It has been stated. However, the statement regarding the eight attainments was made according to the fourfold method (*catukkanaya*).

Both of these are indeed applicable according to the individual practitioner. "Yuganandha" means a pair-bound connection; the analysis (*viggaha*) is "the pair-bound connection of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
Regarding the phrase "by way of attainment, emergence, and insight," this refers to the attainment that has reached mastery (*vasibhāva*).

And the emergence [from attainment] must be grasped. Because there is no obstacle to the requisites bound to one's own body due to the power of the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) itself, there is no need for a separate act of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*);
thus it is said, "having set aside the requisites bound to one's own body.
"Bound in various ways" means bound from various locations; what is meant is that they are placed in various places. "By way of danger" (*parissayena*).
"By way of an obstacle": one should resolve that "let them not be lost," or that they are bound separately and remain undisturbed.
Or, one should resolve: "I shall emerge from this at such a time," which is the honoring of the Saṅgha. The same applies to being summoned by the Teacher.
"The delimitation of the journey" means the examination of the duration of one's own life. For death, indeed, can even be resisted by the power of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).

He was unable [to do so]. Had he died while still within meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), he would not have performed the duties that must be done for fellow practitioners of the holy life (*sabrahmacārī*). For the disciples of the Gotama, the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is one gateway to death;
when one enters it, such-and-such a monk goes to death. It is because of ignoble action (*anariyakamma*).
“For the sake of which” means for the sake of relishing the flavor of practice. “In that purpose” means in that objective. Non-material happiness (*nirāmisa-sukha*).
"Nameless" means happiness devoid of material things. For there are two kinds of happiness: happiness with material things (*sāmisasukha*) and happiness without material things (*nirāmisasukha*).

In this regard, those things in the world known as the five strands of sensual pleasure—which are desirable, lovely, and agreeable—are called "material things" (*āmisa*) because they are to be grasped by the defilements.
And whatever happiness arises in dependence upon those material things is called "happiness with material things. That which [is found] in the world...

They claim as their own divine happiness and human happiness—those very experiences which, while being enjoyed by the great masses of people, surround them on all sides with the fear of the states of misery and the fear of the round of existence (*saṃsāra*). But the happiness of meditative absorption (*jhāna*), the happiness of the path (*magga*), the happiness of the fruit (*phala*), and the happiness of Nibbāna is called non-material happiness (*nirāmisa-sukha*).
It is what is known as the happiness of renunciation (*nekkhamma-sukha*), the happiness of seclusion (*paviveka-sukha*), and the happiness of peace (*upasama-sukha*).
And it is called the bliss of full enlightenment, the bliss of liberation, the bliss of the noble ones, and the blameless bliss.
And when a noble person experiences this, they completely avoid all fears of the states of misery and the fear of the round of existence.

"In the sense of being relished" means that because it is liberated from the hindrances of the defilements, and because its flavor is vast, profound, peaceful, and sublime, it is called "bliss, indeed bliss."
"Even by way of illustrating it, it should be tasted.

262. *Cārittaṃ* means conduct (*caritabba*). It refers to the nature of the ten courses of wholesome action (*dasakusalakammapatha*). By the phrase "by family custom" (*kulācārena*), it is meant by the conduct handed down through successive generations of one's lineage.
In the phrase "by the excellence of relatives, friends, wealth, and enjoyments," the instrumental case is used in the sense of a cause (*hetuatthe karaṇavacanaṃ*).

"Vipule" means extensive (*visāle*). "By that" (*tena*) is the display of the case ending for that word. "By faith" (*saddhāya*) is by way of the faith of confirmed confidence (*aveccappasāda*) in the Three Jewels.

“Of those who have grown” means of those who have increased exceedingly by surpassing the states conducive to decline and the state conducive to stagnation, and by reaching the states conducive to distinction and penetration.
“And of those who are purified” means of those who are purified from faults such as self-exaltation and disparagement of others.
He protects each person; thus he is *nampa*. He dwells in loving-kindness toward all whom he has seen.

It has been said. "To be called" (*āvhātabbo*) means "that which is called" (*avhayo*), i.e., a name. The analysis of the word *nampavhayo* is: "one whose calling (*avhayo*) is by name (*nammo*)," thus it is *nampavhayo*.
The phrase "having made an aspiration" (*paṇidhāya*) is explained as "having wished," while the phrase "having placed firmly" (*bhusaṃ nidhāya*) and so forth serves to clarify its meaning.

The expression "depending upon" (*upādāya*) and "in reliance upon" (*paṭicca*) is a statement of synonyms for that term. The phrase "of those with their own dull intellects" refers to those who are currently living and present.
This is the intention. Therefore he said, "or for the sake of future generations. Compassion (*anukampā*) is the act of compassionating. It is a mental activity directed toward the thought:
"How might these people easily understand the meanings of the Abhidhamma? In terms of its essential meaning, it is simply compassion (*karuṇā*), characterized as non-cruelty.
Therefore he said, "non-cruelty, pity. Or else, "desired" refers to that which the Elder, like a virtuous person, [strives for].
“*Evarūpaṃ pakaraṇaṃ kareyyā*” means “he would compose such a work,” the sense being that it was thus long desired and hoped for.
“*In the Khuddasikkhā-ṭīkā*” is said with reference to the ancient commentary (*porāṇa-ṭīkā*). The intention [of the author] indicates that he was known specifically as Somavihāra in that [place].
In the verse, “*atha*” means “at that time”; “*ettha*” means “in this city”; and as for “*saddo*,” why did the king [utter] such...
He gave the auspicious elephant to the brahmins. An unpleasant sound arose, saying, "It is not fitting that this was done by the king.
"Terrifying" means producing fear, causing dread. "Of the Sivis" means of those dwelling in the kingdom of Sivi.
"Increaser of the kingdom" means he increases the kingdom; thus it is the Increaser of the Kingdom. It was a noble elephant, for it was endowed with all the auspicious marks.
He is a noble-born elephant. In whatever kingdom they perform auspicious rites for him, in that kingdom the rain falls properly, and various fears and calamities do not arise;
thus he is a "world-renowned auspicious elephant. Therefore it is said: "In the prosperity of the Sivi kingdom.
"Extended" means expanded; what is meant is that it is exceedingly extensive.

They are called *dhaññā* because they are desired (*daṭṭhuṃ*) and longed for (*patthīyanti*) by the great multitude; thus they are "fortunate" (*dhaññā*). They possess great supernormal power (*mahiddhikā*).

It is called *adhivāso* because they abide (*adhivasanti*) therein. The compound is "the abode of the fortunate ones" (*dhaññānam adhivāso*). It is called *ajjhāvutthaṃ* because they have dwelt (*ajjhāvasiṃsu*) therein. They rise (*udeti*) and ascend (*uggacchanti*) by way of their fame and virtue;
thus they are "risen" (*uditā*). The analysis (*viggaho*) is "the rising of those who have risen. Therefore he said, "In the midst of the sky," and so forth.
Shame (*sārajjana*) is *sārada*. One from whom shame has departed is *visārada*. The state of being *visārada* is *vesārajja*.
*Vesārajja* regarding the scriptures is *pariyattivesārajja*; it is the knowledge of proficiency regarding the three baskets of scripture (*tepiṭaka-pariyatti*).

Since that is the beginning of this wisdom, it is called "wisdom having the confidence in the scriptures as its beginning" (*pariyattivesārajjādi-paññā*). Those whose nature is to feel shame for evil are "the conscientious" (*lajjin*).
He said, "Those who reproach evil. They are "reproachers of evil" because they censure unwholesome states and speak of their danger by means of their virtue.
"May they recollect" means may they remember again and again. They "become distinguished" or "attain abundance," thus they are "vibhavas.
Since these are both merits and vibhavas, they are "merit-vibhavas. He said "of the abundant" and so forth in order to show that they are vast merits.

The "supreme states" (anuttariya-dhammā) refer to the supremacy of seeing, the supremacy of hearing, and so forth. Among the many forms of seeing in the world, there is no other seeing superior to this;
thus, it is the "supremacy of seeing. This consists of seeing the Triple Gem and seeing the Four Noble Truths.
It also includes hearing discourses on the qualities of the Triple Gem, and hearing discourses on the aggregates, bases, elements, truths, and dependent origination.

This is called the unsurpassedness of sacrifice (*savanānuttariya*). Among those [objects], such as the Three Jewels, the acquisition of faith is called the unsurpassedness of gain (*lābhānuttariya*).
The repeated recollection of those very same objects is called the unsurpassedness of recollection (*anusatānuttariya*).

Service rendered to the Three Jewels by means of the four requisites, or by performing one’s duties and counter-duties, is called the unsurpassedness of service (*pāricariyānuttariya*). Regarding those things prescribed by the Buddha...
Training by undertaking and practicing the three trainings is called the supremacy of training (*sikkhānuttariya*).
Those who "partake in such qualities" are those who necessarily resort to and attain such qualities as the splendor of virtues purified by wisdom.
"We shall become" means: we shall make the effort to become.

They record the compilation known as the Mahāsaṅghīka; that collection of Dhamma and Vinaya prevails in the northern regions (Uttarāpatha), whereas the compilation of the Elder Yasa at Vesālī prevails in the southern regions (Dakkhiṇāpatha). They designate four ages (yugas) in the world:
the Satyayuga, the Dvāparayuga, the Tretāyuga, and the Kaliyuga. Furthermore, "yuga" refers to the measure of a lifespan.
